Feature

General Availability: VPC Flow Logs supports logging for IPv6 encapsulation flows. For more information, see IpConnection field format.

title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.33909v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: What kept breaking in my AI counselor. It was never the prompt.
description:
For the last month I've been building 予安 (Yu An), an AI counselor inside iYarrow, a small divination site I run alone. She talks with a guest about whatever is weighing on them, and when a reading would help she picks a tradition (I Ching, Zi Wei Dou Shu, tarot, a few others) and the guest draws the cast. She is openly an AI. There's a daily free allowance, and past it, talking with her costs credits.

Every change to her goes through a written proposal that says what was wrong, usually with numbers from production. That gives me something most side projects don't have: a record of what kept breaking. I went back through all of it, 25 days and a few dozen changes, expecting to find a lot of prompt fixes.

There were a few. But the bugs that came back, the ones I fixed three or five times, were not prompt bugs. They were places where the architecture let one decision live in two places, or happen in the wrong order. Here are the five patterns, and where each decision lives now.

1. Safety was a branch in the paywall chain

If a guest writes that they don't want to live, she must answer with care and point to a helpline, whatever their balance. That sounds like one rule. It took five fixes, all on the same day, each closing a gap the previous one left:

  1. A text turn ran the credit check before the crisis reply, so a guest with no credit who wrote 「我不想活了」 got an "out of credits" error. Voice calls already skipped the check; text didn't.
  2. The keyword backstop only knew Traditional Chinese. 「我想自殺」 was caught, 「我想自杀」, the same sentence in Simplified, was refused. And a guest who could pay was charged for the crisis turn.
  3. On a day the house spend cap was hit, every crisis turn got a canned paragraph instead of a real reply.
  4. Fixing that made a new path that was unreachable: a guest with no credit couldn't even open a sitting on a capped day, so they never got far enough to be in crisis.
  5. The helpline numbers followed the screen language, so a Chinese-speaking guest abroad was told to dial a Taiwanese number.

None of these was a bad prompt. The root cause was structural: safety was one more branch inside the billing flow, so every new billing rule could get in front of it. The fix was to make it a precondition. The crisis check now runs before the guard is ever asked:

if st.Crisis || (!acted && crisisKeyword(content)) {
    // A guest in crisis never meets a paywall, and the house pays for
    // every crisis turn: the guard is not asked.
    in.crisisHouse, in.crisisFixed = true, h.crisisCapped(ctx, uid)
} else if in.dec, err = h.guard.CheckSitting(ctx, uid, st.freePass()); err != nil {
    // ... (one more house-paid branch and paywall bookkeeping elided)
    return chat.GateError(err, h.logger, uid)
}

Once a sitting is flagged, every later turn runs with an empty toolkit. Not a prompt saying "don't do readings now", but no tools at all. A prompt is a request; an empty toolkit is a fact.

One gap is still open, and I'd rather say so. A crisis line that contains none of the keywords is only a crisis once the model flags it, and the model only sees the line if the guard lets it through. A guest with nothing left who writes something the keyword list misses still gets the ordinary refusal. The credit dialog in her room carries one helpline line for that case. It's a mitigation, not a fix.

2. The gate and the meter lived in different places

Every model call costs money and has to be charged to someone: the guest, or the house. The file that decides this is the most-changed file in the project, 33 commits. Most of those commits are the same bug in new clothes:

  • Free regenerations of a chart essay never checked the cap and never recorded the spend.
  • Regenerating an unlocked reading built a billing decision with no price, so it recorded $0.
  • Changing your birth details gave unlimited free rewrites.
  • Unheard call audio and repeated opening lines weren't counted at all.

The pattern: checking ("may this call happen?") and recording ("this call cost X") were two separate steps in two separate places, so any new code path could do one and skip the other. The spend cap's meaning also changed twice, from "all spend" to "only spend the house pays for". Credit-paid usage is sold above cost, yet a few paying guests on voice calls could use up the cap and lock everyone out, paying guests included.

What it looks like now: the check returns a decision, and the main recording functions take that decision as an argument, so the price comes from the check rather than from whoever is recording. It isn't airtight. The $0 bug was a decision built by hand without a price, and there's still a side door for auxiliary costs that takes no decision at all. But the default path now makes skipping the check awkward instead of easy.

3. State was written before the gate said yes

Three bugs with the same shape:

  • A guest past their daily limit could cast a hexagram. The cast was saved and shown, and then interpreting it failed with a 429. Every one of the 19 unanswered casts in production came right after a guest hit the limit.
  • That refused cast also left behind a conversation thread named after a question nobody answered.
  • If a reply failed and the guest retried, the cards were drawn again. A tarot reading where the cards change on retry isn't a reading.

Each time, something durable (a cast, a thread, a draw) happened before the step that could refuse it. The fix is ordering: a read-only check before anything is written, and the first draw is pinned in the sitting's state before the model runs, so a retry replays the same cards.

4. One decision, several detectors

"What language is the guest speaking?" got decided in at least three places: the reply prompt, the greeting and status lines, and the crisis resources. Each had its own heuristic and its own thresholds.

So they disagreed. Replies followed the UI locale instead of what the guest typed, and 153 of 161 questions written in Simplified Chinese got answers in Traditional. Later, inside a single sitting, the greeting could be in one language and the reply in another. The voice gate nearly billed Mandarin text-to-speech for a Vietnamese guest.

The fix was boring and complete: one function decides the reply language from what the guest wrote, and everything in the room calls it. If you find yourself writing a second "detect X" helper with slightly different rules, that's the bug, before it has a symptom.

5. Rules with a number in them leaked out of the prompt

Some behavior started in the prompt and had to move to code, because the model couldn't see the state the rule depends on:

  • Openers. Her opening line came from a deterministic rule, and I got the identical sentence two visits in a row. Asking the model to "vary your openers" can't work, because it has no idea what it said last time. Code now picks one of 22 opening moves by weight, excluding the last two used, and the prompt gets only the chosen move.
  • Follow-ups. She asked about the same unfinished matter every visit. Now a ledger caps it: 
// The thread caps. They are product rules, not tuning: reference last time
// once, keep the guest's agenda central, never pursue.
const (
    maxThreadAsks      = 2
    ignoredSkipOpeners = 2
    ignoredCooldown    = 7 * 24 * time.Hour
)
  • Reading style. A prompt rule banning one technical term made her drop it even when it mattered. Production showed 34% of replies still opened with cast metadata, and 15 of 40 follow-up replies re-read the whole cast. The fix there stayed in the prompt, but it came with a script that measures reply health on real traffic, because until then nothing measured any of it.

The test I ended up with: if a rule has a number in it ("at most twice", "within seven days", "30 a day"), the prompt can know the rule exists, but code has to hold the count.

The pattern behind the patterns

What broke Symptom Where the decision lives now
Safety inside billing Guest in crisis got "out of credits" Precondition before the guard
Check and record split Calls recorded at $0, or not at all One guard decision, recorded as-is
Write before gate Cast shown, then refused; cards redrawn Read-only check first; draw pinned in state
Many detectors Reply language disagreed with greeting One function, every caller
Counts in the prompt Same opener twice; same question every visit Code picks, ledger counts, prompt writes

Looking at all of it together, the model was rarely the problem. It writes almost everything she says, and it does that well. What broke was everything around it: the order of operations, where a decision was made, and how many places made it. Those are ordinary software bugs, and they recur for the ordinary reason: the architecture allows them.

Not everything that changed was a bug. The "how did it go?" feedback ask was rebuilt three times in three days (a card, then an email, then a line she says in her own words), but that was me not knowing what I wanted, not a structure that made it fail.

Yu An is live at iYarrow, still in beta. If you're building something conversational and drew these lines somewhere else, I'd like to hear where.

title: UI UX Design & App Development Services in Chicago
description:
Chicago has always been a city of builders. It rebuilt itself after the Great Fire, turned its rail yards into the crossroads of the country, and set prices for the world's grain from its trading floors. Today, a lot of that building happens on screens.

A bakery in Logan Square takes pre-orders through an app. A logistics company near O'Hare tracks its drivers in real time. A clinic in the Loop lets patients book a visit in three taps. Behind each of those experiences is a set of decisions about design, code, and how people will find the product in the first place.

What separates the apps people keep from the ones they delete after a week rarely comes down to a single feature. It comes down to how well three disciplines fit together: thoughtful design, solid engineering, and marketing that brings the right people through the door. This guide walks through how those pieces connect, what each one should include, and how to plan a digital product that earns a permanent spot on someone's home screen.

Why So Many Apps Struggle Before They Ever Launch

The most common mistake businesses make is treating design, development, and marketing as three separate purchases. One vendor designs the screens. Another builds them. A third gets hired after launch to "get the word out." Nobody talks to each other until something breaks.

Here is how that plays out. The designer delivers beautiful screens that turn out to be expensive to build. The developers cut corners to stay inside the budget. Then the marketing team arrives and discovers that no one ever defined who the app was for. Every team did good work on its own, and the product still struggles.

The fix is easy to describe and harder to execute: plan all three together from the very first conversation. When the people who will market your app join the discovery phase, they raise audience questions early. When developers review wireframes, they spot the feature that would double the timeline. When designers understand the acquisition plan, they build onboarding that actually converts the traffic marketing sends. Each discipline makes the others better, and that connection is the thread running through everything below.

What UI UX Design and Development Services Really Include

People often use "UI" and "UX" as if they mean the same thing. They don't. UX (user experience) is about how the product works: the flow from opening the app to finishing a task, and how easy or frustrating that journey feels. UI (user interface) is about how it looks and responds: the colors, type, buttons, spacing, and motion that make each screen clear.

Good UI UX design and development services treat these as one continuous process rather than a hand-off. Here is what that process should cover.

Research that shapes the product

Before anyone opens a design tool, someone should be talking to real users. That means short interviews, a look at competing apps, and a clear map of the main jobs your customers are trying to get done. A restaurant app, for example, might discover that regulars care far more about reordering a favorite meal in one tap than about browsing the full menu. That single insight changes the home screen, the navigation, and even the marketing message.

Prototypes you can test before you build

Changing a design in a clickable prototype takes hours. Changing it after the code is written can take weeks. That is why strong teams build interactive prototypes and put them in front of a handful of target users first. Watching five people try to sign up will reveal more problems than a month of internal meetings.

A design system developers can actually use

This is where design and development meet. A design system is a shared library of colors, type styles, and reusable components such as buttons, cards, and forms. When designers and developers build from the same library, the app stays consistent, new features ship faster, and future updates cost less. It is one of the clearest signs that a partner offers true design and development, not two separate services stapled together.

Accessibility from day one

According to the CDC, up to one in four adults in the United States lives with some type of disability. Designing for readable contrast, screen readers, larger text sizes, and simple navigation isn't a niche concern. It widens your market, improves the experience for everyone, and reduces legal risk, since accessibility claims tied to the ADA have become common for digital products. Building it in from the start costs far less than retrofitting it later.

What Strong Mobile App Development Services in Chicago Look Like

Once the design is tested and approved, the engineering work begins. This is where quality differences between providers become very visible, usually a few months after launch.

Choosing the right technology

You will typically choose between native apps (built separately for iOS and Android) and cross-platform apps (one shared codebase using a framework such as Flutter or React Native). Native development offers the best performance and deepest access to device features. Cross-platform development can reduce cost and speed up launch for many business apps. A trustworthy partner explains the trade-offs in plain language and recommends what fits your goals, not what their team happens to prefer.

Security and Illinois privacy rules

This is one area where hiring locally pays off. Illinois has the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), one of the strictest biometric privacy laws in the country. If your app uses fingerprints, face scans, or voice recognition, you need clear consent and careful data handling. Health apps also need to account for HIPAA, and any app that takes payments needs secure processing. Experienced mobile app development services in Chicago will raise these issues before they become expensive problems.

Building for growth

The back end, meaning the servers, databases, and APIs behind the app, needs to handle growth. If marketing succeeds and your user count jumps tenfold, the app should stay fast. That means planning cloud infrastructure, caching, and monitoring from the start rather than patching them in during a crisis.

Testing, launch, and life after launch

Real-device testing, app store submission, and review guidelines all take time. And launch is not the finish line. Apple and Google release major operating system updates every year, so apps need regular maintenance to stay compatible and secure. Ask any partner what their support looks like for the first year after launch.

Why a Chicago partner makes sense

Working with a team in your time zone makes collaboration easier. In-person workshops are possible when a big decision needs a whiteboard. A local team also understands the industries that power the Midwest economy, including logistics, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and food service, along with the customers they serve.

Getting Found: Where Digital Marketing Agency Services Fit In

An app no one can find is an expensive hobby. With millions of apps across the major stores, visibility has to be planned as carefully as the product itself. This is where digital marketing agency services connect directly to design and development work.

A strong marketing plan for an app usually includes:

  • App store optimization (ASO): writing titles, descriptions, and keywords, and designing screenshots so your listing ranks and converts in the App Store and Google Play.
  • Search engine optimization (SEO): building a fast, well-structured website and helpful content so people searching on Google find your product and your brand.
  • Paid campaigns: search ads, social ads, and app install campaigns aimed at clearly defined audiences, with budgets tied to real results.
  • Local visibility: for Chicago businesses, a complete Google Business Profile and neighborhood-focused content help you show up when nearby customers search.
  • Email and push notifications: thoughtful, permission-based messages that bring people back without annoying them.
  • Analytics: tracking that shows where users come from, what they do inside the app, and where they drop off.

Notice how much of this depends on design. App store screenshots are design work. Landing page speed is development work. Onboarding that turns a download into a loyal user is UX work. Marketing can send people to the door, but design and development decide whether they walk in and stay.

The Feedback Loop That Ties Everything Together

The real power of combining these services shows up after launch, when data starts flowing. Think of it as a loop that keeps improving the product:

  1. Design a focused experience based on user research.
  2. Develop it on a stable, secure, scalable foundation.
  3. Market it to the audience defined during research.
  4. Measure what users actually do, using analytics and reviews.
  5. Refine the design and code based on what the data shows, then repeat.

Say analytics show that half of new users quit on the third signup screen. A marketing-only agency would simply buy more traffic. A connected team asks a better question: why are people leaving? Maybe that screen asks for too much information too soon. The designer simplifies it, the developer ships the change, and the marketing budget suddenly goes much further. That is the difference between spending money on growth and building growth into the product.

What to Look For Before You Hire a Partner

Whether you are a startup with a first idea or an established company modernizing an old app, a few checks will save you time and money:

  • Look at their process, not just their portfolio. Ask how they research users and test designs before writing code.
  • Check that design and development share one roadmap. A shared design system and a single project lead are good signs.
  • Ask about privacy and compliance. They should bring up BIPA, HIPAA, or payment security on their own if your app needs them.
  • Make sure marketing is part of the plan. Launch strategy should be discussed before development is finished, not after.
  • Clarify ownership. You should own your code, designs, and accounts.
  • Understand post-launch support. Get maintenance, updates, and response times in writing.
  • Expect clear communication. Regular demos and plain-language updates matter more than technical jargon.

How InstaaCoders Brings It All Together

At InstaaCoders, we built our approach around the idea that design, development, and marketing work best as one team. Our UI UX designers, mobile developers, and digital marketers plan together from the first discovery session, so the app we design is the app we can build well, and the app we build is ready to be found.

We start with your users and your business goals. We prototype and test before we code. We build secure, scalable apps for iOS, Android, and the web. Then we help you reach the right audience and use real data to keep improving. Whether you need full mobile app development services in Chicago, focused UI UX design and development services, or digital marketing agency services to grow an existing product, our goal stays the same: build something people genuinely want to use.

Ready to Build Something Chicago Will Use?

Every great app starts with a clear conversation about who it serves and what it needs to do. If you have an idea, an outdated app, or a product that isn't growing the way it should, now is a good time to plan the next step.

Reach out to the InstaaCoders team to talk through your goals. We'll help you map out a design, development, and marketing plan that fits your budget and turns your idea into a product your customers come back to again and again.

title: What Makes a Travel Enquiry Form Useful for Group Bookings?
description:
Build a Simple Travel Enquiry Form with HTML and JavaScript

A travel enquiry often starts with a message such as “We need a vehicle next weekend.” Before suggesting an option, the operator still needs to know the route, date and passenger count.

A structured form can collect those details together.

This tutorial builds a small browser-only prototype using HTML and JavaScript. It generates an enquiry summary on the page. It does not send information to an operator or confirm a booking.

Choose the Essential Fields

Start with the information needed to understand the journey:

  • Pickup location
  • Destination
  • Departure date
  • Number of passengers

For group transport, luggage requirements and return dates may also be useful. Keep this first version small so the basic interaction remains easy to understand.

Build the Form

The following example includes visible labels, native browser validation and a live summary area.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Travel Enquiry Preview</title>

  <style>
    body {
      max-width: 36rem;
      margin: 2rem auto;
      padding: 0 1rem;
      font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
      line-height: 1.6;
      color: #102a43;
    }

    form {
      display: grid;
      gap: 0.75rem;
    }

    input, button {
      box-sizing: border-box;
      width: 100%;
      padding: 0.75rem;
      font: inherit;
    }

    button {
      margin-top: 0.5rem;
      background: #123b70;
      color: white;
      border: 0;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    pre {
      white-space: pre-wrap;
      overflow-wrap: anywhere;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: #eef5fb;
    }
  </style>
</head>

<body>
  <h1>Prepare Your Travel Enquiry</h1>
  <p>Enter your trip details to generate a summary.</p>

  <noscript>This preview requires JavaScript.</noscript>

  <form id="trip-form">
    <label for="pickup">Pickup location</label>
    <input
      id="pickup"
      name="pickup"
      type="text"
      maxlength="150"
      required
    >

    <label for="destination">Destination</label>
    <input
      id="destination"
      name="destination"
      type="text"
      maxlength="150"
      required
    >

    <label for="departure">Departure date</label>
    <input
      id="departure"
      name="departure"
      type="date"
      required
    >

    <label for="passengers">Number of passengers</label>
    <input
      id="passengers"
      name="passengers"
      type="number"
      min="1"
      step="1"
      required
    >

    <button type="submit">Generate enquiry summary</button>
  </form>

  <h2>Your Enquiry Summary</h2>
  <pre id="summary" role="status" aria-live="polite">
Your trip details will appear here.
  </pre>

  <script>
    const form = document.getElementById("trip-form");
    const summary = document.getElementById("summary");
    const locations = form.querySelectorAll('input[type="text"]');

    locations.forEach((input) => {
      input.addEventListener("input", () => {
        input.setCustomValidity("");
      });
    });

    form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();

      locations.forEach((input) => {
        input.setCustomValidity(
          input.value.trim() ? "" : "Enter a location."
        );
      });

      if (!form.reportValidity()) return;

      const data = new FormData(form);

      summary.textContent = [
        `Pickup: ${data.get("pickup").trim()}`,
        `Destination: ${data.get("destination").trim()}`,
        `Departure: ${data.get("departure")}`,
        `Passengers: ${data.get("passengers")}`,
        "",
        "Enquiry preview only. No booking has been submitted."
      ].join("\n");
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Understand the Validation

The required attribute prevents empty fields from passing browser validation.

For passenger count, min="1" requires a positive value, while step="1" restricts valid values to whole numbers.

The JavaScript adds a check for location fields containing only spaces. It clears that custom error when the user edits the field.

This prototype accepts past departure dates. A production form should apply the operator’s actual date and booking rules rather than assuming every selected date is available.

Display User Input as Text

The summary uses textContent to display the entered values as plain text.

That matters because user input should not become executable page markup. A destination containing HTML-like characters should appear as text in the preview.

The aria-live="polite" region allows assistive technology to announce the updated summary without immediately interrupting the user.

Separate an Enquiry from a Booking

A passenger count alone cannot determine the correct vehicle. Luggage, seating arrangements, route requirements and availability still need discussion.

For example, Urbania Yatra offers Urbania and Tempo Traveller rentals from Ahmedabad. A structured enquiry can provide the starting details for that discussion, while vehicle availability and pricing require confirmation.

This tutorial is an independent prototype, not a description of the website’s existing implementation.

Check the Main Interactions

Before extending the example, try these cases:

  1. Submit with empty fields.
  2. Enter only spaces in a location field.
  3. Enter zero or a decimal passenger count.
  4. Complete the form with valid details.
  5. Enter HTML-like text and confirm it appears literally.
  6. Navigate the form using only the keyboard.

Extend It into a Working Enquiry System

To collect actual enquiries, connect the form to a backend endpoint and validate the submitted data again on the server. Browser validation improves the interaction, but it can be bypassed.

Display a submission confirmation only after the server accepts the enquiry. Keep that message separate from any later confirmation of vehicle availability or booking.

Once that flow works, you can add return dates, luggage notes and a preferred vehicle category.

Meta Details

Field Content
SEO Title Build a Travel Enquiry Form with HTML and JavaScript
Meta Description Build a browser-only travel enquiry form with HTML and JavaScript, including labelled fields, input validation and a plain-text trip summary.
Suggested URL Slug build-travel-enquiry-form-html-javascript
Primary Keyword travel enquiry form HTML JavaScript
Related Keywords HTML form validation, JavaScript FormData, accessible web forms
Image Filename travel-enquiry-form-html-javascript-urbania-yatra.png
Image Alt Text Laptop showing a travel enquiry interface, with an Urbania van outside, the Urbania Yatra logo and an HTML and JavaScript tutorial heading.

Short Description

Create a browser-only travel enquiry prototype with labelled inputs, native validation and a JavaScript summary. Learn how to separate an enquiry preview from a submitted request.

html, javascript, webdev, beginners

title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
description:
arXiv:2611.34686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.

title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
description:
arXiv:2611.34491v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.

title: From Emulators to Physical Devices: Building a More Reliable Mobile Testing Strategy
description:
Every mobile team has lived through it. The build passes every check in the pipeline, the release goes out, and within hours the reviews start arriving: the app freezes on a particular Samsung model, the camera screen crashes on an older iPhone, checkout hangs on a slow 4G connection.

Nothing was wrong with the tests. They were simply running in the wrong place. Emulators and simulators are excellent tools, but they are approximations of a phone, not the phone itself. When a testing strategy leans on them too heavily, the gap between “passed in CI” and “works for customers” quietly widens.

This post looks at where emulators fit, what only physical hardware can tell you, and how to build a layered strategy that combines both without slowing your releases down.

Where emulators earn their place

Emulators (Android) and simulators (iOS) deserve credit. They are a big reason mobile teams can move as fast as they do today.

Speed. They spin up in seconds, run in parallel on ordinary CI machines and need no physical setup.
Cost. There’s no hardware to buy, charge, update or replace.
Debugging. Developers can inspect logs, set breakpoints and reproduce issues right from their IDE.
Early feedback. Unit tests, UI component checks and basic functional flows run well in a virtual environment.

For the first layers of testing, emulators are often the right choice. The trouble starts when they become the only choice, and the final word on whether a release is ready.

What only a physical device can tell you

An emulator runs your app on a desktop processor, with desktop memory, a stable network and a battery that never drains. Real phones live very different lives. Some of the bugs that only show up on physical hardware include:

  • OEM customisations. Android manufacturers modify the OS in ways that affect permissions, notifications, background tasks and battery optimisation. An app that syncs perfectly on a stock emulator can be silently killed in the background on certain brands.
  • Hardware features. Cameras, fingerprint and face sensors, GPS, NFC, Bluetooth and accelerometers either can’t be emulated or are only mocked.
  • Real performance limits. Mid-range and older phones have slower CPUs, less RAM and storage that fills up. Thermal throttling kicks in during long sessions. None of this shows up on a powerful build server.
  • Real networks. Moving between Wi-Fi and mobile data, weak signal, high latency and packet loss expose timeout and retry bugs.
  • Screens and input. Notches, punch-hole cameras, foldables, high-density displays and actual touch gestures behave differently from a mouse click on a virtual screen.
  • Interruptions. Incoming calls, low-battery warnings, OS update prompts and other apps competing for resources.

These aren’t rare edge cases. For many apps, they are the everyday conditions most users experience.

The device lab problem, and how the cloud solves it

Once teams accept they need physical devices, the next question is practical: how many, and who looks after them?

An in-house device lab sounds simple until you run one. Phones need buying, charging, updating and replacing every year. Someone has to track which tester has which device. Remote team members can’t reach them. And even a well-stocked drawer of 30 phones covers only a small slice of what your users actually own.

A real device testing cloud removes most of that overhead. Instead of owning the hardware, teams get on-demand access to hundreds or thousands of real phones and tablets hosted in managed data centres. Key benefits include:

  • Broad coverage. Test on current flagships, budget models, older OS versions and regional devices without buying any of them.
  • Parallel execution. Run the same suite across dozens of devices at once, so wider coverage doesn’t mean slower pipelines.
  • CI/CD integration. Trigger automated runs on every build with frameworks like Appium, Espresso and XCUITest.
  • Remote access for everyone. Developers, testers and support staff anywhere can open a live session on a specific device to reproduce a bug.
  • Rich artefacts. Videos, screenshots, device logs and network traces are captured automatically for every run.

When choosing a real device testing cloud, look at device availability and wait times, how quickly new models and OS versions are added, data security and device wiping between sessions, and whether devices are available in the regions and networks your users rely on.

Performance: where emulators mislead the most

Functional bugs are obvious when they happen. Performance problems are quieter. An app that takes four seconds to open, stutters while scrolling or drains the battery rarely triggers a crash report, but users notice, and many simply uninstall.

Emulators are especially poor at revealing these issues because they run on hardware far more powerful than a typical phone. Performance numbers measured on a virtual device can look healthy while real users on mid-range phones have a very different experience.

That’s why mobile performance testing tools are most valuable when they run on physical devices. The metrics worth tracking include:

  • App launch time, both cold and warm starts
  • Frame rate and dropped frames during scrolling and animations
  • CPU and memory usage, including memory leaks over long sessions
  • Battery drain and device temperature
  • Network request timing, payload size and behaviour on throttled connections
  • App size and storage use

When evaluating mobile performance testing tools, look for ones that capture these metrics on real hardware, simulate different network conditions, compare results across builds so regressions stand out, and plug into your pipeline so performance checks run automatically rather than once before a big launch. Many teams combine platform profilers such as Android Studio Profiler and Xcode Instruments for deep debugging with tools that run on a real device testing cloud for coverage across many models.

The key habit is setting performance budgets, for example a maximum launch time on your lowest-end supported device, and failing the build when they’re exceeded.

A layered strategy: the right test in the right place

The goal isn’t to abandon emulators. It’s to use each environment for what it does best, so you get fast feedback early and real-world confidence before release.

This approach keeps pipelines fast, because most runs still happen on cheap virtual devices, while making sure nothing ships without being checked on the hardware your customers actually hold.

Making the shift: six practical steps

  1. Build your device matrix from real data. Use your analytics to list the devices, OS versions and screen sizes your users actually have. Cover the top ones by usage, plus your oldest and lowest-spec supported models.
  2. Identify device-sensitive flows. Onboarding, login, payments, camera, location and push notifications are usually the first candidates for real-device coverage.
  3. Start small in the cloud. Move your smoke suite to a real device testing cloud first, prove the value, then expand to full regression.
  4. Add performance checks early. Pick one or two mobile performance testing tools, set baseline budgets for launch time and memory, and track them on every release build.
  5. Test under realistic conditions. Include throttled networks, low battery, background interruptions and different locales and accessibility settings.
  6. Review and adjust regularly. Device popularity shifts every year. Refresh your matrix each quarter and retire devices your users no longer use.

Conclusion

Emulators made mobile testing fast. Physical devices make it trustworthy. A reliable strategy needs both.

By running quick checks on virtual devices, using a real device testing cloud for broad hardware coverage, and making mobile performance testing tools part of every release, teams can close the gap between “it passed in CI” and “it works for our users.” Fewer surprises in production, fewer one-star reviews, and far more confidence every time you ship.

Originally Published: https://desertdays.co/from-emulators-to-physical-devices-building-a-more-reliable-mobile-testing-strategy/

title: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
description:
arXiv:2611.34068v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.

title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.34819v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emotionally supportive interactions require large language models not only to avoid overtly harmful content, but also to recognize vulnerability-related risk, regulate their relational stance, preserve user agency, and provide context-appropriate support. Existing safety benchmarks often measure isolated violations, leaving unclear what underlying response competence their scores represent. We introduce VulnSafe, a Chinese capability assessment centered on Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC). VARC organizes relational safety into five complementary constructs: Risk Perception, Safety Preservation, Autonomy Protection, Supportive Response, and Boundary Management. Following an evidence-centered design, 41 scenarios elicit construct-relevant behavior through 2,050 balanced prompts and scenario-specific scoring rubrics. The assessment further separates proactive should-do behavior from prohibitive should-not behavior. Across eight representative LLMs, results show distinct competence profiles and larger disparities than prohibitive requirements. VulnSafe therefore makes relational safety interpretable as a multidimensional model capability rather than as refusal compliance alone.

title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.34250v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.
