title: Supabase PGRST116 "Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object": what it means and how to fix it
description:
You call .single() in supabase-js and get this back:

{"code":"PGRST116","message":"Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object","details":"The result contains 0 rows","hint":null}

Older PostgREST versions say "JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned". The HTTP status is 406.

What it means
You asked for exactly one row. The query returned zero rows or more than one. PostgREST refuses to guess.

Why it happens

  1. The filter matched nothing: wrong id, the row was not created yet, or Row Level Security hides it from this user.
  2. The filter matched several rows because the column is not unique.
  3. You ran .insert(...).select().single() but your SELECT policy does not let the user read the row they just inserted.

How to fix it

  1. If "no row" is a normal state, use .maybeSingle() and handle null: 
const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('profiles')
  .select('*')
  .eq('id', user.id)
  .maybeSingle()
if (!data) { /* create the profile or show onboarding */ }
  1. Filter on a primary key or another unique column.
  2. If the row is in the table but not returned, the problem is RLS. Add a SELECT policy scoped to the owner.

"But I can see the row in the dashboard"
The dashboard bypasses RLS. Your app's role does not. Test the query as the user, not as the admin.

The fix to avoid
Do not "solve" it by making the SELECT policy using (true). Then every user can read every row in that table. PGRST116 itself is not a security problem. That shortcut is.

Check it is fixed
Test as a brand-new user with no row and as an existing user. Neither should throw PGRST116.

Full reference with the same steps: https://proofforge.live/errors/pgrst116 . If you are not sure whether your tables are open to the public, run the free outside check at https://proofforge.live

title: I got tired of juggling cloudflared processes, so I built tuinnel-plus
description:
I run a handful of small services at home and expose them on subdomains of my own domains through Cloudflare Tunnel. It works great, but every service means a cloudflared process, a tunnel and a DNS record. Over time I ended up with processes I'd forgotten about, tunnels I couldn't tell apart, and leftovers in the Cloudflare dashboard.

Where it started

I found tuinnel by Nick Dunas: a terminal dashboard that maps a local port to a subdomain in one step. It creates the Cloudflare tunnel and DNS record for you, and removes both when you delete it. That was most of what I wanted.

What I missed was everything around it. The tunnels lived as long as the terminal did, and I wanted to check on them from a browser, not only from a terminal.

What I changed

So I forked it into tuinnel-plus and added:

  • A background service that owns all tunnels. The terminal dashboard, the CLI and the web UI are just clients of it, so closing any of them leaves your tunnels running. Tunnels that were running come back after a reboot.
  • A web UI with a live tunnel list, logs and metrics, and buttons to add, edit, start, stop and delete. It's password-protected and listens on 127.0.0.1:8484 by default.
  • Optional remote access: publish the web UI itself on a subdomain through its own tunnel, behind your password.
  • service install to run it at login on macOS or as a systemd user service on Linux.
  • purge to find tunnels Cloudflare still has but you no longer use, and doctor to check your token, permissions and network.

Try it

You need Node.js 20+, macOS or Linux, and a Cloudflare account with a domain.

npm install -g tuinnel-plus

# Open the terminal dashboard (the first run walks you through setup)
tuinnel-plus

# Or start a tunnel for port 3000 straight away
tuinnel-plus 3000

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8484 for the web UI; on your first visit you choose a password. To keep it running at login or boot:

tuinnel-plus service install

No Cloudflare account? tuinnel-plus up 3000 --quick gives you a random trycloudflare.com URL.

What's next

It's early (v0.1.4) and I use it every day for my own tunnels. The roadmap is in the repo, and I'd love to hear what's missing or what breaks for you:

👉 https://github.com/mrpap/tuinnel-plus

I built tuinnel-plus with help from Claude Code. I directed the design, review the changes and run it on my own setup every day.

title: Testing Stored Procedures in Postgres — Why PL/pgSQL Only Fails at Call Time, and What a Test Has to Build First
description:
A click on "Duplicate" in the project list, a red notice "The project could not be duplicated", nothing else. The server log has the reason: a procedure reads a column that has not existed for five months. During those five months, the deploy ran green on four environments, production included. The convention check had nothing to complain about, and more than a thousand unit tests were green. None of these nets had ever called the procedure. PL/pgSQL resolves the column names in a body only at call time, and in an empty throwaway database nothing calls the procedure.

This article shows why there is no cheap test layer for the behavior of stored procedures in Postgres, and how to test Postgres stored procedures without installing a tool for it. The means are probes, integration tests against the real database in testing vocabulary: small SQL scripts that build an initial state from synthetic data in the gate's throwaway database, call the real procedure, and check each requirement individually.

The key points up front:

  • Three nets, one gap: A convention check checks the form, the deploy checks that everything can be created, and unit tests stop before the database. None of them checks the behavior of a procedure.
  • A probe is a SQL script that creates test data, calls the real procedure, and writes every result to a table. The checking happens outside SQL, and when it goes red, the stored state comes first, not a guess.
  • The test consists mostly of setup: In the DI² project, 85 percent of the probe code is the SQL files that create test data and call the procedure, 7,266 lines across 22 probes. The checks for them take 1,328 lines of shell script.
  • A probe counts only once it has gone red against the broken state. Performance requirements need volume via generate_series, and a time gate in CI is still a bad idea.
  • Transparency: The project's script, fixtures, and checks come from Claude Code sessions. The maintainer reported the bugs or requested the checks, verified the negative probes, and made the decisions this article is about.

Prerequisite: Postgres and psql, a CI run with a throwaway database as described in GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys, and basic knowledge of PL/pgSQL. All code blocks were executed against PostgreSQL 17.11 in a throwaway Docker container, including the negative probe and the measurement. The examples use a small domain of their own made of customers and orders, and the figures from the DI² project are as of November 5, 2026.

Three Nets, One Gap

In the DI² project, three automated nets stand in front of every merge. A convention check reads every SQL file line by line and checks the form: banners, naming rules, forbidden constructs. What it can and cannot do is in Why sqlfluff Can't Lint Our SQL Conventions. The deploy smoke applies the complete schema to a fresh throwaway database, and it does so twice, so that the second run on an existing state is proven as well. That gate is described in GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys. The application's unit tests check TypeScript, and by an explicit rule only code without database access.

Each of these nets has a job. But no net checks the behavior of a procedure. How big the gap is was measured by a Claude Code session in September 2026, by deliberately removing a working safeguard and then checking whether any net would fire. First it removed from a procedure the block that truncates an overlong text to the column width before the insert, and ran all gates. That block was one half of a fix, the other half lived in the TypeScript. There, a function writes a batch of messages in one transaction. Since the fix, each insert step sits in its own savepoint, so that a failed message rolls back only itself and not the whole batch. The session deliberately removed those savepoints too, ran all gates again, and restored both files afterwards. The question was not whether the safeguard should go, but whether anyone would notice it was gone.

Intervention Convention check Deploy smoke Unit tests
Truncation block removed from the procedure 0 findings green not in scope
Savepoint isolation removed from the TypeScript not in scope not in scope 1,101 of 1,101 green

For the SQL half, the reason is easy to name. The convention check sees form, not behavior. The deploy smoke at the time ran against an empty database, and in an empty database an overlong text never occurs. Both nets were green although the safeguard was gone. For the TypeScript half, it is shorter still: the function accesses the database, and such functions have no unit test by rule. There was nothing that could have gone red.

The case of the vanished column sits one level deeper still, because there not even a call with the right data would have been needed. Any call would have done. The example below reproduces it in the small domain. A procedure copies a customer along with their orders and takes a column legacy_state with it. Three days after this procedure, a schema script removes the column. The next deploy creates the procedure again:

CREATE TABLE shop.customer
(
    id              bigint          GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
   ,name            varchar(100)    NOT NULL
   ,legacy_state    varchar(20)         NULL
);

CREATE TABLE shop.sales_order
(
    id              bigint          GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
   ,customer_id     bigint          NOT NULL REFERENCES shop.customer (id)
   ,amount          numeric(12, 2)  NOT NULL
   ,approved_on     timestamptz         NULL
);

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE shop.sp_dup_customer
(
    IN    p_customer_id        bigint
   ,INOUT p_new_customer_id    bigint
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $procedure$
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO shop.customer (name, legacy_state)
   SELECT
       name || ' (copy)'
      ,legacy_state
   FROM
      shop.customer
   WHERE
      id = p_customer_id
   RETURNING id INTO p_new_customer_id;

   INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount)
   SELECT
       p_new_customer_id
      ,amount
   FROM
      shop.sales_order
   WHERE
      customer_id = p_customer_id;
END;
$procedure$;

-- Three days later, a schema script removes the column.
ALTER TABLE shop.customer DROP COLUMN legacy_state;

-- The next deploy creates the same procedure again, unchanged (abridged here,
-- it is lines 16 to 43 once more). Postgres answers as it did the first time:
-- CREATE PROCEDURE

-- Only the call resolves the body, even with empty tables.
CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(1, NULL);
-- ERROR:  column "legacy_state" of relation "customer" does not exist
-- CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function shop.sp_dup_customer(bigint,bigint) line 3 at SQL statement

Lines 48 to 50 are the point. The repeated CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE goes through although the body reads a column that no longer exists. When creating a PL/pgSQL routine, Postgres checks the syntax and the declarations. The identifiers in the body's SQL statements are resolved only when the statement is executed for the first time, in the example at the first call. A statement in a branch that only a later call passes through is resolved only then. That is how the Postgres documentation describes it in the chapter PL/pgSQL under the Hood, and that is what the context of the error message in line 55 shows: line 3 at SQL statement, not CREATE PROCEDURE. With check_function_bodies switched off, even this check at creation time is skipped, and syntax and declarations are then also checked only at the first call: a body with a typo in the SELECT or an unknown type in DECLARE can be created, and only the CALL reports the error. For the same reason, the schema script in line 46 was allowed to remove the column at all: for the tables and columns that the SQL statements of a PL/pgSQL body use, Postgres registers no dependency, so DROP COLUMN finds no object hanging on the column. A SQL function with a BEGIN ATOMIC body does register them, and there the DROP COLUMN already fails with a hint to the dependent function.

For a CI gate, this means: a deploy that creates a procedure proves that it can be created. What it does, and whether it runs at all, it does not prove.

What Requirement a Probe Checks, and Where It Is Written

A requirement here is a sentence about behavior that the code has to satisfy. "The copy takes over the customer and all orders, but no approval." "An overlong text is truncated to the column width before the insert, without two different texts becoming identical in the process." "No path via the parent table deletes the foreign key of an approved child table." Two of these sentences speak of an approval, a business state of the data. In the DI² project, the owner approves a fully configured table. From that moment on, its configuration is locked: columns can no longer be deselected, the table can no longer be deactivated, and the procedures that try reject the call. In the small domain of this article, an order is approved once the customer has inspected and released the delivery. In the schema, the timestamp approved_on stands for that. A copy starts without approval: what was released was the original, not the copy.

Each probe in the project checks one or a few such requirements, and they are written verbatim in the header of the fixture file, before the first line of SQL. Fixture is the testing term for the prepared initial state a test needs before it can check anything. In this article it means the SQL file of a probe. It creates the test data, calls the real procedure, and writes every result to the result table.

The rule for this is short and came out of the measurement above: SQL behavior belongs in a probe of the deploy smoke. A check is cheap there, because the throwaway database is up anyway and the schema has just been applied. The rule has a counterpart that is just as important. Not every requirement gets a probe. The savepoint half from above, for example, lives in a TypeScript function with database access, and such functions are exempt from unit tests in the project by rule. For every requirement that deliberately stays without a net in this way, the project keeps a row in an inventory table. Its four columns record which requirement it is, why no net checks it, what a refactoring would silently break, and which planned change will close the gap later. Without this entry, a deliberately unchecked requirement would look exactly like one that simply nobody thought of. In both cases there is no test that could go red, and CI is green.

The Initial State Before the Test

What data a single requirement needs is shown by the third one above. "No path via the parent table deletes the foreign key of an approved child table" is one sentence. The probe for it needs two parent tables and two child tables, two foreign keys, a column snapshot of the first parent table, an approval on exactly one child table, and after that seven named cases: deactivating the parent is rejected, deselecting a parent column is rejected, deselecting a different column goes through, the second parent without an approved child may be deactivated, plus three diagnostic rows that record the state afterwards. That is 183 lines of SQL for one sentence.

That is not an outlier, it is the rule. The project's 22 probes consist of 7,266 lines of fixture SQL, and the checks for them of 1,328 lines of shell script. So 85 percent of the probe code is in the SQL files, and in those files only around 15 percent of the lines belong to calling the procedures and recording the results. The rest build the initial state. The three largest probes have 1,030, 944, and 923 lines, and most of that is setup: accounts, projects, memberships, connections, tables, columns, rules, foreign keys, approvals, in the right order and with the right roles.

This is the real complexity of testing database behavior, and it does not lie in the check. The check, in the end, is a counter or a comparison. The work lies in producing a state in which the requirement has any meaning at all. A procedure that protects a foreign key needs a foreign key, an approval, and a caller with the matching role, otherwise there is nothing to protect. And because the probe is supposed to check the behavior against the real database, each of these building blocks has to be real. A stand-in would replace exactly the part that matters. That is where a probe differs from a UI test, which may replace its server with a stand-in that returns a prepared response: a UI test consists of a lot of checking and little setup. A probe consists of a lot of setup and little checking.

The Probe Pattern

The pattern can be shown in full on the small domain. First the corrected procedure, with the requirement in the comment:

-- 155002: The corrected procedure. The requirement on it: the copy takes over the
-- customer and all orders, but no approval.
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Parameter
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
--    p_customer_id        bigint
--       Customer to be copied
--    p_new_customer_id    bigint
--       Id of the copy (returned)
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE shop.sp_dup_customer
(
    IN    p_customer_id        bigint
   ,INOUT p_new_customer_id    bigint
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $procedure$
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO shop.customer (name)
   SELECT
      name || ' (copy)'
   FROM
      shop.customer
   WHERE
      id = p_customer_id
   RETURNING id INTO p_new_customer_id;

   -- Copy the orders, deliberately not the approvals (approved_on stays NULL).
   INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount)
   SELECT
       p_new_customer_id
      ,amount
   FROM
      shop.sales_order
   WHERE
      customer_id = p_customer_id;
END;
$procedure$;

Then the probe. It consists of four parts: a result table, the initial state, the cases, and a check that runs outside SQL.

-- 155003: The probe. Builds an initial state, calls the real procedure
-- and writes every result to a table. The checking happens outside SQL.
-- For throwaway databases only.
SET client_min_messages = warning;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS shop._probe_dup_customer;
CREATE TABLE shop._probe_dup_customer
(
    label       varchar(40)     PRIMARY KEY
   ,sqlstate    varchar(5)          NULL
   ,message     text                NULL
   ,value       text                NULL
);

BEGIN;

-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Initial state: one customer, two orders, one of them approved
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSERT INTO shop.customer (name) VALUES ('_probe_customer');

INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount, approved_on)
SELECT
    T01.id
   ,T02.amount
   ,T02.approved_on
FROM
   shop.customer T01
   CROSS JOIN (VALUES (100.00, NULL::timestamptz), (250.00, now())) AS T02 (amount, approved_on)
WHERE
   T01.name = '_probe_customer';

-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Cases: an error is caught and recorded, not passed through
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DO $do$
DECLARE
   l_source      bigint;
   l_copy        bigint;
   l_count       int;
   l_approved    int;
BEGIN
   SELECT id INTO l_source FROM shop.customer WHERE name = '_probe_customer';

   -- Fixture self-test: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise abort.
   SELECT count(*), count(approved_on) INTO l_count, l_approved
   FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source;
   IF l_count <> 2 OR l_approved <> 1 THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'Fixture incomplete: % orders, % approved', l_count, l_approved;
   END IF;

   -- Case 1: The procedure runs through (expected: sqlstate empty).
   BEGIN
      CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(l_source, l_copy);
      INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
      VALUES ('call_ok', l_copy::text);
   EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
      INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, sqlstate, message)
      VALUES ('call_ok', SQLSTATE, SQLERRM);
   END;

   -- Case 2: Both orders are copied (expected: 2).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('order_count', l_count::text);

   -- Case 3: No approval travels along (expected: 0).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count
   FROM shop.sales_order
   WHERE customer_id = l_copy AND approved_on IS NOT NULL;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('approved_copied', l_count::text);

   -- Case 4: The copy's amounts match the original (expected: 0).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count
   FROM
   (
      (SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source
       EXCEPT ALL
       SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy)
      UNION ALL
      (SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy
       EXCEPT ALL
       SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source)
   ) T01;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('amount_diff', l_count::text);
END;
$do$;

COMMIT;

The result table in lines 7 to 13 is the core of the pattern. Each case writes one row with a descriptive label, plus either a value or, if an error occurred, SQLSTATE and message. The label is the primary key, so a probe that writes the same label twice aborts on its own. The probe decides nothing, it records. There are two reasons for that. A RAISE EXCEPTION at the first finding would hide the remaining cases, and an error message that guesses the cause would regularly be wrong, because several requirements can be violated at the same time.

The initial state in lines 17 to 31 is as small as possible and as large as necessary: one customer, two orders, one of them approved. Whether it came out that way is checked by the self-test in lines 45 to 50 before the first case runs: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise the probe aborts.

The cases in lines 36 to 89 call the real procedure. The call in line 54 sits in its own BEGIN block with an EXCEPTION branch. An error is caught and recorded with its SQLSTATE, it does not tear down the probe. This frame assumes that the procedure can run inside the probe's transaction. A procedure that itself executes COMMIT or ROLLBACK needs a different call, more on that in the section on the limits of the pattern. Which error can be caught in the call is shown by the first block: with the old procedure, 42703 would appear here, because the body reads the column legacy_state that no longer exists, and the message would only come at the CALL. A second example sits in the copy itself: the name gets the suffix "(copy)", and for an original with more than 93 characters it no longer fits into varchar(100), error code 22001. Without the EXCEPTION branch, each of these errors would abort the DO block, cases 2 and 3 would never run, and the check would find an empty table with no hint at the cause. If the probe aborts anyway, the error does not come from the call, because that is caught. Then something is wrong with the probe itself, such as a wrong table name in the setup or a typo in a counting query. Such an abort says something about the probe, not about the procedure. The two counters after it check the two halves of the requirement separately: line 63 counts the copied orders, line 68 counts the approvals on the copy. If the requirement is violated, the label shows which half it is. The counter in line 63 checks only the number of orders, not their content, and a procedure that creates two orders with wrong amounts would stay green with it. That is why case 4, from line 74 on, compares the amounts themselves: EXCEPT ALL in both directions returns every order that occurs on only one side, duplicates included, and the target is zero deviations.

The check reads the table from outside:

#!/bin/bash
# 155004: The check. Reads the probe's result table, shows the stored
# rows first when red, and then aborts.
set -u
PSQL=(psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -tA -d "${PGDATABASE:-probe}")

fail() {
  echo "--- Probe red. Stored rows (label | sqlstate | message | value): ---" >&2
  "${PSQL[@]}" -c "SELECT label || ' | ' || coalesce(sqlstate, '') || ' | ' || coalesce(message, '') || ' | ' || coalesce(value, '') FROM shop._probe_dup_customer ORDER BY label;" >&2
  echo "ERROR: $1" >&2
  exit 1
}

# expect <label> <expected> <message>: exactly one row with this label, without SQLSTATE,
# with value = expected. The expected value "*" requires only the row without SQLSTATE.
# If psql cannot read the table, that is red as well.
expect() {
  local row
  row="$("${PSQL[@]}" -c "SELECT count(*) || '|' || coalesce(max(sqlstate), '') || '|' || coalesce(max(value), '') FROM shop._probe_dup_customer WHERE label = '$1';")" \
    || fail "psql could not read the result table."
  [[ "$row" == "1||"$2 ]] || fail "$3"
}

expect call_ok         "*" "The call aborted or left no row behind."
expect order_count     "2" "Expected 2 copied orders."
expect approved_copied "0" "An approval was copied along."
expect amount_diff     "0" "The copy's amounts differ from the original."

echo "Probe green: 4 of 4 checks passed."

It runs in the shell, because the gate is a shell script anyway and needs an exit code. The function fail in lines 7 to 12 prints the stored rows first when red and only then aborts. Whoever reads the run in the CI log sees the actual state and does not have to reconstruct it from a message. The function expect in lines 17 to 22 requires exactly one row without SQLSTATE for each label and compares the value with the expected one. A missing row is thus red and not green, and so is a psql that cannot read the table. The four lines 24 to 27 are the requirement, broken down into four checks.

The values of a probe are chosen so that each violated requirement stands out individually. The probe for the customer therefore creates two orders instead of one, so that "copies all orders" can be told apart from "copies one". One of the two is approved, the other is not. A procedure that copies approvals along thus shows up in case 3, one that skips approved orders in case 2, and one that changes an amount while copying in case 4. None of these defects hides behind another, because the label says which check is red.

The brief for such a probe is short, because the pattern is in place. The following prompt is reconstructed from the bug report and the fixture file, not quoted verbatim from the session:

The procedure for duplicating a project ran green through the deploy for
five months and was broken all the same, because nothing called it.
Write a probe for the deploy smoke following the pattern of the existing
probes: its own fixture file, a result table with label, sqlstate and
message, checks in the script. The requirement it checks: duplicating
takes over everything that makes up the working state, but no approvals.
The original must contain at least one record from every area.
Acceptance criterion: against the state before the fix the probe goes red,
afterwards green, and the CI run stays green.

From this came the project's largest probe with 1,030 lines, and almost all of them build the original, which contains at least one record from every area. The checks at the end are counters.

When a Probe Counts: Negative Probe and Fixture Self-Test

The last sentence of the prompt is the most important one, and it is the one most often left out. A probe that is green has not proven anything yet. It can be green because the requirement is met, or because it never produces the case that would violate the requirement. Without the approved order in the initial state, case 3 would always be 0, with any procedure. Only the negative probe shows the difference: the probe runs against the broken state and has to go red. In the small domain, that means the procedure copies approved_on along by mistake. The probe then reports:

--- Probe red. Stored rows (label | sqlstate | message | value): ---
amount_diff |  |  | 0
approved_copied |  |  | 1
call_ok |  |  | 2
order_count |  |  | 2
ERROR: An approval was copied along.

Three of the four checks pass, the one on the approval does not, and the dump says with which value. The negative probe thus proves that the probe reacts to this one defect. That it would find every other defect of the procedure, it does not prove. Whoever wants to know that introduces further defects one after another, the way mutation tests do systematically. In the project, this probe is part of the deal before a new probe counts. More than forty bug reports record that the new probe went red against the state before the fix, before the fix counted as done. That is the same principle as the counter-check for automated tests in The Green Test That Proves Nothing: a test that does not react to the code does not check it.

For the initial state there is a second trap that the negative probe does not see. A fixture can become ineffective without anything going red. If the approved order in the customer probe were created without approved_on through a typo, case 3 would stay green forever, and nobody would notice. That is why a fixture checks for itself, before the call, whether it has produced the state it is supposed to produce. In the probe above, those are lines 45 to 50: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise the block aborts with an error message, and the check finds no row call_ok. In the project, the fixtures that are applied between the two deploy runs include such a fixture self-test, and all of them answer the same question: does this test still check anything?

Volume Instead of a Minimal State

A minimal initial state proves behavior. For a performance requirement it is worthless, because a customer with two orders is copied quickly in any implementation. The requirement in the project was that a project of a certain size is duplicated in at most ten seconds. For that, the probe needs a project of that size, and it generates one with generate_series: two connections, 200 tables, 10,000 columns, 500 rules, and 300 foreign keys. In the small domain, the same setup looks like this:

-- 155005: Volume fixture and measurement run. 200 customers with 50 orders each,
-- every customer is copied once. Completeness is checked, the duration is printed.
-- For throwaway databases only.
INSERT INTO shop.customer (name)
SELECT
   'perf_' || lpad(n::text, 3, '0')
FROM
   generate_series(1, 200) n;

INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount, approved_on)
SELECT
    T01.id
   ,(n * 1.5)::numeric(12, 2)
   ,CASE WHEN n % 10 = 0 THEN now() END
FROM
   shop.customer T01
   CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 50) n
WHERE
   T01.name LIKE 'perf\_%';

DO $do$
DECLARE
   l_started     timestamptz;
   l_source      record;
   l_copy        bigint;
   l_expected    bigint;
   l_actual      bigint := 0;
BEGIN
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_expected
   FROM
      shop.sales_order T01
      INNER JOIN shop.customer T02
      ON
        T02.id = T01.customer_id
   WHERE
      T02.name LIKE 'perf\_%';

   -- The clock starts only before the loop: measured is the duration of all 200 calls together.
   l_started := clock_timestamp();
   FOR l_source IN
      SELECT id FROM shop.customer WHERE name LIKE 'perf\_%' ORDER BY id
   LOOP
      CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(l_source.id, l_copy);
      SELECT l_actual + count(*) INTO l_actual
      FROM shop.sales_order
      WHERE customer_id = l_copy;
   END LOOP;

   RAISE NOTICE 'Copied: % of % orders in % ms'
      ,l_actual
      ,l_expected
      ,round(extract(epoch FROM clock_timestamp() - l_started) * 1000);

   -- The gate is completeness, not time.
   IF l_actual <> l_expected THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'Copy incomplete: % of % orders', l_actual, l_expected;
   END IF;
END;
$do$;
-- NOTICE:  Copied: 10000 of 10000 orders in 174 ms

Lines 4 to 19 create 200 customers with 50 orders each, every tenth one approved. The measurement run from line 21 on first determines the expected number, starts the clock in line 39, and then copies every customer once. It records two things: the duration of the whole loop, that is 200 calls including the count after each, and the number of copied orders. Line 55 is the actual check, and it checks completeness, not time. It does not check the content of the copies either, the probe above did that with its minimal initial state. In the container, three runs with the small domain on one day took between 2.2 and 2.9 seconds, ten more on the following days on the same machine between 0.2 and 1.0 seconds. The probe prints this duration but does not decide on it.

That time is not a gate was a deliberate decision in the project, with two reasons. The first is the CI runner, which fluctuates. Before an optimization, the copy under the application role took eleven and twenty-three times the reference, afterwards still seven times, and none of these values works as a threshold. The second reason is more important: the time was a symptom, the cause was the shape of the execution plan. The gate has sat on that plan shape ever since, the duration is only printed, and the ten seconds are measured during the manual check on the development environment.

The most important finding of this probe, however, only came with the third measurement. The first version measured as superuser, because that is how the smoke runs. In operation, the procedure runs under the application role, with row-level permissions and an actor. The actor is the logged-in user that the application passes to the database session, and the row-level permissions refer to them. Only the measurement under this role showed 144 seconds, in one case almost five minutes. As superuser, none of that was visible, because the row-level permissions cost the superuser nothing. Since then, the probe measures three times and requires completeness for each of the three copies. The brief for that, reconstructed:

The performance probe measures the duplication as superuser. That is not
how the procedure runs in the application: there, the application role
with row-level permissions and an actor apply. Please measure the copy
three times, as superuser for reference, under the application role with
an actor and without one, and print all three times. No hard time gate,
the CI runner fluctuates. The only check is that each of the three copies
is complete.

The lesson from this applies to every volume probe: the role is part of the initial state. A measurement under the wrong role measures a different system.

Fixtures Between the Deploy Runs: Backfill and Drift

GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys explains why the gate applies the schema twice: the second run proves that every file is repeatable on an existing state. It proves this, however, only for the state the first run left behind, and that is an empty database with a fresh schema. Two error classes it therefore does not see, and the project closes both with fixtures that are applied between the two runs.

A backfill is a deploy script that brings the existing data up to date after a schema change. In the project, it loops over all active tables and calls, for each one, a procedure that derives new check rules. In the empty throwaway database there is no active table. The loop runs zero times, the call never happens, and the deploy is green. The call runs under the role of the schema owner, and that role once lacked a privilege. On the first environment with data, the deploy would have been red, and in the gate nobody saw it. The backfill fixture therefore creates three records before the second run: a project, a connection, an active table. With that, the loop runs at least once, the call happens, and a missing privilege turns the second run red. How such scripts run exactly once is in Tracking Schema Changes Without a Framework.

The drift fixture simulates an existing database that lags behind the repository: it sets eight check constraints to an old state and creates a row that is valid only under the old constraint. The second run has to bring every definition back to the target state and migrate the row. Without the fixture, there would never be an old constraint for the run to work against.

This is the answer to the open point that "GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys" ends on. There it says that data-dependent effects stay invisible in the gate, and that the common complement is a nightly run against an anonymized production dump. For requirements on behavior, the synthetic initial state in the same gate is the better answer: it runs on every pull request, it is versioned, it contains exactly the constellation that matters, and it needs no real data. The dump keeps its place where it is about data distribution, lock durations, and runtimes on real volumes. Those are different questions, and they do not belong in the PR gate.

pgTAP, plpgsql_check, and the Limits of the Pattern

Anyone who tests Postgres routines knows pgTAP: an extension that provides assertion functions such as ok(), is(), and results_eq() in SQL, outputs results in TAP format, and fits into any test runner via pg_prove. In the DI² project, pgTAP was never evaluated. The probes grew out of the existing deploy smoke, bug by bug, and there was no tool decision. The difference therefore lies in the packaging, not in the idea. A pgTAP file builds the same initial state and checks the same requirements, only the check is written in SQL instead of the shell. For that it needs an extension in the database and a second runner. The shell variant needs only psql and runs in the same run as the deploy. Whoever starts from scratch and plans many probes anyway should look at pgTAP. Whoever has a deploy gate gets by with the pattern here without a new dependency.

For the error class of the vanished column there is, in addition, a cheaper net than any probe. The extension plpgsql_check checks the body of a routine statically, resolving the identifiers as it goes, and reports the removed column without anyone calling the procedure. Against the broken procedure from the first example, version 2.10 in the container returns:

SELECT * FROM plpgsql_check_function('shop.sp_dup_customer(bigint, bigint)');

error:42703:3:SQL statement:column "legacy_state" of relation "customer" does not exist
Query: INSERT INTO shop.customer (name, legacy_state)
--                                      ^

After the fix, the same query returns zero rows. A call of plpgsql_check_function over all routines of a schema therefore belongs at the end of every deploy run as an additional net, in the gate too. It catches orphaned columns and tables at deploy time, in seconds, without test data. What it cannot see is SQL whose text depends on parameters or data only at runtime and runs via EXECUTE. An EXECUTE string that it can assemble from constants in the body, including via format() or a variable, it does check. Conversely, it reports a temporary table that the body itself creates as missing, although the call goes through. Every finding of the check therefore needs a look into the body before it counts as an error. And what it fundamentally does not catch is everything this article is about: whether the copy takes the approval along, whether the truncation keeps two different texts apart, whether the foreign key survives the detour via the parent table. Those are requirements on behavior, and behavior needs a call with data.

The pattern has limits. Three of them are already visible in the project, a fourth is set by Postgres itself. Probes couple themselves to details: the probe for the text truncation knows the width of the column, and whoever widens the column has to touch two files. The runtime of the gate grows with every probe, and 22 probes today run one after another in a single run. And a probe checks only what someone has written down as a requirement. What nobody has written down is either in the inventory or is left to the manual click. The fourth limit concerns procedures that control their own transaction. Postgres allows COMMIT and ROLLBACK in a procedure only if the CALL sits at the top level in autocommit mode. The call in the probe, by contrast, sits between BEGIN and COMMIT, that is in an explicitly opened transaction block, and additionally in a block with an EXCEPTION branch, which internally opens a subtransaction. Either of the two is enough for the error 2D000, and the probe reports red although the procedure runs flawlessly in the application. For such a procedure, the call needs its own psql invocation without a BEGIN before it, and the check then reads its exit code and the state of the tables afterwards.

Summary

  • Creating a PL/pgSQL routine checks syntax and declarations. The columns and tables in the body are resolved by Postgres only at the first call. A deploy gate therefore proves that a procedure can be created, not that it runs.
  • A probe builds an initial state from synthetic data, calls the real procedure, catches errors, and writes every result to a table. The check runs outside SQL and, when red, shows the state first.
  • The test consists mostly of setup. In the DI² project, 85 percent of the probe code is in the SQL files, and in them only around 15 percent of the lines belong to call and recording. The initial state also includes the role under which the procedure runs in the application.
  • A probe counts only after the negative probe, a fixture only after its self-test.
  • For performance requirements, generate_series generates the volume. The gate is completeness, the time is printed.

For practice, as a decision aid:

Starting point Recommended route
A routine reads columns or tables that may change plpgsql_check over all routines at the end of the deploy run
A requirement on behavior: copies X but not Y, rejects Z Probe with a minimal initial state in the gate, validated by a negative probe
A performance requirement Volume fixture via generate_series, completeness as gate, duration as output, measurement under the application role
A deploy script depends on existing data Fixture between the two deploy runs, with self-test
Data distribution, lock durations, runtimes on real volumes Run against an anonymized dump, outside the PR gate

FAQ

How do you test a stored procedure in Postgres without pgTAP?

With a SQL script that creates the necessary tables and rows in a throwaway database, calls the procedure, and writes every result with a label to a table. Errors are caught in a BEGIN block with an EXCEPTION branch and recorded with their SQLSTATE. A shell script reads the table via psql -tAc, compares the values with the expected ones, and exits with a non-zero exit code on any deviation. In CI, the script runs right after the deploy against the same throwaway database.

Why is the double deploy from the CI gate not enough?

The second deploy run proves that every object file is repeatable on an existing state. But it calls no procedure and works against a database without data. A procedure that reads a removed column can be created any number of times, because Postgres resolves the column names in the body only at call time. And a procedure that copies something wrong only does so once there is something to copy. The first needs any call, the second a call with suitable data. A probe delivers both, and a static check with plpgsql_check delivers the first as well.

Can Postgres check a stored procedure for errors without executing it?

Partly, with the extension plpgsql_check. It analyzes the body of a routine statically, resolves table and column names as it goes, and reports, for example, a column that no longer exists, without anyone calling the procedure. It does not check behavior: whether the procedure copies, rejects, or truncates the right thing only shows in a call with data, that is, in a probe.

How do you know that a probe really checks something?

Through the negative probe. The probe runs once against the broken state, that is against the procedure before the fix or against a version from which the checked line was deliberately removed, and has to go red in the process. If it stays green, it does not reach the requirement. For fixtures, a self-test is added that proves the fixture really produced the state, for example through a counter on the created rows.

How do you test a stored procedure that issues COMMIT or ROLLBACK itself?

Not in the probe frame from above, but in a psql invocation of its own. Postgres allows COMMIT and ROLLBACK in a procedure only if the CALL sits at the top level in autocommit mode. Between BEGIN and COMMIT, or in a block with an EXCEPTION branch, the call aborts with the error 2D000 (invalid transaction termination), although the procedure runs flawlessly in the application. The probe therefore calls such a procedure without a BEGIN before it, and the check reads the exit code of psql and then the state of the tables.

May you use real production data as test data?

For probes you do not need it, and for the PR gate it is the wrong place. A probe checks a named requirement, and for that a synthetic constellation of a few rows that touches exactly this requirement is enough. Production data contains personal information that has to be anonymized before any use outside production, and it is large. Where it is about data distribution, lock durations, or runtimes on real volumes, an anonymized dump is the right means, as a separate run outside the gate.

title: The FastAPI Bottleneck Nobody Tells You About Until Production
description:
Everyone benchmarks FastAPI with wrk on a single endpoint that returns {"ok": true} and calls it a day. Then it goes to production, traffic has real payloads and real I/O, and throughput falls off a cliff that the benchmark never showed.

Three things that actually move the needle, in the order we usually find them:

1. Worker count isn't 2 x cores + 1 once you have async I/O. That formula is for sync WSGI workers saturating CPU. With uvicorn workers running async handlers that spend most of their time awaiting a DB or an upstream call, you're often CPU-underutilized with "correct" worker counts. We've seen throughput improve 30-40% just by profiling actual CPU-busy time per request and sizing workers against that, not core count.

2. Gunicorn + Uvicorn workers vs. plain Uvicorn: the difference shows up under load, not at idle. A bare uvicorn process looks identical to gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker in a quick smoke test. Where it diverges is worker death/restart behavior under memory pressure and SIGTERM handling during rolling deploys — gunicorn's process management catches failure modes uvicorn alone doesn't surface until you're already paged.

3. The bottleneck that actually ate our throughput wasn't FastAPI at all — it was connection pool exhaustion on the DB driver. asyncpg's default pool size silently became the real concurrency ceiling, while CPU and worker metrics looked fine the whole time. If your latency graph has a hard ceiling that doesn't correlate with CPU, check your pool max_size before you touch anything else.

None of this shows up in a synthetic benchmark because synthetic benchmarks don't have a database. If you're chasing a req/s number, profile with your actual dependency graph in the loop, not a mocked handler.

We wrote up the full tuning process — including the exact pool-size math and the gunicorn config that stopped our rolling deploys from dropping requests — in a deeper breakdown of the worker-tuning math.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Asset4D-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Editable 3D and 4D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.33728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.

title: How do I automate functional software testing?
description:
Short answer: decide which behaviors matter most, check each one at the lowest layer where it actually lives, give your tests predictable data and fake versions of outside services, then make your CI pipeline run them on every change.

That's the whole loop of automated functional testing. The rest of this post walks through it with a small, concrete example, because "automate your tests" is easy advice to give and surprisingly hard to act on when you're staring at an empty test folder.

The example is a basic online store with a cart and discount coupons. Swap in your own product as you read. The steps don't change much.

Start with a list, not a tool

Most people open a browser tab and start comparing frameworks. That's backwards. The tool matters a lot less than knowing what you're going to test.

Grab a doc and write down three things:

  • The flows that make or lose money, like signup, login, adding to cart, checkout and refunds
  • The last ten or so bugs that reached production
  • Anything you or your QA folks re-check by hand before every release

For our store, the list might start like this: a customer can log in, add items, apply a valid coupon, get a clear error for an expired coupon, and pay with a saved card. Five items. That's plenty for a first pass.

Write the expected behavior in plain words

Before any code, write each item as a short scenario. A simple format works well:

Given a cart with two mugs at 50.00 each
When the customer applies coupon SAVE10
Then the total is 90.00

Given a coupon that expired yesterday
When the customer applies it
Then they get an "expired coupon" error and the total doesn't change

This feels like busywork. It isn't. Half the arguments about whether a test is "right" turn out to be arguments about what the feature should do, and it's much cheaper to settle those in a sentence than in a pull request.

Decide where each check belongs

Now ask where each behavior actually lives in your system.

The discount math happens on the server. So test it by calling the API directly. You don't need a browser to confirm that 100 minus 10% is 90, and a browser test for it will break whenever someone renames a button.

The fact that a customer can get from the product page to a paid order is a journey that crosses the UI, the API and the payment step. That one deserves a browser test.

For our store, the split ends up like this:

Scenario Layer Why
Valid coupon applies the right discount API Pure business logic, fast to check
Expired coupon is rejected API Error handling lives in the backend
Login with wrong password fails API Same reason
Customer checks out with a saved card UI The full journey is what matters

Three API tests and one UI test. That ratio holds up well as suites grow.

A worked example at the API layer

Here's what the coupon tests might look like in Python with pytest and requests. Any language and HTTP client will do the same job.

import uuid
import requests

BASE = "http://localhost:8000"


def new_customer():
    email = f"qa-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.test"
    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/users", json={"email": email, "password": "Passw0rd!"})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {r.json()['token']}"}


def test_save10_takes_ten_percent_off():
    headers = new_customer()
    requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/items", json={"sku": "MUG-01", "qty": 2}, headers=headers)

    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/coupon", json={"code": "SAVE10"}, headers=headers)

    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.json()["total"] == "90.00"


def test_expired_coupon_is_rejected():
    headers = new_customer()
    requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/items", json={"sku": "MUG-01", "qty": 2}, headers=headers)

    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/coupon", json={"code": "OLD5"}, headers=headers)

    assert r.status_code == 422
    assert r.json()["error"] == "coupon_expired"
    assert r.json()["total"] == "100.00"

A few things worth pointing out, because they're where beginners usually slip:

  • Every test creates its own customer with a random email. No test depends on another one having run first.
  • Each test checks one behavior and says exactly what "correct" means. "Status is 200" alone would pass even if the discount were wrong.
  • The expired coupon test also checks that the total didn't change. Bugs love to hide in the "nothing should happen" cases.

Handling the database and outside services

Those tests assume two things exist: a product called MUG-01 priced at 50.00, and a coupon called OLD5 that has already expired. Don't create those by hand in a shared staging database and hope nobody touches them. Someone will.

Put them in a seed script that runs before the suite, against a database that exists only for testing. A throwaway container started in CI is the usual approach. Fresh data every run means a failure points at your code, not at whatever a colleague did on staging last Thursday.

Outside services need the same treatment. If checkout calls a payment provider, your test suite shouldn't depend on that provider's sandbox being up. Replace it with a mock that returns realistic responses, including the unpleasant ones like a declined card or a timeout. Then keep a handful of separate checks that hit the real sandbox on a schedule, so you still find out if their API changes.

If writing mocks by hand sounds tedious, it is. Some teams record real traffic between their service and its dependencies and replay it as mocks, which saves a lot of typing and keeps the mocks closer to reality.

Adding a few UI tests

Once the API layer is covered, add browser tests for the journeys a customer can't live without. Here's the checkout one in Playwright:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('customer can check out with a saved card', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('saved-card@example.test');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('Passw0rd!');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();

  await page.goto('/products/mug-01');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});

Notice it finds elements by their label and role, not by CSS classes. Designers change class names all the time. They rarely change a button that says "Pay now" without also changing what it does.

Keep this layer small. Ten to twenty UI tests covering real journeys will tell you more than a hundred that click every button on every page.

Getting it into CI

Tests that only run on someone's laptop stop running. Put them in your pipeline so they run without anyone having to remember. A minimal GitHub Actions setup looks like this:

name: functional-tests
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  api-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker compose up -d db app
      - run: python scripts/seed_test_data.py
      - run: pip install -r requirements-test.txt
      - run: pytest tests/api -q

Start there. Once that's stable, add the UI tests on merge to your main branch, the full regression set before releases, and a nightly run against staging. Keep the pull request stage under about ten minutes, or people will merge before it finishes and the whole thing loses its point.

Keeping the suite alive

Writing the first tests is the fun part. Keeping them useful is the actual job.

When a test turns flaky, fix it or delete it that week. A retry button teaches the team that red builds don't mean anything, and that lesson is very hard to unlearn.

When a production bug slips through, write the test that would have caught it before you write the fix. Your suite slowly becomes a record of everything that has ever gone wrong, which is exactly what you want it to be.

And review test code in pull requests the same way you review everything else. A test nobody understands is a test nobody will fix when it breaks.

FAQs

What's the first functional test I should automate?

Pick the flow that would hurt most if it broke tomorrow. For most products that's login or checkout. Automate the happy path and one or two common failures, get it running in CI, then move on to the next one.

Do I need to know how to code to automate functional testing?

It helps a lot. Low-code and record-and-playback tools exist and can get you started, but suites written in code are easier to review, version and maintain once they grow past a few dozen tests.

Which framework should I use?

Use whatever fits your stack. For APIs, your language's standard test runner plus an HTTP client is enough. For browsers, Playwright and Cypress are both solid choices. The habits in this post matter far more than the framework.

How long does it take to automate functional testing?

A first useful set, say ten API tests and two UI tests running in CI, is usually a few days of focused work. Getting to a suite the whole team trusts takes months, mostly because of data, flakiness and ownership rather than writing tests.

Wrapping up

Automating functional testing comes down to a short loop: choose what matters, test it where it lives, control the data, and let CI run it every time. Start with five tests, not five hundred. Get them green, keep them green, and add more each time something breaks. That's slower than it sounds on paper, and it works.

title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
description:
arXiv:2611.34363v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql

title: Track your brand in Google AI Overviews with Limelit Open and your own Apify account
description:
Limelit Open is an open-source, self-hosted tracker for "AI visibility": it asks ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI surfaces your prompts, and records whether your brand is named and which sites are cited. Each engine is reached through a provider you choose.

I added one more provider for Google AI Overviews: apify. It runs an Apify Actor on your own Apify account, so you pay Apify directly and the scraping capacity is yours. The pull request is limelit-co/open#72. It is not merged yet, so this post builds Limelit from my fork. When the PR is merged, the normal release works the same way.

Disclosure: I built the Actor this provider runs (Google AI Overview Scraper on Apify). It is a paid Actor; prices are on the Actor page. It returns US English results only.

1. Build Limelit from the fork

You need Go 1.25 or newer.

git clone --branch provider-apify https://github.com/krammer0/open limelit-open
cd limelit-open
go build -o ~/limelit/limelit ./cmd/limelit
cd ~/limelit && ./limelit serve

Open http://localhost:1515. The first visit starts the setup wizard.

2. Set up with only an Apify token

The wizard asks for your domain, competitors and prompts, then for one key.

  1. Brand: I used nerdwallet.com as an example.
  2. Prompts: I kept four:
    • best high yield savings account
    • best credit card for beginners
    • how to improve credit score fast
    • is a roth ira worth it
  3. Key: pick Apify and paste your Apify API token (Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations). Then press Connect and finish.

Connecting the key also adds the target ai_overview:apify. Every prompt becomes one Actor run.

3. Press Run

The server log for my run:

level=INFO msg="run finished" evaluation=1 completed=4 failed=0 took=33s

Four prompts, four AI Overviews, no failures, 33 seconds.

4. What came back

./limelit export writes everything as JSON. This is a summary of my export (2026-11-27):

prompt                               | sources | nerdwallet.com cited at | NerdWallet named
best high yield savings account      |    7    | position 1              | 2 times
best credit card for beginners       |    6    | -                       | 0
how to improve credit score fast     |   11    | -                       | 0
is a roth ira worth it               |   11    | position 10             | 0

For "best high yield savings account", NerdWallet's guide is the first source, and the answer names NerdWallet in the text:

... and NerdWallet highlights Capital One 360 Performance Savings (3.20% APY) for in-person branch/cafe access.

The other cited sources for that prompt were bankrate.com, usnews.com, everbank.com, sofi.com, marcus.com and ally.com. For the two credit prompts, NerdWallet is not cited at all. That is the kind of gap Limelit is built to show.

Each answer is stored with its full text and its sources, so the Answers and Citations pages show the evidence behind every number.

5. Ask Claude about it

Limelit has an MCP server. With Claude Code:

claude mcp add limelit -s user -e LIMELIT_DATA_DIR=$HOME/limelit/data -- $HOME/limelit/limelit mcp

Then ask: "How visible is my brand in AI answers, and which prompts am I losing?"

Notes

  • The provider sends each prompt as one query. Line breaks in a prompt become spaces.
  • A query where Google shows no AI Overview is stored as "no answer surface". Limelit leaves it out of every percentage instead of counting it as an answer that missed your brand.
  • The Actor covers US English only. Limelit returns an error before any request for other countries or languages.
  • The token stays in Limelit's encrypted settings store, or in the APIFY_TOKEN environment variable. It is sent only as a bearer header.

title: Breakfast Special: showing a voice UI through two mascots and one real meal log
description:
Teddy orders two eggs and a latte. Brulee logs breakfast. Then Teddy asks the question that made this worth showing on screen: “How much protein did I get?”

Brulee and Teddy are two of the eight Live Voice mascots in Fud AI. For this short, I wanted the mascots to introduce the feature without asking viewers to take a cartoon’s word for what the app did.

Why the cut to the diary matters

A spoken “logged” is easy to miss. In the iPhone recording you can see which foods landed in the diary, then read the same protein total Brulee gives Teddy: 20 grams for this sample breakfast. That gives the follow-up question a purpose: it connects the conversation to something you can inspect.

The café exchange is scripted and voiced with ElevenLabs. The screen recording uses sample data, and the dialogue is captioned so the demo still makes sense on mute. If you’re making a demo of a voice interface, try watching yours with the sound off: can you still tell what changed?

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.
