title: Pipeline Error Logs: Detect Backend Failures With Attributable Polling Evidence
description:
Detect backend failures in a nightly fintech pipeline by polling structured error logs, then attach account usage before sending a Slack webhook alert; choose this design when the notification needs both failure evidence and an accountable owner, and resist turning account totals into a bill for an individual failed job.

TL;DR: Poll structured error logs, attach an account-usage snapshot, and let a worker own deduplication, cooldowns, retries, and Slack delivery. For a Node.js backend, this is a separate operational worker; the runnable example below uses Python. Search can establish that a failure was observed. Account usage supplies billing context. Neither fact, by itself, establishes what a particular pipeline run cost.

The decision here is about evidence provenance: what can a notification actually justify? A payment failure recorded during an import, a repeated job failure, and a pipeline that never started demand different evidence, even if the same team receives all three alerts. Keep them distinct.

Record the decision before choosing the notification transport

Use a scheduled worker to search recent structured logs for error status, job failures, or payment failures, then deliver a compact notification to Slack or email through a transport the application owns. Keep a durable delivery ledger outside the worker process. A notification should identify the pipeline run and the relevant evidence, with an explicit distinction between measured account usage and any allocation calculated locally.

This is a proposed design, not a benchmark. Its acceptance criteria are concrete: an observed failure produces one incident identity, overlapping searches do not create a fresh incident every time, and a successful account read does not erase an unsuccessful log read. The schedule, search window, and cooldown belong to the deployment configuration. They are not universal constants.

Infrai's self-describing REST API needs no SDK and puts account and observability calls behind one key and one bill, so the collection worker doesn't need separate account and log credentials. Its public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so adding a capability starts with reading one capability description rather than learning another SDK; per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata give the worker useful attribution evidence, although those records still need a local association with the pipeline run.

That association is the architectural work. A shared credential does not invent it.

How should polling error logs detect backend failures without misattributing usage?

The first invariant is that an error observation and a delivery acknowledgment are separate records. Consider a proposed polling interval of 60 seconds and a 300-second cooldown: a restart inside that cooldown must not reset the delivery ledger, and a second observation of the same incident should update its evidence rather than acquire a new identity. These numbers illustrate a policy to test, not a service guarantee. Use a stable event identity where the actual response schema provides one; otherwise define the incident identity from application-owned fields and accept the grouping trade-off explicitly.

A useful application log contract includes a pipeline run identifier, a job name, an operational region label, an owner, and an event classification such as payment failure. These are proposed producer fields, not promised API response fields or search parameters. Keep raw payment credentials and customer identifiers out of the notification. A region label in a record describes the workload; it does not prove where a provider stores that record, so a US or EU SaaS deployment needs a separate residency decision.

The second invariant is that search completeness has to be demonstrated. Pagination, late arrivals, event timestamps, and cursor behavior must be taken from the actual schema before advancing a durable checkpoint. Do not call a partially consumed response a complete interval. Re-reading overlapping intervals is a reasonable worker policy only when the delivery ledger can recognize previously observed evidence.

Failure boundaries matter.

A log with trace_id or span_id offers correlation, not a distributed span tree. A job that never starts may emit no error at all, which calls for a heartbeat tool such as Healthchecks. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, and session replay are separate investigative requirements. Likewise, operational search should not serve as the system of record for erasure, bulk export, retention, or cold-storage policy; those requirements need a separately evaluated data lifecycle, including the obligations described in GDPR Article 17. None of these boundaries should be hidden behind a green Slack delivery acknowledgment.

Compare the evidence each option contributes

The useful comparison is the investigation each choice supports. Notification transport comes afterward.

Option Evidence or role in this decision Trade-off and acceptance boundary
Shared REST account and log capabilities Places account usage and operational search behind the same credential; discovery describes how to call each capability The worker still owns incident identity and delivery state. Account usage alone cannot allocate cost to a run.
Sentry Event grouping and fingerprint mechanics give a concrete basis for grouping repeated errors Evaluate the grouping against the application's incident identity; grouping errors does not establish account-cost attribution.
Datadog Logs plus a vendor console Separates log investigation from the vendor account used for billing context In this proposed two-service arrangement, plan for two service enrollments and two credential sets, then write the join and its ownership rules.
Grafana Loki A log-oriented alternative to evaluate when retaining a separate investigation stack Validate the run-to-record association before adopting it; account reconciliation and notification identity still need explicit ownership.
Healthchecks Covers the missing-run question through a heartbeat-oriented workflow Pair it with error evidence when both silence and explicit failures matter; a missing heartbeat does not identify the failing payment operation.

Sentry's grouping documentation is particularly useful because it makes the grouping mechanism something an engineer can inspect. For Datadog, the relevant alternative here is specifically the vendor-console-plus-logs arrangement, not a claim that every deployment needs exactly two human signups. An organization may already have both accounts. It still needs a way to connect the account evidence, log evidence, incident owner, and delivery state across them.

The trade-off is less credential glue because both capabilities share authentication, at the cost of concentrating dependency risk. Consolidation has a cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Accept that deliberately.

Make the account-to-search handoff explicit

The following Python program is a runnable, read-only collection step for the polling worker. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL in the environment, with the latter pointing to the platform's HTTPS API base ending in /v1, then run it with Python 3. It reads account usage first, carries that response into the collection context, and passes the same context into log collection using the same key and base URL. Both API responses are preserved without assuming undocumented payload fields. No server-side filter parameters are invented.

The handoff is deliberately local: account usage becomes the billing context for the subsequent search result, not an undocumented search filter. The program prints one JSON evidence bundle and exits. It does not claim that fetching two responses implements a complete alerting service. Run it under a scheduler, then build the schema-aware selection and durable delivery stage around that bundle.

import json
import os
import random
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]

def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    if value:
        try:
            return max(0.0, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            try:
                deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
                if deadline.tzinfo is None:
                    deadline = deadline.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
                now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
                return max(0.0, (deadline - now).total_seconds())
            except (ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError):
                pass
    return (2 ** attempt) + random.random()

def read_json(path):
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers={
                "Authorization": "Bearer " + API_KEY,
                "Accept": "application/json",
            },
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Retry budget exhausted")

def collect_logs(context):
    bundle = dict(context)
    bundle["log_search_response"] = read_json("/logs/search")
    bundle["collection_finished_at"] = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    return bundle

def main():
    context = {
        "collection_started_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "account_usage_response": read_json("/account/usage"),
    }
    print(json.dumps(collect_logs(context), indent=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The two response names and collection timestamps are local bundle fields. Collection start and finish bound the worker's activity, not the time range of the returned events, and the two reads are not an atomic account-and-log snapshot. Restrict access to the output as operational data. An HTTP failure terminates collection with its status and response body; route that diagnostic to a protected worker log rather than copying it wholesale into Slack. The example retries rate limits with exponential backoff and honors Retry-After when present. Its four-attempt budget is an example worker policy.

Before adding Slack delivery, inspect the response schemas and implement the actual interval selection, pagination, and incident grouping. Retain the source request metadata where available so a local attribution record can point back to the calls that produced it. An account-usage response can support reconciliation, but dividing an account total by the number of error records would confuse observation volume with consumption. A failed payment may create repeated observations without representing repeated billable work.

Slack delivery needs its own state transition: persist an intent, attempt delivery, then record the acknowledgment. If the process loses the acknowledgment after sending, a retry may duplicate a message; marking it delivered before sending creates the opposite failure mode, a lost notification. Choose and document the acceptable behavior, include the stable incident identity in the message, and retain the uncertain delivery state. A local idempotency key cannot force a remote webhook to deduplicate.

Reject the all-in-one incident ledger for the right reason

The rejected option is treating searchable operational logs as an authoritative ledger for incident delivery, allocated cost, and customer-data lifecycle. It is attractive because one query appears to answer everything. It cannot justify those conclusions without separate invariants: a log match is evidence of an observation, a billing record concerns consumption, and a delivery acknowledgment concerns a transport action. Joining them is useful; treating them as interchangeable is where the design fails.

That smaller operational-search approach still has a valid use case. Choose it for a nightly pipeline whose team needs recent failure evidence and can operate a durable notification worker, with account usage attached as context. If missing runs dominate, add heartbeat evidence; if grouping semantics dominate, evaluate the specialist grouping workflow; if the organization already investigates in a separate log platform, compare the cost of maintaining that join before moving it.

The acceptance test should replay an overlapping search, restart the worker inside its cooldown, and simulate a lost delivery acknowledgment. Each case must preserve incident identity and attribution provenance. Only then does a Slack alert about a nightly failure mean more than a successful HTTP request.

References

  • Sentry, event grouping and fingerprint mechanics
  • Datadog, Log Explorer
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Slack, incoming webhooks
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure

title: SaaS Pricing Page Design: What Makes People Pick a Plan
description:
Originally published on pzhydkykh.com.

Your pricing page is where interest turns into revenue - and where most SaaS websites quietly fall apart. Good SaaS pricing page design is not about making three columns look pretty; the design is about helping a half-decided visitor pick a plan without opening a spreadsheet. After building SaaS sites and pricing pages for several years, I have a clear picture of what makes people commit and what makes visitors “come back later” and never do. Here is the full breakdown.

Key takeaways

  • A pricing page has one job: help a visitor confidently pick a plan - not list everything your product does.
  • Three tiers with one visually recommended plan outperforms both long plan grids and vague “contact us” walls.
  • People do not compare prices, they compare situations: name each plan after the person or team it is for.
  • Billing toggles, seat logic and feature tables are clarity tools - every confusing element sends buyers to the FAQ, and every unanswered FAQ sends them away.
  • Most pricing page fixes are structure and copy, not redesign - you can usually improve conversion without touching your stack.

Why the pricing page decides more than your homepage

By the time someone reaches your pricing page, the marketing has mostly worked. Visitors know roughly what your product does and they are asking the only question left: “what does this cost me, and which option is mine?” The pricing page is where a visitor either picks a plan or leaves, so every unclear line on it costs you sign-ups.

The mistake I see most often is treating the pricing page as a continuation of the marketing site: more benefit statements, more screenshots, more persuasion. But a visitor on this page is past persuasion. That visitor needs decision support - clear tiers, honest limits, and a reason to believe the middle plan is safe. I covered how the rest of the site earns that visit in SaaS landing page structure that converts; this article is about what happens when the click lands on /pricing.

The three-tier pattern - and why it keeps winning

Almost every strong SaaS pricing page converges on the same shape, and that is not a coincidence:

  • **Three visible tiers. **Fewer feels like no real choice; five or more turns choosing into homework. Anchor low, recommend middle, let the top tier make the middle look reasonable.
  • **One visually recommended plan. **A highlighted border, a “Most popular” tag, a slightly larger card. This is not a trick - most buyers genuinely want to be told what people like them choose.
  • *Plans named after people, not sizes. *“Freelancer / Studio / Agency” beats “Basic / Plus / Premium” because visitors self-select by situation. If a visitor cannot find themselves in your plan names in three seconds, the page has already failed.
  • **An honest enterprise path. **If you sell to big teams, a fourth “talk to us” column is fine - as long as the three self-serve tiers still carry real prices.

The psychology underneath - anchoring, decoy pricing, why the $99 tier exists partly to sell the $39 one - is worth understanding once properly. Rob Walling’s short explainer is the best five minutes on the topic: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lC6Gpn0ugFI (SaaS Pricing Models Explained in 5 Minutes, Rob Walling).

People do not buy the cheapest plan or the best plan. People buy the plan that feels safe for their situation.

What each plan card must answer

When I design a pricing card, the card has to answer four questions in order, top to bottom:

  1. **Who is this for? **The plan name and a one-line description of the situation (“For solo founders validating an idea”).
  2. **What does it cost, really? **Price, billing period, and what happens at renewal - with the monthly/annual toggle defaulting to the billing you actually want to sell.
  3. **What do I get - and where is the ceiling? **Five to seven decisive features, not the full matrix. The limit that forces an upgrade belongs here in plain sight.
  4. *What happens when I click? *“Start free trial - no card needed” removes more hesitation than any testimonial. The button copy should describe the outcome, never say “Submit” or “Choose”.

The details that quietly move the numbers

  • Annual toggle with the saving spelled out. Write the saving as money, “Save $58 a year”, rather than “-20%”: a dollar figure feels like money, a percentage feels like maths.
  • Currency and tax honesty. If the card says $49 and checkout says $49 plus tax in a different currency, you will feel the difference in abandoned checkouts.
  • A “you can change this later” line. Fear of picking the wrong plan is a common silent objection.
  • Real usage anchors. “Most teams of 2 to 5 pick Studio” is decision support.
  • A short pricing FAQ on the page. Five questions: trials, refunds, limits, invoicing and cancellation.

Interactive elements - seat calculators, usage sliders, currency switchers - are where no-code tools start to sweat. In Framer this is exactly what code components are for, and a code component is far cheaper than people expect; I showed how that works in Can Framer handle custom code and WebGL? Whether that pushes your whole project towards custom code is a separate question - I weighed that trade-off in should your SaaS site be custom-coded or no-code?.

Mistakes that push buyers away

The anti-patterns I get hired to undo, in rough order of damage:

  1. *No prices at all. *“Contact us” on every tier tells self-serve buyers to leave. Hide prices only if your genuine minimum deal size justifies a sales call.
  2. **The wall-of-checkmarks grid. **Forty rows of identical ticks makes plans look the same and choosing feel risky. Show differences, not similarities.
  3. **Fake urgency. **Countdown timers on subscription software read as manipulation to exactly the technical audience most SaaS products sell to.
  4. **Burying the upgrade trigger. **If users discover the real limit only after they hit the limit inside the product, the pricing page has lied by omission - and churn follows.
  5. **Designing the page last. **The pricing page gets built in the final week of most site projects. The pricing page deserves the same design budget as the homepage, which is also why I insist on scoping the page explicitly - see how much a SaaS website costs to build for where the pricing page sits in a real budget.

A worked starting point

If you are building on Framer and want this structure without starting from a blank canvas, my free SaaS template Verius ships with a pricing section built on this exact pattern - three tiers, a highlighted recommended plan, billing toggle and FAQ block - so you can drop your own plans in and spend your time on the copy, which is where the conversion actually lives.

Want a pricing page people say yes to?

Pavlo Zhydkykh designs and builds conversion-first SaaS websites on Framer - pricing pages, plan structures and the calculators behind the plans included. If your pricing page is your highest-exit page, get in touch and he will tell you honestly whether the page needs a rebuild or an afternoon of fixes.

FAQ

How many pricing tiers should a SaaS pricing page have?

Three self-serve tiers is the sweet spot for most products: an entry plan that anchors the price, a recommended middle plan where most buyers should land, and a top tier that makes the middle look reasonable. Add a “talk to us” enterprise column only if you genuinely sell those deals - and keep real prices on the other three.

Should I show prices on my SaaS website at all?

Yes, unless your minimum contract genuinely requires a sales conversation. Hidden pricing filters out self-serve buyers, who simply move to a competitor that answers the question. Even sales-led products benefit from a published starting price, because it qualifies leads before the call.

Does the monthly/annual toggle actually matter?

It matters more than most visual decisions on the page. Default the toggle to annual if annual is what you want to sell, show the saving as a dollar amount rather than a percentage, and make sure the displayed price updates instantly. A toggle that confuses people about what they will pay is worse than no toggle.

Where should the feature comparison table go?

Below the plan cards, not instead of them. The cards should carry the five to seven features that actually differentiate the plans; the long matrix exists for the minority of evaluators who scroll for detail. Leading with a forty-row grid forces every visitor to do the analysis your design should have done for them.

What makes people abandon a pricing page?

The usual causes are missing prices, plans that all look identical, unclear limits that hint at surprise costs, and no answer to “can I change my mind later”. Most of these are copy and structure problems - fixable in days - rather than design problems that need a rebuild.

Can I build a good pricing page in Framer without custom code?

Mostly yes: tiers, toggles, highlighted plans and FAQs are all standard Framer work. Where code components earn their keep is interactive pricing - seat calculators, usage-based estimates, currency logic. Framer supports those through custom code components, so you get the calculator without leaving the no-code workflow for everything else.

title: Errors, validation and structure: the service that holds
description:
You deploy. The old process gets the signal and dies on the spot, with three requests half-way inside. The clients don't get an error: they get nothing. Measured, with the curl that was waiting:

without handler → 000
process exit without handler: 143

000 is "no response", and 143 is 128 + 15, the signal. Now the same test with four extra lines:

with handler → 200
process exit with handler: 0

That's the difference between a service and a pile of routes. And it isn't the only one: the same project that loses requests on deploy is usually the one handing stack traces to clients and the one that can't tell which request failed because its logs are loose lines.

This is the lesson that turns what you know into something maintainable.

One place for errors

In the previous lesson every route picked its code. With twenty routes that's twenty different decisions and no policy. The pattern is a single error middleware, with four arguments, mounted last.

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, status = 500, code = "internal_error") {
    super(message);
    this.status = status;
    this.code = code;
  }
}

class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(resource) {
    super(`No such ${resource}`, 404, "not_found");
  }
}

A domain error carries its HTTP status and its business code. And the central handler does the only translation that should exist:

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  const known = error instanceof AppError;
  const status = known ? error.status : 500;

  res.status(status).json({
    error: known ? error.code : "internal_error",
    message: known ? error.message : "something broke",
  });
});

With three routes failing in three ways:

curl -s http://localhost:3311/boom
curl -s http://localhost:3311/async-boom
curl -s http://localhost:3311/crash

{"error":"not_found","message":"No such book 7"}
{"error":"not_found","message":"No such async book"}
{"error":"internal_error","message":"something broke"}

The first two are errors you threw and they describe what happened. The third is an unexpected TypeError, and the client sees neither the message nor the trace: it gets a generic one. The full detail goes to the log, which belongs to whoever programs, not to whoever calls.

That's the rule that never breaks: the client gets what it needs to act; the server keeps what it needs to debug. Answer with error.stack and you're publishing your server's layout and your file names.

A 404 is also an error, and it's also centralised

An error middleware doesn't catch "no route matched": that isn't an error, it's Express reaching the end without finding anything and answering with its own HTML page. If your API speaks JSON, that page is noise. You fix it with a normal middleware after every route and before the error one:

app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: "not_found", path: req.originalUrl });
});

curl -s http://localhost:3322/nope

{"error":"not_found","path":"/nope"}

req.originalUrl and not req.url: inside a mounted router, req.url is trimmed to the prefix, and the client needs to see the path it asked for.

async no longer needs help

In Express 4, an exception thrown inside an async function never reached the error handler: it stayed in a rejected promise and, with luck, in an unhandledRejection. That's where express-async-errors came from: it wraps your routes so the exception travels up.

Express 5 doesn't need it. Measured, the async route above returns the same as the synchronous one:

{"error":"not_found","message":"No such async book"}

Express forwards the rejection to the handler by itself. If you see express-async-errors in a new project, it's dead weight from an older version.

What is still yours:

  • try/catch where you actually recover. If the cache fails and you fall back to the database, that isn't an error: it's plan B, and it lives in the route.
  • Never call next(error) after responding. If the body is already sent, the handler tries to answer again and you get Cannot set headers after they are sent.

Validate at the boundary

Everything coming in through a request is hostile until proven otherwise: strings where you expected numbers, null where you expected an object, two megabytes of text where you expected an id. And validating inside the route means repeating it in every branch.

The boundary is a schema, and Zod turns it into code:

import { z } from "zod";

const BookSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1),
  pages: z.coerce.number().int().positive(),
  genre: z.enum(["novel", "essay"]).default("novel"),
});

const ok = BookSchema.safeParse({ title: "Emma", pages: "474" });
console.log("valid:", ok.success, "· data:", ok.data);

const bad = BookSchema.safeParse({ title: "", pages: -3 });
console.log("valid:", bad.success);
for (const issue of bad.error.issues) {
  console.log(" ·", issue.path.join("."), "→", issue.message);
}

valid: true · data: { title: 'Emma', pages: 474, genre: 'novel' }
valid: false
 · title → Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters
 · pages → Too small: expected number to be >0

Three things it does that hurt by hand: it coerces ("474" becomes 474, which is what arrives over HTTP), it applies defaults (genre: "novel"), and it collects every problem with its exact path instead of failing on the first. And what it returns isn't an exception: safeParse hands you a result you can turn into a 400 with the list of failures.

That response shape matters more than it looks. A 400 with { error: "invalid_input", details: [{ field, message }] } lets the client paint the error next to the right input. A 400 with the text "invalid input" tells nobody anything.

Structure: routes, controllers, services

With two routes, everything fits in app.js. With twenty, it doesn't. The split that works is the usual one, because each layer has a different reason to change:

  • Routes: which URL calls which controller. Changes when the API changes.
  • Controllers: translate HTTP into calls. They read req, write res, and nothing else. Change when the protocol changes.
  • Services: the business logic, unaware that HTTP exists. Change when the business changes, and they're the only thing you can test without starting a server.

And two files with similar names worth not confusing: app.js builds and configures the application; index.js (or server.js) starts it, listens on a port and worries about signals. That split is what lets you import app in a test and throw requests at it without occupying a fixed port.

Better still, a factory:

export function createApp({ repository, logger }) {
  const app = express();
  // …
  return app;
}

Dependencies come in as arguments. In a test you pass a fake repository and a silent logger; in production, the real ones. Nothing global, nothing hidden.

And a configuration module that validates at startup, like the one in the files lesson: if DATABASE_URL is missing, the process dies at the beginning, not on the third request.

Logs you can follow

A log line without an identifier is a sentence in a diary with no dates. With twenty simultaneous requests you need to join the four lines of one request.

pino writes JSON, one line per event, and takes structured fields:

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.id = req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? randomUUID();
  const t0 = Date.now();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    log.info({ id: req.id, method: req.method, path: req.url, status: res.statusCode, ms: Date.now() - t0 }, "request");
  });
  next();
});

{"level":30,"time":1794697598645,"pid":1132699,"id":"e5f5f3e3-…","method":"GET","path":"/books/7","status":200,"ms":13,"msg":"request"}
{"level":50,"time":1794697598656,"pid":1132699,"id":"02053e8e-…","err":{"type":"Error","message":"the service exploded","stack":"…"},"msg":"unhandled error"}

Two things: the same id appears on the error line and the request line, so you can rebuild the whole story; and the error carries its trace to the log, where it's useful, while the client gets the generic one.

The identifier is copied from the client when it sends one (x-request-id) and generated otherwise. So when the frontend reports a failing request, its identifier and yours are the same one and nobody has to guess.

And a classic logging trap: the IP. Behind a proxy, req.ip is the proxy's unless you say otherwise:

app.set("trust proxy", 1);

without trust proxy → {"ip":"::1"}
with trust proxy    → {"ip":"203.0.113.9"}

With X-Forwarded-For set, without that line every log says ::1 and every IP-based rate limit points at the same place. With it, the real address. The 1 means "trust the first proxy in front of me"; behind a chain of several, you raise the number.

Shutting down without dropping requests

A deploy doesn't kill a process: it sends SIGTERM and waits for it to leave. What you do with that signal decides whether you lose requests.

const server = app.listen(3000);

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(() => {
    log.info("closed cleanly");
    process.exit(0);
  });
});

server.close() stops accepting new connections and waits for the ones in flight. The test, with an 800 ms request running and the signal at 200:

with handler → 200
process exit with handler: 0

Against the 000 and 143 from the introduction. With one caveat: if a request gets stuck, the close never finishes, which is why almost everyone adds a timer that forces the exit at ten or thirty seconds.

And the piece that separates a correct close from one that hangs: a deadline. If a request never finishes, server.close() waits forever. The complete pattern gives a few milliseconds of grace and then aborts whatever is still alive, with the AbortController from the async lesson.

const control = new AbortController();

app.get("/slow", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    await sleep(2000, null, { signal: control.signal });
    res.json({ ok: true });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.name === "AbortError") {
      res.status(503).json({ error: "shutting_down" });
      return;
    }
    next(error);
  }
});

for (const signal of ["SIGTERM", "SIGINT"]) {
  process.on(signal, () => {
    server.close(() => {
      console.log("closed");
      process.exit(0);
    });
    setTimeout(() => control.abort(), 100);
  });
}

kill -TERM <pid>

in-flight request → 503
exit: 0
SIGTERM · stop accepting, 100 ms of grace
deadline reached · aborting what is left
closed

The in-flight request gets a 503 with a message that tells the truth — "I'm shutting down" — instead of a cut connection. And the process exits with 0, because it did what it had to do. SIGINT is the same story with Ctrl+C: you register both, because locally you kill with the keyboard and in production with a signal.

Exit codes say something and are worth using well: 0 is "I finished fine", 1 is "I failed", and 143 is "I was killed", which is what you'll see in the logs of a container that was sent the signal and ignored it. process.exitCode = 1 lets the process end by itself with that code; process.exit(1) cuts it on the spot, and it's only justified when there's nothing left to finish.

And the two safety nets, with judgement: unhandledRejection and uncaughtException. Their job is to record the error and exit; a process that has seen an uncaught exception is in a state you don't know, and serving requests from there is worse than falling over. Exiting lets the orchestrator start a clean one.

Common problems

Cannot set headers after they are sent

You responded and also called next(error), or the error handler tried to answer an already-sent request. Check res.headersSent before writing.

The error handler never runs

It has three arguments instead of four. Express doesn't warn.

The client receives the error's stack trace

You're sending error.stack or the whole object. Respond with a code and a message, and keep the rest in the log.

Logs don't let me follow a request

There's no identifier, or it isn't on every line. Add it in the first middleware and put it in every log for that request.

Requests are lost on deploy

There's no SIGTERM handler, or the process doesn't wait for server.close(). The orchestrator kills it a few seconds later.

Validation is scattered across routes

Move it to a middleware or the controller, with one schema per endpoint. Repeating if (!body.title) in every branch is how one gets forgotten.

What you take from this lesson

  • An error middleware with four arguments, last in line, decides the code for everything.
  • Domain errors carry their status and code; unknown ones become a generic 500.
  • The client gets what it needs to act; the trace stays in the log.
  • Express 5 forwards async rejections; express-async-errors is dead weight.
  • try/catch only where you recover, and never next() after responding.
  • Zod at the boundary: it coerces, applies defaults and collects problems with their path.
  • Routes, controllers and services, with app.js separate from index.js and a factory that takes dependencies.
  • JSON logs with one identifier per request; the real IP requires trust proxy.
  • A closing 404, after the routes and before the error handler, so the API never returns HTML.
  • SIGTERM and SIGINT with server.close(), a deadline and an AbortController: whatever doesn't finish in time gets a 503 instead of a cut connection. 143 means you didn't do it.
  • unhandledRejection and uncaughtException get logged and exited.

With this the service survives a deploy and a hostile request. There's one code lesson left before the close: the final project, where all of this gets assembled into a real API.

Never stop coding!

title: How to Build a Voice AI Agent in 2026-2027: Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi (Step-by-Step)
description:
Your voice agent works in the demo. Then a real customer calls from an open-plan office.

The agent hears the caller. It also hears the colleague two desks away. It answers both, stops mid-sentence, and the call goes sideways.

If you're:

  • building your first voice agent and picking a framework,
  • moving a prototype from your laptop to real phone calls,
  • or choosing between Pipecat, LiveKit and Vapi,

this guide walks you through all three with the same agent, so you can compare them on code you can actually run.

Short answer: pick Pipecat if you want full control in open-source Python, LiveKit Agents if you want open-source code plus managed WebRTC and telephony, and Vapi if you want a hosted agent you configure instead of code. Whichever you pick, put Krisp voice isolation in front of the agent's ears. All three have a ready-made Krisp integration (on Pipecat, through Pipecat Cloud), and any other pipeline can call Krisp's standalone Voice Isolation API. In my LiveKit test recordings, it cut the words the agent picked up from a background voice from 224 to 35.

How a voice AI agent works

Every voice agent is the same pipeline, whatever framework you use:

  1. Transport brings the caller's audio in (WebRTC, a phone line, a browser).
  2. Voice isolation keeps the caller's voice and removes background voices and noise.
  3. VAD and turn detection decide when the caller is speaking and when they've finished.
  4. Speech-to-text (STT) turns the audio into words.
  5. The LLM decides what to say.
  6. Text-to-speech (TTS) speaks the answer back.

Some agents replace steps 4 to 6 with a single speech-to-speech model, which may also handle step 3. Others merge only part of the pipeline: Deepgram Flux, for example, builds turn detection into speech-to-text. Voice isolation can sit in front of either setup.

It's also the easiest step to leave out.

That's the step that decides whether the rest of the pipeline is working with the caller's words or with everyone in the room.

Speech-to-text handles noise well now. It still transcribes a second person talking near the mic, and the LLM answers it. In Krisp's test for its Voice Isolation 2.5 release, 10 speech-to-text systems averaged 2.10% word error rate on clean single-speaker audio and 35.92% with a second person talking. With Voice Isolation 2.5 in front, that 35.92% fell to 10.90% (release post).

Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi: which one to pick

The three tools sit at different levels of control:

Pipecat LiveKit Agents Vapi
What it is Open-source Python framework for voice and multimodal pipelines Open-source agent framework on top of LiveKit's WebRTC platform Hosted voice agent platform
You write The whole pipeline, frame by frame An agent class and a session config A JSON assistant config
Hosting Anywhere, or Pipecat Cloud LiveKit Cloud or self-hosted Vapi
STT / LLM / TTS Bring your own providers Your own keys, or LiveKit Inference (no provider keys) Picked in the config, billed through Vapi
Krisp voice isolation KrispVivaFilter on Pipecat Cloud; Krisp's Voice Isolation API (or a licensed SDK) for local pipelines krisp.voice_isolation() plugin Smart Denoising, one config field
Best for Teams that want full control over every frame Teams that want code plus managed real-time infrastructure Teams that want an agent live without running servers

I built the same agent on each one: Ava, a support agent for an online store that answers order-status questions in one or two sentences.

1. Build a voice agent with Pipecat

Pipecat is the most hands-on option. You assemble a pipeline of processors and Pipecat moves audio and text frames through it.

I used pipecat-ai 1.16.0 and OpenAI for all three AI services, so the only key needed is OPENAI_API_KEY.

pip install "pipecat-ai[openai,silero,webrtc,runner]" python-dotenv

import os
from pipecat.audio.vad.silero import SileroVADAnalyzer
from pipecat.frames.frames import LLMRunFrame
from pipecat.pipeline.pipeline import Pipeline
from pipecat.pipeline.runner import PipelineRunner
from pipecat.pipeline.task import PipelineParams, PipelineTask
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_context import LLMContext
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_response_universal import LLMContextAggregatorPair, LLMUserAggregatorParams
from pipecat.runner.types import RunnerArguments
from pipecat.runner.utils import create_transport
from pipecat.services.openai.llm import OpenAILLMService
from pipecat.services.openai.stt import OpenAISTTService
from pipecat.services.openai.tts import OpenAITTSService
from pipecat.transports.base_transport import TransportParams

# Krisp VIVA ships preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud; locally the import fails and the bot runs without it
try:
    from pipecat.audio.filters.krisp_viva_filter import KrispVivaFilter
    krisp_filter = KrispVivaFilter()
except Exception:
    krisp_filter = None

INSTRUCTIONS = ("You are Ava, a support agent for an online store. Keep answers short: one or two sentences, "
                "spoken style. If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today.")

async def run_bot(transport, runner_args):
    key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
    stt = OpenAISTTService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4o-transcribe")
    llm = OpenAILLMService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4.1-mini",
                           settings=OpenAILLMService.Settings(system_instruction=INSTRUCTIONS))
    tts = OpenAITTSService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4o-mini-tts", voice="alloy")

    context = LLMContext()
    user_agg, assistant_agg = LLMContextAggregatorPair(
        context, user_params=LLMUserAggregatorParams(vad_analyzer=SileroVADAnalyzer()))

    pipeline = Pipeline([transport.input(), stt, user_agg, llm, tts, transport.output(), assistant_agg])
    task = PipelineTask(pipeline, params=PipelineParams(enable_metrics=True))

    @transport.event_handler("on_client_connected")
    async def on_connected(transport, client):
        context.add_message({"role": "developer", "content": "Greet the caller and ask how you can help."})
        await task.queue_frames([LLMRunFrame()])

    await PipelineRunner(handle_sigint=runner_args.handle_sigint).run(task)

async def bot(runner_args: RunnerArguments):
    params = lambda: TransportParams(audio_in_enabled=True, audio_out_enabled=True, audio_in_filter=krisp_filter)
    transport = await create_transport(runner_args, {"daily": params, "webrtc": params})
    await run_bot(transport, runner_args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pipecat.runner.run import main
    main()

Run python bot.py and open http://localhost:7860/client. Pipecat serves a small playground where you connect and talk to the bot over WebRTC, with no account needed. Mine greeted me, and when I sent "Hi, my order number is 4471. Where is it?" it answered "Your order 4471 is out for delivery today."

Adding Krisp. The KrispVivaFilter goes in audio_in_filter, so it cleans the caller's audio before VAD and STT ever see it. Its dependencies come preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud (base image 0.1.8 or later), and you turn it on when you deploy:

pipecat cloud deploy --krisp-viva-audio-filter tel

Pick tel (models up to 16 kHz, suited to phone audio) or pro (up to 32 kHz). According to Pipecat's docs, the first 10,000 Krisp minutes per month are free, then $0.0015 per minute.

Running KrispVivaFilter outside Pipecat Cloud needs a commercial VIVA SDK license. For local development there's a simpler route: Krisp's self-serve Voice Isolation API. Any pipeline that can open a WebSocket can call it, so you send the caller's audio and feed the cleaned audio into VAD and STT. New accounts start with $30 in free credits. It's a separate integration, not the KrispVivaFilter above. I didn't deploy to Pipecat Cloud for this guide, so my measured Krisp results come from LiveKit below.

Pros

  • Full control over every processor in the pipeline.
  • Open source, runs anywhere Python runs.
  • Krisp VIVA preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud, one deploy flag to enable.

Cons

  • More code to own than the other two.
  • The built-in KrispVivaFilter needs Pipecat Cloud; locally you call Krisp's Voice Isolation API instead (or use a licensed SDK).

Best for: teams that want to own the pipeline end to end.

2. Build a voice agent with LiveKit Agents

LiveKit Agents gives you an open-source agent framework on top of LiveKit's real-time platform. Your agent joins a "room" like any other participant, and LiveKit handles WebRTC and telephony.

I used livekit-agents 1.8.13 with LiveKit Inference, so the only credentials are the LiveKit Cloud project URL, key and secret. STT, LLM and TTS are billed through LiveKit, with no provider keys.

pip install "livekit-agents[silero,turn-detector]" livekit-plugins-krisp python-dotenv

from livekit import agents
from livekit.agents import Agent, AgentSession, inference, room_io
from livekit.plugins import krisp, silero

INSTRUCTIONS = """You are Ava, a support agent for an online store.
Keep answers short: one or two sentences, spoken style.
If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today."""

class SupportAgent(Agent):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(instructions=INSTRUCTIONS)

async def entrypoint(ctx: agents.JobContext) -> None:
    session = AgentSession(
        stt="deepgram/nova-3",          # LiveKit Inference model IDs
        llm="openai/gpt-4.1-mini",
        tts="cartesia/sonic-3",
        vad=silero.VAD.load(),
        turn_detection=inference.TurnDetector(),
    )
    await session.start(
        room=ctx.room,
        agent=SupportAgent(),
        room_options=room_io.RoomOptions(
            audio_input=room_io.AudioInputOptions(
                # Krisp voice isolation before VAD, turn detection and STT
                noise_cancellation=krisp.voice_isolation(noise_suppression_level=100),
            ),
        ),
    )
    await session.generate_reply(instructions="Greet the caller and ask how you can help.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    agents.cli.run_app(agents.WorkerOptions(entrypoint_fnc=entrypoint))

python agent.py download-files   # once: VAD and turn-detector weights
python agent.py dev              # registers the agent with LiveKit Cloud

The Krisp plugin needs no Krisp account and no model files: it authenticates through your LiveKit Cloud project. LiveKit's free Build plan includes 100 voice-isolation minutes, then $0.0012 per minute on paid plans (pricing). For SIP phone calls, use krisp.voice_isolation_telephony() instead.

One setting matters more than it looks. LiveKit's plugin defaults to noise_suppression_level=75. That's LiveKit's default, not Krisp's: Krisp's own default is full strength (100). In my four test recordings below, going from LiveKit's default to 100 roughly halved the word error rate again.

Pros

  • Open-source code with managed WebRTC and telephony.
  • LiveKit Inference: one account instead of three provider keys.
  • Krisp plugin works out of the box with a LiveKit Cloud project.

Cons

  • The Krisp plugin needs LiveKit Cloud for real-time transport, unless you hold your own Krisp license.
  • On Windows, dev mode didn't reload my code changes; I had to restart the worker.

Best for: teams that want to write the agent in code but not run real-time media servers.

3. Build a voice agent with Vapi

Vapi is the no-servers option. An agent is a JSON "assistant" config, and Vapi runs the whole pipeline.

import os
import requests

assistant = {
    "name": "Ava - store support",
    "firstMessage": "Hi, this is Ava from the store. How can I help you today?",
    "transcriber": {"provider": "deepgram", "model": "nova-3", "language": "en"},
    "model": {
        "provider": "openai",
        "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
        "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are Ava, a support agent for an online store. "
                      "Keep answers short. If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today."}],
    },
    "voice": {"provider": "vapi", "voiceId": "Elliot"},
    # Smart Denoising uses Krisp to remove background voices and noise
    "backgroundSpeechDenoisingPlan": {"smartDenoisingPlan": {"enabled": True}},
}

r = requests.post("https://api.vapi.ai/assistant",
                  headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['VAPI_API_KEY']}"},
                  json=assistant, timeout=30)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["id"])

Vapi answered 201 with the new assistant ID, and the response echoed "smartDenoisingPlan": {"enabled": true}. To call it from a web page, Vapi provides the @vapi-ai/web SDK, which uses your public key.

Vapi's docs describe Smart Denoising as Krisp's technology for removing background voices and noise in real time (docs). It replaces the older backgroundDenoisingEnabled flag.

Pros

  • No servers: an agent is one API call.
  • Krisp voice isolation is one config field.
  • Transcriber, model and voice configured in the same request.

Cons

  • Less control over the pipeline than code-first frameworks.
  • Model, voice and transcriber usage is billed through Vapi by default.

Best for: teams that want a hosted agent without running infrastructure.

Test your agent like a real call

A voice agent that works on your laptop mic proves very little. Real calls have other people in them.

So I tested the LiveKit agent the way a real call would hit it. A small script joins the room as the caller and plays a real recording into the agent at real-time pace: four recordings from Krisp's open Voice Isolation Benchmark Dataset, two from working call centers and two from home and office settings, each with a second person talking. Then I captured what the agent's speech-to-text actually heard and compared it with the dataset's hand-written transcripts.

Agent input Word error rate Extra words in the transcript
No voice isolation 58.2% 224
Krisp at LiveKit's default (75) 41.6% 139
Krisp, level 100 21.8% 35

Same LiveKit agent, same four recordings, Deepgram nova-3 through LiveKit Inference. "Extra words" are insertions against the main speaker's transcript, mostly from the background voice. One run per setting, so treat small differences between files as noise.

Without voice isolation, the agent's transcript picked up 224 words the caller never said. With Krisp at level 100, 35. On one office recording, the extra words went from 43 to zero.

That's the gap between an agent that answers the caller and one that answers the room.

Krisp's open voice isolation benchmark points the same way at a bigger scale: across 265 recordings and 11 speech-to-text configurations, word error rate fell from 23.24% to 6.24% with Voice Isolation 2.5.

My relative drop (58.2% to 21.8%, about 63% fewer errors) is almost the same as Deepgram Nova-3 streaming in Krisp's benchmark (20.4% to 8.0%, 61% fewer). My absolute numbers are higher, likely from the scoring and the small sample, but the two results agree.

Going multilingual with Krisp's Voice Translation API

Once the agent hears the right person, the next wall is language. Krisp's voice translation API does real-time speech-to-speech translation across 61 languages, with background voice cancellation built in. Each session translates one direction (I tested English to Spanish); for a two-way call you run one session per direction.

It's a WebSocket: you get a short-lived session key with your Krisp API key, send one config message, then stream 16 kHz PCM.

import asyncio, json, os, requests, websockets

def session_key():
    r = requests.post("https://api.developers.krisp.ai/v2/sdk/tokens/session",
                      headers={"Authorization": f"api-key {os.environ['KRISP_API_KEY']}"},
                      json={"usage_type": "vt", "expiration_ttl": 30})
    return r.json()["data"]["session_key"]

async def translate(pcm_chunks):
    url = "wss://streaming.krisp.ai/vt?authorization=" + requests.utils.quote(f"Api-Key {session_key()}")
    async with websockets.connect(url, max_size=None) as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"config": {
            "audio": {"format": "pcm_s16le", "sample_rate": 16000, "channels": 1},
            "source_language": "en-US", "target_language": "es-ES", "voice": "female",
            "transcript": {"interim": False, "final": True, "translate": True},
            "features": {"background_voice_cancellation": True},
        }}))
        # stream 20 ms chunks with ws.send(chunk); translated audio comes back as binary frames,
        # transcripts and translations as JSON events

I streamed 30 seconds of a real call-center recording through it. It sent back 29.3 seconds of Spanish speech plus both transcripts, for example:

"Thank you, Lilith. Your account 4471-B reflects usage of 512 kW per hour this cycle."
"Gracias, Lilith. Su cuenta 4471-B refleja un consumo de 512 kW por hora en este ciclo."

One gotcha: URL-encode the authorization value. The space in Api-Key <key> made my first handshake fail with HTTP 400.

Production checklist

Before your agent takes real calls:

  • Isolate the caller's voice at the start of the pipeline, and check the level: in my four test recordings, noise_suppression_level=100 cut errors sharply compared with LiveKit's default (75). Krisp's own default is full strength (100). Measure it on your own audio.
  • Use the telephony model for phone calls: voice_isolation_telephony() on LiveKit, tel on Pipecat Cloud.
  • Budget for latency. Krisp voice isolation adds no more than 20 ms, 15 ms of it algorithmic latency; through the SDK, plan for about 25 ms. If you call the WebSocket API, add network time on top.
  • Test with real recordings from calls, homes and offices, not your own mic in a quiet room. A second voice is the case that breaks agents.
  • Watch turn-taking and interruptions. Krisp also ships Turn-Taking and Interrupt Prediction models in its VIVA SDK for teams that run their own pipeline.
  • Load secrets explicitly. An old OPENAI_API_KEY in my Windows environment silently overrode my .env and returned 401s until I used load_dotenv(override=True).

FAQ

How do I build a voice AI agent?

Pick a framework (Pipecat, LiveKit Agents or Vapi), connect a transport, add voice isolation, VAD and turn detection, then speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. All three frameworks in this guide get a basic agent running in under 100 lines of code or one API call.

Pipecat vs LiveKit: which is better?

Neither is better in general. Pipecat gives you full control of the pipeline in open-source Python. LiveKit Agents gives you open-source agent code plus managed WebRTC and telephony. Pick Pipecat for control, LiveKit for infrastructure you don't want to run.

LiveKit vs Vapi: what's the difference?

LiveKit Agents is code: you write the agent and LiveKit runs the real-time transport. Vapi is a hosted platform: you send a JSON config and Vapi runs everything. Vapi is faster to start; LiveKit gives you more control.

Do Pipecat, LiveKit and Vapi support Krisp?

Yes. Pipecat has KrispVivaFilter, preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud; for local development, call Krisp's Voice Isolation API over a WebSocket. LiveKit has the livekit-plugins-krisp plugin with krisp.voice_isolation(). Vapi's Smart Denoising uses Krisp, enabled with backgroundSpeechDenoisingPlan.smartDenoisingPlan.enabled.

Why does my voice agent stop mid-sentence or answer things the caller didn't say?

Usually because it hears more than the caller: a colleague, a TV, another agent on a call-center floor. The agent takes that voice for the caller cutting in and stops mid-sentence, and speech-to-text transcribes its words too. Voice isolation before VAD and STT removes it; in my tests it cut the extra words in the transcript from 224 to 35.

Can a voice agent handle callers in other languages?

Yes. Krisp's voice translation API translates speech to speech in real time across 61 languages. Each session handles one direction, so a two-way call uses two sessions.

The takeaway

Getting a basic voice agent running is the easy part on any of these three frameworks.

Making it hear the right person on a real call is the part that's easy to skip. It's a ready-made integration on all three, and one API call for any other pipeline.
