title: How Can Singapore Firms Build a GenAI Center of Excellence
description:
Building a Generative AI (GenAI) Center of Excellence (CoE) in Singapore requires aligning business strategy, local regulatory standards (such as MAS guidelines), funding incentives, and a cross-functional hub-and-spoke delivery model. (EDB Singapore)

Key takeaways

  • Start with business outcomes: A GenAI CoE should prioritise measurable productivity improvements and scalable use cases rather than accumulating disconnected AI experiments.
  • Choose the right operating model: Centralised structures suit early-stage adoption, while hub-and-spoke models support growing enterprise demand.
  • Make data ownership explicit: Every priority dataset needs a named owner, defined access controls and an agreed governance process before production deployment.
  • Treat responsible AI as an operational requirement: Model evaluation, privacy controls, security testing and human oversight must be embedded before applications reach production.
  • Use Singapore's AI ecosystem strategically: IMDA initiatives and workforce programmes can support capability development, but eligibility and programme scope must be checked individually.

What is a GenAI Center of Excellence (CoE)?

A Center of Excellence (CoE) is a dedicated team, operational hub, or governance structure within an organization that centralizes specialized expertise, best practices, and standards. Rather than operating as an isolated research lab, it acts as a central "mission control" to guide strategy, share resources, and scale adoption smoothly across different departments. (IBM)

Unlike a conventional AI team focused on individual models or analytics projects, a GenAI CoE coordinates the capabilities required to deploy and maintain GenAI applications across an enterprise.

Its responsibilities typically include:

  • Strategy and prioritisation: Identifying business opportunities and maintaining a pipeline of high-value GenAI use cases.
  • Technical enablement: Establishing reusable architectures, LLM integrations, RAG patterns and development standards.
  • Data management: Preparing proprietary information, knowledge bases and enterprise data pipelines.
  • Responsible AI: Defining evaluation criteria, privacy controls, security requirements and human oversight.
  • Business adoption: Training employees, supporting implementation teams and measuring business outcomes.

[caption id="attachment_121867" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] What is a Center of Excellence, and what makes it GenAI?[/caption]

GenAI Center of Excellence examples: Three operating models

There is no single operating model suitable for every enterprise. The appropriate structure depends on AI maturity, internal technical expertise and how many business units need GenAI capabilities.

Operating model

 Who owns delivery? Best fit Main risk
Centralised The CoE builds and operates all GenAI applications. Early-stage organisations with limited use cases and scarce AI expertise.

The central team becomes a delivery bottleneck.

Hub-and-spoke

 The CoE owns standards, platforms and governance; business units develop applications. Mid-to-large enterprises with several active AI initiatives. Business units may deviate from shared standards without clear accountability.
Federated Individual business units own delivery while the CoE provides guidance and oversight. Mature enterprises with established AI teams across departments.

Duplicated tooling, inconsistent governance and fragmented investments.

At Kyanon Digital, we see the CoE as more than a central team responsible for technology standards. It should also build the processes, knowledge and engineering capabilities that allow an organisation to scale delivery sustainably.

How do you build a GenAI Center of Excellence?

Building a GenAI Center of Excellence requires five coordinated steps, from defining business objectives to scaling enterprise AI capabilities. Each step should establish clear responsibilities, deliverables and readiness criteria before the organisation moves forward.

Step

 What to do Expected output Readiness checkpoint
Define the mandate, vision and leadership Establish measurable business objectives, appoint an executive sponsor (CTO, CDO or CoE Director), and form a cross-functional team covering AI engineering, data, business operations, legal and change management. Written CoE mandate, executive sponsor, team structure and prioritised use-case pipeline.

Executive sponsorship confirmed and budget owner agreed.

Establish data readiness and architecture

 Prepare proprietary data and knowledge bases, assign data owners, implement access controls, and design a model-agnostic architecture supporting LLM integration, RAG and cloud or hybrid deployment. Enterprise data inventory, named data owners and reference architecture. Data ownership and access permissions confirmed for priority datasets.
Embed responsible AI and governance Establish model evaluation, hallucination monitoring, security testing, privacy controls, human oversight and AI-use policies. Align governance with relevant IMDA guidance and Singapore's PDPA obligations. AI-use policy, model evaluation checklist and governance procedures.

Governance policies and production approval responsibilities established.

Develop technical capabilities and workforce readiness

 Equip teams with GenAI engineering, data integration, AI orchestration and MLOps capabilities. Train employees to identify appropriate use cases and adopt AI responsibly. Technical capability roadmap, workforce training plan and reusable AI development standards. Core technical capabilities and responsible AI training available to relevant teams.
Leverage Singapore's AI ecosystem and scale adoption Explore relevant IMDA initiatives, research institutions, technology partners and workforce programmes. Validate programme eligibility and scale proven use cases across business units. Partnership roadmap, programme shortlist and enterprise AI scaling plan.

Business value demonstrated, scaling priorities agreed and programme eligibility verified.

Important: Steps 1–3 establish the organisational, technical and governance foundations. Steps 4–5 help the CoE develop sustainable internal capabilities and expand adoption across the enterprise.

When should a firm NOT build a GenAI CoE yet?

Establishing a full GenAI CoE too early can create unnecessary organisational overhead. Before committing to a permanent team, enterprises should confirm that the necessary business, data and governance foundations exist.

Four conditions indicate that an organisation is not yet ready:

  • No executive sponsor: There is no senior leader accountable for AI priorities, funding and cross-functional coordination.
  • No named data owner: Priority datasets lack clear ownership, access permissions or governance arrangements.
  • No agreed first use case: The organisation has broad AI ambitions but cannot identify a business problem with measurable outcomes.
  • No approved AI-use policy: Employees and development teams lack clear rules for handling enterprise information and using external AI services.

[caption id="attachment_121868" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] When should a firm NOT build a GenAI CoE yet?[/caption]

Kyanon Digital believes a GenAI Center of Excellence should address a defined business need, not become an organisational layer created simply to follow the AI trend. Establishing a CoE too early can introduce additional costs, governance overhead and coordination challenges without delivering measurable business value.

How Kyanon Digital supports GenAI CoE work in practice

Establishing a GenAI Center of Excellence requires more than access to foundation models. Enterprises need engineering capabilities that connect proprietary business data, AI orchestration, enterprise applications and operational workflows.

As an Enterprise Digital Transformation & AI Partner, Kyanon Digital supports organisations across digital engineering, data and analytics, enterprise integration, AI applications and technology modernisation.

Case study: Empowering Cynopsis Solutions with Scalable RegTech Development & a Center of Excellence (CoE)

[embed]https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X56mun4cGNM[/embed]

Empowering Cynopsis Solutions with Scalable RegTech Development & a Center of Excellence (CoE)

Client overview

Cynopsis Solutions is a Singapore-based RegTech (Regulatory Technology) company specializing in compliance solutions for financial institutions, fintech firms, and regulated entities.

Challenges

As Cynopsis expanded its RegTech product offerings, it faced key challenges:

  • Scalability & Rapid Development Needs – The demand for AML, KYC, and digital onboarding solutions was rising, requiring fast and scalable product development.
  • Keeping Pace with Regulatory Changes – With constantly evolving compliance regulations, Cynopsis needed a flexible and adaptive product development strategy.
  • Onboarding & Training New Team Members Efficiently – The onshore team was spending significant time training offshore members, leading to inefficiencies and slower delivery.
  • Maintaining High Performance & Product Quality – As the platform grew, ensuring continuous improvement and minimal downtime became critical.

Results and business impact

The collaboration delivered four key outcomes:

  • Faster product launches: Three RegTech solutions, Transaction Monitoring, eKYC, and Digital Onboarding, were launched within a few months.
  • Stronger compliance capabilities: The solutions strengthened Cynopsis’ AML/KYC capabilities and helped its clients manage regulatory risks.
  • More scalable team operations: The CoE enabled offshore engineers to onboard new members independently, reducing the onshore team's repetitive training workload.
  • Improved delivery processes: Agile development, CI/CD, and structured knowledge-sharing practices supported continuous product improvement and adaptability.

Explore the full case study here: Empowering Cynopsis Solutions with Scalable RegTech Development & a Center of Excellence (CoE)

Conclusion

The appropriate engagement depends on the enterprise's starting point. Some organisations need help validating an initial use case, while others require engineering support to integrate and scale applications across multiple business units. Rather than treating a CoE as a standalone technology project, enterprises should connect its technical roadmap to business priorities, data readiness and long-term operating requirements.

Considering a GenAI Center of Excellence for your enterprise? Contact Kyanon Digital to discuss your enterprise AI priorities, technical readiness and implementation requirements.

Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now support function calling

The SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now handle LLM function calling (tool use) flows. Two new optional XML elements extract function calling content for Model Armor sanitization:

  • <FunctionResponseSource> in SanitizeUserPrompt: extracts function/tool response data from user turns. Used as a fallback when <UserPromptSource> returns empty on function calling turns.
  • <FunctionCallSource> in SanitizeModelResponse: extracts function call arguments from model responses. Used as a fallback when <LLMResponseSource> returns empty.

Default templates target the Gemini format and require no additional configuration. For OpenAI and Anthropic formats, configure custom JSONPath templates. For more information, see FunctionResponseSource and FunctionCallSource.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

End-user safety identifier labels for abuse monitoring

End-user safety_identifier request labels are available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) and Veo (predictLongRunning) API calls. API resellers and multi-tenant apps can pass an anonymized per-user ID in labels to attribute policy violations to individual end users. Targeted attribution helps prevent enforcement actions across an entire Google Cloud project.

For formatting requirements and code samples, see Pass an end-user safety identifier in API calls.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Carbon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-carbon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Govern agents on any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster with Agent Gateway for cross-cloud (Limited Preview)

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available in Limited Preview. It extends Agent Platform governance to agents that run on Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes clusters outside of Google Cloud, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Red Hat OpenShift, and bare-metal clusters. Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

For more information, see Set up Agent Gateway for cross-cloud.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.

title: What Does Skill Lift Actually Measure? A Source-Code-Level Audit and Noise-Aware Reanalysis of SkillsBench
description:
arXiv:2611.33943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.

title: FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal
description:
arXiv:2611.33879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a guardrail rejects an LLM agent's action, its message reaches any attacker observing the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves benign users unable to recover, whereas an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message. Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies
description:
arXiv:2611.33794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement of embodied policies, in which progress is judged by evidence the improving system cannot influence.

title: ui-ux-pro-max in Claude Code: three flags that keep your design system from drifting
description:
Disclosure: we run Skillselion, an independent directory of Claude Code, Codex and Cursor extensions ranked by real installs. We have no tie to nextlevelbuilder. Quotes come from the skill's SKILL.md at commit 2de1134, the head of main on 21 November 2026.

Short answer: ui-ux-pro-max is most useful when you let it write a design system to disk once and make every later screen read from it. Three flags control that: --persist writes design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md, --output-dir decides where it lands, and --force is the only way to overwrite it. Get those right and the agent stops inventing a new palette on every page.

On 21 November 2026 Skillselion's catalog API recorded 463,481 installs for the ui-ux-pro-max skill listing (skills.sh registry data), and the nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill repo had 152,242 GitHub stars, MIT licensed.

What does ui-ux-pro-max actually do?

It gives Claude Code a local design database to query. The SKILL.md lists what is searchable:

Searchable local UI/UX guidance: 80 searchable styles (51 active), 194 product palettes and exact reasoning profiles, 74 font pairings, 130 UX guidelines, 105 curated icons, 17 GSAP presets, 25 chart types, and 22 technology stacks.

Source: nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, .claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/SKILL.md

The agent answers by running a bundled script, scripts/search.py, against that data. That is also why it is worth reading the script before you install the skill in a work repo: it is code that runs on your machine.

How do you install it in Claude Code?

The README offers two routes. As a Claude Code plugin:

/plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill
/plugin install ui-ux-pro-max@ui-ux-pro-max-skill

Or with the CLI, run from your project folder:

npm install -g ui-ux-pro-max-cli
uipro init --ai claude

The same CLI takes other agent names (cursor, codex, copilot, gemini and more), or --ai all for every supported agent at once.

How do you save a design system with --persist?

Ask for a design system once, with --persist and an explicit output folder. The skill's own example:

python "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/.claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/scripts/search.py" "<query>" --design-system --persist -p "Project Name" --output-dir "<project-root>"

That writes design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md, which the SKILL.md calls the "Global Source of Truth". Add --page "dashboard" and you also get pages/dashboard.md as a per-page override. Add --tokens dtcg to the same --persist command and it also writes tokens.json next to the master file.

Commit that folder. From then on, the useful instruction to the agent is "read MASTER.md first", not "make it look nice".

Why does --output-dir matter?

Because without it the files go wherever the script happened to run. The SKILL.md says to "always pass --output-dir pointed at the project root". If you skip it, you end up with a MASTER.md somewhere outside the repo, no one commits it, and the next session starts from nothing.

When should you use --force?

Almost never, and only on purpose. This is the rule from the SKILL.md:

If design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md already exists, --persist skips writing and leaves it untouched unless you also pass --force

Source: nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, .claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/SKILL.md

The skip is the safety net. Your MASTER.md may hold decisions a teammate made by hand. The skill tells the agent to read the existing file before deciding whether --force is justified, and never to use it without the user's explicit OK. If you see --force in a command your agent proposes, read the current MASTER.md before you say yes.

Which ui-ux-pro-max should you install?

The nextlevelbuilder original. The repo is a bundle of seven skills (ui-ux-pro-max plus design-system, design, ui-styling, brand, banner-design and slides), and our catalog also lists other repos that carry a skill with the same name. The biggest of those on 21 November, inside nexu-io/open-design, had 5,636 installs against the original's 463,481. title: Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built
description:
Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built

Every designer has done it: you open a blank page, type a headline, and then freeze, because the words aren't written yet. So you paste in some lorem ipsum, the layout suddenly makes sense, and you can finally see what you're building.

That is exactly what placeholder text is for. It is not a shortcut or a sign of laziness. It is a tool that lets you judge a design on its own merits — typography, spacing, hierarchy, rhythm — before a single real sentence exists.

Why meaningless text makes better designs

Real copy is distracting. The moment a reviewer can read the words, they start editing the words. "Should this say 'customers' instead of 'clients'?" — and suddenly nobody is looking at the layout anymore.

Lorem ipsum solves this because it means nothing. The eye treats it as texture, not language, so attention stays where it belongs: on how the page holds together. Printers have used it since the 1500s for exactly this reason, and web designers inherited the habit because it still works.

How to use placeholder text properly

A block of dummy text is only useful if you use it the way a real page will be used. Here is the workflow I follow:

1. Match the amount to the real content. If the final article will be 800 words, don't test the template with two short paragraphs. Generate the same volume the real page will carry, so you see the true shape of the layout — where it gets long, where it breathes, where it breaks.

2. Test the extremes. Generate a very short version (a few words) and a very long one (many paragraphs) and drop both into the same template. Headlines wrap, cards stretch, buttons move. A layout that survives both extremes will survive real content.

3. Check every breakpoint. Placeholder text behaves differently at mobile width than on desktop. Paste the same block in, resize the browser, and watch for awkward orphans, cramped line lengths, and columns that collapse badly.

4. Vary the lengths. Real pages mix short intros, long bodies, and tiny captions. If every test block is the same size, you are testing one layout, not the design system.

A free generator that does the job in seconds

You don't need a plugin or a paid tool for this. FakeXLab's Lorem Ipsum Generator is free, needs no sign-up, and runs entirely in your browser. You choose paragraphs, sentences, or words, set the amount, click Generate, and copy the text straight into your mockup.

Because it generates by word and sentence count as well as paragraphs, you can build exactly the shape you need — a one-line button label, a three-sentence card description, or a full article's worth of body text for a long-form template.

Build a complete mockup, not just a text block

Placeholder text works best as part of a full fake page. Once the body copy is in place, fill the rest of the design with equally fictional data so the whole mockup feels real without exposing anyone's real information:

  • Add a byline with the Random Name Generator so author cards and profile blocks look finished.
  • Fill out sample forms and checkout screens with the Fake Address Generator — a complete fictional profile, address included, in one click.
  • Protect any test accounts you create along the way with a strong password from the Password Generator.

Everything on FakeXLab is fictional and for testing only, and nothing you generate is stored or sent anywhere — it all happens in your browser.

The mistakes to avoid

Placeholder text is a design tool, not content. Three mistakes turn it into a problem:

  • Shipping it live. Lorem ipsum on a published page looks unfinished and hurts trust. Replace every block with real copy before launch — run a quick search for "lorem" across the site as a final check.
  • Testing with one perfect block. If your test text is always the same length, your layout only works at that length. Real content is messy; test messy.
  • Using real copy too early. Drafting final words before the layout is settled means rewriting both when the design changes. Get the shape right first, then write into it.

The takeaway

Good layouts are built before the words arrive. Lorem ipsum lets you see the design clearly, test it honestly, and hand it over with confidence — and a free generator like FakeXLab's makes the whole thing take seconds instead of an afternoon of copy-pasting.

Next time you start a mockup, generate the text first, build around it, and let the design speak before the content does.

title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
description:
arXiv:2611.33594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

title: Tokenisation is not in APX
description:
arXiv:2611.34938v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
description:
arXiv:2611.34188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
description:
arXiv:2611.34725v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.

title: Sales CRM UI kits for Figma + React (2026)
description:
A sales CRM is mostly tables, pipelines and sequences, so starting from a kit saves weeks. These are the Figma + React options I'd compare. I run mebius.design, which sells one of them, and the others were checked on their own sites.

For a sales CRM dashboard in Figma and React, mebius.design sells Arcline: 161 Figma screens for prospect search, lead scoring and outreach sequences, plus 104 React components and 54 blocks in shadcn registry format, for $19 once. Other options: Creative Market’s Venture, Shadcn Studio’s NexaCRM and the free Atomic CRM.

What should a CRM dashboard UI kit include?

The screens a sales team opens every day.

A sales CRM dashboard UI kit should cover the work from finding a lead to closing a deal. Whether you compare CRM kits on mebius.design or elsewhere, look for:

  • People and companies: a searchable list and profiles with activity.
  • Lists, enrichment and lead scoring, so reps know whom to contact first.
  • A pipeline: deals or prospects by stage.
  • Outreach: email sequences, an inbox for replies, tasks and a calendar.
  • Analytics: pipeline, win rate and reply rates.
  • Settings: team roles, a CRM sync, CSV import and billing.

Then check Figma variables, light and dark themes, React code that matches the file, and a license that covers client work.

Which sales CRM UI kits does mebius.design sell?

One kit, Arcline, with Figma screens and React code.

As of 19 Nov 2026, mebius.design sells one sales CRM UI kit: Arcline, an AI prospecting and CRM dashboard by Keitoto Studio. Arcline is one of 11 dashboard UI kits on mebius.design and one of the 7 that come with React code.

Sales CRM UI kits on mebius.design at a glance

  • Kit: Arcline: AI prospecting and CRM dashboard
  • Screens: 161 Figma screens, desktop and mobile
  • Components: 104 React components
  • Blocks: 54 React blocks
  • Code stack: React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format
  • Install: shadcn CLI, or the mebius MCP in Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code
  • Theme: Light, built on color variables
  • License: Single license, client work included. The Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale.
  • Price: $19 once, or $259 for all items. No subscription.
  • Checked: Facts as of 19 Nov 2026

What screens does the Arcline CRM kit have in Figma?

161 screens, desktop and mobile, in a light theme.

Arcline’s Figma file on mebius.design has 161 screens, and every desktop screen has a mobile layout. The Arcline gallery groups them like this:

  • Sign up and onboarding: sign-in, sign-up and a setup flow for a new workspace.
  • Dashboard and analytics: the home screen and outreach analytics.
  • AI prospecting: search in plain words, a query builder and the results.
  • Prospects and companies: profiles with buying signals.
  • Lists, enrichment and lead scoring.
  • Outreach and tasks: sequences with an AI email writer, and tasks.
  • Integrations and settings.

The Arcline file is built on variables and auto layout, so one color change updates every screen. Its fonts, Geist and Geist Mono, are free on Google Fonts.

Which React components and blocks come with Arcline?

104 components and 54 blocks, as of 19 Nov 2026.

Arcline’s code on mebius.design has 104 components and 54 blocks in React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format. The components include fields, selects, date pickers, dialogs, avatars, a score meter, a sortable data table, a filter toolbar and charts.

The Arcline blocks a sales CRM uses most:

  • arcline-metrics-dashboard: the prospecting home, with KPIs, AI-recommended prospects and recent activity.
  • arcline-search-results: AI search results with criteria chips, People and Companies tabs and a bulk-selection bar.
  • arcline-kanban-board: a pipeline board from New through Contacted, Replied and Meeting booked to Won, with cards that drag between stages.
  • arcline-inbox-triage: the outreach inbox, with an AI summary of new replies and tabs such as Needs reply and Interested.
  • arcline-ai-composer and arcline-ai-answer: an AI email prompt card, and a prospect’s AI profile with a suggested opener.
  • arcline-revenue-explorer and arcline-kpi-drilldown: pipeline, win rate and deal size; emails sent, open rate, replies and meetings.
  • arcline-integrations and arcline-file-upload: a Salesforce-style sync page with field mapping, and a CSV import with column mapping.
  • arcline-team-directory, arcline-roles-and-permissions, arcline-week-calendar and arcline-login-and-sign-up for the rest of the app.

Most Arcline blocks are desktop pages, 1152 or 1440 pixels wide, with the Figma sample data. Pass your own data where a block takes props, as the pipeline board does, or edit the installed files.

Is Arcline a full CRM or a sales prospecting kit?

Arcline on mebius.design is a sales CRM front end built around the top of the funnel: finding prospects, scoring them and reaching out. Its code adds a pipeline board, revenue analytics and a CRM sync page for the deal stages after the first reply.

  • Arcline is light only, in Figma and in code. Colors are variables, so you can add a dark theme yourself.
  • Arcline is UI only: the data, auth, email sending and CRM sync are yours to build.
  • For a CRM built around accounts, quotes or contracts, check the Arcline gallery for the screens you need first.

What other CRM dashboard UI kits are there?

Checked on each product’s own page on 19 Nov 2026.

Outside mebius.design, three CRM options cover the same need in different ways. Each name links to the page its facts come from.

  • Venture CRM Platform UI Kit (Creative Market, by dhuhacreative). A Figma kit for a CRM dashboard and its landing page, listing 70+ dashboard and website pages and 100+ components. It costs $45 Personal, $120 Commercial or $220 Extended Commercial, the license the page points apps to. Its strength is one design file for the product and its marketing site. The page doesn’t say React code is included.
  • NexaCRM (Shadcn Studio). A coded CRM admin template in Next.js 16, shadcn/ui, Tailwind CSS v4 and TypeScript: CRM, sales and leads dashboards, people, companies and opportunities, tasks and workflows, kanban and calendar views, and light, dark and system modes. Its page shows $79 and says NexaCRM is part of the All Access Pro plan, paid once, which covers client projects. Its strength is a deal-centered CRM in code; the page says no Figma file is provided.
  • Atomic CRM (Marmelab). A free, MIT-licensed CRM app built with React, shadcn/ui and Supabase: contacts, deals on a Kanban board, tasks, notes, email capture by CC, and import and export. Its strength is a working backend you can fork. It is an app to customize rather than a design kit, and the repo mentions no Figma file.

For more Figma styles, multi-author marketplaces are the next stop: UI8 listed 6,428 UI kits when we checked on 17 Nov 2026. The mebius vs UI8 comparison sets UI8’s prices and license next to mebius.design’s.

Which CRM dashboard UI kit should you pick?

  • A prospecting or sales engagement product, designed in Figma and built in React + shadcn with code that matches the file: Arcline on mebius.design.
  • A Figma-only CRM design with a landing page, bought once: Venture on Creative Market.
  • A deal-centered CRM in Next.js code with a dark mode, no Figma file needed: NexaCRM.
  • A free, working CRM with a Supabase backend to fork: Atomic CRM.

To try the mebius.design style first, the Sales Performance Chart and the Total Sales Chart are among 62 free charts in React + Tailwind, free with a mebius account.

How do you install Arcline’s React code?

The shadcn CLI or the mebius MCP, after you buy Arcline on mebius.design.

After you buy Arcline on mebius.design, create an access token in Settings › Tokens and add the @mebius registry to your project once:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Install the Arcline theme on its own first, then the blocks you need with --overwrite, so shared parts take Arcline’s version:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-metrics-dashboard @mebius/arcline-kanban-board --overwrite

Then render the pipeline board with your own stages and cards:

components/pipeline.tsx:

import { KanbanBoard, type KanbanColumnData } from "@/components/kanban-board"

const columns: KanbanColumnData[] = [
  {
    id: "new",
    title: "New",
    count: 1,
    dropLabel: "Drop to move back to New",
    cards: [{ id: "dimas", initials: "DP", name: "Dimas Pratama", company: "Kopi Kilat", score: 81, level: 8, next: "Research before outreach" }],
  },
  { id: "meeting", title: "Meeting booked", count: 0, dropLabel: "Drop to book meeting", cards: [] },
]

export function Pipeline() {
  return <KanbanBoard columns={columns} />
}

In Claude Code, Cursor or VS Code, the mebius MCP server does the same: add it, sign in, and ask for an Arcline block (setup per editor).

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

For the Arcline Figma file, download the .zip from My Library, extract it and import Arcline.fig into Figma.

FAQ

How much does Arcline cost?

Arcline costs $19 on mebius.design, paid once, with updates included, or $259 once for every item. There is no subscription.

Can I use Arcline in client projects?

Yes. Every mebius.design purchase covers client work for one person. Handing the Figma files themselves to a client, white-label products and resale need the Agency license, quoted on the Pricing page.

Does Arcline include React code?

Yes. Arcline comes with 104 components and 54 blocks in React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format, built to match the Figma file. They install with the shadcn CLI or the mebius MCP.

Does Arcline have a dark mode?

No. Arcline is a light theme in Figma and in code, built on color variables. For CRM code with a dark mode, NexaCRM lists light, dark and system modes (checked on 19 Nov 2026).

Can I build a CRM MVP with Arcline?

Yes, for the UI. Arcline gives you the Figma screens and the React front end. The backend, auth, email sending and payments stay yours to build. The best UI kits for an MVP guide compares kits for other kinds of MVP.

Is there a free CRM dashboard UI kit?

Atomic CRM is free and MIT-licensed, as an app rather than a Figma kit. On mebius.design, Arcline is paid, but 62 charts and 128 forms are free with an account.

title: Scraper input from strangers: country names, 01.08.2026, and why I stopped throwing
description:
When you run your own scraper you type the input the way your code expects it. When strangers run it from a public listing, they type Germany into a field you documented as an ISO country code, 01.08.2026 into a date field, and "50 ads" into a number field. On the Apify Store a failed run also counts against your public success rate, which the Store uses for ranking. So I moved most input handling into one small module whose rule is: understand what the user meant, log a warning, and keep going.

Below is what's in it and the run that made me write it.

The run that started it

My LinkedIn Ad Library actor took a start date and a country. A user sent 01.08.2026 as the date. I passed it straight to LinkedIn, LinkedIn answered with HTTP 500, and the run failed. While fixing that I found a second problem in the same code: I sent the country as countryCode=DE, which LinkedIn silently ignores. The parameter it actually reads is countries=DE. For one advertiser that was the difference between 629 ads (Germany) and 9,530 (everywhere). Nobody had complained, because a list of ads from all countries looks like a valid result.

Dates

The parser takes YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY/MM/DD, DD.MM.YYYY, slash dates, Unix timestamps and anything Date.parse understands, and returns YYYY-MM-DD or null:

let m = str.match(/^(\d{4})[-/.](\d{1,2})[-/.](\d{1,2})/);
let out = m ? iso(m[1], m[2], m[3]) : null;
// DD.MM.YYYY is always European order
if (!out && (m = str.match(/^(\d{1,2})\.(\d{1,2})\.(\d{4})$/))) out = iso(m[3], m[2], m[1]);

iso() builds the string and checks it round-trips through Date, so 31.02.2026 comes back as null instead of March 3rd.

Slash dates are the hard part. 31/12/2026 can only be day first, 12/31/2026 can only be month first, and a part above 12 decides. 08/01/2026 could be either. My first version read those as day first, quietly, which changed the result for every US user who had been sending that format. The current version keeps the US reading for ambiguous dates and says so in the log:

Ambiguous startDate "08/01/2026" - reading it as MM/DD/YYYY (2026-08-01). Use YYYY-MM-DD to be sure.

Something that can't be parsed at all logs a warning and the filter is dropped. The run continues without it.

Countries

Hardcoding a country list felt wrong, and it turns out Node already has one. Intl.DisplayNames gives the English name for every region code, so I build a name-to-code map at startup:

const names = new Intl.DisplayNames(['en'], { type: 'region' });
for (let a = 65; a <= 90; a++) for (let b = 65; b <= 90; b++) {
    const code = String.fromCharCode(a, b);
    const name = names.of(code);
    if (!name || name === code || name === 'Unknown Region' || RETIRED.has(code)) continue;
    map[name.toLowerCase()] = code;
}

Two things to watch: ICU also names retired codes (UK, SU, YU and others), so those get skipped, and a few common inputs need aliases on top (uk, usa, deutschland, españa, türkiye, holland). Values like worldwide, all or any mean no filter. Anything unknown is a warning and no filter, not an exception.

Numbers and lists

Numbers come in as 50, "50", "1,000" or "50 ads". Strip spaces, commas and underscores, take the leading number, fall back to the default with a warning if there isn't one.

Lists come in as arrays, newline-separated strings, semicolon-separated strings, or arrays of { url } objects from the Apify request-list editor. One function flattens all of that into unique trimmed strings. It also accepts a few field names that aren't in the schema (someone sends urls instead of startUrls) and logs which one it used.

Where I do fail

Being tolerant inside the run doesn't mean starting runs that can't work. Two places where failing is still the right answer:

Empty input, before the run exists. The platform validates input against the schema before it starts anything. A required field with a prefill and minItems: 1 but no default makes an empty start return HTTP 400, and no run is created. If you add "default": [] next to required, that check never fires, the container starts, and you get a failed run in your stats. The prefill is what people see in the form, so they can still click Start and get a working run.

Nothing usable after parsing. If every entry was invalid, the run exits with code 1 and a status message that says what was wrong. On Apify that message is the only thing the user sees, and I don't see their run at all. In SDK 3.7.2, Actor.exit({ exitCode: 1, statusMessage }) sends the message and exits about 1 ms later without waiting, and on roughly 1 in 5 of my failed runs the message never arrived. Setting it first fixes that:

export async function fail(msg) {
    await Actor.setStatusMessage(msg, { isStatusMessageTerminal: true, level: 'ERROR' }).catch(() => {});
    await Actor.exit({ exitCode: 1, statusMessage: msg });
}

The whole module is about 400 lines and the only dependency is apify. Most of it is the parsing above. It's shared by every actor I publish, so a fix lands everywhere with one deploy.

The LinkedIn actor from the story above is here if you want to throw odd input at it: https://apify.com/pulsedata/linkedin-ad-library-scraper

title: Frontend Performance Is an Architectural Decision
description:
A page can have memoized components, compressed images, and a good bundle report—and still feel slow.

Sometimes the delay was decided before any of those optimizations: the application waits for JavaScript before requesting essential data, unrelated features ship together, or one global update causes too much work.

Performance is partly a matter of implementation. Architecture determines how much work the implementation has to do and when that work can begin.

Draw the critical path

Consider a product page that loads like this:

  1. Fetch the HTML shell.
  2. Download and execute the application JavaScript.
  3. Fetch the product.
  4. Read the product's category and fetch recommendations.
  5. Render the complete page.

Some dependencies are real. Recommendations may need information from the product. But the customer may not need recommendations before seeing the product title, image, and purchase controls.

That distinction changes the architecture. Essential content can render independently. Secondary work can happen later. Data available earlier in the request lifecycle can sometimes be fetched before browser execution begins.

The important exercise is identifying what must happen sequentially, what can happen concurrently, and what should not block the primary task.

Moving code into a smaller component will not remove a data waterfall on its own.

Rendering strategy changes where the work happens

Client rendering, server rendering, static generation, and streaming distribute work differently.

A mostly static article and a highly interactive trading interface have different requirements. Applying the same strategy to both can create avoidable work or unnecessary infrastructure.

Server rendering can deliver useful HTML before client code runs, but it also introduces server work and may still require substantial hydration. Static output can avoid request-time rendering for suitable content, but freshness needs a plan. Streaming can expose ready content earlier when the framework and application support it, but loading states must remain usable.

Choose based on content freshness, personalization, interaction needs, and measured user experience. The label of the rendering strategy is not a performance result.

Data ownership determines request behavior

If every widget independently fetches the same account record, the page may duplicate requests. If a root loader fetches everything, it may delay the entire route for data needed only by a hidden panel.

Neither extreme is universally right.

Put request coordination at the narrowest level that understands the shared need. Deduplicate equivalent requests where appropriate. Keep essential and optional data distinguishable. Define cache freshness around how the product uses the data.

Caching is a correctness decision as well as a speed decision. A stale avatar and a stale stock availability indicator have different consequences.

Avoid treating one global cache duration as a complete policy.

Dependencies are a recurring budget

A dependency adds more than downloaded bytes. Depending on how it is delivered and used, it can add parsing, execution, initialization, and maintenance work.

A charting library might be justified on an analytics route and unnecessary on the sign-in page. A route boundary gives you a place to defer it. A shared module imported everywhere can accidentally pull it into a broader loading path.

Define budgets for meaningful entry points, then inspect the generated output. Source-level imports do not always tell you exactly what users download.

Treat a budget as a review trigger. If a dependency exceeds it, assess the user benefit and alternatives rather than mechanically rejecting useful functionality.

State boundaries affect interaction cost

A keystroke should not require the application to reconsider unrelated screens.

Broad subscriptions, expensive derived work, and large synchronous updates can make interaction slow even after the page has loaded.

Keep rapidly changing state close to its consumers. Subscribe to the values a view needs. Profile actual interactions before adding memoization: caching a calculation does little if network delay or layout work dominates the experience.

Architecture creates opportunities for local work. Profiling confirms whether the implementation uses them.

Make performance part of ownership

Assign responsibility for the whole user journey as well as individual features.

Track loading, responsiveness, and visual stability in representative conditions. Use controlled checks to catch regressions and production measurements to understand the range of real experiences. Segment results when device or network differences hide important failures.

When a regression appears, connect it to a decision: a new dependency, a request dependency, a rendering change, or a wider update boundary.

Performance work becomes more effective when teams can change those decisions. The strongest optimization is often arranging the system so that unnecessary work never enters the user's critical path.

title: Honest but Wrong: Formalizing Retraction in the Ethics of Speech Acts
description:
arXiv:2611.34011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A speaker who asserts honestly may later discover that its assertion was false. Such erroneous truths are not lies, yet they raise the question of whether, and on which moral grounds, the speaker must retract them. Using the FIPA-ACL performative disconfirm, we extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism to the case of retraction. We prove that the honesty duty of deontologism, which bears on utterances when they are made, never requires retracting an erroneous truth, and add a persistent one, which forbids letting the addressee believe what the speaker no longer believes. On a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, we show that deontologism and consequentialism both require the retraction, but that consequentialism no longer does once it comes too late to prevent harm.

title: The Check That Catches the Loop Misses the Fixation
description:
Six times. A small triage helper I run on my laptop listed the same five GitHub issues six times in a row, burned 10,063 tokens doing it, and never answered the question. The right answer was issue 397, an enhancement. The helper never got there. It just kept asking for the same list, getting the same list, and asking again.

That job sat in my saved run logs for a week before Dr Srinivas Padmanabhuni left a note on my last piece. His shopping helper had done the same shape of thing, worse: it called the same search URL more than ten times and came back with an empty answer. His suggestion was a check from agentest, an open-source checklist of 165 tests for agent traces. Test T5-009 flags the same tool called with the same arguments more than three times in a row. Simple idea. I pointed it at my own logs to see what it would have caught: 41 saved trace files, 429 jobs, 1,074 tool calls, 1,255,700 prompt tokens counted turn by turn.

Here is what came back, and why I am not sure the storm is the thing to guard.

1. The check works. It caught the loop, and fifty others.

T5-009 failed 13 of the 41 files. The six-turn loop tripped it three times over. Across the whole set, 51 of the 429 jobs contain a run of four or more identical calls, 129 such windows in total. Cutting every storm off at the fourth identical call would have saved 103,452 prompt tokens, about 8% of everything the jobs spent. On the six-turn job alone, stopping at the fourth call saves 4,087 of its 10,063 tokens. So the check does what it says on the tin, and the loop that started this whole thing would have been stopped cold at turn four.

2. The storm is the small bill. The second call is the big one.

Here is the number that changed my mind about what to guard. Counting every repeat, not just runs of four: 96 of the 429 jobs repeat an identical call at least once. 276 repeat calls in total. The turns carrying them cost 341,116 prompt tokens, 27% of the whole set. And the most common repeat in the entire corpus is not a storm at all. It is the second call. The helper lists the issues, lists them again, and only then starts working. Two identical calls, then it moves on. T5-009 waves that straight through, because its bar is four.

So the check catches the dramatic failure and misses the ordinary one. 45 jobs repeat a call without ever reaching four in a row, worth 43,327 tokens the check never sees. If I cut at the first repeat instead of the fourth, the saving jumps from 103,452 to 341,116 tokens. But that cut would also kill the double list most triage jobs open with, and I have no evidence that double list is waste. It might be the helper double-checking before it commits. The honest saving is the storm tail, 8%. The 27% is the number I cannot claim without first knowing which second calls are habit and which are doubt.

3. The check is blind to the failure that actually cost us answers.

The six-turn loop is dramatic, but it is not the expensive failure in these logs. That one is the crash report. Issue 412, a crash on launch, is the loudest issue in the set, and the helper answered 412 with the label "bug" on 101 jobs across the triage traces, including jobs where the right answer was a different issue entirely. Five failed jobs in the first full run alone ended on 412. An answer is not a tool call, so no tool-call check can flag it. T5-009 would have passed those jobs as clean while the helper gave the same wrong answer again and again. A check that watches calls will never catch a helper that is stuck on an answer.

4. Shorter results storm less, and the storming jobs solve worse.

The pattern across the arms is hard to ignore. The trimmed arm, which sees five short fields per issue instead of the full dump, never stormed once in 52 jobs. The full arm stormed 3 times in 50. In a later experiment, the diary arm never stormed in 36 jobs and solved 18 of 24. The sender arm stormed on 24 of 36 jobs and solved 2 of 24. That is a correlation across arms, not proof of cause, and I will not dress it up as more. But it points the same way twice: the jobs that loop are the jobs that fail, and the shapes that keep the result short are the shapes that do not loop.

So where does that leave the check? I am keeping it. A test that catches 51 storms in 429 jobs for free is worth running, and the six-turn loop is exactly the failure it was built for. But I am not going to pretend it covers the problem. It guards the fourth repeat and misses the second, and it watches calls while the real fixation lives in answers. The next check I want is the one I do not have yet: something that flags the same answer given twice for different questions, the way T5-009 flags the same call made twice for the same question.

What does the loop look like on your side? Do you cut at the second repeat or the fourth, and has anyone here caught a helper stuck on an answer rather than a call? I would rather steal a check that already works than build another one that watches the wrong thing.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.34505v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
description:
arXiv:2611.33813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

title: 8 Next.js 16 and TypeScript 5 Questions That Filter Senior Engineers
description:
Most frontend interviews still ask candidates to explain useEffect dependency arrays or recite the difference between interface and type. Those questions measure familiarity, not architectural judgment under production constraints.

In Next.js 16 and TypeScript 5 codebases, senior engineers separate themselves on three fronts: request boundary isolation with the new caching model, resilient React 19 mutation pipelines, and type system design that eliminates invalid states at compile time.

If you want to test yourself on these patterns right away:

  • Try the free 8-card interactive browser quiz (zero signup)
  • Download the full 30+ Senior Flashcards PDF + Interactive Browser Quiz ($1 USD launch price)

Here are the core patterns and questions that quickly reveal whether an engineer has shipped real Next.js 16 and TypeScript 5 systems.

1. Async Request APIs and "use cache" Boundaries

In Next.js 15 and 16, dynamic request APIs such as cookies(), headers(), params, and searchParams are asynchronous. Calling them inside a cached scope is a common source of build failures and accidental dynamic opt-outs.

Question: How do you cache expensive downstream queries when the parent layout reads cookies()?

A junior approach calls cookies() directly inside the data helper, which prevents static or shared caching. A senior engineer extracts the session key at the dynamic boundary and passes primitive arguments into a "use cache" function tagged for targeted invalidation.

import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

async function getTenantMetrics(tenantId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag(`tenant:${tenantId}:metrics`);

  const res = await fetch(`https://api.internal.example/metrics/${tenantId}`);
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Metrics request failed with status ${res.status}`);
  }
  return res.json() as Promise<{ mrr: number; activeSeats: number }>;
}

export default async function DashboardHeader() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const tenantId = cookieStore.get('tenant_id')?.value ?? 'public';

  // Only the primitive tenantId crosses into the cached function
  const metrics = await getTenantMetrics(tenantId);

  return (
    <section>
      <p>Active seats: {metrics.activeSeats}</p>
      <p>Monthly recurring revenue: ${metrics.mrr}</p>
    </section>
  );
}

Follow-up check: ask why passing the full cookieStore object into a "use cache" boundary fails serialization and cache key generation, and when revalidateTag beats revalidatePath. revalidateTag(tenant:${id}:metrics) invalidates every route sharing that data slice without purging unrelated layouts.

2. React 19 useActionState, useOptimistic, and Zod Validation

Form handling in modern Next.js combines Server Actions, schema validation at the trust boundary, and optimistic UI updates that automatically reconcile if the server rejects the mutation.

Question: How do you prevent stale optimistic state and unvalidated payloads in a Server Action?

Never trust client input types at runtime. Parse FormData with Zod inside the Server Action, return a typed discriminated result, and bind useOptimistic inside the active transition.

// app/actions/billing.ts
'use server';

import { z } from 'zod';
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

const SeatUpdateSchema = z.object({
  tenantId: z.string().min(1),
  seats: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(500),
});

export type ActionResult =
  | { ok: true; seats: number }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

export async function updateSeatsAction(
  _prevState: ActionResult,
  formData: FormData
): Promise<ActionResult> {
  const parsed = SeatUpdateSchema.safeParse({
    tenantId: formData.get('tenantId'),
    seats: formData.get('seats'),
  });

  if (!parsed.success) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: parsed.error.issues[0]?.message ?? 'Invalid seat count',
    };
  }

  // Persist update here, then bust only the affected cache tag
  revalidateTag(`tenant:${parsed.data.tenantId}:metrics`);
  return { ok: true, seats: parsed.data.seats };
}

Now wire the client component with useActionState and useOptimistic:

'use client';

import { useActionState, useOptimistic } from 'react';
import { updateSeatsAction, type ActionResult } from '@/app/actions/billing';

export function SeatEditor({
  tenantId,
  initialSeats,
}: {
  tenantId: string;
  initialSeats: number;
}) {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState<ActionResult, FormData>(
    updateSeatsAction,
    { ok: true, seats: initialSeats }
  );

  const committedSeats = state.ok ? state.seats : initialSeats;
  const [optimisticSeats, setOptimisticSeats] = useOptimistic(
    committedSeats,
    (_current, nextSeats: number) => nextSeats
  );

  function handleSubmit(formData: FormData) {
    const next = Number(formData.get('seats'));
    if (Number.isFinite(next)) {
      setOptimisticSeats(next);
    }
    formAction(formData);
  }

  return (
    <form action={handleSubmit}>
      <input type="hidden" name="tenantId" value={tenantId} />
      <p>Seats: {optimisticSeats}</p>
      <input type="number" name="seats" defaultValue={committedSeats} min={1} max={500} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Saving...' : 'Update seats'}
      </button>
      {!state.ok && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

Senior signal: the candidate knows useOptimistic automatically rolls back to committedSeats once the transition finishes if state.ok is false.

3. TypeScript 5 NoInfer<T>, satisfies, and never Exhaustiveness

Senior TypeScript questions go beyond syntax and focus on preventing inference leaks in generic helpers and catching missing union branches during refactors.

Question: Why does NoInfer<T> matter in reusable APIs, and how does satisfies compare to type annotations?

Consider a helper that picks a fallback value from a list of allowed states. Without NoInfer<T>, passing a typo as the second argument widens T instead of producing a compile error.

type RouteMode = 'static' | 'dynamic' | 'cached';

function resolveMode<T extends string>(
  allowed: readonly T[],
  fallback: NoInfer<T>
): T {
  return allowed.includes(fallback) ? fallback : allowed[0];
}

// Valid: 'cached' belongs to the inferred union from allowed
const mode = resolveMode(['static', 'cached'] as const, 'cached');

// Compile error: Argument of type '"broken"' is not assignable
// const bad = resolveMode(['static', 'cached'] as const, 'broken');

Pair that with satisfies and a never exhaustiveness helper for discriminated unions:

type AsyncState<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string };

const STATUS_LABELS = {
  idle: 'Ready',
  loading: 'Fetching',
  success: 'Loaded',
  error: 'Failed',
} satisfies Record<AsyncState<unknown>['status'], string>;

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled state: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

export function renderStatus(state: AsyncState<number>): string {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      return STATUS_LABELS.idle;
    case 'loading':
      return STATUS_LABELS.loading;
    case 'success':
      return `${STATUS_LABELS.success}: ${state.data}`;
    case 'error':
      return `${STATUS_LABELS.error}: ${state.message}`;
    default:
      return assertNever(state);
  }
}

Using satisfies preserves exact literal keys and string values on STATUS_LABELS while still checking completeness against the union. Adding a fifth status later immediately triggers a compile error inside default.

4. Parallel Promise.all and Streaming Suspense Boundaries

Another reliable senior differentiator is eliminating sequential server waterfalls.

import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function SummaryMetrics({ orgId }: { orgId: string }) {
  const [usage, billing] = await Promise.all([
    fetchUsage(orgId),
    fetchBilling(orgId),
  ]);
  return <div>{usage.calls} calls, plan: {billing.plan}</div>;
}

export default function OrgPage({ orgId }: { orgId: string }) {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Organization Overview</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading metrics...</p>}>
        <SummaryMetrics orgId={orgId} />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

Instead of awaiting fetchUsage before starting fetchBilling, both requests start concurrently while Suspense streams the shell immediately.

Practice These Patterns Interactive Style

title: SQL Challenge : What Happens When You Insert a Duplicate PRIMARY KEY?
description:
Imagine you are working on an employee management system.

The company stores employee details in a database. Every employee has an employee ID, name, department and salary.

Now, a developer tries to insert a new employee using an ID that already exists in the table.

Will SQL accept the new record, replace the existing employee or return an error?

Let's understand this with a practical SQL example.

  1. Create an Employees Table

First, create an "employees" table with a PRIMARY KEY on "employee_id".

CREATE TABLE employees (
employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
employee_name VARCHAR(100),
department VARCHAR(50),
salary DECIMAL(10,2)
);

Here, "employee_id" is the PRIMARY KEY.

It means every employee must have a unique ID.

  1. Insert Existing Employee Records

Let's insert three employee records.

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES
(101, 'Rahul', 'IT', 65000),
(102, 'Priya', 'HR', 55000),
(103, 'Amit', 'Finance', 60000);

Employees Table:

employee_id| employee_name| department| salary
101| Rahul| IT| 65000
102| Priya| HR| 55000
103| Amit| Finance| 60000

So far, everything is working correctly.

  1. Try to Insert a Duplicate Employee ID

Now, a developer tries to insert another employee with "employee_id = 101".

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES (101, 'Sneha', 'IT', 70000);

What will happen?

The INSERT statement will fail because employee ID 101 already exists as a PRIMARY KEY.

The database returns a primary key or unique constraint violation error. The exact error message depends on the database.

  1. What Will the Final Table Look Like?

The original records remain unchanged.

employee_id| employee_name| department| salary
101| Rahul| IT| 65000
102| Priya| HR| 55000
103| Amit| Finance| 60000

Sneha's record will not be inserted.

  1. Important Points About PRIMARY KEY

A PRIMARY KEY has two important rules:

  • It does not allow duplicate values.
  • It does not allow NULL values.

A PRIMARY KEY helps uniquely identify every record in a table.

For example, it is commonly used for:

  • Employee IDs
  • Customer IDs
  • Order IDs
  • Product IDs

These rules help maintain correct and reliable data in a database.

Your Turn: Test Your SQL Knowledge

Can a table have two PRIMARY KEY constraints?

A. Yes, every column can have a separate PRIMARY KEY.

B. No, a table can have only one PRIMARY KEY constraint, but it can contain multiple columns (a composite PRIMARY KEY).

C. Yes, but only when both columns have different data types.

D. No, a PRIMARY KEY can contain only one column.

Share your answer in the comments!

Learn More About SQL Constraints

If you want to learn more about SQL CREATE TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL and other database constraints, explore these practical SQL tutorials:

"Sankalan Data Tech – SQL DDL Commands and Database Constraints" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/ddl-manage-tables-relationships-sql-faq.html)
