title: Fitting a resume to the page automatically, without breaking it for ATS parsers
description:
This is a layout problem, not an AI problem. Every HTML-to-PDF generator eventually runs into it: the last page that holds only a couple of lines. I'll cover how we hit it, the options we weighed, why predicting page breaks is a dead end, and the trick we ended up using, which is to let the browser measure the layout instead of guessing it. If you generate PDFs from HTML, some of this should be directly reusable.

The situation

I'm the founder of CV by JD. We rewrite resumes for specific job descriptions, and when you're happy with the result, you download it as a PDF.

A resume PDF has two readers. One is a person, often a recruiter skimming a stack of applications. The other is an ATS (applicant tracking system), the software employers use to pull the text out of a resume and search it. A good PDF has to look finished to the first reader and stay easy to parse for the second.

How we got here

We render PDFs on our server with headless Chrome, a copy of the Chrome browser with no window, controlled by code (puppeteer-core with a serverless Chromium build). The PDF uses exactly the same HTML and CSS as the preview in the app, so what you see is what you download:

 In your browser                     On our server
 ───────────────                     ─────────────
 Resume preview      ── "Download" ─▶ The same HTML and CSS, opened in
 (HTML + CSS)                         headless Chrome and printed to PDF
                     ◀── resume.pdf ──

We offer five templates, each with its own fonts, spacing and margins.

The templates were designed for a "typical" resume. Real resumes aren't typical. Some are half a page, some are four pages, and they almost never end neatly at the bottom of a page.

The problem

My own resume was the test case. In one template it ran to four pages, and page four held two lines from the education section followed by white space all the way down.

Nothing was wrong with the content. It just looked unfinished, and that's the first impression a reader gets. The usual fix is manual: open the file in Word, use "Shrink One Page", nudge the margins, and export again. We wanted every export to fit its pages well, automatically, for every template, without ever looking cramped and without changing what an ATS reads.

What we researched

We started by looking at how existing tools handle this. Word's "Shrink One Page" reduces font sizes until the document loses a page. Some resume builders give you sliders for spacing, margins and font size, and leave it to you. Both approaches confirmed the same toolbox: vertical spacing, line height, margins and font size. Both also showed the risk. Shrink too far and the page looks crammed, and text at 8pt is hard to read.

Thinking through how to do this automatically, three constraints narrowed the design:

  1. Free knobs can combine badly. If spacing, line height, margins and font size can each move freely, some combinations fit the page but look wrong, like tiny text inside wide margins.
  2. Word counts don't predict page breaks. Headings that won't sit alone at the bottom of a page, list items that won't split and long URLs all move where a page ends. Two resumes with the same word count can end on different pages.
  3. Rendering real PDFs to search for a setting is slow. The first PDF render after a serverless function starts up takes a few seconds. Trying many settings for every download would keep users waiting.

The options we found

For what to adjust:

Option Problem
Shrink only the font, as Word does Gets small quickly, and does nothing for a page that's too empty
Search four independent knobs Finds strange combinations, and is hard to test or explain
One "fit level" that moves all four together, within limits Fewer possible outcomes, but every one of them looks designed

For how to decide:

Option Problem
Estimate from word count Wrong too often, because page breaks depend on layout
Render real PDFs at several settings and pick one Accurate, but takes many seconds per download
Have the browser lay the document out as pages and measure it, without printing Needs a clever setup, but it's accurate and fast

What we chose, and why

One number per document

Each document gets one fit level, a whole number from −8 to +8. Think of it as a single dial: negative values tighten the layout, positive values loosen it. Level 0 is the template exactly as designed. Each other level is a fixed mix of small changes:

  • vertical spacing, between 70% and 130% of the original
  • line height, within fixed bounds
  • side margins, between 0.35 and 0.58 inches
  • font size, never below 9.5pt for body text

The four settings change together in a fixed order, so none of them runs out of room before the others. When shrinking, spacing tightens first and font size changes last. When growing, margins widen last, because wider margins frame a short page well. If a template's text is already small, we never shrink it further.

We chose this because 17 levels is a small, testable set, and every level looks like a deliberate design rather than an accident.

Let the browser measure the pages

This is the part I'd most like other people to reuse.

Printing and CSS columns split content the same way. Content flows down a box of fixed height, and when the box is full it continues in the next one. In Chrome, both use the same layout engine. So if you put the resume in a hidden container whose columns are exactly the size of one printed page's content area, Chrome breaks it into "pages" for you, side by side on screen:

 ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
 │ page 1 │ │ page 2 │ │ page 3 │ │ page 4 │
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██     │  ◀ 4 columns = 4 pages,
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │        │    and the last one is
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │        │    only about 10% full
 └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘

The CSS is short:

/* simplified */
.measure {
  column-width: var(--page-content-width);
  height: var(--page-content-height); /* one page's content area */
  column-fill: auto;
}

Count the columns and you have the page count. Measure how far the content reaches down the last column and you know how full the last page is. This happens in an ordinary layout pass, with no PDF rendering. Most documents are settled by measuring level 0 alone. When they aren't, a small script inside the page applies each of the 17 levels' styles in turn, lets Chrome lay the document out again, and reads the page count and fill each time, which still takes a fraction of the time of a single PDF render.

One detail matters a lot here. Chrome rounds the printed page's content height up to a whole pixel. On US Letter paper with our margins, the content area works out to 979.2 CSS pixels tall, but Chrome prints it as 980. If you measure with 979.2, a nearly full page gets predicted as spilling onto the next one, and you pick the wrong level. Round up the same way and the predictions match.

A simple rule for choosing the level

With the page count and the fullness of the last page measured at level 0:

What we see What we do
One page Leave it alone
More than four pages Leave it alone. The content needs cutting, not squeezing
Last page 30% full or less Shrink just enough to remove that last page, picking the mildest level that does it. The new last page must stay under about 97% full, so it doesn't look crammed, and shrinking mustn't leave a big blank at the bottom of an earlier page because a block that can't be split, such as a job entry, got pushed onto the next page. If no level qualifies, leave it
Last page between 30% and 60% full Grow slightly so the pages fill more evenly, but only if it keeps the same page count and actually helps
Fuller than that Leave it alone

The thinking behind the thresholds: below 30%, the leftover content is small enough that a modest shrink usually absorbs it. Between 30% and 60%, losing the page would need too much squeezing, so evening out the pages looks better. We tuned these thresholds by rendering 150 test resumes of different lengths at every level as real PDFs and comparing the results.

For my resume, that turned four pages, the last one almost empty, into three pages with the last one nearly full.

Check the real output

In the user's browser, the preview runs the same measurement and picks a level, so what you see matches what you'll download. When you click Download, the server measures again in headless Chrome, prints the PDF, and then counts the pages in the actual file. If the count doesn't match the prediction, it prints again at level 0. We'd rather send the template as designed than a surprise.

Protect the second reader

Fitting must not change what an ATS extracts. Two rules guarantee that:

  1. A document at level 0 is byte-for-byte unchanged. At level 0 we don't add the fitting styles at all, so Chrome receives exactly the HTML it did before this feature existed.
  2. The extracted words never change. Our tests render every template at every level, extract the text with pdftotext, and check that the words match level 0 exactly.

That second test caught a real bug. One template used letter-spacing in em units on its uppercase section headings. At a larger font size the spacing grew enough that pdftotext read "SUMMARY" as "S U M M A R Y", seven one-letter words. An ATS could read it the same way, and a keyword search for "summary" would miss it. We now set heading letter-spacing in pixels.

What you can take from this

  • If the browser can lay it out, the browser can measure it. Multi-column layout makes a surprisingly good page simulator, and it's far faster than rendering PDFs.
  • One bounded setting beats several free ones. It's easier to test, easier to explain, and it can't produce strange combinations.
  • Match the browser's rounding, or your predictions will be off on exactly the pages that matter most: the nearly full ones.
  • Check the real output and keep a safe fallback for when the prediction is wrong.
  • If machines read your documents, test what they extract, not just what people see.

Have you used CSS layout as a measuring tool for something else? I'd like to know what else it's good for.

title: How to Scrape Twitter (X) with Go: Advanced Search Operators, Account Timelines, and a Cron Watcher (2026)
description:
"Twitter advanced search" gets about 18,100 US searches a month, and another 1,900 people a month search for how to "search twitter without account". Both groups want the same thing: type from:golang released min_faves:500 -filter:retweets and get a clean list of posts back, ideally in a script that can run every hour. In 2026 that is harder than it looks. The search page needs a login, the official API bills per post returned, and none of the logged-out tricks that used to work are left.

This post builds xsearch, a small Go tool (standard library only) that does it the other way around: it fetches candidate posts as JSON and then applies X's advanced-search operators locally, in about 800 lines of Go you can read and test. It has three commands:

  1. explain shows how a query is split between "what to fetch" and "what to filter"
  2. search prints matching posts as a table
  3. watch remembers what it has already reported and appends only new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron

Everything below ran on November 27, 2026 (04:10-04:45 UTC) with Go 1.27.3 on a Linux server.

Read this first: X's Terms of Service prohibit scraping. The X Terms of Service (effective October 9, 2026) say that "crawling or scraping the Services in any form, for any purpose without our prior written consent is expressly prohibited", and that you may not access or search the Services "by any means (automated or otherwise) other than through our currently available, published interfaces". The catch-all group in x.com/robots.txt is User-agent: * / Disallow: /. Review the terms and the legal risk for your use case and location before you run anything here. If the official X API covers your job, use it: recent search (last 7 days) and full-archive search are both there, billed pay-per-use (X's pricing page listed $0.005 per post read in November 2026). Keep volumes small, and don't republish other people's posts or build profiles of individuals. The tables below mask the handles of private persons.

Step 1: What a logged-out Go client gets

Before writing a parser, check what X sends to a plain HTTP client:

// probe: what X answers to a logged-out client in 2026. Go standard library only.
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        // Show redirects instead of following them.
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error { return http.ErrUseLastResponse },
    }
    urls := []string{
        "https://x.com/search?q=golang%20min_faves%3A100&f=live",
        "https://api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent?query=golang",
        "https://syndication.twitter.com/srv/timeline-profile/screen-name/golang",
        "https://x.com/robots.txt",
    }
    for _, u := range urls {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/131.0 Safari/537.36")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Printf("%s\n  error: %v\n", u, err)
            continue
        }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        fmt.Printf("%s\n  HTTP %d", u, resp.StatusCode)
        if loc := resp.Header.Get("Location"); loc != "" {
            fmt.Printf(" -> %.70s...", loc)
        }
        fmt.Println()
        if strings.HasSuffix(u, "robots.txt") {
            // Print the catch-all group: the rules for everyone who isn't a named crawler.
            sc := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(string(body)))
            inStar := false
            for sc.Scan() {
                line := strings.TrimSpace(sc.Text())
                if strings.HasPrefix(line, "User-agent:") {
                    inStar = line == "User-agent: *"
                }
                if inStar && line != "" && !strings.HasPrefix(line, "#") {
                    fmt.Println("  ", line)
                }
            }
        } else if len(body) > 0 {
            fmt.Printf("  %.100s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(body)), " "))
        }
    }
}

https://x.com/search?q=golang%20min_faves%3A100&f=live
  HTTP 307 -> /i/jf/onboarding/web?redirect_after_login=%2Fsearch%3Ff%3Dlive%26q%3Dg...
https://api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent?query=golang
  HTTP 401
  { "title": "Unauthorized", "type": "about:blank", "status": 401, "detail": "Unauthorized" }
https://syndication.twitter.com/srv/timeline-profile/screen-name/golang
  HTTP 429
  Rate limit exceeded
https://x.com/robots.txt
  HTTP 200
   User-agent: *
   Disallow: /
   Disallow: /i/u
   Crawl-delay: 1
   Sitemap: https://x.com/sitemap.xml
   Sitemap: https://x.com/sitemaps/finance0

Four doors, four answers:

  • x.com/search answers with a 307 to the login flow. The advanced-search form just builds a /search?q=... URL like this one, so it is behind the same wall.
  • api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent is the official API. Without a bearer token you get 401. With one you pay per post returned.
  • The old syndication timeline (what embedded profile timelines used) is rate-limited to death: 429 on the first request from this machine.
  • robots.txt lists rules for named search crawlers and then closes everything else with Disallow: /.

So "just scrape the search page" is out, and I'm not going to show login automation or cookie reuse. That is exactly what the terms forbid, and the accounts get locked anyway. What's left is to fetch posts from a data source and do the search part yourself.

Step 2: Where the candidate posts come from

The tool reads X through ScrapeAtlas*, using two endpoints:

  • /v1/twitter/user-tweets?handle=golang&trim=true returns an account's latest posts (14-20 per account in my runs) with views, likes, retweets, replies, quotes and the full legacy object. since and until narrow it down, but only inside that latest window: asking @golang for September 2026 returned zero posts with the warning latest_window_limited, even though the account posted in September. It costs 1 credit.
  • /v1/twitter/search/posts?query=... finds posts by keyword through a web index, not through X's own search. Results come back in relevance order, a handful per page, with a cursor like atlas:2 or serper:3 for the next page. It costs 2 credits per page. In my runs the cursor ran out after 3-4 pages, at roughly 10-20 unique posts per keyword. Operators are not supported there: from:golang since:2026-11-01 came back with zero posts.

That split decides the design. A from: query is answered precisely from timelines. Everything else is discovery: the web index proposes posts, the local filter decides. You will not get "every post that mentions X". You'll get a relevant sample that is filtered exactly.

Every response also has a coverage object (complete, order, warnings). The tool prints the warnings on every run, because "0 matches" means something different when the source says complete: false.

Step 3: A client with a disk cache

While you tune a query you run the same fetches over and over. Each response is cached on disk for 30 minutes, keyed by the full URL, so re-running a filter costs nothing. 429 and 5xx are retried with backoff (2s, 4s, 8s). Other errors stop the run instead of being silently skipped.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha1"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.scrapeatlas.com"

type Client struct {
    key      string
    http     *http.Client
    cacheDir string
    cacheTTL time.Duration
    Calls    int // paid requests actually sent (cache hits are free)
}

// envelope holds the fields every ScrapeAtlas twitter response shares.
type envelope struct {
    Success  bool            `json:"success"`
    Status   string          `json:"status"`
    Cursor   *string         `json:"cursor"`
    Posts    []rawTweet      `json:"posts"`  // /search/posts
    Tweets   []rawTweet      `json:"tweets"` // /user-tweets
    Error    json.RawMessage `json:"error"`
    Coverage struct {
        Source   string   `json:"source"`
        Order    string   `json:"order"`
        Complete bool     `json:"complete"`
        Warnings []string `json:"warnings"`
    } `json:"coverage"`
}

func NewClient() (*Client, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    }
    return &Client{key: key, http: &http.Client{Timeout: 60 * time.Second},
        cacheDir: "cache", cacheTTL: 30 * time.Minute}, nil
}

func (c *Client) Get(path string, params url.Values) (*envelope, error) {
    u := apiBase + path + "?" + params.Encode()
    sum := sha1.Sum([]byte(u))
    cacheFile := filepath.Join(c.cacheDir, hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8])+".json")
    if st, err := os.Stat(cacheFile); err == nil && time.Since(st.ModTime()) < c.cacheTTL {
        if b, err := os.ReadFile(cacheFile); err == nil {
            return decode(b)
        }
    }
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if attempt > 0 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second) // 2s, 4s, 8s
        }
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("x-api-key", c.key)
        resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        c.Calls++
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == 429 || resp.StatusCode >= 500 {
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d", path, resp.StatusCode)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != 200 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d: %.300s", path, resp.StatusCode, b)
        }
        env, err := decode(b)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", path, err)
        }
        os.MkdirAll(c.cacheDir, 0o755)
        os.WriteFile(cacheFile, b, 0o644)
        return env, nil
    }
    return nil, lastErr
}

func decode(b []byte) (*envelope, error) {
    var env envelope
    if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &env); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if !env.Success {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("success=false: %.300s", env.Error)
    }
    return &env, nil
}

Calls counts requests that actually went out, so the summary line can tell you what a run cost. A search page is 2 credits, so a 4-page search is 8 credits.

Step 4: Normalizing a tweet

Both endpoints return X's own GraphQL tweet shape. Some details matter for searching:

  • Retweets are shells. The retweet object has favorite_count: 0 and text cut at 140 characters (RT @resend: We rebuilt our email API to Go.\n\nIt took 7 weeks and 140 PRs, and we've been running in production for weeks at roughly half th…). The real text and media are in retweeted_status_result.
  • Long posts live in note_tweet. legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters. In the saved @golang timeline, 5 of 17 posts were longer than that. If you match keywords against full_text, a word in paragraph two never matches. And not every long post has a note: one of NASA's posts ended mid-sentence at 277 characters ("NASA stands ready to") with no note_tweet at all.
  • Text is HTML-escaped. > and & show up in full_text, so unescape before matching.
  • Timeline items have no author object with trim=true. The url field (https://x.com/NASA/status/...) still has the handle in its original case. 
package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "html"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// Tweet is the flat shape the filter and the reports work on.
type Tweet struct {
    ID        string    `json:"id"`
    Author    string    `json:"author"`
    Created   time.Time `json:"created"`
    Text      string    `json:"text"`
    Lang      string    `json:"lang"`
    Faves     int       `json:"faves"`
    Retweets  int       `json:"retweets"`
    Replies   int       `json:"replies"`
    Quotes    int       `json:"quotes"`
    Views     int       `json:"views"`
    ReplyTo   string    `json:"reply_to,omitempty"`
    IsRetweet bool      `json:"is_retweet,omitempty"`
    IsQuote   bool      `json:"is_quote,omitempty"`
    HasMedia  bool      `json:"has_media,omitempty"`
    URLs      []string  `json:"urls,omitempty"`
    URL       string    `json:"url"`
}

type rawUser struct {
    Result struct {
        Core struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"core"`
        Legacy struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"legacy"`
    } `json:"result"`
}

type rawLegacy struct {
    CreatedAt     string `json:"created_at"`
    FullText      string `json:"full_text"`
    Lang          string `json:"lang"`
    FavoriteCount int    `json:"favorite_count"`
    RetweetCount  int    `json:"retweet_count"`
    ReplyCount    int    `json:"reply_count"`
    QuoteCount    int    `json:"quote_count"`
    IsQuoteStatus bool   `json:"is_quote_status"`
    InReplyTo     string `json:"in_reply_to_screen_name"`
    Entities      struct {
        URLs []struct {
            ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
        } `json:"urls"`
    } `json:"entities"`
    ExtendedEntities struct {
        Media []json.RawMessage `json:"media"`
    } `json:"extended_entities"`
    RetweetedStatus *struct {
        Result rawTweet `json:"result"`
    } `json:"retweeted_status_result"`
}

type rawTweet struct {
    TypeName string    `json:"__typename"`
    Tweet    *rawTweet `json:"tweet"` // TweetWithVisibilityResults wraps the real tweet
    RestID   string    `json:"rest_id"`
    Core     struct {
        UserResults rawUser `json:"user_results"`
    } `json:"core"`
    Views struct {
        Count string `json:"count"`
    } `json:"views"`
    Legacy    rawLegacy `json:"legacy"`
    NoteTweet *struct { // posts longer than 280 characters
        Results struct {
            Result struct {
                Text      string `json:"text"`
                EntitySet struct {
                    URLs []struct {
                        ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
                    } `json:"urls"`
                } `json:"entity_set"`
            } `json:"result"`
        } `json:"note_tweet_results"`
    } `json:"note_tweet"`
    URL string `json:"url"`
}

// normalize turns one ScrapeAtlas tweet object into a Tweet. Timeline items
// (trim=true) carry no author object: read it from the post URL, else use
// the handle the caller asked for.
func normalize(r rawTweet, fallbackAuthor string) (Tweet, error) {
    if r.Tweet != nil {
        r = *r.Tweet
    }
    l := r.Legacy
    created, err := time.Parse(time.RubyDate, l.CreatedAt)
    if err != nil {
        return Tweet{}, err
    }
    author := r.Core.UserResults.Result.Core.ScreenName
    if author == "" {
        author = r.Core.UserResults.Result.Legacy.ScreenName
    }
    if author == "" && strings.HasPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/") {
        author, _, _ = strings.Cut(strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/"), "/")
    }
    if author == "" {
        author = fallbackAuthor
    }
    views, _ := strconv.Atoi(r.Views.Count)
    t := Tweet{
        ID: r.RestID, Author: author, Created: created.UTC(),
        Text: html.UnescapeString(l.FullText), Lang: l.Lang,
        Faves: l.FavoriteCount, Retweets: l.RetweetCount, Replies: l.ReplyCount,
        Quotes: l.QuoteCount, Views: views, ReplyTo: l.InReplyTo,
        IsQuote: l.IsQuoteStatus, HasMedia: len(l.ExtendedEntities.Media) > 0,
        URL: r.URL,
    }
    for _, u := range l.Entities.URLs {
        t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
    }
    if n := r.NoteTweet; n != nil && n.Results.Result.Text != "" {
        // legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters; the note has the whole post.
        t.Text = html.UnescapeString(n.Results.Result.Text)
        t.URLs = nil
        for _, u := range n.Results.Result.EntitySet.URLs {
            t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
        }
    }
    if rt := l.RetweetedStatus; rt != nil {
        // The retweet shell has favorite_count 0 and a truncated "RT @x: ..." text.
        // Keep the shell's id and time, but read text and media from the original.
        orig, err := normalize(rt.Result, "")
        if err == nil {
            t.IsRetweet = true
            t.Text = "RT @" + orig.Author + ": " + orig.Text
            t.HasMedia, t.URLs = orig.HasMedia, orig.URLs
        }
    }
    if t.URL == "" {
        t.URL = "https://x.com/" + t.Author + "/status/" + t.ID
    }
    return t, nil
}

Step 5: Parsing advanced-search operators

This is the core. The parser supports the operators people actually type into advanced search:

Operator Meaning
word, "exact phrase" whole-word match, case-insensitive (golang also matches #golang)
a OR b either term
-word, -"phrase" exclude
#tag, @name the hashtag or mention specifically
from:, to: author, reply-to account
lang: X's language code
since:, until: YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, until exclusive
min_faves:, min_retweets:, min_replies: engagement floors
filter:replies, filter:retweets, filter:quote, filter:media, filter:links, url: post type, prefix - to exclude

Anything else (near:, within:, list:) fails loudly instead of being ignored. A silently dropped operator gives you a wider result set than you asked for, and you won't notice.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
    "unicode"
)

// Atom is one search term or operator, e.g. golang, "go 1.27", from:golang, -filter:replies.
type Atom struct {
    Neg   bool
    Op    string // "" for plain words and phrases
    Value string
}

// Query is an AND of clauses; each clause is an OR of atoms.
type Query struct {
    Clauses [][]Atom
    Since   time.Time // inclusive, UTC day
    Until   time.Time // exclusive, UTC day
    MinFav  int
    MinRT   int
    MinRepl int
}

func tokenize(s string) []string {
    var out []string
    for i := 0; i < len(s); {
        switch {
        case s[i] == ' ' || s[i] == '\t':
            i++
        case s[i] == '"' || (s[i] == '-' && i+1 < len(s) && s[i+1] == '"'):
            start := i
            if s[i] == '-' {
                i++
            }
            end := strings.IndexByte(s[i+1:], '"')
            if end < 0 {
                out = append(out, s[start:])
                return out
            }
            out = append(out, s[start:i+1+end+1])
            i += end + 2
        default:
            end := strings.IndexAny(s[i:], " \t")
            if end < 0 {
                end = len(s) - i
            }
            out = append(out, s[i:i+end])
            i += end
        }
    }
    return out
}

func ParseQuery(s string) (*Query, error) {
    q := &Query{}
    orNext := false
    for _, tok := range tokenize(s) {
        if tok == "OR" {
            if len(q.Clauses) == 0 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("query starts with OR")
            }
            orNext = true
            continue
        }
        a := Atom{}
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, "-") && len(tok) > 1 {
            a.Neg, tok = true, tok[1:]
        }
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, `"`) {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(strings.Trim(tok, `"`))
        } else if k, v, ok := strings.Cut(tok, ":"); ok && v != "" && !strings.Contains(k, "/") {
            a.Op, a.Value = strings.ToLower(k), strings.ToLower(v)
        } else {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(tok)
        }
        // Numeric and date operators become fields, not atoms.
        handled, err := q.setField(a)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if handled {
            orNext = false
            continue
        }
        if orNext {
            last := len(q.Clauses) - 1
            q.Clauses[last] = append(q.Clauses[last], a)
            orNext = false
        } else {
            q.Clauses = append(q.Clauses, []Atom{a})
        }
    }
    if orNext {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("query ends with OR")
    }
    return q, nil
}

func (q *Query) setField(a Atom) (bool, error) {
    if a.Neg && a.Op != "" && a.Op != "filter" && a.Op != "from" && a.Op != "to" &&
        a.Op != "lang" && a.Op != "url" {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("cannot negate %s:", a.Op)
    }
    switch a.Op {
    case "since", "until":
        t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", a.Value)
        if err != nil {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want YYYY-MM-DD, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        if a.Op == "since" {
            q.Since = t
        } else {
            q.Until = t
        }
        return true, nil
    case "min_faves", "min_retweets", "min_replies":
        n, err := strconv.Atoi(a.Value)
        if err != nil || n < 0 {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want a number, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        switch a.Op {
        case "min_faves":
            q.MinFav = n
        case "min_retweets":
            q.MinRT = n
        default:
            q.MinRepl = n
        }
        return true, nil
    case "", "from", "to", "lang", "filter", "url":
        return false, nil
    }
    return false, fmt.Errorf("unsupported operator %s:", a.Op)
}

// words lowercases text and splits it on anything that is not a letter, digit,
// '_', '#' or '@', so "Go 1.27!" -> [go 1 27].
func words(s string) []string {
    return strings.FieldsFunc(strings.ToLower(s), func(r rune) bool {
        return !(unicode.IsLetter(r) || unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '_' || r == '#' || r == '@')
    })
}

func containsSeq(hay, needle []string) bool {
    if len(needle) == 0 {
        return false
    }
outer:
    for i := 0; i+len(needle) <= len(hay); i++ {
        for j := range needle {
            if hay[i+j] != needle[j] {
                continue outer
            }
        }
        return true
    }
    return false
}

func (a Atom) match(t *Tweet, raw, bare []string) bool {
    switch a.Op {
    case "":
        if strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "#") || strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "@") {
            return containsSeq(raw, words(a.Value)) // #golang must be a hashtag
        }
        return containsSeq(bare, words(a.Value)) // golang also matches #golang
    case "from":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.Author, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "to":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.ReplyTo, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "lang":
        return t.Lang == a.Value
    case "url":
        for _, u := range t.URLs {
            if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(u), a.Value) {
                return true
            }
        }
        return false
    case "filter":
        switch a.Value {
        case "replies":
            return t.ReplyTo != ""
        case "retweets", "nativeretweets":
            return t.IsRetweet
        case "quote":
            return t.IsQuote
        case "media":
            return t.HasMedia
        case "links":
            return len(t.URLs) > 0
        }
    }
    return false
}

// Match applies the whole query to one normalized tweet.
func (q *Query) Match(t *Tweet) bool {
    if !q.Since.IsZero() && t.Created.Before(q.Since) {
        return false
    }
    if !q.Until.IsZero() && !t.Created.Before(q.Until) {
        return false
    }
    if t.Faves < q.MinFav || t.Retweets < q.MinRT || t.Replies < q.MinRepl {
        return false
    }
    raw := words(t.Text)
    bare := make([]string, len(raw))
    for i, w := range raw {
        bare[i] = strings.TrimLeft(w, "#@")
    }
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        ok := false
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.match(t, raw, bare) != a.Neg {
                ok = true
                break
            }
        }
        if !ok {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

// Handles returns the accounts of the first clause made only of from: atoms
// (from:a OR from:b), or nil when no clause pins the author.
func (q *Query) Handles() []string {
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var hs []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.Op != "from" || a.Neg {
                hs = nil
                break
            }
            hs = append(hs, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
        }
        if hs != nil {
            return hs
        }
    }
    return nil
}

// Keywords returns plain search strings for the web-index search endpoint: the
// positive words and phrases, one string per alternative of the first OR clause.
func (q *Query) Keywords() []string {
    var base []string
    var alts []string
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        if len(clause) == 1 && clause[0].Op == "" && !clause[0].Neg {
            base = append(base, quoteIfSpace(clause[0].Value))
            continue
        }
        if alts == nil {
            plain := true
            for _, a := range clause {
                plain = plain && a.Op == "" && !a.Neg
            }
            if plain {
                for _, a := range clause {
                    alts = append(alts, quoteIfSpace(a.Value))
                }
            }
        }
    }
    if len(alts) == 0 {
        if len(base) == 0 {
            return nil
        }
        return []string{strings.Join(base, " ")}
    }
    var out []string
    for _, alt := range alts {
        out = append(out, strings.TrimSpace(strings.Join(base, " ")+" "+alt))
    }
    return out
}

func quoteIfSpace(s string) string {
    if strings.Contains(s, " ") {
        return `"` + s + `"`
    }
    return s
}

Three decisions worth explaining:

  • Whole words, no stemming. release does not match "released", and api does not match "APIs". X's search doesn't stem either, so the tool behaves the same, and you get used to writing release OR released.
  • OR binds to its neighbours, like X's search: golang OR #go -hiring means "(golang or #go) and not hiring". There are no parentheses, which keeps the parser tiny and covers most real queries.
  • Keywords() fans out OR groups. The web index doesn't understand OR, so scraping OR scraper OR crawler becomes three keyword searches. That's three times the credits, and explain shows it before you pay.

Step 6: Fetch, filter, report, watch

collect picks the source: timelines when the query pins from:, web-index search otherwise, plus any -watch accounts. watch keeps a state file of already-reported IDs (written to a temp file and renamed, so a crash mid-write can't wipe it) and appends new matches to JSONL.

// xsearch: X (Twitter) advanced-search operators, applied locally to posts
// fetched through the ScrapeAtlas API. Go standard library only.
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "text/tabwriter"
    "time"
)

type source struct {
    fetched  int
    warnings map[string]bool
}

// collect fetches candidate posts: timelines when the query pins from:,
// web-index search pages otherwise, plus any extra -watch accounts.
func collect(c *Client, q *Query, pages int, watch []string) (map[string]Tweet, *source, error) {
    seen := map[string]Tweet{}
    src := &source{warnings: map[string]bool{}}
    add := func(env *envelope, list []rawTweet, handle string) {
        for _, w := range env.Coverage.Warnings {
            src.warnings[env.Coverage.Source+":"+w] = true
        }
        for _, r := range list {
            t, err := normalize(r, handle)
            if err != nil || t.ID == "" {
                continue
            }
            src.fetched++
            seen[t.ID] = t
        }
    }
    handles := append(q.Handles(), watch...)
    for _, h := range handles {
        p := url.Values{"handle": {h}, "trim": {"true"}}
        if !q.Since.IsZero() {
            p.Set("since", q.Since.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        if !q.Until.IsZero() {
            p.Set("until", q.Until.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/user-tweets", p)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("timeline @%s: %w", h, err)
        }
        add(env, env.Tweets, h)
    }
    if len(q.Handles()) > 0 {
        return seen, src, nil // from: is answered by the timelines alone
    }
    kws := q.Keywords()
    if len(kws) == 0 && len(handles) == 0 {
        return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("query needs at least one word, phrase or from:")
    }
    for _, kw := range kws {
        cursor := ""
        for page := 1; page <= pages; page++ {
            p := url.Values{"query": {kw}}
            if cursor != "" {
                p.Set("cursor", cursor)
            }
            env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/search/posts", p)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("search %q page %d: %w", kw, page, err)
            }
            add(env, env.Posts, "")
            if env.Cursor == nil || *env.Cursor == "" {
                break
            }
            cursor = *env.Cursor
        }
    }
    return seen, src, nil
}

func filterSort(all map[string]Tweet, q *Query, order string) []Tweet {
    var out []Tweet
    for _, t := range all {
        if q.Match(&t) {
            out = append(out, t)
        }
    }
    sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool {
        if order == "top" && out[i].Faves != out[j].Faves {
            return out[i].Faves > out[j].Faves
        }
        return out[i].Created.After(out[j].Created)
    })
    return out
}

func printTable(ts []Tweet, mask bool) {
    w := tabwriter.NewWriter(os.Stdout, 0, 0, 2, ' ', 0)
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "CREATED (UTC)\tAUTHOR\tLANG\tLIKES\tRTS\tREPLIES\tVIEWS\tTEXT")
    for _, t := range ts {
        text := strings.Join(strings.Fields(t.Text), " ")
        if r := []rune(text); len(r) > 60 {
            text = string(r[:57]) + "..."
        }
        author := t.Author
        if r := []rune(author); mask && len(r) > 2 {
            author = string(r[:2]) + strings.Repeat("*", len(r)-2) // for reports you share
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "%s\t@%s\t%s\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%s\n", t.Created.Format("2006-01-02 15:04"),
            author, t.Lang, t.Faves, t.Retweets, t.Replies, t.Views, text)
    }
    w.Flush()
}

func explain(q *Query) {
    fmt.Println("local filters:")
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var alts []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            s := a.Value
            if a.Op != "" {
                s = a.Op + ":" + s
            }
            if a.Neg {
                s = "NOT " + s
            }
            alts = append(alts, s)
        }
        fmt.Println("  ", strings.Join(alts, " OR "))
    }
    if !q.Since.IsZero() || !q.Until.IsZero() {
        day := func(t time.Time, zero string) string {
            if t.IsZero() {
                return zero
            }
            return t.Format("2006-01-02")
        }
        fmt.Printf("   created in [%s, %s)\n", day(q.Since, "start"), day(q.Until, "now"))
    }
    if q.MinFav+q.MinRT+q.MinRepl > 0 {
        fmt.Printf("   likes>=%d retweets>=%d replies>=%d\n", q.MinFav, q.MinRT, q.MinRepl)
    }
    if hs := q.Handles(); hs != nil {
        fmt.Println("fetch: timelines of", strings.Join(hs, ", "))
    } else {
        fmt.Printf("fetch: web-index search for %q\n", q.Keywords())
    }
}

// watch keeps the IDs it has already reported in a state file and appends
// new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron.
func watch(matches []Tweet, statePath, outPath string) ([]Tweet, error) {
    state := map[string]string{} // tweet id -> first seen (RFC 3339)
    if b, err := os.ReadFile(statePath); err == nil {
        if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &state); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", statePath, err)
        }
    }
    f, err := os.OpenFile(outPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    bw := bufio.NewWriter(f)
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)
    var fresh []Tweet
    for _, t := range matches {
        if _, ok := state[t.ID]; ok {
            continue
        }
        state[t.ID] = now
        fresh = append(fresh, t)
        line, _ := json.Marshal(struct {
            SeenAt string `json:"seen_at"`
            Tweet
        }{now, t})
        bw.Write(append(line, '\n'))
    }
    if err := bw.Flush(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    b, _ := json.MarshalIndent(state, "", " ")
    tmp := statePath + ".tmp"
    if err := os.WriteFile(tmp, b, 0o644); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return fresh, os.Rename(tmp, statePath) // atomic: a crash never truncates state
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: xsearch explain|search|watch [flags] 'query'")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    cmd := os.Args[1]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    pages := fs.Int("pages", 3, "max search result pages per keyword (2 credits each)")
    watchList := fs.String("watch", "", "comma-separated handles whose timelines are also checked")
    order := fs.String("sort", "top", "top (likes) or latest")
    statePath := fs.String("state", "state.json", "watch: ids already reported")
    outPath := fs.String("out", "matches.jsonl", "watch: new matches are appended here")
    mask := fs.Bool("mask", false, "print authors as go*** in the table")
    fs.Parse(os.Args[2:])
    q, err := ParseQuery(strings.Join(fs.Args(), " "))
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "query:", err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if cmd == "explain" {
        explain(q)
        return
    }
    c, err := NewClient()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    var extra []string
    if *watchList != "" {
        extra = strings.Split(*watchList, ",")
    }
    all, src, err := collect(c, q, *pages, extra)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    matches := filterSort(all, q, *order)
    var ws []string
    for w := range src.warnings {
        ws = append(ws, w)
    }
    sort.Strings(ws)
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "fetched %d posts (%d unique), %d match, %d paid requests; coverage warnings: %s\n",
        src.fetched, len(all), len(matches), c.Calls, strings.Join(ws, ", "))
    switch cmd {
    case "search":
        printTable(matches, *mask)
    case "watch":
        fresh, err := watch(matches, *statePath, *outPath)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%d new since last run\n", len(fresh))
        printTable(fresh, *mask)
    default:
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "unknown command", cmd)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

The same tool with a stricter query shows the other edge:

$ ./xsearch search -mask -pages 4 '"web scraping" api OR mcp lang:en -filter:replies min_faves:20'
fetched 21 posts (14 unique), 1 match, 8 paid requests; coverage warnings: web_search:tweets_omitted, web_search:web_index_selection
CREATED (UTC)     AUTHOR           LANG  LIKES  RTS  REPLIES  VIEWS   TEXT
2026-06-20 12:59  @ak************  en    6606   815  134      951560  Web scraping will never be the same. (100% open-source vi...

Fourteen candidates, one match. Most candidates don't contain the exact phrase "web scraping" at all, because the index matches on topic and not on words. Of the few that do, one has no "api" or "mcp", one is in Korean, and some write "APIs", which whole-word api doesn't match. When a discovery query comes back nearly empty, loosen the words first (api OR apis, drop the phrase), then the floors.

Errors that should be errors 

$ ./xsearch search 'near:berlin golang'
query: unsupported operator near:
exit 2
$ ./xsearch search 'lang:en min_faves:100'
query needs at least one word, phrase or from:
exit 1

The second one matters. X would happily run lang:en min_faves:100 across the whole network. Here there is no network-wide stream to filter, so the tool refuses instead of quietly returning a few arbitrary posts.

Watching accounts from cron 

$ ./xsearch watch -state data/state.json -out data/matches.jsonl 'from:golang OR from:github OR from:NASA -filter:retweets min_faves:1000'
fetched 51 posts (51 unique), 13 match, 1 paid requests; coverage warnings: public_api:latest_window_limited, public_api:module_entries_omitted
13 new since last run
CREATED (UTC)     AUTHOR   LANG  LIKES  RTS   REPLIES  VIEWS     TEXT
2026-11-24 19:59  @NASA    en    37785  3322  2162     14042369  As part of a coordinated, whole-of-government effort, NAS...
2026-11-24 16:50  @NASA    en    8447   1041  538      954468    A home away from home 🌕 We're building a Moon Base, where...
2026-11-23 18:59  @NASA    en    6387   792   233      1269140   Happy Thanksgiving from the @Space_Station! https://t.co/...
2026-11-23 16:28  @NASA    en    6135   1011  258      896945    We're on our way to explore the mysteries of Europa, an o...
2026-11-24 22:04  @NASA    en    5228   834   231      1205026   We've decided on key design features and mission details ...
2026-11-20 15:19  @NASA    en    4582   876   237      765059    We 💛 V-G-R On the evening before Voyager 1 reached its on...
2026-11-25 17:24  @NASA    en    3254   587   292      785670    Medicine or engineering? Military or civilian? We're look...
2026-11-20 16:45  @NASA    en    2621   412   182      1002646   LIVE: Watch as an uncrewed SpaceX Dragon spacecraft undoc...
2026-10-30 20:26  @golang  art   2144   91    35       103476    👀
2026-11-24 10:00  @NASA    en    1581   236   115      755869    LIVE: An uncrewed Progress cargo spacecraft carrying food...
2026-11-26 11:30  @NASA    en    1533   260   144      604367    LIVE: Watch the Progress 97 spacecraft arrive and dock to...
2026-11-25 16:00  @NASA    en    1432   233   74       336979    We’re focused on improving all our business operations, i...
2026-08-11 16:53  @golang  en    1219   189   45       142034    AI is your newest teammate—a hyper-productive contributor...

The first run reports everything that matches and records it. "1 paid requests" is not a typo: @golang and @NASA came from the cache of the previous search (same URL, under 30 minutes old), and only @github was fetched. @github had no post over 1,000 likes in its window. The 👀-only post from @golang has the language code art. Posts without real words get codes like that: I saw art and zxx (just a link) in these runs, and X also uses und and qme. lang:en drops all of them.

A later run, after the cache expired:

fetched 51 posts (51 unique), 13 match, 3 paid requests; coverage warnings: public_api:latest_window_limited, public_api:module_entries_omitted
0 new since last run
CREATED (UTC)  AUTHOR  LANG  LIKES  RTS  REPLIES  VIEWS  TEXT

That run was at 04:45 UTC, 34 minutes after the first, with three fresh requests (3 credits). Nobody had posted anything over 1,000 likes in between, so nothing was reported and nothing was appended. That's the normal case for a watcher, and it's why the state file matters: without it, every run would report the same 13 posts again. The state file only tracks IDs, though. A post that crosses min_faves:1000 later is reported on the first run where it qualifies. A post that was already reported is never reported again, even if its likes triple. If you want that, store counts per run instead.

A crontab line that checks every two hours and logs new matches:

0 */2 * * * cd /opt/xsearch && ./xsearch watch -state data/state.json -out data/matches.jsonl 'from:golang OR from:github OR from:NASA -filter:retweets min_faves:1000' >> data/watch.log 2>&1

Each line in matches.jsonl is one post with a seen_at time. Here is the first one, pretty-printed and with the text shortened:

{
  "seen_at": "2026-11-27T04:11:30Z",
  "id": "2125318351341994436",
  "author": "NASA",
  "created": "2026-11-24T19:59:16Z",
  "faves": 37785,
  "retweets": 3322,
  "replies": 2162,
  "views": 14042369,
  "url": "https://x.com/NASA/status/2125318351341994436",
  "text": "As part of a coordinated, whole-of-government effort, NASA has rapidly mobilized..."
}

Twelve runs a day over three accounts is 36 credits a day. The account window (about 20 posts) is the real limit on the interval: for an account that posts 30 times a day, every two hours is too slow, and posts drop out of the window before you see them.

Pitfalls, in one place

  • Logged-out search is gone. x.com/search redirects to login, the API needs a token, the syndication timeline returns 429. Don't build on any of them, and don't automate a logged-in session.
  • Search-by-keyword is discovery, not a firehose. The web index gives about 10-20 relevant posts per keyword, in relevance order, across months. Treat the results as a sample and say so in anything you report.
  • Operators sent to the search endpoint don't work. from:golang since:2026-11-01 returned nothing. Send words, filter locally.
  • Timelines are a window, not an archive. About 20 latest posts. since/until filter inside that window and return nothing outside it (latest_window_limited).
  • Retweet shells have 0 likes and truncated text. Read the original from retweeted_status_result, or exclude retweets.
  • Use note_tweet for long posts. full_text stops near 280 characters, and some long posts have no note at all.
  • Whole-word matching is strict. api doesn't match "APIs". Write the variants with OR.
  • Counts move between runs. The same post had 6,605 likes in one response and 6,606 in the next. Store snapshots with a time if you want trends. Don't compare across runs as if they were exact.
  • Language codes include art, zxx, und and qme. lang:en silently drops emoji-only and link-only posts. A two-word English post can also come back as da (one @golang post did).
  • Credits add up with OR. Every alternative in the first OR group is a separate search, and every page is 2 credits. Run explain first.
  • The official X API doesn't support min_faves. If you move this tool to the official API later, keep the local filter: engagement floors stay client-side there too.

Wrapping up

  • Advanced search can be split in two: fetch candidates, then filter with operators you implement yourself. In Go that's a ~290-line parser plus a table of tests.
  • from: queries are precise; keyword queries are a sample. Print the coverage warnings next to every result, so nobody reads "14 matches" as "14 posts exist".
  • explain before search saves credits and surprises, and watch with a state file turns the whole thing into a cron job.
  • X's terms ban scraping. Read them, prefer the official API where it fits, keep volumes small, and keep individual people's handles out of anything you publish.

*I build it.

title: AI Builds Clean CRUD for Proptech. It Breaks the Moment One User Has Two Roles on Two Properties
description:
Ask an AI coding tool to build a property management app and you'll get working auth, a clean CRUD admin panel, a Stripe checkout flow, and a dashboard that looks fine in a demo. All of that is generic SaaS scaffolding, and AI handles it well because it's been trained on thousands of examples of exactly that pattern. The part that breaks isn't the UI or the database schema for listings. It's permissions, specifically the assumption baked into almost every generated auth system that a user has one role. Real estate doesn't work that way. The same person can be a board member on one property and just an owner on another, in the same account, and most vibe-coded proptech has no data model for that at all.

Where the AI capability line actually sits

AI builds the generic SaaS layer reliably: authentication, basic create-read-update-delete admin panels, Stripe checkout, simple dashboards, landing pages with a waitlist form. A founder with some technical skill can extend that into listing display pages, inquiry forms, and basic tenant directories. What consistently breaks, regardless of how good the model is, falls into four categories: permission modeling tied to real-world structure, integrations with legacy systems that don't have clean APIs, financial workflows touching actual balances, and compliance-sensitive workflows. None of those are language-model problems. They're modeling problems that require someone to think through the real-world structure before any code gets written.

Why "one role per user" is the wrong schema

The default pattern almost every generated auth system produces is a single role column on the user record. That works for most SaaS. It fails immediately for property management, where the same person needs different permissions on different properties, sometimes owner on one unit and board member on another in the same association:

// Wrong: role lives on the user, can't vary by property
User { id, email, role }  // "owner" doesn't tell you which property

// Right: role is scoped to the relationship between a user and a property
UserPropertyRole {
  userId,
  propertyId,
  role,              // "owner", "board_member", "employee", "administrator"
  grantedAt,
}

function checkPermission(userId, propertyId, action) {
  const scopedRole = userPropertyRoles.find(userId, propertyId);
  if (!scopedRole) return deny(action, "no_role_on_property");
  return rolePermissions[scopedRole.role].includes(action);
}

That second pattern is the difference between a system that can actually model a real association and one that only works until the first user with a role conflict signs up. Support access needs the same discipline: a "view as this account" mode should be a logged impersonation event, not a shared admin login that leaves no trail of who looked at what.

What this looked like on a real build

Brocoders built exactly this pattern for C.I.A. Services' HOA management app, which runs five distinct access tiers, owners, multi-lot owners, board members, employees, and administrators, across roughly 150 associations and 50,000 properties. Registration itself is a verification problem: a community code, account number, and PIN get checked against live association records before an account is even created. Support staff get a scoped "view as this account" mode that logs every impersonation instead of sharing credentials. We run this on hard data isolation at both the database and API layer, so a permission bug in one association's records can't leak into another's, with two-factor authentication and audit logging on top. Internal tooling at bcboilerplates.com covers this kind of auth and tenancy scaffolding by default, so new builds start with scoped permissions instead of a single role column that has to be ripped out later.

Other builds hit the same category of problem differently. CondoGenie, a Canadian condo management platform, has needed this same board-versus-resident-versus-manager distinction since inception. Lake, a vacation rental platform, saw connected properties grow 80x with a 210% spike in site activity within three months of a rebuild that included fixing exactly this kind of access modeling. ShineUp's codebase needed a 2-3 week AWS migration at a fixed price with no rebuild required, evidence that not every legacy proptech problem needs a rewrite, some just need the infrastructure moved without touching the permission logic that already worked.

The four questions that tell you if this is a DIY problem or not

  1. Do multiple user types need different property access? A single owner-versus-admin split is DIY territory. Five tiers with overlapping scopes isn't.
  2. Does this integrate with a system you don't fully control? Legacy property management software and MLS feeds rarely expose clean APIs.
  3. Does a permission error carry real compliance or financial consequences? A wrong role assignment that exposes another owner's financial data is a different risk class than a cosmetic bug.
  4. Are there cross-property enforcement rules? Booking limits, amenity availability, and approval chains that span properties need real logic, not a checkbox.

Three or four "yes" answers means this needs a team that's modeled real-world property structures before, not just a capable coding assistant. One or two "yes" answers means DIY territory is probably still viable, at least for now.

Engineering checklist before you scale a proptech permission model

  • Role lives on the relationship, not the user: can the same person hold different roles on different properties without a schema change?
  • Impersonation is logged, not shared: does support access leave an audit trail, or does it use a shared login?
  • Isolation enforced at the data layer: can one association's records reach another's through any code path, even a bug?
  • Legacy integration scoped honestly: does the plan account for a PMS or MLS with no clean API, or assume one exists?
  • Financial workflows get extra review: does anything touching real balances get more scrutiny than a standard CRUD flow?
  • Compliance workflows are explicit: are they designed in from the start, or patched in after the first audit finding? If you're trying to figure out whether your proptech idea needs a real permission model before you keep building on AI-generated scaffolding, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.
