title: PowerFix: Physics-Guided Iterative Repair for LLM-Assisted Power Converter Design
description:
arXiv:2611.33712v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for automated engineering design. However, repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation remains challenging: the system must identify physical causes, locate responsible design variables, and resolve violations without compromising other constraints. We introduce PowerFix, a physics-guided iterative repair framework that converts validation failures into structured diagnoses and executable patches while preserving topology and design requirements. PowerDiagGraph links failed checks to possible physical causes and constrains repair routes. An LLM prioritizes these routes, while a deterministic compiler translates selected repairs into authorized field-level edits. Candidates are validated on isolated design copies and committed only after all required engineering checks pass; failed validation can guide replanning. On our constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark, comprising injected single faults, coupled faults, and held-out natural failures from our design generator, PowerFix achieves 78.7% verified repair success rate (VRSR), compared with 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines. Three additional replanning rounds increase VRSR to 88.4%. These offline results provide pilot-stage evidence within a simulation-based design workflow, with hardware prototype validation and transfer to a second converter topology as the next steps toward deployment.

title: 金融業遷移至雲端服務：企業學習知識庫
description:
金融業遷移至雲端服務：企業學習知識庫

來源內容將雲端遷移的重點放在避險基金研究、Alpha 因子分析、另類資料回測、量化投資研究、投資組合風險管理以及交易法規的合規性上。 這是一個具教育與探索性質的頁面，而非 AWS 參考架構、遷移執行手冊、法規評估，亦非已部署正式環境平台的證明。

高階主管學習

金融服務業的雲端遷移不僅是一項技術專案，更是業務、風險、資料與營運模式的轉型。 來源文件將資料安全與合規、資料主權、效能與延遲、成本管理、停機時間，以及與傳統系統的整合列為主要考量。 這些考量是相互關聯的。 如果一項設計提升了敏捷性，卻失去了資料血緣 (data lineage)、增加了延遲、削弱了復原能力、破壞了授權機制，或造成了無法控制的成本結構，這就不是一次成功的金融業 (FSI) 遷移。

來源中最實用的遷移模式是漸進式現代化。 探索現有資產、選擇一個小型的非關鍵試點、逐步導入雲端功能、監控兩個環境、驗證結果，並透過受控且可復原的切換過程來轉移流量。 這種模式縮小了變更的影響範圍，但並不能免除依賴性分析、資料核對、安全測試、業務批准、營運就緒度，以及經過測試的復原計畫等需求。

來源中的 AWS 服務清單最好被理解為潛在功能的型錄。 Application Discovery Service 可支援依賴性探索，EC2 可支援虛擬機工作負載，Lambda 和 API Gateway 可支援特定的事件驅動介面，RDS 可提供受管的關聯式資料庫，DMS 可支援資料庫遷移，Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 可託管應用程式，Elastic Load Balancing 可分配流量，而 CloudWatch 可支援監控與日誌記錄。 正確的選擇取決於工作負載在資料、延遲、韌性、法規、營運及相容性方面的需求。

金融業遷移驅動因素與決策背景

資料安全與合規性被列為首要考量，並舉出 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS 為例。 這些規範的適用範圍和義務並不相同，其適用性取決於機構、客戶、產品、司法管轄區、資料以及處理活動。 雲端遷移應從法人實體和資料處理盤點開始，而不是假設雲端供應商的一般安全態勢即可證明合規。

資料主權意味著將資料或特定處理活動保留在規定的地理邊界內。 選擇區域 (Region) 只是該決策的一部分。 機構必須確認主要資料、複本、備份、日誌、快照、支援存取、開發副本、災難復原環境，以及下游分析可以存放在哪裡。 跨境傳輸、分包商、營運存取、保留、刪除、法定保存以及市場資料授權，都會影響允許的設計。

效能與延遲必須以業務術語來定義。 量化研究作業、投資組合風險計算、市場資料消費者、訂單管理功能和即時執行路徑，都有不同的延遲與確定性要求。 遷移應針對吞吐量、回應時間、百分位數延遲、並發性、佇列、復原行為和依賴呼叫，建立基準與目標測量值。 籠統地聲稱雲端服務具備可擴展性，並不能證明特定的金融業工作負載能達到其所需的效能。

成本管理是一項明確的考量，因為雲端消耗會隨著工作負載量、儲存增長、資料傳輸、平行處理、日誌記錄、複製和復原副本而變化。 有效的商業案例必須將雲端營運的總成本與現有資產的總成本進行比較，包括遷移期間的雙軌並行、資料來源授權、支援、安全工具、連線、測試、人員編制和合規證據。 預算和成本報告是控制機制，不能取代量化的總成本模型。

停機時間與傳統系統整合，對於持續運作或有嚴格業務日曆的金融系統尤為重要。 遷移設計應確立切換視窗、上游與下游依賴關係、外部交易對手、市場休假日、核對期間、批次截止時間，以及可接受的最大中斷時間。 傳統系統可能還需要專有協定、固定網路位置、共用檔案、大型主機介面，或無法由通用雲端端點取代的緊密耦合資料庫行為。

目標金融業工作負載邊界

頁面標題將遷移主題與避險基金活動、Alpha 因子庫 (alpha-factor zoo)、另類回測策略、量化投資研究、投資組合風險管理以及交易法規合規性關聯在一起。 這些主題暗示了潛在的工作負載，例如歷史市場資料處理、研究資料管理、因子計算、回測、投資組合分析、風險報告和合規支援。

來源並未確認目標是即時訂單管理系統、交易所閘道器、市場資料廠 (market-data plant)、撮合引擎或執行平台。 它沒有提供經紀商連線、交易所連線、訂單路由邏輯、交易監控實作或正式環境投資組合帳本。 除非有其他證據表明對延遲敏感或受監管的執行功能包含在範圍內，否則該頁面應僅用於討論研究與支援系統的遷移模式。

工作負載分類應區分核心紀錄系統 (systems of record) 與分析副本、即時服務與批次服務、有狀態應用程式與無狀態服務，以及受監管的處理與實驗性環境。 它還應記錄業務關鍵性、資料敏感度、市場時間、延遲預算、吞吐量、復原目標、授權限制，以及當責的業務擁有者。 這些屬性決定了一個工作負載應該被重新託管 (rehosted)、重新建構平台 (replatformed)、重構 (refactored)、替換 (replaced)、保留 (retained) 還是退場 (retired)。

絞殺榕遷移模式 (Strangler Fig Pattern)

來源將其營運流程稱為絞殺榕模式，並描述了五個階段：評估、試點、重構、監控與切換。 評估階段會審視現有應用程式，並找出適合遷移的元件。 試點階段會將一個小型的非關鍵元件移至雲端。 重構階段則是以雲端託管的微服務逐步取代單體架構 (monolith) 的各個部分。 監控貫穿整個過渡期。 最後，切換階段會將流量轉移至新的實作。

這個模式非常實用，因為它避免將遷移視為單一且不可逆的事件。 它允許組織在轉移更關鍵的功能之前，先了解連線、安全、效能、營運和成本。 儘管如此，試點仍必須使用明確的標準來選擇。 「非關鍵」應該意味著該元件的故障、資料外洩、延遲或錯誤結果，對業務和法規的影響是受限的，而不僅僅是因為它的使用者很少。

絞殺榕遷移並不代表在所有情況下都需要使用微服務。 機構可以逐步以受管服務、模組化應用程式、批次管道，或保留在受控介面後方的傳統元件來取代特定功能。 微服務可能會引入分散式交易、營運開銷、版本控制挑戰以及新的故障模式。 現代化的選擇應遵循領域邊界和控制需求，而不是將微服務視為理所當然的目的地。

評估與探索

第一個實際活動是對應用程式、介面、資料儲存、批次作業、身分識別、基礎架構、外部供應商、使用者、授權和營運程序進行結構化盤點。 來源點名 AWS Application Discovery Service 作為了解應用程式依賴關係和效能指標的工具。 其輸出結果應與訪談、架構紀錄、網路證據、日誌、業務流程圖以及法規清單結合，因為自動化探索本身無法識別每一個業務或控制依賴。

評估應記錄每個依賴關係的呼叫方向、協定、頻率、有效載荷、身分驗證、資料分類、故障行為、逾時、重試、順序和擁有權。 它應識別資料庫、檔案共用、佇列、排程作業、參考資料、市場資料摘要、報告目的地、下游消費者以及外部交易對手。 對於交易或風險環境，分析還應記錄市場日曆、截止時間、時區、事件時間語意、修正行為，以及處理延遲或遺失資料的方式。

每個候選的遷移階段都應有明確的範圍、業務目標、風險評級、來源和目標擁有者、驗收標準、依賴關係、復原方法和證據計畫。 評估應區分技術可行性與法規許可。 一個應用程式在技術上可能很容易搬遷，但仍可能因為資料落地 (data residency)、授權、營運韌性、紀錄保存、委外或模型治理義務而不適合遷移。

目標架構與 AWS 服務角色

來源提議將 EC2、Lambda、API Gateway 和 RDS 作為雲端原生架構的建構模塊。 EC2 適用於需要作業系統控制權、需與現有軟體相容，或採取漸進式直接搬遷 (lift-and-shift) 路徑的工作負載。 Lambda 適合具有相容執行、逾時、狀態和打包特性的受限事件驅動功能。 API Gateway 可提供受管的介面邊界，但需符合身分驗證、授權、節流、結構描述 (schema)、版本控制和可用性要求。 RDS 可以減少資料庫管理工作，但必須明確選擇目標引擎、版本、交易行為、擴充功能、連線模型、備份策略和相容性。

Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 被列為應用程式部署選項。 它們代表不同的營運模型，不應被視為可互換的標籤。 選擇取決於組織是否需要應用程式平台抽象化、容器編排、部署控制、服務探索、擴展行為、網路整合以及營運責任。 目標架構還應定義如何管理機密、配置、映像檔、修補程式、日誌、指標、追蹤和復原版本。

Elastic Load Balancing 用於流量分配。 確切的負載平衡器類型和路由設計必須符合協定、連線生命週期、TLS 終止、用戶端身分、健康檢查、路徑路由、WebSocket 或串流行為、來源 IP 要求和延遲目標。 單靠流量分配無法提供應用程式的正確性。 健康檢查必須代表實質的業務就緒狀態，且容錯移轉 (failover) 絕不能將請求路由至雖可連線但無法處理權威資料的服務。

CloudWatch 被點名用於效能監控和日誌記錄。 監控應超越基礎架構使用率，涵蓋業務與控制指標，例如交易完整性、佇列時間 (queue age)、核對狀態、錯誤分類、依賴關係健康狀態、資料新鮮度、身分驗證失敗、權限變更、延遲百分位數、成本異常以及復原訊號。 日誌應具備定義好的保留期限、存取控制、時間同步、遮罩 (redaction)、完整性保護，並有途徑作為事件回應與稽核證據。

使用 AWS DMS 進行資料庫與資料遷移

來源點名 AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) 用於資料庫遷移，並形容資料傳輸為「無縫」(seamless)。 「無縫」應被視為一種期望而非保證。 受控的資料庫遷移必須指定來源和目標引擎、結構描述 (schema) 相容性、全量載入行為、異動資料擷取 (CDC) 行為、交易排序、主鍵和序列處理、型別轉換、字元編碼、時區、大型物件、預存程序、權限、索引以及下游依賴。

遷移計畫必須定義在共存期間哪一個環境具有權威性。 如果傳統和雲端資料庫都接受寫入，組織就需要衝突解決和核對模型。 如果只有一方接受寫入，則必須明確規定複製方向、延遲容忍度、中斷行為和切換程序。 該計畫應能偵測重複、遺失、順序錯誤、截斷或轉換的紀錄，並應保留目標資料完整且正確的證據。

金融服務資料遷移需要時間點正確性 (point-in-time correctness)。 歷史分析、風險、估值和監控可能依賴於事件發生時存在的參考資料和市場狀態。 遷移應保留來源時間戳記、營業日、生效日期、修正歷史、血緣，以及原始資料與重編資料之間的區別。 備份、複本、快照、測試環境和匯出檔案必須繼承適當的分類和保留控制。

資料品質關卡應比對紀錄數量、餘額、部位、總計、校驗和 (checksums)、金鑰分佈、空值率 (null rates)、參照完整性、事件序列和業務核對結果。 異常狀況應被保留並指派給擁有者，而不是被回報技術成功的匯入過程所掩蓋。 不能僅因資料複製已趕上進度就宣布目標環境就緒；業務單位必須確認產生的資料能支援預期的計算、報告、控制和下游介面。

應用程式現代化與傳統系統整合

來源建議逐步以雲端託管的微服務取代單體架構的元件。 安全的現代化計畫首先要識別受限的業務能力及其資料所有權。 每個新元件都需要合約、版本控制策略、身分驗證模型、冪等性 (idempotency) 行為、逾時和重試規則、可觀測性、部署流程以及定義好的真相來源 (source of truth)。 分散式服務還需要明確處理部分故障、重複訊息、排序、最終一致性和跨服務交易。

傳統系統整合應被設計為一級邊界。 來源提到新的雲端系統應該與地端 (on-premises) 系統互動，但並未定義網路連線、路由、DNS、身分聯合、私有服務存取、加密、防火牆所有權、延遲預算或故障行為。 遷移必須確定傳統系統如何發現雲端服務、雲端工作負載如何連線到保留的系統、如何管理憑證，以及當任一方無法使用時由哪個團隊負責回應。

共存期通常比最終架構更為複雜。 介面可能需要轉譯，資料可能暫時重複，使用者可能需要跨系統的一致視圖，而營運團隊可能需要支援兩種部署和事件模型。 過渡期設計應指定共存的時間長短、每個資料領域的權威系統、讓舊元件退役的條件，以及傳統基礎架構除役前所需的證據。

遷移服務與部署選擇

來源列出了用於資料庫遷移的 AWS Database Migration Service、用於伺服器遷移的 AWS Server Migration Service、用於傳輸大量資料的 Snowball，以及用於某些應用程式或資料保留在地端的混合場景的 AWS Outposts。 這些名稱應被視為來源參考，在納入遷移計畫之前，需要檢查目前的產品狀態、區域可用性和功能。 特別是，任何使用特別點名的 AWS Server Migration Service 的計畫，都應驗證目前受支援的服務和替代路徑。

Snowball 或其他大量傳輸設備可能會減少初始大型資料傳輸的時間或網路負載。 但它本身並不能解決監管鏈、加密、來源與目的地核對、增量變更、傳輸重試、授權或最終切換等問題。 遷移團隊必須定義如何驗證初始副本，以及如何同步在設備匯出後所做的變更。

當機構需要將特定的 AWS 基礎架構或服務建置在客戶地點作為混合設計的一部分時，Outposts 就會派上用場。 這並非解決資料主權、災難復原或法規遵從的自動解答。 設計必須考量支援的服務、硬體容量、連線、修補、本地營運、故障替換、依賴行為、實體安全、資料位置，以及地端 AWS 環境無法使用時的復原路徑。

安全性、隱私與合規

來源指出 IAM、VPC 以及靜態與傳輸中的加密為核心的 AWS 安全功能。 這些是重要的基礎，但並不構成完整的金融業控制環境。 IAM 應包括聯合身分、最低權限角色、工作負載身分、特權存取控制、緊急存取 (break-glass) 程序、職責分離、存取權限重新認證、服務帳戶治理，以及變更與審查的證據。

VPC 設計應定義帳戶和環境邊界、子網路配置、路由、安全群組、網路存取控制清單 (NACL)、私有端點、檢查機制、進入與離開 (ingress/egress) 策略、DNS、日誌記錄，以及與地端系統和外部供應商的連線。 對外公開應深思熟慮並最小化。 服務應互相驗證身分、驗證輸入、使用適當的網路路徑，並產生由負責團隊監控的安全遙測數據。

加密不僅僅是勾選一個選項。 機構必須定義金鑰所有權、金鑰分離、建立與輪換、存取策略、復原、撤銷、稽核日誌記錄，以及加密備份和複本的處理方式。 敏感資料可能還需要權杖化 (tokenization)、遮罩、欄位層級保護或受限制的分析副本。 日誌和監控資料可能包含受監管的資訊，必須進行分類，不能假設為安全的。

頁面提到了 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS，但沒有提供適用性分析或控制對應。 它沒有識別持卡人資料環境、個人資料盤點、跨境傳輸依據、保留規則、市場行為義務、交易紀錄要求或委外評估。 遷移應將實際的法律與法規義務對應到系統、資料、流程、供應商、證據和控制擁有者。 雲端服務可以支援合規，但若無機構特定的設計和持續營運，則無法保證合規。

韌性、高可用性與業務連續性

來源點出資料遺失、初期效能下降、安全漏洞、意外的雲端成本和切換停機時間等為遷移風險。 它提出安全控制、成本工具、Auto Scaling、多可用區 (Multi-AZ) 部署、沙盒測試和專家指導作為降低這些風險的方法。 這些功能有助於提升韌性，但它們不會自動防止風險發生，也不能證明端到端 (end-to-end) 的可用性。

Auto Scaling 有助於回應特定的容量模式，而 Multi-AZ 部署可減少區域內特定基礎架構故障的影響。 兩者皆無法確立應用程式的復原時間、復原點、交易完整性、依賴可用性，或在故障情況下的效能。 韌性設計應定義服務層級目標 (SLO)、RTO、RPO、依賴假設、備份與還原目標、跨區域復原、網路分區行為、降級模式營運，以及來自受控測試的證據。

來源建議透過 AWS Backup 進行自動備份，使用 Outposts 或其他 AWS 災難復原解決方案的災難復原計畫，CloudWatch 警報，遷移失敗時復原回地端，以及在雲端平台驗證完成前維持地端系統的冗餘。 這些是實用的主題，但實作時必須指定備份範圍、保留期、不可變性、加密、跨帳戶或跨區域副本、還原授權、還原測試、警報擁有權以及支援的復原架構。 「AWS 災難復原解決方案」本身並不是一個足夠精確的設計描述。

冗餘必須包含資料、運算、身分、網路、可觀測性、外部供應商和營運程序。 一個應用程式可以有多個執行個體，但如果它依賴一個資料庫寫入節點、一條身分路徑、一條網路路由、一個市場資料供應商，或一本未經測試的執行手冊，它依然會故障。 連續性演練應根據工作負載的風險設定，測試執行個體、可用區、區域、連線路徑、供應商、資料庫副本、憑證路徑和關鍵依賴項遺失的情況。

切換與還原原則

來源中絞殺榕模式的最後一步是將所有流量切換至雲端實作。 正式環境切換應該是分階段且可復原的，而不是單一次的切換。 團隊應定義流量路由控制、平行驗證、寫入權限、資料核對、觀察視窗、批准權限、還原閾值，以及結案的條件。

在兩個環境都處理了不同的寫入操作後，有狀態系統的還原會變得困難。 在結構描述變更、識別碼變更、外部確認、下游發布或不可逆的副作用發生後，還原也可能變得不安全。 有效的復原計畫必須明確定義權威副本、複製方向、最大還原視窗、處理傳輸中交易的方式、核對流程、使用者與對手方的溝通，以及復原的業務批准。

地端系統應根據風險評估的需求維持可用狀態，但單純保留硬體並不能使還原成為可能。 傳統路徑必須進行維護、同步、保護、監控和測試。 遷移應在最終切換前進行至少一次實際的還原或復原演練，並應記錄證據、限制與補救措施。

成本治理與 FinOps

AWS Budgets 和 Cost Explorer 在來源中被點名為管理和預測成本的工具。 它們能提供可視性與閾值警報，但並不會建立當責或防止每一次的成本超支。 遷移應定義帳戶和環境邊界、標籤 (tagging)、成本分攤、業務擁有權、預算閾值、預測審查、新服務的批准，以及異常消耗的升級呈報流程。

成本模型應涵蓋運算、資料庫、儲存、擷取、快照、備份、複製、跨區域與網際網路傳輸、日誌記錄、監控、安全服務、遷移工具、網路連線、授權、支援、設備、混合基礎架構、測試、雙軌並行、人員配置及專業服務。 它應區分固定與變動成本、正式與非正式環境成本，以及正常營運與韌性/遷移成本。

成本最佳化絕不能妥協資料保留、市場資料權限、可復原性、效能或證據保存。 生命週期策略、排程、規格調整 (rightsizing)、承諾使用量決策和資料刪除，均應根據業務與法規要求獲得批准。 單位成本指標（例如：每次投資組合估值的成本、每次回測的成本、每筆遷移紀錄的成本，或每次監控事件的成本）能讓商業案例比一份加總的雲端帳單更具意義。

監控與營運就緒度

來源提議使用 CloudWatch 進行效能監控與日誌記錄，並提議使用 CloudWatch 警報作為遷移警示。 一個具備營運就緒度的平台應該監控技術、業務、安全、資料和成本訊號。 技術訊號包括可用性、延遲百分位數、錯誤、飽和度、佇列時間、連線健康狀態與依賴狀態。 業務訊號包括交易數量、餘額、部位、資料新鮮度、核對、損益 (PnL)、報告完成度以及異常佇列。

監控必須具備閾值、基準線、通知途徑、升級呈報規則、服務擁有者、執行手冊和證據保留機制。 不會引發當責回應的警報不是有效的控制措施。 日誌應做到時間同步、存取控制、防止未經授權的修改、必要時進行遮罩，並能跨傳統與雲端環境進行關聯，以便在跨越遷移邊界時重建事件脈絡。

在每一次遷移計畫展開之前，都應審查營運就緒度。 審查應確認支援覆蓋範圍、on-call (待命) 責任、部署與還原程序、存取批准、儀表板、警報、容量、備份、復原測試、事件分類、廠商聯絡人、使用者溝通和培訓。 只有當團隊能夠在正常和降級的情況下營運新元件時，試點才算成功，而不僅僅是因為該元件能在沙盒中運行。

治理與遷移營運模型

來源建議尋求 AWS 專業服務 (Professional Services) 和 AWS 解決方案架構師的專家指導，並使用沙盒環境進行測試。 這些可以提供有用的技術支援和安全的學習環境，但無法取代機構對架構、風險承擔、安全、合規、資料治理或正式營運的當責。

企業級遷移需要高階主管贊助、遷移決策機構、業務和應用程式擁有者、雲端平台團隊、安全與隱私擁有者、資料擁有者、網路與身分擁有者，以及營運、財務、合規、法務、供應商管理，還有適當的獨立控制或模型審查團隊。 對於批准範圍、接受殘餘風險、授權切換、宣布還原，以及結案遷移發現，應有明確的職責劃分。

營運模型應包括受管的登陸區域 (landing zone)、帳戶與區域策略、策略執行、集中式日誌記錄、身分生命週期、資產盤點、漏洞與修補程式管理、基礎架構即程式碼 (IaC)、發布控制、證據保留、例外管理、第三方監督，以及定期的韌性演練。 來源並未描述這些機制，因此它們是必須進行的設計工作，而非所列 AWS 服務隱含的功能。

遷移驗收關卡

不應僅因為應用程式已在 AWS 啟動就驗收該遷移階段。 安全驗收應展示已獲批准的身分、網路路徑、加密、金鑰控制、漏洞狀態、日誌記錄和事件回應。 資料驗收應展示完整性、核對、血緣、時間點行為、保留以及異常狀況的正確處理。

效能驗收應將目標與商定的基準在具代表性與壓力工作負載下進行比較，包括依賴呼叫、並發性、延遲百分位數、吞吐量和故障行為。 韌性驗收應展示備份與還原、復原目標、依賴故障處理、監控、營運手冊，以及經過測試的還原或復原路徑。 成本驗收應證明用量、預測、所有權和單位經濟效益皆已被理解。

業務和合規驗收應確認使用者能夠完成所需的流程，報告和計算核對無誤，受監管的紀錄保持可用，資料落地和授權要求得到滿足，且控制擁有者已審查了證據。 每個關卡都應有指定的批准人與記錄在案的例外流程。 只有當殘餘風險被理解、受限、記錄在案並獲得正式接受時，遷移才能帶著殘餘風險繼續進行。

Capital One 案例研究聲明

來源引用 Capital One 作為組織遷移到 AWS 並實現敏捷性、可擴展性和成本節約的真實範例。 它連結到 AWS 案例研究頁面 https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/capital-one。 來源沒有提供遷移範圍、日期、工作負載盤點、基準線、實測節省金額、架構、監管邊界，也沒有說明哪些成果可轉移至其他機構。

這個例子可作為進一步研究的提示，但並不能作為其他金融環境也會產生相同結果的證據。 任何重複此聲明的內部簡報，都應使用目前官方的案例研究，指出其中描述的特定工作負載和成果，區分客戶報告的結果與 AWS 一般能力，並避免將公開的案例研究視為機構特定的商業案例。

來源聲明與驗證邊界

該頁面提出了幾個需要加以限定的廣泛聲明。 它將 AWS DMS 描述為提供無縫資料傳輸、將 Auto Scaling 和 Multi-AZ 描述為確保高可用性、建議 Outposts 或未指定的 AWS 災難復原解決方案作為災難復原計畫，並得出遵循這些步驟即可確保法規遵從的結論。 這些陳述是實用的起點，但都不足以作為實作或保證聲明。

來源沒有包含資料量、交易率、延遲、可用性、成本、節省、遷移持續時間、人員配置、RTO 或 RPO 的量化數據。 除了連結之外，它沒有包含 Capital One 成果的證據、沒有 AWS 帳戶或部署的證據、沒有目標架構、沒有目前產品狀態的驗證，也沒有法規控制對應。 頁面的三張圖片僅作為簡報素材，未增加任何清晰的技術、數值或架構內容。

服務名稱和描述在使用前應與最新的 AWS 文件進行核對。 特別是，所點名的 AWS Server Migration Service 可能是過時的產品參考，應確認目前支援的遷移路徑。 確切的 Elastic Load Balancing 選項、資料庫引擎、DMS 模式、部署平台、備份設計、混合服務和災難復原架構，都必須根據現有功能和機構的需求進行選擇。

內部學習總結

長遠的教訓是：業務能力、資料與控制措施必須同時遷移。 從探索和關鍵性評估開始，選擇一個受限的試點，維持清晰的真相來源，驗證資料和效能，在共存期間審慎營運雙邊系統，並只有在安全、韌性、成本、合規和業務驗收證據皆齊全時才進行切換。

AWS 服務可提供探索、運算、資料庫、應用程式託管、流量管理、資料傳輸、監控、備份、成本可視性和混合部署的建構模塊。 但它們並不能免除架構、治理、測試、營運當責或法規判斷的需求。 對金融業而言，遷移品質的衡量標準不在於將流量轉移到雲端有多快，而在於遷移完成後，機構是否能繼續保護資料、服務客戶、履行義務、從故障中復原、解釋其紀錄，以及控制其成本。

title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.33464v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

title: Two Records, One Card: Keeping the Vault and the Ledger in Agreement
description:
Every Braintree renewal is a meeting between two records that are supposed to describe the same card. The vault holds the credential — the token standing in for a number, an expiry, a billing address. The ledger holds the history — what was charged, what failed, what the failure claimed was wrong. When the two records agree, renewals are boring, which is the highest praise billing infrastructure can earn. When they disagree, the retry logic faithfully charges a card the vault already knows is dead, and the ledger records a mystery.

The most common disagreement is quiet. A customer replaces a card inside your product, or their bank issues a fresh one, and the vault learns the new credential through the account updater or a manual update. Meanwhile the subscription still points at the older payment method, or the retry was scheduled against the stale token before the update landed. Nothing errors. The charge simply goes to the wrong record, fails for a reason that sounds like the customer's fault, and starts a dunning sequence for a problem the business had already solved.

This is why Braintree recovery work is less about retry counts than about reconciliation. Before asking how many attempts a renewal deserves, ask which credential each attempt will use, and when that choice gets locked. A retry fired twelve hours after a failure may use fresher vault data than one fired twelve minutes after. Speed, usually a virtue, can be the mechanism that guarantees the stale card gets charged twice.

There is a second disagreement worth hunting: the descriptor and address record. Issuers weigh the details accompanying a charge, and a vault entry carrying an old billing postcode or a descriptor the customer no longer recognizes invites declines and disputes that look, in the ledger, like funding problems. Auditing the vault for stale addresses is unglamorous work with an outsized return, because it fixes failures before they are failures — the only truly free recovery there is.

For developers, the practical habit is a pre-retry check with teeth. At each attempt, re-read the payment method attached to the subscription rather than trusting the object captured when the case opened. Log which token was charged on every attempt, not just the outcome, so a post-mortem can distinguish "the card declined" from "we charged the retired card again." Those are different bugs with different owners, and blended logs make them indistinguishable.

The customer-facing side matters just as much. When a renewal fails despite a card on file, the message should never imply the customer did something wrong before the business has checked its own records. A surprising share of "please update your card" emails are sent to people whose new card is already sitting in the vault, attached to nothing. Each one teaches the customer that the business does not know what it holds — a lesson subscribers remember at cancellation time.

Braintree dunning read as a records problem — keeping the vault, the ledger, and the retry in agreement about which card is current walks through the platform specifics behind this, including where Braintree's native tooling helps and where the agreement has to be enforced by the layer above it.

None of this argues for more retries. It argues for retries that deserve to succeed: aimed at the current credential, carrying current details, and recorded precisely enough that a failure teaches you something. A ledger full of unexplained declines is usually a vault full of unexamined records, and the fix begins with admitting the two are one system.

That reconciliation habit is built into how Swipe Again watches for replaced cards across the renewal, so a Braintree retry never spends itself on credentials the vault has already retired — check the record first, then spend the attempt.

title: Building a Zero-Library Interactive 2D CAD Canvas in TypeScript: Cursor Zoom, Ortho/T-Junction Snapping & Layered Hit-Testing
description:
When teams start building an interactive floor-plan editor, diagramming canvas, or architectural CAD viewport in the browser, the default instinct is to pull in Fabric.js, Konva, or PixiJS.

For general-purpose drawing boards, a retained-mode scene graph makes sense. For an architectural CAD studio where every wall has a physical thickness in inches, doors live along wall centerlines, rooms are solved dynamically from a planar graph, and dragging one wall slides an entire collinear chain, a generic canvas scene graph quickly becomes a second source of truth you spend half your week fighting.

In PlanCaliber, our 2D CAD editor runs directly on a single HTML5 <canvas> element in pure TypeScript with zero canvas dependencies. All state lives in world inches (1 ft = 12 in), and rendering is a pure function of (solvedPlan, panX, panY, zoom, selection).

Here are the four core interaction primitives that make a raw HTML5 <canvas> feel like native desktop CAD.

1. World-to-Screen Math & Cursor-Anchored Zoom

Every wall vertex, opening offset, and fixture coordinate stays in world inches (+x East, +y South). The camera is just three numbers: panX, panY (in CSS pixels), and zoom (screen pixels per world inch).

interface Point2D {
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

function worldToScreen(wx: number, wy: number, panX: number, panY: number, zoom: number): Point2D {
  return {
    x: panX + wx * zoom,
    y: panY + wy * zoom
  };
}

function screenToWorld(sx: number, sy: number, panX: number, panY: number, zoom: number): Point2D {
  return {
    x: (sx - panX) / zoom,
    y: (sy - panY) / zoom
  };
}

When a user scrolls the wheel or pinches on a trackpad, the single most important invariant is cursor-anchored zoom: the exact world inch under (cx, cy) before zooming must remain under (cx, cy) after zooming.

function zoomAroundScreenPoint(
  factor: number,
  cx: number,
  cy: number,
  state: { panX: number; panY: number; zoom: number }
) {
  const before = screenToWorld(cx, cy, state.panX, state.panY, state.zoom);
  const nextZoom = Math.max(0.2, Math.min(10, state.zoom * factor));
  state.zoom = nextZoom;
  state.panX = cx - before.x * nextZoom;
  state.panY = cy - before.y * nextZoom;
}

Notice we never accumulate rounding error inside panX/panY — each step solves cx = panX + before.x * nextZoom directly. Combined with a ResizeObserver on the canvas wrapper and window.devicePixelRatio backing-store scaling, lines stay crisp at both 0.25 px/in whole-house view and 8.0 px/in cabinet-clearance zoom.

2. Zoom-Aware Snapping: Ortho-First Angle Lock + T-Junction Wall Capture

Raw pixel grids feel terrible in residential drafting. When a user draws a partition wall, they want a strict priority hierarchy:

  1. Existing corner capture (Math.max(13 / zoom, 7) inches): screen-constant pixel magnet so you can close a room reliably whether zoomed out or zoomed in.
  2. Architectural ortho-first angle lock: strongly prefer 90° (±26° capture window) with a lighter 45° detent (±7°), snapping wall length to 1/2" increments unless Shift unlocks free angle.
  3. Cross-plan guide alignment: snap x or y to existing vertices within 4" so opposite walls align effortlessly across hallways.
  4. T-junction centerline snap: project the candidate point onto every existing wall segment (t ∈ (0.02, 0.98)) so interior partitions terminate cleanly on an existing wall centerline instead of stopping 2 inches short and breaking room closure. 
function distPointToSegment(
  px: number, py: number,
  ax: number, ay: number,
  bx: number, by: number
): { dist: number; t: number; projX: number; projY: number } {
  const dx = bx - ax;
  const dy = by - ay;
  const lenSq = dx * dx + dy * dy;
  if (lenSq < 1e-6) {
    return { dist: Math.hypot(px - ax, py - ay), t: 0, projX: ax, projY: ay };
  }
  const t = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / lenSq));
  const projX = ax + t * dx;
  const projY = ay + t * dy;
  return { dist: Math.hypot(px - projX, py - projY), t, projX, projY };
}

function snapVertexPoint(
  wx: number,
  wy: number,
  zoom: number,
  vertices: { id: string; x: number; y: number }[],
  walls: { id: string; startId: string; endId: string; start: Point2D; end: Point2D }[],
  excludeVertexId?: string,
  anchorOther?: Point2D | null,
  freeAngle = false
): { x: number; y: number; snappedVertexId?: string; snappedWallId?: string } {
  // 1. Existing vertex magnet (constant ~13px screen radius, floor 7")
  const snapRadiusIn = Math.max(13 / zoom, 7);
  for (const v of vertices) {
    if (v.id === excludeVertexId) continue;
    if (Math.hypot(wx - v.x, wy - v.y) <= snapRadiusIn) {
      return { x: v.x, y: v.y, snappedVertexId: v.id };
    }
  }

  let sx = Math.round(wx);
  let sy = Math.round(wy);

  // 2. Ortho-first 90 deg / 45 deg polar snap from anchor vertex
  if (anchorOther && !freeAngle) {
    const dx = wx - anchorOther.x;
    const dy = wy - anchorOther.y;
    const len = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
    if (len > 3) {
      const deg = (Math.atan2(dy, dx) * 180) / Math.PI;
      const orthoDeg = Math.round(deg / 90) * 90;
      const diagDeg = Math.round(deg / 45) * 45;
      const snappedLen = Math.round(len * 2) / 2;

      if (Math.abs(deg - orthoDeg) <= 26) {
        const rad = (orthoDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
        sx = anchorOther.x + Math.cos(rad) * snappedLen;
        sy = anchorOther.y + Math.sin(rad) * snappedLen;
      } else if (Math.abs(deg - diagDeg) <= 7) {
        const rad = (diagDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
        sx = anchorOther.x + Math.cos(rad) * snappedLen;
        sy = anchorOther.y + Math.sin(rad) * snappedLen;
      }
    }
  }

  // 3. Cross-plan alignment to existing vertex axes
  for (const v of vertices) {
    if (v.id === excludeVertexId) continue;
    if (Math.abs(sx - v.x) <= 4) sx = v.x;
    if (Math.abs(sy - v.y) <= 4) sy = v.y;
  }

  // 4. T-junction snap onto an existing wall centerline
  const wallSnapTol = Math.max(14 / zoom, 9);
  let bestWall: { x: number; y: number; wallId: string; dist: number } | null = null;
  for (const sw of walls) {
    if (excludeVertexId && (sw.startId === excludeVertexId || sw.endId === excludeVertexId)) {
      continue;
    }
    const hit = distPointToSegment(sx, sy, sw.start.x, sw.start.y, sw.end.x, sw.end.y);
    if (hit.t > 0.02 && hit.t < 0.98 && hit.dist <= wallSnapTol) {
      if (!bestWall || hit.dist < bestWall.dist) {
        bestWall = { x: hit.projX, y: hit.projY, wallId: sw.id, dist: hit.dist };
      }
    }
  }
  if (bestWall) {
    return {
      x: Math.round(bestWall.x * 4) / 4,
      y: Math.round(bestWall.y * 4) / 4,
      snappedWallId: bestWall.wallId
    };
  }

  return { x: Math.round(sx * 4) / 4, y: Math.round(sy * 4) / 4 };
}

Quantizing every returned coordinate to 1/4" (Math.round(v * 4) / 4) aligns the interactive canvas directly with our imperial dimension formatter and planar-graph room healer.

3. Priority-Layered World Hit-Testing (Including Rotated Fixtures & Openings)

Without a retained DOM or scene-graph hit buffer, clicking the canvas calls a deterministic hitTestWorld(wx, wy) function in strict architectural Z-order:

  1. Electrical symbols (small targets on walls/ceilings — highest priority so outlets never get trapped behind cabinets)
  2. Doors & windows (tested in each wall's rotated local frame)
  3. Cabinets & furniture fixtures (rotated bounding boxes)
  4. Walls (point-to-segment distance <= wall.thicknessIn / 2 + tolIn)
  5. Enclosed rooms (ray-casting point-in-polygon fallback)

Checking rotated doors, angled islands, and furniture takes 8 lines by rotating the pointer into the object's local coordinate frame:

function pointInRotatedBox(
  px: number, py: number,
  cx: number, cy: number,
  w: number, d: number,
  rotDeg: number,
  padIn = 2
): boolean {
  const rad = (-rotDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
  const cos = Math.cos(rad);
  const sin = Math.sin(rad);
  const dx = px - cx;
  const dy = py - cy;
  const lx = dx * cos - dy * sin;
  const ly = dx * sin + dy * cos;
  return Math.abs(lx) <= w / 2 + padIn && Math.abs(ly) <= d / 2 + padIn;
}

For a residential floor plan (30–120 walls, 15–60 fixtures), a linear priority pass runs in under 0.05 milliseconds per pointer move — fast enough for live hover highlights without maintaining an R-tree or duplicate hit-canvas. And when the user activates the 1-Wall Calibrate tool, hitTestWorld short-circuits immediately to walls only so clicking a wall behind a countertop never accidentally selects the cabinet.

4. Typing Every Drag Gesture as a Discriminated Union

Canvas interaction bugs almost always come from tangled boolean flags (isDragging, isPanning, draggingWall, draggingVertex). Replacing those booleans with a single discriminated union makes illegal states unrepresentable:

type DragState =
  | { kind: 'pan'; startScreen: Point2D; origPanX: number; origPanY: number; moved: boolean }
  | { kind: 'vertex'; vertexId: string; anchorOther: Point2D | null }
  | {
      kind: 'wall';
      wallId: string;
      startWorld: Point2D;
      normX: number;
      normY: number;
      chainVertices: { id: string; orig: Point2D }[];
      moved: boolean;
    }
  | { kind: 'opening'; openingId: string; wallId: string }
  | { kind: 'fixture'; fixtureId: string; offsetX: number; offsetY: number }
  | { kind: 'electrical'; electricalId: string; offsetX: number; offsetY: number };

Look closely at the kind: 'wall' variant: when you grab a wall segment and slide it perpendicular to its normal (normX, normY), chainVertices stores the original positions of every vertex in its collinear wall chain captured on pointerdown. Moving the pointer computes total offset from startWorld rather than incremental frame deltas — eliminating drift and keeping adjacent corners square even at 120 Hz trackpad rates.

Try the Live 2D/3D Studio

You can test the zero-library 2D CAD canvas, orthogonal/T-junction wall snapping, and instant 3D cutaway sync live in your browser (no signup required to draw) at PlanCaliber.

title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
description:
arXiv:2611.34832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

title: A GBase 8a Performance Case: When NIC Bonding Slows Every DML
description:
A China-domestically developed GBase 8a MPP database often uses NIC bonding for high availability, with links spread across switches to remove a single point of failure. This case study traces a slowdown — loads, DML, everything — back to that bond.

Symptom

The customer reported extremely slow loads, some running past 2 hours without finishing. Normal loads finish within 1 minute, most in a few seconds.

Investigation

Ruling things out layer by layer:

  1. iostat on every node: all machines almost idle, CPU below 30%, IO below 10% — no single-host bottleneck.
  2. ethtool: no link degradation, all 10 GbE.
  3. /var/log/messages: no errors.
  4. Restart the database service: customer restarted the whole cluster; no change.
  5. Network from source to nodes: scp of a 1 GB file from the load source to a cluster node ran at about 50 MB/s — no obvious problem.
  6. Trace log: a trivial insert select of 17 rows took over 1 minute, and the first node was slow on Finish ACK, pointing at that node's network.
  7. Shut down the first node's service and monitor from the second server: slight improvement, but gcadmin kept reporting cluster LOCK, many SQL statements rolled back, and observation became impossible.
  8. gcware service log: the second server repeatedly dropped out of the management nodes, forcing service rebuilds, while other nodes stayed healthy. Historically the second node fbd had far more fault records than the first node fdc. The offline cause was missing heartbeats in both directions — fbd received none from the others, and the others received none from fbd. Conclusion: fbd's network fault was worse than fdc's, with a blocking path between it and every other node.

The on-site bond layout

Site IPs fall into two ranges, fbX and fcX, hinting at cross-switch traffic. The customer confirmed: 2 nodes initially, later expanded by 4 nodes on a new switch; every node had bonded NICs attached to 2 separate switches for redundancy. The system had been healthy, so the question became whether a NIC or switch failover had occurred.

Changing the bond

Force the second node's bond onto NIC 1 and restart the service: the system recovered instantly and stayed stable.

BONDING OPTS="mode=1 miimon=100 primary=eno1"

That points to a blocked or faulty switch port or cable on the second node.

Bonding exists to remove a network single point of failure, but here the standby switch of the original 2 nodes had a communication fault with the 4 newly added nodes — likely UDP broadcast not getting through, or heavy filtering. The switch happens at the OS layer, invisible to the application: traffic on the first switch is fine, and a failover to the second brings the whole database to a crawl. Looking ahead, any gbase cluster with bonded NICs should be tested for performance after failover, not just for link state — a bond that reports "up" can still be the reason a gbase cluster spends two hours on a one-minute load.

title: devnet-fixtures: funded wallets, mints and token balances from a YAML file
description:
An end-to-end test for a Solana app needs a starting state before it can check anything. There must be a wallet with some SOL to pay fees, a second wallet to receive, a mint with known decimals, token accounts, and balances the test can assert on. Most projects build that state with a setup script: a few airdrops, a mint creation, some mintTo calls, then a list of addresses copied into environment variables.

Those scripts tend to break in the same places. Devnet airdrops are rate limited and fail at random. Running the script twice creates a second mint or doubles the balances. And the addresses change on every run, so the test config has to be regenerated each time.

devnet-fixtures is a small CLI for CI pipelines and local end-to-end tests that replaces the script with a description. You write the wallets, mints and token balances you need in YAML. It creates them on a cluster, then prints their addresses as .env lines or JSON.

Two warnings from the README come first. The project is not audited, and it is for devnet, testnet and localnet only: it refuses mainnet, both by URL and by checking the RPC's genesis hash. It also writes throwaway keypairs to disk, so never fund them with real assets, and keep keysDir out of git.

What it does

The spec is one YAML file:

cluster: ${FIXTURES_CLUSTER:-localnet}   # localnet | devnet | testnet | URL
keysDir: .fixtures                        # keypairs saved here (0600), gitignored
# funder: ./funder.json                   # used when airdrops fail (devnet rate limits)
airdrop: { retries: 5, delayMs: 1000, maxSolPerRequest: 2 }
accounts:
  - { name: alice, sol: 2 }
  - { name: bob, sol: 1 }
  - { name: carol }
mints:
  - name: usdc
    decimals: 6
    authority: alice
    mintTo:
      - { owner: alice, amount: 1000 }
      - { owner: bob, amount: 12.5 }
    atas: [carol]
  - name: points
    decimals: 0
    token2022: true
    authority: bob
    mintTo: [{ owner: carol, amount: 42 }]

Running it against a local validator prints the result:

$ devnet-fixtures examples/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899 --prefix e2e
E2E_RPC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8899
E2E_ALICE_PUBKEY=FnJm4NKB…
E2E_ALICE_KEYPAIR=/…/.fixtures/alice.json
E2E_USDC_MINT=93g3h43j…
E2E_USDC_DECIMALS=6
E2E_USDC_TOKEN_PROGRAM=TokenkegQfeZyiNwAJbNbGKPFXCWuBvf9Ss623VQ5DA
E2E_USDC_ATA_BOB=AFjfVXrH…
E2E_POINTS_MINT=2egvfGXW…
...

It never prints secret keys. The output contains public keys and keypair file paths only. A test that needs to sign as alice loads the file at E2E_ALICE_KEYPAIR.

It is idempotent. Keypairs are reused from keysDir. Mints are remembered per cluster genesis hash in keysDir/state.json, and reused while they still exist. SOL balances and token balances are topped up to the target, never added on top. A second run against the same cluster makes no transactions, except to top up SOL that was spent on fees.

Airdrops are handled with care. Each request is split into chunks of maxSolPerRequest and retried with exponential backoff (delayMs × 2^n). If airdrops still fail and a funder keypair is configured, the tool sends a System transfer from the funder instead. Token operations, meaning mint creation, ATAs and minting, are retried in the same way.

Amounts are exact. Values in mintTo are UI amounts, such as 12.5, and they are converted exactly to base units with no float drift.

SPL Token and Token-2022. A mint is created with the classic token program by default, or with Token-2022 when the spec says token2022: true. The output tells the tests which program owns each mint.

How to use it

You need Node.js 20 or later. Clone and build:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/devnet-fixtures
cd devnet-fixtures
pnpm install && pnpm build

Then run it from the checkout:

node dist/cli.js examples/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899   # with solana-test-validator running
node dist/cli.js spec.yaml --format json --out fixtures.json
node dist/cli.js spec.yaml --github-env                               # also append to $GITHUB_ENV

The first command needs solana-test-validator running locally. The second writes JSON to a file instead of .env lines on standard output. The third also appends the variables to $GITHUB_ENV, so later steps of a GitHub Actions job see them without any glue code.

In GitHub Actions, the job has three steps. This is the README's sketch, adapted to a tool that was cloned and built into devnet-fixtures/ in an earlier step:

- run: solana-test-validator --reset --quiet &
- run: node devnet-fixtures/dist/cli.js test/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899 --github-env
- run: pnpm test:e2e      # reads E2E_* env vars

The cluster field accepts localnet, devnet, testnet or a URL, and it supports ${VAR:-default} expansion. That lets the same spec run against a local validator on a laptop and against devnet in CI, with one environment variable to switch.

Things to know

  • Not audited, and never for mainnet. The tool refuses a mainnet URL, and it also refuses when the RPC answers with the mainnet genesis hash, so pointing a custom URL at mainnet does not get around the check.
  • The keypairs are throwaway. They are saved in keysDir with 0600 permissions. Treat them as test material: never send real assets to them, and add the directory to .gitignore.
  • One mint authority per mint, no freeze authority. Token-2022 extensions are not configurable.
  • A harmless warning. @solana/spl-token prints "bigint: Failed to load bindings" when its optional native build is disabled. The README says this can be ignored.
  • What was tested. The 14 unit tests never touch the network. They cover spec parsing and validation, ${VAR:-default} expansion and refusing mainnet by URL. They run the main logic against an in-memory FakeChain to check chunked airdrops, backoff timings, the funder fallback, failure without a funder, idempotent re-runs, refusing a mainnet genesis hash, 0600 keypair files, and env output that contains no secrets. The RPC layer is tested against a mocked JSON-RPC fetch.
  • One manual run. The example spec was also run by hand against solana-test-validator (Agave 4.2). It created 3 funded wallets, an SPL mint and a Token-2022 mint, 4 ATAs and the balances, and a second run reused everything. The README reports no run against public devnet.

Why I built it

Test setup for a Solana project is repetitive, and the usual script has three weak points. It depends on airdrops that fail under rate limits. It is not safe to run twice. And it leaves the test code to find out which addresses were created.

A declarative spec answers all three. Because the tool knows the target state, it can compare it with the cluster and do only what is missing, which is what makes a second run free. Because it owns the airdrop step, it can chunk, back off and fall back to a funder in one place instead of in every project's script. And because it prints addresses under stable names, the tests read E2E_USDC_MINT and do not care how the mint came to exist.

The mainnet refusal and the rule about never printing secret keys come from the same idea. A tool that creates keypairs and runs inside CI logs should be hard to misuse by accident.

Get the code

The CLI, the example spec and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/devnet-fixtures. It is MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: A Developer's Quick Checklist for Messy Java Installs on Windows 11
description:
If you have ever switched between a university project, a Minecraft modding tool and a work codebase on the same Windows machine, there is a good chance you have more than one Java on it. Most of the time nobody notices. Then a build fails with a strange class version error, or a security advisory lands and you need to know exactly what is installed. Here is a short checklist to get a clear picture.

1. Find out which java actually runs

Open Terminal and run:

java -version

The first line is the version Windows uses when anything calls plain java. The next line usually names the vendor (Oracle, Microsoft, Temurin, Zulu and so on). Write down both the major version and the vendor.

Remember the two numbering styles: 1.8.0_xxx is Java 8 in the old format, while 11.0.x, 17.0.x or 21.0.x lead with the major version.

2. List every java.exe on your PATH 

where java

This prints every java.exe Windows can find on PATH, in the order it would use them. If you see three entries, the first one wins, and the other two are just sitting there. This is the single most useful command for "why is my terminal running the wrong JDK?"

3. Check JAVA_HOME separately

Many build tools and IDEs look at the JAVA_HOME environment variable instead of PATH. That means your terminal and your build can quietly use different JDKs. Check it with:

echo %JAVA_HOME%

(in Command Prompt) or $env:JAVA_HOME in PowerShell. If it points to a folder that no longer exists, or to a different major version than java -version reports, fix that first.

4. Cross-check Installed apps

PATH only shows part of the story. In Settings > Apps > Installed apps, search for "Java", "JDK", "OpenJDK", "JRE", "Temurin" and "Microsoft Build of OpenJDK", because each vendor names it differently. Older Oracle installs may show up as "Java SE" or "Java Runtime Environment".

5. Don't forget bundled runtimes

Some applications ship their own private Java. Those copies often don't appear in Installed apps and aren't on PATH, so neither command above finds them. You can't safely swap them yourself; the app's maker has to ship an update.

6. Decide what stays

A simple rule set:

  • Nothing needs it? Uninstall it. You can reinstall later if something complains.
  • A project needs a specific major version? Keep that one and keep it updated from the same vendor you installed it from.
  • Several versions you no longer use? Remove the extras from Installed apps.

After installing or removing anything, open a fresh Terminal window before re-running java -version. An old window can keep reporting stale results.

7. Update only from the vendor

Get updates from the vendor's own site: java.com for Oracle Java 8, Microsoft's download page for the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and adoptium.net for Temurin. Never trust a pop-up or ad saying "your Java is out of date".

This matters right now because of Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), which the OpenJDK advisory of 17 November 2026 lists for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds up to specific versions. TechGuide HQ's guide on how to check which Java versions are installed on Windows 11 includes the affected-version table and the vendor fixed builds, so you can compare your output against it instead of guessing.

Quick recap

java -version, where java, JAVA_HOME, Installed apps, bundled runtimes, then clean up and update from the right vendor. Five minutes, and your machine stops surprising you.

title: How Do You Pace Authorized Web Scrapers So You Stay Within a Site's Fair-Use Limits?
description:
Short answer

Pace an authorized scraper by making the client polite by default: one shared rate limiter, a concurrency cap, retries that honor Retry-After and exponential backoff, a cache so you do not refetch unchanged pages, and a hard stop when the site returns 429, 403, or a terms/robots disallow. Build this in Python around Playwright or HTTPX; use Rust only if you need a fast shared limiter or cache keyed on normalized URLs. Fair-use pacing is about staying inside the site’s published limits and your written authorization — not about looking like a human or bypassing a block.

Scope

This article is for sources you are allowed to collect: public APIs, official bulk downloads, or sites you have permission to access. It is not a guide to evading bot detection, rotating identities to dodge blocks, or ignoring robots.txt and terms of use.

If a target suspends or blocks you, stop and review the authorization and the rate. Do not add an automatic “recover and continue” path.

The pieces that matter

  1. A single limiter for the whole process, not a sleep() in one function and a free-for-all in another.
  2. Concurrency limits. Two or four workers are often enough. More workers can mean more 429s, not more throughput.
  3. Cache first. If you already have a fresh enough copy, do not hit the network.
  4. Backoff that listens. Honor Retry-After. Back off on 429 and 5xx. Give up after a fixed number of attempts and record the failure.
  5. A budget. Max requests per minute and per hour, with a default that is conservative. Make the cap configurable, and log when you hit it.

A shared limiter in Python 

import random, threading, time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, per_minute: int = 20, per_hour: int = 400):
        self.per_minute = per_minute
        self.per_hour = per_hour
        self._hits: list[float] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self) -> None:
        while True:
            with self._lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self._hits = [t for t in self._hits if now - t < 3600]
                last_min = sum(1 for t in self._hits if now - t < 60)
                last_hour = len(self._hits)
                if last_min < self.per_minute and last_hour < self.per_hour:
                    self._hits.append(now)
                    return
                wait = 60.0 if last_min >= self.per_minute else 3600.0 - (now - self._hits[0])
            time.sleep(min(wait, 30) + random.uniform(0, 0.5))

The jitter is only there to avoid a thundering herd when several workers wake at once. It is not a disguise.

Honor Retry-After and stop on a hard refusal 

import time
import httpx

def fetch(client: httpx.Client, limiter: RateLimiter, url: str, attempts: int = 5):
    for n in range(attempts):
        limiter.acquire()
        r = client.get(url, timeout=20, headers={"User-Agent": "ExampleCollector/1.0 (+contact@example.com)"})
        if r.status_code in (401, 403, 451):
            raise RuntimeError(f"stopped: HTTP {r.status_code} for {url}")
        if r.status_code == 429 or r.status_code >= 500:
            retry_after = r.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** n
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2 ** n
            time.sleep(min(delay, 120))
            continue
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r
    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts: {url}")

Identify your client honestly. Include a contact address in the user-agent if the project is long-running. Caching (ETag / If-None-Match, or a local table of URL plus fetched-at) belongs in front of fetch.

Check robots and your written scope before the first request

  • Read the site’s robots.txt and any published API limit. If a path is disallowed, skip it and log the skip.
  • Stay on the documented API or the pages you were authorized to use. Official bulk files (for example an FMCSA census download) are usually a better first choice than a page scrape.
  • Store a run log: start time, request count, 429 count, and when the limiter paused. That log is how you show the job was paced, and how you tune the cap downward if needed.

A small Rust helper can sit behind this if you want a process-wide counter that several Python workers share through a file or Redis-compatible store. The policy still lives in one place: requests per minute, requests per hour, and “stop on 403.”

When the site says no

Pause the job. Alert the operator. Do not rotate IPs, accounts, or sessions to continue. Recovery, if it happens at all, is a manual review of authorization, rate, and the site’s current terms.

FAQ

What default limits should I use?

There is no universal number. Start from the site’s documented cap if it has one. If it does not, start low (for example tens of requests per minute, not hundreds) and only raise the cap when the run log stays clean. This article does not publish a “safe” rate that will keep a site unblocked.

Is a random delay the same as fair use?

No. A random sleep does not replace a real budget, a concurrency cap, or Retry-After. Random delay is not a way to look like a person.

Should I use Playwright or a plain HTTP client?

Use a plain HTTP client when the data is in the response HTML or JSON. Use Playwright when the authorized source actually requires a browser. A browser is heavier; it still must go through the same limiter.

Can Rust help here?

Yes, as a shared limiter or a cache keyed on normalized URLs, especially if several workers run on one host. Python can still own the crawler, the parsers, and the run log.

What about personal data?

Collect only what you are allowed to store, keep a retention limit, and do not log raw personal fields in world-readable run files.

What this is not

This is not advice on bypassing access controls, CAPTCHAs, or blocks, and it does not claim that pacing will keep a SIM, IP, or account unblocked.

I'm Muhammad Afzal, a Rust and Python automation engineer at INDUS Web Agency.

title: Which permission is missing, and what does it switch off? A pure function that keeps an Android app from ever feeling dead
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code. QuickDial is not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

QuickDial adds shortcuts around chat and phone calls on Android: open a chat from a typed number, a call button inside a chat, a chat button while a call is on. Those shortcuts need up to six things from the user, spread across system dialogs and Settings pages. The early complaint was blunt: users did not know they had to allow anything.

The fix was not more screens. It was one pure Kotlin object that answers three questions, and a rule that the app is never "dead".

A snapshot in, a plan out

No Android classes go in. A Snapshot is six booleans read by the permission checker elsewhere:

data class Snapshot(
    val canPostNotifications: Boolean,
    val hasOverlay: Boolean,
    val accessibilityEnabled: Boolean,
    val notificationAccessEnabled: Boolean,
    val hasContacts: Boolean,
    val backgroundRestricted: Boolean,
)

Because it is plain data, the order, the reduced mode and the reminder rule are all unit-testable on the JVM with no emulator.

The order is a design decision, so it lives in code 

fun items(s: Snapshot): List<Item> = buildList {
    add(Item(Kind.ALERTS, s.canPostNotifications, essential = false))
    add(Item(Kind.CONTACTS, s.hasContacts, essential = false))
    add(Item(Kind.ACCESSIBILITY, s.accessibilityEnabled, essential = true))
    add(Item(Kind.OVERLAY, s.hasOverlay, essential = true))
    add(Item(Kind.CALL_ACCESS, s.notificationAccessEnabled, essential = true))
    if (s.backgroundRestricted) add(Item(Kind.BACKGROUND, granted = false, essential = true))
}

Each choice has a reason that would otherwise be lost:

  • Notifications first. It is a single system dialog, and it is what lets the app tell the user later that something else is still off. Without it, a missing permission is silent for ever.
  • The two in-app dialogs next, then the accessibility service before the two Settings pages. Once the service is running it can bring the app back to the foreground after the user visits those Settings pages, so the guided flow does not strand them there.
  • The battery item is conditional. It is only listed when the system has actually restricted the app in the background. Testing showed that the Play install ran fine without an exemption; asking for one anyway adds a scary dialog for no benefit. The list is built from evidence of a real problem, not from a general worry.

Nothing is a gate

The most important function is the shortest:

fun workingFeatures(s: Snapshot): List<Feature> = buildList {
    add(Feature.OPEN_CHAT_FROM_NUMBER)
    if (s.hasOverlay && s.accessibilityEnabled) add(Feature.CALL_BUTTON_IN_CHATS)
    if (s.hasOverlay && s.notificationAccessEnabled) add(Feature.CHAT_BUTTON_DURING_CALLS)
}

With nothing granted, the list still has one entry: opening a chat from a typed number needs none of the six. That gives the UI an honest sentence for every state. Instead of "permissions required", the card can say which shortcut is on and which is off, and what to tap to turn the next one on. Each missing item switches off one shortcut, never the whole app.

Two features each need the overlay permission plus one other thing, which is why the conditions are combined rather than one flag per feature. If the user grants the overlay but not accessibility, the call button in chats stays off and the chat button during a call does not depend on it.

Reminders only for things that matter 

fun needsReminder(s: Snapshot): Boolean = missing(s).any(Item::essential)

Notifications and contacts are marked essential = false. A user who declines contacts is not nagged: they lose name matching, not a shortcut. A reminder goes out only while something that actually switches a shortcut off is missing, and it stops by itself the moment the last essential item is granted.

Tests worth writing

Because the object is pure, the useful tests are small tables:

  1. All six granted: missing is empty, needsReminder is false.
  2. Nothing granted: workingFeatures is exactly one item, never empty.
  3. Overlay granted but accessibility off: the call button in chats is absent.
  4. backgroundRestricted false: the list has five items; true: six.
  5. Order is stable: alerts first, accessibility before overlay.

The pattern is portable to any app with a permission ladder: a snapshot of booleans, a pure ordered plan, a "what still works" function that can never return empty, and a reminder rule that looks only at essential items.

QuickDial is not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

title: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production
description:
Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier and ESLint with a single Rust-powered formatter and linter, but the migration exposes formatting edge cases that break diffs, missing rule coverage for React and accessibility plugins, and configuration translation pitfalls that stall teams mid-sprint. Developers who switch without mapping these gaps face silent behavior changes, thousands of lines of formatting churn in pull requests, and broken CI pipelines that reject commits the old tooling accepted.

A migration starts, hits formatting drift, and fails with broken diffs and CI rejections

The correct approach maps the differences before the migration starts, documents the missing plugins, and stages the rollout to isolate formatting changes from functional commits.

A migration maps gaps first, stages formatting changes, and completes cleanly

Key Takeaways

  • Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier's formatter and a subset of ESLint's rules, but React-specific linting (like eslint-plugin-react) and accessibility checks (like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y) remain gaps as of late 2026.
  • Edge-case formatting differences between Biome and Prettier include line-break decisions in complex JSX expressions, trailing-comma placement in function parameters, and quote-escaping in template literals, all of which surface as thousands of changed lines in the first formatting commit.
  • Configuration translation from .prettierrc and .eslintrc to the configuration file requires manual mapping of formatter options and an audit of which ESLint rules Biome does not yet cover, with the remainder staying in a minimal ESLint config.
  • Performance benchmarks show Biome running 2-5x faster than Prettier alone and 10-15x faster than ESLint plus Prettier combined on codebases over 100,000 lines, but the speed gain matters only if the missing rules do not force teams to keep both tools running in parallel.
  • Production readiness depends on the project: greenfield TypeScript projects with no React-specific linting needs are safe to migrate immediately, while existing React codebases require a dual-tool setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for the React-specific rules) until Biome's plugin ecosystem catches up.

What Biome 2.0 Actually Replaces (And What It Does Not)

Biome 2.0 is a formatter and a linter, not a complete ESLint replacement. The formatter matches Prettier's output on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation, but the remaining 5% consists of edge cases that produce different line breaks, indentation, or quote usage. The linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules (unused variables, missing return types, dangerous equality checks) but omits the ecosystem-specific rules that ESLint plugins provide.

What Biome replaces:

  • Prettier's formatter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, and JSON
  • ESLint's core rules for syntax errors, unused bindings, and code smells
  • Import sorting (Biome includes a built-in import organizer)

What Biome does not replace as of version 2.0:

  • React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react (prop types, hooks rules, JSX accessibility)
  • Accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y (alt text enforcement, ARIA usage)
  • Testing library rules from eslint-plugin-testing-library (async utility usage, screen queries)
  • Framework-specific linters for Next.js, Vue, or Angular

The gap means teams migrating from a full ESLint setup will keep a minimal .eslintrc for the plugin rules Biome cannot cover, running both tools in CI.

Biome covers formatting and core linting but not React-specific or accessibility plugins

Formatting Differences Between Biome and Prettier: The Edge Cases That Break Your Diffs

The migration from Prettier to Biome produces a formatting commit that touches thousands of lines because the two tools handle edge cases differently. The differences cluster in four areas: JSX expression wrapping, trailing commas, quote escaping, and import sorting.

JSX Expression Line Breaks

Prettier wraps long JSX expressions at the opening brace when the expression exceeds the print width. Biome keeps the opening brace on the same line as the tag attribute and breaks at the first operator inside the expression.

Prettier output:

<Component
  disabled={
    user.role !== "admin" && user.permissions.length === 0
  }
/>

Biome output:

<Component
  disabled={user.role !== "admin" &&
    user.permissions.length === 0}
/>

The difference surfaces in every JSX file with complex boolean expressions.

Trailing Commas in Function Parameters

Prettier adds trailing commas to multi-line function parameters when the target is ES5 or higher. Biome omits the trailing comma in arrow function parameters unless the function has type annotations.

Prettier output:

const handler = (
  event: Event,
  context: Context,
) => {
  // ...
};

Biome output:

const handler = (
  event: Event,
  context: Context
) => {
  // ...
};

Quote Escaping in Template Literals

Prettier escapes quotes inside template literals when the string contains both single and double quotes. Biome leaves the quotes unescaped unless the template literal contains an expression.

Prettier output:

const message = `Error: "value" can't be null`;

Biome output:

const message = `Error: "value" can't be null`;

The difference appears identical in this example because Biome matches Prettier's default, but in strings with mixed quotes and expressions, Biome escapes differently.

Import Sorting Order

Biome sorts imports alphabetically within three groups: external dependencies, internal modules, and relative imports. Prettier does not sort imports unless a plugin like prettier-plugin-organize-imports is installed. Teams migrating from Prettier without the plugin will see every import block reordered.

Formatter JSX line break Trailing comma Quote escaping Import sorting
Prettier At opening brace Always in ES5+ Escapes mixed quotes Plugin-dependent
Biome At first operator Omits unless typed Escapes in expressions Built-in alphabetical

The migration strategy isolates the formatting commit in a separate pull request with a title like "chore: migrate to Biome formatter" and no functional changes. Reviewers skip the diff and verify the build still passes.

A migration run exposes formatting drift, isolates changes in a formatting PR, and merges cleanly

Migration Gotchas: Configuration Translation, Git History, and CI Pipeline Changes

The migration from Prettier and ESLint to Biome requires translating configuration files, updating pre-commit hooks, and changing CI commands, all of which introduce points of failure.

Configuration Translation

Prettier stores options in .prettierrc as a flat object. Biome groups formatter options under a formatter key in the configuration file and uses different names for some settings.

Prettier config:

{
  "printWidth": 80,
  "semi": true,
  "singleQuote": false,
  "trailingComma": "es5"
}

Biome equivalent:

{
  "formatter": {
    "lineWidth": 80,
    "indentStyle": "space"
  },
  "javascript": {
    "formatter": {
      "semicolons": "always",
      "quoteStyle": "double",
      "trailingCommas": "es5"
    }
  }
}

The printWidth option becomes lineWidth, and the quote and semicolon settings move into a nested javascript.formatter object. ESLint rules translate to Biome's linter.rules object, but only the rules Biome supports. Teams must audit their .eslintrc and extract the unsupported rules into a separate minimal ESLint config.

Git History Preservation

A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs. Without this step, every line's last edit shows the formatting commit instead of the functional change.

Create .git-blame-ignore-revs:

# Migrate to Biome formatter
a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0

Configure git to use the ignore file:

git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

CI Pipeline Changes

CI pipelines running prettier --check . and eslint . must switch to biome ci or split into biome check and a minimal eslint command for the remaining rules.

Before migration (GitHub Actions):

- name: Check formatting
  run: npx prettier --check .

- name: Lint
  run: npx eslint .

After migration:

- name: Check formatting and lint
  run: npx @biomejs/biome ci

- name: Lint React rules
  run: npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json .

The biome ci command runs the formatter check and linter in a single pass, failing if either finds an issue.

A pipeline translates config, updates hooks, adds blame ignore, and switches CI commands

Rule Gaps and Missing Plugins: What Biome Still Cannot Cover in 2026

Biome's linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules but misses the ecosystem-specific checks that ESLint plugins provide. The gaps fall into three categories: React-specific rules, accessibility checks, and testing library rules.

React-Specific Rules

The eslint-plugin-react package enforces prop types, hooks dependencies, and JSX best practices. Biome does not replicate these rules as of version 2.0. Teams relying on hooks dependency checks (like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps) must keep ESLint installed.

Missing rules include:

  • react/prop-types: enforces prop type validation
  • react-hooks/rules-of-hooks: enforces hooks are called in the correct order
  • react-hooks/exhaustive-deps: warns when effect dependencies are incomplete
  • react/jsx-key: requires keys in list items

Accessibility Checks

The eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y package enforces ARIA roles, alt text on images, and keyboard navigation. Biome does not include these checks. Projects with accessibility requirements must run ESLint with the jsx-a11y plugin in parallel.

Missing rules include:

  • jsx-a11y/alt-text: requires alt text on images
  • jsx-a11y/aria-role: enforces valid ARIA roles
  • jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events: requires keyboard handlers alongside click handlers

Testing Library Rules

The eslint-plugin-testing-library package enforces best practices for React Testing Library, such as using screen queries and avoiding waitFor with side effects. Biome does not cover these rules.

Missing rules include:

  • testing-library/await-async-queries: requires await on async queries
  • testing-library/no-wait-for-side-effects: disallows side effects inside waitFor
Plugin Rules Biome covers Rules requiring ESLint
eslint-plugin-react None All React-specific
eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y None All accessibility
eslint-plugin-testing-library None All testing rules

The workaround is a dual-tool setup: Biome handles formatting and core linting, ESLint handles the plugin rules.

A codebase runs Biome for core checks and ESLint for React-specific rules

Real Migration: Step-by-Step Conversion Without Breaking Your Team's Workflow

The migration follows a staged rollout: install Biome, run the formatter once, translate the config, and update CI.

Step 1: Install Biome

Install Biome as a dev dependency:

npm install --save-dev @biomejs/biome

Step 2: Run the Formatter Once

Run the formatter to see the diff:

npx @biomejs/biome format --write .

Commit the formatting changes in a separate pull request with no functional changes.

Step 3: Translate Configuration

Create the configuration file from .prettierrc and .eslintrc:

{
  "formatter": {
    "lineWidth": 80
  },
  "javascript": {
    "formatter": {
      "semicolons": "always",
      "quoteStyle": "double",
      "trailingCommas": "es5"
    }
  },
  "linter": {
    "enabled": true,
    "rules": {
      "recommended": true
    }
  }
}

Extract the unsupported ESLint rules into .eslintrc.react.json:

{
  "extends": ["plugin:react/recommended"],
  "rules": {
    "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps": "warn",
    "jsx-a11y/alt-text": "error"
  }
}

Step 4: Update Pre-Commit Hooks

Replace Prettier and ESLint in pre-commit hooks with Biome:

Before:

{
  "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}": [
    "prettier --write",
    "eslint --fix"
  ]
}

After:

{
  "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}": [
    "biome check --apply .",
    "eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json --fix"
  ]
}

Step 5: Update CI Commands

Replace Prettier and ESLint in CI with Biome:

- name: Check formatting and lint
  run: npx @biomejs/biome ci

- name: Lint React rules
  run: npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json .

Step 6: Add Git Blame Ignore

Add the formatting commit hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs and configure git to use it:

git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

The staged rollout isolates failures to individual steps, making rollback straightforward.

Migration workflow diagram

Performance Benchmarks: Does Biome 2.0 Actually Save Time in Large Codebases

Biome's Rust implementation runs faster than Prettier's JavaScript and ESLint's Node.js runtime, but the speed difference matters only if the team is not forced to run both tools in parallel.

Benchmark Setup

The benchmark uses a TypeScript monorepo with 120,000 lines of code across 400 files. The machine is a MacBook Pro M2 with 16GB RAM. Each tool runs three times, and the median time is recorded.

Tool Median time Relative speed
Prettier alone 4.2s 1x
ESLint alone 12.8s 3x slower
Prettier + ESLint 17.0s 4x slower
Biome (format + lint) 1.1s 3.8x faster
Biome + ESLint (React) 13.9s 1.2x faster

Biome alone is 3.8 times faster than Prettier alone and 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint. When teams keep ESLint for React rules, the combined time drops to 13.9 seconds, only 1.2 times faster than the original setup.

The speed gain is real when Biome replaces both tools, but projects with React-specific linting needs see a smaller benefit because ESLint still runs.

A benchmark compares Prettier alone, ESLint alone, both together, Biome alone, and Biome with ESLint

Performance benchmark chart

Production Readiness Verdict: When to Migrate and When to Wait

Biome 2.0 is production-ready for projects that do not depend on ESLint plugins, specifically greenfield TypeScript codebases and backend services. React projects or any codebase requiring accessibility checks must run Biome alongside ESLint, which reduces the speed benefit.

Migrate immediately if:

  • The project is TypeScript-only with no React or framework-specific linting needs
  • The team can tolerate a one-time formatting commit that touches thousands of lines
  • CI performance matters and the team is willing to maintain the configuration file instead of .prettierrc and .eslintrc

Wait if:

  • The codebase relies on React-specific rules like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps or accessibility checks from jsx-a11y
  • The team cannot isolate a formatting commit or preserve git blame history
  • The CI pipeline is already fast enough that saving 10-15 seconds per run does not justify the migration effort

For teams in the middle, the hybrid setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for plugin rules) works as a stepping stone until Biome's ecosystem catches up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Biome 2.0 produce identical output to Prettier?

Biome matches Prettier on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation, but edge cases like JSX line breaks, trailing commas, and import sorting differ. The first formatting commit shows the differences.

Can Biome replace ESLint entirely in a React project?

No. Biome does not cover React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react or accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y. React projects must keep ESLint running with a minimal config for the missing rules.

How much faster is Biome than Prettier and ESLint combined?

Benchmarks on a 120,000-line codebase show Biome running 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint when it replaces both. When ESLint stays in the pipeline for React rules, the combined time is only 1.2 times faster than the original setup.

What happens to git blame after a formatting commit?

A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs. Configure git to use the ignore file with git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs.

Is the Biome configuration format stable?

The configuration schema is stable as of version 2.0 according to the Biome configuration documentation, but the nesting structure differs from Prettier's flat .prettierrc. Teams must translate the config manually.

Biome 2.0 delivers on the speed promise but not the full ESLint replacement. Greenfield TypeScript projects gain a faster, simpler toolchain. React projects gain faster formatting but keep ESLint for the gaps. The migration is a tradeoff: less tooling complexity and faster CI in exchange for maintaining a dual-tool setup until the ecosystem catches up. Projects that can live with the gaps should migrate now. Projects that cannot should wait for the React plugin support or accept the hybrid setup as the new baseline.

For related guidance on modern tooling choices, see Biome vs Oxlint Comparison 2026, Correlation IDs in AI Agents, and Create a Modern TypeScript JavaScript Library for 2023.

title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
description:
arXiv:2611.33411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.

title: Full-Page Motion Blueprints vs Component Kits: Choosing Between MovaUI, 21st.dev, Magic UI & Aceternity UI
description:
Disclosure: I build and maintain MovaUI (movaui.com). This is an honest scoping guide based on where our approach helps—and where I'd still reach for 21st.dev, Magic UI, or Aceternity UI first. (Note: MovaUI at movaui.com is unaffiliated with mova-ui.com or movavi.com.)

TL;DR: If you already have a React + Tailwind design system and just need an animated card, marquee, or button, 21st.dev, Magic UI, or Aceternity UI will get you shipped faster. If you are using Claude Code or Cursor to generate a cohesive full-page 60FPS landing page—especially across Next.js, Vue, Astro, or Vite, with looping video backgrounds and frame-budget guardrails—a full-page blueprint system like MovaUI avoids the glue-code mess.

At a glance: five engineering dimensions

Dimension MovaUI (movaui.com) 21st.dev / Magic UI / Aceternity UI
Core deliverable 900+ full-page and section motion blueprints, 218 60FPS looping video backgrounds, and 21 cloud Agent Skills Individual React, Tailwind, and Framer Motion component snippets
Framework support Framework-portable blueprints adapted to Next.js, React, Vue, Astro, Nuxt, and Vite via MIT stack-adapter-skill Primarily bound to React + Tailwind CSS (shadcn ecosystem)
Coding agent MCP Zero-auth Streamable HTTP MCP at /mcp/catalog (Official MCP Registry, Glama Grade A, mcpservers.org, mcptry 99/100 Security Grade A) Component-discovery MCP on some platforms (e.g., 21st.dev Magic) focused on single snippets
60FPS looping backgrounds 218 watermark-free 60FPS seamless loop video backgrounds with responsive React/HTML embed code No dedicated looping video background catalog
Pricing model One-time period plans with zero auto-renewal, plus non-expiring pay-per-prompt Boost Credits Free open-source primitives plus recurring Pro plans or template packs

Why stitching single-component kits breaks down on full-page AI builds

Component kits solve local UI problems cleanly. The trouble starts when you ask Claude Code or Cursor to assemble an entire landing page by pulling five unrelated animated snippets together:

  • Conflicting motion physics: One section runs a stiff spring, the next uses linear CSS keyframes, and the hero uses an uncapped requestAnimationFrame loop.
  • GPU & WebGL budget bloat: Stacking two shader backgrounds and a particle canvas without a devicePixelRatio cap or off-viewport pause turns mobile devices into hand warmers.
  • Framework friction: Copying React + Tailwind v3 shadcn snippets into a Tailwind v4, Next.js App Router ("use client" boundary), Vue, or Astro repo often triggers hydration warnings or broken styling tokens.

A full-page motion blueprint flips the direction of work. Instead of pasting isolated widgets and hoping they harmonize, you hand the coding agent one structured specification covering visual tokens, typographic rhythm, motion curves, and hard 60FPS constraints up front.

Even if you never use MovaUI, adding these four lines to your own system prompt eliminates most AI animation regressions:

- Cap canvas/WebGL pixel ratio to Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2) and dispose GPU resources on unmount.
- Pause continuous loops and shaders when off-viewport using IntersectionObserver + document.visibilitychange.
- Animate compositor-only properties (transform, opacity, clip-path); never use transition-all.
- Honor @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) with a clean static fallback and zero debug/FPS HUDs in DOM.

Choose by delivery granularity

Work backwards from what you are actually shipping this week:

  • 1–2 animated widgets inside an existing design system: Go straight to Magic UI, Aceternity UI, or 21st.dev. Dropping in a single React primitive is faster and adds zero extra workflow overhead.
  • A full landing page or 3D portfolio from 0 to 1 with Claude Code / Cursor: Use a full-page blueprint plus stack detection (stack-adapter-skill) so visual hierarchy, scroll pacing, and 60FPS limits stay consistent from Hero to Footer.
  • Hero atmosphere without shipping a 150KB+ WebGL runtime: Pair a compressed 60FPS looping video background (autoPlay muted loop playsInline + WebP poster + contrast scrim + motion-reduce:hidden) instead of forcing Three.js on every page.
  • Non-React stacks (Vue, Nuxt, Astro, vanilla Vite): Check framework portability before component count—blueprints translate cleanly across stacks, whereas React-coupled component snippets require manual rewrites.

When NOT to use MovaUI

Skip MovaUI if:

  • You just want a single copy-paste React button, bento card, or modal snippet.
  • You want a visual drag-and-drop no-code builder (MovaUI is built for developers and AI coding agents).
  • You want an npm install UI component dependency rather than prompts, backgrounds, and Agent Skills.
  • Your site is purely content/documentation with no need for hero motion or looping video backgrounds.

The lightest tool that matches your delivery scope is always the right pick.

Quick FAQ

Can Vue, Astro, or plain Vite projects actually use MovaUI blueprints?

Yes. The blueprints describe structure, tokens, motion physics, and performance budgets independently of React. Our MIT open-source stack-adapter-skill ships a zero-dependency Node script (detect-project-stack.mjs) that inspects your repo first—router mode, Tailwind v3 vs v4, installed animation libraries—so your coding agent adapts the implementation to your real stack.

Can I test the workflow without creating an account?

Yes—both the interactive prompt builder and the read-only MCP discovery layer work anonymously:

  • MIT Open-Source Starter Skills (4 skills + Node validators): github.com/beautifulboy9527/movaui-skills
