title: Secure MERN JWT Authentication: Beyond Simple Login
description:
Originally published on PEAKIQ

Source: https://www.peakiq.in/blog/stop-treating-jwt-authentication-as-just-a-login-secure-mern-auth

Stop Treating JWT Authentication as Just a Login — Secure MERN Auth in 2026

Most tutorials teach authentication as a simple three-step process:

  1. User submits email and password.
  2. Server validates credentials.
  3. Server generates a JWT and returns it.

That works for a demo.

But production authentication is not just about verifying credentials and generating a token. It is about protecting sessions, handling expired credentials, managing concurrent requests, preventing token theft, revoking access, and keeping the application secure without breaking the user experience.

In 2026, building authentication for a MERN application means thinking beyond the login endpoint.

You need an authentication architecture that can handle:

  • Access token expiration
  • Refresh token rotation
  • Secure token storage
  • Session revocation
  • Multiple devices
  • Concurrent API requests
  • XSS and CSRF risks
  • Logout and account security
  • API scaling

This is the architecture I would use for a production MERN application.

1. The Authentication Stack

For this architecture, we are using a modern MERN stack with a clear separation between authentication, session management, and application APIs.

Frontend

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Axios
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit
  • React Router
  • TanStack Query

Backend

  • Node.js
  • Express
  • TypeScript
  • MongoDB
  • JWT access tokens
  • Refresh token sessions
  • HttpOnly cookies
  • Zod validation
  • Rate limiting

The goal is not to add more dependencies.

The goal is to make authentication predictable, secure, and easy to maintain.

2. The Three Problems Most JWT Tutorials Ignore

Before writing code, we need to understand the real problems.

Problem 1: Token Exposure

If you store long-lived authentication tokens in localStorage, any JavaScript running within your origin that is compromised through XSS may be able to read those tokens.

A stolen token can become a stolen session.

Problem 2: Session Lifecycle

JWTs are stateless, but production applications still need state.

You need to know:

  • Is the user logged out?
  • Is this device still authorized?
  • Has the refresh token been rotated?
  • Has the session been revoked?
  • Has the account been disabled?

Problem 3: Concurrent Requests

Imagine a user opens the dashboard and 10 API requests start simultaneously.

The access token expires.

All 10 requests receive a 401 Unauthorized.

If every request independently calls the refresh endpoint, you can end up with:

  • 10 refresh requests
  • Refresh token rotation conflicts
  • Some requests succeeding while others fail
  • Unexpected logout
  • Duplicate retries

This is why authentication needs to be designed as a system rather than a single endpoint.

3. Stop Storing Long-Lived JWTs in localStorage

The most common implementation looks like this:

localStorage.setItem("token", accessToken);

And then:

const token = localStorage.getItem("token");

This is convenient, but it creates a major security trade-off.

JavaScript can access localStorage. If an attacker executes JavaScript through an XSS vulnerability, they may extract the stored token.

Instead, separate the responsibilities.

Token Storage Purpose
Access token In-memory state Authenticate API requests
Refresh token HttpOnly cookie Renew authentication
Refresh token hash MongoDB Validate and revoke sessions

The access token should be short-lived.

The refresh token should be protected by the browser and managed by the server.

The server should store a hash of the refresh token rather than the raw token.

This reduces the impact of a database leak.

4. Authentication Architecture

The authentication lifecycle looks like this:

flowchart TD
    A[User Login] --> B[Validate Credentials]
    B --> C[Create Session]
    C --> D[Generate Access Token]
    C --> E[Generate Refresh Token]
    D --> F[Return Access Token]
    E --> G[Set HttpOnly Cookie]
    F --> H[React Stores Token in Memory]
    H --> I[API Request]
    I --> J{Access Token Valid?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Return API Response]
    J -->|No| L[Refresh Endpoint]
    L --> M[Validate Refresh Session]
    M --> N[Rotate Refresh Token]
    N --> O[Issue New Access Token]
    O --> P[Retry Original Request]

The important difference is that the refresh token is never returned inside the JSON response.

The browser stores it in a protected cookie.

5. Short-Lived Access Tokens

Access tokens should not remain valid for days.

For most applications, a short lifetime such as 10–15 minutes is a reasonable starting point. The exact duration depends on the application's threat model and usability requirements.

Example JWT payload:

{
  "sub": "user_123",
  "sid": "session_456",
  "iss": "api.peakiq.in",
  "aud": "peakiq-client",
  "iat": 1764200000,
  "exp": 1764200900
}

The token contains:

  • sub — user ID
  • sid — session ID
  • iss — issuer
  • aud — intended audience
  • iat — issued at
  • exp — expiration

Do not put sensitive user data into JWT payloads.

JWT payloads are encoded, not encrypted.

Access token generation 

import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

export function createAccessToken(
  userId: string,
  sessionId: string
) {
  return jwt.sign(
    {
      sid: sessionId,
    },
    process.env.ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET!,
    {
      subject: userId,
      issuer: "api.peakiq.in",
      audience: "peakiq-client",
      expiresIn: "15m",
      algorithm: "HS256",
    }
  );
}

In production, keep signing secrets outside your source code and use strong, separate secrets for access and refresh token mechanisms.

6. Refresh Tokens Are Sessions

The refresh token is what keeps the user logged in after the access token expires.

Instead of treating refresh tokens as permanent credentials, treat them as sessions that can be:

  • Rotated
  • Revoked
  • Expired
  • Audited
  • Associated with a device

I prefer using a cryptographically random opaque refresh token instead of a long-lived JWT refresh token.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export function createRefreshToken() {
  return crypto.randomBytes(64).toString("hex");
}

export function hashRefreshToken(token: string) {
  return crypto
    .createHash("sha256")
    .update(token)
    .digest("hex");
}

The refresh token itself is sent to the browser.

The hash is stored in MongoDB.

7. MongoDB Session Model

A session collection gives us control over authentication beyond JWT expiration.

import { Schema, model } from "mongoose";

const authSessionSchema = new Schema(
  {
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      ref: "User",
      required: true,
      index: true,
    },

    refreshTokenHash: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      unique: true,
    },

    deviceName: String,
    ipAddress: String,
    userAgent: String,

    expiresAt: {
      type: Date,
      required: true,
    },

    revokedAt: {
      type: Date,
      default: null,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
  }
);

authSessionSchema.index({ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 });
authSessionSchema.index({ userId: 1, revokedAt: 1 });

export const AuthSession = model(
  "AuthSession",
  authSessionSchema
);

This gives us a foundation for:

  • Logout
  • Device management
  • Session expiration
  • Revoking individual devices
  • Revoking all sessions
  • Security audit trails

The TTL index is cleanup automation. It is not a substitute for checking session expiration in the authentication logic.

8. Login: Create the Session

When the user successfully authenticates, create:

  1. A session ID
  2. An access token
  3. A refresh token
  4. A hashed refresh token stored in MongoDB
  5. An HttpOnly cookie containing the refresh token 
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { AuthSession } from "../models/auth-session";
import { createAccessToken } from "../utils/access-token";
import { createRefreshToken, hashRefreshToken } from "../utils/refresh-token";

export async function createAuthSession(
  userId: string,
  res: any
) {
  const sessionId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const refreshToken = createRefreshToken();

  const refreshTokenHash = hashRefreshToken(refreshToken);

  await AuthSession.create({
    userId,
    refreshTokenHash,
    expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
  });

  const accessToken = createAccessToken(userId, sessionId);

  res.cookie("refreshToken", refreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
    maxAge: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });

  return {
    accessToken,
  };
}

Notice what we return.

{
  "accessToken": "..."
}

We do not return the refresh token.

The refresh token is delivered through the cookie.

The cookie configuration must match your deployment topology. If your frontend and backend are cross-site, you may need SameSite=None with Secure, plus appropriate CSRF protections.

9. Refresh Token Rotation

A refresh endpoint is one of the most important parts of authentication.

When a refresh token is used:

  1. Validate the existing token.
  2. Hash it.
  3. Find the matching session.
  4. Reject expired or revoked sessions.
  5. Generate a new refresh token.
  6. Replace the stored hash.
  7. Issue a new access token.
  8. Update the browser cookie. 
import { Request, Response } from "express";
import { AuthSession } from "../models/auth-session";
import { hashRefreshToken, createRefreshToken } from "../utils/refresh-token";
import { createAccessToken } from "../utils/access-token";

export async function refreshSession(
  req: Request,
  res: Response
) {
  const currentToken = req.cookies.refreshToken;

  if (!currentToken) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Authentication required",
    });
  }

  const currentHash = hashRefreshToken(currentToken);

  const session = await AuthSession.findOne({
    refreshTokenHash: currentHash,
    revokedAt: null,
    expiresAt: { $gt: new Date() },
  });

  if (!session) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Session expired or invalid",
    });
  }

  const nextRefreshToken = createRefreshToken();
  const nextHash = hashRefreshToken(nextRefreshToken);

  const updated = await AuthSession.findOneAndUpdate(
    {
      _id: session._id,
      refreshTokenHash: currentHash,
      revokedAt: null,
    },
    {
      $set: {
        refreshTokenHash: nextHash,
      },
    },
    {
      new: true,
    }
  );

  if (!updated) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Session no longer valid",
    });
  }

  const accessToken = createAccessToken(
    session.userId.toString(),
    session._id.toString()
  );

  res.cookie("refreshToken", nextRefreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
    maxAge: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });

  return res.json({
    accessToken,
  });
}

Why rotation matters

If a refresh token is stolen and then reused after the legitimate user has rotated it, that reuse can be a signal of token theft.

A production implementation should consider refresh token reuse detection and session-family revocation. It should also handle refresh requests that race with one another, because strict rotation can cause legitimate concurrent requests to fail if coordination is missing.

10. React: Keep the Access Token in Memory

The frontend only needs the access token to make API requests.

You can store it in Zustand:

import { create } from "zustand";

type AuthState = {
  accessToken: string | null;
  setAccessToken: (token: string | null) => void;
};

export const useAuthStore = create<AuthState>((set) => ({
  accessToken: null,

  setAccessToken: (accessToken) => {
    set({ accessToken });
  },
}));

This token disappears when the application reloads.

That is intentional.

On application startup, the frontend calls the refresh endpoint. The browser sends the HttpOnly cookie automatically, and the backend issues a new access token if the session is still valid.

11. Axios: Handle Expired Tokens Automatically

A production application cannot ask users to log in again every 15 minutes.

Axios interceptors can handle token expiration automatically.

The architecture needs to:

  • Add the access token to outgoing requests.
  • Detect authentication failures.
  • Refresh the session.
  • Retry the original request.
  • Prevent multiple simultaneous refresh calls.

Axios client 

import axios from "axios";

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  withCredentials: true,
});

Request interceptor 

import { useAuthStore } from "../store/auth-store";

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = useAuthStore.getState().accessToken;

  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }

  return config;
});

The access token remains in memory and is attached to requests only when needed.

12. Prevent Multiple Refresh Requests

This is where many applications become unreliable.

If 10 requests fail simultaneously, they should not trigger 10 refresh requests.

Instead, use a single shared refresh operation within the current JavaScript runtime.

let refreshPromise: Promise<string> | null = null;

async function refreshAccessToken() {
  if (!refreshPromise) {
    refreshPromise = api
      .post("/api/auth/refresh")
      .then((response) => {
        const accessToken = response.data.accessToken;

        useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(accessToken);

        return accessToken;
      })
      .finally(() => {
        refreshPromise = null;
      });
  }

  return refreshPromise;
}

This ensures requests in the same tab share one refresh operation.

It does not coordinate refresh requests across multiple browser tabs. Multi-tab coordination may require an additional mechanism such as BroadcastChannel, shared state, or server-side handling of rotation races.

13. Retry the Original Request

Once the refresh completes, retry the original API request with the new access token.

api.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,

  async (error) => {
    const originalRequest = error.config;

    if (
      error.response?.status === 401 &&
      originalRequest &&
      !originalRequest._retry &&
      !originalRequest.url?.includes("/auth/refresh")
    ) {
      originalRequest._retry = true;

      try {
        const accessToken = await refreshAccessToken();

        originalRequest.headers.Authorization =
          \`Bearer \${accessToken}\`;

        return api(originalRequest);
      } catch (refreshError) {
        useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

        return Promise.reject(refreshError);
      }
    }

    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

The _retry flag prevents infinite retry loops.

Without it, a failed retry could trigger another refresh indefinitely.

14. Application Startup Authentication

When React starts, it does not know whether the user has an active session.

The access token is stored only in memory, so the application needs to restore authentication.

export async function restoreSession() {
  try {
    const response = await api.post("/api/auth/refresh");

    useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(
      response.data.accessToken
    );

    return true;
  } catch {
    useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

    return false;
  }
}

Use this during application bootstrap.

While session restoration is in progress, show a loading state instead of briefly rendering the login screen.

This prevents unnecessary redirects and improves the user experience.

15. HttpOnly Cookies, CORS, and CSRF

Using HttpOnly cookies solves one problem.

It does not solve every authentication security problem.

Cookie configuration 

res.cookie("refreshToken", refreshToken, {
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: true,
  sameSite: "strict",
  path: "/api/auth",
});

What these options do

Option Purpose
HttpOnly Prevent JavaScript from reading the cookie
Secure Send the cookie only over HTTPS
SameSite Restrict cross-site cookie behavior
Path Restrict where the cookie is sent

CORS configuration 

import cors from "cors";

app.use(
  cors({
    origin: "https://app.peakiq.in",
    credentials: true,
  })
);

Do not use a wildcard origin with credentialed requests.

Your frontend and backend deployment configuration must agree about cookie domain, SameSite, and HTTPS requirements.

CSRF protection

Because cookies are automatically sent by browsers, cookie-based authentication needs a CSRF strategy.

Depending on your deployment, use:

  • Strict origin validation
  • Appropriate SameSite settings
  • CSRF tokens for state-changing requests where required
  • Avoid state-changing GET requests

Do not assume HttpOnly prevents CSRF.

It protects cookie confidentiality from JavaScript, not the browser's automatic cookie sending behavior.

16. Logout Means Revoking the Session

A frontend logout that only clears Zustand is incomplete.

useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

That removes the access token from memory, but the refresh session may still be active.

The backend should revoke the session and clear the cookie.

export async function logout(req: Request, res: Response) {
  const refreshToken = req.cookies.refreshToken;

  if (refreshToken) {
    const hash = hashRefreshToken(refreshToken);

    await AuthSession.updateOne(
      {
        refreshTokenHash: hash,
      },
      {
        $set: {
          revokedAt: new Date(),
        },
      }
    );
  }

  res.clearCookie("refreshToken", {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
  });

  return res.status(204).send();
}

Then clear frontend state:

await api.post("/api/auth/logout");

useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

This creates a real logout.

The refresh session is no longer valid, and the browser cookie is cleared.

For a production application, users should also be able to see and revoke their active sessions from their account security page.

17. Modular Monolith Architecture

Authentication should not be mixed into controllers and utility files randomly.

Keep it inside a dedicated module.

src/
├── modules/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.ts
│   │   ├── auth.service.ts
│   │   ├── auth.routes.ts
│   │   ├── auth.validation.ts
│   │   ├── auth.middleware.ts
│   │   ├── session.service.ts
│   │   └── auth.types.ts
│   │
│   ├── users/
│   │   ├── user.controller.ts
│   │   ├── user.service.ts
│   │   ├── user.model.ts
│   │   └── user.routes.ts
│   │
│   └── projects/
│       ├── project.controller.ts
│       ├── project.service.ts
│       ├── project.model.ts
│       └── project.routes.ts
│
├── middleware/
│   ├── error-handler.ts
│   ├── rate-limit.ts
│   └── validation.ts
│
├── utils/
│   ├── jwt.ts
│   ├── crypto.ts
│   └── logger.ts
│
├── config/
│   ├── database.ts
│   ├── cors.ts
│   └── environment.ts
│
└── app.ts

The auth module owns authentication.

The user module owns user data.

The middleware layer owns reusable request behavior.

This structure is easier to test, audit, and maintain.

18. MongoDB Indexes That Matter

Authentication queries should not become slow as sessions grow.

At minimum, consider indexes for:

authSessionSchema.index(
  { refreshTokenHash: 1 },
  { unique: true }
);

authSessionSchema.index({
  userId: 1,
  revokedAt: 1,
});

authSessionSchema.index(
  { expiresAt: 1 },
  { expireAfterSeconds: 0 }
);

These support:

  • Refresh token lookup
  • Session management by user
  • Cleanup of expired session records

Do not rely only on TTL cleanup to validate sessions.

Every refresh operation must explicitly verify expiration and revocation.

19. Scaling Authentication

You do not need microservices to build secure authentication.

A modular monolith is usually enough to start.

Phase 1 — MVP

  • Login and registration
  • Short-lived access tokens
  • Refresh sessions
  • HttpOnly cookies
  • Logout
  • Rate limiting
  • Password hashing

Phase 2 — Production Traction

  • Device sessions
  • Refresh token rotation
  • Session revocation
  • Reuse detection
  • Security audit logs
  • Multi-tab coordination
  • Email verification
  • Password reset

Phase 3 — Scale

  • Centralized session management
  • Redis for distributed coordination if needed
  • Dedicated security monitoring
  • Risk-based authentication
  • MFA
  • Suspicious login detection
  • Session policy enforcement

The architecture should evolve based on actual traffic and security requirements.

20. Authentication Gotchas

These are the mistakes I would watch closely during implementation.

1. HttpOnly does not prevent XSS

It prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie.

XSS can still perform actions as the authenticated user.

2. Refresh rotation creates race conditions

Multiple refresh requests can invalidate each other if the backend uses strict single-token rotation.

3. Never return refresh tokens in JSON

Use protected cookies instead.

4. Access tokens and refresh tokens should have different purposes

Use different secrets or signing keys if JWTs are used for both, and validate token type, issuer, audience, and expiration.

5. Logout should revoke server-side state

Clearing frontend memory alone is not enough.

6. Cookies require CSRF consideration

HttpOnly is not a CSRF defense.

7. Never log tokens

Avoid logging:

  • Authorization headers
  • Refresh cookies
  • Passwords
  • Authentication request bodies

8. A JWT is not a complete session management system

You still need to manage the session lifecycle.

21. Before Calling Authentication Production-Ready

Here is the checklist I would use before shipping.

  • [ ] Passwords are hashed with a suitable password hashing algorithm
  • [ ] Access tokens are short-lived
  • [ ] Refresh tokens are securely generated
  • [ ] Refresh tokens are hashed before database storage
  • [ ] Refresh token rotation is implemented
  • [ ] Refresh reuse detection is considered
  • [ ] Session revocation is implemented
  • [ ] Logout revokes the server session
  • [ ] Refresh cookie uses HttpOnly
  • [ ] Secure cookies are enabled in production
  • [ ] SameSite policy is explicitly configured
  • [ ] CORS uses an explicit origin allowlist
  • [ ] CSRF protections are in place
  • [ ] Login and refresh endpoints are rate-limited
  • [ ] Concurrent refresh requests are handled
  • [ ] Token secrets are not committed to source control
  • [ ] Tokens are never logged
  • [ ] Session expiration is validated server-side
  • [ ] Authentication failures do not leak sensitive information

Conclusion

JWT authentication is easy to implement.

Secure JWT authentication is much harder.

The difference between a tutorial implementation and a production implementation is not the JWT library. It is how you handle the entire session lifecycle.

A production MERN authentication system needs to think about:

  • Token security
  • Refresh rotation
  • Session persistence
  • Concurrent requests
  • Device management
  • Revocation
  • Cookie security
  • CSRF
  • XSS
  • Scalability

The biggest mistake is treating authentication as a login endpoint.

Authentication is a lifecycle.

If you design that lifecycle correctly from the beginning, your application becomes safer, easier to maintain, and much more predictable as it grows.

title: Build a Daily Game for Reddit with Devvit, React and Redis
description:
By the end of this tutorial, you'll have a daily game running inside a Reddit post. Players make one guess a day, see how they did against everyone else, and a new round posts itself every morning.

We'll build it the way I built Trendline, my entry for Reddit's Game of the Day hackathon. In Trendline, you see the first part of a real chart, draw where the line goes next, then see what actually happened next to the crowd's average guess. The full code is on GitHub, and every snippet below comes from it.


What we're building toward: a reveal that compares your guess with the crowd's. Player names are blurred.

How a Reddit game works

Think of a Devvit app as a tiny website that lives inside a Reddit post. It has a front end (React, in our case), a small server, and its own Redis database. Reddit hosts all three, so there's nothing to deploy to a cloud provider and no database to set up.

The post has two views:

  • The preview that people see while scrolling their feed
  • The expanded game that opens when they tap to play

The server knows which post it's running in and who is playing, so you don't need to build any login.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js, at the version in the template's .nvmrc file
  • Git
  • A Reddit account
  • VS Code or any editor, with its terminal
  • The Devvit CLI, which the template installs for you (I used version 0.15.4)

Step 1: Create the project from Reddit's React template

Reddit maintains a starter project with React, Vite, Hono and TypeScript already wired together. Let's clone it and install its packages:

git clone https://github.com/reddit/devvit-template-react my-daily-game
cd my-daily-game
npm install

You should see added ... packages at the end. Warnings about deprecated packages are normal and safe to ignore.

The template comes with its own git history pointing at Reddit's repository. If you plan to push your game to GitHub, start fresh:

rm -rf .git
git init
git branch -M main

Step 2: Log in and register the app

Log in to Reddit from the terminal:

npx devvit login

A browser tab opens. Log in, click Allow, then come back to the terminal.

Now start a playtest:

npm run dev

Two things tripped me up here, so let's handle them before they happen.

"Please finish setting up your developer account." Choose Open developer account page in browser, accept the developer terms, then come back and choose I have finished setting up my developer account; check again.

"Your app doesn't exist yet." Devvit reads your app's name from devvit.json. If that name was never registered with Reddit, playtest refuses to run, and npx devvit init may say the app is already initialized. Register it properly with:

npx devvit init --force

When it's done, npm run dev should print something like:

✓ Playtest ready
➜ URL: https://www.reddit.com/r/your_app_dev/?playtest=your-app

Devvit creates a private test subreddit for you and installs the app there. Leave this terminal running. Every time you save a file, it rebuilds and uploads, and you refresh the page to see the change.

Step 3: Configure devvit.json

devvit.json tells Reddit what your app contains. Here's Trendline's, with the parts that matter for a daily game:

{
  "$schema": "https://developers.reddit.com/schema/config-file.v1.json",
  "name": "your-app-name",
  "post": {
    "dir": "dist/client",
    "entrypoints": {
      "default": { "inline": true, "entry": "splash.html" },
      "game": { "entry": "game.html" }
    }
  },
  "server": { "dir": "dist/server", "entry": "index.cjs" },
  "menu": {
    "items": [
      {
        "label": "Post today's Trendline",
        "description": "Create today's Trendline chart post",
        "location": "subreddit",
        "forUserType": "moderator",
        "endpoint": "/internal/menu/post-create"
      }
    ]
  },
  "triggers": { "onAppInstall": "/internal/triggers/on-app-install" },
  "scheduler": {
    "tasks": {
      "daily-post": {
        "endpoint": "/internal/scheduler/daily-post",
        "cron": "5 0 * * *"
      }
    }
  }
}

Here's what each part does:

  • post.entrypoints defines the two views. default is the preview, shown inline in the feed. game is the expanded view.
  • server points at your built server code.
  • menu adds a moderator-only menu item to the subreddit, handy for posting a round by hand.
  • triggers runs code when the app is installed. We'll use it to create the first post.
  • scheduler runs a task on a cron schedule. 5 0 * * * means 00:05 UTC every day.

Keep the name that Devvit registered for you in Step 2.

Step 4: Store one guess per player in Redis

A daily game needs one rule above all: one guess per player per day. The tricky part is a player double tapping the submit button. Two requests arrive at almost the same moment, both check "has this player played?", both see "no", and both save.

Redis has an atomic counter that solves this. incrBy increases a number and returns the new value in one step, so only one request can ever see 1:

const keys = {
  playedFlag: (day: number, userId: string) => `day:${day}:played:${userId}`,
  guess: (day: number, userId: string) => `day:${day}:guess:${userId}`,
  sums: (day: number) => `day:${day}:sums`,
  count: (day: number) => `day:${day}:count`,
  scores: (day: number) => `day:${day}:scores`,
};

export async function saveGuess(
  day: number,
  userId: string,
  username: string,
  guess: number[]
): Promise<{ ok: true; streak: Streak } | { ok: false }> {
  // incrBy is atomic, so two quick taps can't both count.
  const first = (await redis.incrBy(keys.playedFlag(day, userId), 1)) === 1;
  if (!first) return { ok: false };

  const chart = chartForDay(day);
  const score = scoreGuess(chart, guess);
  await redis.set(keys.guess(day, userId), JSON.stringify({ guess, score }));
  for (let i = 0; i < guess.length; i++) {
    await redis.hIncrBy(keys.sums(day), String(i), toFraction(chart, guess[i]!));
  }
  await redis.incrBy(keys.count(day), 1);
  await redis.zAdd(keys.scores(day), { member: username, score });
  const streak = await updateStreak(userId, day);
  return { ok: true, streak };
}

redis is imported from @devvit/web/server. Every key includes the day, so each round's data stays separate, and old posts keep their own results.

The last two lines feed the leaderboard and streaks. zAdd puts the score in a sorted set, which Redis keeps in order for you.

Step 5: Build the crowd average from running totals

The obvious way to show the crowd's average is to read every guess and average them. That gets slower with every player.

Instead, look at the hIncrBy loop in the code above. Each guess is converted to a position on the chart between 0 and 1, scaled to a whole number, and added to a running total for each point on the line. Together with the player count, that's everything you need:

const players = await playerCount(day);
let crowd: number[] | null = null;
if (players > 0) {
  const sums = await redis.hGetAll(keys.sums(day));
  crowd = actual.map((_, i) =>
    fromFraction(chart, Number(sums[String(i)] ?? 0) / players)
  );
}

Two Redis reads, however many people have played. The conversion helpers are short:

export const FRACTION_SCALE = 10000;

export function toFraction(chart: Chart, value: number): number {
  const f = (value - chart.yMin) / (chart.yMax - chart.yMin);
  return Math.round(Math.min(1, Math.max(0, f)) * FRACTION_SCALE);
}

export function fromFraction(chart: Chart, scaled: number): number {
  return chart.yMin + (scaled / FRACTION_SCALE) * (chart.yMax - chart.yMin);
}

Storing whole numbers matters because hIncrBy adds integers. Positions between 0 and 10,000 keep plenty of precision.

Step 6: Serve the game from a Hono API

The server is a Hono app. Routes under /api are called by your React client. Routes under /internal are called by Reddit itself, for the menu, triggers and scheduler:

import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';
import { createServer, getServerPort } from '@devvit/web/server';
import { api } from './routes/api';
import { menu } from './routes/menu';
import { scheduler } from './routes/scheduler';
import { triggers } from './routes/triggers';

const app = new Hono();
const internal = new Hono();

internal.route('/menu', menu);
internal.route('/triggers', triggers);
internal.route('/scheduler', scheduler);

app.route('/api', api);
app.route('/internal', internal);

serve({
  fetch: app.fetch,
  createServer,
  port: getServerPort(),
});

The game needs two endpoints. /api/init loads everything the client needs when the post opens. context tells you which post this is and who is playing:

api.get('/init', async (c) => {
  try {
    const { postId, userId } = context;
    if (!postId) {
      return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: 'No post in context' }, 400);
    }
    const day = await getPostDay(postId);
    const username = (await reddit.getCurrentUsername()) ?? null;
    const reveal = userId ? await buildReveal(day, userId) : null;
    return c.json<InitResponse>({
      day,
      chart: publicChart(chartForDay(day)),
      players: await playerCount(day),
      username,
      loggedIn: Boolean(userId),
      reveal,
      streak: await getStreak(userId),
    });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('init failed', error);
    return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: 'Could not load the game' }, 400);
  }
});

Notice publicChart. It sends only the part of the chart the player is allowed to see. The answer stays on the server until they've played, so nobody can find it in the browser's network tab.

/api/guess validates the guess and saves it:

api.post('/guess', async (c) => {
  try {
    const { postId, userId } = context;
    if (!postId || !userId) {
      return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: 'Log in to play' }, 401);
    }
    const body = await c.req.json<GuessRequest>();
    const day = await getPostDay(postId);
    const chart = chartForDay(day);
    const expected = hiddenValues(chart).length;
    const guess = body.guess;
    if (
      body.day !== day ||
      !Array.isArray(guess) ||
      guess.length !== expected ||
      guess.some((v) => typeof v !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(v))
    ) {
      return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: 'That guess looks incomplete' }, 400);
    }
    const clamped = guess.map((v) => Math.min(chart.yMax, Math.max(chart.yMin, v)));
    const username = (await reddit.getCurrentUsername()) ?? 'anonymous';
    const saved = await saveGuess(day, userId, username, clamped);
    if (!saved.ok) {
      return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: "You've already played this one" }, 409);
    }
    const reveal = await buildReveal(day, userId);
    return c.json<GuessResponse>({ reveal: reveal!, streak: saved.streak });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('guess failed', error);
    return c.json<ErrorResponse>({ status: 'error', message: 'Could not save your guess' }, 400);
  }
});

Never trust the client. The server checks the day, the length of the guess, and that every value is a real number, then clamps values to the chart's range before saving.

Step 7: Build the React client

The client is two small React apps, one per entrypoint. Each calls /api/init when it loads.

The preview in the feed should be light and make sense in two seconds. Its job is to get people to tap. requestExpandedMode opens the game entrypoint you defined in devvit.json:

import { requestExpandedMode } from '@devvit/web/client';

function Splash() {
  const [data, setData] = useState<InitResponse | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    loadGame().then(setData).catch(() => setData(null));
  }, []);

  return (
    <main className="splash">
      <p className="kicker">Trendline{data ? ` #${data.day + 1}` : ''}</p>
      <h1>{data?.chart.title ?? 'Where does the line go next?'}</h1>
      {data && <Chart chart={data.chart} />}
      <button onClick={(e) => requestExpandedMode(e.nativeEvent, 'game')}>
        {data?.reveal ? `You scored ${data.reveal.score}. See the results` : 'Draw the rest'}
      </button>
    </main>
  );
}

The button text changes once you've played, so returning players go straight to their results.

Calling the API from the client is a plain fetch to a relative path. Devvit routes it to your server:

async function request<T>(path: string, init?: RequestInit): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(path, {
    ...init,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(init?.headers ?? {}) },
  });
  const body = (await res.json()) as T | ErrorResponse;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error((body as ErrorResponse).message ?? 'Something went wrong');
  return body as T;
}

export const loadGame = () => request<InitResponse>('/api/init');

export const sendGuess = (day: number, guess: number[]) =>
  request<GuessResponse>('/api/guess', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ day, guess }),
  });

Step 8: Post a new round every day

A daily game needs a daily post. One function creates it and remembers which day it belongs to:

import { reddit } from '@devvit/web/server';
import { chartForDay, dayNumber } from '../../shared/game';
import { setPostDay } from './store';

export const createPost = async (day: number = dayNumber()) => {
  const chart = chartForDay(day);
  const post = await reddit.submitCustomPost({
    title: `Trendline #${day + 1}: ${chart.title}. Where does the line go next?`,
  });
  await setPostDay(post.id, day);
  return post;
};

Storing the day against the post ID is what keeps old posts playable. Yesterday's post still loads yesterday's chart.

The scheduler task from devvit.json calls it every day:

import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { createPost } from '../core/post';

export const scheduler = new Hono();

scheduler.post('/daily-post', async (c) => {
  try {
    const post = await createPost();
    console.log(`Daily Trendline post created: ${post.id}`);
    return c.json({ status: 'success' }, 200);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(`Daily post failed: ${error}`);
    return c.json({ status: 'error' }, 400);
  }
});

The menu item and install trigger call the same createPost function, so there's one place to change if you rename your posts.

To decide which day it is, count days since a fixed start date in UTC:

export const EPOCH_UTC = Date.UTC(2026, 10, 25);
const DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

export function dayNumber(now: number = Date.now()): number {
  return Math.floor((now - EPOCH_UTC) / DAY_MS);
}

Set EPOCH_UTC to your own launch date. Note that JavaScript months start at 0, so 10 is November.

Step 9: Playtest, deploy and install

While npm run dev is running, open the playtest URL and play your game. Check the preview, the expanded view, and what happens when you submit twice.

When you're happy with it, upload a release version:

npm run deploy

Then create a public subreddit for your game and install the app there:

npx devvit install YourSubredditName

Leave out the r/. The install trigger creates the first post straight away.

One thing I didn't expect: Reddit held my app's first posts until I approved them as the subreddit's moderator. New app accounts don't have much history, so check your Mod Queue after each daily post until your app's posts go up on their own.

Recap

You now have a daily Reddit game with:

  • Two views: a light preview in the feed and an expanded game
  • One guess per player per day, enforced with an atomic Redis counter
  • A crowd average built from running totals, so it stays fast as players grow
  • A new post every day from the Devvit scheduler, plus a moderator menu item to post by hand

The same pattern works for much more than charts. A daily poll where you guess how the crowd will vote, a prediction game for sports results, or a community challenge that builds up over a week all need the same pieces: one action per player, a shared total, and a fresh post each day.

The complete code for Trendline is on GitHub, and you can play today's chart at r/TrendlineGame.

title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.33897v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

title: P-FedSkill: A Personalized Federated Skill Learning Framework under Task Heterogeneity
description:
arXiv:2611.33707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skill learning has become an important way to improve agent performance. However, agent trajectories often contain sensitive information and cannot be shared across clients, hindering collaborative skill learning. To tackle this issue, federated skill learning (FSL) has emerged as a solution by distilling trajectories into compact skill representations and uploading them to a central server for sharing. However, existing FSL methods typically share skills based on skill similarity without considering their contributions to heterogeneous tasks across clients, thereby degrading agent performance. To address this challenge, we propose P-FedSkill, a personalized FSL framework that comprises three key components: local skill extraction (LSE), personalized skill selection (PSS), and task-aware skill routing (TASR). Specifically, LSE first extracts skill patches (i.e., task applicability conditions and execution strategies) and task execution outcomes from trajectories. PSS then uses these outcomes to evaluate each skill patch's performance on client tasks and incorporates its task applicability condition to construct a personalized skill set for each client. Finally, TASR adaptively selects a task-relevant subset of skill patches based on their applicability conditions to guide agent execution. We further provide a theoretical guarantee for personalized skill selection in P-FedSkill, and extensive experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness.

title: LexaChat new Fine-tuned model
description:
Building LexaChat: A redesigned experience, expanded platform capabilities, and my own fine-tuned AI model.

Over the past three days, I've been working on a major redesign and feature expansion of LexaChat, an AI conversation platform developed under FuncLexa.

This update goes beyond a visual refresh. My focus has been on improving the user experience, platform management, conversation sharing, and AI infrastructure.

What's new in LexaChat?

1. Redesigned User Interface
A completely refreshed interface with a cleaner layout, modern design, and improved navigation to make AI conversations more intuitive.

2. Local Mode and Session Mode
Users can choose how they want to use LexaChat:

  • Local Mode: Start conversations without creating an account, with chats stored locally.
  • Session Mode: Sign in and access conversations across devices.

3. Share Conversations
A dedicated chat-sharing feature that allows users to generate shareable links and make their AI conversations accessible to others.

4. New Admin Dashboard
I've introduced a dedicated administration panel to manage the platform more effectively, including user management, announcements, and administrative controls.

5. Developing My Own Fine-Tuned AI Model

One of the most exciting parts of this update is my work on a custom fine-tuned language model.

I fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B using Unsloth and Hugging Face's TRL library, resulting in my own model:

ansarisultan/lexachat-4b-merged

The goal is to integrate this model into LexaChat as a self-hosted fallback, reducing complete dependence on external AI providers when API rate limits or service interruptions occur.

This is an important step towards building a more independent and resilient AI infrastructure.

What's next?

I'm continuing to work on model integration, reliability, performance, and improving the overall platform experience.

LexaChat is also available on the Microsoft Store, extending the experience beyond the web.

Website: https://lexachat.online

Fine-tuned model: https://huggingface.co/ansarisultan/lexachat-4b-merged

Building an AI product is not just about integrating APIs. It's also about understanding the infrastructure behind them, experimenting with models, solving real engineering challenges, and continuously improving the product.

This is another step forward for LexaChat and FuncLexa.

Built independently. Improved continuously.

title: Open Ontologies 2.0: plan ontology changes before production
description:
Open Ontologies 2.0

Approving a vocabulary mapping because the labels look right is not enough. Downstream, exactMatch means two terms are interchangeable, and a wrong match quietly changes what your data means. Open Ontologies plans ontology changes before they reach production. It reasons over each vocabulary separately and downgrades an exactMatch the evidence does not support, with the reason given. It also reports terms the mapping does not carry. It cannot confirm a match, and a wrong sibling under the right parent can still pass, so treat it as a check, not proof. As of 27 November 2026 it has 2,971 stars on GitHub, is MIT licensed, and the latest release is v2.1.0 from 23 October 2026.

Repo: https://github.com/fabio-rovai/open-ontologies

What you get

  • A plan for ontology changes before they reach production, with a blast radius report and a proof an auditor can re-check
  • Reasoning over each vocabulary separately, instead of trusting labels that look right
  • Unsupported exactMatch matches downgraded, with the reason given
  • A report of the terms a mapping does not carry

Treat it as a check, not proof: it can flag a bad match, but it cannot confirm a good one.

Quick poll

What would you use Open Ontologies 2.0 for first?

  • Planning an ontology change before production
  • Checking a vocabulary mapping for bad exactMatch
  • Reviewing terms a mapping does not carry
  • Reading the docs first

Vote in the comments.

If you found Open Ontologies 2.0 interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Choose AI Gateway providers by headquarters country
description:
Provider headquarters sends your AI Gateway requests only to providers headquartered in countries you choose, so you can meet compliance and procurement rules about where your AI vendors are located.

You can configure provider headquarters to be an allowlist of the countries to use, or a denylist of the countries to block. AI Gateway skips providers in blocked countries and routes requests to the rest of the list, so a model stays accessible as long as it is available in one of its allowed provider locations.

Use provider headquarters with regional hosting and regional inference to control where a request is received, where the model runs, and who runs it.

Set provider headquarters for your team

Pro and Enterprise customers can apply their provider headquarters list to every AI Gateway request across their team. Configure the list in AI Gateway settings.

Provider headquarters settings are applied automatically as AI Gateway adds models and providers. Providers without a headquarters country on record never receive your requests.

Set provider headquarters per request

On any plan, set headquarters in the gateway provider options to restrict a single request. Pass country codes for an allowlist, or prefix every code with ! for a denylist, as in ['!US']. If your team has a list, a request can only narrow it.

In the examples below, requests are only sent to providers based in the US and Germany:

Both settings filter providers, so a model stays available as long as one of its providers is based in an allowed country. If no provider is available in an allowed country, AI Gateway tries your fallback models. If no fallback models are available in allowed countries, or if no fallback models are configured, the request will fail without trying to route to providers in other locations.

title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.33764v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.

title: Multiple Brands: Why I Tie DNS Zone Ownership to Mail Reputation
description:
Give each media brand its own DNS zone when it has a separate team or sending-domain reputation; keep one zone when the names belong to the same product. During a move away from a registrar-specific API, the deciding constraint is whether published records still match each brand's approved intent. A long hostname list alone doesn't justify a split.

Short answer: use separate zones for independently operated publications and one zone for alternate names of the same product. I favor explicit brand-to-zone configuration and an inventory comparison before migration approval. That trades extra verification and rotation work for clearer ownership and an easier future brand sale.

Consider a publisher moving its newsletter and account-verification records away from a registrar-specific integration. This is a proposed architecture decision, not a production migration report. The homepage is only part of the review: an inventory that omits the records supporting mail leaves the most delivery-sensitive part of this move outside the acceptance decision. The useful evidence is a comparison of approved and observed records, attached to a brand, its responsible team, and an explicit zone identifier.

Should multiple brands share one DNS zone for mail reputation?

Mail reputation attaches to the sending domain. Creating a separate DNS zone establishes an administrative boundary; it doesn't itself establish a separate sending-domain reputation. That distinction matters when deciding between many hostnames in one zone and a zone per brand. Brands that send mail independently need their sending identities considered separately, with DNS ownership arranged to support that separation. Counting hostnames answers a different question.

I would separate zones for independently operated publications because their teams need clear ownership and because a publication may eventually be divested. A brand sale should not require someone to infer record ownership from naming conventions. For one publication marketed under several names, a shared zone can remain the better choice: the same team accepts the same mail responsibilities, and splitting adds verification and rotation work without a matching ownership benefit.

Budget that work.

The compliance concern is specific. Handover evidence should show which team approved the intended records and which zone was checked. A matching inventory establishes agreement between two inputs. It isn't a compliance certification or a promise that a newsletter or OTP will reach an inbox. DMARC, described in RFC 7489, belongs in the mail-authentication review; a zone-count decision can't substitute for that review.

The invariants that make drift reviewable

The first invariant is explicit zone configuration.

Never derive the zone identifier from a brand's display name. A rebrand should not silently change the destination of a DNS operation. When replacing a registrar-specific integration, changing the provider binding must be an intentional configuration change too. Keep the approved inventory attached to that binding so reviewers can identify what was checked, rather than reconstructing it from a later configuration.

The second invariant is that intended and observed inventories refer to the same brand and zone. A clean comparison against the wrong zone offers false reassurance. The third is that differences block approval until a responsible person reconciles them. Missing records, changed values, and unexpected records all deserve review; automatically deleting an unexpected entry would turn detection into an unreviewed change. Retain the comparison with the decision so a later owner can understand why the migration was approved.

Use 3 local review outcomes: missing, unexpected, and changed. These are application categories, not provider response fields.

The failure boundary is narrow. A comparison cannot prove that the observed inventory was collected correctly, that every resolver sees the same answer, or that mail authentication and delivery behave as intended. Those require separate checks. Treating matching TXT inventories as a complete deliverability test would leave a gap in both the newsletter and account-verification workflow.

Compare the integration boundary before choosing the provider

Record the zone decision separately from the API decision. A different DNS API does not determine whether two publications are one product. I would evaluate these real options against the same acceptance evidence. The table gives selection conditions, rather than claims about relative mail reputation or performance.

Option When I would shortlist it Trade-off and required evidence
Amazon Route 53 The intended owner wants DNS aligned with its AWS operating model. A direct integration accepts that provider dependency; require explicit brand-to-zone configuration and an inventory mapping.
Cloudflare DNS The intended owner chooses Cloudflare as its DNS administration boundary. Review the direct integration against the same drift check; the provider choice does not settle the brand split.
Google Cloud DNS The intended owner wants DNS administration aligned with Google Cloud. Cloud alignment is a selection condition, not a delivery guarantee; require the same ownership and record evidence.
Common capability API Swapping the vendor behind a capability keeps the application contract stable, without changing application code. One REST API uses plain HTTP, with no SDK to install. Public discovery requires no key and supplies request and response schemas. Runnable examples in 10 languages help the team review an inventory collector in its own runtime; adapter mapping and migration approval remain application responsibilities.

Direct-provider integrations are reasonable when the organization deliberately accepts that dependency. A common capability contract is useful when replacing the dependency is part of the requirement. The additional advantage here is discoverable request and response schemas: reviewers have a concrete contract to examine before approving an inventory adapter. Neither approach decides who owns a publication's records.

These are conditional recommendations. This comparison doesn't establish which provider has the best delivery, latency, or migration success rate. It asks which integration boundary the publisher wants to maintain, then requires every candidate to produce the same reviewable record evidence.

Infrai supplies one API key and one bill across backend services, with 295 routes across 20 modules. Its single REST API uses plain HTTP with no SDK required, so the publisher can keep a Python inventory collector without installing another vendor SDK. Swapping the provider behind a capability keeps the application code unchanged. For newsletter and account-verification flows maintained alongside DNS, the shared credential also reduces the separate keys and invoices the team must administer. The public, self-describing API and runnable examples in 10 languages address a different friction: a reviewer can inspect request and response schemas before granting access. That reduces the setup needed to assess an adapter; it does not remove the need to verify what its inventory means.

Keep approval separate.

Put the comparison on the approval path

This runnable Python example uses only the standard library. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS v1 API base. The read-only domain-list call prints its JSON without assuming an undocumented response shape. It uses 5 attempts and a 30-second request timeout as example settings, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, and surfaces other HTTP errors. No records are written.

The subsequent comparison uses illustrative local inventories, not the printed API response. An inventory adapter must translate the source and destination records into this local contract before the comparator can be used for an actual move. The TXT strings below are review markers, not SPF, DKIM, or DMARC configuration.

The example contains 2 intended records and 1 changed value. Those are fixture sizes, not production measurements. Its zone identifiers are application configuration placeholders, not provider-issued identifiers.

from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def read_domains():
    base = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
    if not base.startswith("https://"):
        raise ValueError("Use the documented HTTPS v1 API base")
    request = Request(
        base + "/dns/domain/list",
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
    )
    for attempt in range(5):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            delay = float(2 ** attempt)
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    requested = float(retry_after)
                except ValueError:
                    deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    requested = (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
                delay = max(delay, requested)
            time.sleep(delay)


def inventory(records):
    grouped = defaultdict(list)
    for record in records:
        key = (record["name"], record["type"])
        grouped[key].append(record["value"])
    return {key: tuple(sorted(values)) for key, values in grouped.items()}


def compare(brand, observed_zone, intended, observed):
    if brand["zone_id"] != observed_zone:
        raise ValueError("Observed inventory belongs to a different zone")
    wanted = inventory(intended)
    actual = inventory(observed)
    differences = []
    for key in sorted(wanted.keys() | actual.keys()):
        if key not in actual:
            differences.append(("missing", key))
        elif key not in wanted:
            differences.append(("unexpected", key))
        elif wanted[key] != actual[key]:
            differences.append(("changed", key))
    return differences


brand = {"name": "Culture Desk", "zone_id": "example-zone-culture"}
intended = [
    {"name": "culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "migration-review=approved"},
    {"name": "news.culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "owner=newsletter-team"},
]
observed = [
    {"name": "culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "migration-review=approved"},
    {"name": "news.culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "owner=previous-team"},
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(read_domains(), indent=2))
    differences = compare(
        brand, "example-zone-culture", intended, observed
    )
    for category, (name, record_type) in differences:
        print(f"{category}: {record_type} {name}")
    print("HOLD" if differences else "READY FOR FURTHER CHECKS")
    raise SystemExit(1 if differences else 0)

The fixture exits with status 1 and reports the changed newsletter marker. Replace the observed value with the intended value to exercise the matching path. A match means the local comparison passed; further checks still have to pass before approval.

The grouped values preserve multiple records under the same name and type. A dictionary that kept only one value per pair could hide a difference by overwriting an earlier entry. That's the quiet inventory error I want this approval path to expose.

This small comparator checks names, types, and values exactly as supplied; it does not normalize provider-specific representations or examine TTLs. Establish adapter rules before using it for approval, and extend the local contract if TTLs are acceptance criteria. For mail records, explicitly review how the adapter represents their values. A normalization rule that conceals a meaningful change defeats the reason for comparing inventories. The local fixture demonstrates the gate, not a complete registrar migration tool.

The rejected option and when it belongs

For separately operated publications, I would reject a single shared zone organized only by hostname prefixes. That makes naming conventions carry ownership information that belongs in explicit configuration. It also leaves a future divestiture dependent on untangling records. A shared zone remains valid when those names represent the same product, the same team owns the records, and the additional verification and rotation work of separate zones has no corresponding benefit.

My acceptance rule is concrete: select the zone boundary from team and sending-domain responsibilities, store its identifier in brand configuration, and withhold migration approval when the intended and observed inventories differ. Then perform the separate mail-authentication and delivery checks. For a media publisher moving off a registrar-specific API, this keeps the decision centered on accountable record ownership instead of hostname volume or a provider's marketing.

References

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/Welcome.html
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation: https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/overview
