title: Before You Merge an AI-Built Landing Page: A 15-Minute Core Web Vitals Review
description:
Disclosure: I work on VibUI, a paid catalogue of website prompts. It appears once, near the end. The review below needs only a browser and whichever AI tool you already use.

Short answer: an AI-built landing page can look finished in the preview and still fail on speed: an oversized hero image delaying the main content, elements that jump as fonts and images load, and scripts that make taps feel slow. Spend fifteen minutes on three metrics (Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift and Interaction to Next Paint), write each finding back into the prompt as a constraint, and regenerate only the section that failed. This applies to output from v0, Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Replit, GitHub Copilot, Framer AI, Google Stitch, Readdy, Aura.build and OpenAI Codex.

The gain is small and concrete: a page you can hand to a client or ship without a "why is it slow on my phone?" follow-up. It is not a promise of any ranking or conversion change.

Why do AI-built pages pass the eyeball test and fail the speed test?

A preview shows a fast laptop on a good connection. The problems are invisible there:

  • Heavy hero media. A full-bleed image or video is requested at original size, so the biggest element on screen is also the slowest to arrive.
  • No reserved space. Images, embeds and web fonts load without width, height or fallback metrics, so text and buttons move after the reader has started reading.
  • Decorative JavaScript. Scroll effects, particle backgrounds and animation libraries are added "for polish" and run on the main thread.
  • Third-party tags nobody asked for. Chat widgets, font loaders and analytics snippets get pasted in by habit.

Which three metrics should you read first?

Metric What it measures Common AI-built cause Constraint to add to the prompt
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) How quickly the main content appears. Google's "good" line is 2.5 s or less. Unoptimised hero image or video, render-blocking fonts "Hero image: modern format, explicit width and height, no autoplay video; preload only the hero asset."
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) How much content jumps during load. "Good" is 0.1 or less. Images without dimensions, late-loading fonts, injected banners "Reserve space for every image and embed; use font-display: swap with a similar fallback."
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) How fast the page responds to taps and clicks. "Good" is 200 ms or less. Heavy scripts, large animation loops, re-rendering widgets "No animation library; CSS transitions only; no script on the main thread that is not needed for the first screen."

How do you run the review in fifteen minutes?

  1. Open the page in a private window and run Lighthouse in DevTools with mobile emulation and throttling on.
  2. Write down LCP, CLS and the biggest items in the "opportunities" list. Do not average runs you have not repeated.
  3. Open the Network panel, sort by size, and look at the top five requests. If one of them is a decorative asset, that is your first fix.
  4. Scroll the page slowly on a throttled profile and watch for jumps.
  5. Tap every button and menu on a real phone, not only in emulation.

Treat these as lab numbers. Real-user (field) data only exists after real visitors arrive, so do not quote a lab score as a result.

What should the performance constraints in the first prompt look like? 

Build the [PAGE] section by section. Performance rules (apply to every section):
- Hero: one optimised image, explicit width/height, no autoplay video, no background animation loop.
- Fonts: at most two families, font-display: swap, system fallback with similar metrics.
- Images: lazy-load everything below the first screen; always set width and height.
- JavaScript: none unless a feature needs it; no animation or carousel library; no third-party tags.
- Layout: reserve space for embeds, forms and images so nothing moves after load.
- Report back: list every external request the page makes.

Ask the tool to list every external request. That one line catches most of the surprise scripts before you open DevTools.

Where does a prompt catalogue fit in a performance workflow?

If you build one page a quarter, keep the block above in a snippets file and skip any paid library. A catalogue earns its place only when you repeat the same section types often and want starting briefs that already carry constraints like these.

If you want to inspect one: The library I work on is VibUI. It has 2,852 website prompt templates (775 full pages, 1,100 sections, 817 components and 160 animated backgrounds), and about 1,000 of them include source code. Payment is one-time with no auto-renewal: $48 quarterly, $99 yearly, or $179 lifetime (listed down from $384). The yearly and lifetime plans also include 2,407 AI video prompts. There are 60 free samples, and a free account can copy 2 prompts. Try a free sample on a real section, run it through the review above, and only consider paying if it saves you setup time on pages you will actually build.

FAQ

Is a perfect Lighthouse score the goal?

No. Use it to find the largest problems. A page that scores a little lower but loads its main content quickly on a phone is better than one tuned to the test.

Should I remove all animation?

Not necessarily. Keep it cheap (CSS transforms and opacity), keep it away from the first screen, and respect reduced-motion settings.

Can the AI tool fix these issues by itself?

It can, if you hand it the specific finding ("LCP element is the hero image, no dimensions") and ask it to change only that section. Vague requests like "make it faster" rarely help.

Do I need to pay for a library to follow this review?

No. Everything above works with free tools and the AI builder you already use.

title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
description:
arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

title: Is Your Coding Agent Actually Helping? Test It on Your Own Old Fixes
description:
"Is Coding with AI Actually Faster and Cheaper?" was the top post on DEV in the week to 22 November, with 229 reactions and 195 comments. It's the right question, and most of us answer it with a feeling: the agent seems to help, or it seems to create cleanup work.

Feelings are a weak instrument here. In METR's early-2025 study, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues from their own repositories. With AI tools allowed, they took 19% longer, yet they "expected AI to speed them up by 24%, and even after experiencing the slowdown, they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%." METR now labels those results out of date, and its February 2026 update says developers are likely more sped up now, but that its new data is "only very weak evidence for the size of this increase." The lesson that survives either way isn't a number. It's that how fast an agent feels and what it actually delivers can be far apart.

You can't run a randomized trial on your own team. You can run something smaller that answers a narrower question: on tasks from my repo, with my setup, does the agent produce changes that pass my checks, and does that get better or worse when I change something? This article builds that in an afternoon from your git history.

What this eval measures (and what it doesn't)

It measures one thing: given the bug report, can the agent produce a change that passes the tests your team wrote for that bug? It does not measure time saved, review effort or code quality. Those still need your judgment. But it turns "the new model feels better" into a pass/fail list you can compare from one change to the next.

Step 1: Pick 10 to 20 past fixes from your history

You already own a good test set: closed bugs whose fix commit also added a test. That's the same idea SWE-bench is built on: 2,294 problems "drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests." You only need a handful from your own repo. Anthropic's guide to agent evals says teams wait too long because they think they need hundreds of tasks: "In reality, 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start." My rule of thumb: ten to start, twenty when you can.

Pick fixes that look like the work you actually hand to an agent: small bugs, validation gaps, edge cases. Skip ones that needed a meeting to understand. For each, write the prompt the way the original bug report read, without hints from the fix.

[
  {"id": "discount-rounding", "fix_commit": "fix-rounding",
   "prompt": "apply_discount(19.99, 15) returns 16.9915. Prices must be rounded to cents.",
   "check": "python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -q"}
]

fix_commit is the commit (or a tag on it) that fixed the bug. The task starts from its parent.

Step 2: Prove each task is fair before you trust it

Two checks per task, before any agent runs:

  1. The original fix passes. The same Anthropic guide recommends a reference solution for each task: "a known working output that passes all graders," which proves the task is solvable and the grader is configured correctly. Your fix commit is that reference.
  2. The unfixed code fails. If the tests already pass on the parent commit, the task can't tell a good agent from one that does nothing.

If a task fails either check, fix the task or drop it.

Step 3: Run each task in a clean copy, with the tests held out

Two details matter more than they look. First, a worktree or a clone of your repo still contains the git history, and the fix is in it. Anthropic describes a related leak in its own evals: Claude gaining "an unfair advantage on some tasks by examining the git history from previous trials." So the runner below exports only the files of the parent commit with git archive, with no .git folder. Second, the tests from the fix commit are held out: the agent never sees those versions, and they're written back after the agent finishes, overwriting any edits it made to them.

Here's the runner. It needs only Python's standard library and git, and it calls whatever agent command you give it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Replay past fixes from your git history as eval tasks for a coding agent.
Usage: python3 eval_runner.py tasks.json LABEL [--reference]
AGENT_CMD is a shell command; the task prompt is in $TASK_PROMPT.
AGENT_FILES (optional): current config files to copy in, e.g. "CLAUDE.md"."""
import csv, json, os, shutil, subprocess, sys, tempfile

tasks_file, label = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
reference = "--reference" in sys.argv
agent_cmd = os.environ.get("AGENT_CMD", "")

def git(*args):
    return subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True,
                          check=True).stdout

def snapshot(commit, dest):
    # files only, no .git: the agent can't read the fix from history
    archive = subprocess.run(["git", "archive", commit], capture_output=True,
                             check=True).stdout
    subprocess.run(["tar", "-x", "-C", dest], input=archive, check=True)

results = {}
for t in json.load(open(tasks_file)):
    fix = t["fix_commit"]
    hidden = [f for f in git("diff", "--name-only", f"{fix}^", fix).split()
              if f.startswith("tests/")]
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as work:
        snapshot(fix if reference else f"{fix}^", work)
        for f in os.environ.get("AGENT_FILES", "").split():
            shutil.copy(f, os.path.join(work, f))  # config under test
        if not reference and agent_cmd:
            env = dict(os.environ, TASK_PROMPT=t["prompt"], TASK_ID=t["id"])
            subprocess.run(agent_cmd, shell=True, cwd=work, env=env,
                           timeout=t.get("timeout", 900))
        for f in hidden:  # restore held-out tests, undoing any agent edits
            os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(os.path.join(work, f)), exist_ok=True)
            with open(os.path.join(work, f), "w") as out:
                out.write(git("show", f"{fix}:{f}"))
        check = subprocess.run(t["check"], shell=True, cwd=work,
                               capture_output=True)
    results[t["id"]] = "PASS" if check.returncode == 0 else "FAIL"
    print(f"{results[t['id']]}  {t['id']}")

passed = sum(r == "PASS" for r in results.values())
print(f"{label}: {passed}/{len(results)} passed")

if reference or not agent_cmd:
    sys.exit(0)  # validation runs are not logged
log = "eval_results.csv"
previous = {}
if os.path.exists(log):
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(log)))
    if rows:
        last = rows[-1]["label"]
        previous = {r["task"]: r["result"] for r in rows if r["label"] == last}
for task, result in results.items():
    if previous.get(task) == "PASS" and result == "FAIL":
        print(f"REGRESSION  {task} (passed in the previous run)")
new = not os.path.exists(log)
with open(log, "a", newline="") as fh:
    w = csv.writer(fh)
    if new:
        w.writerow(["label", "task", "result"])
    w.writerows([label, k, v] for k, v in results.items())

It assumes your tests live under tests/; change that filter if yours don't. Note the snapshot comes from an old commit, so it also contains your old CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. If the change you're testing is a config change, list the current files in AGENT_FILES so each task runs with them.

For AGENT_CMD, use your agent's non-interactive mode. Two examples from the official docs:

  • Claude Code: claude -p "$TASK_PROMPT" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash". The headless docs recommend --bare for scripted calls, but bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md. If your setup is what you're evaluating, leave it off. Without it, a -p session runs the project's hooks and connects its MCP servers "even in a folder you've never trusted," so only do this on your own repo. With --output-format json you also get total_cost_usd per run, which the docs describe as a client-side estimate.
  • Codex: codex exec --sandbox workspace-write "$TASK_PROMPT". Per the non-interactive docs, codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox by default, so it needs workspace-write to edit files.

A demo run (simulated agents, real output)

To show the mechanics, I built a small invented repo: a pricing.py module and three past fixes (rounding to cents, rejecting negative quantities, parsing "$1,299.00"), each fix commit adding one test file. To be clear about what's real: no coding agent ran. The two "agents" are short scripts I wrote that make hand-picked edits, standing in for "my agent before and after a config change." Version 1 fixes two tasks and misses the third. Version 2 fixes the third but rounds discounts to one decimal place. The runner and its output are real, from 27 Nov 2026 with git 2.47.3 and Python 3.13.5 (excerpt):

$ python3 /tmp/eval_runner.py /tmp/tasks.json reference --reference
reference: 3/3 passed
$ python3 /tmp/eval_runner.py /tmp/tasks.json no-agent
no-agent: 0/3 passed
$ python3 /tmp/eval_runner.py /tmp/tasks.json agent-v1
PASS  discount-rounding
PASS  negative-quantity
FAIL  thousands-separator
agent-v1: 2/3 passed
$ python3 /tmp/eval_runner.py /tmp/tasks.json agent-v2
FAIL  discount-rounding
PASS  negative-quantity
PASS  thousands-separator
agent-v2: 2/3 passed
REGRESSION  discount-rounding (passed in the previous run)

The first two runs are the fairness checks from Step 2. The last two are the point of the exercise: both versions score 2/3, so a single total says nothing changed. Per task, one fix was gained and one was lost. That's why the runner compares task by task and logs every run to eval_results.csv.

Step 4: Re-run it on every change

Run the set whenever you change something the agent depends on: model, prompt, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, a new MCP server, a new tool version. Give each run a label that says what changed, so the log reads like a history of your setup.

Read the results with some humility:

  • Small sets are noisy. With 10 tasks, one task flipping is 10 points. Before you conclude anything, re-run the tasks that changed.
  • Agents aren't deterministic. Running each task more than once helps. Anthropic's guide distinguishes pass@k (at least one of k tries succeeds) from pass^k (all k succeed), and the second is the one that matters if you need it to work every time.
  • A task nobody ever passes may be broken. The guide notes that a 0% pass rate across many trials "is most often a signal of a broken task, not an incapable agent." Re-check the prompt and the test.
  • Passing isn't the same as helping. A pass means the held-out test went green. It doesn't tell you how long the review took. Note that next to the result.

I covered the grader side of this in 5 Ways the Evals Might Be Lying, and the basic 10-case set for app agents in Build a 10-Case Eval Set for Your AI Agent.

Checklist

  1. Pick 10 to 20 past fixes whose commit added a test.
  2. Write each prompt like the original bug report, with no hints from the fix.
  3. Check that the fix commit passes and its parent fails.
  4. Run each task in a fresh snapshot without .git.
  5. Hold the tests out and restore them before checking.
  6. Copy in the config you're testing.
  7. Compare per task, not just the total.
  8. Re-run anything that flipped before you believe it.

Where to go next

The free AI Agent Evaluation QuickStart covers the core loop in 5 pages: why agents break traditional testing, Define > Measure > Test > Trust, defining what "good" means, building a small test set (ten real cases to start), choosing programmatic or judgment metrics, and testing on every change.

For the full picture, AI Agent Evaluation & Testing: The Complete Guide goes deeper on LLM-as-judge, evaluating multi-step agents and tool use, regression testing and CI gates, tracing, and a worked support-agent example, in 40 pages.

If you ran this on your own repo, what did you find: did the pass rate match how helpful your agent feels?

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author.

title: Nginx 504 Gateway Time-out, Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff, and MySQL InnoDB Deadlocks: A Triage Cheatsheet
description:
When on-call alerts fire at 2 AM, three infrastructure incidents account for a disproportionate share of wasted debugging time because the symptom hides the real bottleneck one layer below.

1. Nginx 504 Gateway Time-out

Nginx returns 504 when the upstream accepts the TCP connection but fails to send a response header before proxy_read_timeout (default 60s) expires.

  • Raising proxy_read_timeout alone only masks slow DB queries or missing upstream keepalive pools.
  • Check whether upstream_response_time matches your timeout ceiling, and confirm proxy_connect_timeout vs proxy_read_timeout vs Kubernetes Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout).
  • Full tuning walkthrough: Nginx 504 Gateway Timeout & proxy_read_timeout Tuning and Ingress Nginx 504 Upstream Postmortem.

2. Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff (Exit Code 1 vs 137 OOMKilled)

CrashLoopBackOff is not the root error—it is Kubernetes backing off restarts after the container dies:

  • Run kubectl describe pod <pod> and check Last State -> Reason / Exit Code:
    • Exit Code 137 (OOMKilled): container exceeded cgroup v2 limits.memory, often from JVM/Node heap unaware of container limits.
    • Exit Code 1: missing env var, failed migration, or unreachable dependency.
  • Deep-dive guides: Debugging Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff Exit Code 1 and Kubernetes OOMKilled & cgroup v2 Profiling.

3. MySQL InnoDB Deadlocks (Next-Key & Gap Locks)

Under REPEATABLE READ, two concurrent INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE or range SELECT ... FOR UPDATE statements can acquire overlapping gap locks and deadlock even when touching different primary keys.

  • Always run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS immediately and compare lock modes (X,GAP vs X,REC_NOT_GAP) and index order.
  • Full postmortem & lock graph analysis: MySQL Deadlock Postmortem: Gap & Next-Key Lock Patterns.

Offline Diagnostic Utilities (0 Bytes Uploaded)

When inspecting production configs, timestamps, CSS units, or query plans during an incident, keep sensitive dumps strictly in browser memory:

  • PostgreSQL EXPLAIN Visualizer
  • Unix Timestamp Converter
  • PX to REM Converter
  • Zero-Upload Browser DevTools Suite (NerdKit)

title: Avoiding Partially Written Export Files in GBase 8a with Python UDFs
description:
GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP database from GBASE, can export over ftp and sftp. When the export is large — tens of GB — the target file takes time to finish writing. If a downstream job picks it up mid-export, it reads an incomplete file, which shows up as inconsistent data or parse errors. This post uses Python UDFs to add ftp / sftp rename support so the file only becomes visible when it is complete.

The idea

Downstream consumers usually scan for files matching a rule, for example *.csv under a load directory. Making an unfinished file fail that rule can be done two ways, and they can be combined:

  • Name does not match — target is .csv, temporary file is .csv.tmp
  • Path does not match — write to a temporary directory first

Two steps

  1. Export to a temporary file (different suffix, or a temporary directory).
  2. Once the export finishes, use the protocol's rename to switch the temporary name to the final one — changing the suffix or moving across directories.

FTP rename UDF

Stored under gclusterdb, taking host, username, password, source name, target name. Port customisation is not implemented; extend it if you are not on the default ftp port:

use gclusterdb;
drop function if exists ftpRename;
create function ftpRename(server varchar(100),username varchar(100),password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))
returns varchar
$$
from ftplib import FTP
ftp = FTP(server)
ftp.login(username, password)
ftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)
ftp.close()
return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

Calling it:

gbase> select ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv')  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                             |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

SFTP rename UDF

The standard Python library does not speak sftp, so this example uses pysftp (pip install pysftp). Everything else matches the FTP version:

use gclusterdb;
drop function if exists sftpRename;
create function sftpRename(server varchar(100),v_username varchar(100),v_password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))
returns varchar
$$
import pysftp
with pysftp.Connection(server, username=v_username, password=v_password) as sftp:
    sftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)
    sftp.close()
return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

gbase> select sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                             |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

The full flow 

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';
Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.32)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv');
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv') |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.43)

The temporary file can live in a different directory, provided the account has write permission there. This example uses both a temporary tmp directory and a .tmp suffix:

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';
Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv');
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv') |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                                            |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

Both the export and the rename run inside the gbase client, and the consumer's scan rule never matches a .tmp file. Handing atomic visibility to rename means even a tens-of-GB export no longer needs a sleep timer or a human "is it done yet" check — a small UDF turns the database's own export into a safe handoff.

title: November 06, 2026
description:
Agent Registry

Feature

Skill security scanning and governance in Agent Registry are available. You can automatically scan standalone skill revisions for security issues, review Finding resources, enforce scanning policies across your organization using custom Organization Policy constraints, and grant least-privilege skill management access.

For more information, see Scan skills for security issues and Agent Registry roles and permissions.

Feature

Standalone skills in Agent Registry are generally available (GA). You can register, version, search, and govern standalone Skill resources, immutable SkillRevision packages, and verified Publisher details.

For more information, see Skills architecture, Register skills, and Manage skills.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

Blocked query analysis in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is generally available (GA). This feature lets you identify active queries that hold locks and the dependent queries that are blocked by them so that you can terminate the root blockers.

For more information, see Blocked query analysis.

Assured Open Source Software

Feature

The Assured Open Source Software Premium tier supports Google Cloud regions and multi-regions for remote (or proxy) Artifact Registry repositories.

For the list of supported regions, see Supported regions.

BigQuery

Announcement

You can now use BigQuery Graph and run Graph Query Language (GQL) queries when you use on-demand pricing.

Breaking

Starting January 31, 2027, the BigQuery Data Transfer Service for Shopify connector will no longer support the following fields:

  • The legacyMode field from the DeliveryProfile dataset schema
  • The permitSkuSharing field from the FulfillmentService dataset schema

For more information, see January 31, 2027.

Feature

You can now use a custom organization policy to allow or deny specific operations on models in BigQuery. This feature is in preview.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure a Bigtable automated backup policy on SSD instances to create daily hot backups and specify how long the backups remain hot before automatically transitioning to standard backups. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource type is publicly available through the SearchAllResources and SearchAllIamPolicies APIs.

  • Cloud Key Management Service
    • cloudkms.googleapis.com/KajPolicyConfig

Cloud Data Fusion

Feature

Cloud Data Fusion version 6.11.1.5 is generally available (GA). This release includes the following feature:

  • Added support for Dataproc flexible VM machine types, per-selection boot disk types, predefined Compute Engine machine shapes, and ranked fallback priority tiers using runtime arguments (CDAP-21269, CDAP-21274).

Fixed

Fixed in Cloud Data Fusion 6.11.1.5:

  • Resolved an issue in Spark pipelines where failed task attempts were included in aggregated stage record counts on retry. When a task succeeds, stage record counts (records.in, records.out, records.error, and records.alert) emit deduplicated raw metrics tagged by partition (spark_part) and attempt (spark_att). These raw metrics are available only through the Metrics REST APIs (CDAP-21235).

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Frontend configuration for load balancing incoming IPv6 traffic is now generally available (GA) for the following load balancers:

  • Regional external Application Load Balancer
  • Regional external proxy Network Load Balancer
  • Regional internal Application Load Balancer
  • Regional internal proxy Network Load Balancer
  • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancer
  • Cross-region internal proxy Network Load Balancer

To support client IPv6 traffic, you can configure the proxy-only subnet with a stack type of either IPV4_ONLY or IPV4_IPV6 (dual-stack).

For more information, see the following documentation:

  • Forwarding rules overview
  • IPv6 for Application Load Balancers and proxy Network Load Balancers
  • Convert Application Load Balancer to IPv6
  • Convert Proxy Network Load Balancer to IPv6
  • Proxy-only subnets for Envoy-based load balancers

Cloud Trace

Feature

You can reprovision an existing _Trace bucket to satisfy regulatory requirements for data residency and encryption. After reprovisioning, the storage location and encryption configuration of the _Trace bucket match your default settings for observability buckets. Reprovisioning is a destructive operation. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see Remediate data residency and CMEK requirements.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Customizing provisioned IOPS and throughput for Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability persistent directories is generally available (GA) in Cloud Workstations. You can set these values by using the v1 API or the --disk-provisioned-iops and --disk-provisioned-throughput flags of the gcloud workstations configs create and gcloud workstations configs update commands.

Config Controller

Change

Config Controller now uses the following versions of its included products:

Feature

Support for the drop() command is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: End of Gemini Code Assist entitlement for existing subscriptions

Bundled Gemini Code Assist entitlements for existing Gemini Enterprise Standard and Gemini Enterprise Plus subscriptions will end on March 31, 2027. After this date, the entitlement will be removed from existing subscriptions. Support for Gemini Code Assist until March 31, 2027 is limited to the Gemini 3.x model family only. Effective October 9, 2026, new Gemini Enterprise subscriptions no longer include an entitlement to Gemini Code Assist.

To transition your developer workflows, agentic coding assistance is available through Google Antigravity, which is included in Gemini Enterprise editions.

For more information, see the Gemini Code Assist sunset page.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Video generation upgrades to Omni 1.2 Flash

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available (GA) and replaces Veo 3.1 for video generation in the global region. Omni 1.2 Flash improves clarity and instruction following.

To use video generation, an administrator must turn on the Enable video generation setting. For more information, see:

  • Generate a video
  • Manage web app features
  • Gemini Enterprise limitations

Breaking

Gemini Notebook Enterprise: Updated web addresses

The URL path for the Gemini Notebook Enterprise web app is changing in two ways. In both cases, existing links redirect automatically.

"go/" added: Starting immediately, go/ is being added to the URL path:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/
    changes to
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/.

  • For Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise,
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/global/
    changes to
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/go/global/.

The dates for this go/ path change are as follows:

Region Rollout date
global and us Live
eu Rolling out
All other locations Starting November 9, 2026

"lm" removed: Starting November 16, 2026, lm is being removed from the hostname:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Google Identity,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.com.

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Workforce Identity Federation,
    notebooklm.cloud.google
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.

Action is required: if your organization uses a firewall, proxy, or secure web gateway that allows access to Gemini Notebook by a specific URL path. If this applies to you, Google recommends that you add the following URLs to your allowlist:

  1. Allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google.com/* and notebook.cloud.google.com/*

  2. If you use Workforce Identity Federation, allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google/* and notebook.cloud.google/*

  3. If you use Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise, allowlist vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/*.

Google recommends allowing entire domains (/*) so that future path changes don't require additional updates.

If you don't allow /*, you must allow both /REGION and /go/REGION, where REGION is your location value: global, us, eu, asia-northeast1, au, ca, de, europe-west2, in, kr, or sg. For example, notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/ and notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/

Temporary workaround: If your firewall blocks users before you update your allowlist, users themselves can access the original URLs by removing /go from the URL and adding version=legacy. For example: notebooklm.cloud.google.com/eu/?project=1234567&version=legacy. This fix will fail when Google sunsets the legacy version.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Adobe data store (Preview)

The Adobe data store is available in Public Preview in Gemini Enterprise. You can use natural language to search, share, and manage your Adobe Creative Cloud assets, customize Adobe Express templates, apply Lightroom presets, and edit images. For more information, see Connect a third-party data source.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Model availability respects resource location policies

If the resource locations organization policy for your project doesn't allow the global location, Gemini Enterprise administrators can't turn on Gemini models that aren't supported in the app's location, because traffic for these models is routed to the global endpoint. In the Google Cloud console, the toggles for these models are unavailable. If one of these models is already turned on, a warning appears under its toggle so that administrators can turn it off.

For more information, see:

  • Turn on or turn off a Gemini model
  • Data residency for Gemini Enterprise

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Dedicated Memory Bank functionality in the Google Cloud console

You can create, configure, and inspect Agent Platform Memory Bank instances from the dedicated Memory Bank page in the Google Cloud console, with updated memory management controls for deployed agents in Agent Runtime:

  • Memory Bank list and creation: View and manage standalone memory banks on the Memory Bank page (separate from deployed agents on the Deployments page), edit basic information or labels, delete instances, and click Create memory bank to create an instance with default memory settings and Google-managed or Cloud KMS encryption.
  • Memories inspection and filtering: On the Memories tab, switch between Unstructured and Structured views, filter memories by key:value scope pairs or scope chips, edit or delete unstructured memories, inspect structured memory profiles and underlying facts in the Memory details panel, and select View revisions to inspect revision history.
  • Instance and schema configuration: On the Configuration tab, view and edit Details, Generation (memory extraction toggle, perspective, and managed or custom topics), Retrieval (embedding model, configurable before you store the first memory), and Retention (expiration and revision history TTL), or click Schemas to add and edit profile schemas.
  • Agent integration snippets: Click Link to an agent to get installation commands and prefilled Python code (populated with your project, region, and memory bank ID) for connecting with Agent Development Kit (ADK) or retrieving memories.
  • Agent Runtime memory updates: On the Deployments page, deployed agents include key:value scope filtering and View revisions on the Memories tab, along with Generation, Retrieval, and Retention configuration controls under Service configuration in the Memory bank section.

For more information, see Set up Memory Bank, Fetch memories, Memory Profiles, and Memory revisions.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.32

We've released version 6.32 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where abandoned queue records incorrectly calculated wait times from the call's initial queue entry rather than the time the caller entered the specific queue they abandoned from.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter header title on SmartActions and virtual task assistant screens was truncated with an ellipsis, preventing users from viewing the full text.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter froze on Calling and didn't dial the customer during recovery calls following an unanswered in-app call.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls became unroutable and remained stuck in the queue until abandoned if an agent's browser delivered a delayed connection request after a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue in the CCaaS portal where active Spanish IVR queues were incorrectly displayed as Setup is required and grayed out when switching languages from English to Spanish.

  • Fixed an issue where transient network errors during platform validation incorrectly marked virtual agent credentials as invalid.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS and WhatsApp virtual agent chats became unresponsive and didn't escalate to a human agent when encountering a custom payload validation error.

  • Fixed an issue where campaigns didn't resume after being paused, resulting in repeated call session failures and missing participant information.

  • Fixed an issue where call-related actions such as disconnecting or updating status took up to 72 seconds to complete.

  • Fixed an issue where a Not Found banner incorrectly appeared in the call adapter when a phone number couldn't be matched in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where the In-email status bar in the agent desktop appeared white.

  • Fixed an issue where agents in the In-email status couldn't change their status directly from the status bar.

  • Fixed an issue where the first letter of uppercase acronym field names was incorrectly lowercased in virtual task assistant input placeholders.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly set to an Unresponsive status instead of receiving a missed call when a new deltacast offer arrived while the call adapter was already ringing.

  • Fixed an issue where agents became stuck in a projected state and stopped receiving calls after a caller abandoned the call at the moment of routing.

  • Fixed an issue where transient carrier timeouts during outbound callbacks were incorrectly classified as invalid numbers.

  • Fixed an issue where forced virtual agent callbacks booked through the Apps API were incorrectly routed to the original call's queue instead of the requested destination.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback capacity was under-calculated due to a mathematical rounding error.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls were prematurely disconnected if the initial connection request timed out and was retried.

  • Fixed an issue where valid Canadian phone numbers using newer area codes were rejected by the Callback call API.

  • Fixed an issue where certain agents were missing from the directory during outbound calls, preventing other agents from transferring calls or adding them to a call.

  • Fixed an issue where dynamic queues incorrectly offered a minimum of one slot even when WFM staffing was zero or resulted in less than one available slot.

  • Fixed an issue where Dynamic Agent Availability queues were saved without a required custom queue identifier, causing workforce management synchronization to fail silently.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce cases and contacts were incorrectly created for voice calls handled entirely by a virtual agent, even when the Create CRM records for calls attended by Virtual Agents setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where voice transfers addressed to a specific agent were never offered to the target and didn't expire, leaving callers on hold indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where NICE WFM session data exports didn't generate for instances with subdomains exceeding 20 characters.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual callbacks routed through external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) were missing captured virtual agent custom parameters, causing routing engines to lose the caller's intent.

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist transcriptions permanently stopped following transient network or quota errors.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound phone number restriction rules weren't applied to agents with the Allow unrestricted international calling setting enabled.

Looker 26.24 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected final deployment and download available: Tuesday, December 8, 2026

The Looker 26.24 rollout for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Change

The System Activity Conversational Analytics dashboard now displays the estimated cached and uncached input tokens that are used on the instance. The calculation for total estimated input tokens is also updated to reflect how tokens will be billed when Gemini billing goes into effect.

Fixed

Fixed

Fixed

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where passing malformed dashboard filter attributes to the dashboard_filters API endpoints could cause an HTTP 500 error instead of returning an HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity response. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where model set matching treated underscores in model names as wildcards, which could grant self-service access to connections that were linked to similarly named models. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard tag list filters and their drop-down menus resized horizontally when multiple values were selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the data upload file picker could fail to accept XLS files. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where sending a POST /api/token request without a Content-Type header resulted in an HTTP 500 error. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where multi-select filter drop-down menus could immediately reopen after being closed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where Show Percent of Previous arrows and labels overlapped bars instead of appearing between them on column charts that use the Modern visualization theme, custom Group Spacing settings, or unevenly spaced dates. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Time zone settings have been updated so that scheduled job triggers and table calculation time zone evaluations reflect recent regional daylight saving time (DST) changes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where a non-admin user could delete another user's undeployed development project through the API. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where Sankey charts that were created with Chart Config Override could fail with errors such as requires exactly two dimensions or cyclical data is not supported. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where favoriting or unfavoriting a dashboard or Look updated its last-accessed timestamp and erroneously removed the item from the Unused Content list. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Fixed

title: How to Design a Final Year Project Database: ERD and Normalization to 3NF in MySQL
description:
Most FYP database chapters fall apart in the viva for one simple reason: the student drew an ERD that looks nice, then built whatever tables felt right in phpMyAdmin. The first time an examiner asks "why is this field in this table?", there is no answer.

Here is the order that survives questioning, using a hostel management system as the example:

1. Entities come from the problem statement, not from screens.
Read your problem statement and underline the nouns your system must remember: Student, Room, Allotment, Payment, Complaint. If a noun never gets stored, it is not an entity. If it gets stored and changes over time, it probably is.

2. Draw the ERD before you create a single table.
For each pair of entities, write the relationship in a sentence: "One Room has many Allotments over time, but one Allotment belongs to exactly one Room." That sentence gives you cardinality, and cardinality tells you where the foreign key lives. Panels ask about relationships far more than about box shapes.

3. Normalise to 3NF on paper, in this order.

  • 1NF: no repeating groups. A student row with phone1, phone2, phone3 fails this instantly.
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. In an Allotment table with a composite key (student_id, room_id), the student's name depends only on student_id — it moves out.
  • 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Room rent depends on room type, not on the room number — so rent lives in a RoomType table, not repeated on every Room row.

4. Only now open MySQL.
Create tables in dependency order (the "one" side first), add foreign keys with the right ON DELETE behaviour, and seed each table with 5-10 realistic rows. Realistic data is what makes your demo and your test cases believable.

5. Write the viva answers while you design.
For every table, one sentence: "This table exists because…" If you cannot finish that sentence, the table is either missing or should not exist. This is also exactly the justification your Chapter 3 needs — the full chapter structure (methodology choice, use case diagram, DFD levels, and this database design sequence) is laid out in this Chapter 3 guide if you are writing yours now.

Design on paper first, and the database stops being the scary part of the viva.

Are you drawing your ERD before or after building your tables? I am curious how other students were taught this.

title: AI personal assistants: are they a new security threat?
description:
First, a common misclassification worth correcting: models like Claude and ChatGPT are not just chat. They support tool use and function calling, and they work as agents through Claude Code, Computer Use and Agent Mode. So the ability to execute is not what sets an assistant like Instinct apart.

The real difference is in the packaging, not the capability:

  • a hosted system that runs continuously, not a session that ends when the window closes
  • ready OAuth integrations with email, calendar and files
  • long-term memory across sessions
  • background scheduling and event-driven monitoring
  • ordinary channels like iMessage

What used to require building a pipeline by hand with n8n or LangChain is now a ready service.

Does that create a new threat? No. The threat model is stable:

  1. prompt injection from external content (email, web pages)
  2. OAuth permissions broader than needed
  3. data leakage through the provider

All of these apply to any agent, hand-built or ready-made. What is new is accessibility and ease of use, not the nature of the risk.

Mitigation:

  • least privilege
  • human approval for sensitive actions (money, sending)
  • no secrets in chat
  • review execution logs

Takeaway: the risks exist, but they are old and well understood. Security is a decision about permission design before it is a decision to accept or reject the tool.

title: Best robot dog for oil and gas site inspection: B2, X30, A2 or Spot
description:
Short answer: For oil and gas rounds outside classified hazardous zones, the Unitree B2 (40 kg rated payload) or DEEP Robotics X30 (20 kg, IP67 per its maker) is usually the practical choice for a full thermal, gas and acoustic payload; the Unitree A2 suits lighter payloads at lower cost, and Spot (14 kg) suits teams that value its software ecosystem. Do not assume any standard version is certified for explosive atmospheres.

Start with the area classification, not the robot

The first question on any oil and gas site is where the robot will walk. Tank farms, compressor stations, wellpads and process units are often split into classified zones (for example Zone 1 and Zone 2 under IECEx or ATEX). A robot that enters a classified zone needs an explosion-protection certificate for that zone, and so does every sensor on its back. Ask the robot maker for the certificate covering the exact model and zone; do not rely on an IP rating, which only covers dust and water.

Many operators start with routes that stay in unclassified areas or are run under a work permit with gas monitoring, and use the robot for the repetitive parts: walking the same route every shift, logging gauge values, taking thermal images of pumps and motors and sniffing for leaks. That is the job the four robots below are compared for.

The four robots side by side

Robot Own weight Rated payload Built-in perception Maker's protection rating Best fit on an oil and gas site
Unitree B2 60 kg 40 kg 3D LiDAR, front and rear depth cameras IP67 Heavy multi-sensor payloads, long outdoor routes
DEEP Robotics X30 56 kg 20 kg Front and rear LiDAR, depth and wide-angle cameras IP67 Industrial routes in rain, dust and at night
Unitree A2 37 kg 25 kg Front and rear LiDAR, HD camera Check with the maker Medium payloads where cost and handling weight matter
Boston Dynamics Spot 32.7 kg 14 kg 5 stereo camera pairs Check with the maker Teams that value its existing software and integrations

Weights and payloads are the manufacturers' published figures. The rated payload is an upper limit; real routes with stairs, grating and slopes go better well below it.


Unitree B2 carrying a YUANZHI ROBOTICS sensor payload (3D render)

What an oil and gas inspection payload actually weighs

The robot choice usually follows from the payload. A typical oil and gas round combines four jobs: thermal checks on rotating equipment, gas detection, acoustic leak finding and reading analog gauges. Some real component figures:

  • Dual-spectrum PTZ (Hikvision DS-2TD5566T-15/V2): about 4.5 kg and 18 W. Zoom for gauges and radiometric thermal for bearings and motors in one unit.
  • Acoustic imager (CRYSOUND CRY8124): about 1.4 kg; the Fluke SV600 is lighter at about 0.85 kg. Acoustic imaging finds compressed-gas and steam leaks that a thermal camera cannot see.
  • Multi-gas module (Winsen ZCE04B, four gases including CO and H2S): about 50 g and 0.5 W. Light and cheap, but it only measures the air that reaches it, so mounting position and airflow matter.
  • Navigation LiDAR (Livox Mid-360): 265 g and 6.5 W, if the robot's own sensors are not enough for your mapping needs.
  • Onboard compute (Jetson Orin NX 16GB class): budget up to around 40 W at peak for gauge-reading and detection models.

Add brackets, an enclosure, cabling and a 5G or mesh radio, and a full thermal, acoustic, gas and PTZ payload can reach 8 to 10 kg. On a B2 that is a comfortable fraction of the rating. On an X30 or A2 it fits, but you trade some runtime. On Spot you are close to the limit and will usually swap the large PTZ for a lighter camera. Our weight and power budget guide shows how to add this up for your own list.


Optical gas imaging view of a leak plume during a robot dog patrol (scene from the YUANZHI ROBOTICS product film)

Gas detection: point sensors, acoustic or optical gas imaging

Point gas sensors confirm a concentration where the robot is standing; they do not show where the leak is. Acoustic imagers locate pressurized leaks by sound, even in noisy plants, but say nothing about which gas it is. Optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras make hydrocarbon plumes visible and are the most direct way to find methane and VOC leaks, but cooled OGI cameras are heavy, power-hungry and expensive, which pushes you towards the B2. Many sites combine a point sensor for alarms with an acoustic imager for localisation. Our thermal vs optical gas imaging guide explains what each camera can and cannot detect.

Terrain, weather and the route

  • Grating and stairs: process units are full of open-mesh grating and steep steel stairs. All four robots can climb stairs, but check foot slip on wet grating during your trial and keep the payload's centre of mass low and central.
  • Rain, dust and heat: the B2 and X30 carry IP67 ratings from their makers, but the payload enclosure, connectors and camera windows must be sealed to match. A rated robot with an unsealed payload is only as good as the payload.
  • GNSS and localization: open sites suit RTK GNSS; dense pipe racks block satellites and need LiDAR localization. Most real routes need both.
  • Night rounds: thermal works in the dark, but gauge reading needs light. Plan an illuminator and test reading accuracy at night, not just during the day.


Robot dog gimbal reading analog pressure gauges at an inspection point

How to choose

  • Map the route and mark every classified zone. If the robot must enter Zone 1 or Zone 2, start by asking each maker which certified variant exists.
  • List the payload you really need and total its weight and power before you pick the robot.
  • If the total is above roughly 10 kg or includes a cooled OGI camera, shortlist the B2. Between about 5 and 10 kg, the X30 and A2 are both reasonable. Below that, Spot also works.
  • Run a pilot on your worst stretch of route (wet grating, stairs, pipe racks) before committing to a fleet. Our pilot project guide covers what to measure.

Next steps

You can assemble an oil and gas payload on any of these robots in our online payload configurator and see the total weight and power live. Platform notes are on the Unitree B2, DEEP Robotics X30, Unitree A2 and Boston Dynamics Spot pages. For a full build, see our robot payload integration and inspection robot services, or autonomy software if you need custom routes, gauge reading or alarm logic.

Written by the engineering team at YUANZHI ROBOTICS. Original article: Best robot dog for oil and gas site inspection: B2, X30, A2 or Spot
