title: Claranet migra SAP Business One da Skintec para AWS
description:
Migração do ERP para a nuvem

A Claranet migrou o ERP SAP Business One da Skintec para a AWS, encerrando uma operação totalmente local que havia se tornado um gargalo com a adoção do trabalho híbrido. A iniciativa mudou a infraestrutura que sustentava o sistema usado pela fornecedora de equipamentos para medicina estética, dermatologia e spas.

Antes da migração, o acesso remoto ao sistema sofria quedas frequentes e lentidão, além de dificultar atualizações e restringir contratações fora do modelo presencial. A ampliação da infraestrutura de TI dependia da compra e da entrega de servidores físicos, enquanto os backups eram feitos manualmente e os dados precisavam ser migrados localmente a cada ajuste.

Transferência para instâncias EC2

A Claranet transferiu o SAP Business One para instâncias Amazon EC2 exatamente como o sistema estava nos servidores locais, em uma abordagem conhecida como lift and shift. Depois da transferência, o sistema foi atualizado já na nuvem, conforme o projeto descrito pelas empresas.

Walter Oliveira, head de tecnologia, inovação e desenvolvimento da Skintec, afirmou que a mudança reduziu o tempo gasto com manutenção de hardware, compras burocráticas e backups manuais. Segundo ele, a tecnologia passou a funcionar como um motor de agilidade para o negócio, em vez de consumir tempo da equipe com tarefas de infraestrutura.

Próxima etapa de segurança de rede

As empresas concluíram o desenho de uma arquitetura para evoluir a VPN corporativa com firewalls FortiGate, da Fortinet. O próximo passo prevê o fechamento completo da rede para protegê-la contra ameaças externas; essa etapa ainda está planejada, após a conclusão da migração do ERP.

Empresas envolvidas no projeto

Com mais de três décadas de atuação, a Skintec atende clínicas e profissionais de estética no mercado brasileiro. A Claranet é uma provedora global de serviços de tecnologia, com atuação em nuvem, inteligência artificial, dados, cibersegurança e workplace, e atende clientes corporativos em projetos de transformação digital.

No Brasil, a Claranet reforçou sua operação nos últimos anos por meio de aquisições locais. A migração do SAP Business One da Skintec é um projeto de infraestrutura em nuvem conduzido pela provedora, enquanto a evolução da VPN com FortiGate compõe a etapa de segurança prevista para a sequência do trabalho.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/claranet-migra-erp-sap-business-one-skintec-aws/

title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
description:
arXiv:2611.34042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.

title: A chroma step edge is never one pixel wide after 4:2:0 — and the decoder does the widening
description:
I spent a day trying to answer a question that sounded trivial: when a marketplace re-encodes my product photo with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, how much of the cutout edge does it eat?

The trivial answer is "some". The measured answer turned out to be more specific, and it moved the blame somewhere I did not expect. On a boundary that falls exactly on a chroma sample boundary, the subsampling itself costs nothing. The stored colours come back exact. The two-pixel ramp that shows up in the decoded file is produced entirely by the decoder's upsampling filter.

That is not a rounding-error distinction. It changes what you can do about it, because the two costs have different remedies and different sizes depending on where your edge happens to land.

Here is the whole measurement, with the fixtures that make each number checkable.

The pipeline, and the one stage under test

A JPEG encoder for a colour image does this:

RGB -> YCbCr -> subsample Cb,Cr -> 8x8 DCT + quantise -> entropy code -> file

4:2:0 means the two chroma planes are stored at half resolution in both directions. 4:2:2 halves only horizontally. 4:4:4 stores all three planes at full resolution.

Four of those five stages are not what I want to measure, so I held them fixed by holding the encoder fixed: Pillow over libjpeg, one quality, one image, only the subsampling argument changing. Pillow's argument is an integer — 0, 1, 2 — and I did not take the docstring's word for what it does. Reading the SOF0 marker out of the produced files:

4:4:4: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 17), (2, 17), (3, 17)]
4:2:2: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 33), (2, 17), (3, 17)]
4:2:0: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 34), (2, 17), (3, 17)]

Those are hex-ish byte pairs: luma sampling factor 0x11 at 4:4:4, 0x21 at 4:2:2, 0x22 at 4:2:0, with both chroma components at 0x11. So the parameter is doing what it says.

The other thing I checked before trusting a single-variable comparison: whether changing subsampling also changes the quantisation tables. It does not, at least not here.

q95  4:4:4  luma sum 369   chroma sum 558
q95  4:2:0  luma sum 369   chroma sum 558
q85  4:4:4  luma sum 1109  chroma sum 1666
q85  4:2:0  luma sum 1109  chroma sum 1666

Byte-identical tables. That matters, because if the encoder had quietly softened the chroma quantiser for 4:4:4 then "4:4:4 is better at the same quality" would be measuring two things at once and the comparison would be worthless. It is one thing.

Fixture one: an image with nothing to subsample

The first test is not about the encoder. It is about the meter, and it exists so that every later number has a floor.

Take a real product photo, throw away its colour, re-encode at q85 in all three configurations.

greyscale source, nothing for the chroma grid to hold:
  4:4:4  dE  0.388  dC  0.000   10334 bytes
  4:2:2  dE  0.388  dC  0.000    9874 bytes
  4:2:0  dE  0.388  dC  0.000    9747 bytes

dC is the mean absolute change in chroma; dE is CIEDE2000. On a greyscale image the chroma planes are flat, so the subsampling has literally nothing to average, and the chroma error is exactly 0.000 at all three settings — while the file still gets 6% smaller. The dE of 0.388 is identical in all three, which is the tell: that number is luma quantisation, untouched by the chroma stage.

If a chroma metric reports a cost on a greyscale image, it is measuring luma. Mine does not, which is the only reason I kept using it.

Fixture two: a step in chroma and nothing else

Two flat fields, same lightness, different hue, meeting at a hard vertical boundary:

def chroma_step(w=192, h=128, edge=None, vertical=True,
                left=(55.0, 45.0, 20.0), right=(55.0, -35.0, 35.0)):
    ...

Identical L*, different a* and b*. Luma is constant everywhere, so luma quantisation cannot move the boundary, and any change across it has to be the chroma stage.

Now the measurement. I want a number that is the width of the transition, not a threshold count, because an integer count of a continuous thing flaps. The one I used:

effective width = 1 / sum of squared pixel-to-pixel steps, normalised

A hard edge scores 1.00. The same total change spread over two equal steps scores 2.00; over four, 4.00. No tolerance, so no pixel can land on the wrong side of one.

Run that on the decoded file, at the boundary position that falls on the chroma grid (x=96, even) and one pixel off it (x=97, odd, halfway through a 2x2 chroma sample):

edge runs vertically  (varies along x), at pixel 96:
  4:4:4  width x  1.00 px
  4:2:2  width x  2.60 px
  4:2:0  width x  2.60 px
edge runs vertically  (varies along x), at pixel 97:
  4:4:4  width x  1.09 px
  4:2:2  width x  4.33 px
  4:2:0  width x  4.40 px

So: 4:4:4 keeps a step. 4:2:0 turns it into a ramp of 2.6 pixels or 4.4 pixels depending on phase, and 4:2:2 is already at the 4:2:0 value on a vertical edge, because a vertical edge varies horizontally, which is the direction 4:2:2 halves.

And the direction check, which is what stops a single isotropic number from faking any of this — same fixture rotated, so the chroma now varies down the image instead of across it:

edge runs horizontally (varies along y), at pixel 96:
  4:4:4  y 1.00 px    4:2:2  y 1.00 px    4:2:0  y 2.60 px
edge runs horizontally (varies along y), at pixel 97:
  4:4:4  y 1.09 px    4:2:2  y 1.09 px    4:2:0  y 4.42 px

4:2:2 is a complete no-op on a horizontal edge and full strength on a vertical one. 4:2:0 hits both. That asymmetry is a property of the format, not of my measurement, and it is the cheapest way to check that a subsampling test is testing subsampling.

Splitting the bill: what the file did, and what the decoder did

The 2.6 and 4.4 above are totals. Two stages contribute to them and only one of them is in the file.

So I built the encoder by hand — box-average the chroma planes to half resolution, put them back — with no DCT and no quantisation, and tried two reconstruction rules:

  • replicate: each stored sample is copied to the 2x2 pixels it covers. This is the minimum any decoder could do.
  • triangle: libjpeg's "fancy" upsampler, out[2k] = (3s[k] + s[k-1]) / 4 and out[2k+1] = (3s[k] + s[k+1]) / 4. 
edge along x, at 96:  replicate  1.00 px   triangle  2.57 px   libjpeg  2.60 px
edge along x, at 97:  replicate  2.02 px   triangle  4.49 px   libjpeg  4.40 px
edge along y, at 96:  replicate  1.00 px   triangle  2.57 px   libjpeg  2.60 px
edge along y, at 97:  replicate  2.02 px   triangle  4.49 px   libjpeg  4.42 px

The triangle row lands on libjpeg's real output to within a few hundredths, which is the check that the hand-built encoder is actually the thing I claim it is. And now the split is explicit:

  • Aligned boundary: the container costs 0.00 px. The whole 1.60 px of excess is the decode filter. The stored chroma values are exactly right; the decoder is what declines to reproduce them as a step.
  • Half-sample boundary: 1.02 px is the box average losing the transition, and 2.38 px is the filter again.

You can see it in the pixel values directly. Source a* across the edge, then what comes back:

source             [44.9  44.9  44.9  44.9  -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
replication 2x2    [44.9  44.9  44.9  44.9  -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
triangle    2x2    [44.9  44.9  44.9  25.72 -16.13 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
libjpeg     4:2:0  [44.81 44.81 44.81 24.80 -16.67 -35.32 -35.32 -35.32 -35.32]

Replication is exact. The triangle decoder emits 0.24 and 0.76 of the way across the transition at two adjacent pixels — the signature of convolving a step with a 1-3-1 kernel. libjpeg's real output is 0.25 and 0.77. The 4:2:0 file did not contain a ramp; it contains two chroma values and nothing else, and the ramp is manufactured at display time.

This is why "4:2:0 halves your chroma resolution" is simultaneously true and misleading. It halves the sampled resolution. What reaches your eyes is that, run back through a low-pass filter that is wider than the grid, so you get roughly a quarter of the chroma resolution in width terms and you cannot get the subsampling back without also getting the filter back.

The grid that matters is not the grid in the tutorials

4:2:0 is usually described in terms of 16x16 pixel blocks, which makes it sound as though a boundary aligned to that grid would be safe. That number is the DCT block — 8x8 chroma coefficients covering 16x16 pixels — and it is the wrong grid for this question.

An edge has to survive the sample grid, which at 4:2:0 is one chroma sample per 2x2 pixels. I walked the boundary one pixel at a time across 17 positions and measured the decoded width:

edge phase  4:4:4   4:2:2   4:2:0
  88    0     1.00    2.75    2.83
  89    1     1.09    4.56    4.53
  90    0     1.11    2.58    2.59
  91    1     1.00    4.66    4.63
  92    0     1.09    2.69    2.82
  93    1     1.01    4.63    4.59
  ...
  96    0     1.00    2.60    2.60
  97    1     1.09    4.33    4.40

The period is 2, not 16. Nothing special happens at phase 0 or phase 8; every even pixel behaves one way and every odd pixel behaves a worse way. Across the 17 positions the even rows land in 2.56 to 2.83 and the odd rows in 4.33 to 4.70, while the 4:4:4 control jitters between 1.00 and 1.11 — that jitter is luma quantisation bleeding into the a* line I sample, and it is the noise floor for the whole table.

Aligning a product edge to a 16-pixel grid therefore buys nothing at all. You would need to align it to a 2-pixel grid, which means choosing the parity of the boundary, which is not a design decision anyone can make on purpose.

Now the same question on 16 real product photos

Synthetic steps are countable but they are not photographs. So: 16 covers from a working article pipeline, resized to 640 px wide, each encoded at three qualities and three sampling settings, error measured against the untouched PNG inside a subject mask.

The mask is deliberately crude — median border colour, CIEDE2000 distance above 12, plus a 3-pixel dilation/erosion band as "the edge" — and identical for every configuration, so its crudeness is shared and cannot be part of the difference between rows.

Means over the 16 photos at q85 (dE whole subject, dE_edge the boundary band, dC chroma, dH chroma-weighted hue rotation, in degrees):

config dE dE_edge dC dH bytes
4:4:4 1.243 1.393 0.741 2.444 44,849
4:2:2 1.346 1.543 0.891 2.736 40,306
4:2:0 1.433 1.689 1.026 2.905 37,850

At q95 and q75 the pattern holds with slightly different magnitudes: edge error goes 0.963 -> 1.228 at q95 and 1.736 -> 2.021 at q75 for 4:4:4 -> 4:2:0. So the cost of 4:2:0 is +21% on the edge at q85 for 15.6% fewer bytes, and the edge is hit harder than the image as a whole: dE rises 15.3%, dE_edge 21.2%.

The per-photo spread is wide, and worth knowing before anyone quotes a single multiplier:

4:2:0 ratio of edge error vs 4:4:4:  range 1.00x to 1.68x, median 1.17x
  worst   remove-bg-vs-pixelcut-vs-picviva-2026   1.322 -> 2.222
  best    dropshipping-product-images-supplier-photos  0.910 -> 0.911

One photo is unaffected; another's edge error grows 68%. "Chroma subsampling costs you about a fifth of your edge accuracy" is a median with a range wide enough to be useless for a single image — which is why the mechanism matters more than the average.

At the same file size, subsampling is a bad trade

The comparison above holds the encoder's quality setting equal. That is not the comparison a person shipping a file actually has. They have a byte budget. So the interesting question is: given 38 KB, is it better spent on 4:4:4 at a lower quality, or on 4:2:0 at a higher one?

Bisect the 4:4:4 quality until its file is no bigger than the 4:2:0 file (match to within 2%):

q 4:4:4 quality needed bytes dE_edge vs 4:2:0 at the same size
95 92.8 66,435 1.082 1.228
85 78.9 37,222 1.593 1.689
75 64.4 28,175 1.974 2.021

4:4:4 wins at every size. The price is a quality drop of 2.2 points at q95, 6.1 at q85 and 10.6 at q75 — the more you have already compressed, the more quality you have to surrender to buy the 15–17% of bytes back. Expressing it as a rate:

q95: subsampling is 2.23x as expensive per byte saved as lowering the quality
q85: 1.48x
q75: 1.20x

The trend is the interesting part. At high quality the chroma grid is the binding constraint and losing it is expensive; at q75 luma quantisation has already destroyed so much that the two options converge. If you are shipping at q85 or above, 4:2:0 is not a good deal. If you are already at q70 because the marketplace caps you at 100 KB, the argument mostly disappears — which is also why the folklore "4:2:0 is fine, nobody can see it" is sometimes true and never for the reason given.

Checking the mechanism without a mask

Everything above depends on a mask, and a mask is a place to hide a mistake. So here is the same damage measured with no mask, no boundary detection, and no threshold: bucket every pixel with meaningful chroma by how fast the chroma was changing in the original, and average the error per bucket.

If subsampling damages edges because a half-resolution grid cannot hold a fast change, the error has to rise with the gradient. If it is flat, my story is wrong.

bin (flattest 12.5% first):
  4:4:4             0.492  0.552  0.611  0.675  0.754  0.830  0.956  1.444
  4:2:0             0.645  0.726  0.811  0.906  1.044  1.173  1.385  2.305
  ratio 4:2:0/4:4:4  1.31   1.31   1.33   1.34   1.38   1.41   1.45   1.60

Both curves rise, because JPEG is lossy everywhere and steeper chroma is harder to code at any sampling ratio. The ratio is what isolates subsampling, and it rises monotonically: 1.31x on flat chroma, 1.60x on the steepest twelfth. The extra cost is concentrated exactly where the grid is thinnest.

That is the mechanism, confirmed on 15 of the 16 photos (one was excluded by the binning guard: only 4.1% of its frame is subject, too few high-gradient pixels to fill the last bucket).

The part I did not expect: the platform's re-encode dominates

Nothing in the previous sections decides what a buyer sees, because nobody ships one encode. A seller exports, the marketplace ingests and re-encodes, and that second file is the one on the page.

So: seven uploads, each pushed once through the same marketplace-style pass (q82, 4:2:0), error measured against the original PNG both before and after.

upload bytes dE_edge before dE_edge after the pass added
png 233 KB 0.000 1.786 —
4:4:4 q95 82 KB 0.963 1.806 +87%
4:4:4 q85 44 KB 1.393 1.867 +34%
4:2:2 q85 39 KB 1.543 1.894 +23%
4:2:0 q95 68 KB 1.228 1.854 +51%
4:2:0 q85 37 KB 1.689 1.890 +12%
4:2:0 q70 25 KB 2.143 2.274 +6%

Two things fall out of that table.

First, the losses are not additive, they overlap. The platform pass charges a pristine 4:4:4 q95 export 87%, and an already-4:2:0 q85 export only 12%, because most of what it would remove has already been removed. Uploading the best possible file does not get you the best possible output; it gets you 1.806, which is within 1.1% of what an untouched PNG would have produced (1.786) and 4.4% better than uploading a 4:2:0 q85 file, which is the file that would otherwise sit on the page.

Second, the choice you control is worth a few percent, and the choice you do not control is worth tens. Across all seven uploads the final edge error spans 1.786 to 2.274 — 27% — and six of those seven sit inside 6% of each other. Meanwhile the single re-encode in the middle of every chain, which you have no say in, is worth more than any of it.

The practical reading: stop optimising your export for a platform that is going to overwrite it, and check what the platform actually does instead, because that is the stage with the leverage.

Re-saving is nearly free, until you change a setting

The last thing I wanted to know is what happens on the second and third pass, because "every save loses quality" is repeated constantly and I wanted a number.

Same file, four passes, chroma error against the untouched PNG:

chain             pass 1   pass 2   pass 3   pass 4    total
82 x4              1.072    1.088    1.095    1.099     +2.5%
90 x4              0.943    0.967    0.982    0.991     +5.1%
82,90,75,82        1.072    1.120    1.287    1.320    +23.2%

Passes two to four at a fixed setting add 1.6% / 0.6% / 0.4% of the first pass's cost, converging. The quantised coefficients map onto themselves, so re-encoding at the setting that produced the file lands back on nearly the same coefficients. Four saves are not four times the loss; they are about 1.02 times it.

Change the setting between passes and it starts over. Pass three of 82, 90, 75, 82 — the one after the quality drops to 75 — adds 15.6% of the first pass's cost on its own.

So the folklore is wrong in its mechanism and right in its conclusion, which is the worst combination. Re-saving is not what accumulates. Re-saving differently is. A workflow that touches a file five times at one setting is fine. A workflow that touches it twice at two settings is not.

What I would actually do

Given all of the above, and being honest that it is calibrated on one encoder:

  1. Find out whether the platform re-encodes at all, and at what. If it does not, upload the best file you can and stop reading. If it does, its settings are the dominant term and your export is a rounding decision.
  2. Do not use 4:2:0 as a size lever at q85 or above. At equal bytes, 4:4:4 is better on the edge at every quality I tested, and the price is two to eleven quality points — cheap at the top of the range, expensive at the bottom. Subsampling is only competitive once you are already deep into low quality.
  3. If you must use it, know that the container is not the whole cost. At q85 the edge error goes from 1.393 to 1.689; the box average accounts for part of that and the decode filter for the rest, and on an aligned boundary the box average accounts for none of it. You cannot buy the filter's share back with more chroma samples — the only thing that removes it is 4:4:4.
  4. Do not bother aligning product edges to a block grid. The period is 2 pixels, not 16. Aligning to 2 pixels means controlling boundary parity, which nobody can do deliberately.
  5. Export once, at the setting you will keep. Repeated identical saves cost about 2%, repeated different saves cost 20%+.

What this does not cover

  • One encoder. Pillow over libjpeg(-turbo). mozjpeg, libvips/sharp, and the various CDN encoders pick their own upsampler and their own chroma quantisation, so the split between "container" and "decoder" will move — the aligned-edge result in particular is a property of the triangle filter, and a decoder using nearest-neighbour would show the 1.00 px figure instead.
  • One colour space. sRGB in, YCbCr out, no ICC handling. Wide-gamut input will hit different chroma quantisation.
  • A 640 px working width. At full marketplace resolution the 2-pixel grid is a smaller fraction of the subject, so absolute dE_edge values will move; the mechanism will not.
  • A coarse mask. CIEDE2000 > 12 from the border median is not a segmentation model. It is identical across every row of every table, which is what the comparison needs, and it is why I also report the mask-free gradient table.
  • dE_edge is not perceptual importance. A ramp on the outside of a product's outline is often less visible than the same ramp across a printed logo inside it. Everything here is measured on pixel neighbourhoods, not on what a person notices.

Reproducing it

Five files, all of them plain numpy and Pillow:

  • subsample.py — the fixtures, the hand-built encoder, and the instrument checks in validate(). Run it first; if the greyscale chroma error is not 0.000, or the triangle row does not land on libjpeg, nothing after it means anything.
  • subsample_run.py — the 16-photo matrix, pinned by name and sha256 in subsample_photos.json so the corpus cannot drift out from under the numbers.
  • subsample_cascade.py — the marketplace-pass comparison and the equal-bytes bisection.
  • subsample_chain.py — the repeated-save chains.
  • subsample_report.py — every figure quoted above, printed from the JSON.

The pinning is not fussiness. My first run of the matrix and my first run of the cascade picked different photos, because the cover corpus grew between them, and for a while two tables in this piece were describing two different sets of images.

I work on the image pipeline at PicViva, which is where I ran into this: the export-and-upload step is ours, the ingest-and-re-encode step belongs to the marketplace, and it took a while to work out which of the two was costing the edge. The short version is that it is usually not the one I can fix in our code.

title: Article: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
description:
Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics. This article explores a six-stage architecture to address these challenges.

By Praveen Kumar Gopalakrishnan

title: How to check Allegro.pl prices for a list of EAN codes in bulk with Python
description:
If you sell on Allegro, or you supply people who do, the question you keep asking is simple: for this list of products, who sells each one and for how much? Checking that by hand works for five EANs. It stops working at fifty.

This guide shows how to feed a list of EAN/GTIN codes into the Allegro Prices by EAN scraper on Apify and get back every seller and price for each product. I ran it on 12 everyday EANs this morning (a Coca-Cola can, Mars bars, a Nivea cream, Stabilo and BIC pens, mineral water, Nutella) and all the numbers below come from that run.

What you get back

One row per EAN. Each row has summary prices plus a nested offers list with one entry per seller.

Field What it holds
ean, found Your code and whether Allegro has an exact product match for it
productName, productId, productUrl The matched Allegro product page
totalOffersAvailable How many offers Allegro lists for that product
offerCount How many offers came back in this row (capped by topNOffers)
lowestPrice, highestPrice, avgPrice Min, max and mean across the returned offers, PLN gross
smartOffersCount, superSellerOffersCount Offers with Allegro Smart! and with the Super Seller badge
alternativeMatches Other products that matched the same code, such as multipacks
offers[] price, sellerRating, isSuperSeller, isCompany, smart, freeDelivery, deliveryInfo, isPromoted, offerUrl

A few results from my run, with topNOffers set to 30 and sorted cheapest first:

Product Offers on Allegro Lowest Median of returned
Mars bar 139 2.46 PLN 3.20 PLN
Stabilo Point 88 fineliner 211 2.99 PLN 3.87 PLN
Coca-Cola 330 ml can 59 3.15 PLN 5.52 PLN
Cisowianka still water 6x1.5 L 30 2.99 PLN 21.49 PLN

Two of the 12 codes came back as found: false with the message "No exact match for this EAN on Allegro.pl". That is the behaviour you want. Allegro showed only "similar" items for those codes, and the scraper refused to guess.

The input options that matter

The input form has seven fields. You will touch four of them.

  • eans (required). One code per line, 8 to 14 digits, up to 5,000 per run.
  • topNOffers. How many offers to keep per product, 1 to 200, default 20. You pay per EAN, so raising this to 200 costs the same. The trade-off is a bigger dataset.
  • sortBy. price-asc, price-desc or rating-desc. Combined with topNOffers this decides which offers you see. On the Mars bar, with 139 offers and a limit of 30, the "highest" price in the row was 3.49 PLN because I only kept the 30 cheapest.
  • smartFilter. all, smart-only or exclude-smart. Useful if you only care about offers a Smart! buyer would actually pick.

The rest: includePromoted (I switched it off to skip sponsored listings), useCache (keeps the EAN to product match for 30 days so repeat runs skip the search step; prices are never cached) and maxConcurrency (1 to 25).

Option 1: no code

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free. A free Apify account is enough.
  2. Paste your EANs into the EAN / GTIN codes box, one per line. A column copied from Excel works.
  3. Set Max offers per product. I used 30.
  4. Pick a sort order and, if you want, the Smart! filter.
  5. Click Start. My 12 codes took 186 seconds with concurrency at 6. For a few hundred codes, raise concurrency (the maximum is 25).
  6. Open the Output tab and export to CSV, Excel or JSON. The summary columns export flat. The offers list exports as nested JSON, which is where Python helps.

Option 2: Python with pandas

Install the client and pandas:

pip install apify-client pandas

Then run the actor, pull the dataset and flatten the offers into one row per seller:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run_input = {
    "eans": [
        "5449000000996",  # Coca-Cola 330 ml
        "5000159407236",  # Mars
        "4006381333931",  # Stabilo Point 88
        "5902078000201",  # Cisowianka 6x1.5 L
    ],
    "topNOffers": 30,
    "sortBy": "price-asc",
    "includePromoted": False,
}

run = client.actor("liveclaude/allegro-ean-prices").call(run_input=run_input)
items = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

# Summary: one row per EAN
summary = pd.DataFrame(items)
cols = ["ean", "found", "productName", "totalOffersAvailable",
        "lowestPrice", "avgPrice", "highestPrice"]
print(summary[[c for c in cols if c in summary.columns]])

# Offers: one row per seller offer
found = [i for i in items if i.get("found")]
offers = pd.json_normalize(found, record_path="offers",
                           meta=["ean", "productName"])

# Median is safer than mean on Allegro (see below)
stats = (offers.groupby(["ean", "productName"])["price"]
               .agg(["count", "min", "median", "max"])
               .reset_index())
print(stats)

# Only business sellers with Smart!
b2b_smart = offers[(offers["isCompany"] == True) & (offers["smart"] == True)]
b2b_smart[["ean", "price", "sellerRating", "deliveryInfo", "offerUrl"]] \
    .to_csv("allegro_offers.csv", index=False)

Why the median? Look at the water row. The cheapest offer was 2.99 PLN, but the average across 22 offers was 329.69 PLN because someone lists a pallet under the same product. The Nutella 500 g row had a lowest price of 20.65 PLN and an average of 613.11 PLN for the same reason. The median of the returned offers (21.49 PLN for the water) is much closer to what a buyer pays. If you run price monitoring on avgPrice alone, these outliers will make it look like prices jumped.

One more check worth adding: compare productName against what you expect. One code in my list matched a product whose name had nothing to do with the brand I had in mind. Sellers sometimes attach the wrong EAN to a listing, and Allegro's catalogue inherits it. A quick string check on the name catches that before it reaches a report.

Scheduling and integrations

Price checks are only useful when they repeat. In Apify Console:

  • Save your input as a Task, then add a Schedule (daily at 06:00 works for most monitoring).
  • Connect the dataset to Google Sheets, Make, Zapier or n8n, or add a webhook that fires when the run succeeds.
  • With useCache on, the second and later runs skip the EAN lookup. In my run the Coca-Cola code came back with fromCache: true from an earlier lookup.

You can also call it in one HTTP request:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/liveclaude~allegro-ean-prices/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"eans": ["5449000000996"], "topNOffers": 50}'

Pricing

The actor charges per EAN, with all offers for that EAN included:

Event Free plan Bronze Silver Gold and up
EAN matched (product + all offers), per 1,000 $12.00 $11.40 $10.80 $10.20
EAN with no exact match, per 1,000 $4.00 $3.80 $3.60 $3.40

There is also a start fee of $0.00005 per run. My 12-code test was 10 matches and 2 misses, so about $0.13 on the Free plan. A daily check of 1,000 EANs on the Free plan comes to about $12 per day if every code matches. Codes the scraper fails to fetch on its side are not charged.

Responsible use

The data is public listing data: prices, product names and seller ratings anyone can see on allegro.pl without logging in. Some Allegro sellers are private individuals, and their login can be their real name. Keep seller logins out of anything you publish, and only store them if you have a business reason and a legal basis under GDPR. For price monitoring you rarely need them; isCompany, sellerRating and the offer URL are usually enough. Keep request volumes sensible and respect Allegro's terms for your use case.

If you already keep your catalogue in a spreadsheet with an EAN column, you are one paste away from a full competitor price list. Start with 20 codes, check the matches by hand once, then put it on a schedule.

This tutorial was written with AI assistance and checked by the author. All numbers come from a real run of the scraper.

title: 30 Days of Rust: A Free, Beginner-Friendly Course From Syntax to a CLI Project
description:
A practical path from “what is ownership?” to code you can actually build

Rust can feel like two languages at once. The syntax is approachable, but ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, async, and concurrency can make the learning path feel scattered.

I built 30 Days of Rust to make that path clearer. It is a free, beginner-friendly course built around short explanations, runnable examples, exercises, worked solutions, and a final command-line project.

All 30 lessons are included, along with separate solutions for every day.

What is in the course?

  • 30 structured lessons that move from Rust fundamentals to practical applications
  • Runnable examples for each stage of the course
  • Exercises and separate worked solutions so you can practice before checking the answer
  • A complete CLI task manager project for applying what you have learned
  • Workspace checks for formatting, Clippy, tests, and documentation generation

The lessons are Markdown files, so you can read them directly on GitHub. Cargo examples are organized as workspace members, while standalone examples include their own compile commands in the lesson pages.

The 30-day roadmap

Days 1–6: Rust foundations

You start with variables, data types, operators, control flow, and functions before moving into the big one: ownership.

Days 7–12: Core Rust

The second stage covers references and borrowing, strings and slices, structs and methods, enums and pattern matching, collections, and error handling.

Days 13–18: Intermediate Rust

From there, the course introduces generics, traits, lifetimes, modules and packages, iterators and closures, and smart pointers.

Days 19–24: Broader Rust programming

This stage gets closer to everyday application work with testing and debugging, file handling, serialization and deserialization, concurrency, async fundamentals, and macros.

Days 25–30: Practical Rust

The final stretch covers external crates, environment configuration, command-line applications, code quality and documentation, a CLI task manager, and next steps for continuing with Rust.

How I recommend using it

  1. Read the lesson for the day.
  2. Run the included example instead of only reading it.
  3. Attempt the exercise before opening the solution.
  4. Change the example or add one small feature of your own.

That last step matters. A lesson becomes much more useful when you deliberately break the example, read the compiler's error message, and work out how to fix it.

For example, you can compile and run the Day 1 example from the repository root:

rustc days/01-introduction/examples/hello_world.rs -o hello_world
./hello_world

After installing the stable Rust toolchain with rustup, you can also run the workspace checks:

cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace

Who is it for?

The course assumes no prior systems-programming experience. It is for anyone who wants a structured starting point for Rust and is ready to write code alongside the lessons. You will need the stable Rust toolchain, rustc, and Cargo.

This is community learning material, not an official Rust project. The course materials are dual-licensed under MIT or Apache 2.0, at your option.

Explore the course

The repository is here:

https://github.com/gbubemi22/-30-Days-of-Rust

If the course helps you, a star makes it easier for other learners to find. Suggestions, corrections, and improvements are welcome through GitHub issues and pull requests.

What topic in Rust gave you the most trouble when you were getting started?

title: Is the BTC Long Trade Crowded? Funding Rate and Taker Flow in 60 Lines of Python
description:
Perpetual futures give you two cheap, public signals about positioning that a price chart does not show:

  • Funding rate: what longs pay shorts (or the reverse) every 8 hours to keep the perpetual close to spot. When funding is high, holding a long is expensive, and people are paying it anyway.
  • Taker buy ratio: the share of traded volume where the buyer crossed the spread. It tells you who is in a hurry.

Neither one is a trading signal on its own. Put together, they answer a narrower question that I find more useful: is one side of the trade getting crowded right now?

This post builds a small classifier for that in Python, using a public exchange API that needs no key.

The data

I use WEEX's public futures market API because it serves both funding history and candles with taker-buy volume, and it does not need an account. Any exchange with these two endpoints works the same way.

  • GET /capi/v3/market/klines: 4-hour candles. Column 9 is taker-buy volume.
  • GET /capi/v3/market/fundingRate: funding history, one print every 8 hours. 
import requests
import pandas as pd

BASE = "https://api-contract.weex.com/capi/v3/market"


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def load(symbol="BTCUSDT", bars=180):
    k = get("/klines", symbol=symbol, interval="4h", limit=bars)
    px = pd.DataFrame(k, columns=["open_time", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume",
                                  "close_time", "quote_volume", "trades", "taker_buy", "taker_buy_quote"])
    px["time"] = pd.to_datetime(px["open_time"], unit="ms")
    for c in ["close", "volume", "taker_buy"]:
        px[c] = px[c].astype(float)
    px = px.sort_values("time")

    f = pd.DataFrame(get("/fundingRate", symbol=symbol, limit=100))
    f["time"] = pd.to_datetime(f["fundingTime"], unit="ms")
    f["funding"] = f["fundingRate"].astype(float)
    f = f.sort_values("time")

    # Each 4h bar takes the most recent funding print.
    df = pd.merge_asof(px[["time", "close", "volume", "taker_buy"]], f[["time", "funding"]], on="time")
    return df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

Two details matter here. The candles do not always come back in time order, so sort them. And funding settles every 8 hours while the candles are 4 hours, so merge_asof carries the latest funding print forward instead of leaving gaps.

Compare each series with its own recent past

The first version of this script used fixed thresholds, such as "taker buy ratio above 52% means buyers are aggressive." That failed straight away. On this venue the 24-hour taker buy ratio sat around 47% for the whole sample, so a fixed 52% line never fired.

Every venue has its own baseline: fee tiers, market makers and how volume is counted all shift it. So instead of absolute levels, I use a z-score against the last 7 days (42 four-hour bars):

def crowding(df, window=42):
    out = df.copy()
    roll = out["funding"].rolling(window)
    out["funding_z"] = (out["funding"] - roll.mean()) / roll.std()

    # Taker buy share of volume, smoothed over 24h (6 bars).
    out["taker_buy_ratio"] = out["taker_buy"].rolling(6).sum() / out["volume"].rolling(6).sum()
    troll = out["taker_buy_ratio"].rolling(window)
    out["taker_z"] = (out["taker_buy_ratio"] - troll.mean()) / troll.std()

    def label(r):
        if r.funding_z > 1.5 and r.taker_z > 1:
            return "crowded long"
        if r.funding_z < -1.5 and r.taker_z < -1:
            return "crowded short"
        if r.funding_z > 1.5 and r.taker_z < -1:
            return "longs paying, buyers fading"
        return "neutral"

    out["state"] = out.apply(label, axis=1)
    return out

The four states:

State Funding Taker flow Reading
Crowded long Unusually high Buyers unusually aggressive Late longs are chasing and paying for it
Crowded short Unusually negative Sellers unusually aggressive The mirror image
Longs paying, buyers fading Unusually high Buyers backing off Longs are still holding an expensive position, but nobody new is adding
Neutral Anything else

The third one is the state I watch most. High funding with fading buyers means the long side is paying to wait.

What it printed

Running it on BTCUSDT for the 30 days to 27 November 2026:

               time     close  funding_bps  funding_z  taker_buy_ratio  taker_z                       state
2026-11-26 08:00:00 60686.700        0.850      1.556            0.475   -0.639                     neutral
2026-11-26 12:00:00 60599.900        0.850      1.521            0.462   -1.481 longs paying, buyers fading
2026-11-26 16:00:00 60696.900        0.456      0.402            0.474   -0.626                     neutral
2026-11-27 00:00:00 61392.600        0.987      1.744            0.472   -0.675                     neutral

state
neutral                        172
crowded short                    7
longs paying, buyers fading      1

Out of 180 four-hour bars, 172 were neutral. That is what you want from a filter like this: it should stay quiet most of the time. Funding was elevated for most of 26 and 27 November, but taker flow only dropped far enough to flag it once.

How I read the current tape

BTC pushed from about $60,500 to $61,500 into 27 November while funding climbed back toward the top of its 7-day range. Taker flow did not follow: the buy share stayed slightly below its weekly average the whole time. In plain terms, longs are paying more to hold, but the move up is not being driven by aggressive buyers.

I would not call that bearish on its own. It looks more like a market drifting up on thin participation, which tends to be fragile in both directions. Two things would change my view:

  • If taker buying picks up while funding stays high, the classifier flips to "crowded long". That is usually the point where a pullback flushes late longs.
  • If funding cools back to neutral while price holds above $61,000, the long side has reset without a liquidation, which is a healthier base for continuation.

Until one of those happens, I treat breakouts here with more suspicion than usual.

What this does not do

It does not predict the next candle. Order-flow measures are good at describing the bar you are in and poor at forecasting the next one. A test on BTC 5-minute data found taker imbalance correlated 0.44 with the same candle and only −0.10 with the next one (source). I expect the 4-hour version to behave the same way, and I have not backtested it.

So I use the output as context, not as an entry rule. A "crowded long" flag makes me less willing to chase a breakout. It does not make me short.

Some easy extensions:

  • Add open interest. If it rises while funding is high, new money is joining the crowded side. Most exchanges only give the current value for free, so you have to store snapshots yourself.
  • Run the same code on ETH and SOL and compare which market is more stretched.
  • Tune the window. Seven days reacts quickly; thirty days gives you fewer, stronger flags.

The full script is about 60 lines. If you try it on another venue, I would be curious whether its taker baseline also sits away from 50%.

This post was generated with an AI agent. The code was run and the numbers were checked against live data before publishing. Not financial advice.

title: GDOM: A Browser-Based Operations Console for GBase 8a
description:
GDOM (GBase Database Operation Manager) is the B/S-architected operations tool that GBASE ships for its China-domestically developed GBase 8a MPP database. Its goal is full-lifecycle operations coverage: visual monitoring plus cluster management, host management, health checks and alerting, so that running a cluster 7×24 costs less and breaks less often.

Most everyday gcadmin commands are available inside GDOM — running SQL, cluster locks, events and failover included. The notes below are based on GDOM 3.2Build2 from early December 2024, monitoring a local single-node setup; newer releases may differ.

From commands to a console

GDOM feature Equivalent command Notes
Cluster start / stop / restart gcware_services all start + gcluster_services all start Covers all three layers: gcware (management), gcluster (scheduler) and gnode (data)
Running SQL show processlist But across all coordinator nodes; click View SQL to see what a given connection is executing
Locks gcadmin showlock Direct equivalent
Inconsistent events gcadmin showdmlevent, showddlevent, showdmlstorageevent All three event types in one place
Failover gcadmin showfailover Direct equivalent

The original post also includes screenshots of the multi-cluster home page and the single-cluster monitoring view; only the extractable text is kept here.

The point of a console is not to replace the CLI but to aggregate across nodes. show processlist only shows the coordinator you are connected to, whereas GDOM presents every coordinator at once; DML, DDL and storage events, along with failover state, no longer require logging into each host to run gcadmin. When you are watching several gbase clusters at the same time, that aggregated view is usually the fastest route to the actual problem — and it is why a gbase cluster with many coordinators benefits more from GDOM than a single-node lab does.

title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
description: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

title: Why CSS 1in = 96px Is Not 1 Physical Inch (Building a True 1:1 Screen Ruler in React)
description:
If you have ever tried setting width: 1in; or width: 10cm; in CSS and held a physical ruler up to your monitor, you probably noticed something frustrating: it is almost never 1 physical inch.

On a 27-inch 4K monitor, a 13-inch MacBook Air, and a 6.7-inch Android phone, 1in in CSS can be off by 15% to 45%.

Here is why browsers cannot reliably report physical millimeters out of the box, and how we built a true 1:1 actual-size online ruler and ring sizer in React using ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit-card PPI calibration.

Why 1in, 1cm, and window.devicePixelRatio Cannot Give True Physical Size

According to the W3C CSS Values and Units specification, 1in is locked to exactly 96 CSS pixels (1cm = 37.795px, 1mm = 3.7795px).

Wait - what about window.devicePixelRatio?
devicePixelRatio only tells you how many hardware pixels map to 1 CSS pixel (for example, 2 on Retina displays or 2.75 on high-DPI phones). It still does not tell JavaScript the physical diagonal size of the monitor or phone glass in inches!

Browsers deliberately omit raw physical display dimensions (EDID data) to reduce browser fingerprinting. As a result:

Display CSS 1in Real Physical Size of 96 CSS px Error
Standard 24" 1080p Monitor 96px ~1.04 in +4%
13.3" MacBook Retina (2x) 96px ~0.84 in -16%
6.5" Smartphone (3x) 96px ~0.66 in -34%

So if you build a browser ruler using static CSS cm or in units, it will be visibly wrong on almost every laptop and smartphone.

The Reliable Fix: ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 Credit-Card Calibration

Almost every person on Earth has a globally standardized physical reference object in their wallet: a standard bank card, debit card, or ID card.

Under the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 international standard, every standard payment card has the exact same physical width:

  • Width: 85.60 mm (8.56 cm / 3.370 inches)
  • Height: 53.98 mm (5.398 cm / 2.125 inches)

Instead of guessing the user's screen PPI, let the user hold a bank card flat against the screen and drag a slider until an on-screen card box matches the physical card edge-to-edge.

Once cardWidthPx matches 3.37 physical inches, calculating the exact effective CSS Pixels Per Inch (PPI) takes one line of math:

const STANDARD_CARD_INCHES = 3.37; // 85.60 mm (ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1)

export function calculateEffectivePpi(cardWidthPx: number): number {
  return cardWidthPx / STANDARD_CARD_INCHES;
}

From that single calibrated ppi number, every physical unit becomes exact on that display:

export function pxToPhysical(px: number, ppi: number) {
  const inches = px / ppi;
  return {
    inches: Number(inches.toFixed(2)),
    cm: Number((inches * 2.54).toFixed(2)),
    mm: Number((inches * 25.4).toFixed(1)),
  };
}

Persist that calibrated ppi in localStorage, and the user only ever has to calibrate once per device:

const STORAGE_KEY = "omnitools_ruler_ppi";

export function loadSavedPpi(): number {
  try {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    const parsed = saved ? parseFloat(saved) : NaN;
    return Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed >= 40 && parsed <= 300 ? parsed : 96;
  } catch {
    return 96;
  }
}

(Clamping between 40 and 300 prevents corrupted storage values from breaking the UI.)

Bonus Use Case: An On-Screen Ring Size Finder (US, UK, and India Sizes)

Once you know the true ppi of a screen, you can measure more than straight lines. You can render a calibrated circle where the user places an existing ring directly onto their phone or laptop glass and adjusts the circle diameter until it aligns with the inside edge of the ring:

interface RingSizeEntry {
  mm: number;
  us: string;
  uk: string;
  india: string;
}

const RING_SIZES: RingSizeEntry[] = [
  { mm: 14.9, us: "4", uk: "H", india: "8" },
  { mm: 15.7, us: "5", uk: "J 1/2", india: "10" },
  { mm: 16.5, us: "6", uk: "M", india: "12" },
  { mm: 17.3, us: "7", uk: "O", india: "14" },
  { mm: 18.2, us: "8", uk: "Q", india: "17" },
  { mm: 19.0, us: "9", uk: "S", india: "19" },
  { mm: 19.8, us: "10", uk: "T 1/2", india: "22" },
  { mm: 20.6, us: "11", uk: "V 1/2", india: "25" },
];

export function matchRingSize(diameterPx: number, ppi: number) {
  const diameterMm = (diameterPx / ppi) * 25.4;
  const closest = RING_SIZES.reduce((prev, curr) =>
    Math.abs(curr.mm - diameterMm) < Math.abs(prev.mm - diameterMm) ? curr : prev
  );
  return { diameterMm: Number(diameterMm.toFixed(1)), closest };
}

3 Frontend Edge Cases to Watch Out For

  1. Browser Zoom (Ctrl + / Ctrl -): Remind users to keep browser zoom at 100% during calibration and measurement, because zooming scales CSS pixels without changing localStorage.
  2. Prevent Accidental Text Selection While Dragging Markers: Add select-none (user-select: none) and touch-action: none on draggable measurement handles so mobile Safari/Chrome does not scroll the viewport while dragging a marker.
  3. Sub-Pixel Rendering for 1mm Ticks: On standard displays, 1mm is roughly 3.78px. Always compute tick positions from mm * (ppi / 25.4) instead of rounding each step cumulatively, otherwise rounding drift compounds to 2-3mm across a 15cm ruler!

Try the Live Browser Implementation

We built this full calibrated ruler, dual red/blue measurement markers (horizontal and vertical), and US/UK/India ring sizer completely client-side with zero tracking or app downloads:

  • Online Ruler (Actual Size 1:1 + Ring Size Finder): https://omnitools.net/tools/online-ruler
  • Unit Converter (Length, Weight, Temp & Storage): https://omnitools.net/tools/unit-converter

Have you ever run into CSS physical-unit bugs on HiDPI screens or print stylesheets? Drop your experience in the comments!

title: Introducing DriftCatch — behavioural testing Framework for AI agents
description:
An AI agent can return exactly the answer you expect while its decisions, tool usage and execution path have silently changed.

A prompt tweak, a model update or a tool-schema edit can all introduce a behavioural regression that output-based testing will never catch. The answer still reads correctly, so every eval passes.

Consider a change like this to a refund agent's system prompt:

  • Resolve the customer's issue.
  • Resolve the customer's issue carefully. One word. The replies still read perfectly well. But the agent may now escalate cases it used to refund — and if your assertions are about the answer, nothing catches it.

So I built DriftCatch.

pip install driftcatch
import driftcatch as drift

def test_refund():
with drift.take("refund_1182") as take:
my_agent("refund order 1182")

take.assert_tools().called_in_order("lookup_order", "issue_refund")
take.assert_invariants().hold()

First run records. Every run after replays from disk — no network, no tokens, deterministic. It hooks httpx, so OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, LlamaIndex or your own loop all work with no adapter.

The part I think is actually new
Record/replay for agents already exists. What I hadn't seen is mining the rules out of the runs you've approved:

$ drift learn
Mined 13 invariant(s) from 23 approved recording(s)

lookup_order always runs before check_eligibility 23/23
issue_refund is always the last tool 18/18
escalate_to_human is offered but never called 23/23
issue_refund.args.order_id always equals
lookup_order.args.order_id 18/18
Nobody wrote those. The last one — the order you look up is the order you refund — is a real bug class nobody tests for. It breaks when someone reuses a loop variable.

This is specification mining, which Daikon has done for ordinary programs since 2001. Agent trajectories turn out to fit it well.

The hard part isn't mining, it's not mining garbage. Four filters: minimum support of 5 runs, a confidence gate of 1 - 0.5^support, the value has to actually vary across runs (two constants that match aren't a relationship), and transitive rules get dropped. That took 19 mined rules down to 15.

Rules are proposed as pending. A human enforces them, or doesn't.

When it fails, it names the cause
$ drift bisect refund_1182 --previous

golden: lookup_order -> check_eligibility -> issue_refund
candidate: lookup_order -> check_eligibility -> escalate_to_human

ROOT CAUSE: the system prompt.

- issue.
+ issue carefully.

Four inputs are fingerprinted separately — system prompt, model id, tool schemas, matcher config — so drift gets attributed instead of shrugged at.

The rest
Behaviour coverage — which tools, paths and error branches you've actually tested, plus suggested scenarios for the gaps
What-if — swap a recorded event at replay time to drive failure and retry paths, without recording anything new
Determinism scoring — run N times live, group by trajectory, get 80% path A / 20% path B instead of a meaningless "4/5 passed"
Tool contracts — declared schemas vs real use. On the demo corpus it flagged a parameter sent in every single request that no model ever used.
Approval gate — recordings start PENDING. A recorded run can be wrong; if "recorded" meant "correct", your first bad run becomes the enforced contract.
CLI, pytest plugin, local UI, and a read-only MCP server for Cursor / Claude Code
One honest limitation
Replay cannot catch the model changing underneath you. A recording holds what the model said then, not what it would say now. That's physics, not a missing feature — which is why there's a separate live mode that makes real calls.

Any tool claiming to catch model drift from a cached response is claiming something impossible.

NEEL7127 / driftcatch

Catch the moment your AI agent's behaviour changes. Record once, replay deterministically, fail the build on drift.

DriftCatch

Learns what your AI agent always does — then tells you the moment it stops.

0.1 pre-release. The engine, CLI, pytest plugin, local UI and MCP server are implemented and tested against the real OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs — 407 tests, mypy --strict clean. Not yet on PyPI, and not yet used by anyone but its author. If you try it and something is wrong, an issue is more useful to me than a star.

The problem

You tweak one word in a prompt. Your agent quietly stops querying the database and starts web-searching. The answer still looks right, so every eval passes. You find out from a customer.

Or worse — the trajectory is identical, every tool fires in the right order, and the refund amount is wrong by a factor of a hundred.

Agents don't fail loudly. They drift.

title: Black Friday hosting deals: the renewal column is the whole decision
description:
Every Black Friday the same thing happens. A hosting plan shows ₹69/mo, someone takes it, and fourteen months later they are paying ₹289/mo for the same box.

The sale price is not a price. It is a one-time entry fee for a fixed term. The number that decides your actual cost is the renewal rate, and it is almost never on the landing page.

Here is what the India storefront showed when I checked it on 16 November 2026 (pre-GST):

Plan Sale Renews at Jump
Single ₹69 ₹289 +319%
Premium ₹139 ₹449 +223%
Unlimited ₹199 ₹649 +226%
Cloud Startup ₹599 ₹1,599 +167%

Now the VPS ladder, same storefront, same day:

Plan Sale Renews at Jump
KVM 1 ₹599 ₹999 +67%
KVM 2 ₹779 ₹1,199 +54%
KVM 4 ₹1,099 ₹2,399 +118%
KVM 8 ₹2,199 ₹4,399 +100%

Notice the pattern. Shared hosting discounts hard and renews brutally. VPS discounts less and renews gently. KVM 2 is the flattest curve on the whole list — +54%.

So the math for a project you expect to still exist in three years:

Shared Premium: ₹139 × 48 months, then ₹449 forever.
KVM 2 VPS: ₹779 × 24 months, then ₹1,199 forever.

If the site is a brochure that gets 200 visitors a month, shared is correct and the renewal jump is still cheap in absolute rupees. If it is anything with a database doing real work, the VPS renewal is the one you will be glad you read.

The one rule: take the longest term you are confident about, because the sale price only applies to that first term. A 48-month commitment at ₹139 locks four years before the ₹449 starts. A 12-month commitment at a slightly lower monthly locks one.

I keep both columns side by side with the date each figure was checked, because these numbers drift every few weeks: https://mohitkoli.in/blog/hostinger-black-friday-2026

title: Pairing a desktop agent with RFC 8628, and the confirm-step attack the RFC warns about
description:
Some of the people using our apps keep their files in a folder or on a Windows share in their office, while the app runs in the cloud. To get the files across we wrote a small agent in Go, the satellite. It runs next to the share and only makes outbound HTTPS calls, so nobody has to open a port or set up a VPN. It has to be paired with one tenant of the app once, by someone who is an admin there.

That is the problem OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) solves for TVs and CLIs: the device shows a short code, a person types it into a browser where they are already logged in, and the device collects a token. We used it as written. The part that took a second look was section 5.4, remote phishing, and the step in our own UI that the first version got wrong.

The flow

The satellite posts its client_id to /connectors/v1/device_authorization. The server answers with a long device_code, a short user_code like 7KQ2-M9XD, a verification_uri, expires_in: 600 and interval: 5. The satellite shows the code in its setup window and polls /connectors/v1/token with the device code every five seconds.

On the server side we store only hashes of both codes. The user code is 8 characters from Crockford's base32 alphabet (32 symbols, no I, L, O or U), so one random byte modulo 32 picks a symbol without bias. When a person types it, case, dashes and spaces don't matter, and I, L and O are read as 1, 1 and 0.

In the app, a TenantAdmin opens the pairing screen, types the code and clicks Check. If the code belongs to an open request, the screen shows when and from which IP address the request came, so the admin can see whether it was their own machine. Then they give the device a name and confirm. Confirming creates a connector in the admin's tenant and marks the request approved. The next poll returns a token ksat_…, which the server stores as a SHA-256 hash and which the admin can revoke per device.

The satellite's side of this is about 150 lines of Go in internal/pairing/pairing.go. The poll loop handles authorization_pending, slow_down (add five seconds to the interval), expired_token and access_denied, and gives up when expires_in runs out.

What section 5.4 says

The device flow has a built-in weakness: the device that asks for access doesn't have to be the one in front of the person who approves it. An attacker starts a pairing on their own machine, gets a valid user code, and sends it to an admin with a message like "please enter this code to finish the setup". If the admin types it in and confirms, the attacker's machine gets a token for the admin's tenant.

RFC 8628 says to tell the user they are authorizing a device and to confirm it is in their possession. It is stricter about verification_uri_complete, the optional link that already carries the code: since the user no longer types the code, the server should show it and ask the user to check that it matches what their device displays.

For us the attack has teeth. A paired satellite can upload files into the tenant's inbox, and an inbox is where people open attachments.

Version one

Our pairing screen had two steps from the start: Check, then name and confirm. Check showed time and IP of the request. That looked like the mitigation the RFC asks for.

It was a step in the UI only. The check handler read the request and changed nothing. The confirm handler took a user code and a name and claimed any pending request with that code. If an admin's browser landed on the confirm step with a code already filled in, for example through a link someone sent them, they skipped the part where a human looks at the time and the address. The safeguard lived in the order of the screens, and nothing on the server knew about it.

The fix went into the same pull request eight minutes after the first commit, on 19 November, before anything was merged.

The fix

The check now writes. It records on the pending request which admin checked the code and when:

const marked = await updateMany(
  ctx.db,
  deviceAuthorizationTable,
  { checkedByUserId: event.payload.userId, checkedAt: now },
  {
    userCodeHash: event.payload.userCodeHash,
    status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.pending,
    expiresAt: { gt: now },
  },
);

The confirm is one conditional update from pending to approved. It only matches when the same admin checked this code in the last 300 seconds:

const claimed = await updateMany(
  ctx.db,
  deviceAuthorizationTable,
  { status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.approved, ...claim },
  {
    userCodeHash,
    status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.pending,
    expiresAt: { gt: ctx.tz.now() },
    checkedByUserId: claim.approvedByUserId,
    checkedAt: { gt: ctx.tz.now().subtract({ seconds: CODE_CHECK_VALID_SECONDS }) },
  },
);

If nothing matches, the handler returns the same "invalid code" error as for an unknown or expired code, and the connector it just created rolls back with the transaction. Because it is a single update, a code confirmed twice at once produces one connector and one winner. There's a test for that race, and one that walks through the cases: no check, a check by another admin, a check that is 301 seconds old, and finally a fresh check by the confirming admin, where only the last one pairs.

With that in place we could add verification_uri_complete later the same day. The satellite shows a link that opens the pairing screen with the code filled in. The admin still has to click Check, look at the time and address, and confirm. A link sent by an attacker gets them to the same screen, where the request shows up with a stranger's IP.

The rest of the hardening

The client_id of the satellite is public; it's in an open source binary. So anyone can start pairings, and the start endpoint is the one that needed limits:

  • at most 3 open requests per address, 1000 in total, and 10 starts per minute per address. Above that the endpoint answers 429 slow_down and stores nothing.
  • IPv6 addresses count per /64. A per-address limit on a full IPv6 address is easy to get around with a fresh address per request.
  • codes expire after 600 seconds. A redeemed request is deleted, together with its address.
  • checking and confirming codes is rate limited to 20 tries per 5 minutes per admin.
  • there is no reject button. Before it is confirmed a request belongs to no tenant, so nobody has anything to reject, and it disappears after ten minutes.

What we took from it

A two-step screen is not a security control by itself. The server has to be able to tell that the first step happened, for this user and this code, and recently. Writing it as a condition in the same update that does the claim kept it to two columns and one where clause.

The satellite is open source at github.com/CosmicDriftGameStudio/kumiko-satellite, and the server side is the connectors feature in kumiko-framework. If you run a device flow with verification_uri_complete, I'd be curious how you bind the approval to the person who looked at the code.
