title: Calculating percentiles at scale
description:
Some times ago, We designed an analytics dashboard with lots of analytical aggregated information, most of which we didn't know why was needed there.

We had a bunch of Third Party APIs, and based on the requests, their responses and timings used to differ. It was decided that all the requests will be logged in our database for analytics purpose, along with their latencies, the dashboard will have a dedicated section to show the p50, p95, and p99 latencies. Any unusual spikes in latency would be noticed and alerted accordingly.

Before moving forward, let me tell you the tech stack:

  • MSSQL for database
  • Node.js for backend

That's all we need to know.

The mistake

Initially, we tried to calculate the percentiles directly from the raw request logs stored in the database, expecting that simple queries and basic indexing would be enough.

Then came the api integrations, some of these APIs had either extremely high latencies like going upto 40 seconds, some of them required us to poll repeatedly until a certain condition was met. Irrespective of all these, we continued to log them directly in the database. we had a timeout threshold of 60 seconds which means no request will go beyond this point in time.

Our dashboard had filters - date range with minute level granularity, endpoint selection, query params selection, response status, and other important values, and by default, we were showing the latency over the week, with none of the other filters applied.

It didn't take longer to realize that querying raw logs for percentiles was becoming increasingly inefficient and slow, especially as the volume of data grew and the variability in request latencies widened. In the test environment, with limited data, the dashboard APIs started taking more than 26s to return with the default filters.

Trying the fix

We had to launch it, so we didn't had enough time to properly look at the problem. Still we went through couple of iterations:

  • First, we were calculating percentiles after fetching all the records in node. we moved it to calculating percentiles directly in the database using SQL queries.
  • for filters, we created individual indexes and composite indexes on the columns that were frequently used together.
  • In the final iteration, asking claude, we found that our SQL query was calculating p50, p95 and p99 separately, it suggested changes that helped us calculate all in a single pass, bringing down the query execution time significantly.

Finally, the dashboard loaded faster within 5-6 seconds with default filters. However, changing date filters to months, still caused us to wait long and get a timeout eventually. Challenge accepted.

Pre-computing percentiles

The first thing come to my mind was using timeseries or similar kind of db extensions that auto pre-compute and store the percentiles for different time intervals. For now 1m and 1hr buckets would be enough. Then based on time range I just need to do some average or median of these pre-computed percentiles to get an approximate result.

There was a problem, It's not a postgres db. So what, we can build around tables by ourselves and manage them just like timeseries extensions do, by creating and maintaining pre-aggregated tables for different time intervals and updating them as new data comes in.

Only mistake was that I didn't touched the percentile math at all. Thankfully, I went to brainstorm the idea first with claude.

Percentiles are not additive, they don't work like count, sum, avg, min/max where you can combine pre-aggregated values to get the overall result. A percentile is a rank position in a sorted distribution. If a minute bucket has 10 requests, but another minute bucket has 100 requests, simply averaging the percentiles of these buckets will not reflect the true percentile of the combined 110 requests. The distribution of values within each bucket matters, and ignoring it leads to incorrect results.

Deciding tradeoffs and considerations

  1. We don't want exactly accurate percentiles, if we can get appproximate results which are deviating within 5% of the actual value, thats fine. what it means?

    • if the p95 is 100ms, getting a result between 95ms and 105ms is acceptable.
    • if the p95 is 55s, getting a result between 52.2s and 57.7s is acceptable. This would seem huge, but for high-latency operations, a 5% deviation is tolerable and still provides meaningful insights preventing false alerts.

  2. We are ok with reducing some filters, which are hard to support efficiently at scale, as long as the core insights and critical metrics remain accurate and actionable.

  3. We don't want to remove minute level granularity in the date range filters, simply because we are lazy to redesign the date component to allow user to select finer intervals.

  4. It's still a MVP and we don't want to move the data to a separate BI system or introduce complex ETL pipelines at this stage. We aim to keep the solution simple and maintainable within the existing infrastructure.

The approach for efficiently calculating percentiles

The key idea is to pre calculate the counts and distributions of the values within time buckets along with filters.

Instead of storing individual request times, we can store a histogram of latencies for each minute or hour bucket. Each histogram will capture the distribution of latencies within that time interval. When a query comes in for a larger time range, we can merge the histograms of the relevant buckets and then calculate approximate percentiles from the combined histogram. This allows us to efficiently compute percentiles over large datasets without scanning every individual record. Don't worry, I will explain it with example later on.

Our requests usaully have latencies in range of 5s to 1m, after which they get a timeout. we decided to use 1000ms buckets for the histograms, which gives us a good balance between accuracy and storage efficiency. we reduced down these filters:

  • response code - we only care about successful requests, any 4xx or higher status usually returns very early. not contributing to the percentiles.
  • user and other high cardinality attributes, because they are not suitable for histograms.

after this, we are left with the 3 filters and fixed 30×2×3=180 values. still high but manageable, if it's skewed.

so now we have 2 tables representing histograms over time buckets of 1m and 1h, looking like this:

time filter_1 filter_2 filter_3 b0_1s b1_2s b2_3s ... b59_60s total
2026-12-01 12:00 Abc a true 0 0 22 ... 0 590
2026-12-01 12:01 Def b false 1 0 18 ... 0 483

so now we have count of requests that fall under each latency bucket and filter.

calculating percentiles for the date range 12:00 to 12:01, with the filter combination filter_1 = Abc, filter_2 = a, filter_3 = true looks like this:

  • merge the histograms for the relevant time buckets (12:00 and 12:01) for each filter combination.
  • sum the counts for each latency bucket and the total column across the rows from 12:00 to 12:01 that matches the filter combination.
  • results:
b2_3sb3_4sb4_5sb35_36stotal​=22+18=40=18+39=57=0+48=48…=78+29=107=40+57+48+107=252​
  • calculate percentile range:
p50p90​=0.5×252=126=0.9×252=226.8​
  • That means p50 is the 126th request in the sorted order of latencies, and p90 is the 227th request.
  • commulative count of requests by latency bucket:
b2_3s+b3_4sb2_3s+b3_4s+b4_5s​=40+57=97=40+57+48=145​
  • so p50 lies somewhere in b4_5s time range:
126−97=29
  • so the 126th request lies 29 requests into the b4_5s bucket.
  • b4_5s has 48 requests in total, assuming they are evenly distributed into the b4_5s bucket. so the p50 latency is approximately:
4829​×1000ms≈604ms 4s+604ms≈4.604s

Even if it's not perfectly uniform distribution, with this bucket range, the maximum error will be within 1s range, while we accepted the error at around 2.2s in our tradeoffs. so practically, we can increase the bucket size to 2s for better storage efficiency without significantly affecting the accuracy.

The math looks terrible here, lot's of operations, but this is still significantly more efficient than sorting all individual request latencies, especially at scale.
We can do this all computation directly in SQL using queries too, saving a lot of memory and processing time compared to fetching and sorting all individual request latencies.

Scaling further

  • We can improve storage and computation by increasing the bucket size.
  • We also can add another level of aggregation, such as daily or weekly histograms, to further reduce storage and computation requirements for larger date range queries.
  • We can improve the date range filters by restricting to 5minute granularity, which reduces the number of time buckets we need to process.

Note: AI is only used to format the Katex(Latex math) in this document because Dev.to Latex support is terrible

title: NFS2ROOT on CentOS 7: the stock kernel is affected and gets no fix
description:
NFS2ROOT (CVE-2026-99362) is a pre-authentication heap overflow in the Linux kernel's NFS server. A client that can reach TCP 2049 shrinks its NFSv4.1 session reply cache to zero bytes, pads a SEQUENCE request, and nfsd copies the whole reply into the empty slot buffer. No account or export access is needed. The kernel.org CNA rates it CVSS 9.8, Red Hat rates it Critical.

On CentOS 7 it reaches every NFS server running the defaults:

  • Stock 3.10: affected, per Red Hat, and the CentOS 7 source carries the same unbounded copy. nfsd serves +4.1 +4.2 out of the box, and having no exports does not help: the overflow happens during session setup. CentOS 7 gets no kernel updates.
  • ELRepo kernel-lt 5.4.278 and kernel-ml 6.9.7: inside the affected range (3.16 and later), and both lines ended without a fix.
  • CentOS 8: RHEL 8 got the fix on 2026-11-26 (4.18.0-553.190.1.el8_10), CentOS 8 did not. AlmaLinux 8, Rocky 8 and Oracle Linux 8 already ship that kernel, so converting in place is the free way out.

The fix

Disclosure: I maintain this package. GetPageSpeed's kernel-lt has carried the fix since 6.18.62-1, published on 2026-11-07, twelve days before the CVE went public. It uses the same package name as ELRepo, installs beside your current kernel, and is free for any use:

yum -y install https://extras.getpagespeed.com/release-latest.rpm
yum -y install yum-utils
yum-config-manager --enable getpagespeed-extras-corecare
yum -y install kernel-lt
grub2-set-default 0
grubby --default-kernel
reboot

Already on our 6.18 kernel but older than 6.18.62? yum -y update 'kernel-lt*', then check grubby --default-kernel before you reboot: builds before 6.18.62-2 did not move the GRUB default on update. uname -r after the reboot is the check that counts, not rpm -q.

The exposure checks, Red Hat's stopgap (stop nfs-server or firewall 2049) and the rollback are in the full write-up.

title: SOLO: Towards Sample-Faithful and Detectable LLM Watermarking under Repeated Sampling via Content-Anchored Single-Owner Contexts
description:
arXiv:2611.34190v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Providers watermark the outputs of large language models, while applications sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, and uncertainty estimation. We show that deployed configurations of distortion-free watermarks, which deduplicate keyed contexts only within a response, couple the responses of a request: answer templates make all responses query the watermark with the same context before the answer, so collisions across responses, usually assumed rare, become the norm. Key pools reduce or avoid the coupling at the cost of multiple testing, and the exact remedy of a context history shared across the request leaves many positions unwatermarked. We propose SOLO, which keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so that siblings rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses, each detectable with a single key. On five language models from three families and three benchmarks, SOLO preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, also after randomly editing 10% of the tokens, and more than the context history on most clean tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhongliangGuo/solo-watermark.

title: A Snap-Scrolling Vertical Video Feed with CSS and IntersectionObserver
description:
Short-video apps all share one interaction: a full-screen vertical feed where each swipe snaps to the next video and only the visible one plays. You can build that feel on the web with CSS scroll snapping and an IntersectionObserver, no framework needed. This post walks through a version that also works with the keyboard and respects reduced-motion settings.

The markup 

<main class="feed" tabindex="0" aria-label="Video feed">
  <section class="item"><video src="clip1.mp4" muted loop playsinline preload="metadata"></video></section>
  <section class="item"><video src="clip2.mp4" muted loop playsinline preload="metadata"></video></section>
  <section class="item"><video src="clip3.mp4" muted loop playsinline preload="metadata"></video></section>
</main>

muted and playsinline matter: mobile browsers only allow autoplay for muted, inline video. preload="metadata" keeps the page from downloading every clip up front.

Snap scrolling with CSS 

.feed {
  height: 100dvh;
  overflow-y: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: y mandatory;
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}

.item {
  height: 100dvh;
  scroll-snap-align: start;
  scroll-snap-stop: always;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: #000;
}

.item video {
  max-height: 100%;
  max-width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 9 / 16;
  object-fit: contain;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .feed { scroll-behavior: auto; }
}
  • 100dvh (dynamic viewport height) avoids the classic mobile bug where the address bar makes 100vh too tall.
  • scroll-snap-stop: always stops a fast flick from skipping several videos at once.
  • overscroll-behavior: contain prevents the page behind the feed from bouncing.

Play only the visible video 

const videos = document.querySelectorAll('.feed video');

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const video = entry.target;
    if (entry.isIntersecting && entry.intersectionRatio >= 0.6) {
      video.play().catch(() => {});
    } else {
      video.pause();
    }
  }
}, { threshold: [0, 0.6, 1] });

videos.forEach(v => observer.observe(v));

A threshold of 0.6 means a video starts once most of it is on screen, so two videos never play at the same time mid-swipe. The empty catch swallows the promise rejection browsers throw when autoplay is blocked.

Keyboard support

Scroll snapping already works with Page Up / Page Down when the feed has focus, but arrow keys feel more natural:

const feed = document.querySelector('.feed');

feed.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if (e.key !== 'ArrowDown' && e.key !== 'ArrowUp') return;
  e.preventDefault();
  const step = feed.clientHeight * (e.key === 'ArrowDown' ? 1 : -1);
  const smooth = !matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
  feed.scrollBy({ top: step, behavior: smooth ? 'smooth' : 'auto' });
});

Add M to toggle sound on the current video and you have most of the desktop experience:

feed.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if (e.key.toLowerCase() !== 'm') return;
  const current = [...videos].find(v => !v.paused);
  if (current) current.muted = !current.muted;
});

Loading more items

Observe the last item with a second observer and append the next batch when it comes into view. Keep the DOM small by removing items far above the viewport once the list grows past a few dozen; each <video> element holds decoder resources even when paused.

Accessibility notes

  • Give each item a heading or aria-label with the video title so screen-reader users know where they are.
  • Never autoplay with sound.
  • Provide visible play/pause and mute buttons; keyboard shortcuts alone are not discoverable.

See it in practice

Browser-based tools for watching short videos use exactly this pattern. A TikTok viewer in the browser is a good reference for the finished feel: one video per screen, snapping between items, and playback that follows what is visible.

title: ExtractBench Pro: The Long Tail of Document Extraction
description:
arXiv:2611.33791v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present ExtractBench Pro, a schema-guided document extraction benchmark that tests six challenging modes of extraction underrepresented in existing datasets. It is created following a framework for synthetic document generation, in which deterministic document generators assemble challenging components into documents that are designed to be difficult at a level calibrated for frontier systems. We synthesize 100 realistic documents spanning a diverse range of styles. On this data, we evaluate ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations for accuracy, grounding, and their ability to perfectly extract documents. No extraction system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, Claude Code Opus 5.5 and Codex GPT-6 Astra, outperform specialized extraction APIs on both perfect-document rate and Value F1, but at a higher cost per page. Among specialized extraction APIs, LlamaExtract spans the lower-cost frontier, with Agentic Plus Max Effort approaching the strongest coding agent on both perfect-document rate and Value F1 at lower cost per page. Our analysis of coding agent traces identifies intelligent image processing and programmatic reasoning, but also failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams. We release ExtractBench Pro and these evaluation results as resources for the future development of improved frontier extraction systems.

title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
description:
arXiv:2611.34928v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
description:
arXiv:2611.33735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
description:
arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

title: Count Aspect Ratio Changes and Calculate Drift Medians in Python
description:
A staged photo has several properties worth recording separately. The aspect ratio flag tells you whether its frame kept the original width to height proportion. The alignment flag records whether the comparison succeeded. Architecture drift summarizes structural change, with lower scores indicating closer preservation of the room. For a listing, a different ratio prompts an inspection of the edges for cropping and of fixed features for stretching. The fields below come from the public StagingBench data, and you can summarize them with collections.Counter and statistics.median from the Python standard library.

The embedded sample contains one record per tool, for 13 records in total. For each tool with an observed ratio change, the sample uses one changed record. For each remaining tool, it uses one kept record. This selection makes both branches of the counting logic visible and is intended for demonstrating the calculation. Each tuple contains the tool, room, aspect ratio flag, alignment flag, and drift score. Room identifiers stay as strings so that "01" retains its leading zero. A blank alignment entry becomes None, distinct from the False value used for a failed alignment.

The loop increments a total for every record. The expression int(not aspect_kept) adds one when the ratio changed and zero when it was kept. Printing changes over totals for each tool gives the count alongside the number of records examined. Iterating over the keys in totals keeps all observed tools in the output, including those with zero changes. In a larger input, the same logic accumulates multiple records for each tool.

Next, the script appends each drift score to the list keyed by its aspect ratio flag. It also builds a second set of lists using aligned is True, which admits only confirmed alignment. That matters because a failed alignment produces a fallback drift score that cannot be compared with one from an aligned room. The median of the full group describes the recorded values, including fallback scores. The aligned median describes the comparable subset. Printing the number of scores next to each median makes the size of that subset visible. An empty group prints "unavailable".

In the full data, 101 of 129 records kept the ratio and 28 changed it. The full group medians were 21.7 for kept and 21.85 for changed. With confirmed alignment, the medians were 21.35 for 72 kept records and 22.5 for 19 changed records. The script below prints the results for the embedded sample, which has only two aligned records in each ratio group. In that sample, the changed group's aligned median of 35.80 is the midpoint of 52.8 and 18.8. Keeping the sample sizes on the same lines as the medians helps prevent a small demonstration from being read as a benchmark result.

from collections import Counter
from statistics import median

records = [
    ("T01", "01", True, None, 16.2),
    ("T02", "01", True, None, 11.0),
    ("T03", "01", True, None, 28.2),
    ("T04", "01", True, None, 27.1),
    ("T05", "04", False, False, 61.5),
    ("T06", "01", False, None, 18.1),
    ("T07", "01", True, True, 25.4),
    ("T08", "01", True, None, 11.4),
    ("T09", "04", False, False, 10.4),
    ("T10", "01", True, True, 10.6),
    ("T11", "01", False, True, 52.8),
    ("T12", "01", True, None, 18.9),
    ("T13", "05", False, True, 18.8),
]

totals = Counter()
changes = Counter()
all_scores = {True: [], False: []}
aligned_scores = {True: [], False: []}

for tool, room, aspect_kept, aligned, drift in records:
    totals[tool] += 1
    changes[tool] += int(not aspect_kept)
    all_scores[aspect_kept].append(drift)
    if aligned is True:
        aligned_scores[aspect_kept].append(drift)

print("Changed aspect ratios by tool")
for tool in sorted(totals):
    print(f"{tool} {changes[tool]}/{totals[tool]}")

for label, groups in (
    ("All sample records", all_scores),
    ("Aligned sample records", aligned_scores),
):
    print(label)
    for aspect_kept, group_label in ((True, "Kept"), (False, "Changed")):
        scores = groups[aspect_kept]
        value = f"{median(scores):.2f}" if scores else "unavailable"
        print(f"{group_label} median drift {value} (n={len(scores)})")

Output:

Changed aspect ratios by tool
T01 0/1
T02 0/1
T03 0/1
T04 0/1
T05 1/1
T06 1/1
T07 0/1
T08 0/1
T09 1/1
T10 0/1
T11 1/1
T12 0/1
T13 1/1
All sample records
Kept median drift 17.55 (n=8)
Changed median drift 18.80 (n=5)
Aligned sample records
Kept median drift 18.00 (n=2)
Changed median drift 35.80 (n=2)

title: RTL QA checklist: 10 things that break when you launch a Hebrew or Arabic version of your site
description:
Adding dir="rtl" flips the page. It doesn't fix the page. Most RTL bugs come from CSS that was written with "left" and "right" baked in, and from content that mixes directions. Here is the checklist I run on a Hebrew or Arabic page, with the fix for each item.

I built a small test page with deliberate defects to make the examples concrete. Every item below was found on it by a quick scripted pass plus a visual check.

1. dir and lang on the root 

<html lang="he" dir="rtl">

Without dir, the browser lays everything out left-to-right. Without lang, screen readers and hyphenation guess. Check this first; it's the cheapest fix.

2. Physical margins and padding

margin-left: auto on a logo pushes it the wrong way once the page is RTL. Use logical properties:

.nav .logo { margin-inline-start: auto; }  /* not margin-left */
.card { margin-inline-end: 20px; }          /* not margin-right */

A quick way to find candidates: search your CSS for left and right in margin, padding, border, left:, right: and float.

3. Floats

float: left stays on the left in RTL, so card order and gutters come out wrong. Prefer flex or grid with gap, or float: inline-start where it's supported.

4. Text alignment

text-align: left inside RTL content looks broken. Use text-align: start.

5. Arrows and directional icons

A "Continue →" arrow points backwards in RTL. Mirror directional icons (arrows, chevrons, "back"/"next") but not logos, media controls or checkmarks:

[dir="rtl"] .icon-chevron { transform: scaleX(-1); }

6. Form fields that must stay LTR

Phone numbers, emails, URLs and ID numbers (Teudat Zehut, for example) should be typed and displayed left-to-right even on an RTL page:

<input type="email" dir="ltr">
<input type="text" inputmode="numeric" dir="ltr" name="id-number">

Keep the label RTL; only the input flips.

7. Mixed-direction text (bidi)

A Hebrew sentence with "iPhone 15 Pro", a price in ₪ and a date can reorder in surprising ways, especially around parentheses and punctuation. Isolate embedded Latin text:

<p>המחיר של <bdi>iPhone 15 Pro</bdi> הוא 4,299 ₪</p>

or unicode-bidi: isolate on the inline element.

8. Fixed widths on mobile

A width: 700px block forces a 700 px layout on a 375 px phone, so the RTL page gets cut off on the right. That's the side where RTL content starts, so it's even worse than in LTR. Use max-width: 100% and test in a mobile viewport.

9. Carousels, sliders and tabs

Swipe direction and "next/previous" controls should follow reading direction. Many slider libraries have an RTL option that's off by default.

10. Numbers, dates and currency

Decide on one format for dates (31/12/2026 vs 2026-12-31) and currency position (₪99.90 vs 99.90 ₪), and apply it consistently. Mixed formats are a common source of "this looks foreign" feedback from native readers.

A 5-minute scripted pass

Paste this in the browser console on an RTL page to list obvious candidates. Treat it as a pointer, not a verdict:

for (const e of document.querySelectorAll('body *')) {
  const cs = getComputedStyle(e);
  if (cs.float === 'left' || cs.float === 'right') console.log('float', cs.float, e);
  if (cs.textAlign === 'left') console.log('text-align:left', e);
}
for (const i of document.querySelectorAll('input[type=email],input[type=tel],input[type=url]'))
  if (getComputedStyle(i).direction === 'rtl') console.log('LTR field rendered RTL', i);

Then do the visual pass: desktop plus a mobile viewport, looking at navigation, forms and any sentence that mixes Hebrew or Arabic with Latin text and numbers.

Disclosure: I offer this as a written QA report with CSS fixes (an AI-assisted review, layout and direction only, not translation): Hebrew/Arabic RTL website QA on Contra. The checklist above works on its own.

title: Your Leads Are Dying in a Spreadsheet. Here's a 40-Line Node.js
description:
By the WeTakeFwd team. We build automation for small businesses in India, and this is the first thing we set up for almost every one of them.

Every small business we work with has the same file somewhere.

It's called something like leads_FINAL_v2 (1).xlsx. It has names, phone numbers and a "status" column full of things like ??, call back and who added this.

Nobody opens it after the first week.

The problem isn't that the business is short of leads. It's that nobody follows up. A customer says "I'll think about it", and that's the last time anyone speaks to them.

So here's a tiny script that fixes it:

  • reads your leads from a CSV (export it from Excel or Google Sheets)
  • finds everyone who has gone quiet for 2+ days
  • writes a personal follow-up message for each one
  • gives you a page of "Send on WhatsApp" buttons, one tap each

No npm install. No API keys. No WhatsApp Business approval. Just Node 18+.

Why WhatsApp click-to-chat links?

WhatsApp has a public link format: https://wa.me/<number>?text=<message>. Open it, and WhatsApp opens a chat with that number and the message already typed in.

That gives us three nice properties:

  1. Zero setup. No Cloud API, no templates to get approved, no per-message cost.
  2. A human still presses Send. The business owner can tweak the message, and nobody gets spammed by a runaway script.
  3. It works on phone and desktop, with whatever WhatsApp the owner already uses.

The data

Export your sheet as leads.csv. Ours looks like this:

name,phone,last_contacted,status,interest
Rahul,919812345678,2026-11-20,new,deep cleaning for a 3BHK
Priya,919998887776,2026-11-26,new,a product demo
Amit,918887776665,2026-11-18,quoted,a new website
Neha,917776665554,2026-11-19,won,monthly maintenance
Karan,919123456780,2026-11-24,quoted,10 office chairs

The status column drives everything: new and quoted leads get follow-ups, while won (and anything else) is left alone.

The script 

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const FOLLOW_UP_AFTER_DAYS = 2;

// One message per stage. Only these statuses get follow-ups.
const TEMPLATES = {
  new: (l) => `Hi ${l.name}, just checking in about your enquiry for ${l.interest}. Shall I share the details or set up a quick call?`,
  quoted: (l) => `Hi ${l.name}, did you get a chance to look at our quote for ${l.interest}? Happy to answer any questions.`,
};

function parseCSV(text) {
  const [header, ...rows] = text.trim().split(/\r?\n/);
  const keys = header.split(",").map((k) => k.trim());
  return rows.map((row) => {
    const values = row.split(",");
    return Object.fromEntries(keys.map((k, i) => [k, (values[i] ?? "").trim()]));
  });
}

const daysSince = (date, today) => Math.floor((today - new Date(date)) / 86_400_000);

export function dueFollowUps(leads, today = new Date()) {
  return leads
    .filter((l) => TEMPLATES[l.status] && daysSince(l.last_contacted, today) >= FOLLOW_UP_AFTER_DAYS)
    .map((l) => {
      const message = TEMPLATES[l.status](l);
      return { ...l, days: daysSince(l.last_contacted, today), message,
               link: `https://wa.me/${l.phone}?text=${encodeURIComponent(message)}` };
    })
    .sort((a, b) => b.days - a.days); // oldest first
}

const esc = (s) => String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) => ({ "&": "&", "<": "<", ">": ">", '"': """, "'": "'" })[c]);

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) {
  const leads = parseCSV(readFileSync("leads.csv", "utf8"));
  const due = dueFollowUps(leads);
  const rows = due.map((l) => `<li><b>${esc(l.name)}</b> · ${esc(l.status)} · ${l.days} days quiet<br>
    <a href="${esc(l.link)}" target="_blank">Send on WhatsApp</a></li>`).join("\n");
  writeFileSync("followups.html", `<meta charset="utf-8"><h2>${due.length} follow-ups due today</h2><ul>${rows}</ul>`);
  console.log(`${due.length} follow-ups due. Open followups.html`);
}

Run it:

node followup.mjs
# 3 follow-ups due. Open followups.html

With the sample data (run on 27 Nov), it picks out exactly the right people:

Lead Status Quiet for Gets a follow-up?
Amit quoted 9 days ✅ first in the list
Rahul new 7 days ✅
Karan quoted 3 days ✅
Priya new 1 day ❌ too soon
Neha won 8 days ❌ already a customer

Open followups.html, tap a button, and WhatsApp opens with something like:

Hi Amit, did you get a chance to look at our quote for a new website? Happy to answer any questions.

A few details worth stealing

  • Oldest first. The list is sorted by days quiet, so the lead closest to going cold is at the top.
  • Messages per stage. A brand-new enquiry and a lead who already has a quote need different words. Add a key to TEMPLATES for any new stage.
  • Escaping. Names come from a spreadsheet that anyone can type into, so the HTML output escapes them. encodeURIComponent handles the WhatsApp text.
  • The CSV parser is deliberately simple. It doesn't handle commas inside fields. If your sheet has them, swap in a proper parser like csv-parse.

Make it run every morning

  • macOS / Linux: crontab -e, then add 0 9 * * * cd /path/to/leads && node followup.mjs
  • Windows: Task Scheduler → Create Basic Task → Daily → node followup.mjs

Point it at a synced folder (Google Drive, OneDrive), and the owner has a fresh follow-up list on their phone every morning.

Where to take it next

Once a business is hooked on this (they always are), the natural upgrades are:

  1. Read straight from Google Sheets with the Sheets API, so there's no export step.
  2. Write back last_contacted when a message is sent.
  3. Move to the WhatsApp Cloud API with approved templates once volume grows, keeping a human approval step.
  4. Swap the spreadsheet for a CRM when the team grows beyond one or two people.

But honestly? This 40-line version is the one that changes the most, because it turns "we should follow up" into a list of buttons.

A small ask

If you build stuff for small businesses, freelancers and agencies, what's the simplest automation you've built that made the biggest difference? Drop it in the comments. We're collecting ideas.

If you'd like help setting up something like this for your business: https://wetakefwd.online

title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.34373v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.

title: Audit kitchen exhaust scope and photo evidence in TypeScript
description:
The crew marks a duct section cleaned, but the photo index contains only its before photo. The same job records a rooftop fan as inaccessible. Both records need follow-up. One needs an after photo and the other needs an access plan.

Bind each photo to its system and component

Use the pair (systemId, componentId) as the scope key. Two kitchens can both have a HOOD-01. Each photo ID resolves to one system, component, and capture phase. A reference to P-06, the after photo for KITCHEN-B/HOOD-01, fails when attached to KITCHEN-A/HOOD-01. An unknown photo ID or a duplicate index entry also fails before the audit issues a queue.

System / component Reported status Attached photos Follow-up
KITCHEN-A/HOOD-01 cleaned P-01 before, P-02 after
KITCHEN-A/DUCT-02 cleaned P-03 before MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO
KITCHEN-A/ROOF-FAN-01 inaccessible P-04 before INACCESSIBLE
KITCHEN-B/HOOD-01 cleaned P-05 before, P-06 after

Freeze the follow-up queue for each audit

The fixture asks for both phases when a component is marked cleaned. For an inaccessible component, the access status itself creates a follow-up. The audit sorts the queue for stable review and freezes the array and each row. When the correct after photo P-07 arrives for the duct, a new audit returns only the rooftop fan. The original two entries remain available in the previous snapshot.

Run the benchmark

Save the block as hoodcert-benchmark.ts and run node --experimental-strip-types hoodcert-benchmark.ts with Node.js 24. The script needs no packages. Node.js TypeScript documentation

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

type ComponentKey = { systemId: string; componentId: string };
type ScopeRow = ComponentKey & {
  status: "cleaned" | "inaccessible";
  photoIds: readonly string[];
};
type Photo = ComponentKey & { id: string; phase: "before" | "after" };
type FollowUp = ComponentKey & {
  reason: "INACCESSIBLE" | "MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO" | "MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO";
};

function auditScope(scope: readonly ScopeRow[], photos: readonly Photo[]) {
  const photoIndex = new Map<string, Photo>();
  for (const photo of photos) {
    assert(photo.id.trim(), "Photo ID is required");
    assert(!photoIndex.has(photo.id), `Duplicate photo ID: ${photo.id}`);
    photoIndex.set(photo.id, photo);
  }

  const seenComponents = new Set<string>();
  const followUps: Readonly<FollowUp>[] = [];
  for (const { systemId, componentId, status, photoIds } of scope) {
    assert(systemId.trim() && componentId.trim(), "System and component IDs are required");
    const key = JSON.stringify([systemId, componentId]);
    const label = `${systemId}/${componentId}`;
    assert(!seenComponents.has(key), `Duplicate scope component: ${label}`);
    seenComponents.add(key);

    const attached = new Set<string>();
    const phases = new Set<Photo["phase"]>();
    for (const id of photoIds) {
      assert(!attached.has(id), `Duplicate photo reference: ${id}`);
      const photo = photoIndex.get(id);
      assert(photo, `Unknown photo ID: ${id}`);
      assert(photo.systemId === systemId && photo.componentId === componentId,
        `Photo ${id} belongs to ${photo.systemId}/${photo.componentId}, expected ${label}`);
      attached.add(id);
      phases.add(photo.phase);
    }

    const addFollowUp = (reason: FollowUp["reason"]) => {
      followUps.push(Object.freeze({ systemId, componentId, reason }));
    };
    if (status === "inaccessible") {
      addFollowUp("INACCESSIBLE");
    } else {
      if (!phases.has("before")) addFollowUp("MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO");
      if (!phases.has("after")) addFollowUp("MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO");
    }
  }

  return Object.freeze(followUps.sort((left, right) => {
    const a = JSON.stringify([left.systemId, left.componentId, left.reason]);
    const b = JSON.stringify([right.systemId, right.componentId, right.reason]);
    if (a === b) return 0;
    return a < b ? -1 : 1;
  }));
}

const scope: readonly ScopeRow[] = [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", status: "inaccessible", photoIds: ["P-04"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-01", "P-02"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-03"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-05", "P-06"] },
];
const photos: readonly Photo[] = [
  { id: "P-01", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-02", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "after" },
  { id: "P-03", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-04", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-05", systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-06", systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "after" },
];

const queue = auditScope(scope, photos);
const expected = [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", reason: "MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO" },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", reason: "INACCESSIBLE" },
];
assert.deepEqual(queue, expected);
assert.deepEqual(auditScope(scope.toReversed(), photos.toReversed()), expected);
assert(Object.isFrozen(queue) && queue.every((entry) => Object.isFrozen(entry)));
assert.equal(Reflect.set(queue[0], "reason", "INACCESSIBLE"), false);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-01", "P-06"] }], photos),
  /belongs to KITCHEN-B\/HOOD-01, expected KITCHEN-A\/HOOD-01/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-03"] }], photos),
  /belongs to KITCHEN-A\/DUCT-02, expected KITCHEN-A\/HOOD-01/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-99"] }], photos), /Unknown photo ID/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope(scope, [...photos, photos[0]]), /Duplicate photo ID/);
assert.deepEqual(auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-02"] }], photos), [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", reason: "MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO" },
]);

const newPhoto: Photo = { id: "P-07", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", phase: "after" };
const updatedScope = scope.map((row) => row.systemId === newPhoto.systemId && row.componentId === newPhoto.componentId
  ? { ...row, photoIds: [...row.photoIds, newPhoto.id] }
  : row);
const nextQueue = auditScope(updatedScope, [...photos, newPhoto]);
assert.deepEqual(nextQueue, [expected[1]]);
assert.deepEqual(queue, expected);

console.log(`Audited components: ${scope.length} | indexed photos: ${photos.length}`);
for (const { systemId, componentId, reason } of queue) {
  console.log(`${systemId}/${componentId}: ${reason}`);
}
console.log(`After attaching ${newPhoto.id}: ${nextQueue.length} follow-up | original queue: ${queue.length}`);

Verified Node output 

Audited components: 4 | indexed photos: 6
KITCHEN-A/DUCT-02: MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO
KITCHEN-A/ROOF-FAN-01: INACCESSIBLE
After attaching P-07: 1 follow-up | original queue: 2

Keep the scope and photo index with each audit snapshot. That gives the reviewer the exact references behind a missing-evidence flag and preserves the access exception when the rest of the job is documented.

title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
description:
arXiv:2611.34147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.

title: Make Job Cancellation a Durable State Transition
description:
A worker has already claimed a report. An operator clicks Cancel. The worker finishes calculating a result a moment later.

What decides whether that result can become the saved result?

Checking a cancellation flag before calculation leaves a gap. The worker can pass that check, pause, and resume after cancellation has been accepted. Stopping the caller from waiting leaves the same gap in a different place.

This example makes cancellation a durable state transition. Once the cancellation transaction commits, the normal completion path can no longer publish a result for that run. The process may still be alive. An external request it already sent may still finish.

Give the command an exact run

The previous tutorial separated the stable job, an intentionally requested run, and the worker's claim generation. Cancellation needs that distinction too.

Use (job_id, run_id) as its target. If an old cancel request is retried after a new run starts, it must still address the old run. Resolving “the current run of this job” again during the retry would change the target.

The local fixture uses these transitions:

queued  -> running -> succeeded
   |          |
   +----------+----> cancelled

succeeded and cancelled are terminal for this execution. A deliberate rerun is a separate row. The fixture's cancelled state means the run's normal completion path is closed. It is not evidence that the worker exited or a remote operation was reversed.

Put cancellation and completion behind the same database boundary

Cancellation changes only a queued or running row with the exact job and run IDs. It also clears the current ownership fields.

Completion must still match:

  • The exact job and run.
  • The running state.
  • The worker and generation from the originally issued claim.
  • An unexpired lease.

Those predicates are evaluated inside the completion write. A previous application-level read is not permission to skip them.

The two commands can race. The API needs to describe both possible results:

First transition to commit Later command observes Saved result
Cancellation Completion is refused None
Completion Cancellation returns succeeded, with changed=False Original completed result

The caller does not get a successful cancellation merely because it pressed Cancel first. In this fixture, the database's committed order determines which transition wins.

If cancellation commits but its response disappears, repeating the same job/run cancellation returns cancelled with changed=False. It does not start another execution, delete a completed result, or retarget a newer run.

Keep protocol cancellation separate

The MCP cancellation specification, revision 2026-07-28 describes transport-specific cancellation signals and races with completed requests. It also permits a server to ignore a cancellation notification when the request has completed or cannot be cancelled.

A request ID identifies a protocol exchange. The run ID below identifies a durable execution. An application that connects them needs an explicit mapping and authorization check; a disconnected client is not proof that a business job has been cancelled or rolled back.

This tutorial implements a local job-state contract, not an MCP transport or notification handler.

Run the complete fixture

Save the file as cancel_fence.py and run it with Python 3.12 or later:

python cancel_fence.py

It uses the standard library, a deterministic test clock and temporary SQLite files. No queue, cloud account or external API is required. The test that creates run-2 is setup for the old-request case; the earlier article covers acceptance of intentional reruns.

The write methods use short BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions. SQLite allows one writer at a time, so cancellation and completion serialize before inspecting and changing the row. The transaction can still fail because another writer is busy or a database error occurs; those errors propagate instead of becoming a successful cancellation. SQLite documents these transaction rules.

"""A durable local cancellation boundary. Python 3.12+, standard library.
Run: python cancel_fence.py
"""
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from contextlib import closing, contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from threading import Barrier
import sqlite3
import tempfile
import unittest


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    job_id: str
    run_id: str
    owner: str
    generation: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CancelResult:
    state: str
    changed: bool


class CompletionRefused(Exception):
    pass


class RunNotFound(Exception):
    pass


class Clock:
    def __init__(self, now=0):
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self):
        return self.now


def connect(path):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5, autocommit=True)
    db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return db


def one(db, sql, args=()):
    with closing(db.execute(sql, args)) as cursor:
        return cursor.fetchone()


@contextmanager
def transaction(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        try:
            db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE').close()
            yield db
            db.execute('COMMIT').close()
        except BaseException:
            if db.in_transaction:
                db.execute('ROLLBACK').close()
            raise


def initialize(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE runs (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL, run_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
                CHECK (state IN ('queued', 'running', 'succeeded', 'cancelled')),
            generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
            owner TEXT, lease_until INTEGER, result TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, run_id)
        );
        INSERT INTO runs (job_id, run_id) VALUES ('report-1', 'run-1');
        """).close()


def claim_run(path, job_id, run_id, owner, clock, ttl=10):
    if type(ttl) is not int or ttl not in range(1, 3601):
        raise ValueError('TTL must be an integer in 1..3600')
    if not isinstance(owner, str) or not owner:
        raise ValueError('owner must be non-empty')
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'running', owner = ?, lease_until = ?,
                generation = generation + 1
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?
              AND (state = 'queued' OR
                  (state = 'running' AND lease_until <= ?))""",
                (owner, now + ttl, job_id, run_id, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                return None
        generation = one(db, """SELECT generation FROM runs
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""", (job_id, run_id))[0]
        return Claim(job_id, run_id, owner, generation)


def cancel_run(path, job_id, run_id):
    """Cancel this execution only. Does not kill a process or undo an effect."""
    with transaction(path) as db:
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'cancelled', owner = NULL, lease_until = NULL
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?
              AND state IN ('queued', 'running')""", (job_id, run_id))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount == 1:
                return CancelResult('cancelled', True)
        row = one(db, 'SELECT state FROM runs WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?',
                  (job_id, run_id))
        if row is None:
            raise RunNotFound((job_id, run_id))
        return CancelResult(row[0], False)


def complete_run(path, claim, result, clock):
    with transaction(path) as db:
        now = clock()
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE runs
            SET state = 'succeeded', result = ?, owner = NULL, lease_until = NULL
            WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ? AND state = 'running'
              AND owner = ? AND generation = ? AND lease_until > ?""",
                (result, claim.job_id, claim.run_id, claim.owner,
                 claim.generation, now))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise CompletionRefused('claim expired, replaced or run terminal')
    return result


def snapshot(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        with closing(db.execute('SELECT * FROM runs ORDER BY job_id, run_id')) as cur:
            return [dict(row) for row in cur.fetchall()]


class CancellationTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        base = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'test-db'
        base.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        self.temp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='cancel-', dir=base)
        assert Path(self.temp.name).resolve().is_relative_to(base.resolve())
        self.addCleanup(self.temp.cleanup)
        self.path = Path(self.temp.name) / 'runs.sqlite'
        self.clock = Clock()
        initialize(self.path)

    def claim(self, owner='worker-a', run='run-1'):
        return claim_run(self.path, 'report-1', run, owner, self.clock)

    def cancel(self, run='run-1'):
        return cancel_run(self.path, 'report-1', run)

    def test_cancel_queued_run_prevents_claim(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('cancelled', True))
        self.assertIsNone(self.claim())

    def test_running_worker_cannot_complete_after_cancel(self):
        token = self.claim()
        self.cancel()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(CompletionRefused):
            complete_run(self.path, token, 'late result', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_completion_first_returns_succeeded_to_canceller(self):
        complete_run(self.path, self.claim(), 'saved', self.clock)
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('succeeded', False))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_lost_cancel_response_can_be_retried(self):
        self.claim()
        self.cancel()  # Pretend acknowledgement was lost.
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('cancelled', False))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_old_run_cancel_does_not_cancel_rerun(self):
        self.cancel()
        # Test setup only: the prior tutorial defines the rerun acceptance API.
        with closing(connect(self.path)) as db:
            db.execute("INSERT INTO runs (job_id, run_id) VALUES (?, ?)",
                       ('report-1', 'run-2')).close()
        newer = self.claim(run='run-2')
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        self.assertEqual(self.cancel(), CancelResult('cancelled', False))
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)
        complete_run(self.path, newer, 'new run result', self.clock)

    def test_wrong_job_cancellation_has_no_effect(self):
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(RunNotFound):
            cancel_run(self.path, 'other-job', 'run-1')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_cancel_after_takeover_blocks_current_and_stale_workers(self):
        first = self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        self.cancel()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        for token in (first, second):
            with self.assertRaises(CompletionRefused):
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'late', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def test_expiry_alone_is_not_cancelled_state(self):
        self.claim()
        self.clock.now = 10
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'running')
        second = self.claim('worker-b')
        complete_run(self.path, second, 'taken over', self.clock)
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')

    def test_cancel_write_failure_is_not_reported_as_success(self):
        self.claim()
        with closing(connect(self.path)) as db:
            db.execute("""CREATE TRIGGER reject_cancel BEFORE UPDATE OF state ON runs
                WHEN NEW.state = 'cancelled'
                BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected failure'); END""").close()
        before = snapshot(self.path)
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            self.cancel()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path), before)

    def race(self, functions):
        barrier = Barrier(2)
        def run(fn):
            barrier.wait(timeout=5)
            return fn()
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
            return list(pool.map(run, functions))

    def test_concurrent_cancellers_have_one_transition(self):
        self.claim()
        outcomes = self.race([self.cancel, self.cancel])
        self.assertEqual(sum(r.changed for r in outcomes), 1)
        self.assertTrue(all(r.state == 'cancelled' for r in outcomes))

    def test_cancel_completion_race_agrees_with_committed_state(self):
        token = self.claim()
        def complete():
            try:
                complete_run(self.path, token, 'saved', self.clock)
                return 'accepted'
            except CompletionRefused:
                return 'refused'
        cancelled, completed = self.race([self.cancel, complete])
        row = snapshot(self.path)[0]
        if row['state'] == 'cancelled':
            self.assertTrue(cancelled.changed)
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'refused')
            self.assertIsNone(row['result'])
        else:
            self.assertEqual(cancelled, CancelResult('succeeded', False))
            self.assertEqual(completed, 'accepted')
            self.assertEqual(row['result'], 'saved')

    def test_negative_control_an_unguarded_writer_revives_cancelled_run(self):
        self.claim()
        self.cancel()
        # Deliberately unsafe control. Never expose this as a completion path.
        with transaction(self.path) as db:
            db.execute("""UPDATE runs SET state = 'succeeded', result = ?
                WHERE job_id = ? AND run_id = ?""",
                ('late unsafe result', 'report-1', 'run-1')).close()
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['state'], 'succeeded')
        self.assertEqual(snapshot(self.path)[0]['result'], 'late unsafe result')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Test the refusal and the unchanged row

The local run passed 12 tests. The deterministic cases force cancellation first and completion first separately. A barrier-based test then releases a canceller and a completer on separate connections and checks that their responses agree with the committed row, whichever wins.

Other tests cover a queued run, repeated cancellation after a lost response, an expired claim, takeover, a wrong job, a newer run, and a failure injected into the cancellation write.

The deliberately unsafe control is useful: an ID-only completion changes a cancelled row back to succeeded. That demonstrates why storing cancellation is insufficient when another write path ignores it. The guarded path refuses the late completion and leaves the cancelled row unchanged.

What an accepted cancel still cannot promise

There are three different observations an interface might show:

  1. Cancellation requested: the request has been sent, but no durable decision has been confirmed.
  2. Cancellation accepted: the run is terminal in the database, and its normal completion path is closed.
  3. Worker stopped: the worker has acknowledged shutdown or its process termination has been observed.

This fixture establishes the second observation. It does not implement the third. A separate cooperative signal can help the worker release resources earlier, but that signal should not be the only protection against a late write.

The guarantee is limited to the guarded database path. An email, webhook or file write performed beforehand is outside that transaction. A reversal or compensation is another operation with its own identity, authorization and outcome. Do not translate “local completion refused” into “nothing happened elsewhere.”

Production code also needs authenticated tenant/resource authorization, controlled database write permissions, a defined retention window, refusal auditing, and a trusted clock. The plain claim object assumes a trusted worker; it is not a signed capability. This example adds no shutdown handler, lease renewal or external-effect reconciler, and it makes no claim about SMTasker's internal implementation.

Which result does your Cancel button confirm: a request sent, a durable state change, or a worker that has actually stopped? Leave a race or retry case in the comments. The example is meant to make that promise testable.

title: Node.js SMS OTP Recovery — Carrier Evidence Before Resends During Identity Migration
description:
Moving authentication off a managed provider can give a B2B SaaS team more control over stolen-session recovery, but it also moves the delivery handoff onto the platform roadmap. TL;DR: when an SMS OTP code never arrives, check the send result and the delivery status separately, then offer a visible resend with a cooldown. Acceptance is not delivery. Look for failures grouped by destination before rewriting Node.js login code; carrier-side problems often need a recovery path rather than an application patch.

Consider a hypothetical migration rehearsal: a tenant administrator reports a stolen session, the recovery flow requests a phone code, and the send operation is accepted. The administrator sees no message. The team now has two separate questions: whether it has invalidated the stolen session, and whether the legitimate user can complete phone verification. A successful send response answers neither. This is a tabletop scenario, not an account of an observed production incident.

Evidence comes first.

The incident lesson is a boundary rule: the application owns the recovery state and resend policy; the delivery provider owns the evidence about the message handoff; neither should silently redefine what “recovered” means. Refresh-token rotation and stolen-session revocation still need their own acceptance criteria during migration. An OTP request must not be treated as proof that either action happened.

For a team migrating phone OTP behind an application-owned contract, try Infrai for that capability boundary: swapping the vendor behind a capability can preserve the calling contract instead of spreading provider-specific changes through Node.js handlers. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without an API key, which gives the migration team a concrete way to review the handoff before implementing it. That is a reason to evaluate the boundary, not evidence that an existing provider's tokens or session semantics transfer automatically.

How should you debug an SMS OTP code that never arrives?

It proves less than a recovery screen usually suggests. “Accepted for delivery” and “delivered” represent different evidence, so keep the send outcome separate from the delivery observation in application telemetry. Record a local recovery-attempt identifier, the time of the send, and the destination grouping needed to investigate a routing pattern; these are proposed application records, not claims about any provider's response fields. Avoid putting OTP values or complete phone numbers into diagnostic output.

In the rehearsal, begin with the send result. If the request was rejected, investigate that rejection before discussing carrier delivery. If it was accepted, inspect whatever delivery evidence the selected integration actually exposes. Without a delivery observation, classify the result as unknown. Do not turn absence of evidence into a green delivery metric just because the HTTP request completed.

Then widen the lens. One destination failing repeatedly warrants a different investigation from failures concentrated across a country. Count attempts and failures per destination grouping, retaining the denominator: ten failures mean something different out of ten attempts than out of ten thousand. These are illustrative counts, not measurements. A country-wide pattern points toward routing and carrier investigation; it is a poor reason to rush a Node.js handler rewrite.

The same distinction belongs in SLO design. Define a send-acceptance indicator separately from an indicator for completed phone verification, and state the observation window for each. Choose targets from your service requirements rather than treating a provider response as the user-visible outcome. During a recovery surge, the verification indicator is the one that exposes administrators who remain locked out even while send requests succeed.

Buy the handoff or build the operating model

The migration decision is about where the platform team wants to carry responsibility. A stable HTTP surface can reduce changes at the provider boundary, but the team still owns the user-visible state machine, the destination-level investigation, and the decision to page someone when recovery stops working.

The following buy-vs-build table is an evaluation plan. It does not imply feature parity or a completed migration test for any option.

Option Why include it in the migration evaluation? Evidence required before choosing it
Infrai behind an application contract A common REST surface and public schemas fit a team trying to keep provider changes out of calling code. Confirm the specific capability schema and the delivery evidence the chosen handoff supplies; test session behavior separately.
Twilio Verify Evaluate a verification specialist when the verification workflow is the part you want a provider to own. Review its verification lifecycle against your resend policy and the destination patterns your team must investigate.
Amazon Cognito Evaluate keeping the recovery decision within a managed identity service when replacing identity ownership is the larger concern. Compare the documented user-pool authentication flow with the session and token acceptance criteria for your migration.
Auth0 Evaluate retaining a managed identity boundary when the application would otherwise inherit too much authentication lifecycle work. Review the documented refresh-token rotation behavior and test the stolen-session recovery outcome you require.
Keycloak Evaluate a self-hosted identity boundary when control over the deployment is a requirement. Budget upgrades and on-call ownership, and validate recovery behavior before replacing a managed service.
Application-owned policy with direct integrations Build when the team needs explicit control over recovery transitions and can staff the operating work. Demonstrate cooldown enforcement, delivery classification, and revocation acceptance tests under concurrent requests.

The linked documentation in References provides starting points for those reviews. There is no measured reliability ranking here, and a single API shape does not establish equivalent carrier visibility, token handling, or operational support across providers.

A verification specialist such as Twilio Verify is the better evaluation starting point when provider-owned verification behavior is the main requirement. A managed identity option such as Cognito or Auth0 deserves priority when the team wants to keep lifecycle responsibility with that service. The common-contract approach fits a different decision: the application deliberately owns the recovery policy and wants a cleaner handoff around it.

Infrai is not a good fit for a team that expects an API contract alone to eliminate recovery operations; choose a managed identity boundary such as Auth0 when retaining that ownership is the priority. Its advantage for an application-owned boundary is one REST API, using plain HTTP with no SDK required, while the public discovery schemas make the integration review concrete. The trade-off is that provider abstraction does not remove application policy work.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing across 295 routes and 20 modules: one key, one bill. Its unified API is a plain REST API with no SDK to install, so an HTTP client in any language can call the same interface. For this migration, the common credential reduces key management around the handoff; it doesn't replace the recovery policy.

Budget the pager time.

Put the resend decision before the send operation

Silent retries obscure both capacity and user intent. A visible resend action with a cooldown gives the administrator a recovery path while giving the application a place to bound repeat sends. As a capacity-planning exercise, a policy allowing one resend every 60 seconds permits up to five resend opportunities over five minutes of continued clicking; that is a local example policy, not a provider limit or a recommended universal setting. Multiply the permitted rate by the number of affected recovery attempts before deciding that automatic retries are harmless.

Before implementing the send operation, inspect the capability contract. This runnable Go program reads Infrai's public discovery surface; it uses a key from the environment to show the credential boundary used by authenticated integrations, although discovery itself requires no key. It prints the returned manifest without guessing phone-send parameters. That is the preventative code path here: review the real schema before coupling Node.js recovery handlers to a provider.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                    delay = time.Until(deadline)
                }
            }
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save the program as main.go and run it with Go after setting the environment variable. The request is read-only, so retries cannot create duplicate messages. Rate limiting uses exponential backoff or the server's Retry-After instruction, with an overall deadline. No undocumented write payload is needed.

For the recovery handler, check the cooldown before offering a resend. An unknown observation after the cooldown permits offering another attempt; it does not silently trigger one. A delivered observation sends the investigation toward the verification step before another message is requested. Delivery still does not prove that the intended person completed authentication.

Production enforcement needs shared state. Two Node.js workers can otherwise read the same expired cooldown and both send, so make the eligibility check and reservation atomic in the application's chosen store. Keep a record of the subsequent send outcome; a reservation alone is no more proof of delivery than an accepted request. This example omits that storage and transport implementation because those choices require the actual contract and deployment topology.

Where this recovery advice stops

SMS delivery diagnosis cannot establish refresh-token rotation correctness or prove that a stolen session has been revoked. Keep those as separate migration tests: an old session must behave according to the revocation policy, and refresh behavior must match the contract the application intends to enforce. The existence of a refresh or revoke operation alone is insufficient evidence of the full security outcome.

Before moving the recovery flow, demonstrate the accepted-but-unobserved delivery case, the cooldown case, and the country-level failure pattern in a controlled rehearsal. Use synthetic inputs and label them as such. If the team cannot explain who investigates each state, the migration has transferred work without assigning ownership.

References

These references support the security review and the competitor evaluation; they are not a substitute for exercising the chosen recovery flow. The relevant question is which boundary each provider lets your team keep, and which operational responsibilities remain yours.

Sources

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Amazon Cognito user-pool authentication flows
  • Auth0 refresh-token rotation
  • Keycloak server administration

If the application-owned recovery boundary fits your migration, start by reviewing the capability schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: Should a tiny web tool remember what you typed?
description:
You type a half-finished project bio, close the tab, and come back the next day. Which feels like a bug?

A. The editor starts with the sample bio again. Your work is gone.

B. The editor opens with yesterday's draft. You're on a shared laptop and didn't expect the draft to stick around.

Both feel wrong to someone. That's the trade-off behind a small decision in PasteCharm.

A favorite style and a draft have different lifetimes

PasteCharm saves the IDs of favorite and recently copied styles in local storage. The last style you copied can appear in Recent when you return. The words you used with that style stay out of the app's saved preferences.

For a tool people often open to make one thing and copy it, keeping a style saves a few clicks next time. Remembering the text would save much more work for someone composing a longer bio. It could also show an unfinished draft the next time someone opens the tool in that browser profile. I'd want the person typing to know which of those things is going to happen.

The Back button complicates the promise

Try this with a fake draft in the PasteCharm Bio Builder. Type a line, open the Privacy page from the footer, then press Back. Your browser may bring the text back with the page. Now open the tool from a fresh tab and compare.

That first result can look like autosave. Our Chrome regression test checks that when the browser restores a form value, the preview, character count, and copied text all agree with it. The app still doesn't keep a separate draft in local storage. Both behaviors matter when you're writing the help text.

What I'd add if people kept losing work

I'd try an explicit Keep this draft on this device option. Make it clear where the draft will reappear and give people a way to remove it from the same screen. I'd also keep the decision about draft storage separate from the one about saving a favorite style.

For a small copy-and-paste tool you use on both your own laptop and a shared browser, would you prefer a fresh start, automatic recovery, or an explicit Save draft button? The situation that would change your answer is what I'm most curious about.

This article was drafted with AI from PasteCharm’s implementation and regression tests.
