title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
description:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

Get started

Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide, since v5 is a major release.

title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.34831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.

title: Keep a Node.js App Running 24/7 on AWS EC2 with PM2
description:
In my last post, I got my Node app running on EC2 with npm start. It worked until I closed the terminal. Then it was gone.

This post fixes that with PM2. It takes about 5 commands.

Why the app stops

When you run npm start over SSH, the app is a child of your shell. Close the SSH window and the shell exits, so the app exits with it. Ctrl+C does the same thing on purpose.

A server needs the app to run with nobody logged in. That's what a process manager is for.

1. Install PM2 

npm i -g pm2

If you get permission denied, your global npm folder belongs to root. Run it with sudo:

sudo npm i -g pm2

2. Start the app with PM2

From inside the project folder:

pm2 start index.js --name node-api

PM2 prints a table with an ID (0) and the name you gave it. The app is now running in the background. You can close your SSH session, and it keeps running.

3. Check the logs

You no longer see the app's output in your terminal. To read it:

pm2 logs node-api

You can also use the ID: pm2 logs 0. Press Ctrl+C to stop watching the logs. That doesn't stop the app.

4. See what's running 

pm2 list

This shows every app PM2 manages, its status, CPU, memory, and restart count. A rising restart count means your app is crashing.

5. Start it again after a reboot

PM2 keeps the app alive while the server is up. If the EC2 instance reboots, PM2 itself needs to start again. Two commands handle that:

pm2 startup

This prints one sudo env PATH=... command. Copy it and run it. It registers PM2 as a system service.

Then save the current list of apps:

pm2 save

Now, after a reboot, PM2 starts and brings node-api back on its own. Test it with sudo reboot, SSH back in after a minute, and run pm2 list.

Next

The app runs on port 4000. Next, I put Nginx in front of it so people can reach it on port 80.

Video

Here's the 4-minute walkthrough:

Previous step, run the app with npm start: https://dev.to/jahidhiron/run-a-nodejs-app-on-aws-ec2-and-why-it-stops-when-you-close-ssh-3bb5
Full course playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLfeDvEEUyoEJZGnw11rKIET5lJDs6JmhD

title: Cloudflare MoQ CDN: Scale Sub-Second Live Streams in 10 Minutes
description:
You have MoQ running on Ant Media Server, and now you need to serve more viewers than one server can handle. Right now every viewer connects to the relay on your server, and that relay is limited by the server’s network bandwidth. A Cloudflare MoQ CDN takes that load off your server.

HLS solved the same problem years ago with a CDN. One origin server produces the stream, and the CDN caches it near the viewers and serves it from there. MoQ follows the same pattern, so a Media over QUIC CDN is a network of relays instead of caches. Cloudflare runs MoQ relays all around the world, and the Ant Media Server MoQ plugin can push to them with one setting change.

By the end of this post you will have your stream playing through Cloudflare’s relays, and you will know why that scales where a single relay does not. The setup takes about 10 minutes on a server that already has the plugin. If you do not have it yet, start with the MoQ announcement post or the MoQ on AWS walkthrough.

Table of contents

  1. Why does one MoQ relay run out?
  2. How does the Cloudflare MoQ CDN fan out?
  3. Set up the Cloudflare MoQ CDN in 10 minutes
  4. Test it: watch your stream come out of Cloudflare
  5. What’s next once your stream plays from the Cloudflare MoQ CDN?
  6. Before you build production on it
  7. Frequently Asked Questions

Why does one MoQ relay run out?

It runs out of network bandwidth long before it runs out of CPU. Every viewer gets their own QUIC connection, their own encrypted copy of every frame, and their own retransmissions when their Wi-Fi drops a packet. Nothing in that list gets cheaper as the audience grows. The thousandth viewer costs the relay as much as the first one did.

A 1 Gbps port can feed about 330 viewers of a 1080p stream at 3 Mbps, and a 10 Gbps port about 3,300. Adding a 720p rendition does not change that. The server then encodes and sends two streams, and every viewer still uses their own share of the bandwidth. A bigger instance does not move that ceiling by much.

The second limit is distance. Say a viewer sits 150 ms away from your server. Every lost packet takes a 150 ms round trip to recover, and the player’s jitter buffer grows to cover that. A relay 10 ms from the same viewer recovers the same loss in 10 ms, so the buffer can stay at the player’s default of 250 ms.

How does the Cloudflare MoQ CDN fan out?

The CDN keeps one connection per track to your Ant Media Server, no matter how many viewers it serves. Your server publishes each stream to the Cloudflare relay nearest to it. A viewer lands on the relay nearest to them, wherever they are, and that relay pulls the stream across Cloudflare’s network once for all of its viewers. Relays pass the media through without decoding it, so your encoder settings reach the viewer unchanged.

MoQ through a relay CDN gets you WebRTC’s delay and HLS’s way of scaling. A WebRTC edge holds a session for every viewer, so a bigger audience means more edge nodes. An HLS CDN carries the audience for you, but it caches segments, so viewers watch seconds behind. A MoQ relay holds one subscription per track and passes each frame on as it arrives, so it has neither problem. It is still in beta, so run the embedded relay until the server’s bandwidth is the limit, then add the CDN URL.

What does the plugin do with a CDN URL?

It publishes every stream twice. Setting moqCdnUrl adds a second destination, it does not replace the embedded relay. For every stream, and every ABR rendition of it, the plugin starts one extra moq process that sends the already encoded frames to the CDN. Nothing is re-encoded, and the broadcast names are the same on both ends: live/studio1/source, live/studio1/720p.

Everything else is untouched: ingest, playback from your own server, recording, HLS and WebRTC. If the connection to Cloudflare stalls, only the CDN copy drops frames. Viewers on your own relay never notice.

Publish to your server, never to Cloudflare. The CDN only delivers streams to viewers. The browser publisher, OBS and every other source still connect to your Ant Media Server, and the plugin forwards the stream to Cloudflare.

The plugin verifies Cloudflare’s TLS certificate. Only the local connection to your embedded relay, which uses a self-signed certificate, skips that check.

Set up the Cloudflare MoQ CDN in 10 minutes

You need Ant Media Server 3.0.0 or later with the 3.1.0 release of the MoQ plugin installed, and HTTPS on. On a new AWS instance, the MoQ on AWS post gets you there in four steps. On a server you already run, follow the MoQ docs page. You also need a Cloudflare account. Cloudflare’s MoQ docs cover the relay side in more detail than this post does.

  1. Create a relay in Cloudflare In the Cloudflare dashboard go to Media > Realtime > MoQ Relay, select Create relay, give it a name and confirm. You get two tokens, a publish token for your server and a subscribe token for your viewers. They are shown once and Cloudflare does not store them, so copy both now.

You can also create relays through Cloudflare’s API.

The publish token is the whole URL the server will use.

  1. Give the publish token to the plugin Open your application in the web panel, go to Settings > Advanced, and add the key inside customSettings: 
{
  "customSettings": {
    "plugin.moq": {
      "moqCdnUrl": "https://draft-16.cloudflare.mediaoverquic.com/<PUBLISH_TOKEN>"
    }
  }
}

Save, then restart the application so the plugin picks up the new setting. The host has to be draft-16. A draft-14 host is the trap: it accepts the publish and the logs look healthy, but no viewer can ever find the stream. The next stream that starts writes this line to /usr/local/antmedia/log/ant-media-server.log:

MoQ: 2 muxer(s) publishing for stream studio1, with CDN: true

A stream without ABR renditions gets two muxers, one for your relay and one for Cloudflare.

Ant Media Server Settings Advanced with the plugin.moq custom setting and moqCdnUrl.

One key under customSettings is the whole Cloudflare MoQ CDN configuration.

Test it: watch your stream come out of Cloudflare

Now the fun part. Start a stream on your server the way you already do. The plugin’s browser publisher at https://your-domain:5443/live/moq/publish.html is the quickest, and OBS, SRT, WHIP or an IP camera work just as well. Call it studio1.

Use Chrome for this test. Chrome, Edge and Safari 26.4 or later play MoQ, but Firefox is still unstable for it. Open the plugin’s player with your subscribe token as the url parameter:

https://your-domain:5443/live/moq/play.html?url=https://draft-16.cloudflare.mediaoverquic.com/&name=live/studio1/source

Done. The page loads from your server, but the media now comes from the Cloudflare relay nearest to you. Send the link to a friend on another continent. Their copy comes from a relay near them, and your server still sends Cloudflare just one copy.

The quality buttons stay empty on Cloudflare hosts, because the player turns off stream discovery there. To watch a rendition, change name in the URL, for example to live/studio1/720p.

The debug panel under the video shows frame rate and buffer. Set the player beside the source going in, and the two timecodes stay within a fraction of a second of each other. That small gap is what Cloudflare’s path adds for your viewers.

Ant Media Server MoQ player playing a stream from a Cloudflare relay next to the live source.
The same stream playing back from a Cloudflare relay, next to the live source.
What’s next once your stream plays from the Cloudflare MoQ CDN?
Your server now sends each track out once, and Cloudflare carries it to every viewer, wherever they are. The 330-viewer ceiling of a 1 Gbps port no longer caps your audience, and in the side-by-side test the Cloudflare copy stays within a fraction of a second of the source.

If your origin is still a test box, the AWS deployment guide gets a fresh MoQ origin running in four steps, and the same moqCdnUrl setting works there unchanged.

To prove the whole path on your own stream before you commit, from ingest through the embedded relay to the Cloudflare relays nearest your viewers, install the plugin on a MoQ test server under the 14-day Ant Media Server Enterprise Edition trial. No credit card is required, and you can watch your server’s outbound bandwidth stay flat while viewers join through Cloudflare.

Ant Media Server Free Trial – On-Premise or AWS (14 Days)

Choose your Ant Media Server free trial: 14-day on-premise (full control) or 7-day AWS Marketplace (instant launch).

antmedia.io

Contact Us - Ant Media

Contact us and let our experts find the right live streaming solution for you. Reach out today and we'll get back to you shortly.

antmedia.io

Before you build production on it

Check these five limits before you send real viewers through Cloudflare:

  • Cloudflare’s relays are in beta, with no SLA published, and Cloudflare says the API may change.
  • Only the draft-16 host works with the plugin today. Cloudflare already recommends draft-18 for new deployments and keeps draft-16 open for existing clients. MoQ is still an IETF draft, so expect version bumps on every side, including a new Cloudflare hostname.
  • One subscribe token serves all viewers. Per-viewer playback auth through Ant Media Server play tokens is designed but not shipped yet.
  • A viewer who joins late starts at the live edge, because Cloudflare’s relays do not offer rewind yet.
  • Viewers need Chrome, Edge, Brave or Safari 26.4 or later. Firefox has WebTransport, but the plugin docs list it as unstable for MoQ playback.

title: Mapping free street parking from open data with PostGIS and MapKit
description:
This post covers why OpenStreetMap gives kerb-level parking in only some
cities, how I turn a council's paid streets into "likely free" kerbs with
PostGIS, how that guess stays apart from real facts, and how SwiftUI's Map
draws a city's kerbs without stuttering. The app is Easy Find Parking, a free
iPhone and iPad map of free street parking in Berlin, Madrid, Barcelona,
València and Kraków,
on the App Store;
the user's side is in a separate post.

Server: Flask, PostGIS and a self-hosted ParkAPI. Phone: SwiftUI on iOS 17.

OpenStreetMap street parking is mostly a German dataset

My first plan was OpenStreetMap everywhere. Kerbside parking is tagged on the
street itself, with keys like parking:left=lane and parking:right:fee=no
(see Street parking on
the OSM wiki). When I measured in September 2026, this was the share of
drivable streets carrying any parking:* tag:

City Streets with parking:* tags
Berlin 99.9%
Hamburg 54%
Warsaw 26%
Lyon 22%
Milan 11%
Paris 10%
València 7%
Barcelona 4%
Lisbon 0.9%

Fee sub-tags were on about a tenth of those. Berlin works: 64,229 kerb sides and
48,567 car parks from one Geofabrik extract. Elsewhere a tag-driven layer would
be mostly blank, which reads as "no parking here". So outside Germany the
street layer comes from municipal open data, which the city actually enforces.

Reading the tags has traps. The wiki deprecated the older parking:lane=* and
parking:condition=* keys in December 2022 and asks for existing ones to be
converted, so the normaliser reads both. parking:left=no is a value, not an
absence: 43% of Berlin's tagged sides. And without closed_ways_are_polygons
in its config, GDAL put closed amenity=parking ways in the lines layer, where
my highway filter dropped them: Berlin had 42 car-park polygons instead of
63,294.

Deriving "likely free" from what a city charges for

Councils publish what they charge for, because that's what they enforce.
Barcelona's
surface parking dataset
lists its blue, green and goods-delivery segments; Kraków publishes 23 paid-zone
polygons and no kerbs. The complement is the free map: every drivable street
inside the city boundary with nothing regulated near it.

CREATE TEMP TABLE regulated AS
SELECT geom FROM efp.street_parking
WHERE city_id = :'city' AND fee_source IN ('municipal_paid', 'municipal_free')
UNION ALL
SELECT geom::geography FROM efp.paid_zone WHERE city_id = :'city';  -- Kraków's polygons

-- ...
FROM osm_stage.streets_REGIONTAG s
CROSS JOIN (VALUES ('left'), ('right')) AS sides(side)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM city_boundary b WHERE ST_Within(s.geom, b.geom))
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM regulated r
      WHERE ST_DWithin(efp.kerb_offset(s.geom, sides.side)::geography, r.geom, :clearance))
  AND s.highway IN ('residential', 'living_street', 'unclassified', 'tertiary', 'tertiary_link')
  AND lower(coalesce(s.access, '')) NOT IN ('private', 'no', 'customers')

Three of these are there because a looser version published something wrong.

Metres, not degrees. The first version buffered by 0.00025°. At
Barcelona's latitude that's 27.8 m north–south but 20.8 m east–west, and 407
streets 21–25 m from a paid kerb went out as free. Casting to geography makes
ST_DWithin measure in metres; :clearance is 25.

Test the kerb, not the centreline. efp.kerb_offset shifts the street 3 m
to one side, working in EPSG:3857 and dividing the distance by cos(latitude) to
undo Mercator's stretch. That line can sit closer to a paid kerb than the
centreline, so it's the one tested.

Leave out roads with no parking. The first run turned 17,275 regulated
segments into 10,842 free kerb sides, and the map showed dashed "likely free"
lines down Avinguda Diagonal. Arterials have no regulated segments because
nobody parks on them, so "outside every paid zone" came out true. Limiting the
rule to residential, unclassified and tertiary roads dropped 3,156 sides, 29%
of the layer. Service roads stay out: they're car-park aisles and driveways as
often as public kerb.

Kraków's polygons feed the same rule: 21,255 free kerb sides, none within 25 m
of a zone. A test samples 2,000 derived kerbs per city to assert
it. Checking every row took over 150 seconds at 29,000 derived against
105,000 regulated, and a check nobody waits for is a check nobody runs.

Free and likely free are different values

The schema never stores a bare "free". Every row has a fee_state (FREE,
PAID, CONDITIONAL, UNKNOWN) and a fee_source saying where it came from:
municipal_free, osm_tag, operator_feed, municipal_paid_complement and
municipal_outside_zone.

The last one came from Madrid, whose SER map service publishes 87,614 kerb
bands. 53,158 are grey, a colour missing from the service's own legend.
Sampling 300 bands of each colour against the SER boundary settled it: every
blue and green band tested fell inside, no grey one did. So grey bands are
published kerbs outside the paid zone: stronger than an inference from nothing,
weaker than the council saying "free". I first stored them as
municipal_paid_complement, and the overlap test failed, correctly: grey bands
sit next to blue ones on the same street, which for a derived street would be a
bug.

One function turns the pair into a claim, ordered by trust: a current count, a
published fact, a schedule, an inference, an admitted gap.

switch (feeState, feeSource) {
case (.free, .municipalFree), (.free, .operatorFeed):
    return .cityFree
case (.free, .osmTag):
    return .signpostedFree
case (.free, .municipalOutsideZone), (.free, .municipalPaidComplement):
    // This is the inference, and it must never borrow a stronger phrasing.
    return .likelyFree
case (.free, _):
    // A free claim with no provenance is not one we will repeat.
    return .unknown
default:
    break
}

Charging hours the parser can't read resolve to "charged right now": wrong
that way costs a walk, the other way a fine.

On the first build the inferred layer was mint and read as the same free as
the confirmed green. Now it's teal and dashed, which says "not solid" before
anyone reads the legend:

ForEach(model.streets) { street in
    MapPolyline(coordinates: street.coordinates)
        .stroke(street.claim.tint.opacity(0.85),
                style: street.claim.isInferred ? .inferredKerb : .kerb)
}

private extension StrokeStyle {
    static let kerb = StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 4, lineCap: .round, lineJoin: .round)
    /// Dashed: derived from an absence of regulation, not from a sign.
    static let inferredKerb = StrokeStyle(
        lineWidth: 4, lineCap: .butt, lineJoin: .round, dash: [3, 7])
}

Both hedged kinds draw the same dashed teal; the data keeps them apart.

Drawing kerbs with SwiftUI's Map

That ForEach is the whole renderer, and its cost is the count: a city-wide
Barcelona viewport holds around 660 kerbs. The obvious fix is one
MKMultiPolyline per style, about four overlays, but MapPolyline has no
initialiser that takes one. So I rewrote the map as MKMapView in a
UIViewRepresentable. It worked in the simulator and drew no tiles on a real
device. I couldn't reproduce it, and a blank map is worse than a slow one, so I
went back to SwiftUI's Map. What keeps it smooth:

  • Measure first. The database answered in 7.6 ms and the endpoint in under half a second, so the stutter was on the phone.
  • Fetch a ring, draw the screen. The app fetches 30% of the span beyond each edge, skips the request while the viewport stays inside it, and waits 250 ms for the camera to settle. Drawing is clipped to the viewport, about 60% fewer lines, and the array is reassigned only when visible IDs change: an identical array still makes SwiftUI diff every overlay.
  • Slim payload. Street name, zone, capacity and source were 65% of the bytes and none is drawn, so the layer gets four fields per kerb and coordinates rounded to six decimals, about 10 cm. A city-wide response went from 575 KB to 359 KB.
  • Nearest first. The query orders by sp.geom <-> centre with a limit of 1,500, so truncation eats the ring, not the middle of the screen.

One feature from the live API:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": {
    "type": "LineString",
    "coordinates": [[2.174812, 41.403032], [2.174847, 41.403005], [2.174876, 41.402983]]
  },
  "properties": {
    "source_id": "complement-es-barcelona-885702924-left",
    "fee_state": "FREE",
    "fee_source": "municipal_paid_complement",
    "opening_hours": null
  }
}

A cap of 400 drawn kerbs left the edges of a Barcelona screen bare, and a
driver can't tell a capped edge from a street with no parking, so it went.

València publishes individual spaces, 315,303 averaging 2.6 m, so 1,500
features covered a few blocks. ST_ClusterDBSCAN, partitioned by street, fee
state and a grid of about 300 m, now merges adjacent bays into segments with a
bay count: the same view went from 1,500 features and 453 KB to 582 and 135 KB.
Without the grid, nameless paid bays chained into lines 25 km long. A polyline
threaded through the bays zig-zagged across the street, since bays sit on both
sides, so each cluster is drawn as the longest line across its convex hull.

Zoomed out past 0.02° of span, the kerb layer switches off and the gateway
counts kerbs in roughly an 8×8 grid over the viewport, drawn as circles.
These aren't MapKit annotation clusters: the phone never downloads the kerbs at
that zoom. Circle size is logarithmic, because counts span four orders of
magnitude and linear sizing pinned nearly every circle to the maximum.

Live counts go stale after 15 minutes

The old app read api.parkendd.de, which had stopped updating. Now I run my
own ParkAPI v3 (MIT), pulling
realtime data every 300 seconds into the same Postgres as my schema, so the
gateway joins its parking_site table directly. The gateway decides freshness,
so phone and server can't disagree:

STALE_AFTER = timedelta(minutes=15)

def freshness(updated_at: datetime | None) -> str:
    if updated_at is None:
        return 'none'
    age = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - updated_at
    return 'live' if age <= STALE_AFTER else 'stale'

for row in rows:
    row['freshness'] = freshness(row.get('realtime_updated_at'))
    # Keep the number, drop the claim that it is current.
    row['realtime_is_current'] = row['freshness'] == 'live'

ParkAPI's own public API drops realtime fields once they're too old. I keep the
number and label it: a stale count shows grey as "N free when last seen", with
its age. On 9 November 2026, 15 car parks within 2 km of central Basel had a
current count.

Indigo's feed reported zero occupancy for all 558 French car parks, which naive
arithmetic shows as empty, so realtime is off for it. And 28% of upstream
ParkAPI converters were already dead when I set it up, so each source's last
success and error live in a table.

Licences and gaps

OpenStreetMap data is ODbL (© OpenStreetMap contributors). Barcelona and
València publish under CC BY 4.0, Madrid and Kraków under their own open-data
terms, the French national base and Indigo under ODbL. Derived layers credit
both the council and OSM, and the app shows these credits behind its info
button.

Missing: an offline cache, address search, and Warsaw. Its city API timed out
when I checked, and OSM had fee information on 0% of its central streets. Kerb
lines show rules, not empty spaces.

What the app does for the people who use it: Free parking app for Europe: Easy Find Parking for iPhone.

FAQ

How complete is OpenStreetMap parking data in European cities?

Very uneven. When I measured in September 2026, the share of drivable streets
with any parking:* tag was 99.9% in Berlin, 10% in Paris, 4% in Barcelona
and 0.9% in Lisbon, and about a tenth of tagged streets had fee
information. Outside Germany, municipal open data is usually the better source.

How do you find free street parking from a city's paid parking data?

Take the OpenStreetMap road network inside the city boundary and drop any
street side within a clearance (25 m in Easy Find Parking) of a published paid
segment or zone polygon. Limit it to residential, unclassified and tertiary
roads, or arterials come out free, and label the result "likely free".

Should I buffer in degrees or metres in PostGIS?

Metres. On EPSG:4326 geometry, distances are in degrees, and a degree of
longitude shrinks with latitude: 0.00025° is 27.8 m north–south but 20.8 m
east–west in Barcelona. Cast to geography and ST_DWithin takes metres.

How do I draw thousands of polylines in a SwiftUI Map without lag?

SwiftUI's Map needs one MapPolyline per line and can't take an
MKMultiPolyline, so the line count is the cost. Fetch a padded area, skip
requests while the viewport stays inside it, debounce camera changes by about
250 ms, draw only what's visible and send only the fields you draw. Zoomed out,
show area counts instead.

How do you know if a live car park count is still current?

Compare its timestamp with the server's clock. Easy Find Parking treats a count
older than 15 minutes as stale: it keeps the number but shows it as "free when
last seen" with its age, never as spaces available now.

title: Freeze marina haul-out and storage rates in TypeScript
description:
A 30-foot boat rings up $845 for haul-out, prep, and four months of storage. Apply the $200 deposit and the balance is $645. The marina later changes all three rates. Open the approved revision again and the same $645 is still due.

Price the work order at approval

Length overall (LOA) is the billable length for the haul-out in this example. The fixture takes whole billable feet and whole storage months as inputs. If a marina bills fractional lengths, establish the billable quantity under its pricing terms before approval.

Work-order line Calculation Amount
Haul-out 30 ft × $4 per foot $120
Prep One flat charge $125
Seasonal storage 4 months × $150 per month $600
Approved total $845
Applied deposit Receipt DEP-200 −$200
Balance $645

Use bigint cents for rates, charges, and deposits. At approval, copy the live rates and freeze the copied rates, calculated charges, and revision record. Those nested freezes matter because Object.freeze operates on one object at a time. Editing the live card to $5 per foot, $150 for prep, and $170 per month produces a $980 second approval and leaves revision 1 at $845.

Replay the applied deposits

The example ledger contains one row per applied receipt for the work order. Each row carries its receipt ID, work-order ID, and amount applied. Before subtracting the credits, reject duplicate receipt IDs, receipts attached to another order, and totals above the approved price. Replaying the same deposit entries against the saved approval reproduces the balance without reading the live rate card.

Run the benchmark

Save the block as boathaul-benchmark.ts and run node --experimental-strip-types boathaul-benchmark.ts with Node.js 24. The script needs no packages. Node.js TypeScript documentation

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

type RateCard = {
  haulPerFootCents: bigint;
  prepCents: bigint;
  storagePerMonthCents: bigint;
};

type WorkOrderRevision = {
  workOrderId: string;
  revision: number;
  loaFeet: bigint;
  storageMonths: bigint;
};

type DepositApplication = {
  receiptId: string;
  workOrderId: string;
  appliedCents: bigint;
};

function approve(draft: WorkOrderRevision, rateCard: RateCard) {
  const { workOrderId, revision, loaFeet, storageMonths } = draft;
  assert(workOrderId.trim(), "Work order ID is required");
  assert(Number.isSafeInteger(revision) && revision > 0, "Invalid revision");
  assert(loaFeet > 0n && storageMonths >= 0n, "Invalid LOA or storage term");

  const rates = Object.freeze({ ...rateCard });
  assert(rates.haulPerFootCents >= 0n && rates.prepCents >= 0n &&
    rates.storagePerMonthCents >= 0n, "Rates must be nonnegative");

  const haulCents = loaFeet * rates.haulPerFootCents;
  const storageCents = storageMonths * rates.storagePerMonthCents;
  const charges = Object.freeze({
    haulCents,
    prepCents: rates.prepCents,
    storageCents,
    totalCents: haulCents + rates.prepCents + storageCents,
  });
  return Object.freeze({ workOrderId, revision, loaFeet, storageMonths, rates, charges });
}

function reconcileDeposit(
  approval: ReturnType<typeof approve>,
  applications: readonly DepositApplication[],
) {
  const usedReceipts = new Set<string>();
  let appliedCents = 0n;
  for (const entry of applications) {
    const receiptId = entry.receiptId.trim();
    assert(receiptId, "Deposit receipt ID is required");
    assert.equal(entry.workOrderId, approval.workOrderId, "Deposit belongs to another work order");
    assert(!usedReceipts.has(receiptId), `Duplicate deposit receipt: ${receiptId}`);
    assert(entry.appliedCents > 0n, "Applied deposit must be positive");
    usedReceipts.add(receiptId);
    appliedCents += entry.appliedCents;
  }

  const { totalCents } = approval.charges;
  assert(appliedCents <= totalCents, "Applied deposits exceed approved total");
  return { appliedCents, balanceCents: totalCents - appliedCents };
}

const draft = { workOrderId: "WO-030", revision: 1, loaFeet: 30n, storageMonths: 4n };
const rateCard = { haulPerFootCents: 400n, prepCents: 12_500n, storagePerMonthCents: 15_000n };
const deposit = { receiptId: "DEP-200", workOrderId: draft.workOrderId, appliedCents: 20_000n };

const approved = approve(draft, rateCard);
const expectedR1 = {
  ...draft,
  rates: { ...rateCard },
  charges: { haulCents: 12_000n, prepCents: 12_500n, storageCents: 60_000n, totalCents: 84_500n },
};
assert.deepEqual(approved, expectedR1);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved, "revision", 2), false);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved.rates, "haulPerFootCents", 999n), false);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved.charges, "totalCents", 0n), false);
const originalBalance = reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit]);
assert.deepEqual(originalBalance, { appliedCents: 20_000n, balanceCents: 64_500n });

rateCard.haulPerFootCents = 500n;
rateCard.prepCents = 15_000n;
rateCard.storagePerMonthCents = 17_000n;
const revisedApproval = approve({ ...draft, revision: 2 }, rateCard);
const reopened = reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit]);

assert.deepEqual(approved, expectedR1);
assert.deepEqual(reopened, originalBalance);
assert.equal(revisedApproval.charges.totalCents, 98_000n);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit, { ...deposit, receiptId: " DEP-200 " }]),
  /Duplicate deposit receipt/);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [{ ...deposit, workOrderId: "WO-031" }]),
  /another work order/);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [{ ...deposit, appliedCents: 84_501n }]),
  /exceed approved total/);

const { workOrderId, revision, charges } = approved;
console.log(`${workOrderId} r${revision} haul + prep + storage (cents): ${charges.haulCents} + ${charges.prepCents} + ${charges.storageCents} = ${charges.totalCents}`);
console.log(`Applied deposit / balance (cents): ${originalBalance.appliedCents} / ${originalBalance.balanceCents}`);
console.log(`After rate-card edit, r${revision} total / balance (cents): ${charges.totalCents} / ${reopened.balanceCents}`);
console.log(`New approval r${revisedApproval.revision} total (cents): ${revisedApproval.charges.totalCents}`);

Verified Node output 

WO-030 r1 haul + prep + storage (cents): 12000 + 12500 + 60000 = 84500
Applied deposit / balance (cents): 20000 / 64500
After rate-card edit, r1 total / balance (cents): 84500 / 64500
New approval r2 total (cents): 98000

Persist approved snapshots under the work-order ID and revision number. Keep applied receipts with the work order so a marina can trace both the original price and the credits behind a balance.

BoatHaul marina work orders · B2B Ops and FinOps Benchmarks

title: 8 Brand-to-Engineering Handoff Tips That Actually Work
description:
A brand system can look tight in a slide deck and still fall apart in production. The logo is too complex at 16 pixels, the brand typeface adds a second of font delay, and the colour contrast that worked in print fails a basic accessibility check in the product UI.

The tips below are for teams that have to ship a website or an app from a brand identity, not only present one. None of them are a reason to dilute a distinctive brand. They work because engineering constraints show up at launch, whether you planned for them or not.

1. Design Tokens Before a 90-Page PDF

Guidelines that only exist as a PDF will be skimmed once and ignored. The useful handoff is a set of tokens: colour, type scale, spacing, radius, shadows and breakpoints, named in a way a developer can put into CSS or a design-system file.

Keep the names stable and boring (color-text-primary, not “Ocean Dusk”). If a token does not map to a value the product will actually use, leave it out. A short token list that is implemented is worth more than a comprehensive palette that never leaves Figma.

Agree which file is the source of truth, and how a token change reaches the codebase. Otherwise the site and the latest deck will drift within a month.

2. Test the Identity at Product Sizes, Not Just on a Poster

Brand work is often signed off at large sizes: a billboard, a cover, a presentation title. The same mark has to work as a favicon, a nav logo, an app icon and an Open Graph image.

Check the logo in monochrome, on light and dark backgrounds, and at the smallest size it will appear in the interface. If the wordmark falls apart, you need a simplified mark, not a scaled-down poster. The same applies to photography: a campaign image that looks striking in a case study can be too heavy, too cropped, or too low-contrast in a hero slot.

Build a simple page of real components — header, button, form, card, error state — before you call the identity finished.

3. Choose Type With Performance in Mind

Custom fonts are often part of the brand, and they are one of the most common reasons a new marketing site feels slow. Each weight is a network request. A family with four weights and italics can stall the first render if it is loaded carelessly.

Limit the shipped weights to what the UI actually uses. Subset the files, use font-display: swap or a close equivalent, and preload only the critical face. If a secondary display font is only used on the homepage heading, do not make every authenticated view pay for it.

If the brand typeface is not licensed for web use, resolve that before development starts. A last-minute system-font fallback will not match the compositions anyone approved.

4. Check Colour Contrast in the Interface, Not Only in the Palette

Brand palettes are chosen for distinctive look and feel. Product UI also has to be readable. Mid-grey text on a tinted background, or a primary button that fails contrast on white, will create accessibility issues and, in some markets, legal ones.

Run the core combinations — body text, links, buttons, alerts, focus states — against WCAG contrast requirements. If a brand colour cannot pass on the backgrounds you plan to use, define a UI-specific variant rather than telling engineers to “make it work”.

Document focus states and error colours as part of the system. They are easy to omit from a branding deck and hard to invent consistently later.

5. Treat the Website as Part of the Brand, Not a Separate Deliverable

Identity, packaging and a website are often commissioned as if they were unrelated. Users experience them as one thing. Layout, motion, image style and page performance are brand decisions, not only engineering ones.

If web design is going to a different team, give them the tokens, the component list and the performance constraints at the same time as the visual files. The brief is practical: component behaviour, and a site that can be implemented without inventing missing states.

6. Inventory Components, Including the Unhappy States

Most brand presentations show the happy path: a perfect hero, a tidy card, a primary button. Production also needs empty states, validation errors, disabled buttons, loading placeholders, and a cookie or consent banner that does not break the layout.

List the components the site or product actually needs, and design the edge cases for each. Engineers should not be guessing how an error message sits on a form, or what happens when a product name wraps onto three lines. This is also why the handoff works better when identity and the front end are designed together, rather than a PDF being thrown over the wall once the logo is approved. A branding and web design studio such as Abnormal is set up for that kind of work.

If you already have a component library, map the new brand to those components instead of inventing a parallel set. Two button styles for the same action is how a design system starts to rot.

7. Specify Assets the Way a Build Pipeline Will Use Them

Hand over SVG icons that are clean, consistently framed and stripped of editor junk. Provide raster images at the sizes they will be displayed, or clearly larger, and say whether they should be cropped. Avoid “logo final FINAL-v7.psd” as the official file.

Include favicon, app icon, social preview and, if relevant, an email header. Name files in a predictable way. If motion is part of the brand, specify duration, easing and what should be reduced for users who prefer reduced motion. A ten-megabyte animation in the header is not a personality trait. It is a performance bug.

A short README in the handoff folder will save a week of Slack questions.

8. Sit With Engineering for the First Build, Not Only the Sign-Off

The first implementation will surface problems no one saw in Figma: a heading measure that is too long in real copy, a colour that vibrates against a photograph, a nav that cannot fit the actual information architecture.

Budget a review on a staging URL, on a phone, and in the browser your users actually use. Change the tokens if you need to, and record the change in the source of truth. A brand system that cannot absorb a small implementation change will be bypassed.

Once the first release is out, agree who can add a one-off colour or type size, and who cannot. The system survives through that rule more than through the original presentation.

The Bottom Line

A brand that has to live in a product needs tokens, tested sizes, readable colour, a realistic component list and assets a build can use. The PDF is a reference, not a deliverable.

If you sort those things out before development starts, the site will look like the identity you approved, and it will still be fast enough to use.

title: Muse Ember now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Ember from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. It is a lightweight reasoning model for the high-volume parts of an agent run, such as coding sub-tasks, tool calls, and document analysis.

Muse Ember handles the bounded tasks agents repeat many times in a single run, like implementing a helper function, calling a tool, or summarizing a document.

The model accepts text, image, and video input with a 1M-token context window, so an agent can pass it code, screenshots, documents, and clips in the same run. Tool calling lets your application feed each result into the next step. Reasoning effort is adjustable from minimal to max.

title: Kong Plugins for Authentication and Traffic Control
description:
Meta description: Secure and throttle your APIs with Kong: key-auth, Basic auth, JWT, ACL, rate limiting, request size limiting and IP restriction.

What you'll learn

  • How plugins work and where they apply
  • Authentication vs authorization
  • Ways to authenticate
  • How to limit traffic fairly

What is a plugin?

A plugin adds behavior to the request/response flow without changing your backend code. You can attach it at different scopes:

Scope Applies to
Global Every request through Kong
Service All routes of one service
Route Only one route
Consumer Only one caller

When scopes overlap, the more specific one wins.

Part 1: Authentication, "who are you?"

Key authentication (key-auth)

The simplest approach. The client sends a secret key in a header.

# 1. Enable on a service
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins --data name=key-auth

# 2. Create a key for the consumer
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/key-auth --data key=asha-secret-key

# 3. Call
curl -i http://localhost:8000/alpha/hello                                # 401
curl -i http://localhost:8000/alpha/hello -H 'apikey: asha-secret-key'   # 200

Without a key, Kong answers 401 and your backend never sees the request.

Basic authentication (basic-auth)

Username and password in the Authorization header. Simple and widely supported, but use it only over HTTPS.

JWT authentication (jwt)

The client sends a signed token: Authorization: Bearer <token>.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins --data name=jwt
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/jwt     # returns key + secret

Kong checks the token's signature with the consumer's secret and checks it hasn't expired. The token's iss claim must equal the consumer's JWT key.

Method Best for
key-auth Simple service-to-service or partner access
basic-auth Quick internal tools (over HTTPS)
jwt User sessions, stateless tokens with expiry

Part 2: Authorization, "what may you do?" (acl)

Authentication identifies the caller. Authorization decides what they can access. Kong's ACL plugin uses groups:

# put the consumer in a group
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/acls --data group=shoppers

# allow only admins on a route
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/routes/alpha-write/plugins \
  --data name=acl --data 'config.allow=admins'

The ACL plugin needs an authentication plugin on the same route, because it has to know who the consumer is.

401 vs 403. 401 means "I don't know who you are". 403 means "I know you, but you may not do this."

Part 3: Traffic control, "how much?"

Rate limiting

Protects your service from abuse and accidental loops.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins \
  --data name=rate-limiting \
  --data config.minute=30 \
  --data config.policy=local

Responses include headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining-Minute. After the limit, Kong returns 429 Too Many Requests.

Which policy?

  • local: counters in each Kong node's memory (fast, but each node counts alone)
  • redis: shared counters across nodes (accurate across a cluster)

You can also attach a rate limit to a consumer, so a premium customer gets 1000/min and a free one gets 30/min.

Request size limiting 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins \
  --data name=request-size-limiting \
  --data config.allowed_payload_size=1 \
  --data config.size_unit=megabytes

Oversized bodies are rejected with 413 before they reach your backend.

IP restriction

Allow or deny by address, handy for admin routes:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/routes/alpha-write/plugins \
  --data name=ip-restriction --data 'config.allow=10.0.0.0/8'

A typical policy for one API

Route Plugins
GET /items auth, group readers or admins
POST /items auth, group admins only
/orders auth, ACL, rate limit 30/min
everything request size limit 1 MB

Common mistakes

  • Adding acl without an authentication plugin.
  • Using rate-limiting with local policy on several Kong nodes and expecting a global total.
  • Committing real secrets and keys to git. Use environment variables or a secret manager.
  • Confusing 401 and 403 when debugging.

Key takeaways

  • Plugins give you security and limits without touching backend code.
  • Authenticate first, authorize second.
  • Rate limits and size limits are cheap protection; set them early.
  • Attach plugins at the narrowest scope that makes sense.

Next: Transformations and observability.

title: Build a Recipe Step Timer in Vanilla JavaScript
description:
Timers look simple until you build one. Use setInterval to count down from 60, and you will find that it drifts, pauses in background tabs and gets messy when you chain several steps.

In this tutorial we will build a recipe step timer: a list of timed cooking steps that run one after another, with a clean countdown. It is a small project, but it teaches a real lesson about timing in the browser.

For example data, we will use a traditional South Indian rasam recipe, which has a few clear timed stages. You do not need to cook anything to follow along.

No framework, no build step. Just HTML and plain JavaScript.

What We Are Building

A page with a list of steps and a Start button. When you press Start, the timer runs the first step, shows the remaining time, then moves to the next step automatically and shows a message when everything is done.

The Sample Data

A rasam has stages with fixed cooking times, such as boiling the tamarind base, simmering the spices, and covering the pot after the tadka. The step-by-step method in this traditional South Indian rasam recipe gives the cooking ranges. We will use rounded values as example data:

js
const steps = [
{ label: "Boil tamarind, tomato, turmeric and salt", minutes: 7 },
{ label: "Simmer with the rasam masala", minutes: 5 },
{ label: "Cover the pot after the tadka", minutes: 1 },
];

These are only demo numbers. The dal water step and the froth signal are not timed here, because they depend on watching the pot.

Step 1: The HTML
html
<!DOCTYPE html>




Recipe Step Timer



Recipe Step Timer

<ol id="step-list"></ol>

<p id="current-label" aria-live="polite"></p>
<p id="countdown" aria-live="off">00:00</p>

<button id="start">Start</button>
<button id="reset" disabled>Reset</button>




Step 2: Pure Helper Functions

We keep the maths in small, pure functions that do not touch the page.

js
function formatTime(totalSeconds) {
const s = Math.max(0, Math.ceil(totalSeconds));
const minutes = Math.floor(s / 60);
const seconds = s % 60;
return ${String(minutes).padStart(2, "0")}:${String(seconds).padStart(2, "0")};
}

function getRemainingSeconds(deadlineMs, nowMs) {
return Math.max(0, (deadlineMs - nowMs) / 1000);
}

function totalMinutes(list) {
return list.reduce((sum, step) => sum + step.minutes, 0);
}
Why Not Count Down by Subtracting 1?

A common beginner approach looks like this:

js
let seconds = 60;
setInterval(() => { seconds -= 1; }, 1000);

The problem is that setInterval is not exact. Browsers can delay it, especially in background tabs, so after a few minutes your timer is wrong.

A safer approach is to store a deadline and recalculate the remaining time on every tick:

js
const deadline = Date.now() + minutes * 60 * 1000;
// on each tick:
const remaining = getRemainingSeconds(deadline, Date.now());

The tick only decides when to redraw. The truth always comes from the clock, so the timer stays correct even if a tick runs late.

Step 3: Wire Up the Page
js
const listEl = document.getElementById("step-list");
const labelEl = document.getElementById("current-label");
const countdownEl = document.getElementById("countdown");
const startBtn = document.getElementById("start");
const resetBtn = document.getElementById("reset");

let timerId = null;

function renderSteps(activeIndex = -1) {
listEl.innerHTML = "";
steps.forEach((step, i) => {
const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = ${step.label} (${step.minutes} min);
if (i === activeIndex) li.style.fontWeight = "bold";
listEl.appendChild(li);
});
}

function runStep(index) {
if (index >= steps.length) {
labelEl.textContent = "All steps done.";
countdownEl.textContent = "00:00";
startBtn.disabled = false;
timerId = null;
return;
}

const step = steps[index];
const deadline = Date.now() + step.minutes * 60 * 1000;

renderSteps(index);
labelEl.textContent = Step ${index + 1} of ${steps.length}: ${step.label};

timerId = setInterval(() => {
const remaining = getRemainingSeconds(deadline, Date.now());
countdownEl.textContent = formatTime(remaining);

if (remaining <= 0) {
  clearInterval(timerId);
  runStep(index + 1);
}

}, 250);
}

startBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
startBtn.disabled = true;
resetBtn.disabled = false;
runStep(0);
});

resetBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
clearInterval(timerId);
timerId = null;
startBtn.disabled = false;
resetBtn.disabled = true;
labelEl.textContent = "";
countdownEl.textContent = "00:00";
renderSteps();
});

renderSteps();

We tick every 250 ms. That is cheap, and it keeps the display from lagging by more than a fraction of a second. We use textContent throughout, so no raw HTML ever gets injected.

Step 4: Test the Helpers

Because the helpers are pure, you can test them without a browser clock:

js
console.log(formatTime(0)); // "00:00"
console.log(formatTime(65)); // "01:05"
console.log(formatTime(419.2)); // "07:00" (rounds up)
console.log(formatTime(-5)); // "00:00"

console.log(getRemainingSeconds(10000, 4000)); // 6
console.log(getRemainingSeconds(10000, 12000)); // 0

console.log(totalMinutes(steps)); // 13

The expected values above come from running this exact code. Rounding up with Math.ceil means the display shows 00:01 until the very last moment, instead of showing 00:00 while a fraction of a second remains.

Step 5: Make It Better
A sound or notification when a step ends. Ask for notification permission before you use it.
Pause and resume. Store the remaining time when pausing, and compute a new deadline when resuming.
Editable steps. Let the user add steps and durations with a small form.
Persist the recipe in localStorage, and wrap JSON.parse in try/catch.
Untimed steps. Add a step type with a “Next” button for stages like “switch off when it froths”.
Common Mistakes
Decrementing a counter in setInterval instead of using a deadline.
Forgetting to call clearInterval before starting the next step, which stacks timers.
Calling runStep(index + 1) before clearing the old interval.
Using innerHTML with user-provided text.
Treating a timer as the only signal. Real cooking also needs your eyes and nose.
A Note on Real Kitchens

A timer helps, but ingredients still matter. If you are cooking rasam for the first time, a ready rasam powder, one of the Indian spice blends made for a single dish, is a handy shortcut. For a faster, weeknight version of the same dish, see this easy South Indian rasam recipe.

If you plan to buy Indian spices or shop for Indian spices online, look for a full ingredients list, packed-on and best-before dates, and clear seller details. These checks tell you more about authentic Indian spices than any slogan. When you order Indian spices, small packs are easier to finish while they are fresh, and the best Indian spices for a dish like rasam are simply the ones that still smell fragrant when you open them.

FAQ

Why use a deadline instead of counting down?
setInterval can run late, especially in background tabs. A deadline based on Date.now() keeps the display correct no matter how late a tick runs.

Why 250 ms for the interval?
It is frequent enough to feel smooth, and cheap enough not to matter. You can use 1000 ms if you prefer, but the display may lag slightly.

Will it keep running in a background tab?
Browsers may throttle timers in background tabs, but because we use a deadline, the time shown is still correct when the tab comes back.

Can I use it for other recipes?
Yes. Change the steps array, and the rest of the code works as it is.

Should I use a library?
For this size of project, plain JavaScript is simpler and teaches you how timers really behave.

Wrapping Up

In about 70 lines, we built a recipe step timer with drift-safe timing, chained steps and testable helper functions. It is a small project, but it covers Date.now(), setInterval, clearInterval, DOM updates and pure functions.

If you build it, tell me which feature you would add first.

title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.34398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

title: Popular Windows programs hacked to secretly install software
description:
Compromised installers for Q-Dir and DesktopOK distributed a Python-based remote access trojan while executing genuine, digitally signed binaries.

ASEC analysis details how the setup fetched secondary payloads, established scheduled tasks, and evaded security tools.

How did the trap work?

Specifically, the malicious installers for the Q-Dir and DesktopOK tools were found. When someone downloaded and ran these versions, the program appeared to work normally and opened on the screen without any indication that anything was wrong. However, in the background, it secretly downloaded and installed a remote control program.

The threat affected both those who downloaded the programs for the first time and those who upgraded previous installations they already had on their computers. Researchers from the AhnLab research center (ASEC) identified the problem and published their findings on November 26, 2026.

The official applications contained in the installation packages had the normal, valid digital signature of their creator, which made the files appear completely trustworthy. The corrupted installers included versions 12.85.0.0, 12.84.0.0 and 12.83.0.0 of Q-Dir, as well as versions 12.85.0.0 and 12.82.0.0 of DesktopOK.

What could the hidden program do?

When the additional program was installed on the computer, it allowed third parties to execute commands, transfer files, take screenshots, and gather detailed system information. To stay active, the program created automated tasks in Windows, while also monitoring which security and protection applications were running on the computer.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Cyber ​​Attacks & Data Breaches

In a second test of Streamer, Defender recorded 659 non-notification events in the files examined

↗

So far, researchers have not been able to pinpoint exactly how the files were replaced on the official source nor have they attributed responsibility to any specific group, although comments in Chinese were found in the files.

What should those who have installed them do?

Experts recommend that users completely uninstall these programs, download the latest and verified version from the official source, check the digital fingerprints of the files, and look for any unknown scheduled tasks or unwanted connections on their computers.
