title: Spectral Optimal Transport for Dynamics-Aware Sign Language Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.33818v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this issue, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: PGKeeper: Building the bouncer we needed for Postgres
description: This is the story of why and how we built PGKeeper, a scalable and reliable service to support Figma’s rapidly growing products and database workload.

title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
description:
arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.

title: webhook-relay: receive webhooks on a server, handle them on your laptop
description:
Webhooks are awkward to develop against. The sender, whether it is a payment provider, GitHub or a chat platform, needs a public URL to call. Your handler runs on localhost:3000, behind a home router. The usual answer is a tunnelling service, which gives your laptop a public address for a while.

A tunnel gets the request to your machine, and then it is gone. If your handler crashed on it, you have to trigger the event again on the sender's side, which can mean making another test payment or pushing another commit. If two deliveries behaved differently, you compare them by scrolling through logs. And if your laptop was closed when the webhook fired, the delivery simply failed.

webhook-relay is a self-hosted alternative to tunnelling services, built for webhook development. A small server on a public machine receives the webhooks, records every one, and relays them over a websocket to a CLI on your laptop, which calls your local app. Because every request is stored, you can look at it later, replay it after fixing your handler, and diff two deliveries to see what changed.

Stripe/GitHub/… ──POST──► relay-server /h/stripe ══websocket══► relay (CLI) ──► http://localhost:3000
                               │  stores every request                          (your app)
                               └─ inspector UI: list, detail, replay, diff

What it does

Capture first. The endpoint /h/{channel}/{rest...} reads the body up to a limit, strips hop-by-hop headers, and stores the request in SQLite before doing anything else. A delivery is never lost, even when no client is listening. In that case the sender gets 202 Accepted with the request ID, and the request waits in the inspector.

Relay with the real response. Each channel has at most one connected client, and a newer client replaces the older one. The server sends a JSON request frame over the websocket with a random correlation ID, then waits for the matching response frame or the timeout. The response from your local app goes back to the sender, so signature checks and status-code retries behave as they would in production.

Paths are kept. Anything after the channel name is preserved: /h/stripe/v1/events?x=1 arrives at http://localhost:3000/v1/events?x=1.

Failure is visible. If the local target is unreachable, the sender gets a 502 and the error is stored with the request. The client performs the local HTTP calls concurrently, so one slow handler does not block the others.

A connection that stays up. The server pings every 25 seconds to keep proxies from dropping the websocket. The client reconnects with exponential backoff, but it stops on 401 or 403, because a bad token will not fix itself.

Inspector. Server-rendered html/template pages embedded in the binary, with no JavaScript. You get a list per channel and a detail page per request. Replay re-sends a stored request as a new request linked to the original. Diff renders both requests as text (request line, sorted headers, pretty-printed JSON body) and shows a line diff computed with LCS.

JSON API. GET /api/channels/{c}/requests, GET /api/requests/{id} and POST /api/requests/{id}/replay, with a Bearer token.

Storage. The pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite driver, with no cgo, in WAL mode with one connection. Old requests are pruned per channel on insert.

How to use it

Install both binaries with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/webhook-relay/cmd/...@latest

The README also lists prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64 and arm64) on the GitHub releases page. Each archive contains relay-server and relay, and checksums.txt has the SHA-256 sums.

On a server with a public URL, build and start the relay server:

go build -o relay-server ./cmd/relay-server
RELAY_TOKEN=change-me ./relay-server -addr :8080 -db relay.db

On your machine, start the client and point it at your local app:

go build -o relay ./cmd/relay
RELAY_TOKEN=change-me ./relay -server https://relay.example.com -channel stripe -to http://localhost:3000

Then set the webhook URL on the sender's side to https://relay.example.com/h/stripe. The inspector is at https://relay.example.com/, behind HTTP Basic auth: any user name, the token as password.

The server has five flags:

flag default meaning
-addr :8080 listen address (put TLS in front, for example Caddy or nginx)
-db relay.db SQLite file
-keep 500 requests kept per channel
-max-body 1048576 bytes stored and forwarded per request
-timeout 25s how long a webhook waits for your local answer

RELAY_TOKEN protects the websocket, the inspector and the JSON API. The /h/… endpoints are public by design, since the sender has to be able to reach them without your token.

A typical session then goes like this. The provider sends an event and your handler returns a 500. You open the inspector, read the stored headers and body, fix the code, and press Replay. The same request goes through the relay again, and you never have to trigger a new event on the sender's side. If a later delivery behaves differently, Diff shows which headers or JSON fields changed between the two.

Things to know

  • One client per channel. There is no fan-out to several developers. A second client on the same channel replaces the first, so give each developer their own channel name.
  • A single shared token. There are no per-channel credentials and no user accounts.
  • Bodies are capped. A body over -max-body is truncated when stored and when forwarded. Streaming and very large payloads are not supported.
  • It is for webhooks, not general tunnelling. Websocket passthrough is not supported.
  • Single instance. The server keeps waiting clients in memory. Scaling horizontally would need a shared pub/sub.
  • No TLS termination built in. Run it behind a reverse proxy.
  • The UI shows the latest 200 requests per channel. There is no pagination beyond that.
  • What was tested. go test -race ./... includes end-to-end tests that start the relay server and a real client over a websocket in-process, with an httptest server acting as the local app. They cover forwarding (method, path, query, headers, body, status, response headers), storing while no client is connected and then replaying, Bearer and Basic auth, the client giving up on a bad token, invalid channel names, the 502 when the target is down, the inspector pages including the diff output and the replay redirect, and a newer client replacing an older one. There are also unit tests for the store (pruning, round trips) and for the diff.

Why I built it

A generic tunnel solves reachability, and reachability is only the first problem in webhook work. The problems that take the time come after it: reproducing a delivery, understanding why two deliveries differ, and not losing an event that arrived while nothing was listening.

All three have the same answer, which is to keep the request. Once every delivery is stored before anything else happens, replay and diff are small features on top of it, and a closed laptop turns from a failed delivery into a pending one.

Hosting it yourself is the second half of the idea. Webhook payloads can contain customer and payment data, and with this tool they stay in a SQLite file on a server you control. The pieces are deliberately few: one server binary, one client binary, one token, and no JavaScript in the inspector.

Sending the local app's real response back to the sender was also important. A relay that always answers 200 hides bugs, because the sender never retries and a signature failure looks like a success.

Get the code

The server, the client, the inspector and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/webhook-relay. It is MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: From Monitoring Alerts to IT Actions: A Practical Guide to Closing the Loop
description:
A monitoring alert is only useful if it changes what someone does next.

A dashboard can show a full fleet's CPU, disk, and security events and still leave an operator with the same question: "What should I do about this?" The gap isn't a lack of data. It's the missing path from signal to decision.

We think monitoring should be designed around that path. In this article, we'll turn a few common signals into practical, testable actions - and show how to avoid building an alert system that creates more work than it removes.

Start with the decision, not the metric

A metric is not actionable just because it crosses a threshold. "Disk usage is 85%" is a fact. It doesn't say whether the disk is filling steadily, whether a temporary job caused the spike, or who should respond.

Before adding a monitor, write down the decision it should support:

  • What condition is the monitor detecting?
  • What user or service impact could follow?
  • Who owns the response?
  • What is the first safe action?
  • When should the issue be escalated?

If the team can't answer those questions, keep collecting the metric, but don't page on it yet. An unowned alert is a notification with nowhere to go.

Turn a threshold into context

Thresholds are useful for catching immediate risk. Trends are what help distinguish an incident from normal variation.

For example, 85% disk use can mean very different things:

  • A stable volume has been at 85% for months and has enough headroom.
  • A volume has moved from 70% to 85% in a week.
  • A volume grew 2% in the last hour and is still climbing.

The same point-in-time value calls for different responses. Add rate of change, a comparison window, or a known operating baseline where it changes the decision.

A simple rule can estimate time to exhaustion from recent measurements. This Python example assumes the readings are evenly spaced and expressed as percentages:

from collections import deque
from statistics import mean

# (minutes since start, disk usage percent)
readings = deque([
    (0, 72.0),
    (60, 73.0),
    (120, 75.0),
    (180, 78.0),
], maxlen=12)

def estimate_minutes_to_full(samples, limit=95.0):
    if len(samples) < 2:
        return None

    elapsed = samples[-1][0] - samples[0][0]
    if elapsed <= 0:
        return None

    # Percentage points per minute, averaged across the window.
    rate = (samples[-1][1] - samples[0][1]) / elapsed
    if rate <= 0:
        return None

    remaining = limit - samples[-1][1]
    return max(0, round(remaining / rate))

minutes = estimate_minutes_to_full(readings)
if minutes is not None and minutes < 24 * 60:
    print(f"Investigate disk growth: estimated {minutes} minutes to 95%")

This is a starting point, not a forecasting system. A short window can overreact to a backup or deployment, while a long window can hide a sudden change. In production, calculate on a rolling window, account for missing samples, and make the threshold depend on the volume's role.

Give every alert an owner and a first move

An alert should carry enough information to begin triage without a second round of detective work. At minimum, include the affected host or service, the observed value, the time window, severity, owner, and a runbook or first check.

For instance, this configuration describes a monitor in terms of response, not just measurement:

name: disk-growth-risk
scope: customer-host
condition:
  metric: disk.used_percent
  above: 80
  duration: 15m
  trend:
    minimum_growth_percent_per_hour: 1.5
severity: warning
owner: platform-operations
summary: "Disk usage is high and growing on {{ host }}"
first_action: "Check largest directories and recent scheduled jobs"
runbook: "https://docs.example.net/runbooks/disk-growth"
maintenance_silence: true

The exact schema depends on your monitoring stack. The important part is that an operator shouldn't have to infer whether this is urgent, who owns it, or where to start.

Severity should reflect response urgency and impact, not how dramatic a metric looks. A warning that can wait until the next shift is different from a condition that risks taking a customer-facing service offline in minutes.

Use fleet data to find patterns, then scope the response

A fleet-level view is good for spotting patterns: many endpoints reporting the same failure, a patch-related change affecting one OS version, or one customer's machines drifting from their usual baseline. But remediation must stay scoped to the right account and host.

That distinction matters especially in multi-tenant operations. A query that aggregates fleet health can help identify a shared issue, but the action that follows should target only the authorized customer's devices. We built LynxTrac's monitoring and security views around customer-scoped access for this reason: operators need cross-device context without crossing customer boundaries.

A safe workflow looks like this:

  1. Detect a pattern across the authorized fleet or customer scope.
  2. Confirm whether the affected hosts share a relevant property, such as OS version or recent change.
  3. Choose a limited set of hosts for investigation or remediation.
  4. Record the operator, target, timestamp, and outcome.
  5. Verify that the signal changed after the action.

For security findings, keep the evidence attached to the response. File changes, configuration assessment results, and alerts mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics can help an operator understand whether an event is isolated or part of a broader pattern. A flat event list is harder to turn into a defensible decision.

Measure whether monitoring is helping

The number of monitors says very little about operational quality. We'd rather track a small set of measures that reveal whether signals lead to useful work:

  • Alert-to-incident ratio: How many alerts become real incidents rather than being dismissed?
  • MTTA and MTTR: Are the right people acknowledging and resolving issues promptly?
  • Owner coverage: What share of alerts has a named responder?
  • Agent coverage: What share of the managed fleet is reporting current data?
  • Remediation outcome: Did the action resolve the condition, or did it recur?

These measures need context. A falling alert count could mean better signal quality, or it could mean monitoring stopped reporting. Pair operational metrics with coverage and review them over time, not as a single weekly score.

A practical cadence is a short weekly review. Look at the alerts that were dismissed, repeated, or lacked an owner. Remove rules that don't lead to a decision, and improve the ones that produce avoidable investigation. Don't add a new dashboard panel until you know which operational question it answers.

Monitoring is a feedback loop

The useful loop is straightforward: observe a signal, interpret it in context, take a bounded action, and verify the result. If the action doesn't change the condition, or if the alert keeps recurring, the monitoring design needs another look.

That's why we see monitoring as more than a live graph or notification. It should connect infrastructure health, endpoint inventory, security context, access controls, and an auditable record of what happened. The tools can vary; the operational test is whether the next step is clear and safe.

A good starting point is to choose three alerts your team sees every week and ask: who owns each one, what decision does it support, and how do we know the response worked? Which signal in your environment still produces more investigation than action?

title: Veri temiz odasını kodla düşünmek: Normalizasyon, anahtarlı özet, sorgu izin listesi ve asgari küme eşiği
description:
Bir konut geliştiricisi ile bir banka aynı soruyu sorar: "Bizim lead listemizdeki kişilerden kaçı sizin konut kredisi ön onaylı müşteriniz?" Soru masum görünür ama cevaplamanın en kolay yolu, yani iki tarafın Excel dosyalarını birbirine e-postayla göndermesi, kişisel veriyi amacı dışında başka bir şirkete aktarmak demektir. Veri temiz odası (data clean room) bu yüzden vardır: iki taraf ham kayıtları birbirine göstermeden yalnızca üzerinde anlaştıkları toplu sonuçları görür. Ben Koray Yalçın; gayrimenkul projelerinde lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi ve ölçüm altyapıları kurarken bu tür iş birliği taleplerinin genellikle "hash'leyip gönderelim" cümlesiyle başladığını ve tam orada yanlış yola saptığını gördüm.

Kavramın tanımı ve iş tarafındaki kullanımı için Data Clean Room nedir? sayfasına bakabilirsiniz. Bu yazıda konuyu bir geliştiricinin gözünden ele alıyorum: hazır bir temiz oda ürünü kullansanız da kendi küçük kurulumunuzu yapsanız da doğru olması gereken dört katman var. Eşleştirme anahtarının normalizasyonu, anahtarın nasıl gizleneceği, hangi sorguların çalışabileceği ve sonucun ne zaman gösterilmeyeceği. Örnekler Python ve PostgreSQL ile yazıldı. Bu yazı hukuki görüş değildir; KVKK ve GDPR açısından aktarımın dayanağını, aydınlatma metnini ve sözleşmeyi hukuk ekibinizle netleştirmeniz gerekir.

"Hash'leyip gönderelim" neden yetmez?

En sık önerilen çözüm şudur: iki taraf da e-posta ve telefonları SHA-256 ile özetler, özet listelerini birbirine gönderir, kesişimi sayar. Sorun, telefon numarasının çok küçük bir uzay olmasıdır. Türkiye'deki cep telefonu numaralarının olası kombinasyon sayısı, sıradan bir dizüstü bilgisayarın makul sürede tamamını özetleyip bir sözlük çıkarmasına yetecek kadar küçüktür. Yani tuzsuz SHA-256 ile özetlenmiş bir telefon listesi, karşı taraf isterse geri çevrilebilir bir listedir. E-posta için uzay daha büyüktür ama karşı tarafın zaten elinde olan milyonlarca e-postayı özetleyip eşleştirmesi de aynı anlama gelir: siz listeyi "anonim" sanarsınız, karşı taraf kendi müşterisi olmayan kişileri bile tanıyabilir.

Bu yüzden ilk ilke şu: özet, tek başına gizlilik sağlamaz; yalnızca ham değerin ekranda dolaşmasını engeller. Gizlilik, kimin hangi anahtarla özet üretebildiğine ve sonuçta neyin görülebildiğine bağlıdır.

Birinci katman: normalizasyon her iki tarafta aynı kod olmalı

Eşleşme oranının düşük çıkmasının en yaygın nedeni teknik bir gizlilik meselesi değil, biçim farkıdır. Bir tarafta "0532 123 45 67", diğer tarafta "+905321234567" yazıyorsa özetleri asla eşleşmez. E-postada büyük harf, baştaki ve sondaki boşluklar, Türkçe karakterli büyük-küçük harf dönüşümü aynı sorunu yaratır.

Benim tercihim normalizasyonu bir kütüphane fonksiyonu olarak yazıp iki tarafa da aynı sürümü vermek ve sürüm numarasını her çıktıya eklemektir:

import re
import unicodedata

NORMALIZER_VERSION = "2026-11-v1"

def normalize_email(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", raw).strip()
    # Türkçe 'İ' -> 'i̇' sorununu önlemek için önce ASCII dışı büyük harfleri ele al
    s = s.replace("İ", "i").replace("I", "i").lower()
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}", s):
        return None
    return s

def normalize_phone_tr(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", raw)
    if digits.startswith("00"):
        digits = digits[2:]
    if digits.startswith("0") and len(digits) == 11:
        digits = "90" + digits[1:]
    if len(digits) == 10 and digits.startswith("5"):
        digits = "90" + digits
    if not re.fullmatch(r"905\d{9}", digits):
        return None  # yurt dışı numaralar ayrı kurala tabi, burada eşleştirmeye almıyoruz
    return "+" + digits

Burada iki bilinçli karar var. Birincisi, geçersiz değer None döner ve eşleştirmeye girmez; "en yakın tahmin" ile yanlış bir kişiyle eşleşmek, eşleşmemekten daha kötüdür. İkincisi, yurt dışı numaralar bu sürümde dışarıda bırakılmıştır. Kıbrıs gibi çok uluslu alıcı kitlesi olan projelerde bu kural genişletilmelidir, ama genişletme yeni bir sürüm numarasıyla yapılmalı ki iki tarafın farklı kurallarla özet üretip "eşleşme düştü" diye şaşırması önlensin.

Normalizasyon fonksiyonunun birim testleri de iki tarafla paylaşılmalı. Ben test dosyasına gerçek veri değil, uydurma örnek biçimler koyarım: boşluklu, tireli, ülke kodlu, başında sıfır olan, eksik haneli.

İkinci katman: anahtarlı özet ve anahtarın sahibi

Tuzsuz özetin sorununu çözmenin pratik yolu, özeti HMAC gibi gizli bir anahtarla üretmektir. Anahtarı bilmeyen biri sözlük saldırısı yapamaz. Ama burada kritik soru şudur: anahtarı kim tutuyor?

Eğer anahtarı iki taraf da biliyorsa, her biri diğerinin listesini kendi ham verisiyle yeniden özetleyip eşleştirebilir; yani yine kişi düzeyinde kesişim öğrenilir. Temiz oda mantığında anahtar, iki tarafın da doğrudan erişemediği bir ortamda durur: ya güvenilir üçüncü taraf bir platformda, ya da iki tarafın ortak denetlediği ayrı bir hesapta, erişimi kayıt altına alınan bir anahtar yönetim servisinde.

import hmac
import hashlib

def keyed_token(value: str, key: bytes, purpose: str) -> str:
    # purpose: 'email' veya 'phone'; aynı değerin iki alanda aynı jetonu üretmesini engeller
    msg = f"{purpose}:{NORMALIZER_VERSION}:{value}".encode("utf-8")
    return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def tokenize_row(row: dict, key: bytes) -> dict:
    email = normalize_email(row.get("email"))
    phone = normalize_phone_tr(row.get("phone"))
    return {
        "email_token": keyed_token(email, key, "email") if email else None,
        "phone_token": keyed_token(phone, key, "phone") if phone else None,
        "segment": row.get("segment"),        # toplu kırılım için izinli alan
        "created_month": row.get("created_month"),
        "normalizer_version": NORMALIZER_VERSION,
    }

Bu fonksiyon iki tarafın kendi sisteminde değil, temiz odanın içinde çalışmalıdır. Taraflar normalleştirilmiş veriyi şifreli kanalla odaya yükler, oda jetonu üretir ve ham değeri hemen siler. Pratikte bu, yükleme sonrası ham sütunların tutulmadığı, yalnızca jeton tablosunun kaldığı bir iş akışı demektir.

Bir not daha: aynı anahtarı her proje için kullanmayın. Her iş birliği, hatta her kampanya dönemi için ayrı anahtar, jetonların başka bir bağlamda birleştirilmesini zorlaştırır. Anahtar döndürüldüğünde eski jeton tabloları da imha edilmelidir.

Üçüncü katman: sorgular izin listesinden çalışır

Temiz odanın veri ambarından farkı, içeride serbest SQL yazılamamasıdır. "Kaç kişi eşleşti?" sorusuna izin verip "eşleşen kişilerin jetonlarını listele" sorusuna izin vermemek gerekir. Bunu en sade biçimde, onaylanmış sorgu şablonlarını bir tabloda tutarak ve kullanıcıların yalnızca parametre gönderebilmesini sağlayarak yaparım:

CREATE TABLE approved_query (
    query_key       text PRIMARY KEY,           -- 'overlap_by_segment'
    version         int  NOT NULL,
    sql_template    text NOT NULL,              -- parametreli, sabit metin
    allowed_params  jsonb NOT NULL,             -- {"created_month": "yyyy-mm"}
    min_group_size  int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 50,
    approved_by     text NOT NULL,              -- iki tarafın onayı
    approved_at     timestamptz NOT NULL
);

-- Örnek şablon: segment bazlı kesişim sayısı
-- Not: sonuç satır düzeyinde jeton içermez, yalnızca sayım döner
SELECT d.segment,
       count(DISTINCT d.person_token) AS overlap_count
FROM   developer_tokens d
JOIN   bank_tokens b
  ON  (d.phone_token = b.phone_token OR d.email_token = b.email_token)
WHERE  d.created_month = $1
GROUP  BY d.segment;

Buradaki OR eşleşmesi bilinçli bir tercihtir ama aynı kişiyi hem telefon hem e-posta üzerinden iki kez sayma riskini doğurur. Bu yüzden her tarafta önce kişi düzeyinde tek satıra indirgeme (deduplication) yapılır, odada her kişiye bir person_token verilir ve sayım count(DISTINCT ...) ile yapılır. Bu ayrıntı şablon onaylanırken konuşulması gereken türdendir; yani şablonun kendisi de bir kod incelemesinden geçer.

min_group_size değeri bilerek tabloya yazılmıştır. 50 burada örnek değerdir; doğru eşik, veri setinin büyüklüğüne ve iki tarafın risk değerlendirmesine göre belirlenir.

Dördüncü katman: küçük kümeyi gösterme

Toplu sayım bile yeterince dar bir kırılımda kişiyi ele verebilir. "Mağusa'daki 4+1 villa segmentinde, Kasım ayında oluşturulan ve bankanın ön onaylı müşterisi olan kişi sayısı: 2" sonucu, küçük bir projede kimin kim olduğunu tahmin etmeye yetebilir. Bu yüzden sorgu sonucu kullanıcıya dönmeden önce bir eşik kontrolünden geçer:

def apply_threshold(rows: list[dict], min_group: int) -> list[dict]:
    safe = []
    suppressed = 0
    for r in rows:
        if r["overlap_count"] < min_group:
            suppressed += 1
            safe.append({"segment": r["segment"], "overlap_count": None,
                         "note": "eşik altı, gösterilmedi"})
        else:
            safe.append(r)
    # Toplam satır, bastırılan hücrelerin farkla hesaplanmasını engellemek için verilmez
    return safe

Eşik tek başına yeterli değildir; çünkü aynı sorguyu bir kez "tüm segmentler", bir kez "küçük segment hariç" diye çalıştırıp farkı alarak bastırılmış hücre geri hesaplanabilir. Buna fark saldırısı denir. Benim uyguladığım üç önlem şunlar: kırılım alanları sabit bir listeden seçilir, aynı parametreyle tekrar eden sorgular sayılır ve sınırlanır, toplam satırı ancak tüm hücreler eşik üstündeyse döner. Daha ileri kurulumlarda sonuçlara kontrollü gürültü eklenir (diferansiyel gizlilik); ama bu, iş tarafının "sayılar tam tutmuyor" itirazını önceden konuşmayı gerektirir.

Denetim kaydı: kim, neyi, ne zaman sordu?

Temiz odada her sorgu çalıştırması bir satır olarak yazılır. Bu kayıt hem iki tarafın birbirine güven duymasını sağlar hem de bir veri sahibinin "verim nerede kullanıldı?" sorusuna cevap vermeyi kolaylaştırır.

CREATE TABLE query_run_log (
    run_id         uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    query_key      text NOT NULL,
    query_version  int  NOT NULL,
    params         jsonb NOT NULL,
    requested_by   text NOT NULL,
    requested_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    rows_returned  int  NOT NULL,
    rows_suppressed int NOT NULL
);

Ben bu tabloyu yalnızca ekleme yapılabilen (güncelleme ve silme yetkisi verilmeyen) bir rolle yazarım. Haftalık bir kontrol, aynı parametrelerin olağandışı sık sorgulanıp sorgulanmadığına bakar.

Gayrimenkul tarafında somut bir kullanım

Bir lansman projesini düşünelim (örnek senaryo, varsayımsaldır). Geliştirici, son üç ayda Meta ve Google reklamlarından gelen lead'lerini, banka da konut kredisi başvurusu yapmış müşterilerini temiz odaya yükler. Onaylı şablon, lead'leri kaynak kanal ve bütçe segmentine göre kırar ve her hücre için "bankada aktif başvurusu olan" kişi sayısını döner.

Bu sonuçla geliştirici, hangi kampanyanın finansmana yakın kişiler getirdiğini toplu düzeyde görür; banka, hangi proje bölgesinde kredi talebinin yoğunlaştığını öğrenir. Hiçbir taraf diğerinin müşteri listesini almaz. Kişi düzeyinde bir eylem gerekiyorsa, örneğin kredi ön onay teklifi göndermek, bu temiz odanın işi değildir; o kişinin ayrı ve açık rızasıyla yürütülmesi gereken başka bir süreçtir. Benim kurulumlarda en çok dikkat ettiğim çizgi budur: temiz oda analiz içindir, hedefleme listesi üretmek için değil.

Kurulumdan önce kontrol listesi

Kod yazmaya başlamadan önce şu sorulara yazılı cevap almayı alışkanlık haline getirdim:

  • Eşleştirme anahtarları neler, hangi normalizasyon sürümü kullanılacak?
  • Özet anahtarını kim tutuyor, kim erişebiliyor, ne zaman döndürülecek?
  • Hangi sorgu şablonları onaylı, kırılım alanları hangi sabit listeden seçiliyor?
  • Asgari küme eşiği kaç, fark saldırısına karşı hangi sınırlar var?
  • Ham veri ne zaman siliniyor, jeton tabloları ne kadar saklanıyor?
  • Sonuçlar hangi amaçla kullanılabilir, hangi amaçla kullanılamaz?

Bu listenin son maddesi teknik değil gibi görünür ama sistemin tasarımını en çok etkileyen maddedir. Amaç "toplu ölçüm" ise kişi düzeyinde çıktı veren hiçbir yol açık bırakılmamalıdır.

SSS

Veri temiz odası için mutlaka büyük bir platformun ürününü mü kullanmak gerekir?
Hayır. Reklam platformlarının ve bulut veri ambarlarının hazır çözümleri işinizi hızlandırır, ama ilkeler aynıdır: aynı normalizasyon, anahtarı tarafların doğrudan tutmadığı özet, onaylı sorgu şablonları, asgari küme eşiği ve denetim kaydı. Küçük bir iş birliğinde bunları ayrı bir veritabanı hesabında da kurabilirsiniz.

SHA-256 ile özetlemek KVKK açısından veriyi anonim yapar mı?
Genellikle hayır. Geri çevrilebilir ya da başka veriyle eşleştirilebilir özetler kişisel veri niteliğini kaybetmeyebilir. Bu konuda kesin değerlendirmeyi hukuk ekibiniz yapmalı; teknik tarafta yapabileceğiniz, tuzsuz özet yerine anahtarlı özet kullanmak ve anahtarı taraflardan ayrı tutmaktır.

Eşleşme oranı beklenenden düşük çıkarsa ilk neye bakmalıyım?
Önce normalizasyon sürümüne. İki tarafın aynı sürümü kullandığını, telefon biçiminin ülke kodu dahil aynı olduğunu ve geçersiz değerlerin oranını kontrol edin. Ardından iki listenin zaman aralığının gerçekten örtüştüğüne bakın.

Asgari küme eşiğini nasıl seçmeliyim?
Tek doğru sayı yoktur. Veri setinin büyüklüğü, kırılımların ne kadar dar olduğu ve sonuçların kimlerle paylaşılacağı belirleyicidir. Eşiği şablon onayında iki tarafın yazılı olarak kabul etmesi ve tabloda sürümlü tutulması önemlidir.

Temiz oda sonucunu reklam hedeflemesi için kullanabilir miyim?
Toplu sonuçla kampanya bütçesi veya kanal kararı vermek, temiz odanın tipik kullanımıdır. Eşleşen kişilerden bir hedef kitle listesi çıkarmak ise farklı bir veri işleme amacıdır ve ayrı bir hukuki dayanak ile ayrı bir teknik akış gerektirir.

Bu yapı CRM'e nasıl bağlanır?
CRM, temiz odaya yalnızca gerekli alanları (normalleştirilmiş anahtar, izinli kırılım alanları, dönem) aktaran bir dışa aktarma işini besler. Temiz odadan CRM'e kişi düzeyinde veri geri akmaz; yalnızca toplu rapor değerleri, örneğin kampanya bazında eşleşme oranı, raporlama tablosuna yazılabilir.

title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.

title: Your Grant Auditor Can Ask About Your AI Agent Years From Now. Can You Answer?
description:
A how-to for compliance-heavy European organisations that run on public money: universities, research institutes, public hospitals, municipalities, agencies, NGOs and companies in EU-funded consortia.

If your organisation depends on government or EU funding, you already live with a particular kind of accountability. Every euro has conditions. Every claim needs evidence. Auditors can arrive long after the work is done, and what they find can be extended to other grants and recovered with money you may have already spent.

Now add AI agents. They draft cost statements, classify expenses, answer citizens, triage applications, prepare reports and pull data from systems of record. Each of those tasks touches an obligation. And a year or three later, an auditor, a funder, a regulator or a citizen asks the same simple question: how was this decided, and can you show us?

This guide explains why publicly funded organisations face that question earlier and harder than most, how to map agent work to the obligations it touches, and how to build the record that lets you answer. It closes with a 30 day plan.

A note on scope. This is general information, not legal or audit advice. Funding rules differ by programme and member state, so check your grant agreement, national rules and your own legal and audit advisers. The case is an illustrative composite with invented names. Parameter names in code are illustrative. ZizkaDB records events and shows whether the record has been altered. It does not decide eligibility, make a system compliant or replace your audit function.

Why funded organisations are different

Four features set publicly funded bodies apart.

  1. Your costs are conditional. Funding is paid against rules on what counts as an eligible cost. If a cost is later found ineligible, it can be recovered. Under the Horizon Europe model grant agreement, beneficiaries must keep records and supporting documents to confirm proper use of funds and the costs claimed, and a published guide summarising the rules says records must be kept for five years after the final payment for grants over 60,000 euros, or three years for grants of 60,000 euros or less. A national contact point for Horizon Europe adds that the period can be longer in case of ongoing audits or national requirements. Other EU programmes and national funders have their own conditions, so check yours.

  2. Many bodies can audit you, and findings can travel. The model grant agreement includes provisions for checks, reviews and audits, including by OLAF, the European Public Prosecutor's Office and the European Court of Auditors, and a clause on the consequences of audits that deals with extension of findings. In plain terms, a weakness found in one project can prompt questions about others that used the same process. An agent that applied the same classification rule across thirty grants is one finding multiplied by thirty.

  3. Public-law rules on AI apply to you directly. The EU AI Act asks deployers of certain high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before use, and to notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Deployers of high-risk systems must also keep the logs the system generates, where under their control, for at least six months. The Digital Omnibus moved the application date for Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, so check the final text and your timeline. Which of your systems count as high-risk depends on what they do, and that includes systems used to assess eligibility for public benefits and services.

  4. Cyber and incident rules are stricter for public bodies. Under NIS2, public administration entities of central governments are essential entities, regional ones are covered on a risk basis, and member states may extend coverage to local governments. A significant incident triggers an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. If an agent is involved in an incident, you need to reconstruct what it did quickly.

Add to this the usual public-sector layer: data protection law, public procurement rules, freedom of information duties in many countries, and the expectation that public money is spent transparently. The result is an organisation that is asked to prove its decisions more often than almost any other.

The case: the research office and the cost classification agent

This is a composite, with invented names. A university research office, call it Northfield University, uses an AI agent to prepare the cost statements for dozens of EU and national grants. The agent reads time records, invoices and payroll extracts, classifies each item against the cost categories in each grant agreement, and drafts the periodic financial report. A research accountant reviews a sample before submission.

Year one. The agent classifies a recurring item, a shared equipment service contract, as a direct eligible cost for twelve projects. A prompt update in month five changes how it reads certain invoice descriptions. Staff turnover follows. The accountant who set up the review sample leaves.

Year three. After final payment, a funder audit selects one of the projects. The auditor asks about the service contract cost: why was it classified as direct eligible, which version of the grant rules was applied, what evidence supported it, who verified it, and was the same treatment applied elsewhere?

What Northfield has. The final report, the invoices and some application logs. The logs show the output, not the reasoning inputs. The prompt version in force that month is unclear. The reviewer has left. The agent's classification of the same item in other projects cannot be listed without re-running the whole year.

What the auditor does. Finds the cost ineligible in this project, and asks whether the treatment applies to other grants. The university spends weeks reconstructing, and the answers are partly guesses. Recovery is demanded on the one project, and the finding is extended to the others.

None of this requires fraud. It requires only that nobody could show how the decision was made.

What an auditor, funder or regulator will ask
What source documents did the agent use for this item?
Which version of the grant rules and which cost category definitions applied?
Why was it classified this way?
Who verified it, what did they see and when?
Which model, prompt and configuration were in force?
How many other items and projects were treated the same way?
Has the record been altered since?
Can you produce it for the full retention period?
Why ordinary logs fail the funded organisation
They rotate long before the retention period ends, which can be five years or more after final payment.
They record outputs, not the sources, rules and versions behind them.
They cannot list everything affected by one faulty rule.
They do not show who reviewed what.
They can be edited, and an auditor's first question about any record is whether it is original.
They sit in vendor systems you may no longer have access to when the audit arrives.
Step 1: map agent work to obligations

Start with a register, not with technology. List every task an agent performs, and for each one record which obligation it touches.

Agent task Obligation touched Evidence needed later
Classify costs against grant categories Eligibility of costs, record keeping, audit Source docs, rule version, classification, reviewer
Draft periodic technical or financial reports Reporting accuracy Inputs, draft, edits, approver
Answer citizen or applicant questions Duty of care, transparency Question, sources used, answer, handoff
Triage applications or benefits Fundamental rights, non-discrimination, explanation Inputs, criteria, outcome, human review
Draft procurement documents Procurement rules Sources, changes, approver
Handle incidents or alerts NIS2 reporting, security Timeline, actions, evidence

For every row, name an owner. A task without an owner will not have evidence.

Step 2: record decisions as linked chains tied to the funding context

Each decision should be linked to the grant, work package or programme it affects, so that an audit by grant, by rule or by period is a query and not a project.

python
src = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="source_item",
data={"grant": "HE-101012345", "wp": "WP3", "item_ref": "INV-77421",
"doc_sha256": "", "period": "RP2"})

rule = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rules_applied",
data={"grant_rules": "HE-MGA v1.2 Art 6", "national_rules": "UNI-POLICY-2026-04",
"category_table_v": "9", "prompt_v": "v18", "model": "provider-model-2026-03"},
parent_id=src.id)

cls = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="classification",
data={"category": "direct_equipment_service", "eligible": True,
"basis": ["service contract used only for project equipment"],
"confidence": "medium"},
parent_id=rule.id)

Store references and digests of documents, not full copies, and apply redaction before storage for personal data.

Step 3: separate agent judgment from verified decisions

Where money or rights depend on a decision, record the human step with what the person saw.

python
rev = await db.log(agent="research-accounts", event="human_review",
data={"reviewer": "u-acct-12", "saw": ["invoice", "contract", "classification_basis"],
"action": "confirmed", "sample_type": "risk_based"},
parent_id=cls.id)

Do not log only that someone clicked approve. Log what they were shown, what they changed and why. An auditor will weigh a review more heavily when it shows engagement with evidence.

Step 4: add rules outside the model for the costly mistakes

Put deterministic checks around the decisions that matter most. Examples for a research office: a cost above a threshold needs human review, a cost type flagged as ineligible by the programme's rules cannot be marked eligible by the agent, and an item that matches a known risky pattern, such as shared equipment or overheads, must be flagged.

python
await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rule_check",
data={"rule": "shared_equipment_needs_review", "result": "flag", "blocking": True},
parent_id=cls.id)

A flagged item is held for review. The audit record explains afterwards. The rule prevents.

Step 5: use impact queries to answer extension of findings

When an auditor, or your own review, finds a faulty rule, prompt version or classification pattern, you need to know every item that used it, across every grant.

python
affected = await db.impact(rule.id)

Use it before the funder asks. List the items, correct or document each, and approach the funder with a complete picture. Voluntarily scoping and correcting a problem is a stronger position than having it extended to you.

Step 6: align retention with the funding clock

Set retention from the longest obligation that applies, not from your IT default.

Funding. At least the period in the grant agreement, such as five years after final payment for larger Horizon Europe grants, and longer if an audit is open or national rules require.
Legal hold. When an audit, investigation or dispute starts, suspend deletion for the relevant records.
Data protection. Keep personal data only as long as needed, and decide in advance how erasure requests interact with an integrity-protected record. ZizkaDB supports redaction before storage and forget with tombstones, and your data protection officer should approve the approach.
Exportability. Export and archive before systems are retired, and test that archives can be re-imported and verified.
python
export = await db.export_events(agent="grants-cost-agent", since="2026-01-01", until="2026-06-30")
Step 7: make the record tamper evident, with custody you can defend

Every event in ZizkaDB carries a SHA-256 checksum chained to the previous one for that agent. Any edit, deletion or reordering breaks the chain. Verify on a schedule and store the chain head somewhere your own system administrators cannot edit, such as your records management system or your internal audit function.

python
check = await db.verify_chain(agent="grants-cost-agent")

store check.head with internal audit, and log the verification date

When an auditor asks whether the record is original, you can show a verification result and the independently held head. That proves the record has not changed since the head was stored. It does not prove the record was complete.

Step 8: prepare for the incident clock

If an agent is involved in a security or data incident, NIS2-type reporting starts at awareness: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month. Prepare in advance. Make sure you can freeze and export the relevant chain, list every action the agent took in the window, scope affected records through the impact query, and show who did what during the response. Our incident response how-to covers the 72 hour runbook in more detail.

Step 9: give auditors a clean, safe way in

Create an audit access procedure before you need it.

Use read-only, expiring keys scoped to the grant, period or decision set requested.
Provide a standard export with the chain verification result.
Keep a log of who accessed what.
Run a dry audit once a year with someone outside the team.
python
await db.log(agent="audit-desk", event="auditor_access_granted",
data={"auditor_org": "funder-audit-unit", "scope": "grant HE-101012345",
"expires": "2026-12-31", "approved_by": "u-compliance-3"})
Step 10: choose infrastructure that fits public-sector constraints

Publicly funded bodies often face procurement rules, data residency expectations, sovereignty concerns and vendor exit requirements. Design for them.

Self host inside your own environment or an EU-based environment you control, so the evidence stays in your custody.
Avoid lock-in. Choose tools that are open source, so your team and your auditors can inspect the code, and that are model, LLM and cloud agnostic, so you can change providers without losing history.
Keep it small. A single container on Postgres is easier to secure, accredit and operate than a sprawling platform.
Plan exit. Test exporting and re-importing your records.

ZizkaDB's core is AGPL-3.0, runs self hosted in a single Docker container, and can be placed inside the environment you choose. Whether it meets your security and procurement requirements is for your own teams to decide.

Business objectives and how to measure them
Objective Measure
Protect funding from recovery Share of audited items with a complete evidence chain; ineligible cost found per audit
Cut audit preparation time Hours to answer an auditor request, before and after
Contain a finding early Time from discovering a faulty rule to listing all affected items
Support AI governance duties Share of agent decisions with a full record; FRIA evidence ready
Strengthen future bids and procurement positions Evidence packs provided to funders and partners on request
Reduce reputational risk Citizen complaints resolved with a verifiable account
An illustrative exposure example

This is invented, to show the logic. A university manages 40 EU and national grants worth 20 million euros over the reporting period. If a systematic classification weakness caused 2 percent of the claimed costs to be later found ineligible, the exposure would be 400,000 euros, before the cost of the audit itself and the staff time to rebuild evidence. Even a modest reduction in that risk, or in the time to scope it, can justify the effort of recording decisions properly. Use your own figures.

Common mistakes
Treating AI as an IT matter. The obligations belong to finance, research administration, legal and service owners, not only to the technology team.
Keeping logs for 30 days and grants for 5 years. The shortest retention in the chain sets your real position.
Letting an agent decide eligibility alone. Put rules and human review around money and rights.
Recording output only. An auditor needs sources, rules and versions.
Forgetting the review step. Show what the reviewer saw.
One copy, one custodian. Store the chain head elsewhere.
Assuming the vendor holds the evidence. If the contract ends, so can your access.
Ignoring erasure. Decide the approach before the first request.
A 30 day plan

Days 1 to 5: build the obligation register. List agent tasks, the obligation each touches, the retention period that applies and an owner.
Days 6 to 10: choose one high-value workflow, such as cost classification, and define its event model with research administration, legal and your data protection officer.
Days 11 to 15: instrument the workflow with source, rules, classification and review events, and add the blocking rules for the highest risk items.
Days 16 to 20: set retention and legal hold, test export and re-import, and verify the hash chain with the head held by internal audit.
Days 21 to 25: run an impact query on a seeded faulty rule and measure how fast you can list affected items across grants.
Days 26 to 30: run a mock audit with someone outside the team using the eight questions above. Record the gaps, assign owners and agree the next workflow.

Where ZizkaDB fits, and its limits

ZizkaDB is an open source causal audit database for AI agents. It records each decision as a linked event, answers why() for any outcome, lists everything downstream of a faulty input through the impact route, supports replay and drift baselines, and shows whether stored history has been altered through a SHA-256 hash chain. It is model, LLM and cloud agnostic, and it runs self hosted in a single Docker container, with a managed Cloud edition at db.zizka.ai for multi-agent setups.

It does not decide whether a cost is eligible, assess fundamental rights impacts, report incidents or make a body compliant with any rule. It records what your system captures, so the rules and reviews you add are what prevent errors. The open source edition records one agent per install, so fleets and agent to agent flows use the Cloud edition or separate instances. Take advice from your legal, audit and data protection teams on retention, erasure and what the funder requires.

If you rely on public money and use AI agents, choose one funded workflow this week and trace one claimed cost from the source document to the final report. If you can do it in minutes and show the record is original, you are ready for the audit. If you cannot, you have found the gap before the auditor did.

Corrections: if you represent a party mentioned here and believe a statement is inaccurate, contact us and we will review it promptly.

Sources: Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement, Articles 20 and 25 (European Commission, EU Funding and Tenders Portal, version 1.2, June 2026), with guidance summaries from the Canadian ISED Horizon Europe guide and the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG); EU AI Act Article 27 and Recital 96 (AI Act Service Desk and artificialintelligenceact.eu) and Article 26 (AI Act Service Desk); Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) commentary; NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 with Irish NCSC, Finnish NCSC and Morrison Foerster guidance; ZizkaDB documentation.

title: The Product FAQ Block That Only Repeats What the Listing Already Says
description:
We added a FAQ block to 27,000 product pages this week. Four questions per page, matching FAQPage structured data, rendered after the description.

The rule I set before writing a line of it: the answer may only state something the store can already do or already knows. No "we guarantee authenticity". No "100% genuine or money back" unless there is a process behind it that a customer could actually invoke.

That constraint sounds like it makes the block useless. It did the opposite.

The five groups

Products are sorted into five FAQ sets by top-level category: bags, shoes, watches, apparel, and a default for everything else. Each set has four questions.

Bags

  • What are the internal dimensions? (we publish width, base depth, strap drop, weight on every listing)
  • Will a 13-inch laptop fit?
  • Is the photo the actual item I will receive?
  • How is it packed for shipping?

Shoes

  • What is the insole length in centimetres?
  • Does this run true to EU size?
  • Can you measure the boot shaft height?
  • What is the heel height, measured or estimated?

Watches

  • What is the case diameter?
  • Is the bracelet sized before shipping?
  • Are box and papers included?
  • Can you send a photo of the caseback?

Apparel

  • What are the flat measurements for this size?
  • Is the fabric stretch or woven?
  • How does it fit compared to a standard size?
  • Can you measure shoulder to hem?

Every one of these is answerable from data we hold or from an action we will take in the WhatsApp conversation. Not one of them requires a claim about the product's origin.

Why this beats a generic FAQ

The generic version — "Do you ship worldwide?", "How long does delivery take?", "What is your return policy?" — is identical on 27,000 pages and also lives on three other pages of the site. It adds nothing to the page and nothing to the query space. Google has seen that FAQ 27,000 times.

The version above is category-specific and, more importantly, query-shaped. People do not search "what is your return policy do you ship worldwide". They search "chanel mini flap will a phone fit", "are cartier tank straps interchangeable", "what size is a 25cm birkin in inches". A FAQ that answers the concrete version of those questions is the only kind with a chance of matching.

The schema has to match the visible text, exactly

FAQPage markup that does not correspond to on-page text is a manual-action risk and, more practically, a wasted opportunity — Google matches the rendered content.

So the PHP builds one array of question/answer pairs and uses it twice: once to render the <details> blocks, once to emit the JSON-LD. Same source array, no drift possible. Verified on a live page: 4 visible questions, 4 questions in schema, same strings.

Two things to avoid in the FAQ itself:

  • Do not put prices in the answer. They change, the schema goes stale, and stale structured data is worse than none.
  • Do not answer with a link. "See our shipping page" is not an answer. If the fact belongs in the FAQ, state it.

What it looks like in practice

On a Cartier Tank listing, the watch group fires: case diameter, bracelet sizing, box and papers, caseback photo. On a Chanel belt, the default group fires instead, because belts are not a category I wrote a set for — and that is fine, the default set is honest rather than wrong.

The four questions are not going to rank on their own. They exist to do two things: give the page a block of genuinely specific text that no other listing shares, and answer the question before the customer opens WhatsApp, so the conversation that does happen is about the actual purchase.

That second effect is the one I will be watching. If the FAQ works, message volume should drop and message quality should rise — the same thing that happened when we published internal bag dimensions. If message volume does not move, the questions were wrong.

Examples with the block live: a Cartier Tank Solo, a Tank Française 25, and the watches category if you want to open a few in a row.

If you are going to copy this, copy the constraint first. The four questions are easy. Refusing to answer with a claim you cannot back is the part that makes the block worth having.

title: Delete your emoji feature cards (and what to put there instead)
description:
Ask an AI coding agent for a landing page and, somewhere under the hero, you'll get this:

<div class="grid grid-cols-3 gap-6">
  <div class="rounded-2xl p-6 shadow-lg">
    <h3>🚀 Blazing fast</h3>
    <p>Experience lightning-fast performance that scales with your needs.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="rounded-2xl p-6 shadow-lg">
    <h3>🔒 Secure by design</h3>
    <p>Enterprise-grade security keeps your data safe.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="rounded-2xl p-6 shadow-lg">
    <h3>⚡ Seamless integrations</h3>
    <p>Connect with the tools you already love.</p>
  </div>
</div>

Three cards, three emoji, three claims that fit every product ever made. I've been building unslop, a free rule file that AI coding agents read before they build a UI, and this block is one of the first things it removes. This post is why, and what to put in its place.

Why the emoji card grid is a tell

It says nothing a visitor can check. "Fast", "secure" and "integrations" are claims every competitor also makes. A visitor learns nothing about your product.

It hides a missing decision. Three equal cards usually mean nobody decided what the product does better than anything else. If everything gets the same box, nothing is the main feature.

The emoji does the job an idea should do. 🚀 isn't an icon for your feature. It's a placeholder for one.

Everyone ships it. Because it's the average of thousands of templates, it's what models reproduce when nobody specifies a design. So it now reads as "generated" within a second.

The unslop rules say it directly:

Vary the rhythm: not every section is three cards in a row.

and

No emoji as icons or as heading decoration.

The linter also catches the emoji half of it:

npx @deliverwebsite/unslop lint src

warning  emoji-heading  Heading starts with an emoji, a common stand-in for a real icon or idea.
         Fix: Drop the emoji, or use one icon from the project's icon set with a consistent size and stroke.

What to put there instead

Start from one question: what does a buyer need to know right after the hero? Then pick the format that answers it. Here are four that work far better than three cards.

1. One real screen, with the main feature largest

If the product has a UI, show it. Make the main feature the largest thing in the section and explain it in one sentence.

<section class="grid items-center gap-12 lg:grid-cols-[1fr_1.4fr]">
  <div>
    <h2>One inbox for support emails, chat and Instagram messages</h2>
    <p>Every message lands in one queue with the customer's orders next to it,
       so the first reply is the right one.</p>
  </div>
  <img src="/inbox.png" alt="The shared inbox with three open conversations" />
</section>

2. A short list of specific facts

When the features really are small and parallel, a list with real details beats cards. No boxes, just space and a rule between items.

<ul class="divide-y">
  <li><strong>Replies in 6 minutes on average</strong> across 40 support teams [real figure]</li>
  <li><strong>Order history next to every message</strong> from Shopify and WooCommerce</li>
  <li><strong>Instagram DMs in the same queue</strong> as email and chat</li>
</ul>

If you don't have a real number yet, leave a marked gap like [real figure] instead of inventing "10x faster".

3. A before/after or a flow

If the value is a change, show the change: the spreadsheet before, the app after. Or the three steps a user actually goes through, with real screens for each.

4. One quote from a named customer

One real quote with a name and a role does more than three adjectives. If you don't have one yet, skip the section.

The same product, before and after

Here's a customer support tool from a set of 100 pairs I'm building for unslop. Both sides use exactly the same words. Left is the usual AI styling: "Game-Changing Customer Support, Powered by AI!!!" in gradient text, glowing stat boxes, emoji cards and a "Best Customer Support Tool Ever!!!" sticker. Right keeps every word, but follows the rule file: sentence case, one accent colour, the same three features with one icon set instead of emoji, no stickers.

Even with the same weak copy, the right side stops looking generated. The copy rules (a specific headline, real numbers) are the next step.

A quick checklist

Before you ship a feature section, ask:

  • Could this exact section sit on a competitor's site? If yes, rewrite it.
  • Is the main feature the largest thing here?
  • Does every claim have a detail a visitor could check (a number, a name, a screen)?
  • Is there an emoji doing the job of an icon or an idea?
  • Is this a card grid because the content needs cards, or because landing pages "have one"?

Try it on your own project

unslop is free and open source (MIT for the code, CC BY 4.0 for the playbook). One command adds the rule file to your project so Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and other agents read it before they build:

npx @deliverwebsite/unslop init

https://github.com/deliverwebsite/unslop, made by DeliverWebsite UI. If you want sections that already follow these rules, the free components at ui.deliverwebsite.com do.

What do you replace feature cards with on your landing pages?

title: Quotes in a style tag broke hydration in my Framer code component
description:
I sell Framer code components, and one of them worked perfectly in the editor, then threw a hydration error on the published site. The page still rendered, but the console showed React error #425 ("text content does not match server-rendered HTML").

The cause was two kinds of characters in the CSS: quotes and >.

The setup

Framer code components are React components. A common way to ship their styles is a <style> element with a template string inside:

export default function Accordion(props) {
    return (
        <div className="acc">
            <style>{`
                .acc [data-state="open"] .panel { display: block; }
                .acc > .item { border-top: 1px solid #ddd; }
            `}</style>
            {/* ... */}
        </div>
    )
}

In the editor this is fine, because the editor renders on the client only. A published Framer site renders the page on the server first and then hydrates it in the browser, and that's where it broke.

What went wrong

On the server, the text inside <style> was escaped like any other text: " became " and > became >. In the browser, <style> is a raw text element, so those entities are never decoded. The browser kept " as literal characters in the CSS.

So the server HTML and the client render disagreed about the style text, React reported the mismatch, and the selectors with escaped characters stopped matching anything.

The fix

Write the CSS so it has nothing to escape:

<style>{`
    .acc [data-state=open] .panel { display: block; }
    .acc .item { border-top: 1px solid #ddd; }
`}</style>
  • Attribute selectors don't need quotes when the value is a plain word: [data-state=open] works the same as [data-state="open"].
  • Replace the child combinator > with a descendant selector or a class on the child.
  • No content: "..." strings. If you need generated text, put it in the markup instead.

JavaScript inside ${...} in the template string is fine, because it runs before React ever sees the text.

How to catch it before buyers do

The editor will never show this bug. Publish the site, open it in a normal browser tab and check the console for React's "recoverable error" messages, numbers #418, #421, #423 and #425. Those are hydration mismatches. If you see one, look for anything your component renders differently on the server than on the client: escaped text, dates, random ids or window checks.

A related trap: don't build class names or CSS selectors from useId(). Framer's server render adds copies of components for breakpoint variants, so the ids can shift between server and client.

I keep the rest of what I check before submitting a template or component in one place: the Framer template checklist I use before every submission.

Have you hit a hydration error that only showed up on the live site? What caused it?

title: One rules engine, two languages
description:
CheX runs the rules of chess twice: once in TypeScript in your browser, once in Rust on the game's server. Both must agree on every move, every capture and every checkmate, down to the last byte. This post is about how the game keeps two engines in two languages saying exactly the same thing.

Why write the rules twice

Online chess has a trust problem. If only your browser knew the rules, anyone could open the dev tools and teleport a queen. So the server has to be the referee: it checks every move and decides what the game looks like.

But a referee that lives 200 ms away makes the game feel slow. Every tap would wait for a round trip before a piece moved. So the browser needs to know the rules too, so it can show legal moves instantly and play your move the moment you make it.

The browser runs on TypeScript and the server on Rust, for speed and safety. So the game has one set of rules in two languages, and they must never disagree. If they did, the board you see and the game the server records would quietly drift apart.

One engine, designed to be copied

The trick is not clever translation. It is designing the engine so that a faithful copy is easy to write and easy to check. Three choices did most of the work.
1. The game is a pure function. The whole engine boils down to one function: gameReducer(state, action) → state. Same state and same move in, same new state out. No clocks, no randomness, no hidden globals. A pure function is easy to port, because there is nothing around it to port.
2. Every move is a list of small effects. A move does not change the board directly. It produces effects such as relocate, remove, transform (promotion) and spawn, and one small function applies them. Castling is two relocates. En passant is a relocate plus a remove. Both engines only need to agree on six effect types, not on every special case in chess.
3. Variants plug in as rule modifiers. CheX mods, like the knight that can leap like a camel, are not forks of the engine. A mod adds movement rules to a piece kind through one hook, and the engine treats them like the piece's own rules for moves, attacks and check. Charges and cooldowns live in the game state as plain data.
The result is about 1,300 lines of TypeScript and 1,700 lines of Rust, with the same files, the same functions and the same names on both sides. Reading them side by side feels like reading a translation with the original on the facing page.

Keeping them honest: TypeScript records, Rust replays

A copy is only as good as the test that checks it. The game's test is simple: TypeScript plays a game and writes down everything, and Rust has to reproduce it exactly.


A small script plays a game with the TypeScript engine and saves three things to a JSON fixture: the starting state, every action, and the full game state after each one. Each state is everything: the board, every piece, castling rights, the event log, even the mod charges left on each knight.
On the Rust side, a test loads that file, feeds the same actions through the Rust reducer and serializes each result back to JSON. Then it demands an exact match with what TypeScript wrote. Not "same position". The same JSON: the same fields, the same order of events, the same piece ids. If anything differs, the test fails and prints both versions side by side at the exact move where they split.
The test suite keeps two of these recorded games:

  • A classic game of 29 moves, checked at every single step.
  • A knight-camel game of 90 moves, ending with a rematch. The script picks camel leaps 70% of the time when one is legal, so charges, cooldowns and "used up" knights all get exercised. It is checked every 15 moves to keep the file small.

The moves come from a seeded random generator, so the same script always records the same game. When a rule changes, both engines change with it, the game is re-recorded, and the Rust test shows whether the copy is still faithful.

Parity only proves the two engines agree, not that they are right. For that, the Rust engine also runs perft, chess programmers' standard correctness test: count every legal position a few moves deep and compare with known answers. From the starting position that is 20, 400, 8,902 and 197,281 positions at depths 1 to 4. Four more tricky test positions, full of castling, en passant and promotions, are checked too.

What two identical engines do for the gameplay

Moves that never wait for the network. When you move a piece online, your browser runs the move through its own engine and shows it at once, before the server has even heard about it. Because the server runs the same rules, its answer lands on an identical state and silently replaces the browser's. In tests, your move appeared in about 18 ms, even with 600 ms of simulated lag. If the server ever disagrees, the browser rolls back to the server's version.

One message format for both sides. The browser and the server send each other the same game state JSON that the parity test compares. There is no translation layer to go wrong, because the format is the very thing the parity test checks.

Mods ship on both sides at once. Adding the knight-camel mod meant adding one movement rule to each engine and recording a new parity game. The day the Rust test went green, the browser and the server agreed on every camel leap, check and cooldown.

The cost is real: every rule change is written twice, and the fixture has to be re-recorded. For a game where trust and speed both matter, that is a good trade.

If you are building something similar

  • Make the core a pure function of state and action. It is the easiest code in the world to port and to test.
  • Shrink the surface the two sides must agree on. Small effects beat special cases.
  • Test the copy against the original, not against your idea of the original. Record real runs from one engine and replay them in the other, comparing the exact output.
  • Keep a separate correctness test like perft, so both engines are not just agreeing on the same mistake. Next time: how your move shows up before the server even knows about it.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.
