title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
description:
arXiv:2611.33639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

title: Enterprise Software Development: Building Scalable Business Systems
description:
Large organizations often depend on multiple applications to manage finance, operations, customer relationships, inventory, and internal communication.

When these systems operate separately, data becomes fragmented and business processes become difficult to manage.

Enterprise software solutions address these challenges by connecting business operations through integrated, scalable applications.

What Is Enterprise Software Development?

Enterprise software development involves designing and building applications that support the complex operational requirements of organizations.

Unlike smaller standalone applications, enterprise systems often need to support multiple departments, large user groups, extensive integrations, and strict security requirements.

Common examples include:

  • Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems.
  • Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platforms.
  • Human Resource Management Systems (HRMS).
  • Business intelligence platforms.
  • Supply chain management applications.
  • Enterprise workflow automation systems.

Key Components of Enterprise Software Architecture

A typical enterprise application may include:

1. Presentation Layer

Provides interfaces for employees, administrators, customers, and other users.

2. Application Layer

Contains business logic, validation rules, and application services.

3. Integration Layer

Connects internal applications and external services through APIs and messaging systems.

4. Data Layer

Manages databases, reporting systems, and data access.

5. Security Layer

Handles authentication, authorization, encryption, and audit logging.

A modular architecture helps development teams maintain these components as business requirements evolve.

Technologies Used in Enterprise Development

The technology stack depends on system complexity and organizational requirements.

Common technologies include:

  • Java, Python, and .NET: Backend development.
  • React and Angular: Enterprise frontend applications.
  • PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server: Database management.
  • REST APIs: Application integration.
  • Docker and Kubernetes: Containerization and orchestration.
  • Cloud platforms: Infrastructure and deployment.
  • CI/CD tools: Automated testing and delivery.

Challenges in Enterprise Software Development

Enterprise projects introduce challenges that require careful architectural planning:

  • Integrating legacy systems with modern applications.
  • Managing large volumes of business data.
  • Maintaining consistent access permissions.
  • Supporting high availability and performance.
  • Meeting compliance and security requirements.
  • Coordinating changes across multiple teams.

Developers should address these challenges through clear service boundaries, standardized APIs, automated testing, and effective monitoring.

Best Practices for Building Enterprise Applications

Start with business requirements and identify the systems that need to communicate.

Use modular architecture, documented APIs, centralized identity management, and role-based access controls. Establish automated testing and deployment pipelines to improve release consistency.

Also, monitor application performance and maintain audit trails for important operations.

Final Thoughts

Enterprise software development helps organizations connect systems, streamline workflows, and manage complex operations through integrated digital platforms.

The right architecture should balance scalability, security, maintainability, and actual business requirements.

Explore enterprise software solutions to learn more about building connected business applications.

For more software development insights, visit Invertio Solutions.

title: Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models via Agentic Model Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.34036v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-shot adaptation transfers pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to new domains using a small set of labeled images. Most methods fit prompts, representations, or classifiers within an adaptation procedure specified in advance. Yet the visual distinctions needed for recognition can differ substantially across domains, motivating the question: Can an LLM agent use few-shot examples and model observations to design the adaptation procedure itself? We propose Agentic Model Editing (AME), an agentic framework that jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting as an executable, domain-customized adaptation program. The agent inspects images, class semantics, model parameters, intermediate representations, and activations to formulate hypotheses about the target task. It implements and tests candidate programs on the support set, with aggregate validation accuracy guiding refinement and selection. Each program fits a complete domain model that is fixed before testing. The agent and its tools are shared across domains, while each domain receives its own adaptation program. Across eleven datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME achieves the highest average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with back-propagation among the compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate applicability across VLM backbones and LLM agents.

title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
description:
arXiv:2611.34776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.

title: Designing a Reward Points Ledger: Earn, Bonus and Redeem Without Breaking Balances
description:
Every rewards app looks simple from the outside. A customer buys something, they earn reward points, and later they redeem rewards for cash or a gift card. Under the hood, the part that decides whether users trust you is the points ledger.

If balances drift, double credit, or go negative, support tickets pile up fast. Here is a practical way to model it.

1. Never store a balance as the source of truth

Store every movement as an immutable ledger entry and derive the balance from it.

CREATE TABLE points_ledger (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  entry_type    TEXT NOT NULL,  -- EARN, BONUS, REDEEM, EXPIRE, REVERSAL
  points        INTEGER NOT NULL, -- positive for credit, negative for debit
  source_ref    TEXT NOT NULL,  -- order id, scan id, campaign id
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (entry_type, source_ref)
);

The UNIQUE (entry_type, source_ref) constraint is the cheapest protection you will ever add. If a webhook fires twice or a user double taps, the second insert fails and nobody earns twice for the same purchase.

You can still keep a cached balance column for fast reads, but update it in the same transaction as the ledger insert, and rebuild it from the ledger if they ever disagree.

2. Treat bonus reward points as their own entry type

Marketing teams love campaigns like "double points this weekend" or "50 bonus points on your first scan". Do not fold these into the base EARN row. Write a separate BONUS row linked to the campaign.

Why this matters:

  • You can report how much a campaign actually cost
  • You can reverse a bonus without touching the base earn
  • Bonus reward points can have a shorter expiry than regular points

3. Make redemption a two step process

Redeeming is where money leaves the system, so be strict:

  1. Reserve: insert a REDEEM row with negative points inside a transaction that checks the derived balance is enough (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the user row).
  2. Fulfil: call the payout or gift card provider.
  3. Confirm or reverse: on failure, insert a REVERSAL row. Never delete the REDEEM row.

This keeps an audit trail for every rupee or point that moved.

4. Tie earning to a verifiable event

The biggest leak in most programs is fraud on the earn side: fake receipts, shared promo codes, scripted sign ups. A stronger pattern is to tie each earn to a one time token that only a real buyer can get, for example a unique QR code printed under a scratch layer on the product pack.

This is the model used by Assured Rewards, a QR cashback and loyalty platform in India. Each code can be redeemed once, the scan confirms the product is genuine, and the reward lands in a wallet that the user can withdraw through UPI or use to redeem rewards on gift cards. In ledger terms, the scan id becomes the source_ref, so the unique constraint above blocks reuse for free.

5. Handle expiry as a scheduled job, not a query filter

If points expire, write an EXPIRE entry when they do. Filtering old rows out at read time makes balances change silently, which users read as theft.

Wrapping up

A good points system is mostly accounting:

  • Append only ledger
  • Idempotency keys on every credit
  • Separate rows for base points and bonus points
  • Reserve, fulfil, confirm on every redemption

Get that right and features like tiers, streaks or daily rewards deals become easy additions instead of rewrites.

title: I built a swinging lanyard badge in React with no physics library. Here is the whole method
description:
I wanted an ID badge that hangs from a strap, swings when you grab it and flies when you throw it. Every example I found pulled in a physics engine and a 3D renderer for it. That is a lot of code to ship for one card.

It turns out the whole thing is a rope, a weight and one spring. Here is how it works. You can try the finished badge here first: grab it and throw it.

1. The strap is 14 links

A rope is a chain of points that are not allowed to drift apart. I store each point with its current and its previous position:

type Pt = { x: number; y: number; px: number; py: number }

There is no velocity field. The velocity is the difference between the two positions. This is Verlet integration, and it is why throwing works without any extra code: when you let go, the last two positions already contain the speed of your hand.

Each step moves every point by its own velocity, plus gravity:

const vx = (p.x - p.px) * 0.99   // a little air drag
const vy = (p.y - p.py) * 0.99
p.px = p.x
p.py = p.y
p.x += vx
p.y += vy + GRAVITY * dt * dt

2. Then pull the chain back together

After that step the points are too far apart. So for each neighbouring pair, measure the distance and move both points toward the right length. Repeat a few times:

const dx = b.x - a.x
const dy = b.y - a.y
const dist = Math.hypot(dx, dy)
const pull = (dist - segment) / dist
a.x += dx * pull * wa
a.y += dy * pull * wa
b.x -= dx * pull * wb
b.y -= dy * pull * wb

wa and wb decide who gives way. Normally both are 0.5. Three cases are different:

  • The top point is fixed, so it never moves (wa = 0).
  • The card is heavy, so on the last link the rope does most of the moving (0.88 against 0.12). This one number is what makes it hang straight and swing like a pendulum instead of flapping like a ribbon.
  • While you hold the card, it does not give at all.

Ten passes per step are enough for 14 links.

3. The card over-swings on its own spring

If the card simply took the angle of the last link, it would look glued to the rope. A real badge lags behind and overshoots. So the card has its own angle and its own angular speed, pulled toward the rope's direction by a spring:

const want = -Math.atan2(end.x - prev.x, end.y - prev.y)
spin += ((want - angle) * 90 - spin * 9) * dt
angle += spin * dt

The card also leans in 3D with its horizontal speed (rotateY), and a band of light moves across it by the same amount. Both are one line each and they sell the effect more than anything else.

4. Dragging, and the two bugs I hit

While dragging, the last point follows the pointer. Two things went wrong at first.

The rope stretched forever. The top is fixed and so is your hand, so the constraints cannot be satisfied. The fix is to limit the hand: past the strap's length the card only follows 12% of the extra distance. It feels like the strap going taut.

A fast flick launched the card into orbit. Verlet keeps whatever speed the last two positions imply, and a mouse can move very fast between two frames. I cap the release speed.

5. Do not run when nothing moves

A physics loop that runs forever drains batteries. This one counts frames in which the card is slow, the spin is near zero and nobody is holding it. After half a second of that it stops, and a pointer event starts it again. It also stops off screen (IntersectionObserver) and in a hidden tab.

With prefers-reduced-motion the simulation never starts: the badge hangs straight and still flips on click.

What it costs

About 500 lines in one file, styles and markup included, with an SVG path for the strap and a div for the card. The physics uses no library at all. The only import besides React is one hook from Motion that reads the reduced-motion setting.

The finished component, with a flip side and keyboard control, is part of goodui, a React component library I am building. 133 of the components are free and MIT licensed, installed as source through the shadcn CLI. The lanyard badge is in the paid set.

title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration
description:
arXiv:2611.34112v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.

title: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
description:
AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.

Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.

Each canary audit run:

  1. Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run.

  2. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls.

  3. Watches for traffic. A ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, so a canary URL should never receive a request.

  4. Records any request to a canary URL, identifying the provider, model, and run for investigation.

Canary audits complement contractual ZDR agreements and independent audits rather than replacing them.

Read more about AI Gateway security and compliance measures in the documentation.

title: Premiere Pro MCP servers compared (November 2026)
description:
If you want an AI to work in Premiere Pro today, without waiting for Adobe's own MCP beta in 2027, there are already five open-source MCP servers on GitHub. We read the README of each on 27 November 2026 and put what they say side by side. We haven't installed and benchmarked all five, so this is a reading of their docs, not a test.

One disclosure first: we make Concierge LLM, a paid desktop agent that also works in Premiere, so we have a stake in this. It's covered at the end, apart from the open-source projects.

The five servers

Project Stars Last update Bridge into Premiere Premiere versions Tools
hetpatel-11/Adobe_Premiere_Pro_MCP 947 19 Nov 2026 CEP panel (UXP experimental) 2020 and later 283, reached through search_tools and invoke_tool
leancoderkavy/premiere-pro-mcp 591 27 Nov 2026 CEP/ExtendScript, plus UXP see its site 453 core, plus 98 when UXP is connected
ayushozha/AdobePremiereProMCP 152 5 Oct 2026 CEP panel 2020 to 2026 74 in the default profile, more behind other profiles
antipaster/Adobe-Premiere-Pro-MCP 53 29 Oct 2026 CEP panel over WebSocket 2023 and later 170+
morim3/mcp_adobe_premiere 5 Apr 2025 UXP plugin not stated a small set

All five are MIT licensed. Star counts are from the GitHub API on 27 November.

What they have in common

They're bridges. Each one runs a small server on your computer and a panel inside Premiere, and the AI on the other end is whatever MCP client you connect: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor are the ones their READMEs name. So the thinking, and the bill for it, comes from that client. If you use a cloud model, every step of an edit is a paid request.

Four of the five use a CEP panel, and the installers of hetpatel-11, leancoderkavy and antipaster switch on Adobe's CEP debug mode (PlayerDebugMode) so Premiere will load an unsigned extension. That's normal for CEP development, but it's a machine-wide setting, and leancoderkavy's uninstaller deliberately leaves it on so other extensions don't break. Worth knowing before you install on a work machine.

How they differ

Tool count isn't the thing to compare. The bigger servers hide most of their tools behind a search step or a profile, because hundreds of tool schemas in one prompt crowd the model's context. ayushozha's default profile shows 74 tools and hides the risky ones (file I/O, external editors) unless you pick an "unsafe" profile, which we think is the right default.

Maintenance varies a lot. hetpatel-11 and leancoderkavy were both updated this month. morim3 hasn't changed since April 2025.

Telemetry. hetpatel-11 sends anonymous usage telemetry by default. Its README shows how to turn it off with PREMIERE_MCP_TELEMETRY=0.

Seeing the footage

None of them ships a model, so how well shots get chosen depends on what your client can see. leancoderkavy goes furthest: its README lists scene detection, still capture and transcription (which asks for consent first), so a client that reads images can look at frames. With the others, the model mostly works from clip names, markers and metadata.

Where Concierge LLM fits

Concierge LLM is a desktop app, not an MCP server you plug into Claude. It brings its own open model, which runs on your graphics card, and drives Premiere, After Effects and Photoshop itself. It looks at the footage before it picks a shot. Our longest timed job: one request became a 35-shot music edit, cut to the beat on a new sequence, in 11 minutes 46 seconds on one RTX 3090. It's $100 once ($50 right now with code LAUNCH50), and it needs a strong PC: a 24 GB graphics card is what we'd want. https://conciergellm.com/?s=devto&c=premiere-mcp

If you already pay for Claude or Codex and want to script Premiere yourself, one of the five above is the cheaper start. hetpatel-11 and leancoderkavy are the most active.

title: How long should an AI video ad be?
description:
What is the right length for a first ad?

Fifteen seconds is the length I would use for a first ad. It fits one product, one message and about four scenes. It is the length I publish a price for, and it is the length the plans are counted in: Creator makes about 7 videos of 15 seconds a month, and Pro about 19.

I do not have a study on the ideal length for ads, so I will not tell you a duration wins. What I can say is that a short ad leaves less room for error and for confusion.

What are the limits of the studio?

One generation runs up to 30 seconds, and a project can grow to 10 minutes by joining scenes. Most product clips are far shorter than that.

The limits are about what the studio can make. What your ad should be is a separate question, and the answer comes from the placement and the message.

Does length change the cost?

Yes. The credit cost depends on the length and the quality. A 15 second video at 720p is 515 credits, which is $5.15, and that is the only figure I publish. Longer costs more, and so do 1080p and 4K.

For any other length, read the credit cost in the studio before you generate. Do not scale my number by guesswork. More on credits is in how AI video credits work.

Does the placement set the length?

Often it does, and the platform has the final say. Platforms set limits on length and file size, and they change, so check the current rules of the one you use. A vertical slot for short video suits a short ad. A product page or a site banner can take a longer, calmer clip.

The ratio choice goes with it, which I cover in which video ratio to use for each ad placement.

How many scenes fit in 15 seconds?

About four, if each does one job. A simple structure is an opening on the product or the payoff, one detail, one use and a closing frame with the offer.

  1. Open on the product or its result.
  2. Show the detail a shopper should notice.
  3. Show the product in use.
  4. Close on the product with the offer line.

If you find yourself adding a fifth or sixth scene, ask whether the ad has two messages. Two messages usually make two ads.

When does a longer ad make sense?

  • A product page video where a visitor is already interested.
  • A small brand commercial with a short story, where one idea needs room.
  • A video for a website or YouTube, where the viewer chose to watch.
  • A real estate piece that moves through the rooms of a property.

Even then, build it from short checked scenes. Every extra scene is another chance for the product to drift, and each one needs a look against the real item.

How do I test length?

Make a short version and a longer one with the same opening, message and offer, and run both with the same budget. Change only the length. The hook test method in how to test ad hooks with AI video applies here too.

Your ad account will tell you which one works. The studio does not.

How do I cut a longer idea down to 15 seconds?

Pick the one thing a viewer must remember and delete everything else. Write the message in one sentence, then keep only the scenes that carry that sentence. If a scene could be removed without the sentence changing, remove it.

It helps to read the scene list as a storyboard before you generate anything. The scene list shows each moment in order, so a wasted scene is only a wasted line at that point and not a wasted generation.

How does length affect retakes?

Longer videos have more scenes, and each scene is another place where fine detail can drift. A scene that completes and misses the brief still spends credits, so a longer ad usually costs more in retakes as well as in generation.

You can regenerate a single scene and keep the rest, which keeps the cost of a fix small. Still, a short ad checked carefully is better than a long one checked in a hurry.

What should I check before I pick a length?

Open the current spec for the platform and the placement, and write down the maximum length, the file size and the ratio. Then pick the length that fits the message, not the maximum the slot allows.

If you are unsure, export the short version first. You can always build a longer one from the same scenes, and a short ad is quicker to review.

I do not quote platform limits here, because they change and I cannot promise they are right when you read this.

Where do I start?

Make one 15 second ad on Creator, $39 a month, which includes the commercial license for ads. Starter, $9 a month, is for a personal test. The page for brands shows the flow.

title: Go AI Agent Framework With Retries, Budgets and Human Approval
description:
One of my team's main projects has an AI-heavy backend written in Go. I work mostly in Python, where agent frameworks are mature, so I know what the Go side was missing: an agent that's a normal value inside the service, not a Python process reached over a queue. The loop itself takes an afternoon. Deciding what happens at each place it can break is what became Golem, an open-source Go AI agent framework.

This post is about that second part: bad tool calls, provider errors, loops, cost and human sign-off, and where each one lands in a run. It also covers how Golem compares with the other Go options and when you should pick something else. It describes v1.2.0, released on 16 November 2026.

What breaks once the agent loop is running?

The loop is short. The model reads a conversation, asks for a tool, you run it, you feed the result back and repeat until the model answers. Each step then fails in its own way:

  • The provider returns a 429 or a 503 halfway through a run.
  • The model calls a tool with arguments that don't match your schema.
  • The model returns JSON that is almost the shape you asked for.
  • The model asks for the same tool call again and again.
  • A tool needs a person to approve it before anything irreversible happens.
  • A run dies on turn six and you lose the first five turns.

Python has good answers to several of these. Pydantic AI showed that an agent can have typed dependencies and validated output, and I used it as a reference. But copying Python mechanisms into Go would have given me something un-Go-like: decorators are awkward, runtime validation hides what the compiler could check, and exceptions as control flow don't suit a language that returns errors. So the question I started from was what an agent should look like if you begin with Go's strengths.

What is Golem?

Golem is an open-source Go library for building agents. The repository started on 16 August 2026, and v1.0.0 on 25 October 2026 froze the API under a rule written down in ADR 0041: semantic versioning, additive changes only below v2, checked by an API diff against the previous tag.

The short version:

  • Agents are generic: Agent[Deps, Output]. Dependencies and the final output are real types.
  • The module has no dependencies outside the standard library, and needs Go 1.26 or newer.
  • Adapters cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama or LM Studio.
  • An MCP client works over stdio and streamable HTTP, and an MCP server exposes one agent as a tool.
  • Retries, fallback models, self-correction, usage limits, loop detection, streaming and run events are built in.
  • A deterministic fake model lets you test agents offline.
  • It ships with 39 guides, every example runs offline, and statement coverage is 81.6%. 
go get github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

The layering is plain. Your service owns the dependencies, the core owns the run, and everything that touches the outside world sits behind a small interface.

Why build agents in Go at all?

Agent work is mostly waiting on a network, so it's fair to ask whether the language matters. I think it does once the agent leaves the notebook. An agent service holds many conversations at once, calls tools concurrently, streams tokens to clients and has to shut down cleanly. Goroutines, context.Context and a single static binary fit that shape. A deployed agent can be one small container image with no interpreter, no virtualenv and no dependency tree to audit.

The compiler is the second reason. When a tool depends on a database handle and a tenant ID, I want the compiler to tell me if I pass the wrong one. In Golem that's a type parameter, not a convention.

What does a first agent look like?

This is the smallest working agent, from the README:

client, err := openai.New(openai.Config{
    APIKey: os.Getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
    Model:  "gpt-4o-mini",
})
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

agent, err := golem.New[struct{}, string](client,
    golem.DecodeFunc[string](func(_ context.Context, r model.Response) (string, error) {
        return r.Message.Content, nil
    }),
)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "Why is Go ideal for AI agents?")
fmt.Println(result.Output)
fmt.Printf("Tokens: %d input, %d output\n", result.Usage.InputTokens, result.Usage.OutputTokens)

You build the agent once with golem.New and run it many times. It needs a model and an output decoder, and the decoder is the line where untrusted model text becomes a value your program is willing to use. Everything else is an option function. The result carries the typed output, the full normalized conversation and cumulative token usage.

How do typed tools and dependencies work?

Most agent bugs I've seen live in tools. A tool needs a database, an HTTP client or a user identity, and frameworks often solve that with globals or closures, which makes tools hard to test. In Golem a tool is a typed value, and its Exec function receives the run's dependency value directly:

type Database struct {
    Users map[int]string
}

getUser := tool.MustNew(tool.Tool[Database]{
    Name:        "get_user",
    Description: "Look up a user name by their ID.",
    Schema: json.RawMessage(`{
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}},
        "required": ["id"]
    }`),
    Exec: func(ctx context.Context, db Database, args json.RawMessage) (tool.Result, error) {
        var input struct {
            ID int `json:"id"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(args, &input); err != nil {
            return tool.Result{}, err
        }
        name, ok := db.Users[input.ID]
        if !ok {
            return tool.Text("User not found"), nil
        }
        return tool.Text(name), nil
    },
})

agent, err := golem.New[Database, string](client, decoder,
    golem.WithTools[Database, string](getUser),
)

result, err := agent.Run(ctx, golem.RunContext[Database]{Deps: Database{Users: map[int]string{42: "Alice"}}}, "Who is user 42?")

The schema is written by hand and the arguments arrive as raw JSON. That's deliberate. Arguments are untrusted model output, and I'd rather you see the validation than have reflection do it somewhere you can't read. It costs a few more lines per tool, and in return a tool's behavior is visible in the file where it's defined.

What happens when a run goes wrong?

A Golem run is a transparent loop, and each failure has a named place to land.

How does an agent correct bad output?

When the model returns bad output or bad tool arguments, the cheapest fix is often to say what was wrong and ask again. A decoder or tool does that by returning an error that wraps *model.ModelRetry:

if input.N <= 0 {
    return "", &model.ModelRetry{Err: fmt.Errorf("n must be positive, got %d", input.N)}
}

The run feeds that message back to the model. Self-correction is opt-in, with separate budgets from WithOutputRetries and WithToolRetries, so a model can't argue with your validator forever. With no budget, the same error fails the run at a named stage with its cause intact. A failure the model should simply see, like a missing file, is &tool.Failed{Reason}: the model gets the reason as a tool result and no retry budget is spent.

How do you survive provider errors?

Transient provider errors (408, 429, 5xx and transport faults) are retried with WithMaxAttempts. The default is one attempt, so retries are opt-in. Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles and caps at 30 seconds unless you supply your own. Tool and decode failures are never retried by this mechanism, since they aren't transport problems.

When retrying isn't enough, model.NewFallback(primary, backup) tries models in order. For streams there's one rule: a fallback only happens before the first fragment is forwarded, because after the caller has seen output, switching models would replay it.

How do you stop a runaway agent?

Two limits cover it. golem.UsageLimit bounds input, output and total tokens, model requests and tool calls, and a dollar cost if you supply a price table with WithPrice. Token counts come from the provider's reported usage, so a token limit only trips when the provider reports usage, while requests and tool calls are counted by the run itself. Pricing is yours to supply, because I don't want to ship a table that goes stale between releases, and the library says plainly that the cost estimate is only as good as your rates and isn't a billing guarantee.

The second limit is loop detection, added in v1.2.0 (ADR 0051). WithLoopDetection(maxRepeats) counts calls to the same tool with canonically equal arguments across the whole run, and fails the run before the offending call executes. That ordering is the point: a model that polls a tool can't repeat a side effect while you wait for the check. WithLoopPolicy adds checks for repeated results, alternating A-B calls and repeated final text, with a choice between stopping the run and nudging the model.

Oversized tool output is the quieter cost. WithToolOutputLimit caps a tool result before it enters the conversation, keeps the head and tail, and appends a marker with the original size (ADR 0050).

What do you keep when a run fails?

When a run fails on turn six, you still want turns one to five. Golem attaches them to the error as RunError.Partial: the conversation through the last completed turn, the usage so far and the counts of requests and tool executions. Pass Partial.Messages to RunWithHistory to resume instead of starting over, which matters when the run has already spent real money.

How does an agent wait for a person?

Some tools shouldn't run without sign-off: deleting files, moving money, sending email. A tool defers by returning an error wrapping *tool.Deferred, of kind tool.DeferApproval or tool.DeferExternal. The other tool calls in that batch execute, and Run returns successfully with Result.Pending listing what's waiting. No further model call happens.

You resume with RunWithDeferredResults, passing the paused conversation and a decision for each pending call. Approved calls run, denied calls tell the model it was denied, and external results are inserted as given. Because a pause is a returned value, you can store it, show it in a UI and resume it hours later from another process. The reasoning behind that boundary is in the case for keeping meaningful actions with people.

Can a Go agent use MCP?

The Model Context Protocol is now the usual way to expose tools to agents, so Golem includes a client. mcp.NewStdio starts a server as a subprocess, mcp.NewHTTP connects to a remote endpoint, and mcp.AsTools turns the server's tool list into ordinary tool.Tool values with the server's own schema. A server error flagged as isError comes back as a correctable ModelRetry, and protocol or transport failures fail the run instead of being quietly corrected.

The guide says one thing I agree with: don't reach for MCP when a typed Go tool is one function away. A subprocess speaking JSON-RPC has more moving parts than a function call.

How do you test an agent without a model?

Agent tests are usually flaky (a real provider) or meaningless (mocked HTTP). Golem ships testmodel, a scripted in-memory model that plays back the responses you queue and records the exact request the agent sent:

client := testmodel.New().Respond(
    model.Response{Message: model.Message{Role: model.RoleAssistant, Content: "pong"}},
)
agent, _ := golem.New[struct{}, string](client, decoder)
result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "ping")

You can assert on the normalized request, the ordered messages in Result.Messages and which stage failed, with no network, keys or sleeps. The repository's CI runs its suite with the race detector, plus a fuzz target on the message JSON format.

How does it compare with other Go agent frameworks?

I compared Golem with the three other Go options I'd look at: langchaingo, Eino and Genkit for Go. I read each repository's source tree and go.mod on 27 November 2026. Dependency counts are the non-indirect lines in the require block, so they're approximate, and frameworks move fast, so check upstream before you depend on a detail.

Golem langchaingo Eino Genkit (Go)
Direct dependencies 0 About 60 About 10 About 40
License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0
MCP client In the core module Not in the repository Separate eino-ext module Plugin in the repository, client and server
Pause for human approval tool.Deferred, resumable Not found Interrupt and resume in adk Tool approval middleware
Retry and model fallback Built into the run Not found Retry and failover in adk Retry and fallback middleware
Design centre One explicit agent loop with typed dependencies LangChain-style chains and agents Graph and workflow composition Flows with OpenTelemetry tracing

Two things stand out. Golem is the only one with no dependencies outside the standard library, and the only one where a tool receives a typed dependency value for the run. I haven't found an equivalent of RunContext[Deps] in the others, but I haven't audited every API, so read that as what I found, not a proof.

The other half is that Golem is not alone on the guardrails. Genkit's Go module ships MCP, retry, fallback and tool approval as plugins and middleware, and Eino's adk package has retry, failover and interrupt-and-resume. Only langchaingo lacks them in the repositories I read. The Golem README understated Genkit on this.

The others are ahead in other places. Eino's graph model is more expressive than Golem's linear loop for branching, parallel and multi-agent pipelines, and it has more community components. langchaingo covers more providers and vector stores. Genkit has first-party Google tooling and tight Gemini integration. What Golem offers is a smaller surface: one runtime for a single agent inside a service, with the controls in the core module instead of in add-on packages.

When should you pick something else?

Pick Golem if you want agents inside a Go service, typed dependencies, a module with nothing else to audit and tests that run offline. Pick something else if your agent is mostly prompt experimentation, if you need a graph engine for complicated multi-agent pipelines, or if you need a large catalog of prebuilt integrations today. Python is still ahead on that last one, and I won't pretend otherwise. Golem also has no evaluation harness and no durable workflow engine, and v1.0.0 lists both as non-goals.

Herbie, a self-hosted chat and workflow app I built, runs its Go backend on Golem. I don't have production numbers to publish yet, so everything above is design reasoning plus what the repository's tests and examples show.

The documentation site has a guide for each feature, and examples/ has runnable programs for nearly all of them, several with no API key.

  • Project page: the Golem overview and capability matrix
  • Repository: github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem
  • Docs: abubakarsiddik31.github.io/golem
  • API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you try it and something feels un-Go-like, I want to hear about it.

Frequently asked questions

What is Golem?
Golem is an open-source AI agent framework for Go. It provides typed agents, tools with dependency injection, structured output, MCP support, and controls like retries, usage limits, loop detection and human approval.

Does Golem have external dependencies?
No. It uses only the Go standard library.

Which LLM providers does it support?
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Can I test agents without calling an API?
Yes. The testmodel package gives you a deterministic fake model, and the examples run offline.

Does it support MCP?
Yes. The mcp package is a client for stdio and streamable HTTP servers, and mcpserver exposes an agent as an MCP tool.

title: 金融服务业迁移至云服务：企业学习知识库
description:
金融服务业迁移至云服务：企业学习知识库

原始出处将云迁移的重点放在对冲基金研究、阿尔法因子分析、另类数据回测、量化投资研究、投资组合风险管理以及交易法规合规性上。 这是一个具有教育和探索性质的页面，而非 AWS 参考架构、迁移操作手册（Runbook）、监管评估，也不是已部署生产平台的证明。

高管学习

金融服务业的云迁移不仅是一个技术项目，更是业务、风险、数据和运营模式的变革。 来源指出了数据安全与合规、数据主权、性能与延迟、成本管理、停机时间以及与遗留系统的整合为主要顾虑。 这些顾虑是相互关联的。 如果一项设计提高了敏捷性，却丢失了数据血缘、增加了延迟、削弱了恢复能力、破坏了权限控制或产生了无法控制的成本状况，这就算不上是一次成功的金融行业（FSI）迁移。

来源中最实用的迁移模式是渐进式现代化。 发现现有资产，选择一个非关键的小型试点，逐步引入云功能，监控两个环境，验证结果，并通过受控且可回退的割接（Cutover）过程来转移流量。 这种模式缩小了变更的爆炸半径（影响范围），但并不能免除对依赖性分析、数据核对、安全测试、业务批准、运营就绪度和经过测试的回滚计划的需求。

来源中的 AWS 服务列表最好被理解为可用功能的目录。 Application Discovery Service 可支持依赖性发现，EC2 可支持虚拟机工作负载，Lambda 和 API Gateway 可支持特定的事件驱动接口，RDS 可提供托管关系型数据库，DMS 可支持数据库迁移，Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 可托管应用程序，Elastic Load Balancing 可分配流量，而 CloudWatch 可支持监控和日志记录。 正确的选择取决于工作负载在数据、延迟、韧性、监管、运营和兼容性方面的要求。

FSI 迁移驱动因素与决策背景

数据安全与合规性被列为首要顾虑，并以 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS 为例。 这些规范的作用域或义务并不相同，其适用性取决于机构、客户、产品、司法管辖区、数据以及处理活动。 云迁移应从法人实体和数据处理盘点开始，而不是假设云提供商的总体安全态势即可证明合规。

数据主权意味着将数据或特定的处理活动保留在规定的地理边界内。 区域（Region）选择只是该决策的一部分。 机构必须确认主要数据、副本、备份、日志、快照、支持访问权限、开发副本、灾难恢复环境以及下游分析可以存放的位置。 跨境传输、分包商、运营访问、保留、删除、法定保存以及市场数据许可，都会影响所允许的设计。

性能与延迟必须以业务术语来定义。 量化研究作业、投资组合风险计算、市场数据消费者、订单管理功能和实时执行路径，具有不同的延迟与确定性要求。 迁移应建立针对吞吐量、响应时间、百分位延迟、并发性、排队、恢复行为和依赖调用的基线和目标测量值。 笼统地声称云服务具有可扩展性，并不能证明特定的 FSI 工作负载能达到其所需的性能。

成本管理是一项明确的顾虑，因为云消耗会随工作负载量、存储增长、数据传输、并行处理、日志记录、复制和恢复副本而变化。 有效的商业案例必须将云运营的完整成本与现有资产的完整成本进行比较，包括迁移期间的双轨运行、数据源许可、支持、安全工具、网络连接、测试、人员配置和合规证据。 预算和成本报告是控制机制，不能替代量化的总成本模型。

停机时间与遗留系统整合，对于持续运行或有严格业务日历的金融系统尤为重要。 迁移设计应确定割接窗口、上下游依赖关系、外部交易对手、市场节假日、核对期、批处理截止时间，以及最大可接受的中断时间。 遗留系统可能还需要专有协议、固定的网络位置、共享文件、大型机接口或无法被通用云端点替代的紧密耦合数据库行为。

目标 FSI 工作负载边界

页面标题将迁移主题与对冲基金活动、阿尔法因子库、另类回测策略、量化投资研究、投资组合风险管理和交易法规合规性联系在一起。 这些主题暗示了候选工作负载，例如历史市场数据处理、研究数据管理、因子计算、回测、投资组合分析、风险报告和合规支持。

来源并未确认目标是实时订单管理系统、交易所网关、市场数据设施、撮合引擎或执行平台。 它没有提供经纪商连接、交易所连接、订单路由逻辑、交易监控实现或生产投资组合账本。 除非有额外证据表明对延迟敏感或受监管的执行功能在范围内，否则该页面应用于讨论研究和支持系统的迁移模式。

工作负载分类应区分核心记录系统与分析副本、实时服务与批处理服务、有状态应用程序与无状态服务，以及受监管处理与实验环境。 它还应记录业务关键性、数据敏感度、市场时间、延迟预算、吞吐量、恢复目标、许可限制以及负责任的业务所有者。 这些属性决定了一个工作负载应被重新托管（Rehost）、重新平台化（Replatform）、重构（Refactor）、替换（Replace）、保留（Retain）还是退役（Retire）。

绞杀者无花果迁移模式（Strangler Fig Pattern）

来源将其运营流程称为“绞杀者无花果模式”，并描述了五个阶段：评估、试点、重构、监控和割接。 评估阶段检查现有应用程序并识别适合迁移的组件。 试点阶段将一个小型的非关键组件移至云端。 重构阶段则逐步以云托管的微服务取代单体架构的部分组件。 监控贯穿整个过渡期。 最终，割接阶段将流量转移到新实现上。

该模式之所以有用，是因为它避免将迁移视为一次性不可逆的事件。 它允许组织在转移更关键功能之前，先了解网络连接、安全性、性能、运营和成本。 尽管如此，试点仍必须使用明确的标准进行选择。 “非关键”应当意味着该组件的故障、数据泄露、延迟或错误结果对业务和监管的影响是有限的，而不仅仅是因为它的用户少。

绞杀者迁移并非在所有情况下都需要微服务。 机构可以逐步通过托管服务、模块化应用程序、批处理管道，或保留在受控接口后面的遗留组件来替换特定功能。 微服务可能会引入分布式事务、运营开销、版本控制挑战和新的故障模式。 现代化选择应遵循领域边界和控制要求，而不是将微服务视为理所当然的终点。

评估与发现

第一项实际活动是对应用程序、接口、数据存储、批处理作业、身份、基础设施、外部提供商、用户、许可和运营程序进行结构化的盘点。 来源提到了 AWS Application Discovery Service 作为了解应用程序依赖关系和性能指标的工具。 其输出结果应与访谈、架构记录、网络证据、日志、业务流程图和监管清单相结合，因为自动化发现本身无法识别每一个业务或控制依赖。

评估应捕获每个依赖关系的调用方向、协议、频率、负载、身份验证、数据分类、故障行为、超时、重试、排序和所有权。 它应识别数据库、文件共享、队列、计划任务、参考数据、市场数据源、报告目的地、下游消费者和外部交易对手。 对于交易或风险环境，分析还应记录市场日历、截止时间、时区、事件时间语义、修正行为以及对延迟或丢失数据的处理方式。

每个候选迁移波次都应有明确的范围、业务目标、风险评级、源和目标所有者、验收标准、依赖关系、回滚方法和证据计划。 评估应区分技术可行性与监管许可。 一个应用程序在技术上可能很容易移动，但仍可能因数据驻留、许可、运营韧性、记录保存、外包或模型治理义务而不适合迁移。

目标架构与 AWS 服务角色

来源提出 EC2、Lambda、API Gateway 和 RDS 作为云原生架构的构建块。 EC2 适用于需要操作系统控制、与现有软件兼容或采用渐进式直接迁移（Lift-and-shift）路径的工作负载。 Lambda 适合具有兼容执行、超时、状态和打包特征的受限事件驱动功能。 API Gateway 可提供受管的接口边界，但受制于身份验证、授权、节流、Schema（模式）、版本控制和可用性要求。 RDS 可以减少数据库管理，但必须明确选择目标引擎、版本、事务行为、扩展、连接模型、备份策略和兼容性。

Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 被列为应用程序部署选项。 它们代表不同的运营模型，不应被视为可互换的标签。 选择取决于组织是否需要应用程序平台抽象、容器编排、部署控制、服务发现、扩展行为、网络集成和运营责任。 目标架构还应定义如何管理机密、配置、镜像、补丁、日志、指标、追踪和回滚版本。

Elastic Load Balancing 用于流量分配。 确切的负载均衡器类型和路由设计必须与协议、连接生命周期、TLS 终止、客户端身份、健康检查、路径路由、WebSocket 或流式传输行为、源 IP 要求和延迟目标相匹配。 单靠流量分配无法提供应用程序的正确性。 健康检查必须代表有意义的业务就绪状态，且故障转移（Failover）绝不能将请求路由到可达但无法处理权威数据的服务。

CloudWatch 被提出用于性能监控和日志记录。 监控应超越基础设施利用率，涵盖业务和控制指标，如事务完整性、队列时间、核对状态、错误分类、依赖健康、数据新鲜度、身份验证失败、权限变更、延迟百分位、成本异常和恢复信号。 日志应有明确的保留期、访问控制、时间同步、脱敏、完整性保护，以及通往事件响应和审计证据的路径。

数据库与数据迁移（使用 AWS DMS）

来源指出 AWS Database Migration Service 用于数据库迁移，并将数据传输描述为“无缝的”。 “无缝”应被视为一种愿景，而非保证。 受控的数据库迁移必须指定源和目标引擎、Schema 兼容性、全量加载行为、变更数据捕获（CDC）行为、事务排序、主键和序列处理、类型转换、字符编码、时区、大对象、存储过程、权限、索引和下游依赖。

迁移计划必须定义在共存期间哪个环境是权威的。 如果遗留和云数据库都接受写入，组织需要冲突解决和核对模型。 如果只有一方接受写入，复制方向、延迟容忍度、中断行为和割接程序必须明确。 该计划应检测重复、丢失、乱序、截断或转换的记录，并应保留目标完整且正确的证据。

金融服务数据迁移需要时间点正确性。 历史分析、风险、估值和监控可能依赖于事件发生时存在的参考数据和市场状态。 迁移应保留源时间戳、业务日期、生效日期、修正历史、数据血缘，以及原始数据和重述数据的区别。 备份、副本、快照、测试环境和提取的文件必须继承适当的分类和保留控制。

数据质量关卡应比较记录数、余额、头寸、总计、校验和、键分布、空值率、参照完整性、事件序列和业务核对。 异常应被保留并分配给所有者，而不是被报告技术成功的导入所隐藏。 不能仅因为复制已经追平就宣布目标就绪；业务部门必须确认生成的数据能支持预期的计算、报告、控制和下游接口。

应用程序现代化与遗留系统集成

来源建议逐步用云托管的微服务取代单体应用的组件。 安全的现代化计划首先要识别有边界的业务能力及其数据所有权。 每个新组件都需要契约、版本控制策略、身份验证模型、幂等性行为、超时和重试规则、可观测性、部署流程和定义好的单一事实来源（Source of truth）。 分布式服务还需要明确处理部分故障、重复消息、排序、最终一致性和跨服务事务。

遗留系统集成应被设计为一等边界。 来源提到新的云系统应该与本地系统（On-premises）交互，但没有定义网络连接、路由、DNS、身份联合、私有服务访问、加密、防火墙所有权、延迟预算或故障行为。 迁移必须确定遗留系统如何发现云服务，云工作负载如何访问保留的系统，凭证如何管理，以及当任一方不可用时由哪个团队响应。

共存期通常比最终架构更复杂。 接口可能需要转换，数据可能暂时重复，用户可能需要跨系统的一致视图，运营团队可能需要支持两种部署和事件模型。 过渡设计应指定共存的持续时间、每个数据域的权威系统、退役旧组件的条件，以及在遗留基础设施下线前所需的证据。

迁移服务与部署选择

来源列出了用于数据库迁移的 AWS Database Migration Service、用于服务器迁移的 AWS Server Migration Service、用于传输大量数据的 Snowball，以及用于某些应用程序或数据保留在本地的混合场景的 AWS Outposts。 这些名称应被视为来源参考，在放入迁移计划之前，需要检查当前的产品状态、区域可用性和能力。 特别是，任何使用特别指名的 AWS Server Migration Service 的计划都应验证当前受支持的服务和替换路径。

Snowball 或其他批量传输设备可以减少初始大型数据传输相关的时间或网络负载。 它本身并不能解决监管链、加密、源和目标核对、增量变更、传输重试、许可或最终割接问题。 迁移团队必须定义如何验证初始副本，以及在设备导出后进行的变更如何同步。

当机构需要将选定的 AWS 基础设施或服务置于客户地点作为混合设计的一部分时，Outposts 才是相关的。 它不是实现数据主权、灾难恢复或法规遵从的自动答案。 设计必须考虑受支持的服务、硬件容量、网络连接、补丁管理、本地运营、故障替换、依赖行为、物理安全、数据位置，以及本地 AWS 环境不可用时的恢复路径。

安全性、隐私与合规

来源将 IAM、VPC 以及静态和传输中加密确认为核心 AWS 安全功能。 这些是重要的基础，但它们并不构成完整的 FSI 控制环境。 IAM 应包括联合身份、最小权限角色、工作负载身份、特权访问控制、紧急破窗（Break-glass）程序、职责分离、访问权限复核、服务账户治理，以及变更和审查的证据。

VPC 设计应定义账户和环境边界、子网放置、路由、安全组、网络访问控制、私有端点、流量检查、入站和出站策略、DNS、日志记录，以及与本地系统和外部提供商的连接。 公开暴露应是经过深思熟虑且最小化的。 服务应相互验证、验证输入、使用适当的网络路径，并生成由负责团队监控的安全遥测数据。

加密需要的不仅仅是勾选复选框。 机构必须定义密钥所有权、密钥分离、创建和轮换、访问策略、恢复、撤销、审计日志记录，以及加密备份和副本的处理。 敏感数据可能还需要令牌化、脱敏、字段级保护或受限的分析副本。 日志和监控数据可能包含受监管信息，必须对其进行分类，而不是假设其是安全的。

页面提到了 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS，但没有提供适用性分析或控制映射。 它没有识别持卡人数据环境、个人数据盘点、跨境传输依据、保留规则、市场行为义务、交易记录要求或外包评估。 迁移应将实际的法律和监管义务映射到系统、数据、流程、提供商、证据和控制所有者。 云服务可以支持合规性，但如果没有机构特定的设计和持续运营，它们无法确保合规性。

韧性、高可用性与业务连续性

来源将数据丢失、初始性能下降、安全漏洞、意外的云成本和割接停机时间确定为迁移风险。 它建议使用安全控制、成本工具、Auto Scaling、多可用区（Multi-AZ）部署、沙盒测试和专家指导作为降低这些风险的方法。 这些功能有助于实现韧性，但它们不能自动防止风险或证明端到端的可用性。

Auto Scaling 有助于应对选定的容量模式，多可用区部署可减少区域内特定基础设施故障的影响。 两者都不能确定应用程序的恢复时间、恢复点、事务完整性、依赖可用性或故障下的性能。 韧性设计应定义服务级别目标、RTO、RPO、依赖假设、备份和还原目标、区域恢复、网络分区行为、降级模式操作，以及来自受控测试的证据。

来源建议通过 AWS Backup 进行自动备份，使用 Outposts 或其他 AWS 灾难恢复解决方案的灾难恢复计划，CloudWatch 告警，迁移失败时回滚到本地，以及在云平台得到验证之前保留本地系统的冗余。 这些是有用的主题，但实施方案必须指定备份范围、保留、不可变性、加密、跨账户或跨区域副本、还原授权、还原测试、告警所有权，以及支持的恢复架构。 仅说“AWS 灾难恢复解决方案”不足以作为精确的设计描述。

冗余必须包括数据、计算、身份、网络、可观测性、外部提供商和运营程序。 一个应用程序可以有多个实例，但如果它依赖于一个数据库写入器、一条身份路径、一条网络路由、一个市场数据提供商或一本未经验证的运行手册，它仍会发生故障。 连续性演练应根据工作负载的风险状况，测试实例、可用区、区域、连接路径、提供商、数据库副本、凭据路径和关键依赖项的丢失情况。

割接与回滚纪律

来源中绞杀者无花果模式的最后一步是将所有流量切换到基于云的实现。 生产割接应该是分阶段且可逆的，而不是被视为一次性切换。 团队应定义流量路由控制、并行验证、写入所有权、数据核对、观察窗口、审批权限、回滚阈值以及关闭变更的条件。

当两个环境都处理了不同的写入后，有状态系统的回滚将非常困难。 在结构变更（Schema changes）、标识符变更、外部确认、下游发布或不可逆副作用发生后，回滚也可能变得不安全。 有效的回滚计划必须指定权威副本、复制方向、最大回滚窗口、运行中事务的处理、核对过程、用户和交易对手沟通以及恢复的业务批准。

只要风险评估要求，本地系统就应保持可用，但仅仅保留硬件并不能使回滚成为可能。 必须对遗留路径进行维护、同步、保护、监控和测试。 在最终割接之前，迁移至少应进行一次实际的回滚或恢复演练，并应记录证据、局限性和补救措施。

成本治理与 FinOps（财务运营）

AWS Budgets 和 Cost Explorer 被来源列为管理和预测成本的工具。 它们可以提供可见性和阈值告警，但不会确立责任，也无法防止每次成本超支。 迁移应定义账户和环境边界、标签、成本分配、业务所有权、预算阈值、预测审查、新服务审批以及针对异常消耗的升级流程。

成本模型应包括计算、数据库、存储、检索、快照、备份、复制、跨区域和互联网传输、日志、监控、安全服务、迁移工具、网络连接、许可、支持、硬件设备、混合基础设施、测试、双轨运行、人员和专业服务。 它应区分固定和可变成本、生产和非生产成本，以及正常运营与韧性和迁移成本。

成本优化绝不能损害数据保留、市场数据权限、可恢复性、性能或证据保存。 生命周期策略、调度、规模合理化（Rightsizing）、承诺使用决策和数据删除应根据业务和监管要求进行审批。 单位成本衡量指标（例如每次投资组合估值成本、每次回测成本、每条迁移记录成本或每次监控事件成本）比总云端账单能使商业案例更有意义。

监控与运营就绪度

CloudWatch 被建议用于性能监控和日志记录，CloudWatch 告警被建议用于迁移警报。 运营就绪的平台应监控技术、业务、安全、数据和成本信号。 技术信号包括可用性、延迟百分位、错误、饱和度、队列时间、连接健康和依赖状态。 业务信号包括交易计数、余额、头寸、数据新鲜度、核对、损益（PnL）、报告完成和异常队列。

监控必须有阈值、基线、通知路由、升级规则、服务所有者、运行手册和证据保留。 不导致责任响应的告警不是有效的控制。 日志应时间同步、进行访问控制、防止未经授权的更改、在必要时脱敏，并在遗留环境和云环境之间建立关联，以便在跨越迁移边界时重建事件。

每次迁移波次前都应审查运营就绪度。 审查应确认支持覆盖范围、待命（On-call）所有权、部署和回滚程序、访问审批、仪表板、警报、容量、备份、恢复测试、事件分类、供应商联系人、用户沟通和培训。 只有当团队在正常和降级条件下都能操作新组件时，试点才算成功，而不仅仅是因为该组件在沙盒中运行。

治理与迁移运营模型

来源建议使用 AWS 专业服务（Professional Services）和 AWS 解决方案架构师提供专家指导，并使用沙盒环境进行测试。 这些可以提供有用的技术支持和安全的学习场所，但它们不能取代机构对架构、风险接受、安全性、合规性、数据治理或生产运营的责任。

企业迁移需要高管赞助、迁移授权机构、业务和应用所有者、云平台团队、安全和隐私所有者、数据所有者、网络和身份所有者，以及运营、财务、合规、法务、供应商管理以及适用的独立控制或模型审查。 应明确批准范围、接受残余风险、授权割接、宣布回滚和关闭迁移发现等职责。

运营模型应包括受管的着陆区（Landing zone）、账户和区域战略、策略执行、集中式日志记录、身份生命周期、资产盘点、漏洞和补丁管理、基础设施即代码、发布控制、证据保留、例外管理、第三方监督和定期的韧性演练。 来源并未描述这些机制，因此它们是必须完成的设计工作，而不是所列 AWS 服务的隐含特征。

迁移验收关卡

不能仅仅因为某个应用在 AWS 中启动了就接受该迁移波次。 安全验收应展示批准的身份、网络路径、加密、密钥控制、漏洞态势、日志记录和事件响应。 数据验收应展示完整性、核对、数据血缘、时间点行为、保留以及对异常的正确处理。

性能验收应在具有代表性和压力的工作负载下（包括依赖调用、并发性、延迟百分位、吞吐量和故障行为），将目标与商定的基线进行比较。 韧性验收应展示备份和还原、恢复目标、依赖故障处理、监控、运营运行手册以及经过测试的回滚或恢复路径。 成本验收应证明消耗、预测、所有权和单位经济效益已被理解。

业务和合规验收应确认用户可以完成所需的流程，报告和计算核对无误，受监管的记录保持可用，数据驻留和许可要求得到满足，并且控制所有者审查了证据。 每个关卡都应有一个具名的审批人和被记录的例外流程。 只有当残余风险被理解、限制、记录并正式接受时，迁移才能带着残余风险继续进行。

Capital One 案例研究声明

来源引用 Capital One 作为一个迁移到 AWS 并实现敏捷性、可扩展性和成本节约的真实示例。 它链接到 AWS 案例研究页面 https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/capital-one。 来源没有提供迁移范围、日期、工作负载清单、基线、测量出的成本节约、架构、监管边界，或者哪些成果可以转移到其他机构的资格说明。

该示例可作为进一步研究的提示，而不是同样结果也会在另一个 FSI 环境中发生的证据。 任何重复该声明的内部演示都应使用当前官方的案例研究，确定其中描述的具体工作负载和结果，区分客户报告的结果与 AWS 一般能力，并避免将公共案例研究视为机构特定的商业案例。

来源声明与验证边界

该页面提出了几个需要限定的广泛声明。 它描述 AWS DMS 提供无缝数据传输，将 Auto Scaling 和 Multi-AZ 呈现为确保高可用性，建议使用 Outposts 或未指明的 AWS 灾难恢复解决方案作为灾难恢复计划，并得出结论认为遵循这些步骤即可确保法规遵从性。 这些陈述是有用的起点，但没有一项足以作为实施或保证声明。

来源不包含数据量、事务率、延迟、可用性、成本、节约、迁移持续时间、人员配置、RTO 或 RPO 的量化数据。 它不包含除链接之外的 Capital One 成果证明、没有 AWS 账户或部署的证据、没有目标架构、没有当前产品状态验证、也没有监管控制映射。 页面的三张图片为演示资产，没有添加任何可读的、技术的、数值的或架构的内容。

服务名称和描述在使用前应对照当前的 AWS 文档进行检查。 特别是，点名的 AWS Server Migration Service 可能是过时的产品参考，应确认当前受支持的迁移路径。 确切的 Elastic Load Balancing 选项、数据库引擎、DMS 模式、部署平台、备份设计、混合服务和灾难恢复架构必须根据当前能力和机构要求进行选择。

内部学习总结

持久的教训是将业务能力、数据和控制措施一起迁移。 从发现和关键性评估开始，选择有边界的试点，保留清晰的事实来源（Source of truth），验证数据和性能，在共存期间刻意运营双方系统，并且只有在安全性、韧性、成本、合规性和业务验收证据齐备时才进行割接。

AWS 服务可以为发现、计算、数据库、应用程序托管、流量管理、数据传输、监控、备份、成本可见性和混合部署提供构建块。 它们不能消除对架构、治理、测试、运营所有权或监管判断的需求。 对于 FSI 而言，迁移质量的衡量标准不是流量转移到云端有多快，而是在迁移完成后，机构是否能继续保护数据、服务客户、履行义务、从故障中恢复、解释其记录并控制其成本。
