title: 7 Claude Tricks Every Developer Must Know to Write Better Code
description:
Most developers know that Claude can write code.

It can explain Python functions.

Debug JavaScript.

Generate SQL queries.

Review APIs.

And help build applications.

But here's something I've been thinking about:

Are we using Claude as a coding assistant, or are we actually learning how to work with it as an engineering tool?

There's a difference.

Asking Claude to write a function is easy.

Getting it to understand your project, respect architectural decisions, investigate bugs, run tests, and work within clearly defined boundaries is another matter.

And that's where things become interesting.

Today, I want to share seven practical Claude tricks that developers should explore, particularly if they're using Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent.

These aren't magic prompts.

They're ways to make AI-assisted development more structured, reliable, and useful.

1. Stop Explaining Your Project Every Time. Use CLAUDE.md.

Imagine opening Claude Code and repeatedly explaining the same things.

"We use TypeScript."

"Don't add unnecessary dependencies."

"Run the tests before finishing."

"Follow our existing API conventions."

"Don't modify the database migrations."

If you're repeating these instructions across sessions, there's a better approach.

Claude Code supports a project instruction file called CLAUDE.md.

You can create one manually or generate a starting version using: /init

Then refine the file with the information Claude genuinely needs.

For example:

Project Instructions

Stack

  • TypeScript
  • Node.js
  • PostgreSQL

Development Rules

  • Follow existing project conventions.
  • Prefer simple solutions.
  • Avoid unnecessary dependencies.
  • Do not modify database migrations without explicit approval.

Verification

  • Run npm test.
  • Run npm run lint.
  • Report any failing checks.

The benefit isn't simply convenience.

You're making important project context reusable.

But there's a catch.

Don't turn CLAUDE.md into a 50-page instruction manual.

Keep it focused on conventions, commands, and decisions that aren't obvious from the codebase.

And remember: project instructions guide the model; they don't enforce hard security boundaries.

For sensitive actions, use actual permissions and controls.

My takeaway: If you have to explain something repeatedly, it probably belongs in a reusable project instruction.

2. Use Plan Mode Before Claude Touches Your Code

Here's a mistake I think developers should avoid.

You ask an AI coding assistant to implement a feature.

It immediately begins editing files.

A few minutes later, you discover it misunderstood the requirement.

Now you're reviewing changes you never wanted.

Claude Code has a useful feature called Plan Mode.

You can start a session in Plan Mode with:

claude --permission-mode plan

Or switch modes during an interactive session until Plan Mode is active.

In this mode, Claude can inspect the project and propose an approach without directly editing your source files.

Try something like:

I want to add rate limiting to this API.
Before implementing anything:

  1. Inspect the existing architecture.
  2. Identify where rate limiting belongs.
  3. Compare two possible approaches.
  4. Identify security and performance risks.
  5. List the files that would need changes.
  6. Propose a minimal implementation plan. Do not modify any files yet.

This changes the conversation.

Instead of immediately discussing code, you're discussing engineering decisions.

You can challenge the plan.

Remove unnecessary complexity.

Clarify requirements.

Then authorize the implementation.

I particularly like this approach for changes involving authentication, databases, APIs, and existing production systems.

My takeaway: Sometimes the best thing AI can do before writing code is help you decide what code should exist.

3. Give Claude a Test, Not Just a Task

Most developers ask AI to complete a task.

"Fix this function."

"Build this endpoint."

"Add this feature."

But how will Claude know the work is actually finished?

A function that looks correct isn't necessarily correct.

An endpoint that returns HTTP 200 isn't necessarily behaving as intended.

A successful build doesn't guarantee the feature works.

So here's a more useful technique.

Give Claude a way to verify its work.

For example:

The login endpoint fails when a session expires during token refresh.

Investigate the relevant code.

  1. Reproduce the problem with a failing test.
  2. Identify the root cause.
  3. Make the smallest reasonable fix.
  4. Run the relevant tests.
  5. Check for regressions.
  6. Summarize the changes and test results. Do not claim the issue is fixed unless the verification succeeds.

That's a much stronger request than:

"Fix my authentication bug."

Claude Code can run available test commands when permitted and inspect their results.

That doesn't eliminate the need for human review.

But it gives the development process a feedback loop.

And feedback loops are critical.

I've explored a related problem in Most Developers Test Their Code. Why Don't They Test Their AI?.

My takeaway: Don't ask AI to produce a solution without defining how the solution will be checked.

4. Use Subagents to Investigate Problems Without Filling Your Main Conversation

Here's something developers working on larger projects should know.

When an AI assistant explores a large codebase, it may read numerous files, search through logs, and investigate multiple components.

That information consumes context.

And not all of it needs to remain in your main conversation.

Claude Code supports subagents that can perform focused tasks in separate context windows.

For example:

Use a subagent to investigate how authentication and token refresh work
in this codebase.
Identify:

  • Important files.
  • Main execution flow.
  • Failure handling.
  • Potential inconsistencies. Return a concise summary with file references. Do not modify the code. The subagent can investigate and return its findings without dumping every intermediate detail into the main conversation.

You can use the same approach for code review, debugging research, or exploring unfamiliar parts of an application.

However, subagents aren't free performance boosters.

They may consume additional usage and can still make mistakes.

And there's little reason to delegate a trivial task that could be answered immediately.

My takeaway: Use subagents when separating the work improves clarity, not simply because running multiple agents sounds impressive.

5. Learn When to Use /compact and /clear

Have you ever worked through a long AI conversation where the assistant gradually became less focused?

You've discussed one bug.

Then another feature.

Then a database migration.

Then an architecture question.

Eventually, the conversation contains so much information that you can barely remember what the original task was.

Claude Code provides tools for managing that context.

Use:

/compact

to summarize the conversation and reduce its context usage.

You can also specify what should be preserved:

/compact keep the current architecture
decisions, changed files, and test results

And when you're moving to an unrelated task:

/clear

starts a fresh conversation.

These commands serve different purposes.

/compact helps preserve useful continuity while summarizing older material.
/clear removes conversation history from the new task.

Compaction isn't perfect, of course. A summary may omit details you later need.

For important decisions, keep the source of truth in your project files, specifications, or tests rather than relying entirely on conversation memory.

My takeaway: Managing context is part of managing an AI development workflow.

6. Connect Claude to the Tools Your Workflow Actually Needs

One of the more useful developments in AI-assisted programming is the ability to connect models to external tools.

Claude Code supports integrations through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Depending on the integrations you configure, these can help Claude access relevant development resources such as issue trackers, documentation, and other services.

For example, imagine debugging an issue.

Your normal workflow might involve:

Opening a ticket.

Reading the acceptance criteria.

Searching the repository.

Reviewing relevant documentation.

Checking logs.

Then investigating the problem.

With a carefully configured tool integration, Claude may be able to access some of that information within the same workflow.

That's much more useful than copying and pasting disconnected snippets into a chat.

You can inspect MCP connection status in Claude Code using: /mcp

But here's an important warning.

More tool access is not automatically better.

Only connect trusted servers.

Review the permissions you're granting.

Avoid exposing secrets or unnecessary production data.

Treat external tool responses as potentially untrusted input.

And require explicit approval for sensitive or destructive actions.

The objective isn't to give an AI agent unrestricted access to everything.

It's to provide the smallest useful set of capabilities for the task.

My takeaway: Better AI workflows often require better connections, but those connections need boundaries.

7. Automate Your Development Rules With Hooks

This might be one of the most useful tricks for developers working repeatedly with Claude Code.

Suppose you always want a formatter to run after Claude edits source files.

You can write:

"Remember to run the formatter."

But what happens if the instruction is overlooked?

What if the conversation becomes long?

What if another developer uses the same repository?

Claude Code supports hooks that can trigger configured actions at specific points in its workflow.

For example, a PostToolUse hook can run a formatting command after an appropriate file edit.

You can inspect and configure hooks through: /hooks

The important idea is that the formatter is executed through a configured mechanism rather than relying entirely on a conversational instruction.

This distinction matters.

There are rules we want AI to consider.

And there are checks we want the development environment to enforce.

They're not necessarily the same thing.

Examples of useful automated checks include formatting, linting, and selected validation steps.

For more sensitive controls, combine hooks with appropriate permission rules, sandboxing, and normal repository protections.

Hooks can execute commands, so their configuration deserves careful review.

My takeaway: If a check must happen consistently, don't rely solely on the model remembering to do it.

The Bigger Lesson: Claude Isn't Your Engineering Process

After looking at these seven capabilities, I think an important pattern emerges.

None of the most valuable techniques are simply about generating more code.

They're about improving the development process.

CLAUDE.md provides project context.

Plan Mode encourages better decisions.

Tests provide verification.

Subagents help organize investigation.

Context management improves focus.

MCP provides controlled access to useful tools.

Hooks help automate repeatable checks.

Together, these capabilities can make AI-assisted engineering more structured.

But they're not a substitute for engineering judgment.

A bad requirement can still produce a bad implementation.

An incorrect architectural assumption can still cause problems.

Tests can still miss important cases.

And an AI-generated fix can still introduce regressions.

That's why I increasingly believe the developer's job is not just to tell AI what to build, but to design the conditions under which its work can be trusted.

Don't Measure AI Development Only by Speed

Imagine two developers using Claude.

Developer A generates a feature in 10 minutes.

Developer B takes 30 minutes to clarify the requirement, review the architecture, implement the feature, and run verification.

Who is more productive?

We can't answer that from the time taken alone.

What if Developer A's feature introduces a production bug?

What if Developer B's implementation is easier to maintain?

What if both implementations are equally good?

We need to measure the outcomes, not simply the speed of code generation.

This is a principle I also emphasize in my work at ReThynk AI: AI evaluation should consider the quality, reliability, and value of the complete workflow, not merely whether the underlying model produced an output.

For teams looking beyond individual coding tricks, our AI Evaluation Framework: 7 Critical Metrics for AI Success explores how to think more systematically about assessing AI performance.

Because the goal isn't to make developers type fewer characters.

The goal is to help them build better software.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • What's the difference between Claude and Claude Code?

Claude is Anthropic's AI assistant, which can help with programming questions, code explanations, and other tasks through a conversational interface.

Claude Code is designed for development workflows and can interact with project files, execute supported commands, and use development tools with configured permissions.

Several techniques in this article, such as CLAUDE.md, Plan Mode, and hooks, specifically refer to Claude Code.

  • Which Claude trick should a beginner try first?

I would start with Plan Mode.

Before asking Claude to build something, ask it to examine your requirements, identify assumptions, and propose a simple implementation plan.

Then add a clear way to verify the result.

You don't need complicated agent architectures to benefit from structured AI-assisted development.

  • Can Claude Code replace human code review?

I wouldn't treat it as a complete replacement.

Claude can help identify suspicious logic, missing tests, and potential maintainability issues.

But it may misunderstand requirements, overlook vulnerabilities, or recommend unnecessary changes.

Human review and appropriate automated testing remain essential, especially for security-sensitive and high-impact systems.

Final Thoughts

I think we're entering an interesting stage of software development.

Knowing how to ask AI to write a function is becoming commonplace.

The bigger opportunity is learning how to make AI useful across the entire engineering workflow.

Not by adding as many tools and agents as possible.

But by creating better context, clearer boundaries, stronger verification, and simpler processes.

The best Claude trick isn't a secret command.

It's knowing how to turn AI assistance into a reliable engineering practice.

And that's a skill worth developing.

title: Charge Once, Retry Forever: Idempotency Keys in Spring Boot
description:
A client sends POST /payments. The network hiccups, the client times out and sends the same request again. Did the customer just pay twice?

Without protection, yes. Retries are not a corner case: mobile apps retry on flaky connections, API gateways retry on 5xx, users double-click "Pay", and message consumers redeliver. Every one of those can turn into a second charge if the server treats each request as new.

The standard answer is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it in a header. The server promises that the same key produces the same effect once, no matter how many times it arrives. Stripe, Adyen and PayPal all work this way.

The idea is simple. The details are where duplicate charges sneak back in: two requests racing with the same key, a key reused for a different amount, or a provider that fails halfway. I built a small Spring Boot project, idempotency-demo, that handles those cases and proves them with tests. This article walks through what it contains and why each piece is there.

  • Source: https://github.com/josesaid/idempotency-demo
  • Project page: https://josesaid.github.io/idempotency-demo/
  • Diagrams: English · español

What the repo contains

Item Value
Language Java 21
Framework Spring Boot 3.3.5 (Web, Data JPA)
Database H2 in memory, table idempotency_record
Endpoints POST /payments, GET /payments/executions
Tests 3 integration tests, including 8 concurrent requests 
com.mx.development.jose.said
├── idempotency/
│   ├── IdempotencyRecord.java      entity: UNIQUE key, request hash, status, stored response
│   ├── IdempotencyRepository.java  findByKey
│   └── IdempotencyReserver.java    reserve / complete / release, each in its own transaction
└── payment/
    ├── PaymentController.java      POST /payments
    ├── PaymentFacade.java          the idempotency logic
    └── PaymentService.java         simulated provider (2 s latency, counts real charges)

PaymentService sleeps two seconds on purpose, so concurrent requests really overlap, and counts how many times it actually ran. GET /payments/executions exposes that counter, which makes "did we charge twice?" a question you can answer with one curl.

The contract

Every request ends in exactly one of these answers:

Situation Answer Provider called?
New key 201 Created Yes, once
Same key, same body, already completed 200 OK with the stored response No
Same key, same body, still processing 409 Conflict No
Same key, different body 422 Unprocessable Entity No
Provider throws Key released, error returned Retry may charge

Only the first row ever reaches the provider.

The record: a key, a hash and a status 

@Entity
@Table(name = "idempotency_record")
public class IdempotencyRecord {

    public enum Status { PROCESSING, COMPLETED }

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    // The database, not the application, guarantees one row per key
    @Column(name = "idem_key", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 100)
    private String key;

    // SHA-256 of the request body: detects a key reused for another payment
    @Column(name = "request_hash", nullable = false, length = 64)
    private String requestHash;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Status status;

    // What retries get back once the payment is done
    @Column(name = "response_body", columnDefinition = "TEXT")
    private String responseBody;
}

Three fields carry the whole design:

  • unique = true on the key is the real lock. More on that below.
  • requestHash lets the server tell "the same request again" from "a different request with a recycled key".
  • status + responseBody let the server say "still working" (409) or replay the original answer (200).

Reserve before you charge

The facade's main method is short:

public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> createPayment(String key, PaymentRequest request) {
    String hash = requestHash(request);

    Optional<IdempotencyRecord> existing = repo.findByKey(key);
    if (existing.isEmpty()) {
        try {
            reserver.reserve(key, hash);            // try to be first
        } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
            // Another request with the same key won the race: answer from its row
            return handleExisting(repo.findByKey(key).orElseThrow(), hash);
        }
        return process(key, request);
    }
    return handleExisting(existing.get(), hash);
}

The key step is reserve. Before calling the provider, the facade inserts a row with status PROCESSING and commits it. That commit is what lets every other request see "someone is already charging this key".

@Service
public class IdempotencyReserver {

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void reserve(String key, String requestHash) {
        // saveAndFlush forces the INSERT now; a duplicate key throws right here
        repo.saveAndFlush(new IdempotencyRecord(key, requestHash));
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void complete(String key, String responseJson) {
        IdempotencyRecord record = repo.findByKey(key).orElseThrow();
        record.setStatus(IdempotencyRecord.Status.COMPLETED);
        record.setResponseBody(responseJson);
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void release(String key) {
        repo.findByKey(key).ifPresent(repo::delete);
    }
}

Two details matter here:

  1. REQUIRES_NEW: each method commits on its own. If the reservation lived inside one big transaction that also wrapped the two-second provider call, no other request could see the PROCESSING row until the end. That is exactly the window where duplicates happen.
  2. A separate bean: @Transactional works through a Spring proxy. If PaymentFacade called its own @Transactional method, the proxy would be bypassed and the annotation silently ignored. Moving these methods into IdempotencyReserver makes them go through the proxy.

The common mistake

This version looks fine and is wrong:

// ❌ Check-then-act: both concurrent requests pass the check
if (repo.findByKey(key).isEmpty()) {
    PaymentResponse r = paymentService.process(request);   // charged twice
    repo.save(new IdempotencyRecord(key, hash, r));
}

Two requests that arrive together both see "no row" and both charge. The lookup is only an optimization. The protection is the UNIQUE constraint plus inserting before charging.

Who wins a race? The database

Scenario D in the repo sends two (in the test, eight) requests with the same new key at the same time:

  1. Both run findByKey and both get Optional.empty().
  2. Both call reserve. Request A's INSERT commits first.
  3. Request B's INSERT hits the unique index; H2 raises error 23505, Spring translates it to DataIntegrityViolationException.
  4. B catches it, reads A's row, sees PROCESSING and answers 409 Conflict.
  5. A charges, stores the response and answers 201.
  6. When B retries later, it finds COMPLETED and gets 200 with A's paymentId.

The full step-by-step diagram is on the project page: Scenario D · Concurrent requests.

Hash first, then status 

private ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> handleExisting(IdempotencyRecord record, String hash) {
    if (!record.getRequestHash().equals(hash)) {
        return ResponseEntity.unprocessableEntity().build();        // same key, different body
    }
    if (record.getStatus() == IdempotencyRecord.Status.PROCESSING) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).build();  // still running
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(fromJson(record.getResponseBody()));   // replay stored response
}

The order matters. If a client reuses pago-001 for a 999.00 payment, replaying the stored 150.00 response would hide a client bug and the customer would never be charged the 999.00. Checking the SHA-256 of the body first turns that bug into a clear 422, even while the original request is still PROCESSING.

The hash is computed over the JSON that Jackson produces for PaymentRequest:

private String requestHash(PaymentRequest request) {
    byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
            .digest(mapper.writeValueAsBytes(request));
    return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest);
}

When the provider fails: release the key 

private ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> process(String key, PaymentRequest request) {
    try {
        PaymentResponse response = paymentService.process(request);
        reserver.complete(key, toJson(response));
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(response);
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        reserver.release(key);   // free the key so the client can retry
        throw e;
    }
}

Without release, a failed payment would leave its row in PROCESSING forever, and every retry would get 409. Deleting the row, again in its own transaction, makes the key usable again.

One honest caveat: releasing is only safe when you know the provider did not charge. After an ambiguous timeout, a production system should ask the provider for the payment status (ideally passing the same idempotency key downstream) before releasing.

Proving it with tests

The integration test fires eight requests with the same key and counts real charges:

@Test
void peticionesConcurrentesMismaClave_cobranUnaSolaVez() throws Exception {
    String key = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    int before = executions();
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);

    List<Callable<ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse>>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        tasks.add(() -> post(key, request("250.00")));
    }
    List<Future<ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse>>> futures = pool.invokeAll(tasks);

    // ... collect status codes ...
    assertThat(executions() - before).as("real charges").isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(statuses.stream().filter(s -> s == HttpStatus.CREATED).count()).isEqualTo(1);
}

The other two tests check that a retry returns the same paymentId with a single charge, and that a reused key with another body gets 422. When the suite runs you will see seven Unique index or primary key violation lines in the log: those are the seven losers of the race, which is exactly what should happen.

Try it yourself 

git clone https://github.com/josesaid/idempotency-demo.git
cd idempotency-demo
mvn spring-boot:run

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Idempotency-Key: pago-001" \
  -d '{"accountFrom":"ACC-1","accountTo":"ACC-2","amount":150.00,"currency":"MXN"}'
# 201 the first time, 200 with the same paymentId on every retry

curl http://localhost:8080/payments/executions
# {"executions":1}

The diagrams

The project page has an overview (the path of one request, the decision flow and the states of a row) plus one sequence diagram per scenario, in English and Spanish:

Scenario English Español
A · First request (201) Diagram Diagrama
B · Retry with the same key (200) Diagram Diagrama
C · Same key, different body (422) Diagram Diagrama
D · Concurrent requests (201 + 409) Diagram Diagrama
E · Provider failure (500 → 201) Diagram Diagrama

Best practices checklist

  • ✅ Let the database enforce uniqueness of the key; never rely on a read-then-write check.
  • ✅ Reserve before calling the external system, and commit the reservation in its own transaction.
  • ✅ Store a hash of the request and reject reused keys with a different body (422).
  • ✅ Store the response and replay it; the retry must look like success to the client.
  • ✅ Answer 409 while the first request is in flight, so clients back off and retry.
  • ✅ Release the key only when you are sure nothing was charged.
  • ⚠️ Add a TTL or cleanup job; the demo keeps records forever.
  • ⚠️ Scope keys per client or account in multi-tenant systems, so two clients cannot collide.

Performance notes

The happy path costs one indexed SELECT, one INSERT and one UPDATE, each a short transaction. Retries cost a single SELECT and never touch the provider. The losers of a race fail fast on the unique index instead of waiting on a lock. In production, keep idem_key indexed (the UNIQUE constraint does that), keep the stored response small, and purge old rows on a schedule.

Takeaways

Idempotency keys are not about the header; they are about where the guarantee lives. In this repo it lives in a UNIQUE constraint, a reservation committed before the charge, a hash that catches misuse, and a stored response that makes retries boring. Clone idempotency-demo, run mvn test, and watch eight concurrent requests produce exactly one charge.

If you read my previous article on the transactional outbox, this is the other half of the story: the outbox makes sure events are delivered at least once, and idempotency makes sure "at least once" never becomes "charged twice".

title: Back up MongoDB to S3: from mongodump to a verified restore
description:
Most MongoDB backup guides stop at the mongodump command line. That is the
easy part. What decides whether you get your data back is everything around it:
what the dump leaves out, which options change what you will be able to restore,
whether the script really fails when the dump fails, and whether anyone has ever
replayed the file.

This guide covers the whole chain. By the end you will know what a mongodump
holds and what it leaves to the server, when --oplog is worth anything, how to
write a backup script that cannot report success on an empty file, how to
restore the archive by hand in a throwaway container, and which questions asked
in mongosh tell you a restored database actually holds your data.

Everything here works with mongodump, docker and the AWS CLI, and nothing else.

What a mongodump backs up, and what it leaves out

mongodump reads documents over the server protocol, like any other client. So
it backs up data, not a server:

  • users and roles are not part of it. They live in the admin database, in system.users and system.roles; a dump limited to your business database does not hold them, and the restore then gives an intact database where no application account exists;
  • neither is the server configuration: the instance settings, the replica set membership, the sharding layout of a partitioned cluster;
  • nor the other databases on the same server, unless you ask for a full dump.

Indexes, on the other hand, are in the dump — their definition, not their
content. mongorestore writes the documents first, then rebuilds each index. On
a large collection that is where most of the restore time goes, and it is the
reason a restore is almost always slower than the dump that produced it.

A dump is not a copy of the data directory

Both are defensible, but they do not give you the same thing.

A dump is logical: the documents are read back, reinserted, the indexes rebuilt.
It restores into another version of MongoDB, onto another machine, into a
different topology — a dump taken on a replica set reloads onto a standalone
server.

A copy of the data directory (--dbpath) is physical: these are the storage
engine's files. It restores much faster on large volumes, but it is only valid
for the same MongoDB version and the same storage engine, and it cannot be taken
by copying the files of a running server — you have to stop it, or go through a
filesystem snapshot that captures the journal along with the data.

For a database of a few gigabytes, mongodump stays the simple choice: one
file, readable by any recent MongoDB.

The options that decide what you will be able to restore

--archive writes everything into a single stream instead of a tree of BSON
files. That is one object to upload instead of a directory to synchronise, and
mongorestore reads it back as is.

--gzip compresses. With --archive, the compression happens in the stream: no
intermediate file, and mongorestore --gzip reads it back without decompressing
first.

--oplog changes the nature of the backup. Without it, a dump that takes
several minutes mixes documents read at different moments: an order can appear
without the billing line written in the same transaction. With it, mongodump
records the oplog position before starting, then appends the operations that
happened while reading, and mongorestore --oplogReplay replays them at the
end: the result is the state of the database at one point in time. Two
conditions: the oplog only exists on a replica set, and the option only applies
to a full dump of the instance, not to a --db.

Finally, the database name is inside the dump. mongodump records each
collection under its full namespace, shop.orders, and mongorestore
writes it back under that same name. Renaming the file changes nothing. That is
what makes the mistake in the restore section so easy to make.

The backup script 

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

ts=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
dest=s3://backups-shop/mongo

mongodump --host mongo.internal --port 27017 --db shop --archive \
  | gzip > "/backups/shop_${ts}.archive.gz"

aws s3 cp "/backups/shop_${ts}.archive.gz" "${dest}/"

Without pipefail, a failed dump comes out as a success

In mongodump | gzip, the shell only looks at the exit code of the last
link. gzip compresses an empty stream very nicely, so the script returns 0
and cron is happy. set -o pipefail — included in the set -euo pipefail
above — makes the whole line fail as soon as mongodump fails. The variant
without a pipe, --archive=/backups/... --gzip, removes the problem at the
source: mongodump writes the file itself and its exit code is the
command's.

Keep the timestamp in the file name: a file always overwritten under the same
name leaves no chance of going back to yesterday. For retention, a lifecycle
rule on the bucket deletes objects older than N days with no script to maintain.

The account taking the dump needs to read the whole database. A role that is too
narrow raises no visible error: it produces a dump where the collections it
cannot see are simply missing.

That leaves running it every night. A cron is enough, on two conditions: that
its error output goes somewhere someone reads, and that a run dragging on does
not overlap with the next one — flock -n on a lock file settles the second
point in one line.

Restoring once, by hand

A backup is only proven once restored. Do it once, in full, in a throwaway
container — it is also the procedure you will follow the day it matters.

docker run -d --name mongo-test mongo:7
until docker exec mongo-test mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.runCommand({ping:1})'; do sleep 1; done

docker cp /backups/shop_20260918_010000.archive.gz mongo-test:/tmp/dump.gz
docker exec mongo-test mongorestore --archive=/tmp/dump.gz --gzip --drop \
  --nsInclude 'shop.*' --stopOnError

--drop removes each collection before rewriting it: without it, a restore into
a container already used mixes the documents of two attempts. --stopOnError
stops at the first refused insert, instead of carrying on and handing you a
half-restored database that looks like it works.

The database name is the dump's, not the one you want

If the archive was taken on a database named store, the --nsInclude
'shop.*' above matches nothing: mongorestore restores no document,
and exits with success. Nothing in the database warns you, because there is
no database. To restore under another name, you have to say so:
--nsFrom 'store.*' --nsTo 'shop.*'.

Use the same major version as your server instead of mongo:7 if it differs: a dump taken on a newer server does not necessarily replay on an older one.

Note how long it took. That is your real restore duration, the only one worth
comparing to the delay you promised.

What to check in a restored database

mongorestore finishing without an error does not mean the data is there. Four
questions, in this order, from a mongosh opened on the container:

use shop
show collections
db.orders.countDocuments()
db.orders.find().sort({ created_at: -1 }).limit(1)
db.orders.getIndexes().length
  1. The collections are there. An empty list means an --nsInclude that recognised nothing, or an empty dump that replayed perfectly.
  2. The documents are there. countDocuments() really counts, unlike estimatedDocumentCount(), which reads the collection metadata and can report documents that are no longer there. Compare against the order of magnitude in production, not an exact number.
  3. The data is recent. The most recent document should be yesterday's, not last month's. That is what catches a backup job that stopped running without saying anything.
  4. The indexes were rebuilt. A collection back with its documents but without its indexes behaves correctly and answers in seconds instead of milliseconds. On a production database put back in service, that is enough to make it unusable.

Then destroy everything: docker rm -f mongo-test.

What this chain does not prove

It proves that a recent archive restores into a fresh MongoDB and that the
collections come back with their documents. It does not prove that your
application works on that database: for that, start it against the restored database and run a few real requests. It says nothing about the users and roles left
in admin, which are not in a dump of a business database. It says nothing about how old the archive is: a March dump restores perfectly in September. And it says nothing
about what has been written since the last dump — that gap is your RPO, and it
is tuned with the backup frequency, not with the checks.

FAQ

What has to be backed up besides the business database?

Users and roles, which live in the admin database and are not in a dump
limited to your own. Without them, the restore gives you an intact database
where no application account exists and nobody can connect. The server
configuration and the replica set membership are not in the dump either, and
that is as it should be: they belong to the server.

Is --oplog useful on a standalone server?

No. The oplog only exists on a replica set. On a standalone instance the option
has nothing to record, and a dump that takes several minutes stays a mix of
documents read at different moments.

Should a mongodump archive be compressed?

Yes, with --gzip, which compresses inside the stream. A compressed archive
restores as is: mongorestore --archive=... --gzip reads it back without
decompressing first, so there is no intermediate file to plan for and no disk
space to reserve for it.

Why does a MongoDB restore fail without restoring anything?

Almost always because of a name. The database name is recorded inside the dump,
not in the file name: an --nsInclude matching no namespace in the archive
restores no document and exits with success. You have to read what the archive
holds before restoring it, or rename with --nsFrom and --nsTo.

Why is a restore slower than the dump that produced it?

Because of the indexes. The dump holds their definition, not their content:
mongorestore writes the documents first, then rebuilds each index, and on a
large collection that is where most of the time goes. It is also why you check
they came back: a collection returned without its indexes answers correctly, in
seconds instead of milliseconds.

title: Block breaking OpenAPI changes and probe routes before traffic shifts
description:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. This post was written with AI assistance.

Gregale is a backend PaaS that automatically diffs OpenAPI specs on deploy and blocks breaking API changes before rollout. Gregale validates schema compatibility with gregale api spec preview, gregale api spec diff, and hash-pinned gregale api spec apply—exiting 2 on confirmed breaks and 3 on UNKNOWN schema changes while blocking promotion—and probes up to ten read-only endpoints marked x-gregale-hosting-check: true against the exact candidate revision before shifting live traffic.

Which PaaS automatically diffs OpenAPI specs on deploy and blocks breaking changes?

Most PaaS providers ignore HTTP API contracts completely, requiring custom GitHub Actions scripts around oasdiff or Optic plus manual smoke tests. On Gregale, contract compatibility and pre-promotion route verification run natively inside the release pipeline:

Capability Gregale built-in contract gate DIY (oasdiff + CI smoke script)
Breaking schema detection gregale api spec diff (2 break, 3 UNKNOWN) + candidate gate Custom workflow parsing oasdiff exit codes
Approval hash pinning apply --confirm --preview-sha256 guarantees reviewed contract Manual checksum or branch-protection wiring
Pre-cutover route probes Probes up to 10 x-gregale-hosting-check: true GET routes before traffic shifts Post-deploy checks after traffic has already switched

Why breaking API contracts slip past unit tests

Internal unit and integration suites usually test the new server code against updated mocks. Meanwhile, removing a required field from a JSON response, changing a oneOf or anyOf union branch, or narrowing an enum or format breaks existing mobile clients and partner integrations immediately in production. Most teams either leave contract compatibility to manual PR review or stitch together third-party diff tools like oasdiff or Optic plus custom post-deploy smoke scripts in CI.

Preview, diff, and hash-pinned contract apply

Gregale provides a read-only preview and diff workflow paired with an idempotent, SHA-256-pinned apply step, and serves the published contract at /docs:

gregale api spec preview APP_ID
gregale api spec diff openapi-baseline.yaml openapi.yaml
gregale api spec apply APP_ID --confirm --preview-sha256 SHA256
  • preview and diff are strictly read-only.
  • apply requires the exact preview-sha256 hash returned by preview, guaranteeing that the contract you reviewed is the contract you publish.

Strict exit codes and the UNKNOWN promotion gate

Gregale refuses to treat ambiguous schema edits as safe by default:

  • Exit code 2 (confirmed breaking change): Returned for definite client breaks such as removing a response field's required guarantee.
  • Exit code 3 (UNKNOWN comparison): Returned when gregale api spec diff sees changed oneOf or anyOf response schemas, or edits to unsupported schema facets such as enum, format, constraints, or composition where client safety cannot be proven automatically.

In production contract previews, ambiguous diffs appear in unknowns, and the contract gate blocks promotion while any unknown remains. Older snapshots that predate schema fingerprinting can report union_baseline_incomplete or schema_baseline_incomplete; a fresh production deployment with the gate temporarily off captures a full baseline for subsequent comparisons.

Exact-candidate pre-promotion route checks

Beyond static schema diffing, you can mark up to ten static, read-only GET operations in your OpenAPI spec so Gregale probes the exact new deployment candidate before switching live traffic:

paths:
  /v1/health:
    get:
      x-gregale-hosting-check: true
      responses:
        '200':
          description: API is ready

Checks follow strict safety and determinism rules:

  • Only explicitly marked operations are probed, using an empty GET with no redirects, path parameters, or query strings.
  • Pass criteria: 2xx, 3xx, 401, or 403. Treating 401 and 403 as healthy means you can confirm that an auth-protected route is wired and answering on the new candidate without embedding customer credentials in your deploy pipeline.
  • Fail criteria: 404, 429, or 5xx fails the candidate before production traffic moves.

Each route result and the imported OpenAPI document's hash are stored in the deployment hosting receipt. Specs without marked operations fall back to Gregale's standard health and connectivity gates.

What it does and does not replace

Pre-promotion route checks prove that each marked route answered cleanly on the exact candidate revision; they do not parse response JSON bodies against schemas at runtime, nor do they substitute for runtime error monitoring. Pair OpenAPI hosting gates with canary deploys with automatic rollback so any runtime regression in real traffic still rolls back automatically.

See OpenAPI hosting, Release safely, and Errors for full usage details.

FAQ

How does Gregale block breaking OpenAPI changes before deployment?

Run gregale api spec preview, diff and hash-pinned apply --confirm --preview-sha256. Confirmed breaks such as dropping a required response field exit with code 2, while ambiguous oneOf, anyOf, enum, or format edits report UNKNOWN with exit code 3 and block promotion.

How do pre-promotion OpenAPI route checks handle authenticated endpoints?

Mark up to ten static, read-only GET operations with x-gregale-hosting-check: true. Gregale probes the exact new candidate and treats 2xx, 3xx, 401, and 403 as passes while failing 404, 429, and 5xx, proving auth-gated routes exist without storing test credentials.

Do OpenAPI checks replace runtime canary rollouts?

No. Route checks confirm candidate reachability and exit 2/3 rules catch static schema regressions before traffic shifts, while Gregale canary rollouts monitor real production error rates after promotion.

title: How I Built a 93 KB Client-Side GIF89a & WebCodecs Studio Without COOP/COEP Headers
description:
Most browser-based GIF editors take one of two trade-offs: they either upload every frame to a remote processing server, or they ship a ~30 MB WebAssembly FFmpeg bundle that requires strict Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy headers.

While building Offline GIF Editor, I wanted a zero-upload studio that opens instantly under a strict 95 KB raw core JS budget, runs 100% locally in the browser with zero COOP/COEP headers, and still handles real-world edge cases like animated transparency disposal, chat file-size caps, and multi-format video exports.

Here are the four engineering decisions that made the biggest difference:

1. Keep an Immutable baseDelay Per Frame to Eliminate Speed Drift

GIF frame delays are quantized to centiseconds (10 ms ticks). If you multiply frame delays in place when a user clicks 2x and then 1x, rounding error accumulates quickly—and custom loop repeat counts often get silently overwritten.

Instead, store each frame's original baseDelay separately and recompute active delays from that baseline whenever the user toggles 0.5x, 2x, 3x, or 1x. In the GIF Speed Changer, that keeps 2x -> 3x -> 1x bit-exact and preserves custom loop counts.

2. Edge-Connected Flood-Fill Transparency Instead of Global Chroma Key

Global color replacement ruins stickers and UI captures: removing white backgrounds also punches holes through eyes, highlights, or text labels.

Seeding a breadth-first flood fill strictly from the border pixels (plus optional click seeds) with a real-time canvas preview and auto-detected 5-color frame swatches solves this cleanly. You can test the live cutout behavior on the GIF Background Remover, where interior white pixels remain 100% opaque while border regions export clean GIF89a alpha.

3. Lazy-Load gifsicle-wasm Only When Compression Is Requested

Discord animated emojis cap at 256 KB and Slack animated emojis cap at 128 KiB. Shipping a WASM optimizer on initial page load hurts Core Web Vitals, so the core workbench boots with lightweight JS decoding/encoding (gifuct-js + gifenc) and only lazy-imports gifsicle-wasm-browser when the user opens the GIF Compressor or clicks an Auto-Fit preset.

4. Pure-JS Animated WebP/APNG Frame Compositing + WebCodecs MP4

Safari/WebKit still handles multi-frame transparent WebP and APNG inconsistently when drawn straight to a canvas. Extracting frame chunks in pure JS, decoding via createImageBitmap, and compositing disposal rectangles manually keeps 100% alpha parity across Chrome and WebKit in WebP to GIF, while WebCodecs handles hardware-accelerated H.264 exports in GIF to MP4.

Everything runs completely on-device with zero uploads and zero login at offlinegifeditor.com. Feedback from anyone else working with binary image codecs in the browser is very welcome!

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: I Built an Open-Source App Store on Top of GitHub Releases Using Rust and Tauri 2.0
description:
Installing great open-source desktop software usually means jumping from blog post to GitHub repository, scrolling past source tarballs in the Releases tab, guessing which .AppImage, .deb, .dmg, or .exe matches your CPU architecture, and repeating the whole routine manually when an update drops.

I wanted a single interface for that workflow, so I built Open Source Store: a cross-platform desktop app (100% Rust backend with Tauri 2.0 and a vanilla JavaScript + Vite frontend) that treats GitHub Releases as an app store catalog, complete with a live web demo you can open directly in the browser.

  • GitHub Repository: marlonferreira1800-hue/open-source-store
  • Live Web Demo (GitHub Pages): marlonferreira1800-hue.github.io/open-source-store
  • Desktop Installers (v0.1.3): GitHub Releases (Windows .exe/.msi, Linux .AppImage/.deb/.rpm, macOS .dmg)

Why build this instead of using an existing package manager?

Tools like winget, brew, apt, and flatpak are great once you already know what you want to install. They are less helpful when you want to browse visual apps by category, compare project activity and license metadata side by side, or grab the latest release of a smaller GitHub project that hasn't made it into a distro repo yet.

Open Source Store focuses on visual discovery plus direct release installs:

  1. Curated catalog (204 apps): Starts immediately with vetted projects across categories (Development, Utilities, Internet, Multimedia, and more), such as yt-dlp, uv, LocalSend, Logseq, and Ollama.
  2. Live GitHub Search: Searches any public repository on GitHub in real time and applies the store's safety checks before showing an install button.
  3. Local lifecycle tracking: Tracks downloaded apps in installed.json so you can see installed vs. available apps, check for newer GitHub Releases, launch, update, or uninstall them from one tab.

Architecture and Technical Decisions

I kept the stack intentionally lean. The Rust backend (src-tauri/) compiles with opt-level = "s", LTO, and stripped symbols (the Windows NSIS setup binary in v0.1.3 comes out to 2.4 MB), while web/ uses Vite and plain JavaScript modules without a heavy UI framework.

1. Selecting the right release binary across OS and CPU architectures

GitHub Releases do not enforce a naming standard. One project publishes App-linux-amd64.AppImage, another publishes app_0.4.0_x86_64.deb, and both include .sha256 sidecar files and source archives in the same asset list.

In src-tauri/src/platform.rs, asset_score inspects every asset name, filters out source archives and checksum/signature files (.sha256, .sha1, .sha512), rejects mismatched operating systems and architectures (x64 vs. arm64), and scores native installers by preference (for example .msi/.exe on Windows, .AppImage/.deb/.rpm on Linux, .dmg on macOS).

2. Enforcing a 5-gate curation and safety policy

Pointing a downloader at arbitrary GitHub search results carries obvious risks. Every repository and release goes through rules defined in data/curation-policy.json and enforced in src-tauri/src/catalog.rs:

  • Activity and adoption thresholds: Curated entries require at least 3,000 stars, 180 days of repository history, 365 days of owner account age, 3+ releases, and 5,000+ release downloads. Live search uses lighter thresholds (1,000+ stars, 90+ days, 500+ downloads).
  • License allowlist: Accepts recognized open-source licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-*, LGPL-*, BSD-*, MPL-2.0, ISC, etc.).
  • Repo, keyword, and non-app filters: Excludes awesome-lists, documentation-only repos, blocked keywords, and repos without matching platform binaries.
  • Dangerous asset checks: Rejects unsafe asset extensions before offering a download.
  • Strict host allowlisting: Download URLs and HTTP redirects must stay on HTTPS github.com or githubusercontent.com domains.

3. Safe redirects, streaming progress, and SHA-256 checks

GitHub Release downloads bounce through CDN redirects on githubusercontent.com. Rather than letting reqwest follow arbitrary external redirects, src-tauri/src/downloader.rs uses a custom redirect policy that checks every hop, streams bytes to disk while emitting Tauri download-progress events (with cancellation via tokio::sync::watch), and verifies the SHA-256 digest when GitHub reports one on the release asset:

let client = reqwest::Client::builder()
    .user_agent("open-source-store/0.1")
    .redirect(reqwest::redirect::Policy::custom(|attempt| {
        if attempt.previous().len() > 8 {
            attempt.error("Excesso de redirecionamentos")
        } else if is_safe_redirect_url(attempt.url()) {
            attempt.follow()
        } else {
            attempt.error("Redirecionamento bloqueado para domínio externo ao GitHub")
        }
    }))
    .build()?;

4. Handling GitHub API rate limits and the web preview

Unauthenticated requests to the GitHub API cap at 60 requests per hour per IP. Polling 200+ repositories on startup would hit that wall immediately.

To keep startup snappy without requiring a token:

  • The app bundles an embedded snapshot (data/catalog-seed.json) so the initial catalog loads instantly in both desktop and GitHub Pages web mode.
  • The desktop backend caches fetched API responses locally in catalog_cache.json with a 30-minute TTL.
  • Users who do heavy live searching can optionally save a personal GitHub token (save_github_token) in the sidebar settings.

The GitHub Pages deployment reuses the exact same web/ interface with a browser API fallback: you can browse the seeded catalog, inspect security scores and metadata, and run live GitHub searches without installing anything. Only downloading, installing, and updating local apps require the desktop Tauri binary (and the UI tells you when an action is desktop-only).

Try it and help shape what comes next

You can explore the catalog in your browser right now at marlonferreira1800-hue.github.io/open-source-store or download the v0.1.3 installer from GitHub Releases.

The project is MIT-licensed and very early (v0.1.3). I would especially love feedback on:

  • Linux and macOS testing: I develop primarily on Windows, so real-world test reports for the .AppImage, .deb, .rpm, and .dmg packages (and platform.rs asset matching edge cases) are super helpful.
  • Catalog curation: Are there essential open-source desktop apps missing from data/curated.json?
  • Security model: Ideas for tighter signature verification or sandboxed installs.

If this looks useful to you, check out CONTRIBUTING.md, open an issue, or drop a comment below with what you'd expect from a GitHub-powered open-source app store.

title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination
description:
arXiv:2611.33775v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.

title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
description:
arXiv:2611.33165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench

title: A busy database now answers 503 in gophenberg
description:
On 27 November 2026, GitHub Trending's daily Go list is led by tools that put agents to work in parallel: multica-ai/multica gained 173 stars that day and Tencent/LoopForge gained 97, both describing shared task boards or workflows for coding agents. Trendshift's weekly list for the same date shows stablyai/orca gaining 3.2k stars for running a fleet of bots on one subscription, a weekly gain rather than a lifetime total. The dev.to trending page carries a cluster named "Production Error Handling in n8n Automations" with 22 posts in seven days, active one day earlier, about silent failures and retries in automated workflows. Hacker News' front page on that date includes an item on AI agents controlling part of DeepMind's compute at 33 points. The causal link is short: when automated writers share one database, a lock timeout is an ordinary event, and the answer has to name it so the caller can retry instead of believing a save succeeded.

gopherium/gophenberg#681 is one concrete implementation of that answer. gophenberg is a Go publishing server with a Postgres store and a browser editor. The pull request closes issue #550, was opened on 12 November 2026, and was merged on 14 November 2026. Its diff covers 53 files with 935 lines added and 166 removed, across 19 commits. The merge head is 8554209.

What was wrong

A Postgres deadlock or lock timeout arrived at the HTTP layer as an ordinary error with no stable code. errorResponseFor matched a small set of domain errors and auth errors, then fell through to 500 internal. A client reading that answer could not tell contention apart from a real server fault. The release notes in the pull request record two consequences at the editor: a failed save was no longer reported as successful, and unsaved text stayed in the editor so the writer could try again.

The fix has two halves. The store half tags every statement failure with a database class. The server half turns one class into a typed HTTP answer.

The path through the code

At the merge head, internal/postgres/classified.go wraps the database connection in a classified type. Exec, Query and QueryRow each pass the error from the driver through dbkitpg.Classify. The row wrappers do the same for Rows.Err and Row.Scan, so a failure that shows up only while reading results is classified as well. A deadlock detected with SQLSTATE 40P01, or a lock timeout, becomes dbkit.ErrBusy.

internal/server/json.go then maps it in errorResponseFor: dbkit.ErrBusy returns http.StatusServiceUnavailable with the body {"error":"database busy","code":"database_busy"}. Every other unrecognised error still returns 500 internal. There is one deliberate exception. respondReadAfterWrite turns a busy error into the internal answer when a write was already stored, because telling a client to retry at that point could duplicate a save that did land.

A classified deadlock reaches the answer mapper as ErrBusy and leaves as 503 database_busy.

The answer also carries two negative guarantees. wantBusyAnswer in internal/server/busy_test.go asserts that the response has no Retry-After header, so no client retries on its own, and that Cache-Control is no-store, so a busy answer cannot be kept in a cache. The editor shows a message asking the writer to save again, and the decision stays with the person at the keyboard.

What the diff actually contains

The pull request reports 53 changed files. The largest pieces of the diff are these:

File Added Removed
internal/server/busy_test.go 207 0
internal/postgres/classified_internal_test.go 77 0
internal/postgres/groups_failure_test.go 62 17
internal/postgres/classified.go 55 0
frontend/src/test/posts-api.test.ts 37 0

Those figures come from the GitHub files endpoint for pull request #681. The new busy_test.go accounts for 207 added lines on its own, which is why a change that reads as one status code in the API touches 53 files: the class has to be attached at each place a statement can fail, and each response path needs a test that pins the answer.

Authorship

The pull request was opened by Indra Prasetya and merged on 14 November 2026. Nineteen commits are in the branch. Three are authored by me: the first change that surfaced dbkit.ErrBusy, the follow-up on server masking and frontend templates, and the translation entry. Maintainer SirLouen authored the other 16, including the store classifiers, the feature and server tests, the Spanish and French messages, and most of the response changes. The repository belongs to the maintainer. This is a joint branch, not a claim that the whole diff is mine.

Verification I can repeat

At merge head 8554209, internal/server/busy_test.go holds six test functions. Three pin the busy answer for a content save, a media save and a theme change. Two check that a settings patch or a post patch which stored its edit never answers database_busy. The sixth checks that a settings patch storing nothing answers a busy read as database_busy. internal/postgres/classified_internal_test.go holds one more function, which checks that the wrapper marks each failure of the connection. I counted those names from the source files at the merge SHA through the GitHub contents API. I did not run the upstream Go suite on this host, so these are source counts rather than a local test run.

Why this matters

Turning a deadlock into a typed 503 is not a matter of changing one status constant. The database error has to survive three boundaries: the driver, the store wrapper and the HTTP mapper. A read that follows a stored write needs the opposite answer, or a retry would create a duplicate post. Deciding not to send Retry-After keeps the retry decision with the editor and the writer. Those choices are visible in 53 files and 207 lines of new server tests, and they are the part of this fix that a caller can depend on.

Sources: gophenberg#681, its merge head 8554209 and issue #550, retrieved 27 November 2026. Trend sources: Trendshift weekly, GitHub Trending Go, Hacker News and dev.to trending, retrieved 27 November 2026.
