title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2611.33788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models.
  Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
  Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios.
  Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation.
  Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

title: Faster and Better Query (FBQ): Learning Future-Position Probes from the First Generated Token
description:
arXiv:2611.33679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.

title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
description:
arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

title: How to choose Java collection types: List, Set, Map
description:
Originally published at Shipped Code.

Most backend Java code gets by with ArrayList and HashMap, until a method returns a list nobody can add to or a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. How you choose a Java collection comes down to 3 questions. Do you need duplicates and positions? Use a List (ArrayList by default). Do you need uniqueness? Use a Set (HashSet, or LinkedHashSet to keep insertion order, TreeSet to keep it sorted). Do you look things up by key? Use a Map (HashMap, or LinkedHashMap/TreeMap when order matters).

Return List.copyOf(...) from methods so callers cannot change your data, keep LinkedList for the rare case you have measured, and switch to ConcurrentHashMap once several threads write to the same map. The classic trap is removing elements inside a for-each loop, and removeIf fixes it.

This post is for developers who write Java every day. If you are here for a specific exception, jump to Common traps.

Decision table

Need Pick Main trade-off
Ordered items, duplicates allowed, access by index ArrayList Inserting or removing in the middle shifts the elements after it
A fixed list you hand to callers List.of / List.copyOf Throws on any change, rejects null
Unique values, order irrelevant HashSet Iteration order looks random
Unique values in the order they arrived LinkedHashSet A bit more memory than HashSet
Unique values, sorted, range queries TreeSet O(log n) instead of O(1)
Lookup by key HashMap No order; not thread-safe
Lookup by key, keep insertion order LinkedHashMap A bit more memory than HashMap
Lookup by key, sorted, "next key after X" TreeMap O(log n); keys must be comparable
A map shared between threads ConcurrentHashMap No null keys or values

The Java backend roadmap puts collections in stage 1, modern core Java, and lists what to learn next.

Blocks titled Main.java are complete files that run with java Main.java on JDK 21.0.11. The others are excerpts that need imports and a main method.

Lists

ArrayList is the right default for nearly every list in a backend, such as DTOs for a response, rows from a query or items in a cart. It stores elements in one array, so reading by index is O(1), and iterating walks one contiguous block of references.

LinkedList looks better on paper for inserts in the middle, but you first have to walk to that position node by node, and each node is a separate object scattered across the heap. For typical backend lists it rarely beats ArrayList, and this post does not try to prove that with timings. The one job it does well is a queue, and ArrayDeque does that job too, without the per-node objects.

The interesting choice is how to make a list read-only. Java gives you 4 ways, and they behave differently.

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> source = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));

        List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
        List<String> copy = List.copyOf(source);
        source.add("c");

        System.out.println("view = " + view);   // sees the new element
        System.out.println("copy = " + copy);   // snapshot

        List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList("x", "y");
        fixed.set(0, "z");                      // allowed
        System.out.println("fixed = " + fixed);

        try {
            copy.add("d");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("copy.add -> " + e);
        }
    }
}

view = [a, b, c]
copy = [a, b]
fixed = [z, y]
copy.add -> java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

The view changed after it was created, because Collections.unmodifiableList only blocks writes through the wrapper. Anyone holding source can still change what your caller sees. List.copyOf takes a snapshot, and List.of builds an immutable list from values. Arrays.asList is the odd one, because you can replace elements but cannot add or remove them. The last line shows copy.add failing with an empty exception message, which makes the error hard to search for.

For a method that returns a list, return List.copyOf(items); is the safe default, as long as the list holds no null (see Common traps).

Sets

A common use for a Set in a backend is cleaning up ids from a request, for example ?ids=42,7,42,19,7. All 3 implementations remove the duplicates. They differ only in the order you get back.

List<Long> requested = List.of(42L, 7L, 42L, 19L, 7L);

System.out.println("HashSet       " + new HashSet<>(requested));
System.out.println("LinkedHashSet " + new LinkedHashSet<>(requested));
System.out.println("TreeSet       " + new TreeSet<>(requested));

HashSet       [19, 7, 42]
LinkedHashSet [42, 7, 19]
TreeSet       [7, 19, 42]

The HashSet order comes from hash buckets, and the specification does not promise it. If those ids end up in a JSON response or a cache key, use LinkedHashSet so the output is stable and matches what the client sent. Use TreeSet when the result should be sorted anyway.

Hash-based sets decide "same element" with equals and hashCode. A record generates both from its fields, so 2 records with the same values count as one. A plain class without those methods compares by identity.

record SkuKey(String sku, String warehouse) {}

static class SkuClass {             // no equals/hashCode
    final String sku, warehouse;
    SkuClass(String sku, String warehouse) { this.sku = sku; this.warehouse = warehouse; }
}

// add new SkuKey("TSHIRT-M", "HN") twice to one HashSet, then SkuClass twice to another

records: 1
plain class: 2

That second line is how duplicate rows sneak into a "unique" set. Records are the simplest fix for composite keys like this one.

For JPA users, entity collections (Set versus List in Hibernate) have their own rules, which the post on N+1 queries covers.

Maps

The most common map in a service is a lookup by id. You build it once from a list, then each get is O(1) instead of a scan through the list.

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    record User(long id, String name, String team) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<User> users = List.of(
            new User(1, "An", "mobile"),
            new User(2, "Binh", "backend"),
            new User(3, "Chi", "mobile"));

        Map<Long, User> byId = new HashMap<>();
        for (User u : users) byId.put(u.id(), u);
        System.out.println(byId.get(2L).name());
        System.out.println(byId.getOrDefault(99L, new User(0, "unknown", "-")).name());

        Map<String, List<String>> byTeam = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (User u : users) {
            byTeam.computeIfAbsent(u.team(), t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(u.name());
        }
        System.out.println(byTeam);
    }
}

Binh
unknown
{mobile=[An, Chi], backend=[Binh]}

computeIfAbsent creates the list the first time a team appears and returns the existing list after that, which replaces the usual if (!map.containsKey(...)) block. The grouping map is a LinkedHashMap, so teams come out in the order they first appeared. Streams can do the same with Collectors.toMap and groupingBy; the next post in this series covers them.

Reach for TreeMap when the question is "what is the next key after X?". Free appointment slots are a good example.

TreeMap<LocalTime, String> slots = new TreeMap<>();
slots.put(LocalTime.of(9, 0), "room 1");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(10, 30), "room 2");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(14, 0), "room 1");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(16, 15), "room 3");

LocalTime now = LocalTime.of(10, 5);
System.out.println("next slot:   " + slots.ceilingKey(now));
System.out.println("before noon: " + slots.headMap(LocalTime.NOON));
System.out.println("from 14:00:  " + slots.tailMap(LocalTime.of(14, 0), true));

next slot:   10:30
before noon: {09:00=room 1, 10:30=room 2}
from 14:00:  {14:00=room 1, 16:15=room 3}

With a HashMap you would sort the keys or scan all of them for each of these questions. headMap excludes its bound by default, while tailMap(key, true) includes it.

For enum keys, EnumMap and EnumSet are worth knowing. They are backed by an array or a bit vector indexed by the enum's ordinal, and they iterate in declaration order.

Sequenced collections (Java 21)

Java 21 added SequencedCollection and SequencedMap (JEP 431). They give every ordered collection the same methods for the first and last element. That covers List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap.

List<String> events = new ArrayList<>(List.of("created", "paid", "shipped"));
System.out.println(events.getFirst() + " .. " + events.getLast());
System.out.println(events.reversed());

SequencedSet<Long> recentIds = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of(42L, 7L, 19L));
System.out.println(recentIds.getLast() + " " + recentIds.reversed());

SequencedMap<String, Integer> steps = new LinkedHashMap<>();
steps.put("validate", 1);
steps.put("charge", 2);
steps.put("notify", 3);
System.out.println(steps.firstEntry() + " " + steps.lastEntry());
System.out.println(steps.pollFirstEntry() + " -> " + steps);

created .. shipped
[shipped, paid, created]
19 [19, 7, 42]
validate=1 notify=3
validate=1 -> {charge=2, notify=3}

Before Java 21, the last element of a LinkedHashSet meant iterating the whole set. reversed() returns a view, not a copy, and it keeps the original's rules, so calling removeFirst() on List.of("a", "b").reversed() still throws UnsupportedOperationException. I compiled the same file with JDK 17 to check the floor, and it fails with cannot find symbol ... method getFirst().

Sharing a collection between threads (Advanced)

You can skip this section if your collections live inside one request. HashMap is not thread-safe, and when several threads write to it the failure is usually silent. Here, 8 threads each count 100,000 hits into one map.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Main {
    static int count(Map<String, Integer> hits) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) hits.merge("GET /users", 1, Integer::sum);
                });
            }
        } // close() waits for all tasks
        return hits.get("GET /users");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("expected          800000");
        System.out.println("HashMap           " + count(new HashMap<>()));
        System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap " + count(new ConcurrentHashMap<>()));
    }
}

expected          800000
HashMap           139374
ConcurrentHashMap 800000

The HashMap number changed on every run. Across 13 runs it landed between 126,637 and 367,392, never close to 800,000. My first suspicion was that some tasks had died with an exception that submit swallowed into its Future. I wrapped the loop in a try/catch and nothing was thrown, so these are plain lost updates.

ConcurrentHashMap makes merge and computeIfAbsent atomic per key, which makes it the usual pick for an in-memory cache or counter shared across requests. Collections.synchronizedMap also works, but it puts one lock around the whole map. Queues, executors and async composition belong to the concurrency cluster.

Common traps

Removing inside a for-each loop. This one surprised me while preparing the example. My first version removed "expired-2" from ["ok-1", "expired-2", "ok-3"] and did not throw at all.

List<String> tokens = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ok-1", "expired-2", "expired-3"));
for (String t : tokens) {
    if (t.startsWith("expired")) tokens.remove(t);
}
System.out.println(tokens);

[ok-1, expired-3]

Removing the second-to-last element makes the iterator think it has finished, so the loop ends and expired-3 is never checked. With the expired token first, you get the exception everyone knows:

Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
    at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification(ArrayList.java:1095)
    at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.next(ArrayList.java:1049)

The fix is tokens.removeIf(t -> t.startsWith("expired"));, which prints [ok-1] for the list above. The silent version is the worse bug, because nothing crashes; only a test that checks the resulting list catches it.

List.of rejects null. An optional field from a request is enough to trigger it.

String middleName = null;
List<String> parts = List.of("Vu", middleName, "Duong");

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
    at java.base/java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.java:233)

Even List.of("USER", "ADMIN").contains(null) throws the same NullPointerException, while an ArrayList would return false. Filter nulls first, or use new ArrayList<>() if null is a legal value.

A mutable field in hashCode. The Cart class below defines equals and hashCode from couponCode, and the code changes that field after adding the cart to a HashSet.

Set<Cart> carts = new HashSet<>();
Cart cart = new Cart("SALE10");
carts.add(cart);

cart.couponCode = "SALE20";               // field used by hashCode changes
System.out.println(carts.contains(cart)); // same object!
System.out.println(carts.size());

false
1

Warning: the set still holds the cart, but it looks in the bucket for the new hash and finds nothing. The same happens with HashMap keys. Keep fields used by hashCode immutable (a record does this for you, as long as its fields are immutable types too), or remove the object, change it, and add it again.

Arrays.asList is fixed-size. It wraps the array, so set works and add does not.

String[] fromCsv = {"a@x.dev", "b@x.dev"};
List<String> emails = Arrays.asList(fromCsv);
emails.add("c@x.dev");

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
    at java.base/java.util.AbstractList.add(AbstractList.java:155)

Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(fromCsv)) when the list must grow.

Next step

Most of these collections end up feeding streams, through toMap, groupingBy or an Optional from findFirst. The next post in the series covers the patterns worth keeping there and the traps. Other posts on lists, sets and maps are collected under Java collections. For the official overview of every interface and implementation, see the Java Collections Framework guide.

title: How Should Singapore Enterprises Assess AI Delivery Capacity
description:
Singapore enterprises should assess AI delivery capacity by determining whether existing infrastructure, internal expertise, and governance controls can support production AI at a sustainable cost. The assessment should guide a critical investment decision: scale existing initiatives, address capability gaps internally, or engage an AI implementation partner based on verified delivery readiness.

A successful AI pilot does not necessarily mean an enterprise is ready for full-scale deployment. Legacy system dependencies, fragmented data, unpredictable infrastructure costs, and evolving regulatory requirements can turn promising AI initiatives into expensive operational challenges. 

The key consideration is no longer simply whether AI can work, but whether existing capabilities can deliver measurable business value at scale and whether scaling, strengthening internal capabilities, or engaging external expertise offers the most sustainable path forward.

In this guide, Kyanon Digital examines how Singapore enterprises can evaluate AI delivery capacity, identify critical readiness gaps, and make informed decisions about scaling AI initiatives, strengthening internal capabilities, or engaging a specialized implementation partner.

Key takeaways

  • Validate production readiness: A successful AI pilot is not enough. Evaluate whether enterprise data, infrastructure, and engineering teams can sustain real-world workloads.
  • Prioritize measurable business value: Compare expected operational improvements against total implementation and operating costs before expanding AI investment.
  • Balance flexibility with delivery speed: Assess cloud dependencies, vendor lock-in, and switching costs without overengineering infrastructure unnecessarily.
  • Treat governance as a deployment requirement: Address applicable PDPA obligations, AI security risks, and human oversight before introducing AI into business-critical workflows.
  • Close critical capability gaps first: Kyanon Digital recommends validating an end-to-end production workflow before scaling, then deciding whether internal improvements or specialist integration support are needed.

Further reading:

  • How Do You Bridge Data and AI Consulting with Execution? 
  • LLM Integration Services for Enterprise Systems 
  • What Is the True Cost of AI in Manufacturing in Singapore?

Why do enterprise AI pilots fail to scale in Singapore?

Enterprise AI pilots often fail to scale because production environments expose infrastructure limitations, integration complexity, unpredictable costs, and governance gaps. While AI models may perform well in controlled tests, sustainable deployment requires reliable enterprise data, operational ownership, and measurable business value. These gaps can determine whether further AI investment is justified.

According to Gartner (2026), at least 50% of generative AI projects globally were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, largely due to data quality, cost, risk controls, and unclear business value. In Singapore, the Ministry of Manpower's 2026 research found that larger firms identified integration complexity (56.1%) and data security concerns (55.4%) as major barriers to AI adoption.

Key bottlenecks preventing enterprise AI from scaling

  • Fragmented data and legacy infrastructure: Inconsistent data and complex ERP/CRM integrations may require targeted modernization before AI can scale.
  • Unpredictable infrastructure costs: Rising inference, cloud, and maintenance expenses make total cost of ownership (TCO) critical to investment decisions.
  • Security and AI governance risks: Sensitive data exposure and unauthorized AI actions require stronger governance before production deployment.
  • Limited execution capacity: Gaps in AI engineering, MLOps, and operational ownership may justify internal capability development or external expertise.
  • Unclear ROI and business value: Without measurable operational improvements, enterprises risk expanding AI initiatives that cannot justify their costs.

[caption id="attachment_121806" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Overcoming five critical bottlenecks, infrastructure gaps, rising costs, compliance, execution limits, and unclear ROI - is vital for Singapore enterprises to successfully scale AI beyond pilots.[/caption]

Are you risking vendor lock-in with your current AI architecture?

AI vendor lock-in becomes a risk when critical workflows depend heavily on proprietary models, APIs, or cloud infrastructure. For Singapore enterprises, the concern is not using a single provider, but whether future migration, pricing changes, or service disruptions could create unacceptable costs and operational risks.

Key AI vendor lock-in risks to assess

Warning sign Business risk

What to ask your AI vendor

Model and workflow dependency

 Proprietary APIs, RAG pipelines, and agent frameworks increase redevelopment costs. Can critical workflows support alternative AI models?
Cloud and pricing dependency Provider outages, pricing changes, and migration complexity threaten operational continuity.

What are the switching costs and fallback options?

Limited data and IP portability

 Restricted access to business logic, data, or configurations complicates migration and governance.

Who owns these assets, and can they be transferred?

How should enterprises reduce AI vendor lock-in?

Before selecting an AI implementation partner, prioritize three architectural safeguards:

  • Model-agnostic design: Separate business logic, orchestration, and model access to reduce provider-specific dependencies.
  • Open interfaces and portability: Use standardized APIs and modular components where future migration justifies the investment.
  • Tested switching capabilities: Require evidence that an alternative model can support critical workflows with acceptable performance, security, and migration effort.

However, avoiding vendor lock-in should not come at the expense of delivery speed. Managed AI services may be the better starting point when they accelerate deployment without creating unacceptable switching risks.

[caption id="attachment_121808" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] A model-agnostic architecture reduces AI vendor lock-in through modular integration, open APIs, and tested model switching.[/caption]

The key decision: Choose a single-provider architecture when its cost and operational benefits outweigh manageable dependencies. Prioritize greater portability when business-critical AI workflows require long-term flexibility and resilience.

How should enterprises evaluate their AI delivery capacity?

Enterprise AI delivery capacity should be evaluated across business value, data readiness, technical execution, workforce capabilities, and governance. The assessment should test these capabilities against a real business workflow to determine whether the organization can scale AI internally, needs targeted improvements, or requires external implementation expertise.

5 critical areas to assess before scaling enterprise AI

Enterprises should evaluate both internal capabilities and external AI implementation partners across five dimensions before committing to large-scale deployment.

[caption id="attachment_121809" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Evaluating business value, data infrastructure, MLOps, workforce capability, and governance ensures enterprise AI scales reliably and securely.[/caption]

Business value and ROI

  • Baseline performance: Identify existing operational KPIs, such as processing time, error rates, labor costs, and transaction volume.
  • Financial viability: Compare expected business improvements against development, infrastructure, licensing, and maintenance costs.
  • Decision point: Prioritize use cases with measurable business value and clear ownership rather than investing in AI without a validated business case.

Data and technology foundations

  • Data readiness: Check data quality, accessibility, ownership, and compatibility with AI models and RAG pipelines.
  • Infrastructure scalability: Evaluate compute capacity, inference latency, cloud costs, and integration with existing ERP and CRM systems.
  • Decision point: Address critical data and infrastructure gaps before expanding AI workloads.

Technical execution and MLOps maturity

  • Production deployment: Verify experience moving AI solutions from proof of concept into live enterprise workflows.
  • Continuous evaluation: Assess model monitoring, RAG performance, version control, regression testing, and rollback procedures.
  • Agentic workflow testing: For AI agents, evaluate tool usage, execution traces, permission boundaries, and human approval checkpoints.
  • Decision Point: Require production evidence and ongoing maintenance capabilities, not just model demonstrations.

People and operational ownership

  • Technical expertise: Identify gaps across AI engineering, data engineering, cloud, DevOps, and MLOps.
  • Domain knowledge: Ensure business teams can validate AI outputs and manage exceptions in critical workflows.
  • Operating model: Establish clear ownership for deployment, monitoring, incident response, and continuous improvement.
  • Decision point: Determine whether to develop internal expertise, engage external specialists, or adopt a hybrid delivery model.

Governance, security, and compliance

  • Data protection: Review data access, retention, privacy controls, and third-party processing arrangements.
  • AI risk management: Test hallucinations, bias, unauthorized access, and potential information leakage.
  • Auditability: Verify logging, traceability, human oversight, and accountability for AI-generated decisions and actions.
  • Decision point: Resolve material security and governance gaps before deploying AI in business-critical operations.

For Singapore enterprises, AI Singapore's AI Readiness Index (AIRI) provides a broader organizational benchmark, while IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI offers additional guidance for organizations adopting autonomous AI workflows.

How should enterprises turn assessment findings into investment decisions?

The objective is to identify which capabilities are ready, which require improvement, and which need external support.

  • Scale internally: When business value is demonstrated and internal teams can manage production delivery and ongoing operations.
  • Strengthen existing capabilities: When specific data, infrastructure, or engineering gaps can be resolved without replacing the entire technology stack.
  • Engage an AI implementation partner: When complex integrations, specialist engineering, or insufficient delivery capacity prevent internal teams from moving into production.
  • Defer investment: When business value remains unclear or critical security and governance risks are unresolved.

A practical perspective from Kyanon Digital: In its guide to bridging data and AI consulting with execution, Kyanon Digital emphasizes starting with a measurable business decision, prioritizing the first production data path, and establishing accountability beyond deployment.

For example, when evaluating an AI invoice-processing solution, enterprises should test more than document extraction accuracy. They should verify ERP integration, exception handling, approval workflows, processing costs, and the reduction in manual review effort.

The key decision: Invest in the capabilities that make a priority business workflow production-ready. Expand AI deployment only when operational performance, business impact, and ongoing ownership can be demonstrated.

How do you assess the operational risks of undocumented shadow AI?

Shadow AI creates governance gaps when employees use unapproved AI services with enterprise information. An assessment should identify active tools, business purposes, data classifications, access permissions, and approved alternatives. Prioritize sensitive workflows before introducing restrictions or replacing existing tools.

For enterprises needing governed internal AI access, Kyanon Digital's WisdomMind AI platform offers enterprise knowledge retrieval, RAG, access controls, and AI orchestration capabilities.

[caption id="attachment_121812" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] WisdomMind AI by Kyanon Digital enables governed enterprise knowledge access, RAG-powered retrieval, and AI orchestration to help manage shadow AI risks.[/caption]

However, deployment architecture, data residency, provider access, retention, and contractual safeguards must still be verified for each implementation.

How Kyanon Digital scaled AI-powered supply chain automation for a Singapore retailer

Kyanon Digital's Singapore retail supply chain automation project illustrates how enterprise integration and workflow readiness contribute to operational AI delivery.

[caption id="attachment_119807" align="aligncenter" width="960"] AI-powered supply chain automation for a Singapore retailer, integrating supplier document processing, SAP reconciliation, and inventory synchronization into existing enterprise workflows.[/caption]

Challenges

  • Thousands of supplier documents required manual processing.
  • Disconnected SAP, inventory, and financial workflows created reconciliation bottlenecks.
  • Inconsistent inventory information affected omnichannel operations.

Solution from Kyanon Digital

  • Implemented AI-powered supplier document extraction.
  • Integrated automated reconciliation with existing SAP systems.
  • Established event-driven inventory synchronization and exception handling.

Results and impact

[caption id="attachment_115704" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Kyanon Digital helped the retailer automate supply chain operations, improve inventory accuracy, and scale finance workflows without adding headcount.[/caption]

  • 90% reduction in manual data entry time.
  • Supplier invoice processing reduced from days to under 30 minutes.
  • Over 80% reduction in omnichannel inventory discrepancy incidents.

The project demonstrates the value of connecting AI capabilities to existing enterprise systems and controlled workflows. These outcomes are project-specific and do not establish equivalent results for other implementations.

Explore the full case study Scaling Singapore Retail Operations with Intelligent Supply Chain Automation.

Conclusion

Assessing AI delivery capacity helps enterprises determine whether to scale existing initiatives, strengthen internal capabilities, or engage external expertise. Before expanding AI investment, prioritize production readiness, measurable business value, and manageable operational risks. Address critical capability gaps before committing to large-scale deployment.

Considering your next AI investment? Discuss your AI delivery readiness with Kyanon Digital to identify critical capability gaps and determine whether to scale internally or engage specialist support.

title: Is Sara Omar the true author of D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
description:
arXiv:2611.34131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The bestseller D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and na\"ive Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

title: From Map Box to White Model: A Five-Tool Massing Pipeline
description:
I run the same massing pass on small infill sites a few times a year, and the shape of it rarely changes. This time the site was a closed lumber yard behind Main Street: six point four acres, a three-story height limit, a riverbank at the back, and a room full of neighbors who wanted numbers instead of pictures.
Five tools, one afternoon of setup, three options by the end of the week. Here is the actual pipeline, including the parts that broke.

Step 1: CADMapper for the base

Input: an address and a bounding box. Output: a DXF or SketchUp file with street centerlines, parcel lines, building footprints, and contours.
I draw the box one block wider than the site on every side, because half the questions in a massing study are about the neighbors. The free tier caps the area, which is fine at this scale. The contours come in at one-foot intervals, and the site drops about nine feet from the street to the river. That single fact killed my first flat-courtyard sketch before it existed.
The gotcha is precision. This is a planning base, not a survey. I keep a note in the file name that says so.

Step 2: OSM Buildings for the neighbors

Input: the larger downtown area. Output: untextured grey building volumes, no windows, no materials.
This is the context layer. Forty-something buildings around the site, enough to see the three-story wall along Main Street and the low garages along the alley. Heights are estimated, so I spot-checked the tallest few on foot and corrected one that was a story short.
If you skip this step, your white model will look like a spaceship parked in a village. Context is not decoration. It is half the argument.

Step 3: Free3D and Archive3D for scale props

Input: search terms like "white car," "street tree," "bench," "rooftop unit." Output: OBJ or FBX files of varying quality.
White massing models look dead without something human at ground level. I keep a small library of untextured props for this. I downloaded a dozen for this site and kept five; the rejects had bad origins, wrong units, or a license that ruled out commercial work.
The rule I use: props are for scale, never for detail. If a prop takes more than five minutes to fix, it does not go in.

Step 4: GenAnywhere for option generation

Input: a rectangle drawn on the map. Output: a 3D model of a plausible build-out inside that rectangle.
This is the step that replaced my hand-built sketch options. I drew the block boundary, generated three variants, and exported them as white models. No textures, no invented signage, just volume. The three options differed in ways the room could discuss: perimeter block, two bars, townhomes along the alley.
Treat the output as a sketch, not a design. The AI does not know your zoning code, your floodplain, or your neighbor's porch. It gives you shapes to react to, and reacting is faster than inventing.

Step 5: one scene, one origin

This is where most pipelines fall apart. Every tool exports with its own idea of units, origin, and up-axis.
My checklist is short. Set everything to meters. Pick one origin, usually the southwest corner of the site, and move every file to it. Put the context on its own layer, props on another, and the new massing on a third. Then take one screenshot from the same camera for every option, because options compared from different angles are not compared at all.

Handoffs that broke

The CADMapper DXF came in clean. The OSM export needed a unit check, and two building heights were wrong. One Free3D car arrived at ten times scale. GenAnywhere's white model exports were consistent, but the first one came in rotated ninety degrees from the site grid.
None are hard problems, but each one eats an afternoon if you do not expect it.

What I'd automate

Two things. First, a naming convention that carries units and date, so a folder can be rebuilt without opening files. Second, a thumbnail sheet, one image per option from the same camera, generated automatically. The thumbnail sheet is what the meeting actually looks at, and building it by hand is the most tedious part of the week.

The deliverable at the end is not a rendering. It is a folder of white models and a set of screenshots that answer three questions: does it fit, what does it shade, and what does it feel like from the street. That is enough to keep a project moving.

Cache writes are billed at 1.25x the standard input token price by default, and longer retention costs more. For details, see Pricing.

  • Office and OpenDocument file inputs: Supports Microsoft Office (.docx, .dotx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls) and OpenDocument (.odt, .odp, .ods) files inline or from Cloud Storage (gs://), including inside multimodal FunctionResponse parts.

  • Capabilities, consumption options, and endpoints: Supports the GenerateContent API, the Interactions API, the OpenAI compatibility Chat Completions API, function calling, code execution, computer use, URL context, Grounding with Google Search, Google Maps, Enterprise Web Grounding, Parallel and Exa Web Search, Agentic video understanding, Standard PayGo with Usage Tiers, Priority PayGo, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput (685 tokens per second per GSU) on the global endpoint and in the us and eu multi-regions.

Change

In GKE version 1.35.1-gke.1516000 or later, GKE Dataplane V2 clusters use a unified cilium-cni configuration instead of a chained CNI setup. With this change, Cilium configures the Pod default gateway by using its node-local virtual router interface (cilium_host), which has the statically assigned link-local IP address 169.254.4.6.

As a result, node-local kubelet health checks (kube-probe for liveness, readiness, and startup probes) and NodeLocal DNSCache traffic now originate from 169.254.4.6 instead of the .1 address of the node's Pod CIDR range (for example, 10.x.x.1).

If your workloads only accept traffic from specific IP address ranges, for example through application-level IP allowlists or web server ACLs, allow traffic from 169.254.4.6/32 before you upgrade. Otherwise, health checks for these workloads might fail.

For more information, see Using GKE Dataplane V2.

  • Base container images for earlier affected Managed Airflow (Gen 3) and Managed Airflow (Gen 2) builds have been patched across all regions. Newly created environments aren't affected, even when created with an earlier build.

Existing environments continue running cached container images until updated through scheduled maintenance or a manual environment update (such as upgrading the image version, updating a PyPI package, or restarting Airflow workloads in eligible Gen 3 regions). For step-by-step mitigation instructions, see the known issue for Managed Airflow (Gen 3) or Managed Airflow (Gen 2).

Feature

Filter version v4 under the Latest alias includes an updated prompt injection and jailbreak detection filter with the following improvements:

  • Higher recall for indirect prompt injection (IPI) and tool calls.
  • Higher recall for conversational inputs at a lower false positive rate.
  • Higher recall for jailbreak attacks.

For more information, see Filter version history.

Policy Controller

Deprecated

Policy Controller is deprecated as of November 12, 2026, and reaches end of support on December 31, 2027. Starting January 31, 2027, you can't enable Policy Controller in fleet host projects that don't already have Policy Controller enabled. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blocks upgrades to version 1.39 and later for clusters that have Policy Controller installed. Clusters that run GKE version 1.39 and later don't support Policy Controller. On December 31, 2027, technical support, security patching on GKE version 1.38 and earlier, and the Google Cloud console dashboard for Policy Controller end.

Migrate your admission policies to Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicies, Pod Security Admission, or self-managed Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper. For more information, see Migrate from Policy Controller.

Feature

You can deploy Secure Web Proxy as an Agent Gateway to centrally secure, govern, and monitor outbound traffic from AI agents that run on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and Cloud Run. Use this feature to control how your agents interact with large language models (LLMs), Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, remote agents, and external APIs in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. For more information, see Deploy Secure Web Proxy as an Agent Gateway.

This feature is available in Preview.

title: Does This Bama Bound Clip Declare Itself as AI-Generated? Finding, Adding, and Stripping the AIGC Tag Without Re-encoding (Python + ffmpeg, Tested)
description:
Some social apps and some archives want a clear "this is AI-generated" label on the file itself, not only in a caption. I wanted to know whether the official imported field preview on bamabound.app already carries one, and whether I could add or strip that label without touching the picture or the soundtrack.

I re-checked the live studio on 27 November 2026, 15:26:39–15:27:07 CST (Asia/Shanghai, UTC+8). The homepage and the create page still label the clip an "Imported field preview" / "An external reference of the sign clip. Not a result generated by this studio." I copied that file locally. SHA-256 9dcb91afc8f985baaa1bae746380d2e2514b6d84abd5108b3b0284eb1fc6492a, 6,117,241 bytes. I did not upload it anywhere.

What ffprobe already shows 

ffprobe -hide_banner -show_entries format_tags=AIGC,encoder -of default ref.mp4

TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
TAG:encoder=Lavf59.34.101

The braces are part of the stored string. The file is a 720×1280, 24 fps, yuv420p H.264 clip, 193 frames, with 32 kHz stereo AAC. Container and audio last 8.096000 s; the video stream lasts 8.041667 s.

The label does not live in a four-character AIGC box of its own. A walk of the official file finds the string at offset 6,117,171, inside moov/udta/meta, stored as a QuickTime mdta key. The udta box starts at 6,116,883 and is 358 bytes. The keys list has five names: major_brand, minor_version, compatible_brands, AIGC, and encoder. AIGC is the fourth key, at offset 6,117,025.

Stripping the tag with a stream copy

I wrote a tiny ffmetadata file that kept the other format tags and omitted AIGC, then remuxed:

ffmpeg -y -i ref.mp4 -i no-aigc.ffmeta -map_metadata 1 -c copy official_aigc_stripped.mp4

The stripped file is 6,116,980 bytes (261 bytes smaller) and SHA-256 7a87d460ba18f2eeb51f79e7ffc4aca3c147226a78d97f9ad17eedf7e512d465. ffprobe no longer reports an AIGC tag. The remuxer rewrote encoder to Lavf61.7.103, which is expected when this box's ffmpeg (Lavf 61.7.103) writes a new moov. The bitstreams did not move:

  • video annex-B SHA-256 1d3959a35a26e70188de23474a76b1866db3e26c005ab69f3657adb2be869b67
  • audio ADTS SHA-256 084469e3d17abed811d2507a4c523bbcce57afc8fed17fb9f6fb623fd0dbac0e

Those hashes match the official file.

Putting the tag back — and the flag that actually writes it

A plain remux does not write an unknown MP4 key:

ffmpeg -i official_aigc_stripped.mp4 -c copy -metadata 'AIGC={This content is generated by AI}' try.mp4

ffprobe on try.mp4 had no AIGC tag at all. The key was dropped. The mp4 muxer documents use_metadata_tags as "Use mdta atom for metadata." This works:

ffmpeg -i official_aigc_stripped.mp4 -c copy -movflags use_metadata_tags \
  -metadata 'AIGC={This content is generated by AI}' official_aigc_restored.mp4

The restored file is 6,117,240 bytes (one byte smaller than the official original, with the same tag text and encoder=Lavf61.7.103). SHA-256 720e673ef5a301cca585966e2622d092eca5553aedfc0a66742e107ced650dd3. Both bitstream hashes are still the official values. ffprobe again reports AIGC={This content is generated by AI}.

A clean control

I also built a one-second mid-gray 720×1280 clip with no AIGC tag (4,239 bytes). After the same use_metadata_tags write of {DUMMY-AIGC-TEST-LABEL-NOT-A-LEGAL-NOTICE}, the file grew to 4,508 bytes, ffprobe showed that dummy string, and the video annex-B hash stayed 05b2c4d6b1a87cd03930696fb56addd5f70330b0a46269fbec0d7bbf319332e6.

The dummy string is a test label only. It is not a legal notice, and it is not a claim about the official preview.

What this does not prove

This is a container tag. It is not a C2PA Content Credential, and I did not look for one in this run. Stripping the tag does not make the clip "not AI," and adding the tag to some other file does not make the clip a Bama Bound output. The official preview is an imported reference, not a customer render from this studio.

If you want to make your own vertical banner clip from one photo, the live catalogue on bamabound.app/pricing today is $7.98 / 798 credits at 480p, $9.98 / 998 at 720p, $16.98 / 1923 at 1080p, and $24.98 / 3921 at 4k. Packs are $22.99 / 3 credits, $59.99 / 10, and $99.99 / 20. There is no subscription and no free allowance. Buyer tax is added at checkout. The FAQ still says you do not write a prompt.

The script from this run is aigc_check.py. I am not attaching the official preview to this post.

title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
description:
arXiv:2611.33896v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.

title: In a second test of Streamer, Defender recorded 659 non-notification events in the files examined
description:
SOCRadar’s report on Streamer, a Rust-written Windows malware sample, documents a change in detection between two controlled tests.

The revised version connected to its operators’ control system without an alert in the exported Defender log, though 659 events were recorded.

The report does not identify what changed or establish that the result would recur on another device.

This doesn't mean that the second test wasn't recorded. Defender recorded 659 events, including external system connections, data preparation, and account discovery attempts. None of these events in the log had an alert ID.

What did the two tests show?

Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar identified the program as Streamer. Its report, published on November 26, was based on files, screenshots, and Defender logs that connected to the infrastructure of the program's operators.

In the first test, Defender rated the incident as high severity. Four of the 10 alerts were for a program that unexpectedly loaded an extra file. Defender then isolated the computer from the network.

In the October 21 test, Streamer appeared as a security product component. Defender recorded it as an unknown program and marked it as more difficult to control. The device page did not show any known risks, but Defender continued to collect events.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Cyber ​​Attacks & Data Breaches

SAP confirms theft of employee digital keys and access to GitHub

↗

The report doesn't explain what change led to the different result. It also doesn't clarify whether the same version would have passed without notification to another device.

Items linked to other groups

SOCRadar found files for MetaEncryptor/LostTrust, a ransomware platform, on the same development machine. It also found similarities between the infrastructure associated with Streamer and a system called Eclipse, which had been examined by the Atos Threat Research Center. Among the similarities was the same tool and the same creator indication.

The researchers assessed with high confidence that the two infrastructures had a common creator and used common tools. However, they were unable to determine whether the names MetaEncryptor and LostTrust belonged to the same group.

The operator records named 17 organizations in four countries, 14 of which were in the United States. Among them were a federal agency, three energy cooperatives, and a healthcare provider. The records included confirmed activity, operator claims, and one case where only an acknowledgment was made. Therefore, the 17 organizations do not correspond to 17 confirmed breaches or ransomware installations.

For the federal agency's case, the report describes prolonged access and theft of files with the code of a program, as well as a private digital key used to access services.

SOCRadar reported that the researchers did not interfere with the organizations' systems and informed those affected, as well as the relevant authorities.

title: Your logger prints secrets after you redacted them
description:
A redaction hook sees values. The logger prints text. Errors, structs and printf arguments turn into text after the hook has run, so the secret inside them goes out as it came in. We found this in five of the six languages flare-redact supports and fixed it in 1.12.1. Here is the mechanism, the real output, and a test you can run against your own logger.

Short answer: redact what the logger will print, not only the values it is handed. A value the hook does not recognise (an error, a struct, a URL, a %s argument) has to be turned into text the way the logger would, and that text redacted. Then test with the real logger writing to a buffer, never with a fake of its hook.

How we found it

While checking code samples for a round of replies, we logged a database error through our own Go handler:

slog.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: connection refused", dsn))

The password came out in clear. The handler's tests were green, because none of them logged an error. The redactor walks strings, maps and lists. An error is none of those, so the handler passed it on unchanged, and slog's JSON handler called err.Error() when it wrote the line.

So we checked every logging integration the same way: the real logger, a known secret, the printed output. Eight integrations in five languages leaked in at least one path.

The mechanism

Every logger works in two steps:

  1. You hand it values: a message template, arguments, fields, bound context.
  2. Later, when it writes the line, it turns some of those values into text: Error(), String(), toString(), __str__, ToString(), printf's %s.

A redaction hook sits between the two, so it can only redact what is already text when it runs. An error object is not text yet. Neither is a dataclass, a Uri or a struct. If the hook returns unknown objects unchanged, which is the polite thing for a walker to do, the text is created after redaction and nothing looks at it again.

Go slog 

dsn := "postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod"
slog.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: connection refused", dsn))
slog.Info("config", "db", DB{Host: "db.internal", Password: "S3cret-canary-42"})

With flare-redact 1.12.0:

{"level":"ERROR","msg":"db down","err":"connect postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod: connection refused"}
{"level":"INFO","msg":"config","db":{"Host":"db.internal","Password":"S3cret-canary-42"}}

With 1.12.1:

{"level":"ERROR","msg":"db down","err":"connect postgres://app:***@db.internal:5432/prod: connection refused"}
{"level":"INFO","msg":"config","db":{"Host":"db.internal","Password":"***"}}

A key rule in ReplaceAttr, such as if a.Key == "password", would not have helped with the first line: the key is err. The secret is in the value, and the value is not text yet.

pino

pino adds two twists. It builds the message itself from the template and arguments, and passes only the merge object to formatters.log, so a formatter never sees msg. And child() with no options swaps the bindings formatter for one that returns its input, so child bindings skip it too.

log.info('connecting to %s', dsn);
log.error(new Error(`connect ${dsn}: refused`));
log.child({ dsn }).info('pool ready');

With 1.12.0 (stack trimmed):

{"level":30,"msg":"connecting to postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod"}
{"level":50,"err":{"type":"Error","message":"connect postgres://app:***@db.internal:5432/prod: refused"},"msg":"connect postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod: refused"}
{"level":30,"dsn":"postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod","msg":"pool ready"}

Look at the middle line: the same string is masked in err.message and printed raw in msg right next to it. With 1.12.1 all three lines show app:***@db.internal.

Python logging

A logging.Filter sees record.msg and record.args. getMessage() runs later, in the handler, and calls str() on each argument.

log.info("config %s", DB("db.internal", "S3cret-canary-42"))

1.12.0  INFO config DB(host='db.internal', password='S3cret-canary-42')
1.12.1  INFO config DB(host='db.internal', password='***')

This one leaked only with RedactingFilter on its own. install() also wraps the handler's formatter, which redacts the final text, and that caught it. But the filter alone is a common setup, so it had to be right too.

The other five

  • winston: splat arguments and an Error's message and stack, when winstonRedact() runs before format.splat() or format.errors(). Those formats read the raw arguments kept under Symbol.for('splat') and the Error's non-enumerable properties.
  • console (wrapConsole() and --import flare-redact/register): an object with its own toString() printed through %s.
  • .NET Microsoft.Extensions.Logging and Serilog: a Uri, a class with its own ToString(), or a struct passed as a structured value or a scope.
  • Java Log4j2: object values in a MapMessage.

The Rust engine and the Fluent Bit filter only ever see JSON and msgpack values, so nothing is turned into text later. Logback and the Log4j2 pattern converters already redacted the formatted text.

Why our tests missed it

The old pino test called our formatters.log with a record that had a msg field in it. Real pino never puts msg there. The test checked the hook contract as we imagined it, not as the logger implements it, so it passed while the real path leaked. The Go, Python, .NET and Java tests had the same blind spot in a quieter form: none of them logged an error, a struct or an object with its own string form that held a secret.

The fix for the tests was the same everywhere: drive the real logger, write to a buffer, search the buffer for the secret. Every new leak test fails on 1.12.0.

What the fix does

One rule, applied per logger: redact what will be printed.

  • When the hook meets a value it does not walk, it turns it into text the way the logger would (Error(), String(), str(), ToString(), String.valueOf) and redacts that text. In Go, structs, typed slices and maps are redacted as their JSON, decoded with UseNumber so int64 ids stay exact, and a Password field is masked whole by the key rule.
  • Plain numbers and booleans keep their type, so dashboards and queries keep working.
  • Where the logger formats the message itself (pino), the integration hooks in earlier, at hooks.logMethod, to redact the template and its arguments. For a logger whose bound context holds something sensitive, it also redacts the finished line in hooks.streamWrite. That check runs once per logger, so loggers with clean bindings pay nothing extra.
  • If redaction itself fails, the field becomes [REDACTION FAILED]. Printing the original is the one outcome a redactor exists to prevent.

A test you can copy

This works whatever you use for redaction, including your own ReplaceAttr or a regex filter. Pick a canary secret, log it through every path your code uses, and search the printed output. The paths that matter: the message text, format arguments, errors (message, stack, traceback), objects with their own string form, child or bound context, and groups or scopes.

Go 

func TestLogsNeverPrintTheCanary(t *testing.T) {
    const canary = "S3cret-canary-42"
    dsn := "postgres://app:" + canary + "@db.internal:5432/prod"

    var buf bytes.Buffer
    policy, _ := flareredact.Compile(flareredact.Options{})
    log := slog.New(flareredact.NewSlogHandler(slog.NewJSONHandler(&buf, nil), policy))

    log.Info("connecting to " + dsn)                                    // the message
    log.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: refused", dsn)) // an error
    log.Info("config", "db", struct{ DSN string }{dsn})                 // a struct
    log.With("dsn", dsn).Info("pool ready")                             // bound context
    log.Info("pool", slog.Group("db", "url", dsn))                      // a group

    if strings.Contains(buf.String(), canary) {
        t.Fatalf("secret printed:\n%s", buf.String())
    }
}

Node.js with pino 

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import pino from 'pino';
import { pinoRedact } from 'flare-redact/pino';

test('logs never print the canary', () => {
  const canary = 'S3cret-canary-42';
  const dsn = `postgres://app:${canary}@db.internal:5432/prod`;
  let out = '';
  const log = pino(pinoRedact(), { write: (line) => { out += line; } });

  log.info(`connecting to ${dsn}`);                // the message
  log.info('connecting to %s', dsn);               // a printf argument
  log.error(new Error(`connect ${dsn}: refused`)); // an error
  log.info({ db: { dsn } }, 'config');             // a field
  log.child({ dsn }).info('pool ready');           // child bindings

  assert.ok(!out.includes(canary), out);
});

Python 

import io
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass

import flare_redact.log as flare_log


@dataclass
class DB:
    dsn: str


def test_logs_never_print_the_canary():
    canary = "S3cret-canary-42"
    dsn = f"postgres://app:{canary}@db.internal:5432/prod"

    stream = io.StringIO()
    log = logging.getLogger("canary-test")
    log.addHandler(logging.StreamHandler(stream))
    flare_log.install(log)  # your redaction setup goes here

    log.warning("connecting to %s", dsn)  # a format argument
    log.warning("config %s", DB(dsn))     # an object with its own str()
    try:
        raise ConnectionError(f"connect {dsn}: refused")
    except ConnectionError:
        log.exception("db down")          # the traceback

    assert canary not in stream.getvalue(), stream.getvalue()

The Go and Node tests fail on flare-redact 1.12.0 and pass on 1.12.1. The Python test passes on both, because install() already redacted the formatted text in 1.12.0; the Python leak needed RedactingFilter on its own.

Upgrade 

npm install flare-redact@1.12.1
pip install -U flare-redact
go get github.com/flare-collection/flare-redact/sdk/go@v1.12.1

The Rust crate was not affected. Java and .NET are not on Maven Central and NuGet yet; until they are, build sdk/java with mvn install and sdk/dotnet with dotnet pack from the 1.12.1 tag.

What 1.12.1 still does not cover. A Python traceback is only redacted by the formatter, so use install() or add RedactingFormatter yourself; a filter never sees the rendered traceback. In pino, bindings added with setBindings() after a logger's first line are not checked again. A Node Buffer is printed as its byte values and is not scanned.

The code and every test are in the repository, and the full list of changes is in the changelog.
