title: What is geocoding? Forward, reverse and autocomplete explained
description:
I run OpenGeocoding. Originally published on the OpenGeocoding blog. Cross-post formatting was prepared with AI assistance.

Geocoding turns an address or a place name into coordinates: “10 Downing Street, London” becomes latitude 51.5035, longitude -0.1275. Reverse geocoding does the opposite and turns coordinates into the nearest address. Address autocomplete is a third, related job: it suggests complete addresses while someone is still typing one.

Most software that handles addresses needs at least one of the three. A CRM puts customers on a map, a delivery app checks which depot is closest, a fleet log shows “Avenue Anatole France, Paris” instead of a pair of numbers, and a signup form helps people enter an address that the rest of the system can use.

This post explains each one with a real example, how a geocoder gets from text to a point, why two services can return different answers for the same input, and what to check when you choose one. The examples come from OpenGeocoding, the service I run, because those are the answers I can show and explain. The ideas apply to every geocoder.

Forward geocoding: from an address to a point

Forward geocoding, often just called geocoding, takes text and returns a location. Here is what OpenGeocoding returns for “10 Downing Street, London”, trimmed to the useful fields:

{
    "displayName": "10, Downing Street, London, Westminster, England, United Kingdom",
    "geoCoordinates": { "lat": 51.503506, "lon": -0.12754977 },
    "addressDetails": {
        "houseNumber": "10",
        "road": "Downing Street",
        "postcode": "SW1A 2AA",
        "city": "London",
        "countryCode": "gb"
    },
    "goodMatch": true
}

Two things in that answer matter as much as the coordinates. The first is the structured address. The input had no postcode, and the answer adds one, so a geocoder is also a way to clean up and complete address data. The second is a signal of how sure the geocoder is. Send just “Downing Street” with no town or country, and the answer is the town of Downing in Missouri, without the goodMatch flag. There are many Downing Streets, and a bare street name doesn’t say which one you meant, so the geocoder makes a guess and says so. Your code should treat those two answers differently.

Reverse geocoding: from a point to an address

Reverse geocoding starts from a latitude and longitude, usually from a GPS device or a phone, and returns what is nearby. For the coordinates of the Eiffel Tower (48.85837, 2.294481), OpenGeocoding returns “3, Avenue Anatole France, 75007 Paris”, about 50 metres from the point, together with that distance.

That example shows a common surprise: a reverse geocoder answers with the nearest address, not necessarily the name of the place you are standing in. OpenGeocoding returns a house when there is one within range, then falls back to the street, and then to the nearest town, and it tells you which of the three it found. Naming the businesses or venues around a point is a different service, usually called place or POI search.

Reverse geocoding is what turns a trip log, a set of photos or a list of job sites into something a person can read.

Autocomplete: helping people type an address

Autocomplete returns a short list of suggestions for a partial address, updated as the person types. Type “10 Downing” with the country set to the United Kingdom, and the first suggestions are a Downing Road in Dagenham and Downing Streets in Farnham, Dudley and Cambridge. Type “10 Downing Street, Lon” and the only suggestion left is the one in London.

When the person picks a suggestion, the application asks for its full details and coordinates. Autocomplete therefore isn’t a faster forward geocoder. It is a way to let a person resolve the ambiguity themselves, so the address that reaches your database is one the geocoder already knows.

How a geocoder works

Under the hood, most geocoders do the same three things.

  1. Parse the input. The text is split into parts: house number, street, postcode, town, region, country. OpenGeocoding uses libpostal for this, a parser trained on addresses from around the world, and then repairs a few mistakes that would otherwise cost the whole lookup, such as a postcode with a country prefix (“SE-262 73”) or a postcode glued to the town name.
  2. Find candidates. The parts are looked up in an index of addresses, streets and places built from map and address data. This step has to forgive the way people write: one misspelt word (“West 54th Srteet”), abbreviations (“S 5th Street” for “South 5th Street”), and names in another language (“Sevilla” for Seville).
  3. Rank and decide. The candidates are compared with what the input said: does the postcode belong to this street, is the town the one stated, is this the right country? The best one wins. When nothing matches at house level, a good geocoder falls back to the street or the town and says that it did, as in the Downing Street example above.

Reverse geocoding skips the parsing: it searches the same index by distance from the point.

Why two geocoders give different answers

Send the same address to two providers and you will often get two different points. There are a few reasons, and they are useful to know when you compare services.

  • Data sources. Some providers license commercial map data, and others build on open data such as OpenStreetMap, Overture Maps, OpenAddresses and national address registries. A provider can only find an address that is in its data.
  • Precision. An answer can be a building, a point estimated along the street from its house-number range (interpolation), the middle of the street, or the centre of the town. Those can be hundreds of metres apart in a village and kilometres apart in the countryside, and services don’t always say which kind they returned.
  • Coverage by country. Address data is dense in some countries and thin in others. OpenGeocoding is strongest in North America, most of Europe, Australia and New Zealand, and a few others such as Japan and Taiwan. House-level coverage across most of Asia and Africa is still poor, and the coverage measurement and the post about building the engine give the figures by country.
  • Freshness. New streets and new buildings appear only after the provider rebuilds its data.
  • Ranking choices. For an ambiguous input like “Downing Street”, each provider has its own rules for which candidate wins.

This is why a single accuracy number says little on its own. The useful question is how a service does on addresses like yours, in your countries. I wrote about how I measure that in What “accurate” means for a geocoder.

What you may do with the results

The terms of use matter as much as the price, and they differ a lot between providers. Under Google’s Maps service terms, geocoded coordinates may be cached for up to 30 days, so a database of geocoded customers has to be refreshed through the API. Results built on open data can usually be kept: OpenStreetMap’s ODbL licence asks for attribution, and for share-alike if you publish a database derived from it. OpenGeocoding’s results can be stored permanently, with those source licences still applying (attributions).

If you plan to geocode records once and keep the coordinates, read the storage terms before you compare prices.

How to choose a geocoding service

A short checklist that has served me well:

  1. Test with your own data. Take a hundred real addresses or GPS points from your system, including the messy ones, and look at the answers. Most services have a free tier for this; OpenGeocoding’s free plan has 50,000 requests a month and needs no credit card.
  2. Check coverage in your countries, at the precision you need: house, street or town.
  3. Read the storage terms, as above.
  4. Price your real volume. Per-request prices, monthly plans and daily limits look similar until you put your numbers in.
  5. Check the rate limits. The free public Nominatim server, for example, allows at most 1 request per second under its usage policy, which is fine for occasional lookups and not for a production import.

The comparison pages set OpenGeocoding next to Google Maps, Nominatim, OpenCage, Geoapify and Geocodio, with dated prices and terms, and pricing has the plans. To try forward and reverse geocoding on your own addresses, use the demo on the homepage or get a free API key.

title: Zero-Downtime Asynchronous Pipelines: Architecting High-Throughput Event Ingestion with FastAPI and Redis
description:
Zero-Downtime Asynchronous Pipelines: Architecting High-Throughput Event Ingestion with FastAPI and Redis

In distributed systems, the ingestion tier is the absolute bottleneck of your architecture. When a traffic spike hits, blocking I/O operations and synchronous database writes will cascade failures up the stack. To achieve horizontal scalability and bounded latency, we must decouple the API ingestion layer from the heavy backend processing workers.

In this deep-dive, we will design and implement a production-grade, asynchronous event-processing pipeline utilizing FastAPI, Redis Streams, and asyncio.

System Architecture

The following ASCII diagram illustrates the data flow from the external client through the FastAPI ingestion gateway, into the Redis durable log, and finally consumed by background workers.

+----------------+       +---------------------------------------------+
| External Client| ----> |              FastAPI Gateway                |
+----------------+       |  [ASGI/Uvicorn] -> [Validation] -> [XADD]   |
                         +---------------------------------------------+
                                                |
                                                v
                         +---------------------------------------------+
                         |                 Redis Broker                |
                         |        [Redis Stream: event_stream]         |
                         +---------------------------------------------+
                                                |
                                                v
                         +---------------------------------------------+
                         |              Background Worker              |
                         |    [XREADGROUP] -> [Business Logic] -> [ACK]|
                         +---------------------------------------------+

Key Architectural Decisions:

  1. FastAPI & Uvicorn: Chosen for its non-blocking event loop capability, allowing high concurrency per node via ASGI.
  2. Redis Streams (XADD/XREADGROUP): Unlike Pub/Sub, Redis Streams provide persistence, consumer groups, and message acknowledgement semantics (XACK), guaranteeing at-least-once delivery.
  3. Graceful Degradation: If the Redis broker encounters transient network partitions, the API layer fails fast with an HTTP 503 rather than exhausting connection pools.

Production-Ready Implementation

Below is a complete, runnable Python module implementing the architecture above using FastAPI, redis-py (async client), and Pydantic v2.

import asyncio
import logging
import sys
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import AsyncGenerator

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
import redis.asyncio as aioredis

# Configure structured logging
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    stream=sys.stdout,
)
logger = logging.getLogger("event-pipeline")

REDIS_URL = "redis://localhost:6379/0"
STREAM_NAME = "telemetry_stream"
CONSUMER_GROUP = "processing_workers"

class RedisManager:
    def __init__(self, url: str):
        self.client: aioredis.Redis | None = None

    async def connect(self, url: str):
        self.client = aioredis.from_url(url, encoding="utf-8", decode_responses=True)
        try:
            await self.client.ping()
            logger.info("Successfully connected to Redis instance.")
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to connect to Redis: {e}")
            raise e

    async def close(self):
        if self.client:
            await self.client.close()
            logger.info("Redis connection closed.")

db = RedisManager(REDIS_URL)

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncGenerator[None, None]:
    """Manage application lifecycle for connection pooling and background tasks."""
    await db.connect(REDIS_URL)

    # Ensure consumer group exists
    try:
        await db.client.xgroup_create(STREAM_NAME, CONSUMER_GROUP, id="0", mkstream=True)
    except aioredis.ResponseError as e:
        if "BUSYGROUP Consumer Group name already exists" not in str(e):
            raise e

    # Spin up background worker task
    worker_task = asyncio.create_task(event_consumer_worker(db.client))

    yield

    worker_task.cancel()
    try:
        await worker_task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        logger.info("Background worker successfully stopped.")

    await db.close()

app = FastAPI(title="High-Throughput Ingestion Engine", lifespan=lifespan)

class TelemetryEvent(BaseModel):
    device_id: str = Field(..., description="Unique hardware identifier")
    metric_name: str = Field(..., description="Name of the telemetry metric")
    value: float = Field(..., description="Numeric sensor reading")
    timestamp: float = Field(..., description="Epoch timestamp of generation")

@app.post("/ingest", status_code=status.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED)
async def ingest_event(event: TelemetryEvent):
    """
    Ingests telemetry data asynchronously, pushing it directly to a Redis stream
    to maintain sub-millisecond response SLAs.
    """
    if not db.client:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE,
            detail="Storage layer uninitialized."
        )

    try:
        payload = event.model_dump(mode="json")
        # Serialize fields into a flat dictionary for Redis Streams
        stream_payload = {k: str(v) for k, v in payload.items()}

        message_id = await db.client.xadd(STREAM_NAME, stream_payload)
        logger.debug(f"Event enqueued with ID: {message_id}")

        return {"status": "accepted", "message_id": message_id}

    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to write to stream: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
            detail="Internal pipeline execution error."
        )

async def event_consumer_worker(redis_client: aioredis.Redis):
    """
    Background worker simulating distributed stream processing with consumer groups.
    """
    consumer_name = "worker-node-1"
    logger.info(f"Consumer {consumer_name} started execution loop.")

    while True:
        try:
            # Read new messages assigned to this consumer group
            streams = await redis_client.xreadgroup(
                groupname=CONSUMER_GROUP,
                consumername=consumer_name,
                streams={STREAM_NAME: ">"},
                count=10,
                block=2000 # Block for 2 seconds before timing out
            )

            if not streams:
                continue

            for stream, messages in streams:
                for message_id, data in messages:
                    try:
                        # --- Heavy Business Logic Simulation ---
                        logger.info(f"Processing event {message_id}: {data}")
                        await asyncio.sleep(0.05) # Simulate database I/O
                        # ---------------------------------------

                        # Acknowledge successful processing
                        await redis_client.xack(STREAM_NAME, CONSUMER_GROUP, message_id)
                        logger.debug(f"Acknowledged message ID: {message_id}")

                    except Exception as processing_error:
                        logger.error(f"Failed to process message {message_id}: {processing_error}")
                        # Implement dead-letter queue (DLQ) logic or backoff strategies here

        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            raise
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error in consumer execution loop: {e}")
            await asyncio.sleep(1) # Backoff on persistent connection failures

Running and Verifying the Pipeline

To run the application locally, initialize a Redis daemon and execute the module using Uvicorn:

pip install fastapi uvicorn redis pydantic
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4

You can test the ingestion endpoint via curl:

curl -X 'POST' \
  'http://localhost:8000/ingest' \
  -H 'accept: application/json' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
  "device_id": "sensor-alpha-01",
  "metric_name": "core_temperature",
  "value": 84.5,
  "timestamp": 1711900000.0
}'

By decoupling the web thread pool from processing using Redis Streams and Python's asyncio, this pattern guarantees maximal throughput, graceful recovery from downstream outages, and clean extensibility.

For more production-grade systems architecture guides and continuous engineering notes, check out my GitHub Profile.

title: How to Stop Guessing GPU Size: Checking VRAM & Memory Bandwidth Before Provisioning
description:
Most teams size bare metal GPU nodes by looking at parameter count (7B, 70B, 405B) and guessing a GPU SKU. That shortcut breaks in two predictable ways:

  1. You rent an H100 / H200 cluster when a single AMD Instinct MI300X (192 GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s) or FP8-quantized node would avoid multi-GPU tensor-parallel overhead.
  2. You rent a GPU for a sparse CFD/FEA workload like OpenFOAM that is actually memory-bandwidth bound and PCIe transfer bound, where a high-RAM EPYC or Xeon CPU node starting at ₹1,499/mo (~$16/mo) delivers better cost per run.

This guide gives you the exact back-of-the-envelope formulas we use at Hydenring before provisioning any node—and links to our live INR & USD calculator at hydenring.com/compare.

1. The 3-Part VRAM Formula (Weights + KV Cache + Overhead)

Before choosing between bare metal GPU servers (MI300X, H200, H100, B200) or multi-GPU pods, compute total required VRAM:

Total VRAM ≈ Model Weights + KV Cache + Runtime Overhead

A. Model Weights 

Weights (GB) ≈ Parameters (B) × Bytes per Parameter
Precision Bytes / Param 70B Dense Model
FP16 / BF16 2.0 140 GB
FP8 / INT8 1.0 70 GB
INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ) 0.5 35 GB

B. KV Cache (With Grouped-Query Attention) 

KV Cache per Token (bytes) = 2 × Layers × KV_Heads × Head_Dim × Bytes_per_Element

Take a 70B GQA model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, BF16 = 2 bytes):

  • 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes/token (320 KiB/token)
  • At 32,768 (32K) context for 1 concurrent sequence: 32,768 × 327,680 bytes = 10.0 GiB (~10.7 GB)
  • At 16 concurrent 32K sequences: ~160 GiB of KV cache alone

C. Why 141 GB vs 192 GB Changes Node Count (MI300X vs H200)

Add 140 GB (70B BF16 weights) + ~10.7 GB (single 32K KV sequence) + ~8–12 GB (CUDA/HIP workspace & activation buffers) = ~159–163 GB:

  • NVIDIA H200 (141 GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s): Too tight for unquantized 70B BF16 at 32K context on 1 GPU—you must either quantize to FP8 (~70 GB weights) or step up to TP=2.
  • AMD Instinct MI300X (192 GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s): Fits 70B BF16 + 32K KV cache + runtime overhead on 1 GPU (TP=1) with ~30 GB left for batching.

(Note: If your stack already depends on TensorRT-LLM or custom CUDA kernels, staying on NVIDIA H100/H200 often beats ROCm on engineering time. We cover those exact boundaries in our Workload-First Silicon Selection post.)

2. Checking the Decode Memory-Bandwidth Ceiling

Single-stream LLM token generation (decode) is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound. Every generated token must stream the active model weights from HBM into compute units:

Theoretical Max Decode Speed (tok/s) ≈ HBM Bandwidth (GB/s) / Active Weights (GB)

For a 140 GB BF16 70B model (batch = 1):

  • AMD Instinct MI300X (5,300 GB/s): 5,300 / 140 ≈ 37.9 tok/s hardware ceiling (~26.5 tok/s at 70% bus efficiency)
  • NVIDIA H200 (4,800 GB/s, if FP8 70 GB): 4,800 / 70 ≈ 68.6 tok/s hardware ceiling (halving active bytes doubles decode ceiling)

If your cloud GPU pricing quote compares GPUs purely on TFLOPs for a decode-heavy serving API, you are sizing the wrong bottleneck.

3. When to Skip GPUs Entirely (OpenFOAM & Sparse FEA)

The fastest way to waste compute budget is putting a sparse, memory-bound physics solver on an H100:

  • Steady-state OpenFOAM (simpleFoam, icoFoam under 10M cells, or cases with Arbitrary Mesh Interfaces / cyclic boundaries and custom C++/Fortran UDFs) saturates lduMatrix sparse-matrix memory bandwidth and hits PCIe host-to-device transfer bottlenecks when partially offloaded.
  • Implicit FEA (MOOSE, CalculiX) is similarly limited by sparse linear-solver memory latency and MPI synchronization.

For these workloads, a high-memory EPYC or Xeon node starting at ₹1,499/mo (~$16/mo) avoids idle GPU SMs and cuts total cost per simulation.

4. Two Pre-Provisioning Sanity Checks

Before running multi-GPU workloads on bare metal, verify interconnect topology and pin immutable Apptainer container digests:

# AMD Instinct: inspect XGMI / PCIe link topology before setting TP
rocm-smi --showtopo

# NVIDIA: inspect NVLink / PCIe topology matrix
nvidia-smi topo -m

# Pin an immutable @sha256:<digest> instead of mutable :latest tags
apptainer exec --rocm docker://rocm/vllm@sha256:<pinned-digest> python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --help

Compare Live TCO in INR & USD

  • Interactive comparison (no email gate): hydenring.com/compare — compare CPU, AMD Instinct, NVIDIA, and Intel Gaudi 3 economics side-by-side.
  • Submit your solver or model profile: hydenring.com/workload-review — get a bottleneck-first silicon recommendation across India, Europe, and North America (hydenring.com/regions) backed by transparent Mon–Fri 09:30–18:30 IST engineering support (hydenring.com/sla).

title: Building huge go repo
description:
I came across an interesting problem recently when building AzureRM: due to a massive refactoring, the repo now have a lot more files and packages

Ran out of tmp space

First, my WSL box throw tons of write /tmp/go-build123456789/...: no space left on device error. The tmp file system ran out of space.

This can be fixed be mapping another larger volume for compilation: export GOTMPDIR="$HOME/.cache/go-tmp" although I suspect this makes the build slower?

Slow compilation time

A cold build with no cache hit took 12 minutes. A common daily main pull require 5 - 7 mins depending on how much are changing.

I learned that go keep local build cache in $HOME/.cache/go-build and the morning ritual of pulling latest main to warm up the cache is really useful to speed up subsequent build throughout the day.

Stripping debugging info cuts down my build time to 10 minutes, it's not much, but why not if we don't need it? go build -ldflags="-s -w" ..

What about a more powerful machine? In my 16vCPU/64GB devbox (cloud VM), the cold build took 6 minutes, which is half the time, not bad!

Which got me thinking.. wouldn't it be great if devbox and my local can share the cache?

gobuildcache

I found this gobuildcache library which is pretty close to what I want: it allows me to upload the build cache to a blob store. Let's give it a try!

First I installed the binary: go install github.com/richardartoul/gobuildcache@v1

Then I created the blob store that will hold the remote cache:

RESOURCE_GROUP=my-azurerm-buildcache
LOCATION=australiaeast
STORAGE_ACCOUNT=myazurermbuildcachev1
CONTAINER=go-build-cache

az group create --name "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --location "$LOCATION"

az storage account create --name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --kind BlockBlobStorage --sku Premium_LRS \
  --allow-blob-public-access false --allow-shared-key-access false \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2
STORAGE_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --query id -o tsv)

# Grant the signed-in user data-plane access to create the container.
USER_ID=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$USER_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type User --role 'Storage Blob Data Contributor' \
  --scope "$STORAGE_ID"

az storage container create --account-name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --name "$CONTAINER" --auth-mode login --public-access off

Drop a few environment variables to tell go to use gobuildcache (hint use direnv to automate this 😉):

export GOCACHEPROG=/path/to/go/bin/gobuildcache

export GOBUILDCACHE_BACKEND_TYPE=azblob
export GOBUILDCACHE_AZURE_ACCOUNT=myazurermbuildcachev1
export GOBUILDCACHE_AZBLOB_CONTAINER=go-build-cache
export GOBUILDCACHE_READ_ONLY=false
export GOBUILDCACHE_PRINT_STATS=true
export GOBUILDCACHE_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/.cache/gobuildcache/cache
export GOBUILDCACHE_LOCK_DIR=/path/to/.cache/gobuildcache/locks
export GOBUILDCACHE_DEBUG=false

Ran the build again in devbox to warm up my remote cache. And look at how warm and cozy my blob store is now with all the cache populated 😛:

And now for the moment of truth, jumping back to my local, I forced a cold build by clearing the cache: "$GOCACHEPROG" clear-local, then ran a built which hopefully hits these remote cache.

Drumrolls...

Backend cache hits: 6526 (65.8% of GETs)

Promising.. but total time is 10 min 44 second, there's no speed benefit although CPU compute is swapped with 7148 HTTP GET requests 🤣.

So I guess local cache is still the way to go. Maybe I'll setup some cron job that pull and compile daily before I start in the morning.

title: Kagelin v1.54.0: a keyboard-first focus timer and pickers that survive midnight
description:
Kagelin is a local-first task, habit and calendar app built on Next.js 16 with Supabase for sync. v1.54.0 removes friction from three common actions: starting a focus session, picking a date, and editing offline. Most of the work is only visible when it is missing.

Three changes are worth a closer look.

Focus mode should behave like a timer, not a page

The focus screen used to have one large play button and a lot of empty space. It now has a full shortcut set, handled by one window-level listener:

if (e.code === "Space" || e.key === " ") {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (state.isRunning) pause();
  else start();
  return;
}

if (e.key.toLowerCase() === "s" && !e.shiftKey) {
  e.preventDefault();
  skip();
  return;
}

if (e.key.toLowerCase() === "r" && e.shiftKey && isSessionActive) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setStopConfirmOpen(true);
  return;
}

if (e.key === "," && !e.shiftKey) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setSettingsOpen(true);
}

The handler bails out when focus is inside an input, textarea, select, or contenteditable, and when a dialog or popover is open. Space also yields to a focused button so it does not double-fire. The rest is conventional: s skips, Shift+R opens a stop confirmation, , opens settings, Esc leaves focus mode.

The bigger bug was how the timer calculated its total duration. Progress was computed from the current settings:

const totalSeconds = {
  focus: settings.focusDuration,
  shortBreak: settings.shortBreakDuration,
  longBreak: settings.longBreakDuration,
}[state.mode] * 60;

That works until someone changes the focus duration while a session is paused. The finish line moves, the progress bar jumps, and a paused session can look like it has more time left than it started with. The store now stamps the session length when the session starts:

sessionDurationSeconds:
  s.state.sessionDurationSeconds ??
  getDurationForMode(s.state.mode, s.settings),

and every consumer reads that stamp:

const totalSeconds =
  state.sessionDurationSeconds ?? getDurationForMode(state.mode, settings);

const isPausedMidSession =
  !state.isRunning &&
  (state.sessionDurationSeconds != null ||
    state.remainingSeconds < totalSeconds);

Settings changes now only adjust the displayed duration when the timer is genuinely idle. A paused mid-session timer keeps its original length, shows a PAUSED badge, and gets a muted progress fill instead of the brand colour.

The countdown also moved into the tab title. Running sessions show the remaining time and mode; paused sessions get a prefix:

if (isPausedMidSession) {
  document.title = `Paused (${formatMmSs(state.remainingSeconds)}) · Kagelin`;
}

The tab title makes the timer usable from another tab. Accessibility was the bigger gap: the old screen had no live region, so a screen reader user could not tell when a session started or when five minutes remained. There is now a polite live region that announces start, pause, five minutes left, one minute left, and completion. It deliberately does not announce every tick.

A date picker should not make you choose a date before choosing a time

The old picker disabled the Time tab until a date was selected. That is backwards for the common case: you know you want 3pm, and the date is the easy part. The Time tab is now always available, and opening it without a date defaults to noon today:

if (nextStep === "time" && !tempDate) {
  const todayNoon = new Date();
  todayNoon.setHours(12, 0, 0, 0);
  setTempDate(todayNoon);
}

The date step also gained four presets in a 2x2 grid, each with the weekday or time printed on the button: Today, Tomorrow, Next Week, Evening. The hint is generated, not hard-coded, so it stays correct as the week rolls over:

{ label: "Today", hint: format(new Date(), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Tomorrow", hint: format(addDays(new Date(), 1), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Next Week", hint: format(addDays(new Date(), 7), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Evening", hint: "6pm", onClick: ... },

On phones, the calendar event editor now uses a responsive dialog instead of a popover. The same DateTimeWizard component renders in both, but the mobile path gets a bottom sheet with a real title for assistive tech. A popover anchored to a field near the bottom of a phone viewport fights the virtual keyboard. The sheet does not.

Two smaller correctness fixes came with it. Changing an event's start date now preserves its duration instead of resetting the end to an hour later. And an end date before the start is clamped at submit time, so a bad range cannot be saved:

const clampedEndDate =
  safeEndDate.getTime() < safeStartDate.getTime()
    ? getDefaultEndDate(safeStartDate)
    : safeEndDate;

The time picker itself was rebuilt around accessible spinbuttons. Arrow keys increment and decrement hours and minutes, typing a digit moves focus between fields, and AM/PM is a real focus target. The old control was two styled boxes that looked like inputs but were not.

Offline replay needs order and identity

The offline queue was the least visible change and the one most likely to lose data. Mutations were persisted and replayed as a loose pool. A create and an edit of the same row could run in either order, so the edit could hit a row that did not exist yet, or the create could overwrite the edit.

TanStack Query already has the primitive for this: mutation scopes. Each mutation now declares a scope, and replays within a scope are serialized:

client.setMutationDefaults(["createTask"], {
  mutationFn: taskMutations.create,
  scope: { id: "tasks" },
});

The same is done for habits and calendar events. Creates also stamp a stable client ID at the moment the user acts, not when the network returns:

const tempId = input._clientId || crypto.randomUUID();
input._clientId = tempId;

That ID is reused as the row ID, so a retried create is idempotent. Without it, a create that succeeded on the server but failed on the response would be retried and produce a duplicate.

The second bug was dates. Habit start dates used to be filled in inside the mutation function:

start_date: input.start_date || new Date().toISOString().split("T")[0]

Two problems. toISOString() is UTC, so a local evening in a negative-offset timezone can already be tomorrow in UTC. And the value was computed at replay time, so a habit created at 23:55 and replayed at 00:05 got the wrong day even in UTC. The date is now captured when the mutation is enqueued, using the local calendar:

const today = format(new Date(), "yyyy-MM-dd");
input.start_date = input.start_date ?? today;

Tasks, habits, habit entries and calendar events all have regression tests that create and edit offline, cross midnight, reconnect, and assert the original local date survived. The tests matter as much as the fix. The next person to touch the queue will otherwise reintroduce the bug.

Smaller changes

Vim selection used to be a border that vanished against some surfaces. It is now an inset ring plus a lighter row background, applied consistently to list rows and board cards.

There is a branded 404 page instead of the framework default (but needs more work), and production responses now send Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains. Telemetry consent and any queued events are cleared on sign-out and account switch, so a shared device does not inherit the previous person's choice.

Try to break it

The focus shortcuts are the part I most want stress-tested: Space while a button is focused, s inside an input, Esc with a dialog open, a paused session across a reload. The offline queue is the other: create something offline, edit it, cross midnight, reconnect. If the order or the date is wrong, I want the reproduction.

  • App: app.kagelin.app (guest mode works, no account needed)
  • Source: Achyuth072/kagelin
  • Full changelog: Settings, then What's new

title: Support Report SMS Timeouts: 4 Checks for Idempotent Retries and Status Polling
description:
For SMS event notifications, a timeout should trigger reconciliation before a retry can create duplicate sends. The page to design for is a customer-support report notification whose submission outcome is still unknown. The on-call view should identify the support case, generated report revision, notification job, template revision, and last reconciliation attempt. This is a proposed alert design, not an incident account. Don't trust a green send-rate dashboard to explain that particular customer's message. What page fired?

Short answer: persist the notification job before sending an SMS, preserve its idempotency identity across timeout retries, and poll status or events before deciding to resend. For a generated report sent as an email attachment, give the email and its companion SMS separate job identities, with one accountable owner for each template. An SMS update cannot establish that the report attachment reached the customer.

The four checks are job identity, submission evidence, reconciled status, and template ownership. They support a postmortem question that a successful-request counter cannot answer: which customer-visible action was justified by the evidence available at that moment?

How should idempotency govern an SMS retry after an event notification timeout?

A timeout establishes that the caller stopped waiting. It does not establish whether the downstream service accepted the notification, which means an automatic fresh send can turn a communication delay into duplicate customer messages. The earlier signal should therefore describe an unresolved notification job and its age, rather than treating every timeout as either a definitive failure or an invitation to send again.

Keep uncertainty visible.

Consider a design example: support case CS-157 has generated report revision 3, an email job carrying that report, and a separate SMS job announcing its availability. These are illustrative application identifiers, not provider request fields. A support editor owns the customer-facing wording; engineering owns delivery policy and the durable job transition. If an editor revises the SMS while submission is unresolved, that edit must not silently create a second notification identity. Conversely, a genuinely new report revision may justify a new notification, subject to the team's communication policy. Those two decisions need separate review paths because one changes wording and the other changes what the customer receives.

The trap is using the attempt identifier as the notification identifier. Every network retry then looks like a new business action. Store both: one durable logical job identity and separate attempt records, including the template revision actually selected for submission. Freeze that revision while reconciling an uncertain result. It makes the eventual postmortem about an identifiable message instead of whatever template happens to be current when someone opens the dashboard.

Reconstruct the send before authorizing another one

Start with the stored job. Record submission intent durably before the request, save the provider identifier when one is returned, and retain the evidence used to authorize every later action. Where a provider supports idempotency for that operation, reuse the same key for the same logical notification; verify its scope and retention before treating it as a recovery guarantee. Local uniqueness still matters because it governs your worker's decisions outside the provider's deduplication window.

Then reconcile. A provider identifier gives a polling worker something concrete to inspect. Without that identifier, the job remains ambiguous: do not invent an identifier, assume the message was rejected, or generate a fresh idempotency key to get past the uncertainty. A request-level deduplication contract can help with a retry of the original submission, but it is different from proof of delivery. An application cannot promise exactly-once customer delivery merely because it stored a key.

For this workflow, Infrai combines one API key and one bill with a self-describing REST API whose public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a capability begins with inspecting its contract instead of learning another SDK. That single-key model reduces credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation between the report-email worker and SMS reconciliation worker. Its specified idempotency convention adds a useful supporting mechanism, with an Idempotency-Key header and a default 24-hour deduplication window; check the chosen capability's idempotency declaration before relying on that convention. Delivery reconciliation uses status or event polling, so include a polling worker in the design.

The application owns the decision.

Use bounded exponential backoff for retryable requests, honor Retry-After when supplied, and distinguish polling retries from sending retries. A rate-limited status check should not create a new customer message. Exhausting a polling budget should escalate an unresolved job for review, rather than convert uncertainty into permission to resend. For a Node.js Express application, the request handler can persist intent and return control while a worker performs this reconciliation; the lifecycle matters more than which language hosts it.

This Go status probe is deliberately read-only. Save it as main.go and run it with Go after setting SMS_API_BASE to the HTTPS API base ending in the version segment, INFRAI_API_KEY to your key, and SMS_ID to the identifier already stored on the job. It prints the actual response without guessing undocumented status fields; a production reconciler must interpret those fields against the response schema and persist its observation. There are 3 attempts, each with a 10-second HTTP timeout. A timeout exits with an error and never sends another message.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("SMS_API_BASE"), "/")
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" || key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set HTTPS SMS_API_BASE, INFRAI_API_KEY, and SMS_ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+"/sms/status/"+url.PathEscape(id), nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("status unresolved: %w", err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if proposed := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; proposed > delay { delay = proposed }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if proposed := time.Until(deadline); proposed > delay { delay = proposed }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("status unresolved after retry budget")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Put template ownership in the comparison

Choose the system in which the responsible team can review a template revision and reconstruct its use. The following are evaluation boundaries, not claims that every product supplies the same delivery semantics. In particular, an email template feature should not be scored as an SMS recovery guarantee.

Option Relevant template surface to inspect Fit and boundary for the support workflow
Twilio Messaging Content templates and messaging documentation Evaluate for the SMS notification leg; review its status callbacks as an alternative to a polling design. Establish separately who owns the report email and its attachment.
SendGrid Dynamic transactional email templates Evaluate when support needs ownership of the report email's wording. Verify attachment handling and how a template revision is associated with an application job; assess the SMS leg separately.
Amazon SES Email templates and sending documentation Evaluate when engineering can own the email integration and template lifecycle. Review the attachment sending contract, and make the SMS ownership decision separately.

Each is a real candidate for a different part of the communication path. None earns a complete workflow recommendation merely by appearing in a table. The referenced documentation is the place to validate the selected integration; this article does not present an authenticated comparison test or measured delivery results.

There is a trade-off here: an editor-facing template workflow can reduce engineering involvement in copy changes, while application-managed revisions can make deployment review and job reconstruction more direct. Decide which team is allowed to change customer-facing text during an active support incident. Then require the integration to preserve evidence of that choice. For the attachment itself, validate the selected email API's actual request schema before implementation; an SMS send contract says nothing about attachment fields or limits.

Instrument the decision the responder needs to make

Add application-level records for job creation time, logical notification identity, template revision, attempt time, provider identifier when available, and the last successful reconciliation. These are suggested internal fields. They are not an invented vendor payload. Track unresolved-job age separately from request duration, and distinguish a worker that cannot poll from a job whose latest observed state remains inconclusive. Otherwise a stalled reconciler can masquerade as a healthy system simply because it produces no new send errors.

One practical handoff record should answer all four checks: is this the original logical job; what submission evidence exists; when was its state last reconciled; and which template owner can explain the submitted revision? Keep customer message content out of routine alert text where a case reference and revision are sufficient. The responder needs a decision trail, not an attachment copied into a pager notification.

Scheduled communication adds another policy decision. Reconcile the outcome of an SMS cancellation before assuming a delayed notification has been suppressed. Treat scheduled report email cancellation as a separate contract requirement, and use an application-owned scheduling policy if that requirement cannot be established. Email fallback codes likewise need an explicit application design; do not assume a messaging integration supplies a managed email OTP flow.

Scope the evaluation to email and SMS. If the support workflow requires SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, make those independent selection criteria rather than implying that a shared messaging interface covers them. Country restrictions and geographic abuse controls also belong in the application's policy review. Record per-job accounting information internally when the team needs reporting by support category, and keep an application template inventory so recovery does not depend on discovering mutable template state during an incident.

Close the postmortem with the cost of a noisy threshold

Set the unresolved-job age threshold from the support team's acceptable notification delay and the polling schedule it can actually sustain. No measured delivery-time distribution is established here, so a universal timeout number would be false precision. Start with an explicit service expectation, inspect the resulting alerts, and revise it using observed outcomes.

Page on actionable uncertainty.

A threshold shorter than ordinary reconciliation can page repeatedly for jobs that resolve without intervention, consuming the same responder attention needed for a stalled worker or a report that never gets its notification decision resolved. A threshold set too generously can leave support waiting on an ambiguous message while the dashboard remains green. The useful postmortem action is to connect the threshold to a named owner, a known template revision, and a safe next action. If the alert cannot explain why another send is justified, its default action should remain investigation.

Further reading

References for validating the alternatives and the recovery model:

  • Twilio Message resource and delivery status callbacks
  • Twilio Content templates
  • SendGrid dynamic transactional email templates
  • SendGrid Mail Send API, including attachment parameters
  • Amazon SES email templates
  • Amazon SES attachments
  • RFC 9110, idempotent methods and retry semantics

title: SaaS Dashboard UX: How to Turn Complex Product Data Into Better User Decisions
description:
A SaaS dashboard can display dozens of metrics, charts, reports, and activity logs. But none of that matters if users still struggle to understand what is happening inside their product.

This is one of the most common problems in SaaS product design. Teams invest heavily in analytics, reporting capabilities, and backend functionality, yet the interface often makes users work harder than necessary to find meaningful information.

The real challenge isn't displaying more data. It's designing an experience that helps users interpret that data, identify what needs attention, and decide what to do next.

Effective dashboard UX starts with understanding user workflows, organizing information around real tasks, and reducing the cognitive effort required to make decisions.

Here are the practical design considerations that make a SaaS dashboard genuinely useful.

  1. Design Around User Workflows, Not Available Features

A common mistake in dashboard development is starting with a list of available features.

The product team asks:

Which analytics can we display?

How many charts should we include?

Which filters should be available?

What information can we pull from the database?

These are implementation questions, not UX questions.

A better starting point is understanding what users actually want to accomplish.

For example, consider a marketing analytics platform. A marketing manager might open the dashboard to answer three questions:

Which campaigns are performing below expectations?

Where is the advertising budget being wasted?

Which campaigns need immediate attention?

These questions should influence the dashboard structure.

Instead of presenting every metric with equal importance, the interface should prioritize campaign performance, budget efficiency, and actionable alerts.

Practical approach: Map the primary user journeys before creating dashboard components. Identify the decisions users make most frequently, then organize the interface around those activities.

  1. Establish a Clear Information Architecture

Information architecture determines how dashboard content is grouped, prioritized, and accessed.

Without a logical structure, even a visually attractive dashboard becomes difficult to navigate as the product grows.

A useful SaaS dashboard usually separates information into meaningful layers:

Overview layer: Key performance indicators, account summaries, and important notifications.

Analysis layer: Detailed charts, historical comparisons, trends, and performance breakdowns.

Action layer: Tasks, alerts, approvals, and operational controls.

Detail layer: Individual records, customer information, transactions, and supporting data.

This structure allows users to move from a high-level understanding to detailed investigation without overwhelming the initial screen.

For larger SaaS applications, navigation should also reflect how users mentally categorize their work. For example, billing, team management, reporting, and account settings should not be mixed into an unpredictable menu structure.

The objective is simple: users should understand where information lives without having to explore the entire application.

  1. Make Every KPI Explain Something

A dashboard KPI should provide context, not just a number.

Displaying revenue as $48,500 might look informative, but users cannot determine whether that performance is positive or negative without additional information.

A more useful KPI includes:

The current value.

A comparison against a previous period.

The percentage or absolute change.

A clear definition of the measurement.

The relevant reporting timeframe.

For example:

Monthly Recurring Revenue

$48,500

+12.4% compared with the previous month

This provides a much stronger understanding of business performance.

However, comparison periods must be consistent. Comparing the last seven days with an entire previous month can produce misleading conclusions.

Also, avoid presenting every KPI as equally important. Identify the metrics that directly influence user decisions and give them appropriate visual priority.

  1. Treat Data Visualization as a Communication Problem

Charts are useful when they make relationships easier to understand.

They become unnecessary decoration when users need additional effort to interpret them.

Choose chart types according to the question being answered:

User question

Suitable visualization

How has revenue changed over time?

Line chart

Which product category performs best?

Bar chart

How is the budget distributed?

Stacked bar or carefully used pie chart

How do conversion rates compare?

Bar chart

Where are operational bottlenecks?

Funnel visualization

A few additional considerations matter:

Avoid using too many colors without a consistent meaning.

Label axes and measurement units clearly.

Do not truncate scales in ways that exaggerate differences.

Provide tooltips for additional context.

Make important data points accessible without relying exclusively on hover interactions.

A chart should reduce interpretation time. If users need to study the visualization before understanding its message, reconsider the design.

  1. Design for Different Data States

One of the most overlooked aspects of SaaS dashboard UX is what happens when data is unavailable.

Designers frequently focus on the ideal scenario, where all information loads correctly and every account has sufficient data.

Real applications are not that predictable.

A production-ready dashboard needs carefully designed states for:

Empty state: The user has not generated any data yet. Explain what belongs here and provide a useful first action.

Loading state: Information is being retrieved. Use appropriate skeletons or progress indicators rather than leaving unexplained blank spaces.

Error state: A request has failed. Communicate what happened and provide a recovery option.

Partial data state: Some metrics are available while others are still processing. Make the limitation clear instead of presenting incomplete information as final.

These states are not secondary UI details. They directly influence whether users trust the application.

For example, an empty revenue chart should not simply display a blank area. It should explain that revenue data will appear after the first transaction and guide the user toward the relevant setup step.

  1. Build Responsive Dashboards Around Real Usage

Responsive design for SaaS dashboards requires more than shrinking desktop components.

The information density, interaction patterns, and navigation requirements can change significantly between devices.

A desktop dashboard might comfortably display:

Multiple KPI cards.

A detailed analytics chart.

A sidebar navigation.

Several data tables.

On a smaller screen, displaying everything simultaneously creates unnecessary complexity.

A better responsive strategy prioritizes information based on user needs.

For mobile layouts:

Keep the most important KPI visible early.

Stack cards according to their importance.

Simplify navigation.

Make filters accessible through compact controls.

Avoid horizontal scrolling for essential information.

Preserve readable chart labels and interactive targets.

It is also important to test actual interactions, not just visual breakpoints. Date pickers, dropdowns, tables, and chart tooltips can behave differently on touchscreens.

  1. Make Accessibility Part of the Design System

Accessibility should be considered during component design rather than added after development.

Dashboard interfaces often contain dense data, small labels, status indicators, and complex interactions. These elements can create usability barriers if accessibility is ignored.

Important considerations include:

Color contrast: Ensure text and graphical elements remain distinguishable against their backgrounds.

Color-independent communication: Do not use red and green as the only indicators of failure and success. Add labels, icons, or other visual cues.

Keyboard navigation: Users should be able to navigate menus, filters, dialogs, and interactive components using a keyboard.

Readable typography: Maintain appropriate text sizes, spacing, and hierarchy.

Accessible data tables: Use meaningful headings and logical reading order.

WCAG 2.2 provides useful accessibility criteria for evaluating these experiences, including keyboard accessibility, contrast, and non-text visual information.

Accessibility improves the overall usability of a product because it encourages more predictable and understandable interactions.

  1. Validate Dashboard UX With Actual Product Usage

A dashboard can look excellent in a design presentation and still perform poorly in real-world usage.

The difference becomes clear when actual users start interacting with it.

Instead of relying exclusively on internal opinions, evaluate the interface through usability testing and product analytics.

Some useful measurements include:

Time required to complete a common dashboard task.

Number of interactions needed to find a specific metric.

Filter usage and abandonment.

Frequency of report exports.

Errors during important workflows.

Feature discovery and adoption.

User feedback about confusing or unnecessary information.

For example, if users repeatedly export a report because they cannot understand the information displayed on the dashboard, the problem might not be missing functionality. It could be poor information hierarchy or unclear data presentation.

Use these observations to identify friction points, redesign individual components, and measure the impact of each change.

A Practical SaaS Dashboard UX Review Checklist

Before releasing a dashboard, review the following:

Does the main screen answer a clear user question?

Are the most important KPIs visually prioritized?

Do metrics include meaningful comparisons and timeframes?

Are charts appropriate for the information being communicated?

Are filters understandable and predictable?

Do empty, loading, and error states provide clear guidance?

Does the layout work across desktop, tablet, and mobile?

Can users navigate essential interactions with a keyboard?

Are status indicators understandable without color?

Have real users tested the most important workflows?

This checklist can help teams identify design issues before they become recurring usability problems.

Final Thoughts

A successful SaaS dashboard is not defined by how many charts it contains or how sophisticated its interface looks.

Its value comes from how effectively it helps users understand information and complete important tasks.

Good dashboard UX requires a combination of information architecture, interaction design, data visualization, accessibility, and continuous usability testing.

For a deeper look at the design principles behind effective data presentation, read this guide on SaaS Dashboard UI/UX Design: 8 Principles for Clear Data.

It explores practical ways to organize dashboard information, establish KPI hierarchy, improve empty states, and make complex product data easier to understand.

Ultimately, the best dashboards don't simply show users what is happening. They help users understand what matters and what to do next.

title: MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.33822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Rust Anything: Port to Rust and Verify Behavior
description:
title: "Rust Anything: Port your code to Rust and check that it still behaves the same"
published: false
description: "An open-source tool that records how your code behaves and replays those cases against a Rust port."

tags: rust, opensource, tooling, ai

When you port a piece of software to Rust, getting it to compile is just the beginning. The harder question comes next: Does it still behave like the original?

I came across Rust Anything, an open-source project by Erkam Yaman that helps you answer that question by migrating one component at a time and using the original implementation as a baseline.

How it works

  1. Rust Anything runs the original code and records inputs and outputs.
  2. A coding agent writes the Rust implementation.
  3. Rust Anything replays the recorded cases against the port and flags any differences.

The project reports matching results for all 3,414 recorded cases in its Fuse.js port. It also documents a port of PEAR XML_Util, a PHP library that calls into Rust through PHP’s ext-ffi extension.

Where I’d start

In a PHP or TypeScript backend, I’d start with a component whose inputs and outputs are easy to reproduce, such as a parser or file transformer. I’d include malformed inputs and edge cases in the comparison, then benchmark both implementations with a representative workload to see whether the port is worth keeping.

If you already have Cargo, you can install the tool and set up integrations with coding agents such as Codex, Claude Code, or OpenCode:

cargo install rust-anything
rust-anything setup
  • Rust Anything website and documentation
  • Source code on GitHub

What part of an application you maintain would you try porting to Rust first?

title: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
description:
AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers.

The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path.

Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. Baseten, Modal, and Wafer are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy.

Audited ZDR builds on two steps we took toward stronger governance earlier this year:

  • We launched team-wide Zero Data Retention (ZDR) so teams could route traffic exclusively to providers stating a ZDR policy.

  • We completed our ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, which put Vercel’s own AI systems under independent third-party audit.

We are now asking inference providers for the same thing we asked of ourselves: independent verification.

Why a contract is not enough

ZDR guarantees rely on contracts and self-attestation. A provider agrees not to retain prompts or completions, and customers take that commitment on faith.

For teams sending proprietary code, customer information, or regulated data through models, self-reported ZDR contracts don't provide enough assurance.

  • Are prompts landing in debug logs, crash dumps, or tracing pipelines?

  • Can a rate limit push a request marked ZDR to a non-ZDR endpoint?

  • Can a support engineer's debugging tools surface a customer's prompt?

Answering these questions means running a bespoke security review for every provider and the models they host. An audit answers them in public.

What Audited ZDR verifies

To qualify for Audited ZDR on AI Gateway, an inference provider engages an independent security firm, chosen from among respected third-party auditors, to run the audit. The firm then tests the provider's zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic.

The audit confirms that customer data is never written or retained on durable storage in any system. Customer data means prompts, completions, system prompts, embeddings, files, images and audio, tool and function-call payloads, and any derived data that could identify them. Coverage spans request logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, prompt caches, abuse monitoring, analytics, backups, support tools, and training, fine-tuning, and evaluation datasets.

The audit confirms that once a response is returned to AI Gateway, that content is deleted from the inference provider’s systems. Where a request uses caching, such as a KV cache, the cache stays in RAM only, is never written to disk, and the behavior is disclosed.

The audit also confirms:

  • That a request marked ZDR never fails over to a non-ZDR endpoint, tool, or feature

  • That no human or automated process accesses customer data outside handling the request itself

  • That sub-processors with access comply with all of the above

  • That no training on customer data occurs

Auditors verify this by reviewing the inference provider's serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then running live tests. They send marked prompts through AI Gateway and search the provider's logging, caching, and storage systems for any trace of them.

Every passing provider publishes the report under the auditor's name. It covers scope, methodology, dates, findings, and fix status, with any exceptions disclosed and redactions limited to exploit detail. AI Gateway links directly to the report.

Canary monitoring between audits

An independent audit checks a provider's code and infrastructure at a point in time, but production systems change. To add a detection layer between independent audits, Vercel also runs canary audits against inference providers on AI Gateway.

Each run sends prompts containing unique, unindexed URLs mapped privately to a provider, model, and run. Because a ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved. Canary checks cannot detect prompts written to disk and never read, so they complement independent code and infrastructure audits rather than replacing them.

How Audited ZDR works in AI Gateway

We are adding an independently Audited ZDR provider tier and a team-wide toggle in AI Gateway policy settings. When enabled, AI Gateway routes and fails over your team's requests only across providers with published audits that meet the bar.

Launch partners have started their audits, and each provider enters the tier as soon as its report is published. Launch partner reports are expected to be published by December 8, 2026.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries and failover for higher uptime than connecting to providers directly. It reflects provider pricing with no markup and charges no platform fee on inference, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. Read the AI Gateway documentation to get started.

The audited tier works alongside AI Gateway's other compliance controls. Regional inference pins where a provider runs inference to the US, EU, Australia, or Japan, per request or team-wide, and any data the provider stores at rest stays in that region. If AI Gateway can't honor the region, the request fails rather than running elsewhere.

Provider headquarters filters routing by who owns the provider, so a request only reaches providers whose parent company is headquartered in a country you allow.

Private inference connects your own self-hosted or fine-tuned model endpoints to AI Gateway, called as private/<slug> with the same SDKs, auth, and observability as catalog models and scoped to your team.

title: text-wrap pretty made my pills overflow on phones
description:
In October, Framer's Marketplace review took four of my templates down. One of the problems they flagged looked tiny: on phones, the text in some pills and price tags ran past the edge of the pill. A price like "€6,900 / week" spilled out of its card.

The cause was a setting I had turned on to make text look better.

The setup

In Framer, text styles have a Text Wrap option: default, balance or pretty. Balance evens out line lengths, and pretty avoids a single word stranded on the last line. Both map to the CSS text-wrap property, and both make headings and paragraphs look more polished.

So I had set pretty wrap on almost every text style, including the label and button styles. Those styles are used inside pills that size themselves to their text, which in Framer means auto width (in CSS terms, the pill shrinks to fit its content).

What went wrong

On desktop everything looked fine. On a narrow phone, where a pill had to wrap or squeeze, the text stopped fitting inside it. Framer publishes these text layers with white-space: pre-wrap, and with balance or pretty wrap on top, the auto-width pill ended up sized by its longest word rather than by its text. The rest of the text overflowed the pill instead of the pill growing or the text wrapping cleanly.

It only showed at small widths, so I never saw it at the three breakpoints I usually looked at.

The fix

Set Text Wrap back to default on the label and button styles. That fixed every pill at once, because they all shared those styles.

In plain CSS terms:

/* Pills, tags, buttons: let them wrap normally */
.pill, .button, .tag {
    text-wrap: wrap;
}

/* Keep the nicer wrapping where it helps: headings in containers with a set width */
h1, h2 {
    text-wrap: balance;
}

I still use balance on big headings, where a lone word on the last line looks bad and the container's width doesn't depend on the text.

How to catch it

  • Check your published site at a 320 px phone width, not just the breakpoints your tool gives you. Small phones show wrapping problems first.
  • Look at every component that sizes itself to its content: pills, tags, chips, buttons and badges.
  • Change shared text styles carefully. One setting on a style touches every layer that uses it, which is how one checkbox broke pills across a whole template.

The other two things that review flagged were a hover zoom that grew past its frame and buttons that linked to a deleted page. I wrote all three up, together with the rest of my pre-submission checks, here: the Framer template checklist I use before every submission.

Where do you use text-wrap: balance or pretty, and have you seen it misbehave?

title: The LXD OIDC Patch Plan: 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2
description:
The LXD OIDC Patch Plan: 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2

CVE-2026-135384 has a clear fixed-release boundary, but the repair also requires configuration checks. Canonical lists LXD 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2 as patched versions for an improper authentication flaw in OIDC bearer-token verification. Administrators should plan the upgrade around the deployed release line and verify the identity path after the service restarts.

The CVE record identifies CWE-287 and assigns CVSS 4.0 score 9.2 Critical. The GitHub advisory entry displays 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The difference should be documented in the change record, but it does not change the affected versions, the authentication impact, or the fixed release list.

What the patch addresses

The advisory says LXD checked an OIDC token's issuer, signature, and expiry. Unless oidc.audience was set, the server did not bind the token to LXD. A token from the same provider for another application could therefore be accepted. The advisory also describes a token without a user name being authenticated with an empty name, an ID token being accepted in place of an access token, and unverified email claims being used for the user name when oidc.claim was unset.

The fixed releases are intended to remove these accepting paths. The rest of the security work is to ensure the deployment uses the intended provider, audience, claim, and authorization model after the binary changes.

Identify the release line first

Use the LXD version and packaging records to place each server in the 5.0, 5.21, or 6.10 line. Confirm whether the package, snap, or source build is within an affected range. A version displayed by a client can differ from the server's running version, so collect the server value through an authenticated management path.

For systems outside these lines, consult Canonical support and the CVE record rather than applying another branch's patch by assumption. For a supported branch, the target is the fixed release listed by the vendor. The fixed release should be installed through the normal package or snap channel and followed by a service restart if the deployment requires one.

Build the upgrade order

Prioritize internet-reachable management interfaces and servers with broad OIDC authorization first. The advisory says an authenticated OIDC client has full control in the default configuration where clients are not routed through OpenFGA or a scriptlet. A delegated setup may reduce the blast radius, but an affected authentication path still needs remediation.

Group servers by evidence available: version confirmed, OIDC enabled, provider shared with other applications, email-based identities, and management exposure. This produces a defensible order without claiming that every product match is exploitable. Include cluster members and recovery nodes, since a repaired primary with an older peer can leave another management path available.

Apply temporary controls if needed

The advisory recommends setting oidc.audience to a value that the provider places only in LXD access tokens. It also recommends setting oidc.claim to a value users cannot edit, such as sub, or configuring the provider to release only verified email addresses.

These controls should be documented as temporary risk reduction. Test them with the same provider and client flow that production uses. A value copied from a different application's configuration is not sufficient unless the provider actually places it in LXD access tokens. An ID token flow must be tested separately from the normal access-token flow.

Administrators should also review access paths. If external management is not required, remove the exposure. If it is required, restrict it to trusted networks and preserve access for authorized administrators. Firewall changes are compensating controls and do not replace the fixed release.

Validate after the patch

After the upgrade, query the running server version and confirm the expected build. Test a normal OIDC login with an account that has the correct LXD permissions. Test a token with the wrong audience and verify that it is rejected. Test an ID token where an access token is expected and verify rejection. Test an unverified email identity against a non-production account to confirm the configured claim mapping behaves as intended.

Preserve the test evidence with the release and configuration snapshot. If the server uses multiple applications at one provider, test a token from a neighboring client. The purpose is to confirm the boundary that the advisory says was missing while also checking that the new package starts.

Review authorization after upgrade

Authentication repair does not automatically correct every mapping decision. Review OpenFGA or scriptlet rules, group claims, identity-provider groups, and user records created from email addresses. If the deployment relies on email, make sure the provider releases only verified addresses. If it uses a subject claim, confirm the subject is stable across provider accounts.

The advisory describes the issue as copied from an Incus advisory while listing LXD software and patched versions. That wording should not be used to broaden the product scope. Treat the LXD advisory, LXD documentation, and CVE record as the product-specific basis for the change.

Monitoring and rollback

Monitor authentication failures and successes around the deployment window. A burst of failures can indicate an audience or claim mismatch after the change. A successful login from an unexpected application suggests the configuration still needs review.

Keep a rollback plan that restores the previous service state only under an approved incident process. Rolling back to an affected release reopens the authentication weakness. If an upgrade fails, the safer immediate state is usually a restricted management interface plus the documented compensating controls, not an indefinite return to the vulnerable version.

Exposure context

The frozen ZoomEye observation recorded 12,271 matches for app="LXD" and zero for vul.cve="CVE-2026-135384". The product count is useful for finding inventory and validating change coverage. It does not confirm that a host uses OIDC or that it is running a vulnerable version.

References

[1] Canonical LXD security advisory GHSA-v3m9-p36m-qjqc

[2] CVE Program record for CVE-2026-135384

[3] LXD 6.10.2 release notes

[4] LXD server configuration reference
