title: November 09, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

The following AlloyDB AI features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • Smart batching for AI functions: AI function acceleration is generally available for ai.if, ai.rank, ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, ai.extract, ai.classify, and ai.generate on AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 17 and later. Smart batching automatically batches and offloads eligible AI operations for asynchronous evaluation. It improves query execution speed without requiring you to rewrite queries into complex array structures. In PostgreSQL 18 and later, this feature is enabled by default. For more information, see Accelerate performance for queries with AI functions.

  • Sentiment analysis: the ai.analyze_sentiment function is generally available on AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 17 and later. This built-in function classifies the sentiment of text as positive, negative, or neutral directly within SQL queries in real time. For more information, see Analyze text sentiment.

title: How to Build Unified Bid Request Mapping Systems for Multiple DSP and SSP Integrations
description:
Here's the specific trap every AdTech platform integrating multiple partners walks into. The spec says OpenRTB 2.6. The integration docs from 15 SSPs and 40 DSPs all cite OpenRTB 2.6 compliance. You code against the spec, ship the integration, and discover that every single partner interprets the spec slightly differently. Content taxonomy versions drift, impression ID formats clash, user ID arrays arrive in four different shapes, geo fields contradict each other, and video placement types mean different things on different exchanges.

Modern OpenRTB Development teams building unified bid request mapping systems solved this years ago. The engine normalizes incoming requests from every SSP into a canonical internal schema, enriches with missing fields, routes to DSPs in each DSP's preferred dialect, and handles version drift per integration. Platforms running on "spec compliant" integrations without a proper mapping layer burn impressions on field mismatches and lose fill every single day.

That's not a documentation problem. That's a specific engineering problem. The 2026 reality is that OpenRTB 2.6 is the live spec across most exchanges, OpenRTB 3.0 adoption is slow-rolling, and every major partner carries protocol extensions, deprecated field handling, and custom interpretations. Platforms engineering proper mapping middleware integrate 50+ partners cleanly. Platforms treating OpenRTB as a universal translator eat integration bugs quarterly.

Why OpenRTB Isn't a Universal Translator

The OpenRTB spec is a specification document. It is not a wire protocol validator, not a field dictionary enforcer, not a behavior guarantee. Every partner's implementation sits somewhere inside the spec's permissible interpretations, and the overlap between any two implementations is smaller than engineers expect.
The commercial cost shows up at scale. A field a DSP requires that your SSP doesn't send drops that DSP's bids entirely. A video placement type you send wrong gets filtered pre-auction. A deal ID formatted differently from the partner's expectation doesn't match. Each of these failures looks like "low fill" in the dashboard; the actual cause is mapping, not demand.

The Specific 5 Mapping Challenges

IAB Content Taxonomy Version Drift
IAB Content Taxonomy 1.0 (categories like IAB2-3), 2.0 (hierarchical with underscore separators), and 2.2 (current stable) all live in parallel across partners. Some SSPs send 1.0 codes, some send 2.2, some send both in different fields. The mapping layer maintains a translation table across versions and normalizes to the canonical internal version before routing to buyers.

IAB Taxonomy 1.0, 2.0, 2.2 all live in parallel:Translation table per direction.
Canonical internal version normalization: One schema inside, dialects at the edges.

Impression ID Normalization

OpenRTB imp[0].id is the standard. Some SSPs put correlation IDs in bid request ext fields, some use their own impression identifiers for post-auction reconciliation. The mapping layer preserves the original SSP-side ID for win notification, stores the canonical internal ID for cross-partner tracking, and maps both directions for billing reconciliation.

User ID Mapping Across EIDs Array**

Post-cookie, user identity flows via the OpenRTB EIDs array carrying UID2, ID5, LiveRamp RampID, EUID, Google PPID, and dozens of proprietary identifiers. Each DSP accepts different EIDs, with different hashing expectations, different source field requirements, and different fallback behavior when IDs are missing. The mapping layer normalizes incoming EIDs, enriches via ID bridges where available, and formats outgoing EIDs per DSP expectations.
EIDs array carries UID2, ID5, RampID, EUID, Google PPID: Each DSP accepts a subset.
Enrichment via ID bridges fills gaps: Where deterministic links exist.

Geo Enrichment and Field Discrepancy

Country codes arrive as ISO 3166 alpha-2 (US) or alpha-3 (USA) depending on partner. Postal codes come as 5-digit, 9-digit, or alphanumeric international. DMA codes versus metro codes versus city names versus lat/long coordinates all show up. The mapping layer standardizes to a canonical geo schema, enriches missing fields via MaxMind GeoIP2 or IP2Location where the request is under-specified, and formats per DSP preference.

Video Spec Translation and Placement Semantics

OpenRTB video objects carry mimes, protocols, playbackmethod, placement (deprecated in 2.6), plcmt (the 2.6 replacement), api frameworks (VPAID 2.0, OMID 1.0), and dozens of other fields. The placement vs plcmt transition is still mid-rollout across exchanges. Some SSPs send only placement, some send only plcmt, some send OpenRTB DSP Integration both with conflicts. The mapping layer handles both, normalizes to plcmt semantics internally, and sends whichever the target DSP expects.

Schema Registry and Version Management

The schema registry maintains canonical schema definitions, per-partner version tracking, and field deprecation warnings. Named tools: Confluent Schema Registry for Avro or Protobuf schemas, custom JSON Schema stores, or OpenAPI specs managed in version control. The registry becomes the source of truth for every adapter's input and output expectations, with automated contract testing catching integration drift before production.
Adapter-per-integration keeps mapping encapsulated: 5-10 days per onboarding vs 30-60 scattered.
Schema registry with contract testing catches drift: Confluent, custom JSON Schema, or OpenAPI.

title: Accept crypto payments in Spring Boot
description:
How to connect Moonvex to a Spring Boot 3 app: RestClient creates a checkout and returns the link to the page where the customer picks the coin, and the webhook controller receives the body as byte[], verifies the signature with javax.crypto.Mac and marks the order in a transaction.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. In Spring Boot inject them into application.properties from environment variables.

# application.properties — values come from environment variables
moonvex.secret-key=${MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY}
moonvex.webhook-secret=${MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET}

2. Create a checkout with RestClient

A RestClient (Spring Framework 6.1+) with the base URL and the Authorization header is built once. The request has no network, so Moonvex creates a checkout where the customer picks the coin and network. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl (https only) is where the Back buttons lead. The amount is BigDecimal.toPlainString(), never a double. The controller responds 303 with Location set to paymentUrl.

// MoonvexClient.java
@Service
public class MoonvexClient {
    private final RestClient http;

    public MoonvexClient(@Value("${moonvex.secret-key}") String secretKey) {
        this.http = RestClient.builder()
                .baseUrl("https://api.moonvex.org")
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, "Bearer " + secretKey)
                .build();
    }

    public JsonNode createCheckout(long orderId, BigDecimal amount, int attempt) {
        return http.post()
                .uri("/v1/payments")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "order-" + orderId + "-" + attempt)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(Map.of(
                        "orderId", String.valueOf(orderId),
                        "amount", amount.toPlainString(), // BigDecimal → "25.00", not a double
                        "currency", "USD", // no network: the customer picks the coin on the checkout page
                        "description", "Order #" + orderId, // shown as “You are paying for”
                        "returnUrl", "https://shop.example.com/orders/" + orderId)) // the Back buttons
                .retrieve()
                .body(JsonNode.class); // {"object": "checkout", "id": "inv_…", "paymentUrl": …}
    }
}

// PayController.java
@RestController
public class PayController {
    private final MoonvexClient moonvex;
    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public PayController(MoonvexClient moonvex, OrderRepository orders) {
        this.moonvex = moonvex;
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @PostMapping("/orders/{id}/pay")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> pay(@PathVariable long id) {
        Order order = orders.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
        JsonNode checkout = moonvex.createCheckout(order.getId(), order.getTotal(), 1);
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SEE_OTHER)
                .location(URI.create(checkout.get("paymentUrl").asText()))
                .build();
    }
}

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook.

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. A @RequestBody byte[] parameter receives the body without Jackson getting involved, and those are exactly the signed bytes. Signatures are compared with MessageDigest.isEqual and hex is parsed with HexFormat (Java 17+).

// MoonvexWebhookController.java
@RestController
public class MoonvexWebhookController {
    private final ObjectMapper json;
    private final OrderService orders;
    private final byte[] secret;

    public MoonvexWebhookController(ObjectMapper json, OrderService orders,
                                    @Value("${moonvex.webhook-secret}") String secret) {
        this.json = json;
        this.orders = orders;
        this.secret = secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    // byte[] gives the body as is, without Jackson conversion
    @PostMapping("/moonvex/webhook")
    public ResponseEntity<String> webhook(@RequestBody byte[] raw,
                                          @RequestHeader(name = "Moonvex-Signature", required = false) String signature) throws Exception {
        if (!verify(raw, signature)) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body("bad signature");
        }
        JsonNode event = json.readTree(raw);
        String type = event.path("type").asText();
        if (type.equals("payment.confirmed") || type.equals("payment.overpaid")) {
            orders.markPaidOnce(event.path("id").asText(), event.path("data").path("orderId").asText());
        }
        // payment.cancelled also arrives when the customer switches coins: do not cancel the order on it
        return ResponseEntity.ok("ok");
    }

    private boolean verify(byte[] raw, String header) throws Exception {
        if (header == null) return false;
        String ts = null;
        List<String> sigs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String part : header.split(",")) {
            String[] kv = part.split("=", 2);
            if (kv.length != 2) continue;
            if (kv[0].equals("t")) ts = kv[1];
            else if (kv[0].equals("v1")) sigs.add(kv[1]);
        }
        if (ts == null || !ts.matches("\\d+")) return false;
        if (Math.abs(Instant.now().getEpochSecond() - Long.parseLong(ts)) > 300) return false;

        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
        mac.update((ts + ".").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        byte[] expected = mac.doFinal(raw);
        for (String s : sigs) {
            try {
                // MessageDigest.isEqual is a constant-time comparison
                if (MessageDigest.isEqual(expected, HexFormat.of().parseHex(s))) return true;
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException ignored) {
                // not hex, skip it
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open. @Transactional plus INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: jdbc.update returns 0 on a redelivery.

// OrderService.java
// CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id text PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public OrderService(JdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void markPaidOnce(String eventId, String orderId) {
        int fresh = jdbc.update("INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", eventId);
        if (fresh == 0) return; // a redelivery
        jdbc.update("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = ? AND status <> 'paid'", Long.parseLong(orderId));
    }
}

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • With Spring Security, exclude /moonvex/webhook from CSRF (csrf.ignoringRequestMatchers) and allow it without authentication (permitAll).
  • Do not bind the webhook body to a DTO or a Map: after Jackson the bytes differ and the signature will not match.
  • Money is BigDecimal only; send toPlainString() in JSON so you never get 2.5E+1.
  • Move heavy work to @async or a queue: the webhook response must go out within 10 seconds.
  • Need one fixed coin instead of the customer's choice? Add network (and asset when currency is USD) to the same request, for example "network", "TRON", "asset", "USDT" in Map.of: that is the classic payment in one coin. The checkout above is the recommended flow.

FAQ

Can I use WebClient or OkHttp instead of RestClient?

Yes, the protocol is plain: POST /v1/payments with JSON and the Authorization: Bearer and Idempotency-Key headers. The example uses RestClient as Spring's own synchronous client.

Why is amount in the webhook higher than the order price?

The checkout returns your price as is in amount and currency. The payment the customer starts (data in webhooks) is in the chosen coin, and its amount is the total due including the Moonvex fee on top. Your price stays in pricing.amount, and what you receive on a full payment is in merchantAmount. Reconcile orders by orderId and pricing.amount.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/java-spring

title: $\mu$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.34920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $\mu$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $\mu$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

title: Make the agent use the existing Badge component, not a one-off colored span
description:
The PR marks a row as "Paid" with a rounded <span>, a hard-coded background, and 11px text. The repo already has a Badge (or Tag / Chip) component with tone variants, a size scale, and contrast that was already checked against the surface tokens. Nearby tables use it. The new span uses a different radius, a different font size, and a color that does not exist on the badge variant list.

I've started treating a one-off colored span as a missed component, not as a lighter label. The word is the easy part. Tone, padding, and contrast are why the Badge exists.

Why the homemade badge shows up

A tutorial "status pill" is a span and a background color. The model can write that without finding components/Badge. Your primitive may be named Tag or Chip, or it may live under a status folder, which is easy to miss if the prompt only says "show a paid label."

You also skip the existing icon slot, the rule about not inventing a new tone, and the contrast work that already happened on success, warning, and neutral.

A simple Badge policy

  • New status and count labels use the existing Badge component
  • Do not add a one-off colored span in a feature file
  • Pick an existing tone (success, warning, neutral, and whatever the system already names)
  • A new tone or size is a Badge change, with a story

If the copy is a filter or a removable label, use the Tag or Chip variant the system already has. Do not turn a Badge into a close button in the feature file.

What to put in the prompt 

Use the existing Badge (or Tag / Chip) component for this status label.
Do not build a colored span or a one-off pill in this file.
Pick an existing tone and size. Do not invent a new hex or font size.
If you need a new tone, extend the Badge; do not fork it here.

Paste one existing Badge usage and the variant list. In review, search the diff for a raw <span> with a background, a hard-coded hex or Tailwind color on a pill, and a "Paid" / "New" / "Beta" label that is not the shared component.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A feature-level status pill that reimplements the Badge
  • A new tone or hex that is not on the Badge variant list
  • A Badge used as a removable filter when a Tag or Chip already exists
  • A second badge component added for one table

Accept

  • A status or count that uses the existing Badge
  • A Badge PR that adds a documented tone or size and a story
  • A removable filter that uses the existing Tag or Chip, not a forked pill

title: Extracting Prediction Confidence from Scikit-Learn Classifiers
description:
QuackBuilds has released a new snippet: Scikit-Learn Classifier Prediction Confidence.

This tool addresses a common need when working with classification models: understanding how confident your model is about each individual prediction. While a classifier provides a predicted class, knowing the underlying probability can offer deeper insights into its performance and reliability.

The snippet demonstrates the process of extracting these prediction probabilities directly from a scikit-learn classifier. It shows how to access the confidence scores for each class, which can then be used to evaluate the model's certainty for its chosen output. Additionally, it includes methods to identify and flag predictions where the model's confidence is notably low. This feature is useful for pinpointing ambiguous cases or areas where the model might require further training or data.

This is intended for developers and data scientists who use scikit-learn for classification tasks and need to go beyond simple class labels to understand model behavior.

title: WormHole: AI Vulnerability Discovery for Complex Systems
description:
Most security tools answer a question you already know how to ask. Is this endpoint authenticated? Does this version of the library carry a known CVE? Run the checklist, get a list, work the list.

That approach holds up while the flaw is a pattern. It stops holding up when the flaw is a sequence: an approval that the requester can grant to themselves, a step that stays replayable after it was revoked, a retry that moves a record forward twice. No scanner reports those. Nothing in any single request looks wrong. The bug is in the order of events.

WormHole is an AI vulnerability discovery and penetration testing tool built for that kind of system. Not any website — multi-tenant SaaS, internal platforms, APIs, onboarding and approval flows, the places where a business rule is the attack surface.

Three layers, one engine

The product page splits the work into workflow, services and code. The split matters because each layer hides a different problem, and a tool that only sees one of them keeps missing the others.

Workflow. Multi-step processes with approvals, retries and reversals. This is where most automated testing dies and where the real flaws sit: a revoked step that can still be replayed, a retry that advances state twice, an approval granted to its own requester.

Services. The boundary between components. A weak API on its own is unremarkable. The same API trusting a service account with more permission than the task needs is an attack path. Single-hop testing never sees it, because every hop passes on its own terms.

Code. The repository. Runtime proof answers whether something can be exploited. The source answers why it exists and where: the missing authorization check, the unsafe data flow, the key committed three releases ago. The two views are linked, so a runtime finding lands on a file, a line and a route.

The four questions a finding has to answer

Question What comes back
What did we not think to test? Findings that surface only when the tool follows an assumption across business rules, state and service boundaries
How far does the path reach? Isolated findings joined into the route an attacker would take, ranked by the data or admin surface it reaches rather than by score
Where is it in the code? File, line, route, plus the code-level risks that never appear at runtime
Can it be reproduced? The request, its response, the object affected, and the recipe to re-run after the fix

Those four are the whole deliverable. A finding that cannot be re-run after the patch is a description, and descriptions do not survive a review meeting.

Anyone who has sat through a findings review knows why. The argument is never about whether a scan ran. It is about whether the thing is real, whether it matters, and whether it can be shown to someone who was not in the room when it was found.

What a session looks like

You describe the target and the risk you care about in plain language. The tool builds a model of how the system behaves, forms hypotheses from that model, and decides its own next test instead of walking a fixed list. When something looks off it keeps following the thread across the boundary rather than logging a line and moving on. At the end you get a finding set, the objects each one touches, and the requests to reproduce them, which you review before anything reaches a report.

No code writing is required. Pointing it at a repository is optional, and it is what turns "this can be exploited" into "and here is the missing check on line 214".

Scope comes first. A session starts with a list of hosts, paths and accounts it is allowed to touch, and it stays inside that list. Pointing it at an environment that mirrors production data is a decision worth making with whoever owns that data, not a default.

Who it is for

  • Platform teams running multi-tenant SaaS, where tenant isolation lives in application logic rather than in the database.
  • Fintech and marketplace products with approval, quota, onboarding or settlement flows, where the state machine is the product.
  • Internal platforms and admin surfaces behind SSO, assumed safe because they are internal.
  • Security teams that already run a scanner and keep collecting findings nobody can turn into a decision.

Take a case that shows up again and again in this class of system. A tenant admin invites a user, the invite expires, the seat is released, and a scheduled job later reactivates it. Every step is a normal feature, documented and tested. Together they hand back access that was revoked on purpose. No regex finds that. It is a state machine allowing a transition nobody intended, and the only way to see it is to run the sequence against a real deployment.

If the system is a brochure site, this is more tool than the job needs. If the risk you worry about is somebody doing the right steps in the wrong order, it is aimed at you.

Open source and Pro

Same engine, one decision about the model.

The open source build takes any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The PoC library and product fingerprints are yours to extend and keep current, and deployment can be self-hosted.

Pro ships model credits so there is no API key to manage, plus an expanded PoC and fingerprint library maintained with each release, a tuned concurrency pool and priority support.

The engine, the evidence and the report are identical in both. What changes is how much maintenance you want to own.

Scope and limits

WormHole tests systems you own or have written authorization to assess, and a session opens with a scope list it will not step outside. It is a testing tool, not a substitute for authorization; compliance stays with whoever runs it.

It also does not promise coverage of everything. On a complex system, "we tested all of it" is not a claim anyone can make honestly. What it does promise is that whatever it reports arrives with the proof to check it.

FAQ

Can I use it without writing code?

Yes. You describe the target and the risk in natural language, and what comes back is a set of findings, the objects they affect and reproducible requests. You review that before it goes into a report.

We already run a scanner. Is this a replacement?

For pattern-shaped bugs, keep the scanner. WormHole covers the class it cannot reach: business rule bypass, state machine flaws, race conditions, cross-service trust gaps, secrets in source. Plenty of teams run both and use this one where the scanner returns nothing worth reading.

Does it replace a penetration tester?

No. It replaces the enumeration and the repetition, and it hands a tester evidence to start from instead of a blank page. Judgement about business impact, the decision to chain something further, and the sign-off all stay with people.

What does one finding actually contain?

A request and its response, the object that changed and how to tell, the file and line that explains it, and the steps to re-run after the fix.

WormHole is an AI vulnerability discovery and penetration testing tool from HACKBOX.AI, built for complex business systems. Test only systems you own or have written authorization to assess.

title: KeyDeck: Multi-Paper-to-Slide Generation via Cross-Paper Synthesis and Reference-Guided Personalization
description:
arXiv:2611.33715v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) is the task of constructing a unified presentation from multiple research papers by selecting, organizing, and synthesizing information across sources. This task introduces two main challenges: (i) combining multiple sources into a coherent narrative requires identifying cross-paper relationships and synthesizing their content, and (ii) the desired organization and emphasis varies substantially across presenters, making personalization essential for user satisfaction. Motivated by these challenges, we propose KeyDeck, the first multi-PTSG framework that integrates per-paper and cross-paper analysis to identify relationships among sources and synthesize their contributions into a coherent narrative, and reference-guided personalization to infer presenters' narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences and adapt slide generation accordingly. To evaluate generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction, we introduce KeyBench, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations, together with a comprehensive evaluation framework. Our results demonstrate that KeyDeck outperforms existing approaches in multi-PTSG quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction.

title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
description:
arXiv:2611.34785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.

title: Should Service Requirements Be Scalarized or Constrained When Minimizing Costs? A Case Study on HVAC Control
description:
arXiv:2611.33946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action. In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.

title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
description:
arXiv:2611.34137v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

title: Malt freelancer ratings in Python: choose the right denominator
description:
You're about to publish a reputation comparison. The spreadsheet has an average rating, a review count and a reassuringly tidy weighted average.

The weight is where the trouble starts: reviewCount counts client recommendations, while ratingCount counts appraisals containing a rating.

A recommendation count is not automatically the denominator behind an average rating. Weighting avgRating by reviewCount gives you a recommendation-weighted average of profile averages. It doesn't establish an average across individual ratings.

A row is a profile, not a review

The Actor returns freelancer records. Each record can carry a stable profileId, a profile-level rating and several counters, but it doesn't contain the individual appraisals behind those aggregates.

That distinction matters before you write any arithmetic. You can compare public profile summaries; you can't expand a counter into the underlying observations.

This Example input collects profiles without imposing reputation thresholds:

import os

import pandas as pd
import duckdb
from apify_client import ApifyClient

run_input = {
    "mode": "searchFreelancers",
    "searchQuery": "python developer",
    "market": "de",
    "maxItems": 20,
}

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor(
    "dataspryva/malt-freelancer-skill-and-rate-finder"
).call(run_input=run_input)

if run["status"] != "SUCCEEDED":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Actor status: {run['status']}")

items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items

Search returns a randomised public sample, then de-duplicates profiles by their identifier. That makes the returned dataset useful for describing those profiles, without making it a representative survey of freelancers.

Your chart's population starts with the collection method, before missing values get their turn.

The counters describe different evidence

Here's the field map for the reputation comparison. The analytical types below are choices for the loader: the output descriptions give meanings, but don't specify a complete JSON type and formatting contract.

Field What it holds Analytical type The trap
profileId Stable profile identifier Nullable string Counting rows across combined extracts can count a profile repeatedly.
avgRating Average client rating, bounded by 0–5 Nullable float A profile average isn't an individual appraisal, and its exact aggregation formula isn't specified.
reviewCount Client recommendations Nullable integer Its name invites you to treat it as the number of rated appraisals.
ratingCount Appraisals containing a rating Nullable integer It describes rating volume, but doesn't establish that it is the exact weight behind the supplied average.
missionsCount Completed missions Malt reports Nullable integer A mission count isn't an identified population of eligible review invitations.

The split is easier to see without the familiar word “reviews” doing everyone's job:

Public profile
  ├─ avgRating      → average client rating
  ├─ reviewCount    → recommendations
  ├─ ratingCount    → appraisals containing ratings
  └─ missionsCount  → reported completed missions

Different counters do not establish shared membership or timing.

A difference between the counters is therefore an audit finding, not automatically an error.

If recommendations exceed rated appraisals, subtraction tells you the numerical gap. It doesn't identify which recommendations lack ratings, or prove that the counters describe nested sets.

Column names are cheap. Set membership is more expensive.

Choose types without inventing a format

Unfilled fields are omitted rather than returned as nulls or placeholders. There's no field-specific promise explaining every possible omission for these counters.

We'd preserve that distinction during ingestion. An absent key, supplied text that won't parse and an out-of-range number should never quietly become the same analytical zero.

The loader below retains the original values, tracks key presence and parses numeric-looking text after trimming whitespace. It deliberately doesn't guess a thousands separator or decimal locale where no formatted numeric convention is specified.

It also keeps malformed or out-of-domain values available for inspection:

fields = [
    "profileId", "avgRating",
    "reviewCount", "ratingCount", "missionsCount",
]
count_fields = ["reviewCount", "ratingCount", "missionsCount"]
numeric_fields = ["avgRating", *count_fields]

raw = pd.DataFrame(items).reindex(columns=fields)
present = pd.DataFrame(
    [{field: field in item for field in fields} for item in items],
    columns=fields,
).astype("boolean")

typed = pd.DataFrame(index=raw.index)
typed["profileId"] = (
    raw["profileId"].astype("string").str.strip().replace("", pd.NA)
)
audit_parts = []

for field in numeric_fields:
    text = raw[field].astype("string").str.strip()
    parsed = pd.to_numeric(text, errors="coerce").astype("Float64")

    if field == "avgRating":
        valid = parsed.between(0, 5).fillna(False)
        typed[field] = parsed.where(valid)
    else:
        valid = (
            parsed.ge(0)
            & parsed.lt(2**63)
            & parsed.mod(1).eq(0)
        ).fillna(False)
        typed[field] = parsed.where(valid).astype("Int64")

    audit_parts.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "field": field,
        "raw_value": raw[field],
        "omitted": ~present[field],
        "supplied_missing": present[field] & raw[field].isna(),
        "parse_failure": raw[field].notna() & parsed.isna(),
        "domain_failure": parsed.notna() & ~valid,
    }))

audit = pd.concat(audit_parts, ignore_index=True)

The integer storage boundary is a loader constraint, not a claimed marketplace limit. Fractional counts are rejected because counting appraisals or missions requires whole quantities.

For profileId, the string representation is an analytical key; raw retains its original representation. Don't interpret an identifier numerically or use its apparent order as chronology.

Missing fields change who enters the mean

An omitted recommendation count doesn't establish that a freelancer has no recommendations. An omitted rating doesn't belong at the bottom of the rating scale.

Those substitutions would change the story: absence of public evidence would become evidence of poor reputation.

Keep the counters side by side before selecting an average. When combining extracts, also quarantine missing or repeated identifiers until you've decided which observation to retain.

This cell creates the comparison table and calculates gaps only where both operands survive parsing:

identity_ok = (
    typed["profileId"].notna()
    & ~typed["profileId"].duplicated(keep=False)
)

comparison = typed.copy()
comparison["identity_usable"] = identity_ok
comparison["recommendation_rating_gap"] = (
    comparison["reviewCount"] - comparison["ratingCount"]
)
comparison["mission_rating_gap"] = (
    comparison["missionsCount"] - comparison["ratingCount"]
)

identity_audit = pd.Series({
    "returned_rows": len(typed),
    "rows_with_usable_identity": int(identity_ok.sum()),
    "rows_requiring_identity_review": int((~identity_ok).sum()),
})

The gaps remain missing when either input is unavailable. Filling those gaps would manufacture relationships between quantities you haven't observed.

Duplicate identifiers deserve similar restraint. Silently keeping the first row can select an older or less complete observation merely because it arrived first.

Which average are you publishing?

An unweighted mean of avgRating gives equal influence to each included profile with a usable average.

Weighting by ratingCount emphasises profiles with more rated appraisals; using reviewCount instead emphasises recommendation volume.

Those are different estimands: different quantities your calculation is trying to describe.

Even the more intuitively relevant appraisal count leaves an arithmetic catch: if supplied averages are rounded, multiplying them back by counts needn't recover the underlying rating total.

This cell calculates explicitly labelled alternatives and retains the contributing population for each:

profiles = typed.loc[identity_ok].copy()
rated = profiles["avgRating"].notna()

def weighted_profile_mean(frame, weight_field):
    usable = (
        frame["avgRating"].notna()
        & frame[weight_field].gt(0).fillna(False)
    )
    subset = frame.loc[usable]
    weights = subset[weight_field].astype("Float64")
    weight_sum = weights.sum(min_count=1)
    numerator = (
        subset["avgRating"] * weights
    ).sum(min_count=1)

    mean = (
        numerator / weight_sum
        if pd.notna(weight_sum) and weight_sum > 0
        else pd.NA
    )
    return {
        "mean": mean,
        "contributing_profiles": len(subset),
        "weight_sum": weight_sum,
    }

estimates = pd.DataFrame.from_dict({
    "unweighted_profile_average": {
        "mean": profiles.loc[rated, "avgRating"].mean(),
        "contributing_profiles": int(rated.sum()),
        "weight_sum": pd.NA,
    },
    "rating_count_weighted_profile_average":
        weighted_profile_mean(profiles, "ratingCount"),
    "recommendation_weighted_profile_average":
        weighted_profile_mean(profiles, "reviewCount"),
}, orient="index")

Don't compare those means without comparing their contributing profiles. Missing weights can change both the weighting and the membership of the calculation.

For publication, “mean public profile rating among returned profiles with usable ratings” is defensible wording. “Average client satisfaction” claims a broader population and a measurement interpretation these aggregates don't establish.

Thresholds don't create a rated sample

The inputs minRating and minReviews filter present values below their thresholds. Profiles without the corresponding public value aren't excluded.

That means a filtered result isn't automatically a collection of rated, sufficiently reviewed profiles. You still need an explicit analytical eligibility rule after collection.

The input types also differ: minRating accepts a number, while minReviews accepts an integer. Neither input becomes an output counter you can audit row by row.

Keep your chosen input settings with your analysis. If you later exclude missing ratings locally, report that exclusion separately from the Actor's threshold behaviour.

The worked example uses Malt Freelancer Skill & Rate Finder. Its thresholds define collection rules; your publication needs a separate statement of analytical eligibility.

Keep the denominator audit beside the chart

You need to know how many profiles contribute to each proposed figure before deciding which figure earns a headline.

This DuckDB query counts usable fields and the paired, positive-weight populations used by the weighted calculations:

connection = duckdb.connect()
connection.register("reputation_profiles", profiles)

denominator_audit = connection.execute("""
    SELECT
        COUNT(*) AS profiles_with_usable_identity,
        COUNT("avgRating") AS profiles_with_rating,
        COUNT("reviewCount") AS profiles_with_recommendations,
        COUNT("ratingCount") AS profiles_with_appraisal_count,
        COUNT("missionsCount") AS profiles_with_mission_count,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (
            WHERE "avgRating" IS NOT NULL
              AND "ratingCount" > 0
        ) AS rating_weight_eligible_profiles,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (
            WHERE "avgRating" IS NOT NULL
              AND "reviewCount" > 0
        ) AS recommendation_weight_eligible_profiles
    FROM reputation_profiles
""").df()

connection.close()

Keep denominator_audit, identity_audit and the parsing audit with the calculation. They explain why a returned profile did or didn't contribute, rather than leaving that decision buried in pandas' missing-value handling.

If you compare groups, apply the same audit within each group. Equal-looking averages can rest on very different amounts of public evidence.

Rating volume describes evidence quantity. It doesn't independently establish service quality.

A mission count can't supply a response rate

Dividing ratingCount by missionsCount produces a ratio of public counters. Calling it a review response rate requires more: an eligible population, aligned observation periods and a known relationship between missions and appraisal opportunities.

These records don't establish those conditions. You can't infer the experiences of clients who left no visible appraisal.

A defensible denominator needs a population, not just a convenient column.

Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.

title: Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode needed an object boundary
description:
Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode needed an object boundary

Template engines are often described as presentation layers, but a server-side template can call objects, read properties, and invoke application services. Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode exists to limit that power when a template is not fully trusted. CVE-2026-136410 concerns a bypass that used expression objects to perform actions that restricted mode should have blocked.

The GitHub advisory and VulnCheck describe the issue in Thymeleaf before 3.1.6.RELEASE. The public scoring reaches roughly CVSS 9.0 in some feeds because an unauthenticated remote attacker may influence a template expression. The practical risk depends on whether the application exposes user-controlled expressions, how the expression context is built, and which objects are available to the template.

Restricted mode is a policy, not a sandbox

Thymeleaf evaluates expressions against a context. A restricted expression mode can reduce the set of methods, types, and objects that a template may access. The control is only as strong as the boundary between the template and the application objects. If a permitted object exposes a method that returns a more powerful object, the template may reach functionality outside the intended set.

Expression objects are useful because they provide reusable helpers for formatting, links, and data access. They also enlarge the surface. A bypass may not look like a raw Java call. It may be a chain of property reads and method calls that begins with an object the application intended to expose.

Identify applications that evaluate untrusted templates

Inventory services that use Thymeleaf and allow users, tenants, integrations, or lower-privileged administrators to supply templates or expression fragments. Examples include email templates, report builders, notification editors, CMS integrations, and workflow configuration screens. A template supplied only by developers in a reviewed repository has a different risk profile from a template saved through a web form.

Check the Thymeleaf version and the application's expression context. Search for custom expression objects, utility beans, SpringTemplateEngine, TemplateEngine, and code that constructs variables from request data. Review whether the application enables restricted mode and whether it also passes a broad root object into the evaluation.

Upgrade to 3.1.6.RELEASE or later through the dependency-management path used by the service. A transitive dependency may require an explicit version constraint. Rebuild the image and confirm the runtime classpath. A stale cached artifact can make a source change look successful while the deployed application still uses the old library.

Do not rely on a single template flag

Restricted mode is one layer. Applications should separate developer-controlled templates from user-controlled content. If business users need configurable output, prefer a constrained data model and a small set of safe formatting operations. Avoid exposing service beans or arbitrary object graphs to the expression context.

Apply least privilege to the process that evaluates templates. A template service should have only the credentials and network reach needed for its job. Keep secrets out of the context unless the template truly needs them. Review custom dialects and utility objects for methods that can load classes, access files, execute commands, or make network requests.

Run regression tests with representative malicious expressions in a safe test environment. The tests should assert that restricted mode blocks access to forbidden classes and methods, and they should verify that an application error is not being mistaken for a policy denial. Test chained calls and object properties because that is where a type check can be incomplete.

Detection and response

Review application logs for template compilation or evaluation from unexpected users, repeated render failures, suspicious property names, and template changes outside the normal workflow. Correlate those events with outbound network requests, filesystem access, and process creation by the application server. A template vulnerability can be used as a data read or as a step toward command execution.

If the application evaluates untrusted templates, temporarily disable that feature or restrict it to trusted administrators while the upgrade is completed. Preserve the submitted template and the application context for analysis. Remove stored templates that are no longer approved.

The patch fixes the known bypass. The durable control is a smaller expression context with a clear trust model. CVE-2026-136410 should prompt teams to ask which objects a template can reach and why each one is necessary.

References

  • Thymeleaf, GHSA-2wmw-5fmc-m25v
  • Thymeleaf, 3.1.6.RELEASE
  • CVE Program, CVE-2026-136410
  • VulnCheck, Restricted expression mode bypass advisory
