title: The Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark: Do Language Models Know the Foundations of Early-Grade Literacy?
description:
arXiv:2611.34823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many languages of instruction in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are poorly represented in the data used to train language models. Before these models can support early-grade literacy in such languages, we need to know whether they hold the linguistic knowledge of each language that literacy teaching relies on. To test this, we present the Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark and the reproducible, largely automated pipeline that turns curriculum documents, teacher guides and pupil books into a vetted question set organised on a fixed grid of nine linguistic domains and seven grade levels. The pipeline combines LLM-driven source survey, feature consolidation, item generation and quality control with an item-selection step inspired by item response theory and a final expert review. We instantiate it for Kiswahili (Kenya; 135 items) and English (United Kingdom; 137 items) and evaluate 121 and 119 models respectively. Frontier models exceed 90% accuracy in both languages, but accuracy falls steeply for smaller and cheaper models, and more so in Kiswahili. The two best models under 10 billion parameters reach 91.7% and 73.0% in English but only 51.9% and 40.7% in Kiswahili, and the mean accuracy of models deployable on mobile and tablet hardware is 47% in English against 24% in Kiswahili. The models most practical for low-resource classrooms are therefore the least capable in the languages they would serve. We release a 20-item sample per language, all pipeline prompts, open-source code, and a public leaderboard. This is the first rung of a three-level evaluation ladder for measuring and generating decodable text to support foundational literacy.

title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
description:
arXiv:2611.33617v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.

title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
description:
arXiv:2611.34044v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.

title: Print a Web Page to PDF in Go: chromedp and IronPDF
description:
A shipment tracking page has to become a PDF, filed by a Go service as proof of delivery. One route drives a browser, and in Go that browser can be controlled by chromedp, an MIT-licensed module that speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol with no external driver.

Our IronPDF for Go is coming soon, with early-access sign-up. The chromedp print path comes first here, then the parts of that path that fall to the service team, and then what the Go edition is designed to put in its place.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

How does chromedp print a page to PDF after v0.19.0?

It navigates to the page and then runs one PrintToPDF action, which returns the file as a byte slice. That action arrived in v0.19.0, released on October 4, 2026, on top of the generic API from v0.17.0, in which chromedp.Run takes one action and returns its value along with an error, while chromedp.Do runs actions that return nothing. Three names belong to the earlier API, page.PrintToPDF().Do(ctx), chromedp.ActionFunc and chromedp.Tasks, so a snippet that contains any of them predates the generic API.

The listing below prints the tracking page on A4 paper with custom margins and backgrounds.

// The first action run on this context starts the browser, and cancel stops it.
ctx, cancel := chromedp.NewContext(context.Background())
defer cancel()

url := "https://track.example.com/shipments/48213"
if err := chromedp.Do(ctx, chromedp.Navigate(url)); err != nil {
    return err
}

// Since v0.17.0, Run takes one action and returns its value with the error.
buf, err := chromedp.Run(ctx, chromedp.PrintToPDF(
    chromedp.PDFPaper(chromedp.PaperA4),
    chromedp.PDFMargins(0.9, 0.6, 0.9, 0.6),
    chromedp.PDFPrintBackground(),
))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
return os.WriteFile("delivery-proof-48213.pdf", buf, 0o644)

With no options, PrintToPDF produces Letter paper in portrait, 1 cm margins, no header or footer and no backgrounds. Letter paper and missing backgrounds come from the browser's own print behavior, so a tracking page with a colored status banner loses its color until the call asks for backgrounds.

Where does the browser come from in a container?

It has to be installed in the image, because chromedp drives a browser that must already exist on the host. On Unix-like systems the package searches at start-up for an executable by name, beginning with headless_shell and headless-shell, moving on to chromium, google-chrome and their variants, and falling back to the name google-chrome when nothing turns up. A machine that already has Chrome or Chromium installed passes that search. A bare container image fails it until a browser is added.

The project publishes a chromedp/headless-shell container image, a slimmed-down Chrome built to support the package, and the documented route for headless environments is to run the Go program inside it. The package also sets container-friendly defaults. It sends shared memory to the temp directory, because /dev/shm is small in many containers, and it adds --no-sandbox when the process runs as root unless that default is turned off.

Each of those settings is a decision the service team makes about a browser, and the shared-memory default trades away some speed and can let memory grow.

Who looks after the Chrome process once it runs?

The service does, under rules that the project's FAQ spells out. The first Run on a context starts the browser and ties its life to that context. A timeout on that context stops the browser when it expires, so the working pattern is a long-lived parent context with no timeout and a derived, timed context for each print. Concurrent requests follow the same shape, with one parent browser context and a child per goroutine.

When the connection to the browser drops, chromedp cancels the context and the caller sees context canceled. That happens when the browser is closed or its process is killed, and if the process died on its own, the error includes its exit error. A browser that never comes up reports chrome failed to start: followed by Chrome's own output. In containers, the headless-shell image should run with --init so that zombie processes are reaped.

The print options and automation chromedp offers

The print options in chromedp go well past the listing above, with header and footer templates, page ranges, scale, CSS page size, tagged output for screen readers and a streaming mode in which the browser sends a large file in pieces. The same package handles clicks, waits and screenshots when a page needs interaction before it prints, and the project's migration document lists every renamed and removed name.

What does IronPDF for Go put in place of the browser?

An in-process engine, by design. According to the IronPDF for Go page, the edition will run IronPDF Universal, the IronPDF engine rebuilt as WebAssembly, inside the application itself, with no server, no remote call and nothing extra to deploy next to the app. The engine is designed to run in a Wasmtime sandbox, with one pair of modules for every operating system and architecture, and the page says one package update will deliver a security patch.

For the tracking page, a design with nothing extra to deploy would leave no Chrome binary to add to the image. The page lists HTML conversion from strings, files and URLs, with HTML, CSS and JavaScript rendered to PDF. Beyond conversion, it lists document assembly, page edits such as headers, footers, watermarks and bookmarks, forms and digital signatures, extraction and comparison, and security work such as passwords, redaction, compression and PDF/A.

Where should a Go service start the move?

Start with a list of every endpoint that prints a web page to PDF in Go, and mark the ones where Chrome exists only to print. Those endpoints are the first candidates for the Go edition, because they gain the most when the browser leaves the image.

  1. Pick the hardest page: choose the tracking page with the colored status banner, its scripts and its web fonts, and keep a reference PDF from the current endpoint.
  2. Stabilize the current endpoint: remove any timeout from the context that starts the browser, move timeouts to per-print child contexts, and run the container with --init.
  3. Sign up for early access: register the team so the reference page can be rendered with IronPDF for Go as soon as a build is available, then compare the two PDFs side by side.
  4. Move endpoint by endpoint: if the reference page matches, point the next print-only endpoint at the Go edition and remove its share of the browser setup.

The chromedp details in this article come from the project's repository, documentation and migration notes. Sign-ups for the Go edition's early access go through the IronPDF for Go page on ironpdf.com, and the first page we would try with it is the one that has given the team the most trouble.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the chromedp calls and defaults were checked against the chromedp source at tags v0.20.0 and v0.24.0, its README and its migration notes, the release history against its tags and release notes, and the IronPDF for Go claims against its product page.

chromedp, Chrome, Chromium, Google, Go and Wasmtime are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the chromedp repository, its documentation and release notes and the IronPDF for Go page on ironpdf.com.

title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2611.33745v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.

title: Can Its Own Misses Teach an MLLM to Find Small Brain Metastases?
description:
arXiv:2611.33836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.

title: EVA: Evidence-seeking Visual Agent for Hallucination-Resistant Multimodal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.33706v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.

title: Claude Code /ship command and Claude Ship costs
description:
On 23 November 2026 Anthropic announced Claude Ship, agents that review and fix GitHub pull requests and can approve the ones a team's policy allows. Alongside it, Claude Code got a command of its own called /ship, which does a similar job from your terminal. On 26 November we gave /ship low to a fresh Claude Code 2.1.330 session as its starting prompt, in a scratch repo where we had planted a bug. It refused: "Nothing started. /ship starts only from a line that you type, not from claude -p or a program." The /code-review command, which /ship uses for its review step, started fine the same way and found the bug in about 11 seconds.

So /ship only starts when a person types it, and Anthropic's troubleshooting page lists that exact message with the fix "Type the command yourself at the Claude Code prompt." After that, per the docs, it can commit, push, open the pull request and then keep looking after it, which the docs call a watch. You can't put it in a scheduled job or hand it to another agent. /steward, its sibling, works the same way. The docs give no reason. My guess is that Anthropic wants a person to ask for something that pushes commits with that person's credentials for up to seven days, and I think that's the right call.

This post covers what the product and the command are, what /ship does once typed (from the docs, since our run stopped at the first line), what our review run showed, what Claude Ship costs, and what people have already reported.

What our run and the docs showed

  1. /ship and /steward both refused to start from a session's opening prompt on Claude Code 2.1.330. Nothing was committed, pushed or opened.
  2. /code-review low did start that way. It read the branch with a single shell command (two git diff runs), flagged the off-by-one at textkit.py:11 as "important", gave the right fix, and posted nothing to GitHub.
  3. At low effort the review skips test files ("test-file changes are not reviewed at this level", its own instructions say). /ship reviews at high by default.
  4. Claude Ship (the organisation product) and /ship (the command) are billed differently. Claude Ship's promotional credits, $10,000 to $50,000 for eligible Enterprise organisations, don't pay for /ship or for any of the commands you run in your own session.
  5. The public Claude Code changelog has no line about /ship in 2.1.330, 2.1.331 or 2.1.332. The version requirement comes only from the docs.

What is Claude Ship, and how it differs from the /ship command

Claude Ship is the organisation product. Per the Claude Ship docs it is three agents on your GitHub repositories. Code Review leaves inline comments ranked by severity. PR Steward picks up failing checks and review comments and pushes commits to fix them. Claude Approvals is a check that reports who still has to approve, based on a policy file you write in YAML (a plain settings format), .claude/approvals.yml. Code Review is generally available, and the other two are in public beta. It is for Claude Team and Enterprise plans on GitHub. Some organisations can't use it at all: those with Zero Data Retention, customer-managed encryption keys or the configuration for HIPAA (the US health-data privacy law). A person with the Owner role in the Claude organisation (its top admin role) turns Code Review and PR Steward on under Organization settings > Claude Ship. Approvals starts when someone commits a policy file to the repository.

/ship is a command in the Claude Code CLI (the terminal program) and runs in your own session, in your local clone. The ship-command page says "Cloud sessions don't have them", meaning /ship and /steward. No admin has to switch it on. It can still be missing, though. Managed settings can turn it off, and so can settings that stop feature-flag fetching (for example DISABLE_TELEMETRY). On a third-party provider such as Bedrock it needs 2.1.331. It counts against your own Claude Code usage. A commenter in the Hacker News launch thread (89 points, 36 comments when we read it) asked whether it needs Claude Code on the web and API billing. For the command, it needs neither.

What /ship does after you type it, according to the docs

Our run never got past the first line, so this section comes from the docs. /ship has four steps:

  1. Pull request. If the branch has no pull request yet, it can commit your uncommitted changes, push the branch and open the pull request as you. On the default branch it commits on a new branch and switches your checkout to it.
  2. Review. It runs /code-review on the change.
  3. Watch. It keeps checking the pull request from your session, works on whatever breaks or gets commented on (its own review findings included) and pushes fixes as it goes.
  4. Merge. You do that yourself.

/steward skips the first two steps. It starts a watch on your own open pull request, or restarts one that ended.

There is no confirmation prompt. Before the commit and again before the push, a line ending Esc to cancel says what is about to happen, and "If you do nothing, /ship continues after a few seconds." A commit made before you cancel stays (git reset HEAD~1 undoes it). I'd have liked a real yes/no here. A prompt would stall the unattended part, though.

You need Claude Code 2.1.330, GitHub CLI (gh) 2.63 signed in with gh auth login, and git 2.38 at least. With an older gh no watch starts. We had 2.1.330, gh 2.100.0 and git 2.54.0, so nothing needed an upgrade.

In a public repository it doesn't commit your uncommitted changes at all, and I'm glad, because half-finished work pushed to a public repo is the worst way for this to go wrong. In a private one, an uncommitted file whose name suggests a secret, such as .env, stops it from committing or pushing anything. It checks names only, so the docs tell you to look inside your files yourself. And if someone else has a pull request open for the branch, it commits nothing and starts no watch.

The permission mode (how much Claude Code may do without asking you) matters too. Auto mode is the one for unattended work. In Manual or acceptEdits mode it waits at every prompt, and in bypassPermissions no watch starts. From 2.1.331 it won't start in plan mode. If I were trying it for the first time, I'd do it on a branch nobody else pushes to.

Arguments go after the command. The first sets how hard the review tries, from low to max (default high); a number or URL picks the pull request, and +botname makes it read that bot's comments as well. The docs' own example is /ship low 41 +my-lint-bot.

/ship refused our script: "Nothing started. /ship starts only from a line that you type"

We set up a private scratch repo holding a small Python module, textkit.py. A GitHub Actions check (CI, the tests GitHub runs on every pull request) runs python -m unittest. Then we added a function, truncate_words, that keeps one word too few (words[: limit - 1]), plus a test that expects truncate_words("one two three four", 2) to return "one two...". Locally the test failed, which was the point.

Our fleet starts Claude Code sessions in visible terminal tabs from a script, with the first prompt passed in. We passed /ship low. The transcript held one reply, the refusal, and git status still showed the two modified files with no new branch or commit. Thirteen minutes later, after we had opened the pull request by hand, /steward gave the same answer.

The troubleshooting page lists this message, and next to it a separate one for a session that another session started. Either way you can't build /ship into a nightly job, a CI step or an agent pipeline. The ship-command page lists the alternatives: Auto-fix (/autofix-pr) for fixes from a cloud session, and Claude Ship for whole repositories, billed to the organisation. PR Steward, its fixing agent, is started per repository or with an @claude steward comment.

Claude Code's /code-review command found the planted bug in 11 seconds

/code-review is the review /ship runs, and it has no such rule. We opened the pull request ourselves (git push, then gh pr create) and the check failed, as planned.

Then we started a new session with /code-review low. It ran as a background agent on claude-opus-5-5 at low effort, made one tool call (a shell command, git diff main...HEAD; git diff HEAD) and answered 11 seconds after the prompt.

It was right. It also caught a case our test didn't cover: with limit=0 the slice becomes words[:-1] and keeps every word except the last (in Python, "a b c".split()[:-1] gives ['a', 'b']). It suggested words[:limit], then asked "Want me to apply the fix and run the tests?" It changed no file and wrote nothing on the pull request.

It read the local branch with git diff and never called gh, although the pull request was open. Version 2.1.329 changed /code-review <pr number> to read the pull request with gh pr diff, so pass the number if your checkout and the remote branch might differ. It also left test_textkit.py out, which is the low-effort rule. Here the bug sat in the code, so that cost nothing, but at low a wrong assertion in a test goes through unread.

It was cheap. The main session wrote 375 output tokens and the review agent 276, with the rest of the context cached. I can't turn that into a dollar figure, because a subscription seat doesn't show a price per command.

What a /ship watch can do with your GitHub sign-in

I'd read this part twice before typing /ship in a repo other people push to. The watch uses your gh and git sign-ins. In auto mode it pushes commits and resolves review threads without asking. While Claude acts on its own, Claude Code blocks any gh or git command that would merge, approve or force-push, and /ship terms prints the full list of limits.

Those limits cover Claude's own commands only. The docs still warn that the watch "could merge a pull request that your repository's branch rules let you merge without another person's approval". If auto-merge is on for the pull request, for example, a fix the watch pushes can end up merged once the checks pass. And if you type a message while Claude is idle, the limits are off while it answers you. The docs add: "Run a watch only where you trust everyone who can merge to the base branch or push to your branch. Any of them can run programs on your computer with your credentials." I wouldn't run one on a repo that takes pull requests from outside contributors.

Your git hooks get skipped too. The docs say the watch pushes with git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null push, so your repo's hooks don't run on those pushes. A deny rule on Bash(git push *) makes /ship leave the steps to you. An ask rule on that pattern doesn't match the hooks-off form, so you need one on Bash(git *).

To stop it, type /ship stop (what Claude pushes in the current turn still lands) or press Esc once. A watch also ends after seven days, on merge or close, or when you switch branches. An organisation can switch the command off for everyone with the managed setting skillOverrides set to "ship-local": "off" and "steward": "off". Some teams already had a /ship skill of their own, and the built-in now hides it (a commenter in the Hacker News thread and issue #111946 both raise this). The troubleshooting page's fix is to remove any "off" entry for your command under skillOverrides, then set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHIP=1 (2.1.331 or later). That turns off both built-ins and lets yours load.

What Claude Ship and its Code Review agent cost

There's no flat price per review, which I find annoying when you're trying to budget a team. The Code Review costs page says each review is billed on tokens through the organisation's usage credits, separate from plan usage, and that the cost depends on the review level, the size of the change and the code around it. To estimate, the docs suggest a pilot. Read the average cost per review for one repo, then multiply by your pull requests a month (and by pushes per pull request if reviews run on every push).

PR Steward "has no spend limit of its own until you set one." Turning off usage credits doesn't stop an agent that is on either; it keeps running and billing. Claude Approvals has no base charge, but a policy that names claude/code_review in a condition can start billed reviews on every push, and observe mode (where the policy reports but doesn't block) is billed too. The docs' turn-off order is Approvals, then PR Steward, then Code Review. If I ran the organisation, PR Steward's spend limit is the first thing I'd set.

Eligible paid Enterprise organisations can claim $10,000 to $50,000 in promo credits, set by active Claude Code seats, until 23:59 UTC on 15 January 2027, to be used within 30 days. They don't pay for /ship, /steward or the /code-review command.

For a rough comparison, GitHub's Copilot code review docs estimate $0.25, $1.50 and $10 per review across its three levels, and by default its reviews don't count toward required approvals. If you're comparing vendors, we wrote up how Atlassian is moving its Rovo code reviewer to Rovo credits from 3 December.

Where people are already tripping over it

Four issues about /ship were open in the anthropics/claude-code tracker when we looked on 26 November:

  • #111946, the built-in /ship hiding a user's own skill called ship.
  • #112018, /steward refusing a pull request when the git remote is an https:// URL with a user name in it.
  • #112183, /ship falling back to review-only on a branch name with Korean characters.
  • #112154, a request for Code Review on self-managed GitLab.

I'd expect more of these in the first month. Three days in, these are mostly about setups people already had.

Press coverage went another way. ITPro put Anthropic's own warning in its headline: Claude Ship "may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues" (the docs carry the same line). Decrypt worried about one model reviewing code written by a similar model, and The Register quoted an engineer calling it "a glorification of what I already use Claude on". TechCrunch describes the approval policies as natural language. The policy file itself is YAML with fixed keys, where only purpose is free text; plain English comes in through custom classifiers, a model asked a question in plain English whose answer a rule can test.

Anthropic's own numbers are the strongest case for it. On the claude.dev blog the Claude Code team says the share of its internal pull requests with substantive review comments went from 16% to 54% when the review launched, and that from June to September the share of merged pull requests later reverted fell by more than 40%. Those are self-reported and I can't check them. I'd still like to see them from a team outside Anthropic.

Use /code-review now, and type /ship only behind branch protection

I'd start using /code-review now. It took 11 seconds, it can be started from a script, and it found the bug plus an edge case our test missed without touching GitHub. Pass it the pull request number, and use a higher effort than low if your tests matter.

/ship is a person's command that turns your terminal into an agent acting as you for up to a week, and a program can't start it. Before typing it in a shared repo, make sure branch protection requires another person's approval and auto-merge is off. If you want the same work done with nobody at a keyboard, the options are Auto-fix from a cloud session or PR Steward, which is the organisation's call and the organisation's bill.

If you've had a watch run overnight on a real repo, I'd like to know what it pushed. And if you're wiring Claude Code into tools that act on your behalf, our post on a Claude Code agent hitting a Jira workflow validator covers the same question from the Jira side.

title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
description:
arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.

title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
description:
arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.

title: The Transactional Outbox Pattern in Postgres and NestJS: Ending Dual Writes Between Your Database and Your Queue — Field Notes
description:
Headline: Saving a row in Postgres and then publishing a message to a queue is a dual write, and it loses or invents events whenever the process dies between the two calls. The transactional outbox pattern fixes it by inserting the event into an outbox table in the same Postgres transaction as the business change, then letting a relay publish pending rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event ID.

For a long time my NestJS services created an order and then pushed an order.created job to a queue on the next line. It passed every test, because tests never kill the process between two awaits. Production does: SIGTERM during deploys, OOM kills, broker timeouts. These are my notes from replacing that code with a transactional outbox.

Key takeaways

  • A dual write is one operation that writes to two systems with no shared transaction, such as a Postgres row plus a Redis, RabbitMQ or Kafka message; a crash between the writes leaves the systems disagreeing.
  • The transactional outbox stores each event as a row in the same database transaction as the state change, so the commit makes both durable or neither.
  • A relay claims unpublished rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes them and marks them published; several relay instances never claim the same row.
  • The outbox gives at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so consumers record processed event IDs under a unique constraint and skip repeats.
  • Polling is the simplest relay; change data capture with Debezium removes polling latency but adds Kafka Connect and a replication slot to operate.

What is the dual-write problem, and why don't retries fix it?

The dual-write problem is that two independent writes cannot be made atomic from application code, so a failure between them produces an inconsistency that no retry can see. This is the code I used to ship:

// orders.service.ts — the dual write
async createOrder(input: CreateOrderDto) {
  const order = await this.ordersRepo.insert(input);             // write 1: Postgres commits here
  await this.queue.add('order.created', { orderId: order.id });  // write 2: Redis
  return order;
}

It fails in two directions:

  • Lost event: Postgres commits, then the process dies or the queue call times out. The order exists, but no confirmation email, invoice or stock reservation ever follows.
  • Phantom event: the message is published first, or inside the transaction before COMMIT, and the transaction rolls back. A consumer receives order.created for an order that does not exist.

A retry loop cannot fix the dual write, because the process that would retry is the process that crashed. Publishing inside the transaction only swaps lost events for phantom events while holding a transaction open across a network call. Two-phase commit (XA) would solve it on paper, but Redis, Kafka and most managed brokers cannot join a Postgres transaction.

How does the transactional outbox pattern work?

The transactional outbox pattern turns "publish a message" into "insert a row", which Postgres commits atomically with the business change. A separate relay reads committed rows later and does the actual publishing. This is my table:

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id              uuid        PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type  text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. 'order'
  aggregate_id    text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. the order id
  event_type      text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. 'order.created'
  payload         jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at    timestamptz,
  attempts        int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_error      text
);

-- The relay only ever reads pending rows; a partial index keeps that scan cheap
CREATE INDEX outbox_pending_idx ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

The write side is one Drizzle transaction in the NestJS service, so the order and its event commit together or not at all:

// orders.service.ts — the outbox write
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

async createOrder(input: CreateOrderDto) {
  return this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const [order] = await tx.insert(orders).values(input).returning();
    await tx.insert(outbox).values({
      id: randomUUID(),
      aggregateType: 'order',
      aggregateId: order.id,
      eventType: 'order.created',
      // Snapshot what consumers need now; a later read could see a newer state
      payload: { version: 1, orderId: order.id, customerId: order.customerId, totalCents: order.totalCents },
    });
    return order;
  });
}

The same shape works with Prisma's interactive prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => …) and TypeORM's dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => …). I put a version field in every payload because the outbox row outlives the code that wrote it.

How does the relay publish outbox rows safely with several workers?

The relay claims a batch of pending rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes each one, and marks the successes as published before committing. FOR UPDATE locks the claimed rows; SKIP LOCKED makes a second relay skip those rows instead of waiting, so I run the relay in every API replica.

// outbox.relay.ts — DB, Database, EventPublisher and the outbox table come from this app's own modules
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';
import { and, asc, eq, inArray, isNull, lte, sql } from 'drizzle-orm';

@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelay implements OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OutboxRelay.name);
  private running = true;

  constructor(@Inject(DB) private readonly db: Database, private readonly publisher: EventPublisher) {}

  onApplicationBootstrap() { void this.loop(); }
  onApplicationShutdown() { this.running = false; } // requires app.enableShutdownHooks()

  private async loop() {
    while (this.running) {
      const claimed = await this.drainBatch().catch((err) => { this.logger.error(err); return 0; });
      if (claimed === 0) await sleep(500); // idle: poll every 500 ms; a busy relay loops immediately
    }
  }

  private drainBatch(): Promise<number> {
    return this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      const rows = await tx.select().from(outbox)
        .where(and(isNull(outbox.publishedAt), lte(outbox.nextAttemptAt, sql`now()`)))
        .orderBy(asc(outbox.createdAt))
        .limit(50)
        .for('update', { skipLocked: true });

      const sent: string[] = [];
      for (const row of rows) {
        try {
          // The outbox row id travels with the message as the deduplication key
          await this.publisher.publish(row.eventType, { eventId: row.id, payload: row.payload });
          sent.push(row.id);
        } catch (err) {
          // Back off this row only: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … capped at 5 minutes
          await tx.update(outbox).set({
            attempts: sql`${outbox.attempts} + 1`,
            nextAttemptAt: sql`now() + least(power(2, ${outbox.attempts}), 300) * interval '1 second'`,
            lastError: String(err),
          }).where(eq(outbox.id, row.id));
        }
      }
      if (sent.length > 0) {
        await tx.update(outbox).set({ publishedAt: new Date() }).where(inArray(outbox.id, sent));
      }
      return rows.length;
    });
  }
}

Three details took me more than one attempt:

  • Per-row error handling. My first version let one failing publish roll back the whole batch, so one poison row blocked everything behind it. Now a failure only bumps that row's attempts and next_attempt_at, and a broker outage delays delivery without losing anything.
  • Publish timeouts. The claim transaction stays open while the relay talks to the broker, so the publisher needs a short timeout. For slow targets such as third-party webhooks, I use a lease instead: set locked_until, commit, publish outside the transaction, then mark the rows published.
  • Ordering. Postgres now() returns the transaction's start time, so an event whose transaction commits late can be published after a newer one. The relay never skips that row, because it re-queries every pending row, but several relays remove global ordering entirely. For per-aggregate order I run one relay or shard relays by aggregate_id, and consumers discard stale versions.

Why is outbox delivery at-least-once, and how do consumers deduplicate?

Outbox delivery is at-least-once because the relay can crash after the broker accepts a message but before published_at commits, so the next run publishes that row again. The fix lives in the consumer: an inbox table keyed by event ID, written in the same transaction as the consumer's work.

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
  event_id     uuid        PRIMARY KEY,
  processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

// invoice.consumer.ts — the handler's work runs once per event ID, however often it is delivered
async handleOrderCreated(event: OutboxMessage<OrderCreatedV1>) {
  await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const fresh = await tx.insert(processedEvents)
      .values({ eventId: event.eventId })
      .onConflictDoNothing()
      .returning();
    if (fresh.length === 0) return; // duplicate delivery: already handled

    await tx.insert(invoices).values({ orderId: event.payload.orderId, totalCents: event.payload.totalCents });
  });
}

INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING returns no row for a known event ID, so a duplicate becomes a no-op. For side effects outside the database, such as charging a card, I pass the event ID as the provider's idempotency key; Stripe's Idempotency-Key header is the standard example.

Should the relay poll, use LISTEN/NOTIFY, or use change data capture?

Polling is the right default; change data capture pays off when you already run Kafka or need sub-second latency at high volume:

Relay strategy Latency Extra infrastructure Main catch
Polling with SKIP LOCKED Up to one poll interval None beyond a worker Constant small query load, even when idle
Polling plus LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-ups Near-immediate One dedicated session connection Notifications are not durable, so keep the poll as a fallback; transaction-mode PgBouncer does not support LISTEN
CDC with Debezium's outbox event router Near-immediate, in commit order Kafka Connect or Debezium Server, wal_level=logical, a replication slot An abandoned replication slot retains WAL until the disk fills

Change data capture (CDC) reads row changes from the Postgres write-ahead log through logical replication instead of querying the table; Debezium ships an outbox event router transform for this table shape. NOTIFY is transactional, delivered only if the sending transaction commits, so it is a safe wake-up signal for a poller.

How do I keep the outbox table healthy in production?

Keep the outbox small and alert on its lag. A scheduled job deletes published rows older than a few days, in batches; at higher volumes, partitioning by created_at and dropping old partitions is cheaper. The alert I would not ship without tracks the oldest pending row:

SELECT count(*)                                         AS pending,
       coalesce(max(now() - created_at), interval '0')  AS oldest_pending_age,
       coalesce(max(attempts), 0)                       AS max_attempts
FROM outbox
WHERE published_at IS NULL;

A growing oldest_pending_age means a stuck relay, a down broker or a poison row. None of these is visible from the API, which keeps returning 201 because the order itself was saved.

FAQ

Q: Do I still need an outbox if my queue is BullMQ on Redis?

A: Yes. Writing a Postgres row and enqueuing a BullMQ job in Redis is a dual write. The alternative is a Postgres-backed queue such as Graphile Worker, whose graphile_worker.add_job() SQL function enqueues a job inside your own transaction, making the job table the outbox.

Q: Does the transactional outbox give exactly-once delivery?

A: No. The transactional outbox gives at-least-once delivery; exactly-once processing comes from consumers that deduplicate by event ID.

Q: Can I write to the broker first and to the database second?

A: No. Reversing the order still leaves two independent writes and turns lost events into phantom events for rows that never commit.

Q: Should the outbox payload contain the full entity or only its ID?

A: A versioned snapshot of the fields consumers need. An ID-only event forces every consumer to call back to the producer, which may already hold a newer state.

title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
description:
arXiv:2611.33322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
description:
arXiv:2611.34331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

Today we’re launching Vercel X, a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages.

Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers.

The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners.

Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below.

title: Designing a Bridge From the Post-Mortems: Wormhole, Ronin, and the Phantom-Deposit Drains
description:
Designing a Bridge From the Post-Mortems

Bridges are where crypto loses its money. Not in ones and twos — in nine-figure single events, and usually not because the cryptography failed. The signatures verify fine in most bridge post-mortems. What fails is everything around them: a check that doesn't check, a quorum that isn't independent, an event nobody verified actually happened.

So when I built the bridge for Machine — my Solana-derived L1 (Agave 2.3.13 fork, its own genesis, $MACHINE as native gas) — I didn't start from a template. I started from the post-mortems, treated each one as a failing test the design had to pass, and wrote down which defence answers which incident. The bridge is a plain lock/mint design: SPL tokens lock in a program-owned vault on Solana, wrapped copies mint on Machine, burning the wrapped copy unlocks the original. Nothing exotic. All the work is in the parts that decide whether a crossing is real.

The status, up front: the programs and relayer are written and tested locally — 821 tests across the repo, 241 in the bridge workspace — but the bridge is not deployed and not audited, Machine is a single-node localnet today, and no asset has ever crossed. This is a design article, not a launch announcement.

Failure class 1: verification that doesn't verify — Wormhole

February 2022: an attacker minted 120,000 wETH (~$326M) on Solana with no ETH locked behind it. Wormhole's Solana program verified guardian signatures by reading the instructions sysvar through a deprecated API that never checked the account it was handed actually was the sysvar. The attacker passed a fake account containing a forged signature set, the program believed the guardians had approved, and minted. The cryptography was never broken — the program just never confirmed it was looking at real verification output.

The defence is to not hand-roll the step that failed. My bridge programs do no in-program signature cryptography at all. The submitting transaction carries an ed25519-precompile instruction holding the relayer signatures over the message hash; the Solana runtime verifies those signatures before any instruction executes. The programs then read the attestation back from the instructions sysvar and require at least 3 distinct, currently registered relayers on exactly that hash — the standard verification path, with the set membership checked on-chain. The off-chain collector independently re-verifies every signature with the same verifier the programs use before submitting, and a forged signature in the exchange fails closed rather than being counted toward quorum.

The message itself is bound tight so a valid attestation can't be repurposed: the hash covers the direction (a Solana→Machine attestation can't replay as Machine→Solana), the source mint — which both destination programs check against the mint registered in their config — the source transaction signature (one deposit can't fund two mints), and a timestamp window. Attestations expire; a signed message whose lifetime exceeds 400,000 seconds, or that is submitted after its expiry, is rejected, so a quorum-signed message can't be stockpiled and used months later.

Failure class 2: quorum in name only — Ronin

March 2022: ~$625M left the Ronin bridge in two transactions. The threshold was 5-of-9 validators — respectable on paper. In practice, four of the nine keys belonged to one company, and the fifth signature came from a DAO validator that had given that company signing access months earlier for a temporary traffic spike. The access was never revoked. One infrastructure compromise produced all five signatures. Then the second failure: nobody noticed for six days, until a user couldn't withdraw.

Three defences, aimed at three different parts of that story:

  • Independence is a property of the set, not the number. My relayer set is 5 with a 3-of-5 quorum, composed so no single operator is close to threshold: one relayer per validator plus two operators who run no validators, each with its own keypair, and relayer keys, admin keys, and validator keys are distinct keypairs held for distinct roles. One relayer key alone is useless; the attack needs three independent compromises.
  • Assume the quorum falls anyway, and bound the blast radius. Caps are enforced in the programs, not the relayer, so even a fully compromised quorum can't bypass them. Two layers, both must pass: absolute per-transaction and daily caps, and on the Solana unlock side, dynamic caps — a single unlock can move at most 1% of the vault's locked total, a day's window at most 5%. The vault also has a ceiling set at initialization that no instruction can raise; changing it means a new deployment.
  • Make outflows impossible to miss. Ronin's six silent days are a monitoring failure, so every crossing in my design writes evidence as it happens: a receipt PDA per crossing (message hash, amount, recipient, destination slot) that anyone can derive and read without trusting the relayers, an on-chain event record per crossing that external watchers can enumerate and reconcile against balances, and a proof bundle — receipt, canonical message, signatures, and the set they were checked against — that a third party can verify fully offline. And every unpause after an incident automatically tightens the dynamic caps to a quarter of normal (0.25% per transaction, 1.25% per window) for a full cap window, relaxing on their own by slot count — a bridge that was just paused does not reopen at full speed.

Failure class 3: the event that never happened — the 2026 phantom deposits

The most instructive recent cases are the phantom-deposit drains, and my relayer's source code names one directly: Coreum, August 2026, where relayers attested to a transaction that moved the bridge's own wrapped token between two attacker wallets and treated it as a deposit — because nothing checked that the transaction actually delivered funds to the bridge. A record existed; the transfer backing it didn't. Variants of the same shape — forged or misread events, a decoy transfer in the same transaction standing in for the real one — keep recurring because "a transaction exists and mentions the right accounts" is treated as proof.

So the relayer verifies the transfer, not the event. Before signing, it fetches the parsed source transaction and requires all of this:

  • The transaction succeeded — a failed transaction created nothing, whatever its contents claim.
  • Inside the inner-instruction group of the one top-level instruction that created this event record, there is an SPL Token program transfer of exactly the record's amount, into the vault (for a deposit) or burning the wrapped mint (for a burn). A transfer elsewhere in the transaction doesn't count; a decoy top-level transfer doesn't count; the wrong amount, destination, or mint doesn't count. If the creating instruction's own group holds no matching transfer, the relayer refuses to sign — fail closed, no partial credit.
  • The event is finalized, plus a 16-slot safety margin. Never a confirmed-only transaction.
  • The source transaction's own block time exists. Expiry is derived from it; a transaction without one is never signed, rather than substituting a local clock.

The test suite pins the incident shapes by name — phantom_deposit_rejected_coreum_case is a literal test — alongside wrong-amount, wrong-destination, decoy-transfer, and batched-transaction cases (one genuine transfer must not verify two records).

Failure class 4: the incident after the incident — rotation that doesn't rotate

The freshest lesson is from this month. The Cyber bridge post-mortem follow-up (Bitquery, 22 November 2026) describes a bridge whose verifier was effectively a single key — and, worse, the response: after the first rotation, a third forged message was still approved the next morning, because the keys the thief had used remained accepted. Rotating during an incident is exactly when teams are tired, rushed, and most likely to leave the old set half-alive.

So the incident sequence is a tested code path, not a runbook hope. Pause and rotation compose in the order an incident actually demands: pause first (2-of-3 admins, or any 2 of 5 relayers — a low threshold for stopping, a high one for moving funds), rotate the set while paused — rotation is not blocked by the pause, or a compromised set could never be removed mid-incident — and the bridge stays paused until a separate admin unpause. The test rotation_while_paused_takes_effect_without_unpausing pins the whole sequence, including the part Cyber got wrong: after the sequence completes, attestations from the old set are dead, not just immediately after rotation but at the end of the drill, and only the new set's quorum moves funds.

Two more valves, kept distinct because they answer different questions. Pause halts movement in both directions while it is active — it is an emergency stop, and only admins can lift it once the cause is understood; it can stop the bridge, but it holds no funds and moves none. The kill switch is the one-way version: 2-of-3 admins permanently disable minting, while burns — the exit back to Solana — stay open forever. If minting itself is ever compromised, users can still leave.

The honest limits

A post-mortem-driven design is still a design. What it doesn't fix:

  • 3-of-5 relayers is a trust assumption. It is weaker than validator-set attestation, which is a later phase, and I don't present it as decentralization. The caps exist precisely because I assume the quorum can fail.
  • The upgrade authority is a single key in the code today. No multisig, no timelock. Assigning it to a multisig with a minimum 48-hour timelock is a hard requirement in the deployment gate — before any real asset crosses — not a shipped feature, and the docs say so in those words.
  • Nothing here is live. The deployment gate is a written list — a real multi-validator net, public RPC, fresh production keys generated on the deployment hosts (the keys in the repo are throwaway), an independent audit with the report published, and worthless-amount crossings in both directions with pause and outage drills — and until every item exists, the bridge stays off. A bridge without an audit does not hold other people's funds.

The post-mortems are free. Every bridge team gets to learn from Wormhole's $326M, Ronin's $625M, and the 2026 drains, or from their own. I know which tuition I'd rather pay.

The code, the design document this article is drawn from, and the threat model: https://github.com/yourmememachine/mememachine

title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?
description:
arXiv:2611.34303v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.

title: Learning from Unreliable Operator References: Claim-Level Rewards for Customer Support Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.34341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Even a correct operator reply can be an unreliable training target for a customer-support agent. About a quarter of the factual claims in these replies lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. We treat operator replies as claims to verify rather than answers to imitate. Unverified claims guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools. Verified claims serve as coverage targets in a claim-level GRPO reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved for its answer. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the GRPO agent's text answers were flagged for hallucinations, compared with 13.6% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system increased the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%.

title: HTML Template to PDF in Scala: OpenHTMLtoPDF and IronPDF
description:
A Scala service turns an order into order-confirmation.pdf from a template and a handful of values. Then the order form gains a delivery note field, customers type whatever they like into it, and that text lands in the same template. The question for the renderer changes from how it lays out a page to what exactly reaches it.

Our released IronPDF for Java already runs in Scala services, and IronPDF for Scala is coming soon, with early-access sign-up. Before either of them, the same template goes through OpenHTMLtoPDF.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

How does OpenHTMLtoPDF render a template from Scala?

It renders through a builder that takes a source and a target and then runs once. OpenHTMLtoPDF is a pure-Java library that lays out a reasonable subset of well-formed XML or XHTML, and some HTML5, with CSS 2.1 and later standards. Output goes to PDF through Apache PDFBox, and the library can also produce images. It grew out of Flying Saucer, and Scala calls it like any other Java dependency.

import java.io.FileOutputStream
import com.openhtmltopdf.pdfboxout.PdfRendererBuilder

// The builder takes a well-formed XHTML file and an output stream.
val out = new FileOutputStream("order-confirmation.pdf")
val builder = new PdfRendererBuilder()
builder.withUri("file:///srv/templates/order-confirmation.xhtml")
builder.toStream(out)

// One call lays out the document and writes the PDF.
builder.run()
out.close()

That render stays inside what the project recommends, because the file is well formed and nobody outside the team wrote a character of it.

What changes when the template takes user text?

The renderer starts to receive input that a customer wrote. The delivery note reaches the page through one line.

// The customer's note goes straight into the template string.
val note = order.deliveryNote
val page = template.replace("{{deliveryNote}}", note)

OpenHTMLtoPDF expects strict XML by default, so an HTML5 template with an unclosed <br> needs converting first. The documented route parses the page with Jsoup, converts it with the fromJsoup method of W3CDom and hands the result to builder.withW3cDocument(doc, url). Every HTML5 template therefore carries a conversion step that the team owns.

The project's position, repeated across its changelog, is that untrusted SVG and XML are strongly advised against. A note passed through as markup, tags and all, is user-supplied XML arriving at the renderer, which is exactly the input the project advises against. A note that is escaped first, so that a typed <b> prints as three visible characters, stays a data value in a fixed template.

Which dependency fixes has OpenHTMLtoPDF shipped?

Its changelog records CVE fixes in its dependencies and one fix in its own code marked as security. The dependency entries name Apache Batik, which draws SVG, PDFBox, which writes the file, and xmlgraphics-commons, which is also used in SVG rendering. Batik moved to 1.14 and PDFBox to 2.0.24 in version 1.0.9, and xmlgraphics-commons moved in 1.0.10. The fix in the library's own code stopped an almost endless loop on deeply nested content with page-break-inside: avoid, also in 1.0.10.

Version 1.0.10, the last release under the com.openhtmltopdf group on Maven Central, is dated September 13, 2021, and the last commit on the project's default branch is dated April 1, 2022. On those artifacts, any dependency version newer than the ones 1.0.10 pulls in is a line the team adds to its own build.

OpenHTMLtoPDF strengths on a JVM back end

Several of its features suit server-side JVM code. It runs on Java 8 or later with no native binary to ship, and it generates accessible PDFs under Section 508, PDF/UA and WCAG 2.0, as well as PDF/A. Its README also lists footnotes, font fallback, CSS3 transforms and built-in SVG and MathML plugins, and the project runs automatic visual regression tests across many end-to-end cases.

How does IronPDF for Java handle the same template in Scala?

It renders the HTML5 template as web content, with no XHTML conversion in front. IronPDF for Java is a released library that supports Java, Scala and Kotlin on Java 8 or later, and a Scala service calls it as it would any Java library.

import com.ironsoftware.ironpdf.PdfDocument

object OrderConfirmation {
  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    // The HTML5 template renders as written, with its stylesheet and scripts.
    val confirmation = PdfDocument.renderHtmlFileAsPdf("order-confirmation.html")
    confirmation.saveAs("order-confirmation.pdf")
  }
}

Rendering an HTML file also loads the stylesheets, scripts and images that the file references by relative path. In the PDF from that listing, the layout follows the stylesheet, the total is the figure that the template's script computed, and the delivery note prints its <b> tags as text.

IronPDF for Java also handles the steps that usually follow a confirmation, including running headers and footers and digital signatures. According to its product page, the dedicated IronPDF for Scala edition will let Scala code produce and edit PDFs.

Which Scala template should switch to IronPDF first?

The template that takes user text should switch first, since it carries the conversion step and the input question together.

  1. Escape the note in the current renderer: until the move is done, print the delivery note as text so the template stays inside what OpenHTMLtoPDF asks for.
  2. Render the HTML5 version with IronPDF for Java: use the template as written, without the Jsoup conversion, and compare it with the current PDF page by page.
  3. Move the remaining templates: point each one at IronPDF for Java once its output matches, and remove the conversion step from the build.
  4. Register for the Scala edition: use the sign-up form on the IronPDF for Scala page on ironpdf.com to try that edition when it opens.

Everything said here about OpenHTMLtoPDF traces to its repository, README and changelog. In our run on November 26, 2026, the IronPDF for Java listing compiled with Scala 2.13.10 against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 and turned the HTML5 confirmation, stylesheet and script total included, into a one-page PDF. We would start with the template behind the delivery note, rendered in the existing sbt project with IronPDF for Java under a 30-day trial key.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the IronPDF for Java listing was compiled with Scala 2.13.10 on Java 17 and run against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3. The OpenHTMLtoPDF listing and the Jsoup route were compiled against openhtmltopdf-pdfbox 1.0.10, the other OpenHTMLtoPDF claims were checked against its repository, README and changelog, and the IronPDF for Scala claims against its product page.

OpenHTMLtoPDF, Flying Saucer, Apache PDFBox, Apache Batik, Jsoup, Scala and Java are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the OpenHTMLtoPDF repository, README and changelog, the IronPDF for Java documentation, our run of the IronPDF for Java listing and the IronPDF for Scala page on ironpdf.com.
