title: Why did my AI chat stop? Using stoppedBy from AI SDK 7 in a React chat
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Details come from the Vercel AI SDK release notes and docs, checked on 27 November 2026. We didn't call a real model. Everything below ran against MockLanguageModelV4 from ai/test on ai@7.0.183, so this tests the wiring your app sees, not how any model behaves.

A tool-calling chat can end for very different reasons. The model gave its answer. Your step limit kicked in halfway through a task. A tool is waiting for the user to approve it. Or the model called a tool that only the browser can run. Until now you had to guess which one happened from finishReason, and that field only describes the last model call. A loop that hits its step limit still says tool-calls.

ai@7.0.181, published November 23 (UTC), adds stoppedBy to the generateText and streamText results, the onEnd callback, and the final finish stream part. Per the AI SDK loop control docs it has four values:

  • model: the model finished without tool calls that keep the loop going. Check finishReason to tell stop from length.
  • stop-condition: a stopWhen condition was met, such as isStepCount(3).
  • tool-without-execute: a tool call needs a result from a tool with no execute function.
  • approval: a tool call needs approval.

The same release adds a per-call onWarning callback. The docs say WorkflowAgent and HarnessAgent don't report stoppedBy yet.

Getting it to the browser

stoppedBy lives on the server-side stream. The UI message stream's finish chunk that useChat reads carries finishReason and messageMetadata, but not stoppedBy. So pass it through message metadata:

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
import {
  streamText, convertToModelMessages, tool, isStepCount,
  type UIMessage, type StoppedBy, type FinishReason,
} from 'ai';
import { z } from 'zod';

export type ChatMessage = UIMessage<{ stoppedBy?: StoppedBy; finishReason?: FinishReason }>;

const tools = {
  searchDocs: tool({
    description: 'Search the docs',
    inputSchema: z.object({ query: z.string() }),
    execute: async ({ query }) => ({ hits: [`result for ${query}`] }),
  }),
  deleteDraft: tool({
    description: 'Delete a draft',
    inputSchema: z.object({ id: z.string() }),
    needsApproval: true,
    execute: async ({ id }) => ({ deleted: id }),
  }),
  askUser: tool({
    description: 'Ask the user a clarifying question',
    inputSchema: z.object({ question: z.string() }),
    // no execute: the browser answers this one
  }),
};

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages }: { messages: ChatMessage[] } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai('gpt-6.2-sol'),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    tools,
    stopWhen: isStepCount(3),
    onWarning: ({ warnings }) => console.warn('model warnings', warnings),
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse<ChatMessage>({
    messageMetadata: ({ part }) =>
      part.type === 'finish'
        ? { stoppedBy: part.stoppedBy, finishReason: part.finishReason }
        : undefined,
  });
}

On the client, useChat<ChatMessage>() gives you message.metadata.stoppedBy on the last assistant message. Only two cases need new UI:

export function LoopStatus({ message, onContinue }: { message: ChatMessage; onContinue: () => void }) {
  const { stoppedBy, finishReason } = message.metadata ?? {};
  if (stoppedBy === 'stop-condition') {
    return <p>Paused after the step limit. <button onClick={onContinue}>Keep going</button></p>;
  }
  if (stoppedBy === 'model' && finishReason === 'length') {
    return <p>The answer hit the length limit and may be cut off.</p>;
  }
  return null; // approval and client-side tools already show up as tool parts
}

We wire onContinue to sendMessage({ text: 'Continue where you left off.' }). The approval and client-side tool cases already appear as tool parts in approval-requested and input-available states, so those parts can render their own buttons.

What the test showed

We ran six scripted scenarios through the route handler above (with the mock model swapped in) and read each response the way useChat does, using parseJsonEventStream and readUIMessageStream.

Scenario Model calls stoppedBy finishReason
Plain answer 1 model stop
Cut off by max tokens 1 model length
Three searches, limit of 3 3 stop-condition tool-calls
Delete needs approval 1 approval tool-calls
askUser (no execute) 1 tool-without-execute tool-calls

The last three rows are the point. finishReason is the same in all three, while stoppedBy tells them apart. The metadata arrived on the client every time.

The sixth scenario had the mock return a provider warning. With onWarning set, the callback got {"type":"unsupported","feature":"temperature"} and nothing was printed. Without it, the same warning went to the global warning logger. That matches the streamText reference, which says warnings skip that logger when onWarning is set.

The other change: a 64 MiB cap per streamed event

@ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.84 (November 25, UTC) fixed a crash risk. Before, parseJsonEventStream buffered a server-sent event with no size limit, so a stream that never finished an event could use up memory. Now a single event is capped at 67,108,864 characters. Per the release notes, this cap also covers the streams useChat and useCompletion read. 5.0.85 a day later let the OpenAI and xAI Responses models accept events of up to 512 MiB, because response.completed repeats every output item, including base64 images.

We pushed one SSE event through parseJsonEventStream with the UI message chunk schema:

  • A 10 MiB text delta parsed fine.
  • A 70 MiB delta failed with ParseError: Buffered data exceeded max buffer size of 67108864 characters.
  • The same 70 MiB delta passed with maxEventSize raised to 128 MiB.

For a chat app, the practical rule is to keep big payloads out of single events. If a tool returns a generated file, send a URL in the tool output instead of base64. In ai@7.0.183, we found no maxEventSize option on DefaultChatTransport, so you can't raise the cap from useChat.

Honest limits

  • No real model. These results show what the SDK sends and reports. They don't show how often a real model hits your step limit.
  • The browser UI wasn't exercised. The route and the React components type-check against @ai-sdk/react@4.0.188, and the stream was read with the same parser useChat uses. We didn't click through a rendered page.
  • "Keep going" is a new turn. It sends another user message, which costs another model call with the full history.
  • Patch-level features. stoppedBy is optional in the types, so treat undefined as "unknown" if you share code with older versions or agents that don't report it yet.

Sources

  • ai@7.0.181 release notes (stoppedBy, onWarning)
  • Loop control: Why the loop stopped, AI SDK docs
  • streamText reference (onWarning), AI SDK docs
  • @ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.84 release notes (64 MiB event limit)
  • @ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.85 release notes (512 MiB for OpenAI and xAI Responses)
  • OpenAI API changelog (gpt-6.2-sol model ID)

If you'd rather not build the message list and tool-status rows yourself, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style AI chat components that fit this setup.

title: 4 Tells That Make a React and Tailwind UI Look Generic (Plus a Clean 4px Token Setup)
description:
Open five SaaS dashboards generated in a hurry and you will see the same visual footprint: glowing purple gradient cards, misaligned metric rows, jittering counters, and muted gray text that barely clears readability checks.

The fix is not adding more animations or inventing a massive design system. Four concrete engineering choices remove that generic template look immediately.

  • Live interactive MIT React components
  • QuietCraft UI Pro (24 production components, theme switcher, and Figma tokens, $2.00 USD with code FIRST10)

Tell 1: Decorative Gradients and Soft Glows Competing With Data

When every card header uses a violet or cyan gradient and heavy box-shadow, nothing on the screen has hierarchy. Replace multi stop glows with a disciplined neutral graphite ramp and crisp 1px borders.

/* tokens.css */
:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --surface: #f8fafc;
  --surface-elevated: #ffffff;
  --border: #e2e8f0;
  --text-primary: #0f172a;
  --text-muted: #475569;
  --accent: #0f766e;
}

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #09090b;
  --surface: #111114;
  --surface-elevated: #18181b;
  --border: #27272a;
  --text-primary: #fafafa;
  --text-muted: #a1a1aa;
  --accent: #2dd4bf;
}

Notice that surface elevation comes from subtle tonal separation and crisp borders rather than blurry colored shadows.

Tell 2: Numeric Columns Without tabular-nums

In KPI cards, pricing calculators, and financial tables, proportional digits shift horizontal width whenever values update or align vertically. Always enforce font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on numbers.

interface MetricCardProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  delta: string;
  positive?: boolean;
}

export function MetricCard({ label, value, delta, positive = true }: MetricCardProps) {
  return (
    <article className="rounded-lg border border-[var(--border)] bg-[var(--surface)] p-4">
      <p className="text-xs font-medium uppercase tracking-wide text-[var(--text-muted)]">
        {label}
      </p>
      <div className="mt-2 flex items-baseline justify-between gap-3">
        <span className="text-2xl font-semibold tracking-tight text-[var(--text-primary)] tabular-nums">
          {value}
        </span>
        <span
          className={
            positive
              ? 'text-xs font-medium text-emerald-600 tabular-nums'
              : 'text-xs font-medium text-rose-600 tabular-nums'
          }
        >
          {delta}
        </span>
      </div>
    </article>
  );
}

In Tailwind CSS, adding the tabular-nums utility class ensures every digit occupies identical horizontal width so totals, percentages, and deltas align cleanly across rows.

Tell 3: Arbitrary Spacing Instead of a Strict 4px Scale

Generic AI layouts mix p-3, p-5, gap-2.5, and mt-7 across adjacent components. Locking everything onto a 4px rhythm (4px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px, 32px) gives dense dashboards effortless visual calm.

:root {
  --space-1: 4px;
  --space-2: 8px;
  --space-3: 12px;
  --space-4: 16px;
  --space-6: 24px;
  --space-8: 32px;
}

Rule of thumb for component internals:

  • 16px (p-4) for compact cards, KPI strips, and table cells
  • 24px (p-6) for modal bodies and main section wrappers
  • 12px (gap-3) inside button groups and filter bars

Tell 4: Low Contrast Secondary Labels

Subtle labels often ship with #94a3b8 on white or #52525b on near black, failing WCAG AA 4.5:1 contrast. Keep muted text at #475569 or darker on light backgrounds and #a1a1aa or lighter on dark graphite surfaces.

export function TokenStrip() {
  return (
    <section className="grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 sm:grid-cols-3">
      <MetricCard label="Monthly Recurring Revenue" value="$58,240" delta="+14.2%" />
      <MetricCard label="Operating Expense" value="$4,820" delta="-3.1%" />
      <MetricCard label="Net Margin" value="72.4%" delta="+2.4 pts" />
    </section>
  );
}

title: Adobe opens Photoshop and Premiere to outside AI agents in 2027. Ours already works in them.
description:
At MAX this month Adobe said outside AI agents, ChatGPT and Claude among them, will be able to work in Photoshop, Premiere and the other Creative Cloud apps on your own computer through local MCP connections. That opens as a private beta in early 2027, and Adobe hasn't said what it will cost or which agents get in.

We make Concierge LLM, a desktop agent that already does this, so read the rest as coming from a vendor. It runs an open model on your own graphics card and drives the Adobe apps you have installed through their own scripting. The work lands in your project the way you'd have built it by hand, as layers, sequences and markers, so you can take over at any point.

The longest job we've timed

One chat request: cut a music video to the beat. The agent looked through the footage, picked 35 shots and built them into a new Premiere sequence with the song and beat markers. It took 11 minutes 46 seconds, with the model running on one RTX 3090.

What changes when it runs locally

Nobody bills you per request, because the model is yours, so you can ask for a recut ten times and it costs nothing more. And your footage never leaves the machine, which matters if you cut client work under an NDA.

What you pay instead is hardware. We'd want a 24 GB graphics card and 64 GB of memory. It runs on less, just slower. Our speed numbers for one 3090, and the cards we haven't tested, are in this repo: https://github.com/conciergellm/local-llm-agent-benchmarks

What we'll do in 2027

When Adobe's beta opens we'll run the same edit through it and post both timings side by side.

Concierge LLM is $100 once, $50 right now with code LAUNCH50: https://conciergellm.com/?s=devto&c=adobe

title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
description:
arXiv:2611.34120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

title: FyroDB อ้างแทน Redis ได้ แต่ยังไม่ใช่ drop-in เต็มตัว
description:
บทความนี้เริ่มจากคลิป TikTok ของบัญชี @github.signals ที่โพสต์เมื่อ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ความยาว 38 วินาที คลิปแนะนำ FyroDB ว่าเป็นตัวแทน Redis ที่พูดโปรโตคอลเดิม จึงไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด เร็วกว่าเพราะออกแบบแบบ thread-per-core และยังเป็นพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ที่ตอบคิวรีซ้ำในราวหนึ่งไมโครวินาที โค้ดอยู่ที่รีโป Rana718/FyroDB บน GitHub

ผมเทียบคำพูดในคลิปกับ README เอกสารทางการ และหน้ารีลีสของโปรเจกต์ ผลคือตัวโปรเจกต์มีอยู่จริงและฟีเจอร์หลักตรงกับที่คลิปเล่า แต่คำว่า drop-in กับตัวเลขความเร็วกว้างกว่าที่เอกสารของโปรเจกต์เองรองรับ ผมไม่ได้ติดตั้งหรือรันเบนช์มาร์กเอง ทุกอย่างในบทความนี้มาจากการอ่านเอกสาร ไม่ใช่ผลทดสอบในเครื่องจริง

มุมที่ผมใช้คือคนทำแอปที่ใช้ Redis ผ่าน redis-py หรือ ioredis อยู่แล้ว และมี Postgres ที่โดนคิวรีอ่านซ้ำจาก ORM จนหนัก คำถามคือ FyroDB เหมาะกับงานแบบไหนตอนนี้ และควรระวังอะไรก่อนเอาไปใกล้โปรดักชัน

คลิปพูดอะไร และรีโปยืนยันอะไรได้

คำพูดในคลิปมีสี่ประเด็น ใช้โปรโตคอล Redis จึงไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด, เร็วกว่าในหน่วยความจำเพราะ thread-per-core, เป็นพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ที่ล้างแคชตามตาราง และเขียนด้วย Rust แคปชันปิดท้ายด้วยลิงก์ไปที่รีโป FyroDB ภาพในคลิปเป็นการเลื่อนหน้า README ของรีโปนี้

ข้อเท็จจริงที่ตรวจจาก GitHub API ของรีโป ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 คือรีโปสร้างเมื่อ 16 กรกฎาคม 2026 ภาษาหลักเป็น Rust มี 99 ดาวและ 14 ฟอร์ก โปรเจกต์จึงอายุราวสี่เดือนและยังมีผู้ติดตามไม่มาก

รีลีสล่าสุดคือ v0.6.0 ที่เผยแพร่ 22 พฤศจิกายน 2026 เวลา 21:30 น. ตามเวลาประเทศไทย ส่วน v0.5.0 ออกเมื่อ 21 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ห่างกันวันเดียว ไฟล์ Cargo.toml ระบุเวอร์ชัน 0.6.0 ตรงกัน เลขเวอร์ชันที่ยังไม่ถึงหนึ่งกับรอบรีลีสที่ถี่ขนาดนี้บอกว่าโค้ดยังเปลี่ยนเร็ว

เรื่องสถาปัตยกรรม หน้า Introduction ของเอกสาร เขียนว่าใช้ thread-per-core โดยมี epoll loop หนึ่งชุดต่อ CPU และรับการเชื่อมต่อผ่าน SO_REUSEPORT ข้อนี้ตรงกับคลิป แต่เป็นคำอธิบายการออกแบบ ไม่ได้พิสูจน์ว่าเร็วกว่าในงานจริงของใคร

เรื่องลิขสิทธิ์ ไฟล์ LICENSE ในรีโป เป็น Apache License 2.0 และ Cargo.toml ระบุ Apache-2.0 แต่ README บอกว่าเลือกได้ระหว่าง Apache 2.0 กับ MIT ขณะที่รูทรีโปมีเพียงไฟล์ Apache ถ้าทีมของคุณมีฝ่ายกฎหมายตรวจไลบรารี ให้ยึดไฟล์ LICENSE ไว้ก่อน

ใช้ไคลเอนต์ Redis เดิมได้ แต่ยังไม่ใช่ drop-in เต็มตัว

README ระบุว่า FyroDB พูด RESP2 และ RESP3 และยกตัวอย่างไคลเอนต์ redis-cli, redis-py, ioredis, go-redis และ redis-rs ส่วนนี้ตรงกับคลิปที่บอกว่าใช้ไคลเอนต์เดิมได้ ถ้าแอปใช้แค่ GET, SET, INCR หรือคำสั่งพื้นฐาน การเปลี่ยนโฮสต์และพอร์ตก็น่าจะพอสำหรับการทดลอง

แต่หน้า Introduction เขียนเองว่ารองรับชนิดข้อมูลหลักและ 150+ คำสั่ง ไม่ได้อ้างว่าครบทุกคำสั่งของ Redis ทีมที่ใช้ฟีเจอร์ลึก เช่น ACL, consumer group ของ Stream, โมดูล หรือสคริปต์ Lua ต้องเช็กทีละคำสั่งเอง ผมยังไม่ได้ไล่ตรวจรายการคำสั่งครบทุกหน้า

ความต่างเชิงปฏิบัติข้อแรกคือพอร์ต หน้า Getting Started ระบุว่าเริ่มที่พอร์ต 8000 เป็นค่าปริยาย ไม่ใช่ 6379 แบบ Redis ตัวอย่างใน README แก้ด้วยการแมปพอร์ต 6379:8000 ใน Docker ซึ่งทำได้ง่าย แต่ถ้าลืมก็จะเชื่อมต่อไม่ติดตั้งแต่ขั้นแรก

ข้อที่สองคือระบบปฏิบัติการ หน้า Getting Started ระบุว่าต้องใช้ Linux เพราะอาศัย epoll, SO_REUSEPORT และ signalfd เครื่อง dev ที่เป็น macOS หรือ Windows จึงควรรันผ่าน Docker แทนการคอมไพล์ตรง

ข้อที่สามคือไฟล์ข้อมูล หน้า Persistence อธิบายว่าสแนปชอตขึ้นต้นด้วยค่า magic FLDB ซึ่งเป็นฟอร์แมตของ FyroDB เอง ไม่ใช่ไฟล์ RDB ของ Redis แม้ตัวแปรตั้งค่าจะชื่อ FYRODB_RDB_PATH ก็ตาม จากเอกสารนี้ผมจึงไม่เห็นทางย้ายไฟล์ดัมป์ Redis เดิมมาใช้ตรง ๆ ถ้าจะย้ายข้อมูลต้องเขียนสคริปต์อ่านจากต้นทางแล้วเขียนใหม่

รวมสามข้อนี้ ความเห็นของผมคือคำว่า "ไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด" ใกล้ความจริงในระดับไลบรารีไคลเอนต์ แต่ระดับการดูแลระบบยังมีเรื่องต้องเปลี่ยน ทั้งพอร์ต ระบบปฏิบัติการ การสำรองข้อมูล และการตรวจคำสั่งที่ใช้จริง

พร็อกซีแคช Postgres ล้างแคชได้เฉพาะการเขียนที่ผ่านมัน

ฟีเจอร์ที่ต่างจาก Redis ทั่วไปคือพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ตามหน้า DB Cache Proxy แอปชี้ไดรเวอร์ Postgres มาที่พอร์ตของพร็อกซีแทนฐานข้อมูล พร็อกซีพูดโปรโตคอล PostgreSQL ทั้งแบบ simple query และ prepared statement แคชผล SELECT ไว้ และส่งคิวรีที่แคชไม่มีต่อไปยัง Postgres

การล้างแคชเป็นแบบตามตาราง เมื่อ INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE หรือ DDL ผ่านพร็อกซี ผลที่แคชไว้และแตะตารางนั้นจะถูกลบ หน้า Introduction ยกตัวอย่างตาราง users ที่เขียนแล้วแคชของทุกคิวรีที่แตะ users หายทันที ข้อนี้ตรงกับคลิปที่บอกว่าลบรายการเก่าอัตโนมัติเมื่อมีการเขียน

เงื่อนไขที่คลิปไม่ได้พูดคือการเขียนต้องผ่านพร็อกซี หน้า DB Cache Proxy มีตัวอย่างการล้างแคชด้วยมือ "after a bulk load outside of FyroDB" แปลว่าถ้ามีงาน batch, migration, cron หรือบริการอื่นเขียนตรงเข้า Postgres แคชจะไม่รู้ และผลเก่าจะค้างอยู่จนหมด TTL

ค่า TTL จึงเป็นตัวกำหนดว่าข้อมูลค้างได้นานแค่ไหน เอกสารเดียวกันแนะนำ FYRODB_PROXY_CACHE_TTL_MS ช่วง 30000 ถึง 60000 มิลลิวินาที และมีตัวอย่างตั้งเป็น 0 ซึ่งหมายถึงไม่หมดอายุเลย ถ้าตั้ง 0 ในระบบที่มีการเขียนอ้อมพร็อกซี ข้อมูลอาจค้างไปเรื่อย ๆ จนกว่าจะล้างเอง พร็อกซียังต้องเปิดด้วย FYRODB_PROXY_ENABLED เองด้วย ที่มา: DB Cache Proxy

ผมไม่ได้ทดสอบว่าการล้างแคชครอบคลุมทริกเกอร์ ฟังก์ชัน หรือ view ที่อ้างตารางอื่นหรือไม่ ทีมที่สนใจควรเทียบกับทางที่คุ้นกว่า เช่น connection pooler หรือแคชในชั้นแอปที่ควบคุมคีย์เอง ก่อนวางพร็อกซีไว้หน้าฐานข้อมูลหลัก

ตัวเลขความเร็วที่ยังเทียบกันไม่ได้

คลิปบอกว่าพร็อกซีตอบคิวรีซ้ำในราวหนึ่งไมโครวินาที ตัวเลขนี้มีที่มาจริง หน้า DB Cache Proxy เขียนว่าเรียกครั้งที่สองแล้ว latency ลดลงเหลือราว 1 ไมโครวินาที แต่ไม่มีตารางวัดค่า latency ระดับไคลเอนต์ที่รองรับประโยคนั้นในหน้าเดียวกัน ตารางที่มีเป็น throughput เช่น Simple query TCP ราว 7.6 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที

ตัวเลข latency ที่โปรเจกต์วัดผ่านเครือข่ายจริงอยู่ใน README จาก redis-benchmark บน loopback TCP 16 ไคลเอนต์ GET มี p50 ที่ 0.119 มิลลิวินาที และ SET 0.127 มิลลิวินาที หรือราว 120 ไมโครวินาที ช้ากว่าหนึ่งไมโครวินาทีประมาณร้อยเท่า แท็กไลน์บน README ที่โผล่ในคลิปก็ใช้คำว่า sub-millisecond ไม่ใช่หนึ่งไมโครวินาที

ใน README เองตัวเลขก็ไม่ตรงกัน ส่วนฟีเจอร์เขียนว่า p99 ต่ำกว่า 0.2 มิลลิวินาที แต่ตาราง redis-benchmark ในไฟล์เดียวกันมี p99 ของ GET ที่ 0.287 มิลลิวินาที และ MSET 0.325 มิลลิวินาที ที่มา: README

ตัวเลขเทียบกับ Redis ก็กระจัดกระจาย หน้าแรกของเว็บโปรเจกต์ แสดง Go benchmark แกนเดียวว่า FyroDB ทำ GET ได้ 24.39 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที เทียบ Redis 2.65 ล้าน และ Dragonfly 0.99 ล้าน การที่ Dragonfly ออกมาช้ากว่า Redis ในชุดนี้เป็นสัญญาณให้อ่านวิธีวัดก่อนเชื่อผล

หน้า Benchmarks รายงาน pipelined GET ที่ 49.75 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาทีด้วย 12 workers ส่วน README มีตาราง pipelined GET 97.69 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที ชุดทดสอบพร็อกซีแบบ smoke บนหน้า Benchmarks ได้ Simple query TCP 1.75 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที ต่ำกว่าตัวเลข 7.6 ล้านในหน้าพร็อกซีหลายเท่า และหน้าเดียวกันเตือนว่ารันสั้นจึงอ่อนไหวต่อโหลดเครื่อง

ทุกชุดเป็นผลของผู้พัฒนาบนเครื่องของตัวเอง ส่วนใหญ่ระบุเป็น Intel i5-11400H หกคอร์ ผมไม่พบเบนช์มาร์กอิสระจากบุคคลที่สาม คำว่า "เร็วกว่า Redis มาก" จึงยังพิสูจน์ไม่ได้ ไม่ได้แปลว่าผิด แต่ยังไม่มีหลักฐานจากภายนอกให้ใช้ตัดสินใจ ที่มา: Benchmarks

ถ้าจะลองในทีม ควรเริ่มอย่างไร

ส่วนนี้เป็นความเห็นของผมจากเอกสาร ไม่ใช่คำแนะนำของโปรเจกต์ ทางที่เสี่ยงน้อยคือรันใน dev หรือ staging ผ่าน Docker ตามหน้า Getting Started ใช้ภาพ rana718/fyrodb บน Docker Hub ซึ่งมียอดดึง 1,275 ครั้ง ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 แล้วชี้ redis-py หรือ ioredis เดิมไปที่พอร์ตที่แมปไว้

ก่อนลอง ให้ดึงรายการคำสั่ง Redis ที่แอปใช้จริงจาก log หรือโค้ด แล้วรันชุดทดสอบเดิมกับ FyroDB ถ้าคำสั่งไหนไม่ผ่านจะรู้ตั้งแต่ staging ไม่ใช่ตอนลูกค้าใช้งาน การวัดความเร็วควรทำบนเครื่องและรูปแบบโหลดของทีมเอง เพราะตัวเลขในเอกสารต่างกันตามเครื่องและวิธีวัด

ทีมไทยจำนวนมากเช่าเครื่องเล็กบนคลาวด์ ไม่ได้มีหกคอร์ต่อหนึ่งงาน การออกแบบ thread-per-core จะได้เปรียบแค่ไหนบนเครื่องสองคอร์จึงต้องวัดเอง ผมไม่มีข้อมูลยืนยันในเรื่องนี้

สำหรับพร็อกซี Postgres ให้ลองกับแอปที่อ่านซ้ำมากและเส้นทางเขียนชัดเจน ทำรายการทุกจุดที่เขียนเข้าฐานข้อมูลก่อน ถ้ามีงานที่เขียนอ้อมพร็อกซีอยู่ ให้ตั้ง TTL สั้นและยอมรับว่าจะเห็นข้อมูลเก่าได้ในช่วงนั้น ส่วนการเอาไปแทน Redis ในโปรดักชัน ผมคิดว่ายังเร็วเกินไปสำหรับโปรเจกต์อายุไม่กี่เดือน

ข้อจำกัดของบทความนี้

ผมไม่ได้คอมไพล์ รันคอนเทนเนอร์ วัดเบนช์ หรือทดสอบไคลเอนต์และพร็อกซีจริง ข้อสรุปทั้งหมดมาจากคลิป README เอกสาร และหน้ารีลีส ซึ่งเขียนโดยผู้พัฒนาเอง ความเข้ากันได้และความเร็วในงานจริงจึงยังพิสูจน์ไม่ได้จากบทความนี้

ผมไม่ได้ไล่รายการคำสั่งที่รองรับครบทุกหน้า และไม่ได้เปิด changelog ย้อนหลังทุกเวอร์ชัน คำว่า "safe" ในคลิปไม่มีนิยาม แม้เอกสารจะพูดถึง Rust และสแนปชอตแบบ crash-safe แต่ความทนทานในโปรดักชันยังไม่มีแหล่งอิสระยืนยัน

โปรเจกต์ออกรีลีสถี่ เอกสารและตัวเลขอาจเปลี่ยนหลังวันที่ผมตรวจ ตัวเลขดาว ฟอร์ก ยอดดึง Docker และเวอร์ชันเป็นค่า ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ตามหน้ารีโป ถ้าอ่านภายหลังควรเปิดหน้ารีลีสล่าสุดเทียบอีกครั้ง

title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
description:
arXiv:2611.34051v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

title: How to Scrape Twitter (X) with Go: Advanced Search Operators, Account Timelines, and a Cron Watcher (2026)
description:
"Twitter advanced search" gets about 18,100 US searches a month, and another 1,900 people a month search for how to "search twitter without account". Both groups want the same thing: type from:golang released min_faves:500 -filter:retweets and get a clean list of posts back, ideally in a script that can run every hour. In 2026 that is harder than it looks. The search page needs a login, the official API bills per post returned, and none of the logged-out tricks that used to work are left.

This post builds xsearch, a small Go tool (standard library only) that does it the other way around: it fetches candidate posts as JSON and then applies X's advanced-search operators locally, in about 800 lines of Go you can read and test. It has three commands:

  1. explain shows how a query is split between "what to fetch" and "what to filter"
  2. search prints matching posts as a table
  3. watch remembers what it has already reported and appends only new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron

Everything below ran on November 27, 2026 (04:10-04:45 UTC) with Go 1.27.3 on a Linux server.

Read this first: X's Terms of Service prohibit scraping. The X Terms of Service (effective October 9, 2026) say that "crawling or scraping the Services in any form, for any purpose without our prior written consent is expressly prohibited", and that you may not access or search the Services "by any means (automated or otherwise) other than through our currently available, published interfaces". The catch-all group in x.com/robots.txt is User-agent: * / Disallow: /. Review the terms and the legal risk for your use case and location before you run anything here. If the official X API covers your job, use it: recent search (last 7 days) and full-archive search are both there, billed pay-per-use (X's pricing page listed $0.005 per post read in November 2026). Keep volumes small, and don't republish other people's posts or build profiles of individuals. The tables below mask the handles of private persons.

Step 1: What a logged-out Go client gets

Before writing a parser, check what X sends to a plain HTTP client:

// probe: what X answers to a logged-out client in 2026. Go standard library only.
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        // Show redirects instead of following them.
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error { return http.ErrUseLastResponse },
    }
    urls := []string{
        "https://x.com/search?q=golang%20min_faves%3A100&f=live",
        "https://api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent?query=golang",
        "https://syndication.twitter.com/srv/timeline-profile/screen-name/golang",
        "https://x.com/robots.txt",
    }
    for _, u := range urls {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/131.0 Safari/537.36")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Printf("%s\n  error: %v\n", u, err)
            continue
        }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        fmt.Printf("%s\n  HTTP %d", u, resp.StatusCode)
        if loc := resp.Header.Get("Location"); loc != "" {
            fmt.Printf(" -> %.70s...", loc)
        }
        fmt.Println()
        if strings.HasSuffix(u, "robots.txt") {
            // Print the catch-all group: the rules for everyone who isn't a named crawler.
            sc := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(string(body)))
            inStar := false
            for sc.Scan() {
                line := strings.TrimSpace(sc.Text())
                if strings.HasPrefix(line, "User-agent:") {
                    inStar = line == "User-agent: *"
                }
                if inStar && line != "" && !strings.HasPrefix(line, "#") {
                    fmt.Println("  ", line)
                }
            }
        } else if len(body) > 0 {
            fmt.Printf("  %.100s\n", strings.Join(strings.Fields(string(body)), " "))
        }
    }
}

   Sitemap: https://x.com/sitemaps/finance0

Four doors, four answers:

  • x.com/search answers with a 307 to the login flow. The advanced-search form just builds a /search?q=... URL like this one, so it is behind the same wall.
  • api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent is the official API. Without a bearer token you get 401. With one you pay per post returned.
  • The old syndication timeline (what embedded profile timelines used) is rate-limited to death: 429 on the first request from this machine.
  • robots.txt lists rules for named search crawlers and then closes everything else with Disallow: /.

So "just scrape the search page" is out, and I'm not going to show login automation or cookie reuse. That is exactly what the terms forbid, and the accounts get locked anyway. What's left is to fetch posts from a data source and do the search part yourself.

Step 2: Where the candidate posts come from

The tool reads X through ScrapeAtlas*, using two endpoints:

  • /v1/twitter/user-tweets?handle=golang&trim=true returns an account's latest posts (14-20 per account in my runs) with views, likes, retweets, replies, quotes and the full legacy object. since and until narrow it down, but only inside that latest window: asking @golang for September 2026 returned zero posts with the warning latest_window_limited, even though the account posted in September. It costs 1 credit.
  • /v1/twitter/search/posts?query=... finds posts by keyword through a web index, not through X's own search. Results come back in relevance order, a handful per page, with a cursor like atlas:2 or serper:3 for the next page. It costs 2 credits per page. In my runs the cursor ran out after 3-4 pages, at roughly 10-20 unique posts per keyword. Operators are not supported there: from:golang since:2026-11-01 came back with zero posts.

That split decides the design. A from: query is answered precisely from timelines. Everything else is discovery: the web index proposes posts, the local filter decides. You will not get "every post that mentions X". You'll get a relevant sample that is filtered exactly.

Every response also has a coverage object (complete, order, warnings). The tool prints the warnings on every run, because "0 matches" means something different when the source says complete: false.

Step 3: A client with a disk cache

While you tune a query you run the same fetches over and over. Each response is cached on disk for 30 minutes, keyed by the full URL, so re-running a filter costs nothing. 429 and 5xx are retried with backoff (2s, 4s, 8s). Other errors stop the run instead of being silently skipped.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha1"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.scrapeatlas.com"

type Client struct {
    key      string
    http     *http.Client
    cacheDir string
    cacheTTL time.Duration
    Calls    int // paid requests actually sent (cache hits are free)
}

// envelope holds the fields every ScrapeAtlas twitter response shares.
type envelope struct {
    Success  bool            `json:"success"`
    Status   string          `json:"status"`
    Cursor   *string         `json:"cursor"`
    Posts    []rawTweet      `json:"posts"`  // /search/posts
    Tweets   []rawTweet      `json:"tweets"` // /user-tweets
    Error    json.RawMessage `json:"error"`
    Coverage struct {
        Source   string   `json:"source"`
        Order    string   `json:"order"`
        Complete bool     `json:"complete"`
        Warnings []string `json:"warnings"`
    } `json:"coverage"`
}

func NewClient() (*Client, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    }
    return &Client{key: key, http: &http.Client{Timeout: 60 * time.Second},
        cacheDir: "cache", cacheTTL: 30 * time.Minute}, nil
}

func (c *Client) Get(path string, params url.Values) (*envelope, error) {
    u := apiBase + path + "?" + params.Encode()
    sum := sha1.Sum([]byte(u))
    cacheFile := filepath.Join(c.cacheDir, hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8])+".json")
    if st, err := os.Stat(cacheFile); err == nil && time.Since(st.ModTime()) < c.cacheTTL {
        if b, err := os.ReadFile(cacheFile); err == nil {
            return decode(b)
        }
    }
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if attempt > 0 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second) // 2s, 4s, 8s
        }
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("x-api-key", c.key)
        resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        c.Calls++
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == 429 || resp.StatusCode >= 500 {
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d", path, resp.StatusCode)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != 200 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d: %.300s", path, resp.StatusCode, b)
        }
        env, err := decode(b)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", path, err)
        }
        os.MkdirAll(c.cacheDir, 0o755)
        os.WriteFile(cacheFile, b, 0o644)
        return env, nil
    }
    return nil, lastErr
}

func decode(b []byte) (*envelope, error) {
    var env envelope
    if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &env); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if !env.Success {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("success=false: %.300s", env.Error)
    }
    return &env, nil
}

Calls counts requests that actually went out, so the summary line can tell you what a run cost. A search page is 2 credits, so a 4-page search is 8 credits.

Step 4: Normalizing a tweet

Both endpoints return X's own GraphQL tweet shape. Some details matter for searching:

  • Retweets are shells. The retweet object has favorite_count: 0 and text cut at 140 characters (RT @resend: We rebuilt our email API to Go.\n\nIt took 7 weeks and 140 PRs, and we've been running in production for weeks at roughly half th…). The real text and media are in retweeted_status_result.
  • Long posts live in note_tweet. legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters. In the saved @golang timeline, 5 of 17 posts were longer than that. If you match keywords against full_text, a word in paragraph two never matches. And not every long post has a note: one of NASA's posts ended mid-sentence at 277 characters ("NASA stands ready to") with no note_tweet at all.
  • Text is HTML-escaped. > and & show up in full_text, so unescape before matching.
  • Timeline items have no author object with trim=true. The url field (https://x.com/NASA/status/...) still has the handle in its original case. 
package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "html"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// Tweet is the flat shape the filter and the reports work on.
type Tweet struct {
    ID        string    `json:"id"`
    Author    string    `json:"author"`
    Created   time.Time `json:"created"`
    Text      string    `json:"text"`
    Lang      string    `json:"lang"`
    Faves     int       `json:"faves"`
    Retweets  int       `json:"retweets"`
    Replies   int       `json:"replies"`
    Quotes    int       `json:"quotes"`
    Views     int       `json:"views"`
    ReplyTo   string    `json:"reply_to,omitempty"`
    IsRetweet bool      `json:"is_retweet,omitempty"`
    IsQuote   bool      `json:"is_quote,omitempty"`
    HasMedia  bool      `json:"has_media,omitempty"`
    URLs      []string  `json:"urls,omitempty"`
    URL       string    `json:"url"`
}

type rawUser struct {
    Result struct {
        Core struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"core"`
        Legacy struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"legacy"`
    } `json:"result"`
}

type rawLegacy struct {
    CreatedAt     string `json:"created_at"`
    FullText      string `json:"full_text"`
    Lang          string `json:"lang"`
    FavoriteCount int    `json:"favorite_count"`
    RetweetCount  int    `json:"retweet_count"`
    ReplyCount    int    `json:"reply_count"`
    QuoteCount    int    `json:"quote_count"`
    IsQuoteStatus bool   `json:"is_quote_status"`
    InReplyTo     string `json:"in_reply_to_screen_name"`
    Entities      struct {
        URLs []struct {
            ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
        } `json:"urls"`
    } `json:"entities"`
    ExtendedEntities struct {
        Media []json.RawMessage `json:"media"`
    } `json:"extended_entities"`
    RetweetedStatus *struct {
        Result rawTweet `json:"result"`
    } `json:"retweeted_status_result"`
}

type rawTweet struct {
    TypeName string    `json:"__typename"`
    Tweet    *rawTweet `json:"tweet"` // TweetWithVisibilityResults wraps the real tweet
    RestID   string    `json:"rest_id"`
    Core     struct {
        UserResults rawUser `json:"user_results"`
    } `json:"core"`
    Views struct {
        Count string `json:"count"`
    } `json:"views"`
    Legacy    rawLegacy `json:"legacy"`
    NoteTweet *struct { // posts longer than 280 characters
        Results struct {
            Result struct {
                Text      string `json:"text"`
                EntitySet struct {
                    URLs []struct {
                        ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
                    } `json:"urls"`
                } `json:"entity_set"`
            } `json:"result"`
        } `json:"note_tweet_results"`
    } `json:"note_tweet"`
    URL string `json:"url"`
}

// normalize turns one ScrapeAtlas tweet object into a Tweet. Timeline items
// (trim=true) carry no author object: read it from the post URL, else use
// the handle the caller asked for.
func normalize(r rawTweet, fallbackAuthor string) (Tweet, error) {
    if r.Tweet != nil {
        r = *r.Tweet
    }
    l := r.Legacy
    created, err := time.Parse(time.RubyDate, l.CreatedAt)
    if err != nil {
        return Tweet{}, err
    }
    author := r.Core.UserResults.Result.Core.ScreenName
    if author == "" {
        author = r.Core.UserResults.Result.Legacy.ScreenName
    }
    if author == "" && strings.HasPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/") {
        author, _, _ = strings.Cut(strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/"), "/")
    }
    if author == "" {
        author = fallbackAuthor
    }
    views, _ := strconv.Atoi(r.Views.Count)
    t := Tweet{
        ID: r.RestID, Author: author, Created: created.UTC(),
        Text: html.UnescapeString(l.FullText), Lang: l.Lang,
        Faves: l.FavoriteCount, Retweets: l.RetweetCount, Replies: l.ReplyCount,
        Quotes: l.QuoteCount, Views: views, ReplyTo: l.InReplyTo,
        IsQuote: l.IsQuoteStatus, HasMedia: len(l.ExtendedEntities.Media) > 0,
        URL: r.URL,
    }
    for _, u := range l.Entities.URLs {
        t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
    }
    if n := r.NoteTweet; n != nil && n.Results.Result.Text != "" {
        // legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters; the note has the whole post.
        t.Text = html.UnescapeString(n.Results.Result.Text)
        t.URLs = nil
        for _, u := range n.Results.Result.EntitySet.URLs {
            t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
        }
    }
    if rt := l.RetweetedStatus; rt != nil {
        // The retweet shell has favorite_count 0 and a truncated "RT @x: ..." text.
        // Keep the shell's id and time, but read text and media from the original.
        orig, err := normalize(rt.Result, "")
        if err == nil {
            t.IsRetweet = true
            t.Text = "RT @" + orig.Author + ": " + orig.Text
            t.HasMedia, t.URLs = orig.HasMedia, orig.URLs
        }
    }
    if t.URL == "" {
        t.URL = "https://x.com/" + t.Author + "/status/" + t.ID
    }
    return t, nil
}

Step 5: Parsing advanced-search operators

This is the core. The parser supports the operators people actually type into advanced search:

Operator Meaning
word, "exact phrase" whole-word match, case-insensitive (golang also matches #golang)
a OR b either term
-word, -"phrase" exclude
#tag, @name the hashtag or mention specifically
from:, to: author, reply-to account
lang: X's language code
since:, until: YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, until exclusive
min_faves:, min_retweets:, min_replies: engagement floors
filter:replies, filter:retweets, filter:quote, filter:media, filter:links, url: post type, prefix - to exclude

Anything else (near:, within:, list:) fails loudly instead of being ignored. A silently dropped operator gives you a wider result set than you asked for, and you won't notice.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
    "unicode"
)

// Atom is one search term or operator, e.g. golang, "go 1.27", from:golang, -filter:replies.
type Atom struct {
    Neg   bool
    Op    string // "" for plain words and phrases
    Value string
}

// Query is an AND of clauses; each clause is an OR of atoms.
type Query struct {
    Clauses [][]Atom
    Since   time.Time // inclusive, UTC day
    Until   time.Time // exclusive, UTC day
    MinFav  int
    MinRT   int
    MinRepl int
}

func tokenize(s string) []string {
    var out []string
    for i := 0; i < len(s); {
        switch {
        case s[i] == ' ' || s[i] == '\t':
            i++
        case s[i] == '"' || (s[i] == '-' && i+1 < len(s) && s[i+1] == '"'):
            start := i
            if s[i] == '-' {
                i++
            }
            end := strings.IndexByte(s[i+1:], '"')
            if end < 0 {
                out = append(out, s[start:])
                return out
            }
            out = append(out, s[start:i+1+end+1])
            i += end + 2
        default:
            end := strings.IndexAny(s[i:], " \t")
            if end < 0 {
                end = len(s) - i
            }
            out = append(out, s[i:i+end])
            i += end
        }
    }
    return out
}

func ParseQuery(s string) (*Query, error) {
    q := &Query{}
    orNext := false
    for _, tok := range tokenize(s) {
        if tok == "OR" {
            if len(q.Clauses) == 0 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("query starts with OR")
            }
            orNext = true
            continue
        }
        a := Atom{}
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, "-") && len(tok) > 1 {
            a.Neg, tok = true, tok[1:]
        }
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, `"`) {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(strings.Trim(tok, `"`))
        } else if k, v, ok := strings.Cut(tok, ":"); ok && v != "" && !strings.Contains(k, "/") {
            a.Op, a.Value = strings.ToLower(k), strings.ToLower(v)
        } else {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(tok)
        }
        // Numeric and date operators become fields, not atoms.
        handled, err := q.setField(a)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if handled {
            orNext = false
            continue
        }
        if orNext {
            last := len(q.Clauses) - 1
            q.Clauses[last] = append(q.Clauses[last], a)
            orNext = false
        } else {
            q.Clauses = append(q.Clauses, []Atom{a})
        }
    }
    if orNext {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("query ends with OR")
    }
    return q, nil
}

func (q *Query) setField(a Atom) (bool, error) {
    if a.Neg && a.Op != "" && a.Op != "filter" && a.Op != "from" && a.Op != "to" &&
        a.Op != "lang" && a.Op != "url" {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("cannot negate %s:", a.Op)
    }
    switch a.Op {
    case "since", "until":
        t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", a.Value)
        if err != nil {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want YYYY-MM-DD, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        if a.Op == "since" {
            q.Since = t
        } else {
            q.Until = t
        }
        return true, nil
    case "min_faves", "min_retweets", "min_replies":
        n, err := strconv.Atoi(a.Value)
        if err != nil || n < 0 {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want a number, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        switch a.Op {
        case "min_faves":
            q.MinFav = n
        case "min_retweets":
            q.MinRT = n
        default:
            q.MinRepl = n
        }
        return true, nil
    case "", "from", "to", "lang", "filter", "url":
        return false, nil
    }
    return false, fmt.Errorf("unsupported operator %s:", a.Op)
}

// words lowercases text and splits it on anything that is not a letter, digit,
// '_', '#' or '@', so "Go 1.27!" -> [go 1 27].
func words(s string) []string {
    return strings.FieldsFunc(strings.ToLower(s), func(r rune) bool {
        return !(unicode.IsLetter(r) || unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '_' || r == '#' || r == '@')
    })
}

func containsSeq(hay, needle []string) bool {
    if len(needle) == 0 {
        return false
    }
outer:
    for i := 0; i+len(needle) <= len(hay); i++ {
        for j := range needle {
            if hay[i+j] != needle[j] {
                continue outer
            }
        }
        return true
    }
    return false
}

func (a Atom) match(t *Tweet, raw, bare []string) bool {
    switch a.Op {
    case "":
        if strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "#") || strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "@") {
            return containsSeq(raw, words(a.Value)) // #golang must be a hashtag
        }
        return containsSeq(bare, words(a.Value)) // golang also matches #golang
    case "from":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.Author, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "to":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.ReplyTo, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "lang":
        return t.Lang == a.Value
    case "url":
        for _, u := range t.URLs {
            if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(u), a.Value) {
                return true
            }
        }
        return false
    case "filter":
        switch a.Value {
        case "replies":
            return t.ReplyTo != ""
        case "retweets", "nativeretweets":
            return t.IsRetweet
        case "quote":
            return t.IsQuote
        case "media":
            return t.HasMedia
        case "links":
            return len(t.URLs) > 0
        }
    }
    return false
}

// Match applies the whole query to one normalized tweet.
func (q *Query) Match(t *Tweet) bool {
    if !q.Since.IsZero() && t.Created.Before(q.Since) {
        return false
    }
    if !q.Until.IsZero() && !t.Created.Before(q.Until) {
        return false
    }
    if t.Faves < q.MinFav || t.Retweets < q.MinRT || t.Replies < q.MinRepl {
        return false
    }
    raw := words(t.Text)
    bare := make([]string, len(raw))
    for i, w := range raw {
        bare[i] = strings.TrimLeft(w, "#@")
    }
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        ok := false
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.match(t, raw, bare) != a.Neg {
                ok = true
                break
            }
        }
        if !ok {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

// Handles returns the accounts of the first clause made only of from: atoms
// (from:a OR from:b), or nil when no clause pins the author.
func (q *Query) Handles() []string {
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var hs []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.Op != "from" || a.Neg {
                hs = nil
                break
            }
            hs = append(hs, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
        }
        if hs != nil {
            return hs
        }
    }
    return nil
}

// Keywords returns plain search strings for the web-index search endpoint: the
// positive words and phrases, one string per alternative of the first OR clause.
func (q *Query) Keywords() []string {
    var base []string
    var alts []string
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        if len(clause) == 1 && clause[0].Op == "" && !clause[0].Neg {
            base = append(base, quoteIfSpace(clause[0].Value))
            continue
        }
        if alts == nil {
            plain := true
            for _, a := range clause {
                plain = plain && a.Op == "" && !a.Neg
            }
            if plain {
                for _, a := range clause {
                    alts = append(alts, quoteIfSpace(a.Value))
                }
            }
        }
    }
    if len(alts) == 0 {
        if len(base) == 0 {
            return nil
        }
        return []string{strings.Join(base, " ")}
    }
    var out []string
    for _, alt := range alts {
        out = append(out, strings.TrimSpace(strings.Join(base, " ")+" "+alt))
    }
    return out
}

func quoteIfSpace(s string) string {
    if strings.Contains(s, " ") {
        return `"` + s + `"`
    }
    return s
}

Three decisions worth explaining:

  • Whole words, no stemming. release does not match "released", and api does not match "APIs". X's search doesn't stem either, so the tool behaves the same, and you get used to writing release OR released.
  • OR binds to its neighbours, like X's search: golang OR #go -hiring means "(golang or #go) and not hiring". There are no parentheses, which keeps the parser tiny and covers most real queries.
  • Keywords() fans out OR groups. The web index doesn't understand OR, so scraping OR scraper OR crawler becomes three keyword searches. That's three times the credits, and explain shows it before you pay.

Step 6: Fetch, filter, report, watch

collect picks the source: timelines when the query pins from:, web-index search otherwise, plus any -watch accounts. watch keeps a state file of already-reported IDs (written to a temp file and renamed, so a crash mid-write can't wipe it) and appends new matches to JSONL.

// xsearch: X (Twitter) advanced-search operators, applied locally to posts
// fetched through the ScrapeAtlas API. Go standard library only.
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "text/tabwriter"
    "time"
)

type source struct {
    fetched  int
    warnings map[string]bool
}

// collect fetches candidate posts: timelines when the query pins from:,
// web-index search pages otherwise, plus any extra -watch accounts.
func collect(c *Client, q *Query, pages int, watch []string) (map[string]Tweet, *source, error) {
    seen := map[string]Tweet{}
    src := &source{warnings: map[string]bool{}}
    add := func(env *envelope, list []rawTweet, handle string) {
        for _, w := range env.Coverage.Warnings {
            src.warnings[env.Coverage.Source+":"+w] = true
        }
        for _, r := range list {
            t, err := normalize(r, handle)
            if err != nil || t.ID == "" {
                continue
            }
            src.fetched++
            seen[t.ID] = t
        }
    }
    handles := append(q.Handles(), watch...)
    for _, h := range handles {
        p := url.Values{"handle": {h}, "trim": {"true"}}
        if !q.Since.IsZero() {
            p.Set("since", q.Since.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        if !q.Until.IsZero() {
            p.Set("until", q.Until.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/user-tweets", p)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("timeline @%s: %w", h, err)
        }
        add(env, env.Tweets, h)
    }
    if len(q.Handles()) > 0 {
        return seen, src, nil // from: is answered by the timelines alone
    }
    kws := q.Keywords()
    if len(kws) == 0 && len(handles) == 0 {
        return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("query needs at least one word, phrase or from:")
    }
    for _, kw := range kws {
        cursor := ""
        for page := 1; page <= pages; page++ {
            p := url.Values{"query": {kw}}
            if cursor != "" {
                p.Set("cursor", cursor)
            }
            env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/search/posts", p)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("search %q page %d: %w", kw, page, err)
            }
            add(env, env.Posts, "")
            if env.Cursor == nil || *env.Cursor == "" {
                break
            }
            cursor = *env.Cursor
        }
    }
    return seen, src, nil
}

func filterSort(all map[string]Tweet, q *Query, order string) []Tweet {
    var out []Tweet
    for _, t := range all {
        if q.Match(&t) {
            out = append(out, t)
        }
    }
    sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool {
        if order == "top" && out[i].Faves != out[j].Faves {
            return out[i].Faves > out[j].Faves
        }
        return out[i].Created.After(out[j].Created)
    })
    return out
}

func printTable(ts []Tweet, mask bool) {
    w := tabwriter.NewWriter(os.Stdout, 0, 0, 2, ' ', 0)
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "CREATED (UTC)\tAUTHOR\tLANG\tLIKES\tRTS\tREPLIES\tVIEWS\tTEXT")
    for _, t := range ts {
        text := strings.Join(strings.Fields(t.Text), " ")
        if r := []rune(text); len(r) > 60 {
            text = string(r[:57]) + "..."
        }
        author := t.Author
        if r := []rune(author); mask && len(r) > 2 {
            author = string(r[:2]) + strings.Repeat("*", len(r)-2) // for reports you share
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "%s\t@%s\t%s\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%s\n", t.Created.Format("2006-01-02 15:04"),
            author, t.Lang, t.Faves, t.Retweets, t.Replies, t.Views, text)
    }
    w.Flush()
}

func explain(q *Query) {
    fmt.Println("local filters:")
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var alts []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            s := a.Value
            if a.Op != "" {
                s = a.Op + ":" + s
            }
            if a.Neg {
                s = "NOT " + s
            }
            alts = append(alts, s)
        }
        fmt.Println("  ", strings.Join(alts, " OR "))
    }
    if !q.Since.IsZero() || !q.Until.IsZero() {
        day := func(t time.Time, zero string) string {
            if t.IsZero() {
                return zero
            }
            return t.Format("2006-01-02")
        }
        fmt.Printf("   created in [%s, %s)\n", day(q.Since, "start"), day(q.Until, "now"))
    }
    if q.MinFav+q.MinRT+q.MinRepl > 0 {
        fmt.Printf("   likes>=%d retweets>=%d replies>=%d\n", q.MinFav, q.MinRT, q.MinRepl)
    }
    if hs := q.Handles(); hs != nil {
        fmt.Println("fetch: timelines of", strings.Join(hs, ", "))
    } else {
        fmt.Printf("fetch: web-index search for %q\n", q.Keywords())
    }
}

// watch keeps the IDs it has already reported in a state file and appends
// new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron.
func watch(matches []Tweet, statePath, outPath string) ([]Tweet, error) {
    state := map[string]string{} // tweet id -> first seen (RFC 3339)
    if b, err := os.ReadFile(statePath); err == nil {
        if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &state); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", statePath, err)
        }
    }
    f, err := os.OpenFile(outPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    bw := bufio.NewWriter(f)
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)
    var fresh []Tweet
    for _, t := range matches {
        if _, ok := state[t.ID]; ok {
            continue
        }
        state[t.ID] = now
        fresh = append(fresh, t)
        line, _ := json.Marshal(struct {
            SeenAt string `json:"seen_at"`
            Tweet
        }{now, t})
        bw.Write(append(line, '\n'))
    }
    if err := bw.Flush(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    b, _ := json.MarshalIndent(state, "", " ")
    tmp := statePath + ".tmp"
    if err := os.WriteFile(tmp, b, 0o644); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return fresh, os.Rename(tmp, statePath) // atomic: a crash never truncates state
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: xsearch explain|search|watch [flags] 'query'")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    cmd := os.Args[1]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    pages := fs.Int("pages", 3, "max search result pages per keyword (2 credits each)")
    watchList := fs.String("watch", "", "comma-separated handles whose timelines are also checked")
    order := fs.String("sort", "top", "top (likes) or latest")
    statePath := fs.String("state", "state.json", "watch: ids already reported")
    outPath := fs.String("out", "matches.jsonl", "watch: new matches are appended here")
    mask := fs.Bool("mask", false, "print authors as go*** in the table")
    fs.Parse(os.Args[2:])
    q, err := ParseQuery(strings.Join(fs.Args(), " "))
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "query:", err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if cmd == "explain" {
        explain(q)
        return
    }
    c, err := NewClient()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    var extra []string
    if *watchList != "" {
        extra = strings.Split(*watchList, ",")
    }
    all, src, err := collect(c, q, *pages, extra)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    matches := filterSort(all, q, *order)
    var ws []string
    for w := range src.warnings {
        ws = append(ws, w)
    }
    sort.Strings(ws)
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "fetched %d posts (%d unique), %d match, %d paid requests; coverage warnings: %s\n",
        src.fetched, len(all), len(matches), c.Calls, strings.Join(ws, ", "))
    switch cmd {
    case "search":
        printTable(matches, *mask)
    case "watch":
        fresh, err := watch(matches, *statePath, *outPath)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%d new since last run\n", len(fresh))
        printTable(fresh, *mask)
    default:
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "unknown command", cmd)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Each line in matches.jsonl is one post with a seen_at time. Here is the first one, pretty-printed and with the text shortened:

{
  "seen_at": "2026-11-27T04:11:30Z",
  "id": "2125318351341994436",
  "author": "NASA",
  "created": "2026-11-24T19:59:16Z",
  "faves": 37785,
  "retweets": 3322,
  "replies": 2162,
  "views": 14042369,
  "url": "https://x.com/NASA/status/2125318351341994436",
  "text": "As part of a coordinated, whole-of-government effort, NASA has rapidly mobilized..."
}

Twelve runs a day over three accounts is 36 credits a day. The account window (about 20 posts) is the real limit on the interval: for an account that posts 30 times a day, every two hours is too slow, and posts drop out of the window before you see them.

Pitfalls, in one place

  • Logged-out search is gone. x.com/search redirects to login, the API needs a token, the syndication timeline returns 429. Don't build on any of them, and don't automate a logged-in session.
  • Search-by-keyword is discovery, not a firehose. The web index gives about 10-20 relevant posts per keyword, in relevance order, across months. Treat the results as a sample and say so in anything you report.
  • Operators sent to the search endpoint don't work. from:golang since:2026-11-01 returned nothing. Send words, filter locally.
  • Timelines are a window, not an archive. About 20 latest posts. since/until filter inside that window and return nothing outside it (latest_window_limited).
  • Retweet shells have 0 likes and truncated text. Read the original from retweeted_status_result, or exclude retweets.
  • Use note_tweet for long posts. full_text stops near 280 characters, and some long posts have no note at all.
  • Whole-word matching is strict. api doesn't match "APIs". Write the variants with OR.
  • Counts move between runs. The same post had 6,605 likes in one response and 6,606 in the next. Store snapshots with a time if you want trends. Don't compare across runs as if they were exact.
  • Language codes include art, zxx, und and qme. lang:en silently drops emoji-only and link-only posts. A two-word English post can also come back as da (one @golang post did).
  • Credits add up with OR. Every alternative in the first OR group is a separate search, and every page is 2 credits. Run explain first.
  • The official X API doesn't support min_faves. If you move this tool to the official API later, keep the local filter: engagement floors stay client-side there too.

Wrapping up

  • Advanced search can be split in two: fetch candidates, then filter with operators you implement yourself. In Go that's a ~290-line parser plus a table of tests.
  • from: queries are precise; keyword queries are a sample. Print the coverage warnings next to every result, so nobody reads "14 matches" as "14 posts exist".
  • explain before search saves credits and surprises, and watch with a state file turns the whole thing into a cron job.
  • X's terms ban scraping. Read them, prefer the official API where it fits, keep volumes small, and keep individual people's handles out of anything you publish.

*I build it.

title: 8 Product Tips for Regulated Investment Platforms
description:
Investment platforms are judged on two things at once: whether a first-time investor can understand a deal, and whether a regulator could reconstruct what that person was shown. Those goals pull in opposite directions if you treat compliance as a footer and the product as a marketing page.

The tips below are for teams building or reviewing a platform that lists discrete deals — fixed income, notes, private-market offers — and takes money from retail or accredited investors. They are not legal advice. They work because most of the harm happens when key facts are technically present but practically hard to find.

1. Put the Deal Facts in One Place, in a Stable Order

Every listing should show the same core facts in the same order: what the investor is buying, the rate or return figure and its basis, the tenure, the minimum amount, the currency, fees, and when interest or principal is supposed to be paid.

If a number is “net”, say net of what. If a rate is historical or illustrative, label it as such on the same line, not in a footnote three scrolls down. People compare deals the way they compare pricing tables. A layout that changes from deal to deal makes comparison, and later complaints, worse.

Keep a signed factsheet or term sheet attached to the same record. The page and the document should not be able to drift apart without someone noticing.

2. Do Not Hide Risk Below the Fold

A risk section that only appears after a carousel of testimonials is not a disclosure. It is a design choice that will be read uncharitably later.

Put material risks on the deal page itself: what the money is used for, what the investor’s claim is on any underlying asset, what happens if a borrower is late, and that capital is at risk. If there is collateral, a charge, a guarantee or a buy-back arrangement, describe it in plain language and say what it does not guarantee.

Links to a 40-page information memorandum still matter. They do not replace a clear summary on the page where the investment button sits.

3. Make Fees and Timing Impossible to Miss

Investors remember the headline rate. They forget platform fees, spread, early-exit rules, and whether interest starts on funding day or on a later deployment date.

Show fees next to the return figure, and show the scheduled payment dates next to the tenure. If principal is returned only at maturity, say so. If a deal can be extended, say who can extend it and what the investor can do about it.

If you change a fee or a date after a deal is live, record the change on the deal record and tell the people who already committed. Silent edits to a live listing are a product failure, not a copy tweak.

4. Design Onboarding as a Checkpoint, Not a Funnel to Be Maximised

Know-your-customer checks, appropriateness questions and cooling-off periods exist to stop the wrong person buying the wrong product. A UX that treats them as friction to be minimised will eventually push a user through a flow they did not understand.

Explain why each step is there, allow people to save progress, and do not pre-tick agreements. If a user fails an eligibility check, tell them clearly and do not offer a back door on the next screen.

Keep an audit trail of what was asked, what was answered, and which version of the terms was accepted. If you cannot reconstruct that later, the flow is not finished.

5. Write Deal Pages as a Product Surface, Not a Brochure

The temptation is to dress a listing like a campaign: lifestyle photography, slogans, and a large “invest now” button. That can be fine, as long as the decision-grade information is complete and easier to find than the slogans.

The test is simple: can a careful reader state the risk, the fees and the timetable without opening a second document? If they cannot, the page is not ready, no matter how polished it looks.

6. Keep Client Money and Status Language Precise

Platform copy often says “your funds are secure” or “capital protected” when the legal structure is more limited: an independent account, a charge over an asset, or a process that has worked so far. Those are not the same thing.

Use the same terms the legal documents use, then explain them. If money is held by a custodian or a cash administrator, name the role and what it means when a deal is delayed. If there have been no defaults to date, that is a historical statement, not a promise about the next deal. On a regulated real-estate-backed platform such as BigFundr, the deal page, the factsheet and the account status have to agree, because the investor is committing to a specific tenure and structure rather than a generic fund unit.

In-product status also needs this precision. “Processing”, “funded”, “live” and “matured” should map to a defined state, visible to the investor and to your operations team, not to a designer’s sense of momentum.

7. Build for the Awkward Mid-Deal Moments

The happy path — browse, invest, receive interest, get principal back — is the easy part. The product is defined by what happens when a payment is late, a deal is withdrawn before funding, a user dies or loses access, or a factsheet is updated.

Specify those flows before you scale marketing. How is the investor notified? What can they do in the account? Who can they talk to, and with what identification? If a deal is oversubscribed or cancelled, when does the money come back, and in which currency?

A help centre article is useful. An in-product message at the moment the status changes is better.

8. Version Everything the Investor Could Have Relied On

Deal pages change. Terms are restated. Risk wording is tightened. If you overwrite the previous version, you will not be able to show what a given investor saw on the day they clicked confirm.

Version the factsheet, the deal-page summary, the terms accepted at onboarding, and the email or push notification that accompanied a material change. Store them against the user and the deal, not only in a CMS history that a future redesign might drop.

This is unglamorous infrastructure. It is also the difference between a platform you can explain and one you can only apologise for.

The Bottom Line

A regulated investment product is only as clear as its listings, fees, risk wording and onboarding trail. Design those as core product surfaces, and keep the mid-deal failures and the historical versions as carefully as the first “invest” button.

If a patient reader can understand a deal from the page in front of them, and you can later prove what they saw, the platform is doing its job.

title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
description:
arXiv:2611.33821v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.

title: I built "ask your database" where each person only sees the tables they're allowed to (now on AppSumo)
description:
Most "chat with your database" tools give everyone the same view. Connect the company database and the intern can ask about salaries. schemagate lets each person's AI see only the tables and columns that person is allowed to read.

What it does

  • Connects to PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Oracle or SQL Server (presets for Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL, PlanetScale and TiDB). Or upload CSV/Excel files, or paste a Google Sheets link.
  • Access per person: a hidden table gets the same refusal as one that doesn't exist.
  • Read-only. PostgreSQL and MySQL sessions refuse writes at the database level.
  • Your rows never go to the AI, only table and column names.
  • Charts, CSV export, saved questions, dashboards, and a "Make it faster" button that only suggests a rewrite if it returns the same rows and runs faster.

The engine underneath is the open-source schemagate library (13,000+ PyPI downloads, listed in LangChain's retrievers). It scores 74.34% on the BIRD hidden test set and is #1 on UniQL's Oracle column (64.93%).

Lifetime deal, 10% off until Dec 1: Starter $4.50 · Team $53.10 · Business $107.10 · Agency $179.10. A 7-day free trial is also available, no card needed.

What it doesn't do: it never writes to your database. SQL Server relies on a SELECT-only check, not a database-level lock.
