title: Secure AI Apps on Spring Boot: Typed Prompts with AISL, Apps as Pimi with pim-core
description:
Unlike OpenClaw, Knoden PIM is built to be secure. Its skills aren't instructions written as informal text. Each one is a typed Java interface, so what goes to the model and what comes back is checked like any other code. Agents aren't let loose: they ask before using any tool that isn't on their allowed list. PIM is never given root access, and it only loads pimi whose checksum or signature checks out.

The architecture is built on a stack developers already trust: Java, Spring, Spring AI and Ollama. And PIM is designed with developers in mind, to be extended. Its engine, pim-core, is a set of Spring Boot libraries: an event bus, storage, security and an AI layer. Apps plug into it as pimi, modules with their own data, logic and AI skills. The fifteen apps that come with PIM are pimi too, written to show what can be built.

Every prompt in PIM goes through a small library of ours: AISL. It turns a prompt into a Spring bean you inject and call like any other. It's LGPL-3.0, so you can use it in any application, open or closed.

This article has two parts. The first is a walk-through: from an empty project to a typed Java record filled in by a model on your own machine, then the bug that the types didn't catch and the two ways we fix that kind of bug. The second is what pim-core adds when one prompt becomes an app, and how that app is packaged and loaded as a pimi.

What you need

  • Java 25 and Gradle (or the wrapper).
  • Ollama, with the default model pulled: ollama pull gemma4.

AISL is in a public GitLab package registry, so there's no token to set up, but it isn't on Maven Central yet, so Gradle needs one repository block:

// settings.gradle.kts
rootProject.name = "aisl-demo"

dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        exclusiveContent {
            forRepository {
                maven { url = uri("https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/86960067/packages/maven") }
            }
            filter { includeGroup("com.knoden.aisl") }
        }
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

// build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    java
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
}

java { toolchain { languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(25)) } }

dependencies {
    implementation(platform(org.springframework.boot.gradle.plugin.SpringBootPlugin.BOM_COORDINATES))
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("com.knoden.aisl:aisl-runtime:0.8.1")
}

That's every dependency. aisl-runtime brings Spring AI and its Ollama starter.

A prompt is an interface

We want to turn "Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm" into an appointment. First the shape of the answer, as a plain record:

public record Appointment(String title, String date, String start, String end) {
}

Then the prompt. It's a method on an interface: the system prompt goes on @AislPrompt, a {placeholder} is filled from the parameter marked @AislParam, and the first plain parameter is what the user typed:

public interface AppointmentSkill {

    @AislPrompt(system = "Today is {today}. Turn the user's request into one appointment. "
            + "Dates as YYYY-MM-DD, times as HH:MM in 24-hour time.")
    Appointment parse(String request, @AislParam("today") String today);
}

There's no implementation. @EnableAislSkills finds the interface and registers a bean for it:

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableAislSkills
public class DemoApp {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApp.class, args);
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner run(AppointmentSkill skill) {
        return args -> System.out.println(skill.parse(
                "Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm",
                LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 25) + " (a Wednesday)"));
    }
}

Because the method returns a record and not a String, the call goes through Spring AI's structured output: the model is asked for JSON matching the record, and the reply is mapped onto it. ./gradlew bootRun:

Appointment[title=Dentist, date=2026-11-30, start=15:00, end=16:00]

It compiled, it ran, every field is filled in, and the times are right. And November 30, 2026 is a Monday.

The bug the types didn't catch

We ran it five times with gemma4, the default. It said Friday the 27th twice. The other three times it said Monday the 30th (twice) and Friday, December 4, a week late. The record only guarantees the shape of the answer. A small model is good at language and bad at calendar arithmetic, and "this Friday, given that today is Wednesday the 25th" is arithmetic.

We've seen this before: in our own model tests, a small Gemma 4 put an appointment on the wrong Friday in all five runs (how we test the models). There are two ways out.

1. A bigger model for just this skill. Every skill is a bean with a name (the interface's name, first letter lower-cased), and one property moves that skill alone to another model:

aisl.skill-models.appointmentSkill=gemma4:26b

With gemma4:26b it was Friday the 27th, five out of five. Everything else in the application stays on the small, fast model. That's the point of the setting: you don't move your whole application to an 18 GB model for one prompt that needs it.

2. Don't ask the model to do arithmetic. Ask it for what it's good at, which day the person meant, and let Java compute the date. The record can use real Java types; Spring AI maps them:

public record Booking(String title, DayOfWeek day, LocalTime start, LocalTime end) {
}

public interface BookingSkill {

    @AislPrompt(system = "Turn the user's request into one appointment: what it is, the day of the week, "
            + "and the start and end time.")
    Booking parse(String request);
}

Booking b = skill.parse("Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm");
LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 25).with(TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(b.day()));

Booking[title=Dentist, day=FRIDAY, start=15:00, end=16:00] -> 2026-11-27

Five out of five on the small model, and the prompt got shorter: it no longer needs today's date. DayOfWeek is an enum, so the model can only name one of seven days; there's no date left for it to get wrong.

We use both in PIM. The second one is the better habit: types tell you the answer has the right shape, so make the shape carry as little of the reasoning as you can.

When you have more than a few prompts

For a larger set of skills there's a second way to write them: .aisl files, a short declarative format that a build-time compiler turns into the same kind of bean. An output_schema block in the file also generates the Java records, and a skill can record its own model and whether a thinking model should think. The user guide has the format and the Gradle setup for the compiler. The interfaces above need no build step, so start there.

From a skill to an app: pim-core

AISL handles one prompt. An app needs more: somewhere to keep its data, a way to talk to the rest of the system, and limits on what it and its AI may do. That is pim-core, PIM's engine, published as Spring Boot libraries (com.knoden.pim.core, AGPL-3.0). You take only the modules you need:

  • Event bus (pim-events-core). Modules work by sending each other messages, not by calling each other. The kernel has no AI dependency.
  • Storage (pim-storage-core). Data is kept per person. Other modules store data by sending storage a message over the bus; only storage touches the database or the disk. A file goes into the person's own folder under the app's name, and a path that could leave that folder is refused.
  • Security (pim-security). Credentials (PBKDF2/BCrypt, lockout), crypto, an optional key store, and the encrypted backup format (AES-256-GCM).
  • AI (pim-ai-core), the only module that carries Spring AI: conversations, retrieval, memory, and agents. An agent has a list of tools it may run freely. Any other tool pauses the run until the person says yes or no, and that answer covers only that one call. By default a run stops after 6 tool calls or 3 minutes.
  • The pimi loader (pim-workspaces), below.

The same registry block as above, with pim-core's registry added, gets you any of them; the pim-core page has it.

An app is a pimi

A pimi is an app packaged as a plain jar: its own classes in its own package, its own tables as Flyway migrations, and its own AISL skills. Here is Notes, PIM's simplest app:

pimi.properties
db/pimi/notes/V1__notes.sql
db/pimi-grants/notes/R__notes_grants.sql
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesPimiConfiguration.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/DefaultNotesEventService.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesPersistenceEventService.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesRecord.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesRepository.java
...

# pimi.properties
id=notes
name=Notes
type=Journal
description=Quick, freeform notes for anything you want to remember.

At startup pim-core's loader puts the workspace's pimi on the class path before Spring scans, so a pimi's beans are ordinary Spring beans. Nothing loads on trust:

  • A pimi loads only if its SHA-256 matches the one configured for it (pim.workspaces.trusted.notes=<sha256>) or a publisher-signed catalog vouches for that exact build (ECDSA P-256).
  • The loader accepts only classes in the pimi's own package (com.knoden.pim.pimi.notes) and its generated skills. A library the pimi brings is relocated into its package at build time, so two pimi can't clash over a library's version.
  • The app's code never depends on the AI stack. Its skills are .aisl files, and pim-core's AI module runs them on request over the bus, on whatever model the application is configured with.

The fifteen apps that come with PIM, from Notes and Calendar to Mail and Finance, are built exactly this way, in pim-apps. They are there to show what a pimi can do. Calendar books "dentist Friday at 3" for real, and it avoids the bug from part one in a third way: it gives the model the dates of the next two weeks with their weekdays, so the model looks the date up instead of working it out.

Rough edges

  • Pre-1.0: APIs can still change between minor versions.
  • Not on Maven Central yet, hence the repository block.
  • Built around Ollama: the per-skill model and thinking settings are Ollama options.
  • A method can't return List<Appointment> directly; wrap the list in a record.
  • pim-core is pre-1.0 too (0.64), and its agents are for PIM's own apps so far, not yet for pimi.

Links

  • AISL, code at gitlab.com/knoden/aisl-core (LGPL-3.0)
  • pim-core, code at gitlab.com/knoden/pim-core (AGPL-3.0)
  • PIM's apps as pimi: gitlab.com/knoden/pim-apps (AGPL-3.0)
  • Both on one page: For developers

Questions and bug reports are welcome as GitLab issues.

title: Running LibRaw, WebGL2 Color Grading, and Memory-Bounded Video Reversal in a Browser Tab (Zero Uploads)
description:
Every "free online RAW converter" or "online video cutter" follows the same playbook: upload your 40 MB Sony .ARW or 4 GB action-camera .MP4 to a remote bucket, wait in a server queue, and hope the output doesn't come back with a watermark or heavy recompression.

When you come back from a shoot with hundreds of camera RAWs and multi-gigabyte 4K clips, uploading gigabytes of personal footage just to cull keepers, grade colors, or trim a few clean subclips makes no sense. Modern browsers already ship WebAssembly SIMD, WebGL2 3D textures, WebCodecs, and Worker threads.

So I built CutCull — a free, watermark-free, zero-upload RAW photo developer and multi-subclip video trimmer that runs entirely inside a browser tab (as the instant-access web companion to our upcoming native macOS/Windows desktop culling app). Your original files never leave your device.

Here are the three core engineering problems we solved to make real sensor-level RAW development, real-time WebGL2 color grading, and multi-gigabyte video processing fast and stable inside browser memory limits.

1. Real Sensor Demosaicing for 20 Camera RAW Formats (Not Embedded JPEG Extraction)

Most lightweight browser "RAW viewers" cheat: they scan the file header for the embedded preview JPEG that cameras write for their rear LCD screen, extract that 1600px 8-bit preview, and call it a conversion. The moment you push shadows or recover bright sunset highlights, 8-bit banding falls apart.

To do genuine sensor-level RAW development in the browser, we compiled LibRaw plus the GoPro GPR SDK (for VC-5 compressed .GPR RAWs) to WebAssembly:

  • 20 camera-tested RAW extensions: Sony .ARW, Canon .CR3 / .CR2 / .CRW, Nikon .NEF / .NRW, Fujifilm .RAF (X-Trans & Bayer), DNG .DNG (DJI, Leica, Ricoh, phones), OM System / Olympus .ORF / .ORI, Panasonic .RW2, Leica .RWL, Hasselblad .3FR / .FFF, Phase One .IIQ, Pentax .PEF, Samsung .SRW, Minolta .MRW, GoPro .GPR, and Sigma .X3F (plus batch .HEIC conversion).
  • Worker isolation: Demosaicing a 45–60 MP Bayer or X-Trans sensor buffer takes hundreds of milliseconds of CPU work. Running the WASM decoder inside a dedicated Web Worker keeps UI scrubbing, filmstrip navigation, and slider drags responsive at 60 fps.
  • Batch export without opening every file: If you drop 20 .CR3 or .ARW files into the workspace, grade three hero shots, and hit batch export, unedited RAWs automatically decode and export at full sensor resolution (JPG quality 90 or lossless PNG) alongside your graded picks.

2. Shared Rust Color Math & a Single-Pass WebGL2 Grading Shader

Once demosaiced wide-gamut pixels arrive from WASM, running pixel math on the CPU in JavaScript is far too slow for interactive sliders. At the same time, chaining half a dozen separate WebGL passes wastes memory bandwidth on high-megapixel photos and 4K HDR frames.

We defined a single color math specification in Rust (cutcull-core) mirrored by a single-pass WebGL2 fragment shader in the browser (and matching export pipelines), so interactive preview and final export stay consistent across photos and video:

  1. As-Shot Anchored Kelvin White Balance: Camera white balance coefficients from the RAW metadata anchor an intuitive Temperature (Kelvin) and Tint control alongside one-click Auto grade.
  2. Highlight-Safe Tone & Presence Controls: Interactive Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Dehaze, Vibrance, and Saturation math evaluated in linear/perceptual space within a single fragment pass, paired with non-destructive spatial aspect-ratio crop (Original, Free, 16:9, and social presets).
  3. Hardware sampler3D .cube 3D LUTs: Built-in creative looks (Warm, Cool, Black & white, Teal + orange) plus custom user .cube 3D LUT files uploaded into a WebGL2 3D texture for single-fetch hardware trilinear interpolation.
  4. Consumer HDR Pipeline & Strict Local Privacy: Preserves consumer HDR (HLG / PQ 10-bit video and gain-map photos) end to end — while zero media bytes, filenames, custom LUTs, or edit parameters ever touch a network socket.

3. Multi-Subclip Stream-Copy Cutting & Windowed Video Reversal Without OOM

Standard ffmpeg.wasm demos usually read an entire video into in-memory MEMFS, transcode it from start to finish, and crash the tab as soon as the input crosses a few hundred megabytes.

For action-camera, drone, and vlog footage, we built two specialized local execution paths:

Instant Multi-Subclip Cutting (-c:v copy)

Instead of a heavy multi-track NLE timeline, CutCull gives you J / K / L shuttle keys and I / O markers to tag multiple independent keeper ranges on a single long source video, then exports every range as its own clean file via lossless stream copy — no re-encoding, zero generation loss, and near-instant output.

Memory-Bounded Video Reversal

Reversing a video (vf=reverse,af=areverse) normally requires decoding every frame of the entire clip into uncompressed RAM at once — a 3-minute 1080p clip easily exceeds the 2–4 GB Wasm32 heap ceiling.

To make longer 1080p clips reverse reliably in a browser tab, CutCull splits the job into 2-second keyframe-aligned sliding windows:

  1. Decode only one short keyframe-bounded window into raw frames inside worker memory.
  2. Reverse video frames and audio samples for that window, encode the reversed segment, and immediately free the raw buffers.
  3. Concatenate the reversed segments seamlessly into a single MP4 download.

Peak memory stays flat whether your clip is 10 seconds or several minutes long. We pair this with pitch-preserving 0.1x–10x speed control and instant one-click audio track muting without video re-encoding.

Try It in Your Browser (No Sign-Up, No Watermark)

You can drop a camera RAW photo (.ARW, .CR3, .CR2, .NEF, .RAF, .DNG, .ORF, .RW2, .GPR, …), an iPhone .HEIC, or an .MP4 / .MOV clip directly into https://cutcull.com — no account required, no watermarks, and zero uploads.

We are also building the native macOS & Windows desktop edition of CutCull for high-volume SD-card culling (hundreds to thousands of clips per shoot, Lightroom/Bridge-compatible .xmp sidecars, and one-click FCPXML / Premiere XML / EDL handoff to DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, and Final Cut Pro).

If you work with WebAssembly media pipelines, WebGL2 color shaders, or camera RAW formats, I'd love to hear your feedback and edge cases!

title: Your commit says Tuesday. It might be lying.
description:
A commit can say it was made on Tuesday night when it was really made on Thursday morning. Git will happily write that date for you.

I ran into this while building Vigilante, a browser game where your real GitHub pushes open the next day of the story. If you build anything that counts "coding days" (a streak bot, a #100DaysOfCode tracker, a team dashboard), you hit the same question sooner or later:

Someone pushes at 12:03 am. Which day does it count for?

Keep that question in your head. I'll answer it at the end, and the answer isn't the one I started with.

First, the boring but necessary parts. Here's how I'd take a GitHub push webhook and turn it into "yes, this person coded today", in plain Java, no framework.

Step 1: prove the request really came from GitHub

A webhook endpoint is just a public URL. Anyone can POST JSON to it. If your "verified day" logic trusts whatever lands there, it isn't verified.

When you set a secret on the webhook, GitHub sends an X-Hub-Signature-256 header. It's sha256= followed by the HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the request body, keyed with your secret. You compute the same thing and compare.

Two details matter:

  1. Hash the raw body bytes, before any JSON parsing. Parse first and re-serialise, and the bytes change, so the signature won't match.
  2. Compare in constant time. GitHub's docs say outright never to use a plain ==. 
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public final class GithubSignature {

    public static boolean isValid(byte[] rawBody, String header, String secret) {
        if (header == null || !header.startsWith("sha256=")) return false;
        try {
            Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), "HmacSHA256"));
            String expected = "sha256=" + HexFormat.of().formatHex(mac.doFinal(rawBody));
            // MessageDigest.isEqual is a constant-time comparison
            return MessageDigest.isEqual(
                    expected.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                    header.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;
        }
    }
}

GitHub's docs publish a test vector, which makes a nice unit test. The secret It's a Secret to Everybody and the body Hello, World! should give:

@Test
void matchesGithubTestVector() {
    byte[] body = "Hello, World!".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    String header = "sha256=757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17";
    assertTrue(GithubSignature.isValid(body, header, "It's a Secret to Everybody"));
}

If that test passes, your HMAC code is right. If production still fails, something between GitHub and you (a proxy, a body parser) is changing the bytes.

Step 2: don't count the same push twice

Every delivery carries an X-GitHub-Delivery header, a unique ID for that event. Store it and ignore any ID you've already seen. In a real app that's a unique column in your database, not an in-memory set:

// sketch: in production, a UNIQUE constraint on delivery_id does this job
if (!seenDeliveries.add(deliveryId)) {
    return Response.ok("already processed");
}

The commit IDs deserve the same treatment. Push the same commit to main and then to a release branch, and it shows up in two push events. The payload's commits array marks each commit with a distinct flag for exactly this case. I'd still keep my own set of counted commit SHAs as a backstop.

One more limit to know: the commits array holds at most 2048 commits. Nobody pushes that many in a normal day, but if they do, you'll need the Commits API for the rest.

Step 3: decide what a "real" commit is

This is where streak apps quietly break. An empty commit is a commit. So is a lockfile bump that a bot made. If those count, the streak means nothing.

Each commit in the push payload lists the files it added, modified and removed. That's enough to drop the obvious noise without ever reading the code:

private static final Set<String> NOISE = Set.of(
        "package-lock.json", "yarn.lock", "pnpm-lock.yaml",
        "Gemfile.lock", "poetry.lock", "Cargo.lock");

static boolean looksLikeRealWork(JsonNode commit) {
    if (!commit.path("distinct").asBoolean(true)) return false;

    List<String> files = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String key : List.of("added", "modified", "removed")) {
        commit.path(key).forEach(f -> files.add(f.asText()));
    }
    if (files.isEmpty()) return false;              // empty commit

    return files.stream()
            .map(path -> path.substring(path.lastIndexOf('/') + 1))
            .anyMatch(name -> !NOISE.contains(name)); // not lockfile-only
}

Merge commits are trickier, because the push payload doesn't list a commit's parents. You can ask the Commits API, or filter on the Git side. I wrote a separate post about sorting merge, empty and lockfile noise with a git script, so I won't repeat it here.

Notice what this code never touches: the diff. File names and commit IDs are enough to say "this person changed real files today". You don't need anyone's code to verify their effort, and I think you shouldn't ask for it.

Step 4: the question from the top

Now the fun part. You have a valid, deduplicated push with real commits in it. Which day is it?

The obvious answer is the commit's timestamp. It's right there in the payload, and it's when the person actually wrote the code. Feels honest.

It isn't. That timestamp comes from the committer's own machine, and Git lets you set it to anything:

git commit --date="2026-11-24T21:00:00" -m "totally did this on Tuesday"
# or for the committer date too
GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-11-24T21:00:00" git commit --amend --no-edit

Missed Tuesday? Backdate a commit on Thursday, push it, and a tracker that trusts commit dates gives you Tuesday. People build whole GitHub contribution graph "art" this way.

So the commit date is a claim. The only clock you control is your own: the moment your server received the push. Bucket that into the user's time zone and you get the day:

static LocalDate countedDay(Instant receivedAt, ZoneId userZone) {
    return receivedAt.atZone(userZone).toLocalDate();
}

Which brings back the 12:03 am push. The commits were written at 11:58 pm, the push landed five minutes after midnight, and this rule says it counts for the next day.

At first that feels unfair to the person coding late.

Then I flipped it around. A commit sitting on your laptop hasn't shipped anything. Your work becomes real for everyone else the moment you push it. So the honest rule is simple: the day you pushed is the day you shipped. If you want it to count for tonight, push before midnight. That's a better habit anyway.

Recap

  • Verify X-Hub-Signature-256 against the raw body, in constant time.
  • Deduplicate on X-GitHub-Delivery, and on commit SHAs.
  • Count commits by what files they touch, never by reading the code.
  • Trust your server's clock, not the commit's. Commit dates are self-reported.

If you're doing #100DaysOfCode and want days checked this way instead of by screenshot, Vigilante has a free 100 Days of Code tracker (full disclosure, I built it): vigilante.ocix.in/100-days-of-code

And if you've built a streak counter yourself: which clock did you trust?

title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.33748v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit multi-stage verification evidence rather than a single pass/fail outcome.

title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33962v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.

title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
description:
arXiv:2611.34092v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.

title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
description:
arXiv:2611.33402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.
